text: This is so amazing.  This was maybe the third game I bought for my Nintendo 64, after Shadows of the Empire and Goldeneye.  I loved this game so much.  The sounds, the feel of the game, all of its miasma was preserved in this port and all of a sudden I was awash in memories from twenty years ago and was blown away.  Perfect!
Pure nostalgia...a must own.

Turok: Dinosaur Hunter on the Nintendo 64 was one of those many games in my childhood that I played and remembered fondly, but never finished. The world design, sound design, and weapons stuck with me. Trying to play it now can be a little cumbersome, so playing it with modern controls and resolutions make it alot easier to play. You can actually find the abandonware of the PC edition - but it is probably missing music and doesn't support modern resolutions and I think you can't rebind keys - also it costs $50 Amazon.  I'm not 100% sure on the development of the game, but it is some sort of hybrid of the N64, a PC engine and maybe the PC version. There are improved graphics (anti-aliasing, lighting), depth of field options (which reduces the distance fog for you AND enmies), and even a recently added Level editor and Workshop/Mod support - I recommend the iddqd_textures (HD Textures)
The game is largely the same as the N64 version, though there are some minor level detail edits/editons that I don't remember from the N64 classic and didn't see in the PC version - so extreme purists might be turned off, but I don't think any "level flow/pathing" has changed. One of the updates mentions the game uses the N64 sounds which were apparently better than the PC version - which is welcome because I loved some of the classic soundtrack (especially Lv 1, Underwater, and Cave themes) and Turok 1 has some of the best death grunts in FPS history. I didn't realize until playing far into this game how prevalent first person platforming is, which will turn some gamers of. Also, some enemies have hitscan weapons - it doesn't make sense how a blowdart can hit me from behind the shooter or the pulse rifle shots hit me near instantly while mine travel a bit slower. You can exploit the AI the bit and most humanoid enemies can be killed in 1-3 knife hits.
I recommend Turok. It comes from a passionate developer that makes blog posts lamenting over minor issues many gamers wouldn't notice.  The $20 tag is high for an old game, but it has at least that amount of work put in to make it happen. At least wishlist it and wait for a sale if you liked the game or have a fondness for classic FPS games.

Ah, Turok. One of my favourite games from my childhood. Grew up mostly playing this one and Evolution, but man oh man is it a great series. This game in particular is probably one of the best and this remake does it even more justice.
Pros
- Amazing, powerful, hilariously unrealistic weapons. From the Bow to the Chronoscepter, they're all useful in all stages of the game and incredibly fun to use (my personal favorite being the Grenade Launcher).
- Fun sense of exploration. All of the levels have different secrets to be found, many are in very unsuspecting spots. They are also fairly complex and not so straight-forward.
- Good selection of graphical, audio, video, and gameplay options. I'm so thankful to be able to play with  110 FOV.
- Very Quake-like. Secrets, the weapons, etc.
- Level Editor! The devs released this pretty recently to open up the community to making their own levels and the like. I've been having a bit of trouble with playing some custom levels, but its not a huge deal.
Cons
- Lack of story. Not really a major con, as it doesn't really affect the gameplay. You gotta read the comics to get a basis of the game and understand why you're a Native American man running and gunning other men, dinosaurs, dinosaurs WITH GUNS, aliens, robots, etc.
- A LOT OF JUMPING PUZZLES AND PLATFORMING. This isn't something that can really be changed, but it is what it is. They're just a little frustrating on some levels.
Verdict: 9/10
This is a fantastic game and definitely worth the price.  I'm really looking forward to the remake of Turok 2: Seeds of Evil!

Lifeless planet is a pretty unique game, and be warned, one that many will probalby dislike, one that many will find utterly boring. The Steam tags for this game are "Adventure" and "Action", well truth said, it's neither an adventure game, and especially it ain't no action game. I'd rather tag it "exploration game". Lifeless planet is made for Sci-Fi fans who enjoy exploring an alien world. Folks that spend hours watching the web cam of that Mars Robot will prolly enjoy Lifeless Planet. It's not so much about what you can do --as there is actually little that you can do--, but it's about wanting to find out what'd behind the next corner. It's about wanting to find out the secret of this planet, and that's it. The game has charme, no doubt. But don't expect too much. The game is not overly long, it has close to zero Adventure elements, no inventory, almost no items, your tasks are limited to ridiculously easy mechanical riddles and jump sequences (which could be called "the action part") and that's it. If you are of the curious type who just wants to explore this beautiful and mysterious planet, and if you don't mind the lack of "action", this game is for you. And I sure enjoyed this game.

If XCOM told the story of Game of Thrones, while being set on Discworld, then you'd have a game pretty close to Massive Chalice. And Massive Chalice is pretty close to being very good.
First of all, if you enjoyed XCOM, you'll enjoy Massive Chalice. It's got the strategic and tactical layering. It's got the persistence. It's got the simplified, board-game-like rules that allow emergent tactical depth. It's got the skill trees and the soldier nicknames. It's got the panic levels. It adds the bloodline mechanic, where you combine your soldiers together to try and found a family of supersoldiers. Also, it's funny as heck. Definitely pick it up during a sale or something.
Where Massive Chalice falls short of being great, though, is failing to go all the way with its new idea. In XCOM, you get attached to and invest in your troops. Massive Chalice wants you to do that, but after two or three battles with any given soldier...they reach old age. I wish Massive Chalice had gone out of its way to get you attached to the *houses,* instead of the individuals in them. I would have loved to see a family tree in each house, with important or venerated house members highlighted. (Battle veterans, Standards, partners and regents, or people who were involved in game events. They could even blank out Sagewrights entirely, so that "Sagewrights must forsake all family ties" actually had meaning.) As another example, two of my houses got into a feud. Did I hear songs about how the other house stunk when I click on the first house's keep? Did house members take advantage of the chaos of battle to murder each other? No, there was just a minor penalty to accuracy if feuding house members were in battle together.
The other thing that XCOM did much better than Massive Chalice was to give the plot a sense of progression with well-times changes in objectives and cutscenes that shifted the player's priorities and focus. Massive Chalice just tells you the goal at the beginning, and...that's it. Get to the end.
This game is a lot of fun, and if you have the imagination to fill in those blanks, you'll really enjoy it. Personally, I think the game world is rich for expansion, and I'd like to see more. (Hopefully including some features to differentiate the great houses in meaningful ways, too)!

Too small in terms of content and some poor execution in mechanics makes it get stale very fast. I got through my first playthrough, but there's nothing in the game that keeps me wanting to play through the other difficulties. Add on the fact that modding is not available, or (as I hear) planned, I don't see myself coming back to this game.
I want to like this game, the core mechanics are good, but it's just a very shallow game.
Examples of shortcomings:
Most choices you make in management, like marraiges, don't seem to make huge differences. By the end of the game, I had generally positive traits, but it still didn't feel like there were enough traits to make it seem like any one family was really special in a good or bad way.
Classes were kind of neat, but there are only 3, each with 2 variations, and your control over what classes you get are constrained by traits due to their inclusion in the marriage mechanic.
There aren't many enemies, and the main crowd control mechanic is hard movement of enemies. It does add more depth to the combat that I saw at first, but that was about as deep as it got.
Relics are random, and absurdly strong. There are really no other options. You can research a few weapons per class that mimic enemy mechanics, but they still pale in comparison.
Research is limited to a few techs, that never change based on playthroughs(though they may be unlocked in a marginally different time frame). I also disliked the idea of having to "research" more troops to recruit. I see why they did it, but it seems silly.
Perma-death doesn't hurt much in the long run, really just for that battle. If the dead person carried a relic, it is passed on. If the person had good traits, well you chose someone else for marriage instead of them, who likely had even better traits. I would have liked to see more units needed for battles, and the inclusion of regents in the fighting forces, to raise the stakes. The finale was neat, and if the mechanics of battle were better, it would be incredible to play.
Lastly, I'd like to see more done with the overworld. It's the same everytime and is, in the grand scheme, rather small. Basically 5 areas, with 2 divisions (10 total), where only the outer region carries any value. On top of that, the invasion mechanic is painfully simple. Bad guys invade 2-3 areas at once. Defend one area to reduce 1 corruption points, other regions gain 1 corruption point. None of that matters unless a region reaches 3 corruption points, at which point it just disappears. I'd like to see regions be affected by corruption, and lost regions do more than just go away.

We are alone and surrounded. The Cadence never rests and their sole purpose is to destroy us. But there is a glimmer of hope, an ancient relic that can wipe out our demonic enemy once and for all. However, it will take three hundred years to charge up the divine chalice to have enough power to destroy the Cadence. During those three hundred years, your heroes will live, fight, reproduce and die. As an immortal ruler, you will remain vigilant. You cannot leave the keep or the chalice, but you can oversee the entire land and dictate everything.
This is the premise of Massive Chalice, Double Fine’s fantasy turn-based strategy easiest described as a mix between XCOM’s tactical battles and Crusader King’s marital simulation. But it’s not quite as simple as that. The way those two elements come together is what really sets Massive Chalice apart. You start off with a central keep that houses the chalice and five royal families. In the rest of the provinces you can build further keeps and assign your heroes to them. Their duty as regents will be to procreate and thus provide new heroes in order to sustain the centuries-spanning battle against the Cadence. You can also build two separate keeps that will either provide research bonuses or faster training of young heroes. Heroes assigned as regents, sagewrights or standards cannot fight so you constantly have to bear in mind that you need at least five battle-ready heroes. This is a bit tricky at first because deaths are permanent and heroes will die both in combat and of natural causes.
There are three main hero classes. Hunters are ranged specialists, Alchemists are great for crowd control as they carry explosive flasks and Caberjacks deal damage with brute melee force. Each class has two sub-classes which you gain by marrying different main classes. Also, every class and sub-class has their own unique skill tree. For example, a Trickshot is an offspring of a Hunter regent and an Alchemist partner and has the unique ability to fire off a long-range explosive flask using his/her bow and arrow. Apart from that, each hero has positive and negative physical attributes and personality traits which they can potentially transfer to their children. So you will want to pay attention as to who you’re marrying as it will influence the class and traits of your future heroes. You don’t want to find yourself two hundred years into the fight with nothing but sickly, nearsighted, drunk heroes or even worse, lacking a vital class.
The enemies also come in a range of shapes and sizes with different abilities. Some will run up to you and explode, some will shoot from a distance and stun your heroes whereas others have the ability to spawn additional minions and throw explosive substances. In a rather unique twist, one type of enemy will actually age your heroes while dealing damage. This could potentially lead to your hero dying of age, not by damage, on the battlefield. Even if they survive the battle, they will most likely die soon after. That’s where your research comes in. Over the years you can assign various research and develop better armor, weapons and items that negate the aging attack, among others. The battles take place on grid-based procedurally generated maps. The battle system isn’t the deepest out there, but it is engaging and satisfying enough to quench that tactical itch.
Another unique aspect of the game are relics. Once a particularly valiant hero passes away, their weapon may become a relic that can be passed down through generations, but only within that bloodline. Throughout the years, the relic itself will gain experience points and become more and more powerful. As the ruler, you will also be tasked to solve random problems or situations similar to the ones in The Banner Saga. I’m not sure if I just had really bad luck, but almost every choice had horrible repercussions. A few times my choice didn’t lead to any change at all and I never managed to resolve a situation in such a way to get something good out of it. But the biggest problem I had with this feature was that, unlike in The Banner Saga, it just felt impersonal, distant and irrelevant. I didn’t feel the plight of the people and I wasn’t immersed into those more whimsical situations.
The game’s presentation is absolutely great. What stood out to me the most was the superb soundtrack which hits just the right notes. It has a bit of a melancholic vibe to it which makes sense in the grand scheme of things as you will see dozens and dozens of your heroes die over three centuries. The art style is very nice as well. The environments looks lush and beautiful, the colorful enemy designs are wholly unique as well. Ironically, it’s the heroes that visually lack personality, they seem too plain and bland. Also, male and female models are actually quite difficult to tell apart.
Double Fine needed this. The famed independent developer lost quite a bit of good will recently as Broken Age didn’t turn out as people expected and the less said about Spacebase DF-9, the better. Massive Chalice is a step in the right direction to regain people’s trust. But even if you disregard all that, Massive Chalice is a great strategy game in its own right with an engaging combat system, engrossing marital simulation and stellar presentation.
8 OUT OF 10 (GREAT)

To start off, I would like to get some review-based♥♥♥♥♥♥posting out of the way. So, without further delay:
Drunk Sledgehammer Fight Simulator 2016

With that done, I feel that any honest suggestion of this game has to at least mention the fact that this game exists as a testing ground for the mechanics the devs intend to use in their larger (and far more ambitious) game, Sui Generis. As such, the phrase "Glorified Tech Demo" is not completely inapt. However, this does not mean that this is not a full game (in progress), but just that the scope of the game is limited in part by its position in the overall plans of the devs.
Exanima is at its core a dungeon crawl, and it does that completely adequately. The dungeon is large and maze-like. There are keys that open doors. There are enemies, treasure chests, and puzzles. If it sounds like I am unenthusiastic about this game, that would be incorrect. However, this aspect of the game, the “Shell” of the game so to say, is not what makes the game interesting. All of these things are good enough; At worst, underwhelming, and at best, average. However, there are two things that make this game stand out: the atmosphere and the combat.
The world of Exanima and Sui Generis is a low and dark fantasy setting. This world is incredibly well communicated through the environment, items, and enemies. Magical equipment exists, but is rare, and most of the time, upgrades are simply higher quality or built differently than their predecessors. Most items look suitably worn, and the environment is dark, foreboding, and filled with hints of activity before its abandonment. Scrolls are sprinkled throughout the dungeon, giving hints of these activities. The lighting is excellent, casting deep shadows through the dungeon, making each corner dark and mysterious. Overall, the atmosphere is sufficiently dark, grim, and makes for an excellent world to explore.
The second, and largest part of what makes Exanima worth playing, is its combat. Instead of simply pressing a button to make an attack with a pre-canned animation that if it connects does a constant amount of damage (ignoring target armor/stats), each attacks damage in Exanima is based on physics. Defence is handled automatically, with characters attempting blocks and parries at any attacks coming at them from the front. Attacking is more complex, relying on positioning, timing, and accurate movements. While swinging a weapon, movements of both your and enemy characters can affect how the weapon strikes an enemy. Stepping into a stab increases its damage, stepping back lowers it. A polearm swing at to close a target that strikes the enemy with the pole does far less damage than a proper strike with the head. This, combined with a remarkably detailed armor system, makes combat very realistic-ish. At its core, the basic moves of real combat are there. Stepping into lunges, rotating with your hips into a swing to increase its power, maintaining effective range, all there. However, it is much slower and often looks clumsier than real combat, hence the drunk sledgehammer fight joke. I remain unconvinced that this system is necessarily better than a traditional animation based system. As I said, it leads to clumsy looking fights. It is by necessity slower than a traditional system. Slightly wonky physics can lead to odd clipping errors, such as getting an arm twisted and stuck behind the players back. Despite all this, I can confidently say that it is the most interesting combat system I have played. Because the damage is physics based, big hits feel satisfying. A hit from a sledgehammer can knock an opponent into a ragdoll. Stepping into a stab produces excellent looking stabs with real impact. Despite the many oddities that the system brings, overall, the combat is, while not flashy, interesting, impactful, and most importantly, fun. It’s a very unique system that makes this game interesting enough to be worth checking out.

I remember a similar game called Die By the Sword that had mouse combat for swinging your sword, and one of the reasons why it worked so much better than it does in this game is because the camera was behind your character and swiping the mouse actually translated to similar motions. Spent more time fighting my controls than my opponents. Imagine a bowling ball attached to a long stick, then wielding that around. That's basically how it feels.  Physics? Kinda. Fun? No.  Disappointing too, because I prefer realistic games and wanted to like this one. I'm sure there's a way to make this work better, but they haven't quite found it yet.

This game has likely flown under the radar of practically everyone here on Steam, and that is somewhat of a shame.
The Haunted Hells Reach is a horde based wave shooter in which you play as four stereotypical badasses with no difference other than how corny their lines in combat are. You face wave after wave of the undead as you fight to survive with an ugradable arsenal of Knife, Shotgun, Machine Gun, and pistol. Each weapon has it's own upgrade tree, with the knife becoming a chainsaw at somepoint whilst your pistol becomes two revolvers. Along with this, you can pick up several other exotic weapons like a bow with explosives or a rocket launcher. You can also find explosives such as grenades and mines as well.
The online community at this point is dead in the water for this game, a shame since it is best enjoyed online. However physical copies of the game exist and for as little as a dollar, it's utterly worth it in my opinion. The more players, the more challenging the game becomes. And there is even a mode in which you can play as the demons in an effort to murder your friends.
The graphics are decent enough, servicable if you will, the animations aren't awful, and the textures for the environments are solid enough, though you don't have much time to admire because enemies come from everywhere.
Luckily, enemies rarely become all aggressive, which makes the game a hell (HA!) of a lot better. If you have some friends then this game will be an enjoyable time of 8/10.
However if horde based games aren't your thing then perhaps Doom might be more your speed.

I’ve had the fortune of being alive during most of the major changes and improvements to computers and gaming in general.  I was more of a Nintendo fan back then so the N64 was my main console over the PS1 granted I was till a PC kid but once the N64 games started pumping out games like Goldeneye 64 and Turok I mainly played them for quite some time.  While the N64’s hardware was lacking in a few ways I still loved the console even if by today’s standards looking back it was horribly antiquated compared to disk based console systems.
Turok was a good game back then, I don’t remember a lot about it but I do recall it running moderately well compared to higher fidelity games like Perfect Dark 64 (even with the extra ram).  It may have been even one of my first semi open world/exploration kind of games that I ever got into but I’m not sure, still though the different worlds/levels and weapons always added some refreshing gameplay from time to time.
This remake of the original PC port is every way better then the 64 version by far, now that it’s on PC you can now mod the game to have say user made higher def textures and now the developer Nightdive studios has added a level editor, something that the original N64 version did not have.  The game itself is everything that I remember it from my younger days yet runs at least 10 times better as far as performance which should go without saying given how powerful PCs are today compared to back then.  If you had fond memories of this game back then or even recently if you are a retro gamer then you will get those same feelings.
Turok is an early platformer and because of this you will probably die to falls quite a bit or have to redo sections because you fell off or missed a jump.  That is one thing that at times frustrated me because it is quite prevalent in many levels and while the extra performance boost for this port is helpful so that there is little to no input lag you will still probably die or fall many times.
I’m glad that Nightdive is continuing support for the game, as they just recently released the map editor and now the Steam version has Workshop support for user created levels.  I eagerly await Turok 2 if this is the type of quality that I should expect from this developer, and considering they have done other games like a remastering of System Shock 1 and 2 which players seem to like quite a bit.
If you are into retro play or you were alive and playing on an N64 platform you will enjoy this for sure.  Though while the price is a bit steep given how old the game really is, I’d say it’s mostly worth it but I’d still get Turok on sale unless $20 is not that big of a deal for you.

The game is a "manage your criminal organization" strategy game, with turn-based combat missions and a setting in 1920's Atlantic City.
First of all, the mood and atmosphere is excellent.  The graphics and music are really good.  The voice-acting is fairly decent.  Although the story is rather stereotypical, it isn't bad by any means.
About the gameplay, I like to compare it to Xcom Enemy Unknown, because they both combine  a management game with turn-based combat missions.  Xcom EU won several prices last year, including strategy game of the year, and got generally high reviews.
From what I heard, the reason Omerta got bad criticism was mostly due to bugs and the management aspect being fairly simple.  Funny enough, I feel the same applies easily to Xcom EU: base management is totally simplified compared to classic Xcom, and multiplayer is so bugged it's hardly playable.  The difference is Xcom patches only seemed to scratch the surface, while I've recently played a lot of Omerta and haven't encountered a single bug.
And what about the turn-based combat ?  Well, I actually prefer Omerta, I really feel they did a great job on that.  Especially "line of sight", which is a serious issue in XCom, is well executed in Omerta.  Everything also seems to be nicely balanced.  I'm not sure how active the multiplayer community is, I'm afraid it's pretty dead thanks to the bad publicity the game received.
Bugs: no big issues I'm aware of
Management part : fun, but pretty casual, not that much replay value
Turn-based strategy missions : excellent
Gangster setting : great
Maybe I'm biased because I really like both the genre (management + turn-based strategy) and the setting (gangsters).  So it probably depends what you're looking for.  Biggest issue seems to me the limited replay value.

Solid gameplay, mostly replayable and interesting because of the well-programmed AI, but the overall experience suffers from the hedious artstyle that leaves a bad first impression.
SotS is an turn-based strategy game, inspired by the perfect Advance Wars series, which are only playable on Nintendo devices. The former is not as deep and doesn't follow the 'grid rule' (like a chessboard) like the latter. You move units anywhere within a certain radius, and you are limited to five actions per turn (in contrast to AW, where you can spent a whole lot a time in one turn moving your whole army). Games like these need a good competitive AI player to fight against. 17-bit knows and shows that.
The downfall is when you have trouble overseeing the battlefield. The artstyle of the units tend to blend in with other units and surroundings. I often didn't notice that I had another unit behind my archer, making me reload the last autosave. The free-movement also makes it difficult, at first, to understand why you can't move a unit between other units or objects. Even the AI seems to fidget around specificly with that. In the end, these annoyences aren't gamebreaking, but they do leave a bad first impression, which means you'll get used to them.
The 'stretching animations' and the corny - sometimes fourth wall breaking - jokes aside, I can full-hearthedly say that I enjoyed the music, challenge and general length of the game. I didn't check it out myself, but apparantly the multiplayer is really fun too. I should warn completionists, though, for more than 50% of the achievements are either time-consuming or just difficult to unlock because they require you to build specifc setups/arrangements in the battlefield.

I’ve always been a Broken Sword fan, even throughout the awkward 3D box pushing, filling Prague with Russians phase. Then the fourth one came out and I only played it once and there was some bimbo blonde instead of Nico, and then Nico shows up with this weird voice actress and just doesn’t look like herself and it’s probably the weakest episode in the series, so no wonder Broken Sword gets quieter than ever. But somehow, even without my knowledge, the guys do a crowd-funding of this one, and, as it should, it drives nostalgia like a new muscle car. The dorky humor of both protagonists is back, it gets the classic 2D point and click treatment and the logic of your tasks is mostly within reason. The game doesn’t do anything special or revolutionary (hah, the irony of that, considering the studio), but we all know how that turned out last time, so that’s all cool. The weird cell-shady 2D/3D aesthetic took a little time for me to get used to and frankly, the animation is sometimes hilariously bad – namely mouth movements and occasionally the way the characters are stood when talking to each other. The puzzles are sometimes dumb as all hell, though that may be intentional in an attempt for subtle humor (whether that works for you or not is another thing). But the voice acting is good, the story intriguing and it is definitely one of the better Broken Sword games.

Game Corp DX is way too simplistic to give me any feeling of attachment to the "games" I am making or the workers working on it. I'll definitely admit that my expectation of a "game development tycoon" is tainted by Game Dev Tycoon - the low price and near child like art style of the game envokes a game simple enough for children and teens, but is overall uninteresting and unrewardng enough to keep them and myself playing.
Hiring workers doesn't involve much decision making. Build a workstation and click it to hire somebody - you three choices, which are usually poor choices when you are starting. You can hire one of the three, or waste another day (which potentially wastes money) to reroll for workers again, which are also likely to suck. There's no way to influence the kind of workers you can get outside of pure luck and the previous success of your studio.
Building a game requires choosing a project size, which determines the amount of people you can put on the project. Since none of your workers will have any stats at the beginning, your early games will almost certainly get bad reviews until you build up your team's experience. Thankfully, at least the game is forgiving with poorly reviewed games and you can still make some money to stay in business.
I was hoping the build feature would be a nice component of this game - the ability to customize your building further to make your building stand out from others, or to give you more attachment to your building than in Game Dev Tycoon. Instead, building is just a roadblock to progress. Not enough workers? Build more stations. Untrained workers? Build training stations. Bad work environment? Buy some plants? Bulding too small to make additions? Delete some walls and add some more further down. The building is purely simplistic placing of tiled objects that only conflict if there isn't a space "under it" for somebody to get to the object/use it. You can upgrade your building to get even larger offices, but the button that is supposed to let me upgrade never appeared - you're supposed to hire max workers, but eventually the game said I couldn't hire anymore in my city - so I saw no way to progress. There was one button I saw about moving to San Francsico, but that required $100M and there was another requirement I didn't meet. I just barely made $1M and I'm certianly not spending the hour it took to get to $1m times 100 to get that much money.
GCDX may be a decent little mobile game to not pay much attention to, but I wasn't entertained the entire time. I felt no attachment to my games since I couldn't make sequels to them or research why a game I made went well or bad or not being able to develop engines or work with publishers. After my third game, I let Game Corp auto-name all my games because there was no point to rename them. Game Corp DX is nothing but clicking boxes to select your game genre and which worker works on a game and hope the game does well.

It's a good old graphic point'n click adventure with all the things that made good old point'n click adventures as good as annoying. I wish there was a neutral button. That's what I'd hit. Since there isn't one, I have to go with the negative evil thing: The bad just outweights the good.
I want slow adventure games to succeed. I really, really do. I love stories. I love characters. I love puzzles. I love getting involved into fantasy stuff. I love... ermm.. slowness in games? The Serpent's Curse managed to drag me into nostalgia, I suppose. And it's very much like its predecessors, almost like a copy. Still, things just don't add up anymore nowadays. It's like the devolpers haven't learned anything since 2006. How long can you drag nostalgia out?
The good:
- It's fairly heavy on story. I'm not at the end yet but still wanna find out about those mysteries
- It has beautifully drawn background graphics
The bad:
- Oh god, the voice acting. Nothing feels natural. I tried three different audio languages and I'm still lost here. In German (1st language), it's like listening to 3rd-graders reciting a play. English audio has hilariously spoken accents everywhere, Even I could hear the fake, and that says something. Finally I tried French and... well scratch that, my French has somehow dissolved over the years. Hopefully you'll get luckier with your audio.
- Holy hell, the puzzles. I forgot how annoying these can be sometimes. You often know EXACTLY what you need to do: Talk to this guy, give him that. Repair the machine using X. But it's never that easy, isn't it? Things have to be complicated. THEY HAVE to be, because point'n click adventure game. Oh man. I'm writing this review from a point in the game where I definitely know that I have to drive a frigging seagull off a lamppost by honking a horn. Problem: I have about 0,5 seconds to make three things at once happen. Even with a guide at hand, I've tried seven times so far. This whole situation is horrible. I hate guides. I don't wanna use them. This game gives me no choice though. I don't wanna run around offering everyone a banana for five hours and hope it'll stick. So, there's that.
Conclusion: This game is heavily outdated and only a thing for hardcore nostalgists. or masochists. Or people who like to google for solutions. Or ones who like to do the same things over and over again.

and now onto the review
Sumer is a digital boardgame loosely based on M.U.L.E. and ancient poetry from the civilization of Sumer (modern day Iraq). There are two phases, harvesting and sacrificing for the Goddess Inanna and bidding for goodies the Goddess.
-Gameplay-
There are four players, if not enough human players are entered the game will automatically add AI to the mix, who start off randomly in the lower regions of a temple. The narrator lets the players know whats happening, then buildings rise randomly from the temple and players must then wake up to start doing their sowing. In the first year you are given very limited options for you and your followers(2 game pieces), to raise goats (currency) or harvest barley (used for sacrifices, baking, other materials). The goal is to have the most FAVOR from the Goddess as at the end of the game she will choose the player that paid their dues to her. How you do that is the strategic portion of the game. Absolutely everything you do from the beginning counts towards the favor you will need to impress Inanna. After the players have met the sacrifices at the top of the temple.
The game year will end and the players will be pushed into the bidding phase, where you can use the goats you cultivated to win prizes such as buildings, more servants (or game pieces), statues, wings (that make you faster) among other advantages. The players engage in a bidding war, how you wish to spend is up to you. (personally I love making my opponents spend way more money than they need to for an item)
After the bidding is over if you are playing the 2 year portion you are ushered into the last year where the sacrifices on the top of the temple are much greater. Players rush to be the last person to place their sacrifise and get a bonus for doing so in FAVOR.
After all the rituals and sacrificing is done, the game is over and Inanna places her judgement on the four participants. Like I said previously, there she will judge you for everything.
How many goats you have.
How much material you have left over.
What sacrifices you did over the course of the game.
How much FAVOR you have.
The Statues you have.
EVERYTHING.
Finally players are floating towards the Goddess and one by one will drop until the winner of the game is announced and declared the new ruler of Sumer.
-Graphics, Sound & Artstyle-
Sumer's overall feel is absolutely astounding, the simplicity and perfectly crafted artwork of the board game and pieces combined with the awesome 7 song soundtrack bring the ancient civilization back to life in front of our eyes.
-Price-
The retail price is 14.99 USD
-How many hours estimated?-
Being a board game afficianado I can honestly say that this will be a game I will pump hundreds of hours into especially once Online is a feature. There are three different game lenghts. 2, 4 and 6 years. 2 taking about 15 mins. 4 taking about 25 mins and 6 taking around 45-50 mins.

I'm writing this review after spending many hours playing the Kickstarter beta version.
We're a big fan of board games, and really like multi-player party games like this. We learned of this game through one of the developers, Josh Raab, who seems to have great skill at developing simple games that have great depth.
The game mechanic is largely worker placement and auction.
During the worker placement phase you're trying to earn as many points as you can. You collect resources and can sacrifice them, or 'invest' them in ways that will earn more points later. There is a racing element to it as well. You try to get to buildings before the other players, so you can block them, but there area always alternative ways to earn points if you get blocked.
The auction phase is a lot of fun. You bid excess resources to gain bonuses or extra buildings. There are a lot of ways to try to trick each other to get a better price or force them to spent too much. You can also 'overbid' which is to sacrifice points to try to win a bid that is key to your strategy. Once you buy your buildings you get to place them on the temple, which has strategy as well, trying to block other players or trying to claim a bigger part of the temple for yourself.
The game is simple enough that our 5 year old wins the short games frequently. The longer games have enough depth that my wife and I are still figuring out new ways to beat each other.
A short '2 year long' game is usually done in 10-15 minutes, or you can go up to an 6 year game that will have a lot more depth and cool power-ups. It lets you plan ahead further for bigger bonuses at the end. The 6 year games seem to take about 30 minutes.
The game has an awesome theme. Love the art and quality of the look.
We've played the game with our keyboard, mouse, and an SNES style gamepad, they all work well."

A long time ago, I remember one of the designers of Doom 3 talking about realistic physics in a game and pointing out that truly, absolutely realistic physics would be a pain--would you really want your shotgun to get stuck on a doorpost you didn't properly circumnavigate, or trip over every bit of scenic debris on the floor? The designers of Exanima would apparently answer each of these--originally rhetorical--questions with a resounding "YES!!!" Add to that a character movement system that goes against just about every way your natural instincts could be translated into a keyboard and mouse approach, and you get an experience that is roughly equivalent to being dropped into a dungeon after being severely drugged and barely in control of your own nervous system. Sure, you could argue that taking six or so hours to learn utterly counter-intuitive controls in order to barely get your character to do what you'd like him or her to do is "innovative." For me, the experience is more like getting teeth pulled without anesthesia by a dentist who claims that it's the "artisanal" thing to do. A realistic fencing system may be the holy grail of fantasy gaming. Alas, Exanima has brought us nowhere closer to it--unless you really enjoy the idea of fighting for your life while drunk out of your mind at the same time. Thanks, but no thanks.

As the store page claims, Exanima is entirely based around physics based combat system. This however does not mean that the combat is realistic. What it means is that the game is a physics experiment and plays like one. I'm for all sorts of weird stuff, but in this case the end result doesn't appeal to me. Playing the game feels more like balancing ball on a plate or like playing Surgeon Simulator than fighting with a sword or other deadly implement. But while Surgeon Simulator was more of a goofy game, this one takes itself very seriously and new players should expect to spend many hours in the arena mode or replaying the first level (because manual saves break immersion) before getting the hang of the clunky controls.
So is it fun? Well, maybe you enjoy this sort of thing. Maybe you even enjoy Surgeon Simulator, who knows. As for me, I'll rather go and play Dark Souls.

::For the time being this review has been set to "Friends Only" until I have had time to give the game a second go."
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I have seldom seen controls in a game that were as unresponsive and unintuitive as in Exanima. That includes attacking as well as moving in and out of combat.
To make things even worse, while the combat/attacking system is already severely lacking in responsiveness, the character your are controlling (or not...) always automatically performs certain actions during combat that take away what little is left of the control that I as the player have over the actions of my character.
In particular, the fact that you cannot control when and how your character blocks/parries an attack, or starts pushing around the opponents with their hands in a melee fight, completely destroys any notion of a reponsive combat system with any degree of depth to it.
Finally, movement of your character in this game is beyond akward. While I do not mind the concept of moving your character with either the mouse only, or with M&KB, it has never been executed as poorly in a game is in Exanima. Even Neverwinter Nights back in 2000 with their Aurora Engine already had a movement system by mouse that was leagues better and beyond than what is being offered here. And what is being offered here can be summarized with the words: clunkiness, and unresponsiveness in relation to the degree of control input.
These issues are especially prevelant during combat, when moving your character is reduced to being able to take only baby steps (almost literally; the dodge moves are just as unresponsive and almost not noticeable), and since the camera cannot be fixed to a certain position (compare fixed chasing cam in other isometric games) but instead would have to controlled with your mouse (which is already used to control, well, everything esle!) you end up with the perfect ingredients for whole lot of annoyance and frustration for absolutely no good reason.
While the approach that the developers have taking is indeed an interesting one, I think that unless they refine the movement system, its responsivess (especially during fights), and allow the player more control over what their character is doing (such as turning off automatic blocking and giving us a block key) I cannot see how this concept is going to win over many more of the gaming community save for the most hardcore of us. Only that hardcore here doesn't mean the type of Souls hardcoreness achieved through unusually challenging content, but rather those who are willing to invest hours upon hours into a game the primary challenge of which it is to master a set of clunky and unresponsive controls...
Edit: The implementation of a proper tutorial that introduces new players to not only the basics of the game's controls and mechanics, but also the its (alleged) subtlelties, could probably do much to alleviate the unneccessary frustration that new players are bound to run into.

Listen, I like this game.
But it has so many problems I can't recommend it to everyone.
First, the planets are boring - there may be around 20 or 30 biomes, but some planets, like the aquatic ones, are made of literally 3 set pieces and 2 major locations.
Then there are some interesting planets, like Scorched, with their post-apocalyptic atmosphere
and Toxic, which have probably the most variety, but are nearly impossible to traverse - radiation and costant poison debuffs await unprepared players.
Some planets have very stupid underground layering, like a molten hot volcano planet with a thick layer of dirt, or some set pieces on lava planets still having water.
The bosses are mostly bullet sponges or take around a minute to defeat, most of them encourage heavy use of medicinal items, like bandages. While they might have interesting patterns and concepts, they just don't work. If you ask me, healing items should have a cooldown or be nerfed.
Speaking of battles...
The battle system is absolutely horrendous!
Shields work similarly to armor in Payday 2 where, as long as you have at least 1 HP left on the shield, you take no damage at all!
And the worst of all, crouching in front of a shooting enemy makes it miss 90% of its shots, especially if it's a humanoid enemy. I've seen games where the AI couldn't handle water, but here they can't handle such a simple task as aiming slightly lower to hit you!
Throwing weapons, while limited, are overpowered af.
I beat the final boss in around 1 minute after finding out that throwing weapons deal around 100 damage to it.
And it doesn't help that there is a huge variety of weapons,
when most of them feel under- or overpowered.
You can hold a grenade launcher along with any other 1-handed weapon for some really crazy shenanigans and for making rocket launchers obsolete, guns come with some of the stupidest addons I've ever seen, like a sniper rifle or shotgun with a grenade launcher attached and not a single assault rifle of mine had one.
Now some things I absolutely love:
Space encounters - they spice up the gameplay from looting everything on multiple planets to flying around in a huge golem and destroying fleets of enemy space ships, with a surprise at the end! The mechs also work like the ones from Megaman X while on land, so extra points for me!
Damage types - weapons can be found with one of four damage types (posion, fire, ice or electric), each of them have different effects on enemies and some enemies are resistant or weak to certain elements.
Enviro Protection Pack - this thing will save your life on moons, radioactive, cold and hot planets.
It can also be modified to increase one of your stats, but it's best to hold on to the best augments until you get the cooling upgrade, as upgrading the EPP makes it lose its augment - that's stupid.
Graphics - the backgrounds are amazing, add atmosphere and sometimes create the whole planet or biome. I love how ores are easy to distinguish, placed on top of blocks and even walls, the lighting is top-notch: the flashlight is simply beautiful and all blocks look great.
From what I thought could be better than Terraria, it turned out to be a pretty good game, but I cannot find any replay value in it after finding out there are only 10 armor sets with different stats, while Terraria has over 20 or 30 very diverse armors.
The vanity items are a problem for me - I personally learned to hate goofy costumes and opt for more serious-looking, armor-like clothing, but this game simply has too many "funny" clothes.
And lastly, can I touch upon the dungeons for a second?
They all suck.
The sewer dungeon has got to have the most overpowered monsters in the game and the highest risk and lowest reward out of all of them.
Other dungeons at least serve the purpose of speeding up your progress
in the missions, which always go like this:
scan enough objects of X race -> meet Esther -> dungeon -> boss -> artifact -> repeat
I am aware this game has a big roleplay potential and most people prefer it for roleplay, but that doesn't appeal to me at all as I personally hate roleplaying.
I wouldn't call it a No Man's Sky level disappointment, but I personally don't find repetitive games enjoyable, except when they're done right.

MASSIVE CHALICE suffers from Sporetosis. So many unique elements of gameplay are crammed in that no single aspect of the game really stands out. It's as though Double Fine Productions got together at an IHOP late one night, and after a few dozen mugs of bottomless coffee, started coming up with all these fantastic ideas for a turn-based tactical game. With nothing but a green sharpie and the back of a napkin, they jotted down as much as they could before the caffeine-induced coma.
-Xcom combat system
-Game of Thronesy overview map
-Massive time scale
-Eugenics
-Omniscient ruler
-Witty advisory banter
-Inheritance based class system
-Random event scenarios
-Heirlooms passed through generations
To be fair, all of that stuff is actually in the game. There was probably a deadline, and not wanting to upset anyone, DFP made sure to get each and every idea in the game, even if just barely. So you really are an immortal, omniscient ruler who, over several hundred years, really does lead dozens of generations of soldiers to battle in a Game-of-Thrones-esque hellscape complete with knee-slapping back n' forth from your two trusty advisors.
There’s just not a whole lot of depth here to explore.
But yes, you can totally make an inbred army of mentally handicapped, myopic drunks. And I did. And it was kinda fun.
Can't wait for MC2.

Creeper World is a tower defense with very unique gameplay and design. Unlike most tower defense games your enemy isn't a horde of monsters, but is instead a steadily expanding mass known as 'creeper'. Defeating the creeper isn't as simple as having strong towers - you have to know how to hold back the creeper while expanding your own area of influence, taking into account the the creeper will ooze in from multiple angles and will build up in areas of low elevation to eventually climb up onto higher ground.
Your own building mechanics are quite interesting as well. Instead of having independent towers, you instead build a web-like network of resource gatherers, utility structures, and attacking towers. Managing this web can get quite tricky at times, because all resources must flow through a command center and take time to traverse the network. Done incorrectly you could end up building a tower but not being able to arm it in time to defend against the creeper.
Also, while the creeper acts as a steadily growing mass, the player often ends up mirroring the creeper in many ways. Collectors - the primary resource generator - are most effective when spread out, forcing the player to expand their area of influence if they want more resources to spend. There are also many resource deposits around the map which must be contested, forcing the player to expand their area of influence even more. Aiding this playstyle is the fact that attacking towers can be respositioned, allowing you to leapfrog towers to slowly but steadily push the creeper back.
Overall the game is an excellent example of a unique twist on a genre and very polished gameplay. It's an extremely satisfying game to play and I highly recommend it to anyone who finds the concept interesting. Don't worry about not playing the previous games - they give more of the story, but this game is fully functional as a standalone experience.

I did not enjoy this game nearly as much as I expected I would.
Lifeless Planet is exactly that: a barren, lifeless planet; basically the least interesting envrionment you could possibly think of. Of course it's not really lifeless, because there's the whole soviet village thing. The first several areas are really pretty dull (baren, lifeless planet), but things do start to get more mysterious. Unfortunatly, my interest in the plot died about as quickly as the Russian colonists. Lifeless Planet quickly becomes Follow-the-Radioactive-Soviet-Pixie-Dust Simulator as you track the trail across a seemingly enless expanse. The voiced plot-points are predicible and the collectable documents read like a bad 70's alien invasion/Cold War crossover movie.
I probably would not have noticed/cared about the weak story if the other parts of the game were better than they are. Aside from a noticible smattering of death-related glitches, there are a number of game mechanics that don't work well of don't make sense. Calling them out may seem nit-picky, but by their powers combined, they really detract from the quality of the game:
-When transitioning into a new scene that should be geographically adjacent to the previous scene, the scenary changes as if you traveled a distance between scenes with no apparent explaination
-A burst from your jetpack at the right time can save you from hitting the ground too hard... unless of course you're falling into the valley that isn't part of the trail you're supposed to follow, in which case you die before you hit the ground to prevent you from going out of bounds
-The character is capable of pushing around boulders that are as tall as he is, but requires three sticks of dynamite to clear a blockade consisting of a couple of packing pallets and a barrel
-You can only deply the robotic arm in very specific situations (i.e. puzzles)
The only thing that I actually like about Lifelss Planet is the robotic arm. The specialized GUI is the envy of my inner Kerbal cargo engineer.
In conclusion: if you're looking for graphically appealing exploration/mysterious story walking simulator, I strongly reccomend Dear Ester. If you're looking for a retro sci-fi mystery/adventure, read Space Cadet by Robot Heinlien. If you need an example of a game that was good in theory but was poorly executed, add Lifeless Planet to your list of references.

So there you are, looking at this game like you're some kind of hot shot. "Oooh, look at me! I'm so badass! I could lift ten times my weight before breakfast!" Well, time for a wake-up call, sweetheart. With this simple, yet surprisingly hard to master little gem, you'll be doing war against the Creeper, an ever evolving, ever growing purple monstrosity, like the Smooze if it was genocidal and emotionless. You'll be taken back by how much strategy you have to implement to wage your war against the creeper. See, unlike your average RTS/tower defense, you can't just rush guys in and tire the enemy out. No, he'll be doing that to you. You have to cleverly work a way around using a multitude of offensive and defensive technologies. Standards like shields which protect you from the ever-increasing reach of the Creeper, to aerial units which provide ground support, and a landing pad for you to stage a beachhead against the amorphous beast. If you think you're Mr. Bigshot after hearing that, then prove it. Beat the creeper and send him to the reaper!
With that all said and done, I fully recommend this game. Especially when it took me about 15 hours to complete my first playthrough. I have to say that's not bad at all. And looking back, i even had tons of replay value checking out the other game modes, such as custom maps made by the developers, and those made by the community. Gotta really appreciate the simplicity of the game, which lends itself to such enjoyment.
EDIT: And after almost 100+ hours of enjoyment, I think I may be addicted.
EDIT2: After 400 hours, I ask you: Someone send help, I'm addicted to this damn game.

Lifeless Planet is a walking simulator, essentially developed by David Board.
What David Board did rather well:
What David Board did not rather well:
Gameplay:
The core of Lifeless Planet is a walking simulator, but the mantle is a sub-average 3D platformer. And the crust consists of a few puzzles which are not difficult.
The sections where you have octuple jumps are quite nice, being able to jumping eight times is almost like having a jetpack, partially because the character is an astronaut and has kind of a jetpack.
Rather not nice was the section where you have to ride geysers. It was next to impossible, I only made it through with trial and error and a bit of luck.
Some of the grabbing arm sections where difficult to control as well, especially because they provide no good perception of depth, yet another issue in communication design.
Pricing:
A walking simulator for 20€ is rather expensive, and so is Lifeless Planet. Definitely wait for a sale or an indie bundle.
I still recommend Lifeless Planet. It may just be a walking simulator, but then it is a very fancy and atmospheric one. Also note that, despite being out of Early Access, David Board still patches the game, some of the issues I mentioned might be resolved by the time you read this.

The need to combine the space key for jumping with camera control by left-handed mouse and cursor keys for movement is so awkward that this game becomes unplayable, considering that it requires very precise jumping.
Too bad, because I was really interested in experiencing this game's story.
I really do not understand why developers are willing to spend so much time on developing a game and then do not allow key remapping, which is quite easy to implement. Effectively, they are shutting out about 10% of their player base.

I haven't spent a single cent on this game but I find myself playing it more than any other game on Steam or my android.  The great thing about Solforge is that all you have to do is login once a day and/or win a game and you get free cards and Silver.  The Silver you win can even be used to purchase additional booster packs with more cards!  After a week or two of playing the computer, I had a decent enough collection to build my own decks and play against others online.
If you download the android version, it syncs with your PC account so you can take your collection with you to the toilet.
The game isn't perfect.  I think the interface could be improved especially in deck building mode.  This is more of an issue with the mobile version of Solforge as opposed to the PC version.  There are still some balance issues to work out with individual cards but that's what patches are for.  Some players will let the timer run out on their turn if they are losing and force you to sit there for 10 minutes because they refuse to concede.  This is more of an issue with the community rather than the game but it's the only time I have ever been frustrated with Solforge.
If you are a fan of Magic: The Gathering or Adventure Time's Card Wars, you will enjoy Solforge.  It's easy to learn but difficult to master.

I really like how they chose a system that would be impossible in a physical format, yet feels very traditional.
Compared to other games it is rather simplistic, but it's still a lot of fun and still let's you create some pretty interesting combos and tactics.
Due to it's leveling system the rounds start out slow but come to a fevered pace where one wrong placement can lead to losing or victory.
Ultimately it is fun and for free I'd definitely suggest it. A nice change of pace, at the least.

I have absolutely loved this game and it is a shame it is not more popular than it is. I have played this game more than any other game on steam, and besides the $20 I spent to buy the game before it went F2P, I have not spent any money on it. Solforge loses complexity by only, generally, having the option to play two out of the random five cards you draw each turn. However, it makes up for this lack of strategy by forcing the player to not just play whatever card is most optimal in the given situation, but also consider what cards you are leveling up and how this will impact your late game (a card "levels up" into a new version of that card whenever you play it which makes it more powerful by increasing health, damage, and sometimes granting or changing abilities. Generally a card has three ranks and your hero levels up every 4 turns allowing you to play cards of the next rank and all previous ranks). I absolutely love this element of strategy that, as far as I know, is unique to this solforge. It also helps that the card art is absolutely gorgeous. The only negative thing I can say about Solforge is that it has some minor p2w elements, however they have mostly been fixed by the latest patch. This patch made booster packs easier to get, have more cards,  and have a better chance of more rare cards. It also allowed you to purchase specific cards with in game currency if you are tired of rolling the dice with booster packs. Stoneblade has continued to support Solforge by adding tournaments and new tournament options, necessary balance fixes and relatively frequent releases of new cards. I look forward to seeing what they continue to do with Solforge.

I disagree that this game is pay to win, i have never paid for anything within this game and even after not playing for half a year and returning, I find that my old decks still hold up very well vs swarms of new cards I had never seen before including the ones that can go up to level 4.
*edit* After checking the shop for the first time in ages I've noticed they have bumped the price of free in game currency card packs by a ridiculous amount, which I suppose could make the game quite a bit more grindy when you are starting out, they have bumped the price from 900 silver to 5k which is ridiculous considering you normally get about 4-6k silver from your 3 wins bonus per day. This is clearly an attempt to make people purchase boosters with real money which is a shame.
That being said, what I like about this game is how the combat works, everything gets a lane and everything is required to attack, there is no saving a monster on the field for later nor in your hand as it gets refreshed every turn. This also prevents people from being total asses and just destroying all your monsters and leaving you alive forever like in other CCGs. When you use a card it levels up into the next tier and becomes unusuable until  you yourself level up, as the cards go through levels they get stat boosts and ability boosts, some of them even gain abilities they don't start with.
This IS a game you will have to play daily  if you want to have a decent deck though, you need 3 wins per day in order to get all the free rewards which include silver(free currency that can be used to buy basic boosters) and a random item that can be  an event ticket, a card(which is usually terrible and the worst reward) or a booster pack of any tier(I think I received 3 premium packs in the first month of playing). After about the first 2-3 weeks you should be able to assemble a decent deck and after that it's all a matter of tweaking. you are allowed to use cards from 2 out of the 4 factions in your deck which also creates some interesting combos.
Legendaries are well...legendaries, they either fall into the massive stats and terrible abilities type or the very  very squishy but amazing ability  type. Legendaries tend to start off way weaker at the first level but become better at endgame, what this means is that if you can put the pressure onto your enemy and  force them to put up normal monsters in order to defend, do it. This will cripple their lategame and potentially make the difference on whether you win or not.
Spells are also a major part of the game, there are no traps or secrets just regular spells. They can be buffs like armor, damage,  heals, special abilities like moving on the board or damage that goes through defending monsters etc. Or debuffs and damage: straight up nukes, poisons, debuffing of hp and attack(debuffing hp to negative CAN be used as a killing technique and has the benefit of going directly thorugh armor at the cost of usually doing way less damage than a nuke does).
It is a different system to get used to but once you do I find it is quite fun, matches are quite quick and you can play multiple at the same time, plus they just got android support so you can officially play it on just about any tablet or phone now. As long as you long in once a day and do your 3 wins (you can even play against bots if you're lazy since they're very easy) you will have very nice cards. The only cards you cannot get for free are the alternate arts*(essentially shiny cards) they release once a week

This game is terrible its seems they have tried to be as counter-intuitive as possible with the control system as you struggle to discover how to perform simple actions. it quickly becomes a giant PIOTA as you blunder in the dark trying to make some sense of what should be straightforward. It looks good but it feels bad, so bad I decided to forget my wasted $AUD20 and go looking for something professional.

Full disclosure:  I bought this game and refunded it just before the two hour mark because I got the strong impression it's just not ready yet, even from an Early Access point of view.  I am hopeful that it will improve in the future and I can change my stance on it, but we'll just have to see.
Exanima has the skeleton of a good game inside it, you can easily see that from the media they provide on the store page.  It has a wonderfully gritty and realistic style about the art, and the light and shadow and darkness is gloomy in that way I love in my RPGs, and their design goals are in the right place for the most part- the physics integration is especially cool, as I can't even think of another game I've played where it's possible to trip by running over an obstacle too fast.   But there are a few things I think really need to be said:
The controls are bad.  There's no two ways about it.  The barrier the game places between what you want your character to do and actually being able to pull it off, let alone with any kind of consistency, is unacceptably massive.  Now some of you are probably going to argue that you managed to eventually learn how to actually play the game and fight effectively, but the fact that the controls are possible does not make them bad, and I'm not going to waste my time learning the needlessly complicated rituals necessary to make my physics-controlled onscreen avatar do what I want them to.
An example:  In order to swing a weapon from left-to-right instead of the default right-to-left, you need to put the mouse cursor in some vague, undefined area to the left of the character.  This would be fine, except your character also turns to face the cursor, which means no only do you need to click precisely in an undefined area of the screen, but you have to chase this hotspot around like an invisible ghost in order to do so.  In the midst of all of this process, you might have just turned halfway away from your adversary, who has taken the opportunity to stab you violently in the back.  Why they didn't just add another keybind to do the alternate attack (like the other alternate attack they already have) I have no clue.
Another difficulty with the control is that you move with WASD, but but W is always forward, A and S are sideways, D is backwards no matter what direction you're facing, and there's no control to keep the camera automatically centered behind you.  Furthermore, for a game attempting to base itself on realistic physics, there is apparently a limited degree to which you can move while attacking even taking a step while you're in the process of swinging doesn't seem to be an option.  These issues might be able to be overcome with practice, but it just feels unintuitive and disorienting, and generally leaves the feeling that it could have been done much better.
I have more gripes than those two, but I don't think they need to be brought up in a review, some things just get on my case.  Everything else that I was able to experience looked good and seemed promising, but given the fact that combat is most of the experience as presented, apart from manipulating items to inspect the environment, it was rather limited how much of the content I could experience.  It's possible I could have gone further with time and effort, but I had zero desire to try to fight the poor controls and my own frustration in order to get there.
Those are my few cents at least, and I hope these things change for the better before full release, there's fantastic potential here.

Recommend because I got my money's worth. Still work to be done but I think it's worth the price in the game's current state. I don't think it's for everyone. You will probably get bored of the game after some time, but I think there's enough here to keep you entertained for a while if the trailer suits your fancy. Some thoughts on the game:
-The physics based combat is pretty fun and I haven't seen anything like it. It's real satisfying to gain some level of mastery over it and wreck most of the AI opponents. Practice mode offers a safe environment to learn the ins and outs.
-Arena mode can be pretty addictive - "just one more fight" - and it really delivers a steady stream of the solid core gameplay.
-The campaign / story mode I think could use some work. I really wish the game had a map. I get the whole spooky dungeon you've never been in before etc. but I am not the only one who has found the story mode to get tedious after being lost for tens of minutes. It's not so scary or atmospheric after you clear most of the hallways of hostile undead and just want to get to the next place. Surely there is some solution that doesn't involve the jury-rigged maps you can find online or randomly tripping over a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥until you eventually find the exit.
-I think the AI is very well done. You can tell when you're fighting lower-tier opponents and when they're higher tier. Harder opponents are harder because they're better fighters, and are not inherently more spongy (HP, as far as I can tell, is the same between humans).
-Armor system is pretty cool - good armor saves your life, but encumbers you without the conditioning to wear it. A well aimed shot can get around armored bits and deliver some dangerous stuff. Layering of armor to give different kinds of protection, like a gambeson beneath chain mail.
-Camera and controls can be difficult to play with - even after 42 hours (as of now). It may be the best solution so far, but it sometimes feels like I'm playing with a bucket on my foot against the sometimes more agile AI, who can get in your♥♥♥♥♥♥and fire away if you're not on it.
-Wide variety of weapons delivering different kinds of damage. Morning stars, barchides, axes, spear, swords, sledgehammers, and so on. If online PVP were introduced, I suspect most people would grab the 2h sword and spam away like the AI does until you're dead.
-Sometimes the weapons get stuck in the player model. For example I've had my guy hold his halberd between his legs for way too long during fights, other time he has held his sword behind his back like a dumbass. On a positive note, combatants can get tangled up as they would in real life and sometimes fall to the floor because of it.
-Blocking is still a bit of a mystery to me... Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. I've totally been hit when I didn't deserve and and I've dished it out when the AI blocked. Against dual wielding opponents, forget it.
Absolutely awesome despite being incomplete.  Arena is fun and I recommend doing it before going into campaign.  Can't wait for more updates, they're coming

Pros
+ Very similiar style to first two Broken Sword games
+ Good 2D graphics (for the most part)
+ Cheap
Cons
- Story is stupid
- Character animation is poor and very limited
- Some/most characters come across as annoying
- The writing is amateur-ish
As a big fan of the first two Broken Sword games, I was excited to see the series return to its roots after the last few releases. At first, I wasn't disappointed; the graphical style was spot on, and Rolf Saxon was back voicing the main character, with a similar witty approach.
However, that's where the similarities ended. I started to notice a lack of variation in the character animation, and when interacting with objects, mimed with empty hands instead of holding them. The cut scenes were ok, but some of the 2D style backdrops made me feel motion sick as they 'moved' to create a sense of perspective in panning shots.
Though the voice actors put in a good performance (mostly), that can't overcome the poor quality, amateur-ish script. A lot of the dialogue was clunky, and any humour felt false and out of place. The overarching story started well, but by the end was just over-the-top stupidity. The ending felt like the writer had had enough and just stuck any old crap on the end just to finish the game. Details such as how the police acted were also badly written, as if the writer didn't have the first idea of what police officers actually do. Yes, those characters were supposed to be a bit silly, but it crossed the line into ludicrousness.
In short, the only thing that got me to the end of the game was my love for the original two games. Although that was clearly what the developers were going for, that is all they went for, not quality or originality, but a pastiche with many original characters stuck into the game just because they could.

Skulls of the Shogun is a turn based strategy game set in a humorous rendition of the ancient Japanese afterlife where you play as a General by the name of Akamoto, who arrives after being mysteriously murdered in battle. Many turn-based strategy games rely less on strategy and more on rock-paper-scissors like tactics in order to counter your enemy's units rather than out-thinking them. Skulls of the Shogun shakes up the genre by being rather fast paced, especially for a strategy game, and forcing you to make decisions under multiple different kinds of constraints that have to be worked around. These constraints force you to use strategy and essentially play parts of the game more as a puzzle game than a turn-based strategy, and that's mainly where Skulls of the Shogun tends to stand out.
As I said many times before Skulls of the Shogun is a turn-based strategy game, which means that it has plenty of competition. So the question then is, what makes this Skulls of the Shogun different from all the other turn-based strategy games out on the market. The main difference is the orders system, limiting you to only being able to use 5 actions a turn. Those actions could be moving and attacking or maybe buying a new unit, regardless of what the action is though it always costs one order, represented by the scrolls at the top of your screen. I really liked how this actually influenced gameplay, it made me have to think about which unit I should be moving and actually plan my game out instead of moving first and planning later. Seeing as in almost every battle you're outnumbered significantly, you're going to be doing a lot of planning so that you can overcome odds that are certainly not in your favor. You start with a handful of units, but on pretty much every level there are shrines that you can use to buy more units with rice, the game's currency. Rice is acquired by haunting rice paddies with your units, a task that takes a turn and leaves the unit doing the haunting defenseless for said turn. The paddies are normally put in locations that tend to provoke conflict with the opposing side, so you have to strategize as to which ones you can take or hold. Rice paddies, like mineral fields in C&C or Starcraft, eventually run out so you are somewhat on a timer and will eventually reach a point where you run out.
Now in Skulls of the Shogun you're going to be using 4 types of units: cavalry, archers, infantry, and your commanding general unit. You also have different monk shrines that can be haunted to give you special monk units with themed abilities, which massively change how you play the game. I found that the hardest part of the game was actually fully utilizing each kind of unit, but I got better at it as the game progressed. When enemies are killed, they drop skulls, which can be eaten by one of your men to give them a health buff. If 3 skulls are consumed on one specific unit, then they turn into a demon and can attack more often and hit harder. So strategy in Skulls of the Shogun is not only about the usual things like positioning and knowing when to attack, but you also have to work with both a small number of moves and units, as well as knowing when to upgrade your men. The best part about Skulls of the Shogun is that I found as the game progressed, I didn't feel like I was playing a strategy game and instead felt more as if it was closer to a puzzle game in some places. Finding the right combination of moves to successfully out-think your enemy was incredibly satisfying, and at times difficult, but in the end I always found myself looking back fondly on just about every level.
Skulls of the Shogun is a colorful and refreshing take on strategy games that switches up the monotony with faster paced combat and gameplay in places that feels almost like solving a puzzle, let down only by its lackluster story.
