It's like a strange mish-mash of SNES Sim City, Rollercoaster Tycoon 2, Lords of the Realm II, and Banished. At its heart, K&C is a survival-builder/management sim, but it's not nearly as unforgiving as some of the other titles in the genre, and is more about building cool cities, surrounding them with walls, and spearing the heck out of invading beasties.
Pros:
+ It is super addicting.
+ It updates with some frequency.
+ The game has cool, pseudo-throwback graphics.
+ It's really hard to "lose." In fact, I haven't had a deserted town (unlike Banished, where any small mistake will end the game :P).
+ It's a rock-solid platform, at least for me. I've had no crashes.
+ There are a lot of maps, even if they don't really have that big an impact on gameplay.
+ Great soundtrack... if a bit limited. But the tracks that do exist are really catchy.
+ The AI is smart. Even in medium difficulty, I was constantly attacked where most vulerable; peasants don't generally get lost; there are basically zero pathing issues.
+ It's as rewarding to play small-ball as to go big. Try building and maintaining a small walled outpost instead of a mega metropolis. Both are pretty enjoyable in their own way.
+ The interface is pretty slick. There are shortcuts from tree-cutting, etc. that assist in speeding things up.
Cons:
+ There's almost nothing in the way of a tutorial. It takes a while to understand what's necessary to maintain a balanced budget and keep peasants happy.
+ If trees grow back, I haven't seen it happen. You have to "plant" via logging huts, but these cannot be constructed without timber nearby. Thus, if you deforest an island you're building on, you're just SOL.
+ The player-built armies are pretty much worthless. All defense can (and should) be done via towers.
+ The game is heavily focused on peasants, and gives zero screen time to gentry/nobility/royalty. I understand that *I* am the King, but a Kingdom is more than just the guy with the crown and a bunch of peasants.
+ There's no marketplace by which to resource trade. I really want a structure that allows me to buy, say, stone from a neighboring kingdom when I have cash on hand.
+ After a while, no matter how many ogres the AI lands, it isn't enough. I find that the threat from dragons/vikings significantly diminishes in the late game. It would be insteresting to see full enemy kingdom-armies attack at some point instead of this pillaging rabble.
+ I really wish there was an alternative to farming - say, cattle or pigs or sheep or something. It would be nice just to mix things up, even if it was still "farming."
+ The late-game demands for charcoal are just ridiculous, easily outstripping any resource with the exception of food. It's hard not to, at some point, be totally charcoal-starved (and have your peasants go ballistic).
Overall? Totally, completely worth $10. Would pay $50 for how much playtime I've had with this sucker. I love the game, and look forward to playing more over the next several years.

The Haunted: Hells Reach is a third-person, wave/survival shooter set in demonic themed reality set in a western-style backdrop.  The objective is simple: join the side of good (or evil.) Shoot, punch, kick and blast numerous demonic minions across five or so waves (depending on the mode) Defeat the great hulking demon Adadon in the final battle.  Overall the game possesses a Painkiller aesthetic with a Killing Floor feel.
+ V. good and stable netcode with listen server mode.
+ Nice designed and streamlined gameplay makes for a very fun game.
+ Weapon classes maybe limited to three but the upgrades are very different and satifying to use.  Upgrading is so well ingraved in the action that choosing which weapons to upgrade is done on the fly.
+ Very well conceived achievements.  Only one grinding achievement and a two tricky but easy to get achievements.  Overall very satisfying to unlock for achievement unhunters/completionists.
+ Good range of difficulty levels from: Beginner to Nightmare, provides an excellent learning curve.
- Enemies are quite fast and will be upon you on harder levels before you can react.  Giving the impression of getting overwhelmed quickly.  Put me off playing at first.
- Spawn frequency doesnt seem to be that well geared towards difficulty
- Dead community.  Although there are a very few die hards from time to time you will struggle to get anyone to join your game or find one on going.  Which is a real shame!
- The games heavy demonic theme may put you off if thats not your cup-of-tea.
- Doesnt scale to well with more players.
* A really nice selection of game modes including: wave survival, versus (pvp) and a mix of both allow for some change-up when you feel the need.
* Well-rounded characters with good one-liners and _ voice-overs.
* While the graphics maybe dated by todays standard they held up very well and immerse players in the setting.
* The use of soulstones to keep players on their toes is a nice touch.  Fail to get these before time runs out and the pace, franticness increases.  Includes some nice environmental changes to penalise the player some more.
* An average soundtrack which switches from one track to a second when gameplay changes normal pace to
* Its a port with console style gameplay moves and controls.  But its a decent one and it works well on PC at all levels.
Dropped like a hot potato when first played, I really did not take to Haunted: Hells Reach.  I found the game slow, difficult and frustating.  Nothing made sense.  After a few years gathering dust I decided to give this another try.  Suffice to say I was really glad I did!
By starting on easier difficulty and learning the game's mechanics, I really enjoyed my experience during this second pass.  Graphics may become dated but for the time being they hold their own.  Game mechanics are concise and robust, making for fluid gameplay.  Sure its very repetitive and at times five waves seem a little long but despite these its alot of fun.  The combination of destroying soulstones within the time limit and weapon upgrading work well keeping you invested in playing. The range of enemies require some tactics especially when they enter rage mode, increasing the challenge to a satisfying level.  Probably one of the highlights are the range of characters and the very apt one-liners they spit out as you slaughter the devils minions!
Potential downsides are the slightly clunky controls and 'on-top of you' enemy spawning which together, can cause premature death!  The Haunted plays fine in solo but is much better fun with other players.  PvP where players can choose to play on the side of good or control the evil minions could actually have been very good!  Its just a shame that there is no community to speak of anymore.
Overall its actually far better than I had originally thought.  If youre looking for an ultimate challenge from a coop wave survival shooter, you cant get much harder than on Nightmare.   Despite its age its a very underrated title.  One I would recommended mostly on a decent sale.  Be aware that now that its under new ownership the brand looks about to be re-vitalized.   At least with a new dlc.

This is actually pretty fkn fun.  Monster design is freaky, comes with lots of variety and I love how fast and in-your-face they are.  The character controller is surprisingly good.  Granted, animations aren't fluid or 3A industry standards but play really well with the game.  Gun control, combat control and jumping is very responsive and satisfying and has a bit of parkour going with it, which is great.  For a "yo, lets play something quick" co-op game, this is perf.  Worth it for the sale price, honestly.  I'm glad I got it.
EDIT: After a bit more playing, this game is seriously good.  Really hard.  Might be the hardest shooter I ever played for coop survival.  Harder then Killing Floor 2 on HoE and that's even on NORMAL difficulty!  Take that in!  I know you don't believe me because you don't know my level of skill, but I can 'zerk in KF2 on HoE solo with 100% success rate at this point.  The community says "Normal" is an untested difficulty...and it has +2 more difficulties above normal.  I barely beat normal.
The combat mechanics are fantastic.  It's damn near cartoony over-the-top holywood, but, the mechanics play out very well.  Melee and unarmed combos mix up well with ranged attacks and level up your inventory.  You can prioritize which weapons to upgrade.
Certain monsters are immune to ranged when enraged (when u fail to finish them off during their stun period) and thus hafta be taken care of in close combat.  If you have someone prioritizing close combat/melee then they can go in and assassinate raged enemies before it gets out of hand.
When a player dies a totem spawns with player's soul that must be touched to respawn them;  However, a monster can steal the soul and run away, getting lost in horde, forcing co-op team to risk going after it.  Health totems spawn and hafta be dealt with in same way.  Really cool mechanic and clutch for such a steep difficulty curve.  It's very satisfying getting combos off as each enemy kill regens ur health (but less and less on higher difficulties).
They made this game long time ago for a contest, then refined it and fixed the bugs.  It was worth the effort, very unique co-op survival game.  I'm buying copies for lan and online parties since its fun and easy to get into but hard to master.

Despite the negative reviews it has received, this is a quite solid strategy game.
The writing and voice acting certainly leave a lot to be desired, and the game world can be static and formulaic, but there is definitely an interesting strategic challenge. The campaign does a good job of focusing the player through various restrictions and objectives, ensuring that missions offer different experiences and challenges and forcing the player to vary their style.
The area in which the game really shines is combat. The player has access to a variety of characters and their performance in combat is quite diverse thanks to the effect of attributes, perks, abilities and weapons. While some of the battles towards the end of the campaign seem almost impossible, it is very satisfying to learn through trial and error and finally get a win against the odds.
The sandbox mode exposes some of the flaws of the game, but the campaign mode is long enough to get good value out of the game. There is also DLC if it really captures your imagination.
Well worth a go.

This remaster is superb, breathing life into the classic FPS. Reinvigorating the sprawling levels and less-than-intricate hidden areas.
The gameplay remains identical, focusing on a combination of oldschool FPS and platforming puzzles, of which Turok strikes a near perfect balance and offering players comfortable with their jumping prowess certain (albeit rare) unique oppertunities to shortcut certain levels or reach secret areas with increased ease.
The level design isn't anything special, usually relying on players overthinking to hide treasures essentially in plain sight. However, each level feels unique, enjoyable, and the vast majority of the secret areas feel rewarding to locate.
All in all, great game and definitely worth picking up if it's on sale.

Lifeless Planet is a puzzle-platformer where you're an astronaut travelling to another world 20 lightyears into the future, but, twist, the USSR beat us there in 1979 because plot and, twist, they ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ed everything up.
The good:
The controls were fluid and responsive, or at least for me. I also have an appreciation for exploration and puzzle games, but...
The ugly:
Meh.
That's the best way I can sum up this game. Just... meh.
Voice acting? Meh.
Graphics/Art? Meh.
Gameplay? Meh.
Music? Meh.
Plot? Meh.
Meh? Meh.
It seems like the project tacked on too much. Like... okay, great example- the plot. I understand it's suppsed to be plot-heavy, right? But, there's the astronaut, and the russians, and the ancients, and the dead wife, and the plant chick, and it's just a complete mess. The game's 4-6 hours long, and the plot's trying to go fourty different ways. By the time I hit the end, they're hinting at this twist with the dead wife, and I know I'm supposed to feel something, but I just... *sigh* I just don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥
The gameplay itself seems like it doesn't know what it wants to do. Open-world exploration, without being open and nothing to explore; puzzler, with only one actual puzzle that I remember; a platformer that's unchallenging and monotonous.
The gameplay is repetitive and dull, the scenery gets old after an hour of seeing just desert and rocks, there's four soundtracks and only one of them is decent, and the entire time, there's this hide-and-go-seek challenge to find minerals scattered around the world.
That's right. You're supposed to find hidden minerals amongst the barren, rock-filled landscape.
LIFELESS PLANET: WE GOT ROCKS. LIKE ROCKS? FIND SOME ROCKS. GET ACHEIVEMENTS WITH ROCKS. ROCKS WITH ROCKS ON ROCKS. ROCK SIMULATION 2014. 10/10 GAME OF THE YEAR, ALL YEARS.
The game's trying to be this grandoise art piece, but it's not really focusing on anything. And yet...
The ugly:
It's still charging my credit card like it's some grandoise art piece. This game is not worth $20. I complained about AntiChamber being $20, and that is a fantastic puzzle-platformer. This? I /might/ pay $5 for it, if I was drunk.
Final words:
This game was so close to being something worthwhile, but a lack of focus and a short gameplay meant that this became a bland, uninteresting mess. It's not awful per se, but just the sheer medicocrity of it is almost insulting considering I paid $20 for it.
Final score: 4.5/10
Cost: $19.99 USD

My Super Tower 2
While I never got to play My Super Tower 1, I don’t think I am missing much. My Super Tower 2 is a botched attempted at a tower defense game. When loading the game up, you can either launch the game, or launch a manual. Clicking manual will send you to a Steam Guide, in which you are greeted with Russian and English guide. The guide, which is short enough to place in game, is pretty basic and doesn’t give you much.
When I launched the game, I immediately noted the UI, with its blocky, comic sans type text, oversized buttons and huge VK button up in the top corner. The customization is relatively basic and allows for basic, personal optimization, but the game really isn’t that graphics intensive.
The problems start to arise when playing the game. When trying to place towers, the game doesn’t allow you to place them on certain place, and requires a lot of moving of the mouse to find the right place. To place the tower, you have to hold down the mouse button and it if you move, it stops the placement process.
The enemies are unoriginal and basic. Graphically, the game is a very simplistic 3D rendering of what TABS would look like if it were a TD.
The game is not only unoriginal, but it is also filled with bugs. I was able to break the game in 10 different ways with only clicking my mouse.
In all honesty, the game is bugged, broken and rough around the edges. It isn’t worth it, even if you have a coupon. It is unoriginal take on a TD game, it has no theme and no point. I am going to give it a 3/10, for lack of content, lack of originality, but a plus for concept.

This is a qualified recommendation.  I bought this game for $10 during the 2015 Steam Summer Sale and I think it was probably a good use of $10.  I really enjoyed my first playthrough, the graphics have a very interesting style, and the characters and monsters show a ton of variation.
The basic idea is x-com, but with less research and upgrade options, but much better gameplay, much more balanced and interesting combat scenarios and much less random nonsense, and with a natural "retirement" mechanic in which you generally get no more than 3 or 4 combats out of any specific hero.
Instead of getting attached to certain heroes, you get attached to their liniage, raising other members of their family to replace them, etc.
The game basically gives you no hints regarding build order or strategy, but despite that I beat the game pretty easily the first time on normal difficulty, so I don't think it's too hard or anything.
Overall I think it's a lot of fun and better than X-Com.  I don't know if I see myself playing through it again, but on the other hand I never played through X-Com a second time either so that's not really a huge knock on the game.
I think if you're looking for a lot of depth or options, I"m not sure there's that much here for a 2nd or 3rd playthrough but it's still a good few dozen hours of fun for your money.

The best and quickest way I can descibe this game is to say that it's fantasy XCOM (the newer ones) with elements from Hero Generations.
And I don't mean that as a bad thing, I love XCOM, and I'm really enjoying MASSIVE CHALICE, but it really is XCOM. The management simulation sections are similar to XCOM, and even feature similar research mechanics. The combat interludes are similar to XCOM, even down to the 2-AP turns. The character pregression is similar to XCOM, esspecially as far as the two-path ability tree format and equipment layout prior to a fight.
The biggest difference is that MASSIVE CHALICE features a "character breeding" mechanic. Your heroes will age and, eventually, die of old age. To keep yourself well-stocked with battle-ready warriors, you need to arrange marriages between heroes. They will do the deed, have children with their physical traits, raise them into warriors with their personality traits, and, eventually, die as well and need to be replaced from their own bloodline. It's kind of neat, and keeps your hero-pool continually changing, instead of letting you just stick to the same five heroes forever like XCOM does, also giving a sense of dread as you realize your best troops are getting old, and you need to decide whether to keep them in the field or settle them down to make kids who are, hopefully, a quarter as amazing as they were before they drop from age.
All-in-all, I'm enjoying it a lot. I recommend it to anyone else who enjoys games like XCOM or Jagged Allience: Management games with tactics-RPG combat interludes. If you're looking to get into the genre, I'd even say to start here and work your way to those others, MASSIVE CHALICE is a bit more forgiving than some.

Right! Completed a campaign on the starting difficulty. I reckon it took about ten hours all told, and at various points I was ♥♥♥♥ing sick of everything but Massive Chalice has some interesting enough points that it's worth discussing.
First off: the obvious comparison to make is X-Com. It's the same basic template of a squad of five engaging in turn-based percentage-themed combat with alien-looking-things.  Backing that all up is a world map where events emerge and you react. There's some research where you use alien-looking bodies. There's a timer. Surely just a rip-off? Well...
...not quite. Let's take a step back: What's the premise? The MASSIVE CHALICE is a superweapon of sorts, charging up to once and for all defeat the dastardly Cadence, a vague orangey blob around the map there that is planning to destroy you and everyone you care about. But it's gonna take a while to charge up - 300 years in fact, so your elite squad is going to be experiencing a lot of change. They've got a fighting lifetime of maybe 50 years if you get lucky, so you don't invest in single supermen, you invest in super-bloodlines.
Each of your castles on the map is occupied by heroic families. The Kuan! The Leones! The Aabershots! The Berrys! Heroes all! Keep 'em married and not covered in orange goo and they will provide you with a fine selection of heroes. Then you cross-breed them with special tweezers to try and encourage positive traits to emerge. I mean in theory you do, I just married off people with high fertility so I could get maximum manpower, which led to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ super soldiers indeed.
The research you're doing is gradually improving their equipment, both in stats and fancy stuff, and during their short lifetimes, they'll level up themselves and unlock special powers of their own.
Basically it is a balancing act, trying to keep the conveyor belt of babies rolling consistently enough that you always have a good enough five-man force to call upon while trying to boost up the long-term bonuses - I've mentioned research but there's also relics which have to be passed down bloodlines, and gain power every time they're used in battle.
As long as you make sure to build a few keeps at the start to house your families, minion numbers aren't really an issue, so then it's going to be battles which could be your downfall. Every ten years or so the cadence strikes in 2/3 provinces, and you defend one. Three strikes and they vanish forever.
You're inevitably gonna lose something. What you have to do is not lose battles, as that will accelerate the process of loss, and at the difficulty I was on, this wasn't a taxing task either. I lost one battle out of maybe thirty, which meant a lot of those 300 years were boring , waiting for the next fight to emerge so I could get it over with.
About 200 years in, I'd unlocked enough stuff, advanced my soldiers enough, and came across bad enough dudes, that the occasional interesting battle slipped in. Everything I've said so far is functional and boring, but let's get in the praise for MASSIVE CHALICE now, which is the diversity of battlefield options.
There's Cradles - upside down jellyfish who spit out babies. Roided-out blue guys called Twitchers, who can instantly swap position with anything. Ghostly Lapses, who causes your heroes to forget how to do things. Spiky Ruptures, who only exists to explode, leaving behind damaging sludge puddles. There's also baddies that can only be hit once and go invulnerable (Bulwarks), and baddies who cause your heroes to age years in a single punch (Wrinklers), potentially having them die of old age in the middle of a fight.
Your heroes are also pretty damn fragile, which means everything can suddenly go 100% to pot in a moment. So at its best, MASSIVE CHALICE is this little battlefield puzzle, where you have a huge amount of enemies around you that you can't possibly all kill this round, so how do you prioritize? Can you chain-reaction the ruptures? Can you knock some of them into a tree so they get knocked out for a turn? Can you smash up the local flora?
In my favourite battle (barring the final showdown which I shall not go into cos I want it to be a surprise if you play it), I found myself against a very large number of bulwarks, who go almost invincible after their first damage instance each turn. I did not have the damage to take out eight of them simultaneously, so I couldn't just start locking and loading as they would ♥♥♥♥ing murder me, but I had invested in some bulwark armour (researched with their corpses), which does exactly the same for your men.
So the big men waddle into the centre and absorb the hits and hope they don't run out of health while the alchemist stands at the back lobbing crates of bees at the enemy, which meander around, causing damage to everyone and the hunters prowl around in the shadows looking for pickoffs as the blundering bulwarks try and escape the bees.
Later on I got something from the Twitcher corpse research called Skipping Stones, which let you be the one who swaps positions with anything - there's some really inventive things you can do with them, to force enemies onto certain paths, to save people, to drag baddies into range. I kept a guy alive on 1HP for a good ten minutes on the final battle by swapping him all over the shop
The other thing which got better as the game went on was my feeling towards Bloodlines rather than specific heroes. X-Com is all about that one sniper who is the best at killing aliens, and you give him a name and ooh isn't he the best. Whereas with MASSIVE CHALICE, your heroes are going to see at most five battles before they die, so you better get used to them fast. Ultimately - I can barely name anyone who fought for me, but I have a strong recollection of the bloodlines they came from (always rely on the Aabershots) but you're not going to be able to tell the same stories about them.
In summary: MASSIVE CHALICE starts off immensely boring, and gradually increases in challenge and options until it becomes interesting. My normal campaign took about ten hours, so it depends whether you have that time to spare.

Fantasy X-Com with a dash of Rogue Legacy. This sort of game is built on the idea of becoming vested in these families and their members, so that it really hurts when ill befalls them, and this is a feature that would have really enhanced that aspect. It also would have been nice, particularly given how the game ends, to have a New Game+ mode of some sort, perhaps where the families you had persist, but you're given a new generation at half their current level and the difficulty is scaled up. Lacking these two qualities, I'm unlikely to ever go back to the game, but I still very much enjoyed my dozen or so hours going through the first time. 20 minutes in and I'm already giving up.  Framerate was awful... maybe 15 fps on a new Mac.  Tutorial said I could hit the [End] key to perform an action but this is a Mac and it does not have an [End] key; their QA team should have caught that.  I tried dialing back the video settings to get better fps but even at the lowest settings the framerate was still lame.  So I clicked [Reset] to restore the defaults but when I clicked [Apply] nothing happened; I had to restart the game again to apply the settings.  They seem to have implemented their own proprietary keyboard driver which basically ignores my OS settings where I just tap the touchpad to perform a click... with this game I actually have to depress the trackpad hard to do a basic left click.  Maybe this game is good but after so many annoying and preventable issues so early on, I'm cutting my losses and moving on.

UPDATE 9/30/2016  Well, after having and playing the game for awhile, my initial positive impression has worn off quite a bit.  I still like the atmosphere of the game, and the mechanics are still "unique" but the game itself isnt all that rewarding to play.  My biggest gripe involves the combat system but not because of the games "ragdoll" movement/combat mechanics.  Most of the time you must carry a torch to see where you're going because most of the area's are so dark.  When you have to fight, you have to switch from your torch to your weapon.  Seems logical, yes?  BUT, you cannot move even the tiniest bit while switching from a torch to a weapon or else your charector wont do the switch.  Oh and it takes time to do the switch. That means that a spoon weilding zombie can and most likely will kill you before you can even finish dropping your torch to grab your weapon to get into the fight.  This could easily be fixed by allowing you to move to avoid being hit while switching weapons.   It wouldnt even be cheating since you could do such a thing in real life.  But so far, the developers seem to believe that this kind of artificial difficulty provides "challenge".  It doesnt.  It provides only frustration.
My next complaint is vaguely related to the first.  Every single item in the game is in the exact same place in every single walk through.  This means that if you have played the game a couple of times, you already know where all the important stuff is.  There is no reason to explore-nothing special to find, no happy(or upsetting) suprises.  There is no reason to travel anywhere except directly to the containers where you know there will be a useful item.  And since my first complaint leads to you dying so easily and often, and since the deaths of your charectors are permanent, you will have to travel through the same corrodors and rooms and retrieve the same objects from the exact same containers over and over and over again.  The more often you have to start over this way, the less likely you will be to bother starting again.  It gets very old and very boring very quickly.
Finally, there is no way to heal your charector in this game and he/she does not heal over time either.  This means that the best way to make it very far in the game is to avoid fighting at all since every little nick and bump that you receive in battle brings you that much closer to the perma-death of your charector.  I dont mind the perma-death idea but put in some kind of way to heal yourself-like food or rest.  Make finding food or a safe place to sleep rare if they like but give us the oportunity to keep our game going by the skin of our teeth if thats what it takes. Please dont tell me that such a thing wouldnt be realistic.  For one, its a game.  It isnt real to begin with.  For two, how is your charector surviving in a pit without any food in the first place?
Anyway, bottom line is that combat in the game is already a fun challenge because of the "ragdoll" movement mehanics.  Dont add artificial difficulty with the torch/weapon switching issue.  Standing completely and utterly still to drop a torch and pull a weapon while an enemy beats your health down to zilch is NOT challenging.  Its frustrating and dumb.  Then you die and have to start all over again.  Next, move the loot around!  Give us a reason to search the place.  Finally, either get rid of perma-death, allow some mechanism for regaining a bit of health or let us save our games!  Im so so sick of having to do the first layer of the dungeon over and over and over just because of no health regen + permadeath.  Ive stopped playing the game because of it.

首先，这个游戏很不错，结合了沙盒和ORPG游戏的特点。系统也不是很复杂。人物成长跟日常的养成联系很密切。

地图
地图不是很大，但是无缝衔接，缺憾是目前视乎开放的区域不够大，而且地图缩览图过于简单，我觉得应该在大地图界面加入罗盘和玩家自定义标记。以方便在满地图找资源的时候不至于迷路。
资源
地图中资源分布好像缺乏规划，山脉和巨石附近找不到矿石群，动物们凌乱的分散在各个地方，城镇和村庄有点小，而且地产资源有些分散。草药可见度很低，也很少。然而树木到处都是。水资源采集量太少。
其他系统

A game with a LOT of potential!
Since it's in Early Access it's understandable that issues like lag, bugs and missing content is possible, but NeoJack has been at the front of the battallion working hard to add new content and patch bugs. He's often present at the official Discord channel, checking the bug reports, reading our suggestions and answering questions about the current content and what's to come.

With less than a few weeks of launching the economy system is yet to be at its full potential. Right now everyone is crafting everything for themselves and most find it hard to part with their hard-earned cash when they really don't need to, but once the playerbase grows and cash becomes more abundant we'll see the player-driven economy advertised in the game description.
Repeating my first statement, this game has A LOT of potential, and I'll love to be here to see it flourish.

So I backed this game in its Alpha, about 3 years ago, played it a little back then and then put it away. Having picked it up again a few days ago, I just can't believe how far it has come. I've literally played for 30 hours straight and still have about 10 biomes to see (meaning planet types), still have quite a few buildings and upgrades to check out, and I have almost completely ignored the main quests in order to tech faster. I still have to upgrade my ship, create a space station, create an animal farm to harvest monster drops easier, create a colony with tenants, collect Pokemon style pets and use them as battle companions, upgrade my mech to be able to actually fight in space, test all the amazing legendary weapons, explore all randomly generated dungeon types, fight hostile ships in space, then there's multiplayer servers, community mods... And I hear they're about to launch an update that enables you to hunt down most wanted criminals between planets. Can't wait for that to happen!
It did take 3-4 years of development but I have to say it was worth the wait. There is so much to explore and do even long after what I estimate to be ~100 hours to just discover/test every feature of the game, as the game is ultimately a sandbox, so you are free to collect, organize and use everything your matter manipulator can collect. The gameplay is just so relaxing and the graphics are so atmospheric for a pixel art game: going through a sandstorm in the middle of the night on a foreign planet while struggling to see anything with your flashlight, then bumping into a small village when you least expect it, being pixel art it lets your imagination fill in so many gaps, which enriches the atmosphere of the game. Even simple activities such as mining for some needed ore can be so relaxing, while still providing enough risk-reward through the dangers you encounter while going deeper and deeper into the planet. And if you ever have enough, you can always start a fresh character and do things differently.

Maybe this will sound weird, but I find this game very much alike the X-COM game, yet it is also nothing alike it.
This is a fantasy game. Lovely artwork. Yet the strategic elements in the battles and the way you build up your "base", or in this case, kingdom, reminds me of how X-COM works.
Your goal is to defend your kingdom for 300years, and a large part of the manner in which you achieve this goal is by breeding your heroes, your nobels. They make up both your soldiers, but also researchers, trainers and parents of future heroes/soldiers.
I get great fun out of trying to fit together in arranged couples those who will pass on the most desired traits to their offspring. Yet at time I have had to pick whomever I had left at said time. You start with three base classes yet breeding toghether different classes can yield new classes.  I have yet to complete my first playthrough but will definitly play though it several times (even as I doubt that I will manage to move from the normal difficulty setting).
The management side aside, ever so often your kingdom will get attacked. Often two or three times at once, yet you can only send out one team of heroes. Leaving you at the hard choice of which parts of your land to possibly loose.
The battles themselves are as stated before turn based. Enemy difficulty has thus far always felt challanging enough, with a good (yet not overly large) amount of varied opponents. Nothing has felt OP even as there are some leaps in difficulty from time to time.
If you like games that are a mix of management and turnbased strategy, then this is really a game for you to try.

At the moment of writing this review I have not completed my first playthrough but I think 8 hours is enough to evaluate my experience.
It is good. Game is challenging in every aspect, as you have to make choices on things that will follow up throu entire game and there is rarely an obviously good option to take and it will impact things like what heroes you can deploy in battle, or what bonuses will you get for controlling (with a keep) a region.
Although one must understand that the very mechanics this game is based on may be a bit frustrating for some as you don't care for heroes, you care for lineages. You have to tailor marriages that will give you valuable descendants and classes you will need later in game. There is no telling what will be the perfect composition of classes in next generation as in every battle you have different set of enemies that will require different tactics.
Combat itself is propably strongest aspect of game as enemies are challenging and interesting and you have a really fun mixture of skills to use in battle.
Question is what are this game's downsides?
Well, game can get repetitive after a while. Strategic aspect of game lacks options and feels shallow after first few decades. Events that happen sometimes are a bit to rare and most of the time lacks impact. This game needs an expansion of that aspect. I guess more buildings, events or even lands would make it more interesting and less repetitive.
Still I can recommend this game as it will give you few nice evenings and for its discounted price (~10 EUR right now) it's hardly a bad choice.

First Fight: Holy hell, is this guy drunk? Am I drunk? What is this?
One hour in: Ok, ok. So moving forward and swinging is pretty good. But what if I use my drunken shove and combo it?
One hour, thirty minutes in: OH SWEET BABY JESUS THERE'S AN ALTERNATIVE ATTACK?! Stab, stab, swing, lounge push, swing... ... ...
Three hours in: Judging by the trajectory of this guy's movements and his previous attempts at coming at me from the side, he's going to move to the left to flank, and that gives me an opportunity to feint after a solid parry to put him on the defensive and back him into a corner. Then... ... ..
Look, this game is great.
It brings a fresh new formula to combat in top-down action RPGs. At first it feels rather choppy as you flail about to get ahold of the controls, but it turns out to be a system that flows well and keeps you on your toes, regardless of who your enemy is (the AI is very good so far, and beating enemies on equal-footing is always a rewarding feeling).
Exanima is very difficult, has a fun learning curve (crazy thought, I know), and overall has pretty great gameplay. The atmosphere is relatively similar to the Dark Souls series in that the dark, gritty setting is coupled with a complete lack of hand-holding and the story is entirely dependant on how much you want to look into it.
The development of this game appears to be coming along very well, and the devs appear to be quite responsive to their community. I'm quite happy with the progress, which shows no signs of slowing, and I think it's worth every penny of $15- especially if you're already a fan of the genre.

I have to say, as someone who has always loved the isometric, DnD-esk RPG, Exanima does it well. It's been a long while since I last went for an early access game as the system is too often abused, but I am glad that I gave Exanima a shot. While it is clear that the game is still missing that last bit of spit-and-polish (it is an early access game after all!) the core mechanics, atmosphere, and overall player interaction clearly show that a lot of time when into the development process.
The mechanics are such a suprising delight and demonstrate an agreeable direction for the natural progression of the core mechanics introduced years ago and seen in many dungeon-crawl/baulder's gate type games. Adding a new depth of interaction and the corresponding introduction of a physics-based world will set this game apart from those it draws inspiration from and defintely prove satisfying for years to come. I still need to put many more hours in to fully grasp the interface, but just from a short test drive I can tell there's not only depth to the mechanics, but unlike many rougelikes or action RPG types that typically rely on mastery of a cheese-strat, this is appreciable, rewarding depth. There's just so much for the player to work with both in and out of combat.
The atmosphere was a pleasant suprise as well, as those degrees of consideration tend to get backburnered for a large portion of the development. Textures looked good both from far away and up close, character development was wonderfully, needlessly complex, and being dropped into the world with just a torch, wandering very confused, and getting immediately killed by the literal first enemy set the tone that the world of Exanima is not to be taken lightly.
All in all, at this point, I would certainly recommend trying this game out. The mechanics are deep, the world seems legit, and to top it off the developers seem to genuinely care about their product. For the last point alone I think that's worth some weight as steam is far too riddled with "developers" selling asset-flipped garbage for $15 a pop.
TL;DR
Recommend it. I am genuinely excited to see where this game (and developer) goes in the future.

Adventure or try your hand at merciless permadeath as the world's clumbsiest human!
In short, this game is an amazingly fun and quite challenging to master! (I haven't mastered it yet)
It is essentially an isometric combat game in lieu of diablo, but the combat is based entirely on physics. You have to carefully maneuver and swing your weapon about. Left clicking makes a swing, but you still need to amplify the swing by moving the mouse. Alternate attacks are possible, such as stabbing and overhead, but keep in mind that your entire body is a physics object, meaning I literally tripped over a corpse while fighting! It's nearly impossible to describe but truly, truly groundbreaking, and worth playing.

Imagine yourself on a precipice, staring out across a vast gulf of empty space. Far below you, as you teeter on the airy brink of a screaming descent, you are just barely able to make out a teeming, seething mass of color and light; tantalizing, gleaming with a banal allure, its glittering generality draws you in, calling to you with a melancholic siren's song, tempting you to take the step and plunge willingly into its garish embrace.
However, your lofty vantage point, and the laborious climb you undertook to ascend to this megalithic perch reminds you of why you are here; and like a lungful of biting cold mountain air, you see with painful clarity the hollow emptiness of the false promises of those plaintive voices, which to the weak and cowardly sound like the lyre and flute of a lonely goddess.
That is Exanima. That is the difficulty and reward for mastering a game which I can only describe as revolutionary, ambitious, and truly different from all the other RPG's, triple-A titles, formulaic franchises, and other money-making schemes of the big publishers and their ilk.
Many of you are skeptical of Steam Early Access games, and for good reason. Oftentimes investing in an unfinished product leaves that product in a perpetual cycle of development, where the developers lose their incentive for fixing anything or adding meaningful content as they rake in more and more money from people like you, the people who give their money and time in the hopes that the creators will actually use your "support" towards the common (and advertised) goal. Why would you financially support their endeavor otherwise?
These developers care. They care about making something which is not only totally different in the way the core gameplay operates, but is also helped along and advised by the players and community. They have made a game where every action, every duel, every combat and subtle move made and choice in positioning has weight (pun intended) and impact (pun intended there too) in your playthrough. Every object, every part of your character, your equipment, your weapons and armor, have a physical presence in the game world which no other game has ever come close to realizing. Yes, there is indeed a steep learning curve, but the reward for your time and patience in mastering the technique is truly satisfying, as is the knowledge that the money you paid for this game goes not only to further Exanima support and development, but also towards Bare Mettle's magnum opus Sui Generis.
If you have been searching for something different, something difficult, something rewarding and worth your time, you've found it. I don't write reviews much, but Exanima and Bare Mettle Entertainment have earned my praise a hundredfold. Please support this game and these developers, it's worth every penny.
Good luck. And good hunting.

This was a difficult "Yes" to give. As far as real time city builders go, Kingdoms and Castles has a lot going for it. It does a great job of a lot of genre defining traits such like: really enjoyable graphics as your city develops, balancing population growth with industry and employment, city planning and some logistics to the randomly placed resources.
So what is there, is very good. What makes me give this game a "meh 6/10" is what's not there.
There is no campaign, multiplayer and sandbox only. It will only take a few hours for a player (using no guides) to master the economy and see all there is to see. Town building uses a system similar to games like cities XL but with less depth: Build all of your residences within the active ranges of the supportive buildings to keep happiness high. Once you hit a point where you're no longer balancing growth with employment you'll have a population explosion and the city management aspect becomes trivial.
The combat, very lackluster. Waves of enemies come occasionally from different directions. Very slowly getting stronger.  While it's kind of neat to see an ogre bash through a castle wall, the whole experience is pretty bland with only one type of ground troop and two types of defense towers.
If you really like the city building genre, this game is worth a play through, but I don't know if it has enough content to warrant the price tag. Grab it on sale.
If the developers read these, adding in some goal based missions or a campaign of sorts would do wonders to extend the longevity of this game.

While the second game is obviously superior, there are a few things that the first does better.
- Everything from the shooting to the flying is faster and more responsive, if a bit unrealistic. For example, stunt jumps aren't necessarily affected by gravity, planes never stall, and helicopter propellor blades can touch almost anything without affecting control.
- The entire game can be taken at one's own pace, with side missions free to perform at the player's choosing.
- The world has one central theme, Caribbean jungle, as opposed to every type of biome crammed into one country. This makes the locations memorable by relying on clever geography and buidling placement, instead of the false illusion of a major change of global locale. Plus, it's just pretty to look at, most of the time.
That being said, the game isn't perfect. There are plenty of bugs to look out for, both fun and bad. I've gotten trapped inside garages simply by respawning. I've driven a motorcycle so fast that I crashed into a person's house and became stuck inside. All of those incidents required me to load a previous save. Then there are the police who never EVER shut up, and the idiotic AI that deems it fit to pilot a helicopter into the side of a mountain or skyscraper. There's a monster truck with hollow tires. There are also the occasional missing or misapplied textures.
Yet, on the other hand, I come back and find new bugs, or perhaps just oversights, every time I play. Rico is capable or rocket-jumping with the correct equipment, something I never thought I would see outside of FPS. He can kill himself with a heavy drop. Hell, once I took down a passing helicopter simply by requesting a vehicle at the right time. I've toyed around with the camera by grappling onto boats outside of the game's invisible ocean walls. It's even possible to do some sweet tricks by letting the cannon on a tank touch an immovable object. It's not often I see a big vehicle like that spinning and flipping that quickly.
All in all, it's a good sandbox game, but don't expect a lot of depth.

Get Just Cause 2 instead. It's basically the same game, except actually finished. This one only has inklings of ideas which were never developed, and simply has no polish whatsoever. For example, take the settlement takeover missions, which are a cool idea and which you'll probably be doing a lot. "Missions" might be too generous. There's basically only one (shoot enemies, destroy roadblock #1, shoot enemies, destroy roadblock #2, shoot enemies, destroy roadblock #3, rush to flag / kill a specific enemy - the only difference you can spot between them is that when taking over cities you don't have to destroy roablocks), which you will be doing over and over and over and over again. Do you at least get something cool for your troubles? Nope, just a new save point and a color of some pixels flipping on the map. Or take the combat, which you'll be doing a lot of. The game has only two levels of enemy threat. "Light drizzle" if they are using bullets, "instagib" if they're using explosives. For your own part, you'll have tiny, hard to see crosshairs (if you play at any real resolution)... or extremely intrusive autoaim which kicks in while you're manning vehicle weapons (which are another cool idea on their own) and which will actually very often prevent you from shooting what you want to shoot (say, the barricade rather than all the random soldiers all over the place). Or take the grappling hook, which is an amazingly fun tool in JC2, and which is an unreliable and unwieldy piece of crap in this game. The whole thing is just extremely rushed and upolished.
Again, just get JC2 instead. I can assure you, you will not miss out on anything by skipping JC1.

Lifeless planet is a somewhat linear exploration platformer game that focuses mainly on story and atmosphere. You play as an astronaut that took a long journey through space to a reach a planet that could be colonized by the human race. You, and the rest of your crew crash land on what was supposed to be a lush green planet with breathable oxygen. Instead, you arrive at a vast and lifeless wasteland. There is evidence that someone has been here before you (spooky..). The environments are big, and there are a lot of logs that are written by your character, and that you pick up as you progress through the game to further the story. The sound is quite good and really helps set the mood. The platforming bits are a little too easy, but get more fun when you activate the extended jetpack. Some very minor puzzles too. It took me around 3 hours to finish the game at a casual space. Not that high replayability, unless you want to find all of the secrets, and every log. It was quite alright. I would strongly suggest waiting for a sale if this game seems interesting to you, before purchasing it.

This may seem like a scything review, but bear in mind that it is overall positive.
Lifeless Planet is like a rather gripping story book made game, in a very engaging way.  I enjoyed the story quite well, visual clues and backstory presented in a way that "keeps you turning pages", as it were.  In the end, you feel you have little to no control over the events taking place, which fits into the storybook motif.
There are a few minor puzzles, but they make no sense whatsoever in the context of the story, or the puzzles themselves.   The achievements are poorly designed, with one achievement going only to cheaters.  That achievement is to "Beat the game without dying on your first playthrough".  That, can only be achieved through dumb luck or reading ahead which totally breaks the exploration of the story.   To give an idea, one of the other achievements was to get killed without knowing what killed you.  (Which actually happens a lot.  There's invisible death-walls that are there to say "No, you can't go that way.")
Lastly, if you're used to playing with a joystick, then the controls will make perfect sense.  The Keyboard controls are a bit nausiating and inconsistent.  A Joystick pretty much is the only way to play this one.
All this negativity aside, the game was quite enjoyable.  But does leave me with one unanswered question - "Why have I been carrying this rock for the last 3 chapters?"

At first I thought this would be - in absolutely best case - a decent remake. Now as I have played my way though half of the game and just completed Level 4 I have to say that buying this game (even only at -75%, sorry Nightdive) was absolutely one of my best buys this year.
This game brings back so much memories and is so fun to play. I thought like "what the hell, 97% positive reviews ... they can not be serious" before, but i pretty much like it too. This is one gold old FPS from "good old times" :)
One thing I was a bit confused about is that Level 1 is at some points DIFFERENT from the Level 1 on N64 (PAL Version). I only can compare it to N64 PAL version, not to the original PC Version.
This might also apply to some other Levels. I guess you originally were NOT able to get the Minigun in Level 2 (a few metres away from the end portal) because you could not destroy the "spikes" with a Tek-Arrow. In Level 3 it seemed like there have been some backpacks added, but some Tek Armors are missing. I played it more than 15 years ago for the last time, so maybe I remember something wrong^^
The games is apparently faster than before and I think this is really good.
Still each level untill now took about 45-60 minutes for me to complete it.
I liked the robots in N64 PAL version more than the humans in this version, because the robots colours were more different from the environment, while I have got sometimes problems to see enemie humans near some walls. Moreover the robots just disappeared when they were dead, while the humans sometimes still keep on moving some seconds and you can not be sure if they are really dead already.
The only pretty bad issue:
Your characters positioning is sometimes very frustrating. Back on N64 I could very good use the character arrow on the minimap and center it on some plattforms at areas requiring lots of jumping. The center of the arrow was the center of your character. NOW the tip of the arrow is the center of the your character. When you look down to where your feets are supposed to be and then go to the edge of a plattform, you will fall down (visually through the plattform) even if you see yourself still standing on the plattform.This feels and plays really different from the original. especially in Level 3 directly before the boss I messed up more jumps than ever before in all complete playthroughs of Turok.
This problem also occurs at some stairs in Level 3. If you a close to a stair and want strafe to the left or right, then you can not move. It feels like if there is a invisible wall.
When you turn around 180°, then you can understand both of these issues, as your view then is completely different from before. Then you can see, that you are leaving the plattform and you can see that you are still next to the stairs.
Something is pretty wrong with it to be honest.
And one more smaller issue... dodging the falling down rocks at some point in Level 2 really is a PAIN. If you dont look at the sky (where you can see them hanging^^) and are REALLY slowly and carefully, then you will get smashed. If you walk straight forward and hear the sound of them falling, they it is already too late and you will die.
Moreover I had wished that you (even though it also was not possible in the original game) can change the ammo of Bow and and Shotgun, so that you can choose on your own whether to use arrow or tek-arrow and regular shotgun ammo or explosive shotgung ammo. I pretty much never use all of my explosive shotgun ammo (dont wanna waste it^^), so I barely ever could collect any regular shotgun ammo.
But still this is really a great old-school FPS, which I absolutely can recommend, but - sorry again Nightdive studios - not for the full price of 20 bucks. I bought it at -75% and if I had knewn before how good and fun it is, i would have bought it before already at -50%.
At max. 10 Bucks you can not do anything wrong buying it, when you are a fan of old FPS games.
EDIT:
Now I have completely finished the game after about 8 hours. More or less 1 hour each level, but Level 8 took longer. I could not remember how big it is^^
Just to add: In one Level I had some technical problems which only could be fixed by restarting the game. I am not really sure if they really had an influence on the gameplay or if they just were some graphical bugs.

An interesting and entertaining MMORPG that is in early access.
While the game is still quite raw and is certainly unfinished, the current content and community make it worth the time to play. It is a seamless world (no zones or loading) with only 2 major towns (one is more like a large barebones city) with some settled farmlands, forests and plains in-between.
The crafting system is easy to work with (but every crafted item requires a recipe and ingredients which surprises some players.) Gather, refine and craft is the basis of the current crafting system with a handful of recipes available at the moment to introduce players to try their hand at making everything they might need.
The player-driven economy is still developing, so stuggling to buy a plot of land to own (or rent) has been a struggle for most, with some powerhouses claiming prime real estate.
PVE combat is lackluster with only a few weapon options and imprecise actions versus enemies, but it has the makings of a reasonable system which should develop over the next wee while.
A small number of quests exist in-game, with a set of tutorial quests that can help acclimitise new players into the basic flow of play as well as familiarising new players with key locations in the starting town.
There is currently NO PVP, but it is expected as the game develops.
The art style is stylised and could be considered cartoony by some, but I find it easy on the eyes.
While it may be considered as a sandbox, it isn't what I would call a true sandbox (do whatever you want wherever you want whenever you want).
Player housing is active in-game and works well enough, with the possibility of owning farmland for budding farmer-wannabes. Farming itself doesn't seem to be fully active though, so more exploration and research could be needed to understand how the system works.
The skill system is learning-by-doing, so chopping trees increases a lumberjacking skill giving access to a few spell-like abilities to help you survive against the passive chicken threat that is just waiting to explode! Skills also increase some stats (STR, DEX, END and more which in turn affect other composite stats.) Skill gain is a little faster than expected, but a recent patch should have reduced skill gain to a slower but managable level. In-game actions, skills and stats are part of the RPG aspect of progression and customisation (as well as min-max for those so inclined.)
There are no dungeons or dungeon-equivalents at the moment, but there are at least 2 planned with a possible 3rd under speculation. It has been said that some dungeons will be open world and others may be instanced, so we are waiting for more information in this regard.
How can you get in on this action? You can purchase the game on Steam or through the official
website if you want founder packs (currently only available on their website and not on steam.) Just another reminder, the game is in EARLY ACCESS and is not production-ready for mass consumption. Support the devs and join us in-game!
Will there be a wipe? Who knows, but there is fun to be had now!
TL;DR: Still a lil buggy, not as stable as I would like but hours of engagement with a supportive community.

Steampunk. Tower Defense. RTS. FPS. Co-op.
Did I just blow your mind?
This game is rough around the edges, (not super modern graphics, for instance, and the game is still in the process of being balances as of Nov 2010), but it's a LOT of fun.
You're defending a ramshackle rebel base from the bourgeouis imperialists, and you need power to do it. You collect power by shooting the bad people, or collecting gold (don't ask questions), and you use that power in several ways:
You can unlock/upgrade weapons for personal use, from machine guns to sniper rifles to mines, you can upgrade your character's health/speed/attributes, or very uniquely, you can enter a top-down RTS view and build/upgrade defensive structures like MG nests, fuel bombs, and supply depots.
I don't think you can exclusively play in either mode, so a wee bit of FPS and RTS knowledge is good, but even better you can play with up to 8 friends cooperatively, and it is quite a ride.
I'd recommend buying at ~5$.

I got about two thirds of the way through and gave up out of boredom. I YouTube'd the ending, out of curiosity, and am glad I didn't bother getting there myself. I'm a big fan of BS1 and 2 and I backed 5 on Kickstart. I'm glad that point and click adventures continue to get made and I've got my fingers crossed for a Beneath The Steel Sky 2, but I found Broken Sword 5 to be rather limp and flat. I can put up with some silly puzzles if the writing and humour are there, but they weren't. It was all pleasant enough, but I think the game played it very safe; there was no cheeky spark or wit. I found myelf playing the game with the sound off, while having one eye on whatever was on the TV in the background. That was when I realised I should play something else.
(Mild, but possibly helpful spoiler!) And acknowleding the infamously unfair goat puzzle from the first game with... an unfair goat puzzle? You establish that George isn't an action hero, and that the game isn't a third person action game, so why can he suddenly do certain very physical things mid game that he couldn't do before and with very poor signposting? The game breaks its logic to have a laugh about the logic breaking in the first game. (spoiler end)
Lovely backgrounds weren't enough to make me care about the story or its flat delivery. It's the first BS game where I didn't care much about any of the characters either. Currently the game is overpriced too. Might provide a pleasant and undemanding Sunday afternoon for someone who's bored and happens upon the game during a sale. Alternatively, try the superior BS1, 2 or a good book.

I will preface this review by saying that Broken Sword 2 was the first video game I ever played when I got my first PC about 17 years ago. It left a huge imprint on my gamer psyche and made me an avid fan of point and click adventures. After finishing The Smoking Mirror, I went to the original installment and my mind was blown - it was even better. The old games didn't have the best graphics in the modern sense, but their world felt rich, alive and intricate. Every character felt real, tangible and memorable. I never felt as though I was only playing a video game - it felt like an entire new world, with its own characters, stakeholders and conspiracies. Every location was a treat and seemed alive and genuine.
Sadly, not many of these things can be said for The Serpent's Curse. The game attempts to cater to the original fanbase by doing a lot of fan service, such as reintroducing certain characters and puzzles from the previous games, but it fails miserably at evoking the feelings of The Shadow of the Templars and The Smoking Mirror. The few locations that are introduced feel bland, static, unalive and uninteresting. The characters are even more boring and lifeless. The game attempts to buy cheap points by taking us to familiar locations such an art gallery in Paris and an old mansion in Spain, and this particular manipulation is obvious from the very beginning. The whole world of BS 5 feels static and fake. Sure the graphics are nice, but that's not enough to offset the constant feeling of emptiness and as though the game was rushed in order to maximize its profit margin. The ending is particularly bland and disappointing, and it's hard to imagine that such poor writing actually made it into the game.
Whether I recommend playing The Serpent's Curse or not depends on what you're looking for. If you want to relive the experience and memories of the old games, give this one a wide berth. If you're simply looking for a somewhat decent pont and click adventure, it might be worth a playthrough... but keep your expectations in check.

Still - it has beautiful backgrounds and it's entertaining enough. Not my favourite Broken Sword game, though (that would be either BS1 or BS2), but bettrer than its predecessors 3 and 4.

Finally a good game in the series and a great way to end this mediocre marathon.
After 2 failed attempts to make a 3D game BS series finally does it by mixing it with 2D. Beautiful 3D models with 2D and just as beautiful background, no pixelated images and a tasteful color palette... Graphics are simply superb.
As for the gameplay, they went back to P&C. The game has almost the same gameplay as the first two. They polished some rough edges of course (but completely ignored making a double-click function to make the characters move faster). They changed the second lead character Nİco's voice yet again, thankfully not for the worse,  and I'm starting think they are doing this on purpose seeing as no voice was used a second time but I'm missing the point of it entirely. Anyway, puzzles are a delight for the most part. There are still overcomplicated unimportant puzzles like every adventure game ever but most of them are just as they should be especially the second half of the game(Yes there are two main parts).
Story is also the best in the series imo. I love christian mythology (no I'm not a follower of the religion) and this is one of the best ones I've seen. The symbolisms, the background, the puzzles... They really connect and you can see they really put effort in it. But the other guys in the story department clearly didn't do as much. Not surprising twists are not surprising, bad guys are cliche at best and ending is disappointing (
). All in all it's a fun story.
To sum up: I you liked the previous ones you ARE going to love this one. If you didn't like them or didn't play them it's still a good game worthy of your time.

I'm in love with the concept of Bloodlines and family traits for a generation-spanning RPG, but the appeal of that is killed by the fact that the game is a strategy RPG. Additionally, I imagined handsome heroes growing up from adolescents who are learning their craft to young adults honing it, to mature adults achieving their legacy, to elders securing and nurturing it, but the art is so stylized that the humans look monstrously mishapen. . .  I'm not wondering what my hero's kids will look like because it will just be some flavor of ugly.
Unfortunately, Massive Chalice's ideas had some great traits, but they were bread with some ideas with bad traits, the resulting offspring has suffered.

I bought this game and initially loved it.  On the surface it has a lot going on and seems like tons of fun.  Sadly, it only takes a few hours to realize how shallow the gameplay really is.  The breeding, training, and research all seem like good ideas but I can't really immerse in it too far after discovering that the only classes worth using are Hunters and Hunter-derivatives.
The meat of my complaint: they have virtually the same starting health and damage as the other two primary classes, can stealth their way across the map, and eliminate enemies from range with no limit to the number of attacks.  I'm sure the other two classes could be good with a lot of work and research, but why bother?  They fill no roll.  You can literally start breeding nothing but Hunters right out of the gate with zero regard for traits and stats and win every single fight hands down.

It really feels like a near miss.  The components are there for a solid game, but the core of it - the fighting - is horribly broken by design.  The worst part is Double Fine seems to be satisfied.  Don't expect any DLC's or patches adding content or changing mechanics.  This thing is done, and it's just not where it should be.

Exanima is one of the few current games that has piqued my interest, and consequently I've put in many hours. There are a few things to take into account with this game. The combat and controls have an extremely high learning curve that surpasses many games. It allows for high precision and control over the arc of your swing, granted you have a steady hand and can anticipate the movements of enemies. This point should not be discounted; the skill cap potential for this game is extremely high.
As for the general atmosphere, the game features a low fantasy dungeon crawler setting. There are also numerous puzzle elements that have clever solutions. The graphics are high quality, and the game features an engine which was made purely from scratch. The AI patterns are quite sophisticated, and against unskilled players will feel ruthless.
Footwork is important in this game, and understanding how the WASD keys augment your damage by adding force to a swing is integral. The overhead and thrusting motions are fantastic and there are multiple weapon classes with different weight and swing speeds. The different weapon types feel extremely responsive once you are familiar with the timing.
The arena mode is another game type which is extremely addictive. I recommend playing the arena mode first to aid in developing your combat skills.
When reading these reviews take into account the hours played by the reviewers. This game is not one that can be properly assessed unless you've developed your familiarity with the combat, and can master the controls. Otherwise you're listening to frustrated players who want to blame the game rather than admitting they aren't very good.
The developers are hard at work on Exanima but are currently limited by a small staff. However, it's clear when reading the forums and seeing the responses that they are very invested in this project and are extremely perfectionist in their work. The game is well worth the current price, even if it is only 5/14 levels completed.
Takeways:
- Incredibly difficult; not for the fainthearted
- High skill cap
- Wonderful art style
- Unfinished, but continuous updates

Simply a great, unique and fun yet challenging game.
Ever wondered what would happen if we had a ragdoll fighting game? Well, here it is!
Exanima is a heavily physics-based game where everything in your screen counts. Never liked how sword games have a crappy "hitbox" mechanic? that's no problem here, your weapons are literally what do the damage, not just programmed and scipted "press m1 to attack", well, technically it is, but not as other games.. to attack, you hold the mouse and swing it in the direction you want to attack, for example, you wanna do a left to right swing, you click on the left side of your character, hold it down while sliding it to the right and if you're lucky enough, your sword did some serious damage.
Talking about that, damage is all about momentum. weak and slow attacks will most likely just poke enemies while a heavy wide attack with a greatsword could 1-hit an enemy.
Besides it's awesome combat, the game has dark and scary yet great exploration. You can interact with most props laying around (unless it's just too big for your character), and as useless as it may see, when it comes to puzzles.. oh boy, they're just great.
Only problem might be the perma death system it comes with.. if you die, its over. Thankfully for new players, in options there is a checkpoint option to make it more forgiving. (it'll save after each floor)
The game's updates are a bit slow, I'd say they might take up to 4 months if we're unlucky, however, quantity doesn't equal quality.
I rate it 8.5/10, still a few silly glitches and animations that need to be worked with, but nothing gamebreaking so far... I'm looking at you, weapon stuck in wall bug..

This game had me for about three hours.
The rest of the time I spent in a sort of trance, wherein I wasn't really enjoying myself but I couldn't quite put it down, hoping I'd find some spark that would reignite my enjoyment of this title.
The strong point of this game is the period setting of 'Atlantic' City, replete with boardwalks, hooch smugglers, strongarm mobsters and bad accents.  A small crew (starting with 3, capping out at 6) operates around a particular segment of the city, working their way into local businesses, strangling the cash flow and occasionally shooting up other mobsters.
The city management element of the game is a fairly simple juggle of three resources (beer, liquor, firearms), two types of money (dirty and clean) and police attention (gained by doing more of the things that get you the aforementioned items).  While I enjoyed seeing the city turn through its day-night cycle, the interaction was shallow and repetitive.  The best means of expansion across the urban setting is to reveal all local businesses via informants (who can be asked, forced or paid to do so), set up a supply chain of materials (a brewery to make beer, for instance, and a bar to consume it) and wait for the money to trickle in.
And wait.
And wait some more...
In the interim, you can harass local businesses for immediate rewards, but these come with diminished income options and lots of police attention - which is the one way to attain a Game Loss state.  If the police meter tops out, the investigators come a-knockin'.  They can be paid off (the fee doubles each time), you can throw another business under the bus (worsening relations with all goods providers), call in a favor from a bribed official (if one was buttered-up prior) or you can engage in a single combat encounter to try and destroy the evidence.  Fail to provide one of these, and the game ends.
But the waiting gets silly.  There is a fine point where your income and expenses are evenly matched and you're racing the margin curve to watch your influence spread across the town... But once you have it all, there's nothing to do with it.  Just watch the money numbers go higher as your Hotels and Casinos roll in totally legit *cough* moneys into your grubby coffers.
But wait! The game features a turn-based combat mechanic with your squadmates! (whom you pay to retain every morning in-game).  There is a decent amount of attention to the environments, and your fragile mobsters will have to make good use of cover to avoid gut-shredding volleys of lead from your opposition.
The interface is a mixed bag; on one hand, if you set a travel path for your character to take, the game helpfully counts out the steps (in Movement Points), tells you when an intersecting line of sight for an opponent comes up and displays available abilities cleanly; But then the camera obscures critical cover or registers a movement point for a character on the WRONG FLOOR and sends a goon running out into the open, making for a flight of stairs he won't reach for three turns!
The gunplay is vicious, as enemies and allies both have shallow HP pools and guns do what guns do best.  There are also knives, brass knuckles and baseball bats, but it takes a truly hardy character to withstand being shot to death by four opponents before their next turn.
It's disappointing that a game with good intentions for its environments does so little to help you customize or get to know your team.  There is a levelling mechanic (but in the campaign the level-ups are event-locked to missions, not combat encounters) wherein every level allows for a team member to grab a new perk.  These range from increasing core stats to raising critical chances and giving new abilities.  Of course, seeing as your henchmen never get stronger on their own, a single combat mistake can send your veteran to jail or the morgue.  Oh, there are also persistent injuries, wherein your character might lose half of their stamina bar or move at 1/3 normal rate.  No punches pulled here, folks.
While you can purchase new weapons in the game and assign one to any given character, there is no cosmetic change on the models and the weapons lack flavor within their subclass; By this I mean that while I greatly appreciate 'the revolver' actually being two separate pistols, able to retalliate at the first shot fired and spray lead in a cone as a special attack (a great touch of flavor!), any one revolver behaves like any other, be it a common or a unique weapon.
And as many reviews have pointed out, the game simply gets boring.  There is little incentive to advance within the story, except to discover how the various buildings you can set up in the city can synergize - or how snipey a Sniper can become, given enough accuracy and critical perks.
But this game simply fails to inspire.  It looks nice, but it's far more shallow than one would hope.
While it's worth a look at a discount or a bundle, I only managed to enjoy about 5 hours of its mechanics (not counting the plodding tutorial) and the rest was spent holding my breath for more.  Eventually my lungs collapsed and I died.  But then I got better and regretted the time spent not breathing.
