Long, long ago, i played this game once. There was a clan-server, on which three of its members lived happily...
But then I came onto the server...
Even though they already played for like ten minutes, i quickly went first place. Something they had a hard time to handle.
At one point, i could hear one of them complaining over voice chat: "He´s always attacking me with grenades"
Bad attempt, considering i cant remember this game having friendly fire. I wasnt attacking him, but the enemys around him.
Later, i could enjoy the sight of them throwing explosives at me, doing no damage whatsoever.
Their rage became undeniable, when we reached the "Mine"-Map. If a player dies in this game, he "respawns" in form of a crystal. The other players must destroy this crystal in order to bring the dead teammate back.
When i died, they ignored my crystal... For several minutes... It appears they tried to get rid of me that way, hoping that i´d quit, since they apparently had no kicking-power... But i didnt.
But thanks to divine justice, their plan was condemned to fail. You see, when a players crystal isnt destroyed fast enough, a enemy NPC will pick them up. These NPCs then stop attacking and run around on the map, on hardcoded routes.
On the Mine-Map, this route is bugged. Sooner or later, the NPC will jump down a hole and land in a lava-pit, thus killing himself and destroying the crystal.
Thus i came back to live and ruined the clan-members game once again with my skill.
Finally, the time had come for the final battle. Time for us four to face Abaddon. One by one they fell like unskilled scrubs, until only i was left.
Unlike them, i wasnt a childish little ♥♥♥♥♥ and would have brought them back a.s.a.p but divine justice struck again:
In the final battle against Abaddon, there is no revival. Once a player dies, he stays dead.
Thus the three little scrubs had no chance but to spectate me being better than them. Alone, this battle used up alot of time, since i had to fight the boss while dealing with all the mobs.
But i wasnt giving up, i kept fighting and Abaddons health kept going down. After about ten minutes of watching me, hoping that i´d fail, the first clan-♥♥♥♥♥ couldnt take it anymore and left the server. For a brief second his voice-chat symbol showed up, he was telling his teammates something. Surely it was something like "Guys just leave, he´ll die soon anyway".
The second followed quickly after that, while the third one stayed for another five minutes, desperately trying to find an explenation that could explain why he and his friends didnt make it longer than five minutes, while i just kept fighting, surviving everything Abaddon threw at me.
Finally, he also left, bailing out in shame probably thinking i would die soon. But i didnt. Yet another ten minutes later, i dealt the final blow to Abaddon, beating the boss and winning the game.
When i bought this game it was like what? 10€? Yeah, money well spent!

My brief summary for this game would be that it is a hugely overpriced missed opportunity.
In theory it sounds great. Building up your own gang and taking over the city. All with turn-based combat similar to X-Com. I desperately wanted to like this game as it ticks all of the strategy boxes that I like. Unfortunately, the disappointment began immediately upon release as the price was ridiculously high. I have finally got a steam code for a reasonable price and picked up the DLC cheap on here so I can actually play it for myself.
At first, it seemed quite interesting. A small tutorial area guides you through the basic concepts, including taking over businesses, building up your gang, and combat. Once this has been achieved, the story takes you into your first full area where you are let loose on your own. You have an overall objective that will advance the story but are free to investigate the rest of the area at will. Unfortunately, this is where the limited appeal of the game starts to become apparent. Although there seems to be plenty to do, none of it is particularly interesting. You send a gang member off on a job and then get a text report back as to whether they succeeded or not. Occasionally, a job will result in combat and this is the only bit where the game actually shines. The turn-based combat is excellent and makes good use of strategic cover. If the game was purely this (and cost a lot less) I would have no hesitation in recommending it.
This seems to have been envisaged as a combination of Tropico and X-Com, which is an admirable intention as they are both excellent series. Unfortunately, it pales next to both of them. I would strongly recommend taking the money you were thinking of spending on this and buying Tropico 4 and/or X-Com: Enemy Unknown as they are both infinitely more enjoyable.

I backed this in its early crowdfunding stages, and finally circled around to it now a long way after launch. It ended up being pretty much what I wanted out of it - an expansive 2D sandbox with a straightforward adventure storyline leading you through the world and encouraging you to expand your crafting and equipment opportunities. I had a fun time with it overall, exploring the world and finding new and better resources to build better tools and weapons. Once I'd finished the main quest and several of the pre-written side quests, though, I did kind of feel like I'd had my fill.
There are "procedural" quests and quest lines given by NPCs living in random settlements, but they're essentially pre-written quest lines with a few fill-in-the-blanks substitutions and precisions to make the quest fit into the local geography; they don't really stay compelling after running them a few times, and they very quickly cease to be surprising. And for all that there were supposed to be procedural monsters, I felt like I was encountering a lot of hand-crafted creatures repeated across multiple planets.
There's also a farming system that's pretty fun, there are a wide variety of supplementary systems like fossils and mech missions and armour dyes and what have you, and there's a whole space-station construction element along with colonization and tenants that I only really dipped into. There's a lot to do, but the more intricate side systems require a lot of grinding - grinding for mech parts and blueprints, grinding for unique racial or biome furniture, and so on - so that put me off really diving deep into these side systems.
Still - even if it didn't blow me away quite the way I had hoped, I had a good time overall, got as much as I felt I needed to out of the game, and I'd heartily recommend it to people looking for a fun little interstellar sandbox to pass the time.
Note that it didn't take me 80+ hours to finish the main story - I played a bit in beta and also had a save on another laptop, but since there are no cloud saves I ended up restarting rather than digging up my old laptop. I think it took me around 50 hours from scratch to finish the story and several of the major side missions as well as get nice sets of top-tier gear, play with the extra side systems, and fully upgrade my ship.

You begin by dropping on-planet, setting up energy collectors and ore mines, and trying to stay one step ahead of the goo by running relay lines (think high-voltage lines) to power the various weapon systems you'll need to fight it. Cannons, mortars, sprayers, and other tools are at your disposal. Interestingly, you are able to reposition them as the situation on the ground changes. From there, it is a systematic war of resources and logistics to reach the Emitters that produce the Creeper/Goo. You then build a nullifier which charges up and fires a high-powered beam into the emitter, destroying it.
I'll be the first to admit I haven't made it far yet. Two hours in, and several missions in the story mode. I love every useful goodie I find on planets and put to use as I go. I'm sure there are many others out there to find. Icing on the cake to me. It's fun without being overly complex, and very easy to get caught up in the deadly "just one more turn" syndrome.
For two bucks, hours of fun. Grab it and give it a try...if you dare! *Muahahahah!*

Review written after 10 hours of play.  Summary, well executed, fun and satisfying game but turn the volume down.
Interesting RTS that doesn't follow the usual formula.  You are fighting against a rising liquid tide and have to plug your defenses then expand outward.  Has a simple yet effective art style that conveys all the information you need.  Playstyle is reminiscent of tower defense but more immediate, at the same time levels can often feel like a puzzle.  This combination means finishing a level is usually very satisfying.  The game does an excellent job of gradually introducing the mechanics and units and the levels where they are introduced do a good job of teaching you how to use them effectively without holding your hand.  The creep behaves intuitively leading to emergent strategies that the game never outright tells you about but make perfect sense, particularly as regards the terraforiming.  You can make walls and trenches to control the flow of the creep, or push back an area then build walls around it to expand into a large pool.  So far the levels have been varied enough that each new level has made me think 'ah interesting, how am I going to deal with this?'
About the only negative I've found is that the sound design.  Weapon sound effects can be very repetitive, especially when you are in the late stages of a level and have many mortars and strafers firing at once.  Also the music while by no means bad is very penetrating and booming and combined with the sound effects can be extremely irritating for other people in the house who aren't playing the game.   Easily sorted by turning the volume down and the games other qualities make this a relatively minor grumble.

tl;dr - forget this, go buy Game Dev Tycoon :-)
long version:
This game isn't inherently bad. It just focuses on wrong things.
It's nice to have 40+ workers after an hour or two, it's nice to rebuild your office every few minutes and enhance it with flowers and statues... But is this what game development is about? I don't think so...
Do you want to know all your developers by name? Well, they just become numbers in few minutes.
Do you want to create fantasy games? Sci-fi? History? Sorry, not here.
Do you want to develop sequels, DLCs, expansions? MMO or MOBA maybe? Nothing like this here.
After few attempts, game development shrinks to looking at numbers and bars - genre does not matter, people don't matter,  even game name does not matter, since the randomly generated one is fine and you wanna go for quantity anyway.
Campaign is done for in 3 hours (and doesn't tell you it's over, just goes on without any endgame), and "challenge" game is just a sandbox game with more achievements.
I guess it just makes a good EA GAMES simulator - horde of anonymous workers, developing games which are all the same, dubious work, big profits, but almost no fun.
If you want to really play game developer, go buy Game Dev Tycoon instead, or buy this in sale, the dollar or two of price just may be ok for few hours of gameplay.

I'm a huge fan of the Broken Sword series.  George and Nico are second only to Guybrush and Elaine.  I tried not to mind too much when the series shifted to 3D and some action for the third and fourth installments because Revolution were clearly handling the games with care and love for the genre.  Still, I was thrilled when it became clear on Kickstarter that the fifth game would be 2D and action-free.
The artwork in the game is about the best of this style that I have ever seen in a game.  Scenes are beautiful and detailed (and that really helps when you have to notice a slightly pink spot on a sort of orange spot).  I had to resist taking screenshots because they would all be spoilers.
The game presents you with pretty standard environment, inventory, and dialog puzzles, but they all work pretty sensibly, even the decrypting puzzles late in the game.  I never got stuck due to some ridiculously obtuse puzzle structure.
The worst I can say about the game is that there are so many spots to interact with, so many comments to hear (although still less than in a typical Daedalic game, by comparison) that you can progress pretty slowly and it's possible to get bored.  Still, the story is well written with a typical Indiana Jones plus reluctant hero approach as in the other Broken Sword games.  I did find it to be slightly less boring than the fourth game (which is finally on Steam, by the way).  The religious aspect of the story focuses on a conspiracy-flavored long line of Gnostics protecting an artifact that could upset the balance of Jehovah and Lucifer, so you kind of know the story will take you around Europe and eventually to the Middle East.
So if you like the very best that standard point-and-click gameplay can offer, reasonable puzzles, and the best 2D artwork anywhere, this game is a must-play. Depending on your ability and your choice of pace, it's about a 12 hour game at least, possibly as much as 14 hours, longer than that other crowd-funded classic adventure game two-part installment that still isn't finished (ahem-cough-Broken-Age-cough).

Broken Sword 5 is an awesome adventure game and hails the return of one of the best game franchises in adventure game history. The graphics are awesome, even if some of the animations are a little stiff and awkward. The voice acting for the most part is superb with standout performances from george and nico. The story is amazing and is right up there with broken sword 1 and 2. Now for some basic pros and cons.
PROS
1. voice acting
2. overall story is very well done that kept me engaged the whole way. I always loved the Indiana Jones aspects of the broken sword series and this game is no exception. its full of intrigue and suspense.
3. puzzles for the most part are well thought out and not too hard, but as in any adventure game there are some hard ones and some solutions that are basically just trial and error. there is a built in hint system that can help you, im pretty proud I ony had to use it on two puzzles. overall I give the puzzle difficulty of it a 6/10 in the fact that for the most part they will challenge you but not frustrate you.
4. The hand drawn backgrounds all look fantastic, and I mean FANTASTIC.
5. The length of the game is also really good, I beat the the game in about 12.5 hrs, which I think is the perfect length for a game.
CONS
1. Animations are a little wonkie and im not a huge fan of the 3d models they used for the characters, I wish they were hand drawn like the backgrounds
2. Humor and jokes while at times are truly funny, I believe this game misses on the jokes more than they hit. not a huge deal but I wanted to point it out.
3. While the cutscenes still look good, they are no where the level they were in broken sword 1 and 2.
4. the game for the most part ran smoothly but did crash on me twice, the good part though is it does auto save frequently, so was not a huge issue.
5. While I love the fan service and cameos I thought they had too many cameos and returning characters, and one to many goat puzzles lol.
CLOSING COMMENTS
This game is great I got it on sale and I cant reccomend it enough to anybody, especially if you played the other games in the series and enjoyed them, or if your an adventjure game fan in general. Although you should first play broken sword 1 and 2 bc even though this is the 5th game in the series, im pretty sure it follows the events of broken sword 2. they are also on sale right now. Broken Sword 5 is a great entry into the series, if I had to rank my fav broken sword games in order it would go
1. broken sword 1
2. broken sword 5
3. broken sword 2
4. broken sword 3
5. broken sword 4

Being the first game in the Just Cause series, you shouldn't expect it to be perfect, because it's not. But for all it's flaws, it's glorious because of how massive in scope and epicness it is.
Something like ~365 sq miles, the world is your playground, and not because of the sidequests, which are many yet repetitive; i.e; help the guerillas take over political territory, and help the Rioja family expand and defeat the other competing/mafia type family. The side quests are many and they do have their advantages when advancing through the game for opening safe houses and extra weapons, but are otherwise unnecessary.
No, the world is your playground because of how ridiculous it is. Police everywhere, villages are spread out, mountains, mountains, and mountains are all over with hills, rivers, cliffs, etc. The only thing that kept the diverse landscape vague was the color, which is pretty much all green. There's grass everywhere, you can't go anywhere without seeing grass unless you drive a boat out to sea.
A game released in 2006, this could have easily been on all next gen systems, but you can tell Avalanche had focused with the Xbox and PC while also trying to transition to 360, as the models are pretty good, but the textures are certainly at the end of the Xbox and PS2 era.
As for travel, you get planes, helicopters, tanks, cars, trucks, etc. There's an infinite amount of vehicles at your disposal. Again, you'll have to advance the sidequests to unlock some of the cool ones, but completely unnecessary.
The plot is okay. It's nothing special, run and gun doing espionage esq type missions, sort of like James Bond espionage, but less stealthy. You are Rico and are sent by the Agency to help rid the country island of San Esperito of its corrupt El Presidente and followers. It's fun, but rather short, you can probably beat it in 4 or 5 hours, depending on the difficulty and amount of time you spend in between missions.

As someone who helped with the beta, I received this product for free.  If you had asked me for a review upon release, I would have given this a thumbs down.  Probably a 2/5 stars.  This is my first Open Canvas product, so everything has been completely new for me.
Things have turned around, and I'm really liking their changes.  The main fix is that my XP PEN STAR 05 now works when I switch to a different tab and then back to the program.  It was a serious issue OC has had since its beta, but I recently decided to give it another chance today and LOVED it.  I'd give it a good 4/5 stars now, and still haven't uncovered all of its little features.
Pros:
Advanced user interface mixed with simpler user interface.
Now works better with (some) non-Wacom tablets.
Sorted brushes
Variety of default brushes
Grids
Variety of docking/layout setups premade into the program to choose from.
Cons:
The advanced parts of the program can be rather confusing.
A few little quirks in the program are different or strange compared to other drawing tools (SAI, Firealpaca, Krita, etc.)
No button to easily move around the canvas that I've found.
No reset to fit the whole canvas to the available screen size.
Docking doesn't really seem to dock, more of just awkwardly places the windows where you want them.
I'm still working with the program to learn every little thing it has to offer and now that I can easily use my tablet, I'm very happy with it and looking forward to using it more often for drawing.

Nice detective kinetic novel for one or two afternoons I guess (yeah, there are actually no choices at all) and one that is completely FREE at that. It's full of overused tropes and it doesn't take itself seriously at times but I certainly wouldn't call it bad either as it leaves some food for the thought in the end, so it's probably somewhere in between.
So yeah - it was enjoyable yet also flawed experience for me. Women characters here are mostly likeable and detailed but all man except captain and protagonist father would benefited from more developement. The pacing was actually pretty good but the mystery was maybe way too easy for me as I guessed the culprit and how everything happend right after the murder happened. Which is good and bad at the same time but thankfully the rest of the story was interesting to follow at least. But the main flaws were probably both main characters - detective Butler and main character (Golder's son) unfortunately.
While the first one felt like self-entitled and overconfident bragger that would be thrown out of the ship right away after someone noticed he took and kept what he shouldn't have (noone really questioned that, really?) and it was really unnatural and borderline stupid how everyone trusted him completely, told him everything and let him go everywhere. The second one was mostly fine but then he went way too emotional suddenly or made some stupid or would be wise speeches or illogical decisions at times that I almost had to facepalm. I also expected some kind of clever twist regarding existence of both of them in the end but it didn't happened, sadly. And I certainly didn't like how almost noone make anything of the murder after that scene happened, even joking here and there while they should be scared instead.
On the other hand I have to say I like MC's backstory scene, Cobalt couple part and the actual epilogue was wrapped up nicely. The music was good mostly and character sprites were great but have to say I didn't like some choice of soundtrack at some places (disco for the dining room for example) and hand-drawn backgrounds would probably suited this game a lot better even though I didn't mind that much towards the end.
Some other cons:
- The prologue is really badly written, the logic is flawed there and it almost made me ditch the game.
- Maps were good but it would be good if it actually served some purpose other than showing the area.
- There are some inconsistencies regarding time, it says 1:30 at one place and 1:55 elsewhere for example.
I would also appreciated it more if players was given a choice to name the culprit by theirselves in the end - based solely on their own undestranding of the case - which would lead to interesting different conclusions and implications to be intepreted by player only, not necessarily showing which one was good.
All-in-all, the game would certainly benefited from yet another author's pass to fix all the odd texts. But I also wouldn't say this was bad experience. When looking back I had actually fun following the story and constant discovering of new clues kept my attention all the time. I actually look forward to Episode 2 to see some improvement. Journal was really well done for example. So give it a try, maybe, you may enjoy it - just don't expect anything stellar.

I came to Omerta after I completed X Com and wanted another turn based strategy game to try. This game is a big disappointment for those that want to get into the genre and doesn't even come close to X Com on a gameplay perspective.
While the concept of having Gangstas might be fun to begin with, it is hard to overlook some flaws.
Its extremely hard to find pros for this game when compared to a more refined product such a X Com. My biggest gripes with Omerta are:
- City management becomes repetitive. After a few hours, you will always follow the exact same process of trying to weed out other gangs using the exact same methods.
- You are only limited to a maximum of 4 party members for each mission despite the fact you can have a roster of 20+.  Its a big waste of potential as a lot of the gangsters you will never use as they are inferior. You are not encouraged to experiement as some weapons/gangstas are always superior than others.
-Stupid AI. Even on Hard difficulty, the AI rarely work together to bring your ganstas down e.g they rarely focus fire. The toughness usually comes from AI having superior numbers (vs your 4 gangstas) rather than actually being smart
- Bad Voice Acting. Its really sub par for a $40 game.
- Price. In no way is this worth $40. It may be worth a shot when it is discounted to $10 but at full price it is a massive rip off.

SolForge is the only online CCG I have seen that makes good use of the online medium: most online CCGs could just as easily be done in cards, and most of them fall short of MtG; leaving me little reason to play them. SolForge, however, uses a leveling mechanism that could not be done in a paper CCG; and exploring the leveling system and the need to think not only what you want to play now; but also what you want leveled for later in the game, makes SolForge the one online CCG I am likely to keep playing.

I will start by saying that stoneblade has produced a card game with an innovative and very interesting core mechanic. However I have exhausted a considerable amount of time into the game and have come to the conclusion that RNG 'feels' like it plays too large a hand in the game.
Without going into specifics becuase people who are reading this may not have experienced the Solforge leveling system, I will say that more often than not you will lose matches and 'Feel' like you had absolutly no power. And unlike magic wereby matches you lose due to RNG are lost in the first few draws due to mana, Solforge matches are lost turn 20-30 around 10+ mintues into a match.
Basically an average game of solforge has you play a card you will need leveled later and then you cross your fingers in the hope that you draw that card when you need it. But more often than not you will never see that card again and if you do see it there may be no benefit in playing it.
In conclusion I don't mind losing when the game is close but the majoritiy of time you will lose because the level 1 creatures you draw will NEVER beat those level 3's your opponent keeps playing.

The first Broken Sword and its first sequel remain among my favourite point-and-click adventure games. (Remember to check the Director's Cut versions of those games!) #3 and #4 changed the art style (to 3D) and lost some of the magic in the process, although those aren't bad games either. After that, it took a long, long time for the fifth game (back to gorgeous 2D) to come out. Based on the middling reviews, I wasn't expecting much. Luckily I was pleasantly surprised.
The new 2D art is beautiful. More importantly, the opening scenes in Paris re-capture the atmosphere of the early games. The characters - George and Nico et al - remain the same, love'em or hate'em.
The game feels stuck in the past. That is not ENTIRELY a bad thing. However, it means that the interface is clunky; inventory is messy; puzzles can be obtuse; there's even a goat puzzle involved (!). Luckily there's a VERY useful hint system incorporated. Whenever I got stuck (every 30 minutes or so), all I had to do was to click the "hint" button.
If you don't like old-school adventure games, this game is probably not for you. If you have no prior experience with the series, many of the inside references and jokes will be lost on you. And you should really start with the first game. That one's a better game. But this one FEELS right, like an authentic Broken Sword game - even down to replicating the flaws and quirks of the original. For nostalgic fans of the series, especially of the first two games, this one is a worthy sequel.
Rating: 8/10

As a CCG, SolForge is one of the most solidly constructed games I've played in years. It takes full advantage of the fact that it exists in virtual space to explore mechanics that would be difficult or even impossible in real space. Also, instead of banning or restricting cards, if a card becomes unbalanced in play, they won't hesistate to update it to make it more functional. However, they don't go overboard changing cards all the time, either.
Like all the best games, it is fairly easy to learn, but hard to master. The basic concept is simple. You draw a hand of 5 cards, of which you can play two. There are spells and creatures. Creatures occupy one of 5 lanes. When you play a card, it levels up into another version of itself, usually a better version. How much better varies from card to card. Each turn you battle, any creature that doesn't have summoning sickness attacks the creature across from it, and if there is nothing across from it, it deals damage to the opposing player. At the end of your turn, you discard your entire hand, and draw 5 new cards. After four turns, you level up, meaning you reshuffle all your cards back into your deck, except now some of those cards are higher level. And this repeats, with your deck getting stronger as the game goes on.  There are four factions, and each of them plays differently. Decks are 30 cards, and can be made of one or two factions.
From that simple structure, there is a lot of depth in the game. This game was designed by Stoneblade Entertainment, the same company that created the Ascencion deckbuilding game, with the help of Richard Garfield (creator of Magic: The Gathering). Most of them are Magic protour veterans as well. The plan, for now, seems to be to release one major set and one minor update each year. There are timed and untimed matches, as well as tournaments and drafting. The game is built to be free to play, although it is still in beta, so many things like a single-player campaign and trading cards between players are not in yet, but the game is updated fairly regularly. I definitely recommend it to anyone who is keen on strategy games or CCGs, and the free to play nature makes it easy to try out.

While the central mechanics are interesting, they feel poorly put together. Each turn is basically a coin toss as to whether or not you will be able to do anything good. While strategic play can influence this to a point, the fact that you discard what's left of your hand and draw a brand new one each turn makes planning ahead difficult, not to mention that going several turns drawing level-1 cards which no longer have any impact once the stronger level-2 and level-3 cards appear is incredibly common and will often lead to losing any advantage you may have had, if not to losing the game outright.
Aside from the fact that luck is far too great an element in this game, the balancing is an issue as well. Having spend 150 hours of in-game time on this game, I managed to acquire a grand total of 3 legendary cards and there were plenty of heroic cards I hadn't even seen at that point. At this point, I feel like I should mention that not only are the interesting effects mostly limited to legendary and heroic cards and many (if not most) deck archetypes are completely based around them, but in the few cases where they can be compared to the less rare cards they are almost always better. Who'd rather have a nexus core than a thundersaur? Who could make a removal deck without dreadbolt, a lifegain deck without Oros/Arboris or a metamind deck without Drix? Why is Chrogias better than scrapforge titan, echowisp better than ether hounds, hinterland watchman better than cypien infiltrator, etc?
When we take the combination of poor balancing, slow releases, and the always overhanging element of luck and then add a UI that would've looked bad in 2005, the fact that card effects trigger in a random order, the fact that there is no reason to play more than 3 games a day, locking drafts to an average of 6 games (not 6 drafts, 6 GAMES) a week if you win half your games, the poor matchmaking and the frequently exploited fact that there are no turn timers - only a chess clock of 20 minutes, we get a game with interesting basic mechanics but unspeakably poor execution.
While the review says I don't recommend this game, I actually recommend that you play this ONCE if you're intersted in TCGs, because the mechanics at the base of SolForge are actually fairly interesting and might change some things you take for granted in a TCG. But I do not recommend playing more than that and I beg you not to spend money on this. SolForge might be worth returning to one day, but do not expect that day to come anytime soon.

The Good: Solid card game with a good balance between strategy and fun. Many possible deck variations choosing from 4 different card pools. Nice short games (usually). Very generous with booster pack unlocks and in-game currency. Syncs with mobile versions of the game. Nice level-up mechanic that introduces addition strategy into the very act of playing the cards. Simple, easy to read interface. Great artwork and some of the cards have a neat evolution of appearance as the cards level up. Recent updates slowly add a new expansion set of cards.
The Bad: A bit simple if you're a veteran of Magic: the Gathering. Hard to see what the opponent plays sometimes because it flashes by too quickly (although you can go back to the log to look). Only 4 schools/houses of spells. Not as well polished as Hearthstone which has nice spell animations and creature sounds and highlights spells and effects as they happen. Deck construction is a little messy the way the cards are displayed although the filters do help. Slightly clunky menus and interface in general.
Overall: Great card game that is worth spending your time in. Great on the go, especially if you link the game to a mobile device. Simpler than Magic but still fun. Lacks the polish and oomph of Hearthstone's sound and animation but far more generous with free card/booster unlocks and in-game currency. That's honestly the main thing that really keeps me hooked to logging in daily. Otherwise, I'd probaly spend more time grinding Blizzard's game which requires a lot more grinding to unlock cards unless you want to spend cash. Ultimately, I am divided between both online CCGs and find them both equally enjoyable in different ways.

From Goldbar Games comes a casual, free to play murder mystery anime visual novel. Released in only May, 2017, this surprisingly popular game has already wowed many Steam players and have had people looking forward to what else Goldbar releases.
In this game, you follow Detective Butler and his sidekick, Gilligan, as they try to solve a seemingly impossible murder case on a haunted cruise ship's maiden voyage. Is the ship actually haunted and the ghosts are at work, or is the crime a little more human than people first thought?
I got this game for a little bit of fun. I didn't really know what to expect from it, and I was a little disappointed in the fact that there were no choices to make. This is pretty much a book, with the option to interrogate who you want to - but you have to interrogate all of them when this pops up, so there isn't really much to do. The story, however, really caught my attention.
This has an amazing eye to detail, and a lot of it is really well written out. This is the kind of murder mystery I expect to find in a novel, perhaps by Agatha Christie, or maybe Ian Rankin. The creators of this game have done absolute wonders with it. I was left with my mouth open when things were finally revealed - I was completely lost for words. I had it all wrong.
Now, I know a lot of people are around to play games, rather than constantly read what's happening in the game, but this was actually a really stunning game. I was left really confused, and when I thought I had it all figured out, it all changed and left me struggling to comprehend what had just happened. I was wrong countless times. Part of the charm of this game is purely trying to figure out who did it before it's revealed in the game - and who doesn't like trying to crack a mystery that's set out in front of them?
The achievements are all relatively easy to collect, except maybe Skipper if you don't know what you're doing. The game is really well thought out and I had a lot of fun playing through this twice to get all the achievements - even going through it twice, I only logged 70-80 minutes of game time, so it is a relatively quick game! I'd definitely recommend this one to both achievement hunters and anime-favoured gamers. This was a lot of fun, and I'm really glad I downloaded it and gave it a shot.

Okay, I will try to make it short this time: this game was developed and released by Double Fine -- a company well-known for it's interesting concepts (Psychonauts, Broken Age, The Cave, Costume Quest, Brutal Legend, etc -- google it or use Steam search). One of the also well-known phenomenons with this company is that it abandons games after they're released (The Cave, Spacebase DF-9, some more, I think).
Now, Massive Chalice is a pretty interesting concept -- it's a fun strategy game with turn-based "medieval XCom"-ish battles. You have to actually raise your heroes -- firstly, you'll have to "marry" two of your heroes, then (if everything would go okay) a child will be born, then he (or she) will come of age, and only after that you'll be able to recruit him/her.
Concept is interesting, because children are able to inherit traits and personalities of their parents. If father is a raging alcoholic (-speed in battle) and mother is insightful (+intuition) it would be wiser to take their children to the researches, assigning them as sages, instead of taking them to battles in your vanguard.
On the strategic map you will build forts and assign regents (and choose their spouses) there, develop new weapons in your capital, intrude in your heroes' personal life from time to time by choosing a path which they should go. For example, one of your heroes find a hermit that wants to teach him to see the way of communicating with the corruption -- and it's your choice if he goes to live with the hermit for a few years, or stays with you.
Your global mission is to win the war of 300 years. Your enemies are spawns of some sort of corruption that threatens to swallow the whole kingdod if not for your efforts.
Now, this all sounds pretty fun, doesn't it? It actually does. And it actually is fun. The sad thing is, the game lacks content... and balance. Once you'll crack the code on how to beat the battles, the game would start to bore you. Your squad would be consisting of only one hero class (I won't spoil it to you, which one, but you'll get it yourself pretty fast). You would be equpping all of the heroes with the same items. You will be marrying your regents in the same manner, maxing only one parameter.
You will basically repeat the same action 10-15 times before you beat the game.
Don't get me wrong -- XCom was repetitive too, especially before the Enemy Within update. But developers were working with balance, so people won't be recruiting exclusively snipers with ghost armor, for example. Alas, I have my doubts that Massive Chalice would get any updates any time soon.
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
The game is pretty good overall, it's definitely worth buying... on a sale. Paying $5-10 for this title is okay, game's definitely worth it. If it'd be updated with balance changes, new enemies, new items and new building (which I strongly doubt), it might be worth even more.
Right now, I'd advise you to wait for the game to go on 50-75% sale and buy it. Then complete it one time on Normal difficulty with Iron Man option on (which implies that you won't have any saves, except for when you quit the game), and move on to the next game.

I'd love if the devs add some more content, bigger maps and fix the performance. But in general a enjoyable game for some hours.

Broken Sword 5 is a classic old-school point&click adventure. It is the 5th part of a series with ups and downs and it is definitly not one of the downs.
Obviously some people learned their lesson after Broken sword 3 which always seemed like a very weak action adventure in some parts but still had a decent story and Broken Sword 4 which was clearly one of the worst adventure games I ever played. Broken Sword 5 is obviously "back to the roots". No more crate puzzles, no more running aroud using your keyboard with messed up controls to escape someone you can't even see properly because of the bad camera position... Just simple and plain point&click!
The story is clearly told and makes some sense (to be honest I didn't understand all the twists of Broken Sword 4 and it had some logical flaws, so this is a point I realy appreciated) although of course it has some mystical components (this is a Broken Sword game, after all).
You will meet some old faces, of course. I don't think I will spoil all too much if I say that Pearl and Douane have their appereance and, other than Douanes appereance in Broken Sword 4, this appereance isn't utterly nonesense.
The graphics are beautiful. The music is good enough. The german dialogues were mostly well translated.
Any cons?
Well, the solutions to some of the puzzles are a little bit stupid. And I hated the one music puzzle. But fortunately, they re-inserted the hint function which gives cummulative hints until you get the solution, so you won't ever need to watch a walkthrough and spoil your fun (because most people will rely on a walktrough once they have googled it).
Recommendation? Yes!

This ended up being a fantastic Broken Sword game. Definitely a worthy entry in an already great series!

Decent adventure game with zero Dragon's Lair-type scenes (like one of the earlier Broken Swords). Storyline was quite intriguing and I actually went to see if the painting was real :) The history portion is fascinating in a Dan Brown way.

Finally, George and Nico are back. There’s always something special about my favourite American tourist and French journalist stumbling into conspiracies, mysteries and dangers that threaten the world if not stopped in a timely manner and “The Serpent’s Curse” is no exception. The adventure unfolds once again in Paris, City of Lights, Love, Art and Death. George, currently employed by an insurance company, and Nico, still freelancing for La Liberté, meet at the opening of an exposition at a rather small gallery which is suddenly interrupted by a gun-wielding pizza delivery boy, stealing one of the many paintings and fatally shooting the gallery owner. The hunt for the thief/murderer and the stolen painting eventually uncovers a a threat for humanity itself and leads the dynamic duo to a place of biblical mythology.
There are many nods to the serie’s origins and beloved characters from other parts do – as is traditional – make rather surprising re-appearances during the course of the game and prove to be as helpful now as they were when you first encountered them. The game play is that of a classic point-and-click adventure and easy to handle, though on occasion not very exact. In the German version, which I’ve played, I noticed several translation errors, most notably the flower shop owner’s mouse over which identified her as the “intercom”. However this doesn’t affect the game play negatively at all, so I suppose there’s really no reason to complain. The game’s riddles aren’t that difficult and the new Hint System actually gives the kind of hints which enable you to solve the problems on your own rather than clicking your way through to the solution or googling a walkthrough.
I love the game’s style which is as close to the original comic style as possible while giving it a modern 3D look. The music is amazing, too, and a certain flowery tune has been stuck in my head for a while now. The game has many humerous scenes and examining items or hotspots can be quite entertaining, as always when George’s (or Nico’s) opinion is requested. Of course as always, the game is well-researched and rather engaging.
Unfortunately there are also a few downsides. The game is indeed rather short and I feel somehow that the – for lack of better term – ‘philosophical’ part of the storyline could have been expanded on. On precisely two instances, I had problems with the game not working properly: both times the game could either not play or exit a cut scene. This appears to be a bug that has been around for a while. It is quite annoying and I therefore advise you to save your game, and save often, as the auto-saved file is likely to give your grief in these instances.
Nevertheless, if you love this genre, George & Nico and brain teasers, this game is for you. I recommend it wholeheartedly. Even if you haven’t played Broken Sword before, you will find this entertaining.

About the game then:

the story through letters that you find throughout your journey.
The game itself has a very diabloesque feeling (think Diablo 1)
Allthough the combat system differs fundamentally, It's 100% physics driven, you control how your sword will swing using the mouse sweeping, thrusting, overhead strikes and taunting etc

The game is still in early access, and even though updates could be released at a faster intervall, the content available makes this game well worth the price for me.

A 2D tactical RPG, Skulls of the Shogun takes inspiration from other classic games like Final Fantasy Tactics, and Advance Wars.  Taking place in a colorful cartoon world, Skulls of the Shogun takes this inspiration and rolls with it in all sorts of fun and intuitive ways.
Set in ancient Japan, you take the role of a recently deceased Shogun.  Killed by his own lieutenant during battle, he is relegated to the afterlife as a skeleton. Faced with waiting in line with thousands of other fallen soldiers to the end of time waiting to get into the afterlife, the general instead decides to take matters into his own hands and raises an army to push his way to his rightful reward.
The playful art style mixes well with the almost constant shade of humour in the game.  Dialogue and character choices are both funny, and light hearted.  The third wall is broken often as the characters question not only the game mechanics, but the player's actions.  This cleverness tends to fade a little as the game proceeds, but not so much that it isn't still funny at times.
Each character class has a unique look and animations.  The only fault visually is occasionally the screen becomes crowded with units and objects and it can be difficult to pick out the object you want, though the game does try to assist with a pop up when several items are selected close together.
Each battle is a 1v1 turn based affair.  The game starts you out with very basic commands and units and does a good job of dishing out new elements with each new battle.  Every different unit comes with it's own stats and abilities.  Infantry have solid defence and good knockback, but are slow and don't deal that much damage.  Calvary have long movement range and high attack, but no knockback.  There are various other units like archers and magic casters to fill out the ranks.  Your general is also controllable in battle and gains new abilities as the story progresses.
Each of these units can be upgraded during any single battle in the unique manner of eating the skulls of fallen foes, even though as they will tell you themselves, it's pretty gross.  Each skull adds hit points to your units including your general, and when 3 skulls are consumed your unit becomes a demon and gains an extra action each turn.  This extra action can be extremely useful in most battles.  Along the way you will also find various potions and power ups to assist you in winning.
On later maps you will also be tasked with some minor resource management.  Rice paddies can be conquered to give you rice to pay for new troops at barracks.  There are also other buildings to be conquered to give you access to more powerful units.  Rice paddies are limited, and each one including the other buildings can be conquered by the opposing force at any time.  Controlling the map becomes very important on these levels.
Each map has different objectives, and several can be won in different ways.  Defeating the enemy general, defeating all troops, or moving a unit to a specific marker may all be ways to win.  Several maps have multiple stages and differing objectives in each stage.  This with the overlapping humour keeps the game fresh and fun throughout.
This is a fun game with a long campaign, multiplayer options and a ton of laughs.  With a regular price of $10.99 on Steam it's definitely a bargain, and will fill up hours of your time.  If you are a fan of strategy games, good humour and want a game that is easy to get into, this is a great one for you.

Man, 60% of this game is absurd and irritating. If fighting a pirate penguin piloting a UFO sounds too out there for you, you may not have enough of an open mind for this game. I admit that I cringed at stuff like that myself.
You will however eventually find yourself immersed in other ways if you are experienced with these kind of games and/or imaginative enough to develop a connection to your character and their racial lore.
But that other 40% of the content to me makes up for any perceived silliness 200%, mostly the exploration, survival, gathering of materials, recipes, schematics, construction and furnishing: sandbox stuff, managing a huge planetwide colony you built yourself if you wish.... developer Chucklefish has something special here. I've greatly enjoyed the building and survival aspects and have proudly created some awesome stuff and storylines for my characters just using my own imagination supplemented by the vast plethora of options available.
While I mostly use the game as a fantasy building simulator the inevitable combat and loose rpg mechanics are surprisingly complex, responsive and enjoyable.

I went in not taking it seriously at all but once I started surviving and building my first structure I already knew I was about to gladly sacrifice many hours of my life just finding out what else there was to explore, collect and build.

I still haven't gotten around to completing the storyline so can't comment much on that, but what I have isn't terrible and to me the potential of this game is high and is easily worth the few dollars

Pros: As GTA3 clones go, adding extreme sports and OTT stunts is one of the ideas that make it worthwhile, introducing things that you find yourself wishing were in GTA3. Tremendous freedom, with multiple approaches to two thirds of the main missions(parachute in, burst through the front, sneak in, etc.). If you're in a vehicle moving fast, or you make a vertical jump of about a dozen meters or more, you can engage your parachute, from where you can comfortably shoot or grapple to any vehicle. Shooting is like a proper third person shooter, not like GTA3 and Vice City. Vehicles include cars, motorcycles, boats, helicopters and planes, all of these types can come armed with machineguns and/or rockets, and all of them useful: sail, since you're in an island paradise, and going across water may be the shortest distance between two points; helicopter flight is easily the most flexible way to travel, because of mountains and sea; and planes are by far the fastest way to travel far. Control is great, no matter what you travel by. Fairly challenging. Limits on ammo and weapon carry capacity(two pistols, two types of C4, and another two guns - choose carefully between SMGs, assault and sniper rifles, RPGs and a grenade launcher) ensure that you are careful in shootouts. A fun arcade game.
Cons: Very clearly rushed, with glitches and bugs. Nothing to do once you've completed the short story and liberated all enemy zones and/or completed a certain number of the uninspired, crushingly inconsequential and repetitive side-missions. Characters are bland, and there's little to the story, meaning there's almost no "meat" to what's going on(the fun stuff is all in the game-play). I've been an openCanvas user for nearly ten years and it's my main painting program. Back when Portalgraphics released version 6, I was excited about the prospect of more brush options and layer masks. I got those, but lost a lot of staple features like patterns, legacy brush tools and a condensed Option window. As such, I never upgraded past oC 5.5. When oC 7 was announced, I participated in the beta testing and sent the developers a slew of recommendations to make this new release as versatile as oC 5.5. Do you know how many of my suggestions were implemented? Two: A typo fix and removal of a nag window. Whoop dee doo.
This is horrible! What really kills oC 7 for me is its blindingly unwielding tool options. For brushes, Portalgraphics have combined the paintbrush and airbrush with the default pencil tool, which uses one keyboard shortcut. Let me say that again: ALL OF THE BRUSH TOOLS USE *ONE* KEYBOARD SHORTCUT! ONE!! Think you can switch between the pencil and airbush with the click of a key? Nope! You have to manually select the right tool from the Brush window. This is a pure time-waster and it was the FIRST thing I told the developers to change (highlighted in bright red). It baffles me that programs like SAI and Clip Studio Paint allow users to set keyboard shortcuts to individual brushes, but openCanvas does not. Even if you somehow forgive the lack of accessibility, you won't excuse the fact that the Burn and Dodge tools are COMPLETELY MISSING! Why were these removed? It's just another mark of this latest version's inferiority.
Those aren't the only shortcomings. Event playback (like an oekaki recording) is still unacceptably slow. (This was complaint #2 on my list.) It's been this way since oC 6 and Portalgraphics promised to fix the issue, but never did. An event file that takes 30 seconds to play in oC 5.5 takes two minutes to play in oC 7! Why is a newer version four times slower than an old one? It also insists on exporting a GIF of the image after every playback, which is really annoying. Oh, and patterns are still missing, even though they appear in event playacks. WTF?
openCanvas 7 is rife with problems. The type mask is also conspicuously absent and canvas scrollbars have vanished. You can't disable anti-aliasing to improve playback speed or view a layer mask like in Photoshop. The layout suffers too. You can't switch from a dark to light interface and there's some pointless waste of space. Watching playbacks generates a HUGE pop-out Event window that obscures the canvas, and the Navigator options have been needlessly enlarged. I believe that older versions of openCanvas were designed during a time when users had smaller screens, which is why everything felt neater and more compact. This is especially useful for artists who paint on laptop screens and still the preferred option over this new release.
For all the improvements Portalgraphics boasts, oc 7 feels poorly designed and poorly optimized like a repackaged beta. Others might say that the fault lies in an early build, but oC 6 had the same underdeveloped feel upon release and Portalgraphics concerned themselves more with minor bug fixes rather than drastic improvements. With the shuttering of the PGN Community, the company has been going downhill for the last few years and this newest version proves it. Don't expect any major new features in the future, just stick with openCanvas 5.5. Despite the lack of layer masks and brush jitter, it's still the best version of the program to date. Unless Portalgraphics get their act together, they won't encourage me to update any time soon.

Quick Review:
Detective Butler: Maiden Voyage Murder is a free to play Kinetic Novel created and published by Goldbar Games.
Following Gilligan Goldar and the abrasive Detective Butler we observe their attempts to solve a locked-room murder during a cruise ship's maiden voyage while learning more of Gilligan Goldars history.
While as a Kinetic Novel the game allows the player has no input in the development of the story Goldbar Games instead try to challenge the player to solve the mystery before the solution is revealed, the players are given all the clues as and when the characters discover them. As a fan of tradition who-du-its and murder mysteries this was a refreshing change from many books in the genre who often hold back vital clues until the reveal, so even if you are able to guess the method you may not understand the motive.
However this does mean that the dialogue and descriptions within the game comes under far more scrutiny than other visual novels, minor mistakes and contradictions which would normally overlooked become evidently more obvious and at times can make solving the mystery a little difficult.  It should also be noted that many of these errors seem to be minor details that have been overlook and are easy to miss through the various different versions of the games plot whose victim(s) and culprit have changed whilst still in draft.
Overall though the writing in the game is of a decent quality varying between scenes
The journal system within the game is also extremely useful by automatically updating with condensed versions of the important information acquired making it easy to follow along with the mystery.
The characters are varied though somewhat sterotypical with the clumsy enthusiastic maid, smug detective and smart yet geeky business woman all make an appearance, this is not a bad thing and their characterisation presentation had a similar feel to the Phoenix Wright games in style.
Whilst the titular character is Detective Butler Gilligan Goldar is the actual main character of the game with the majority of the events seen from his viewpoint, the first five chapters focus almost entirely on building up the history and mindset.
The game itself seems to be about his change from a aimless, depressed underachieving rich kid in his fathers shadow to actually growing in confidence and taking some control over his life, so if your looking to dive directly into the mystery you will be sorely disappointed.
Much like many modern versions of Detectives, Butler comes across as slightly smug and is often condensing to those around him, this becomes somewhat grating after a while and it is only his budding mentorship to Gilligan than really saves his from been a completely unlikeable character.
This is made all the worse by Gilligan failing to really aid in the mystery other than clue gathering and relying on Butler for the solutions, the failure for some characters to miss obvious solutions or their gullibility towards some of the utter garbage Butler says while trying to get his way actually had me shouting at the screen in frustration.
As a free game it was well worth the try and overall I enjoyed it more than it frustrated me.

No, not to when dinosaurs existed. To 1997! A time when 3D graphics had firmly supplanted 2D on consoles, and analog control was new. A time when reflection mapping and particle effects meant a game was realistic, and we considered these derp faces highly detailed.
A time when platforming meant insanely challenging precision hopping 1,000 feet in the air between what one magazine article of the era lamented as "floating rocks the size of dinner plates." All with slippery, floaty controls compared to what you're likely used to today, and a draw distance we all didn't know better than to think was just "ambient fog" that added atmosphere to our games.
An era where grey, green, and lava red were considered a stunningly vibrant array of colors.
This game... ohhh, this game! When I purchased an N64 back in the 90s, I got four games with it. Doom 64 (still my favorite classic style Doom ever,) Mario 64, Star Wars Shadows of the Empire (someone please remaster it with modern controller support and upscale like this game, please!) ... and Turok: Dinosaur Hunter.
By today's standards, this is a brief, ridiculously challenging on any difficulty above easy from the second or third level on, very ugly, less than ideally controllable (although it feels fine with mouse and keyboard) first person shooter. But in 1997, it felt revolutionary. With a speed and polish something akin to the original Quake, graphics which at the time were gorgeously slick, the appeal of fighting dinosaurs and soldiers in jungles, and plenty of secrets, it was a big hit and a staple on the system.
This is a fairly no frills port, but adds modern controller support, FOV settings (I recommend the lowest one for something akin to the original game's FOV, but crank it up for that high speed feeling fisheye effect if you want it,) vibrancy settings (with Reshade - use version 3 and OpenGL incidentally - and vibrancy turned on but all the way down, the game really pops and looks like the original but with much higher contrast,) FXAA, bloom, *massively increased draw distance*and other bells and whistles. There is no retexture, but existing textures natively scale all the way to 4K resolutions. So everything looks sharp, if dated.
There are eight levels, and one hub stage. The goal of the levels is to find all the keys which unlock subsequent stages (so if you miss any, you'll need to replay them a bit.) Saves work via manual save points, and a checkpoint system only restores you after death during your current session. Loading always takes you to your last manual save point. Old school.
The game is much more challenging than I remember. Some of that is due to revamped AI toughness, but mainly it's just that this is a pretty challenging game, especially the platforming sections. I'm much better at it now than I was in the 90s, thankfully. But expect a tough time due to the save system.
Using a controller, the game works fine (native dual analog control just like you'd expect,) but even after tweaking the sensitivity and turn acceleration settings for more than an hour, I couldn't ever get it to feel quite as precise as modern games do. The acceleration curves are very dated. Mouse and keyboard feel great, however. That said, I did adapt and play with my 360 controller. I wanted to relive the console experience, just with twin analog.
Level variety is decent. Jungles, treetop villages, lost ruins, volcanic plains, and mechanical bases. Enemies are pretty epic in my opinion. Dinosaurs, soldiers, soldiers riding dinosaurs, dinosaurs modified with weapons, and later on, some fairly intimidating mechs. And this Suburban Commando era Hulk Hogan looking boss that I completely forgot about until replaying the game after 20 years.
Weapon variety is nice. Exploding arrows, a variety of guns, advanced energy weapons... all the things you'd expect. This game and its sequel always stuck out in my mind as the point where modern, animated weapons, and crazy alien tech with blue glowy energy started showing up in first person shooters. They still look pretty good, and as mentioned, have some pleasing particle effects. Honestly at times while replaying this, I was reminded of the Halo games' arsenals. Which may give you some idea of how modern it felt for 1997.
Anyone cool with old school games in the vein of Quake, but with a more outdoor vibe. Anyone who doesn't mind old school save systems, and challenging platforming.
Anyone who doesn't want tough platforming sections, limited lives, manual save points, and dated visuals. Anyone who was hoping for a true HD retexture.

Turok: Dinosaur Hunter is an FPS that originally appeared on Nintendo 64 in 1997 and later ported to the PC, unbeknownst to some. The Turok series has always been a strange one: Largely popular on the N64 platform it was best known for, but it had absolutely nothing on PC shooter competition even in the year it came out. Its sequels would take radical turns in gameplay style and features, often with mixed results, with Turok 2: Seeds of Evil typically being regarded as the last great Turok game, at least the last one most similar to its predecessor. A lousy reboot in 2008 simply called Turok all but killed off the semi-popular franchise, at least until last year when Night Dive Studios resurrected the first title and gave it a bit of a facelift (remaster, not remake) bringing the N64 classic to a wider audience. I never owned thus never played it on the N64 but I did acquire the PC version many years ago and enjoyed it quite a lot despite its shortcomings.
Turok was originally a comic book, Turok: Son of Stone in the 60's, a relatively innocent series of books about two Native American brothers who went on adventures in a desolate valley populated with dinosaurs. In the early 90's Valiant Comics brought back a revamped series called Turok: Dinosaur Hunter and the setting was vastly altered: the valley is now 'The Lost Lands', a place where time moves in a self-contained loop. With dinosaurs, aliens, demons and future tech in a bizarre unison. The villain is an entity known as Mothergod who uses the Lost Land as a base of operations and outfits dinosaurs with intelligence-boosting implants turning them into 'bionisaurs'. From there on there's things like a post-apocalyptic future Earth, various Lovecraftian abominations and high-tech future warriors. Yeah, the 90's were here. There's many elements in this iteration that would show up in the games. Later on another series was published by Acclaim Comics in 1998 as a tie-in for Turok 1 and 2.
Turok is not a character's name but a title meaning 'Son of Stone'. For many generations the mantle of Turok has been bestowed upon those who saw the protection of the barrier as their sacred duty, the barrier between this world and the others. The axis of all being the Lost Lands. Turok travels between alternate dimensions stopping those who would try to conquer the Lost Lands and thus all of the multiverse with it. In this game you are Tal'Set, a time-travelling Saquin warrior tasked with stopping The Campaigner, an evil warlord who controls a vast army of creatures in addition to his own troops, seeking pieces of the Chronoscepter in the Lost Lands. This ancient artifact, once assembled contains the power to rule the known universe.
Turok's gameplay is standard for the era but closest I can compare it to would be the first Quake. Movement speed and jumping height are excellent and grant you a lot of mobility which allows you to easily sidestep and jump over enemy attacks. And jumping you will be doing a lot of, for even the most rudimentary skill it is absolutely mandatory to master if you're going to finish the game. Platforming is commonplace but not hard to pull off and is very responsive. Among this there's an assortment of keys you obtain in each level which are used to unlock the next, and a piece of the Chronoscepter in each level as well. The majority of the game takes place in outdoor environments with the occasional indoor section. Exploration is key as there's all kinds of stuff hidden around. Interactivity is decent with being able to scale certain walls, swimming, collapsing trees with explosive weapons and hunting deer and warthogs for extra health (tip: use regular shotgun shells for best results). There's no use function so activating things requires a simple approach or stepping on pressure plates. There's only eight levels but they're pretty large and take anywhere from 45 minutes to a little over an hour to finish.
The bestiary is surprisingly varied, well animated and different from one another. It's a bit ironic that the game's subtitle is Dinosaur Hunter since 6 of the 8 levels contain mainly humanoid enemy types like poachers, evil natives and the Campaigner's own troops. But there's a host of other lifeforms like cave dwelling leapers, giant beetles, the ape-like Purr-Linn, and of course dinosaurs, mainly biomechanical velociraptors and dimetrodons. The enemies get more bizarre the further you go, with aliens, demons and robots near the end and of course a few bosses sprinkled along the way. Death animations are also pretty violent, but nowhere near as gory as the sequel, considering this was on the N64 but by that time Nintendo had backed off with its censorship. People grab their throats with blood jetting out of their neck and raptors produce a crimson volcano from their maw more often than not, but it's pretty tame by today's standards.
The weapons were another highlight from this time period as most shooters had little more than 10 or so but Turok boosts a whoppin' 14 in all. From a lowly knife and Tek Bow to high-tech death dealing in the form of the atomic energy Fusion Cannon to the Chronoscepter itself. And all manner of shotguns, miniguns, grenade and rocket launchers, and alien technology in between. They're all great fun to use and are one of the main selling points of the game. The iconic Cerebral Bore from Turok 2 isn't in this one but what's here already is more than sufficient to get the job done.
Visuals are obviously aged with early 3D models and low res textures but they're still competent like Quake's IMO and leave little guesswork as to what the hell you're looking at. As stated earlier everything's animated well and the addition of updated graphics options in this remaster do make things look a bit nicer. Originally the draw distance for the fog was abysmal due to console restrictions, the FOV was insanely low and the frame rate for the original PC version was capped at something odd like 42. Now the draw distance allows you to see more things (and some things you probably weren't meant to see), the FOV isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the frame rate's a silky 60 easily making this the superior version of the game. Audio's low quality as they come straight from the source but they're not too ear-grating. The music's not bad though and mostly consists of fitting tribal beats, dreary ambient pieces and a sinister industrial style on the final level. The levels are mostly set in a jungle or ancient temple but throw some curve balls later on. Night Dive greatly reduced frustration in exploring these by doing some very minor streamlining, removing redundant hallways or reworking a section to flow better, and the placement of certain keys and some extra save zones on the tougher maps.
Criticisms include the low difficulty in combat as most enemies aren't that challenging to fight and are easily exploited due to their animation, but hitscanners can be annoying and the pulse rifle wielding Campaigner sergeants are extremely aggressive and require a lot of jumping around while laying into them to not get hit. Hard difficulty isn't that much harder and just makes everyone bullet spongy and removes pickups from dead enemies, effectively screwing you out of the Mortal Wound pickup (permanently raises base health) if killing with the knife or regular arrows. Limited save areas as a result of consoles and the amount of platforming can be tedious, and the Chronoscepter piece on level 7 is very out of the way (useful hint: not all lava hurts you). Lastly if you can score hits with the Chronoscepter on the Campaigner it massively cheeses him.
Overall, Turok is a very 90's FPS in its design but that's largely what makes it so unique and fun to play and I highly recommend it to fans of the genre. Happy hunting.

Overall:
This is an excellent game which I've enjoyed playing both solo and co-op. The loads of different maps, each of which may require a different strategy for optimal results, provides great replay value. Unlocking additional weapons, traps, trinkets, etc. offers the chance to spice things up. When you've played though all the maps, you can revisit them at the same difficulty or more challenging settings in co-op mode, and some of the maps are definitely easier with a friend.
Graphics/video:
The graphics run smoothly on even old computers. I've never had any issues with freezing or lingering artifacts. The only thing that could be considered annoying is the occasional odd camera angle which leads to disorientation.
Sound/audio:
The sound effects never seem to get tedious. The quips from the heros are entertaining, as are the verbal responses from the orcs. I never minded the music, but keep it muted most of the time so any audio cues that orcs have breached defenses in another section of the map won't be missed.
Challenge:
Especially at Nightmare difficulty setting, the maps can be a real challenge, but most players should be able to complete almost all the maps on at least the easiest difficulty setting over time. The endless mode provides additional challenges if the campaign has been completed.
Achievements:
Just a side note about weird requirements for those who are focused on achievements. The Stay Classy achievement requires you to purchase Orcs Must Die 1 and complete its levels.  The Six Degrees achievement requires you to play through a stage with another player who has already earned the achievement. Both achievements are kind of lame and you should be aware of them if you're serious about achievements.

What I can say about Massive Chalice is odd. It's a game that is at the same time very neat, and very clunky.
For example the combat (one of the things you'll be doing the most) is laid out in a neat way, the UI is good. You get a lot of information (although not enough like the game not telling you if you'll be in the range for a melee attack) without it cluttering the interface.
That however doesn't make the actual combat any better. While at first it might be enjoyable to experiment with various classes you quickly discover strategies that work best for your current line-up and stick to them.
For example if you play with a lot of hunters you'll be doing a lot of sneaking and alpha striking the enemy to blow him up before he can react, as kaberjacks you'll notice that enemies take damage by getting knocked back into walls AND into units. So you'll abuse that fact for more damage+stun potential, alchemists are really only good against the weakest enemies in the game. so after the start they only really serve to make kaberjack and hunter hybrids. But that creates a problem for the other game mechanics.
The breeding. It is supposed to be a big part of the game but really it turns into a chore. The mechanics are never explained properly so you have to do a lot of guesswork to understand how to do it properly. It is important to remember that your kids will not only get the traits of the parents, but also possibly random ones or traits from the OTHER members of the family tree, OR perks that you didn't even know the family has. This is extremely frustrating in the early game and if not managed properly becomes a problem in the mid and even late game.
Imagine this scenario. You decide that you'll base your early game on kaberjacks (and you have to decide who to base it on early because you only get one castle at start). Cool. You built your castle, you find a good young couple with a high fertility rating and good kaberjack stats and mush them together. Recipe for success right? No.
Now it took your super fertile mating pair anywhere between 0 and 40 years to pop their first baby. They might NEVER get one even though the release day patch supposedly altered the numbers. But hey, there is a kid! Oops he's asthmatic and anaemic. So he can't run and he has reduced hp. WHy is that?! Oh because both family trees had those perks hidden in their genes and you had absolutely NO way of knowing that. Enjoy.
Now imagine you're doing this for 300 in-game years while having to constantly bring in new blood (and new bad traits) because upkeeping a family that is provided for is apparently a really hard task.
So yeah, neat idea, pretty dull and clunky execution. Same you could say for most of the game.
Honestly if this is how Double Fine keep doing things I think I'll just stop buying things from them altogether.

Massive Chalice combines aspects of tactical squad-based games like XCOM with a eugenics simulator to create a pretty unique strategy experience. Broadly speaking, the game divides into two distinct segments: the "grand" strategy map, where you'll mostly make choices with regards to things like what to research, who to marry to whom, how to react to certain events etc., which are interrupted by enemy attacks in the tactical maps, which play out very similarly to XCOM missions if without quite as much detail or tactical flexibility.
There are some genuinely intriguing design decisions here - marrying off heroes of two separate classes will create hybrid classes, opening up new options in the tactical maps. High-level heroes will leave behind heirlooms when they die, letting their legacy live on through those relics (which can also be levelled). The Cadence (the evil guys) will always attack more than one region at a time, leaving you to make broader strategic choices as to how to defend your territory with the ultimate aim of surviving for the 350 or so years the game spans.
The graphics are charming, albeit simplistic. They do fit the theme of the game, which is light-hearted and fun. That doesn't mean it's a simple game; it's just simple to get into. The controls are easy to pick up, but it's the broader context of the game that's harder to master. Building lasting bloodlines, ensuring a sufficient diversity of hero classes through shrewd marriages and the like...all the while cheering for the battlefield victories of individual heroes you'll come to know, love and mourn as they pass. RIP SpaceJesus Doodlebats, gone but never forgotten.

I'm a big fan of city building/thriving games, so this seemed to be right up my alley. The game is interesting, I will say, but I'm often frustrated by areas that feel either unnecessary or really not fleshed out. Some big gripes:
- Even a small, optional tutorial mode would be helpful to learn buildings and controls. For instance, the bakery takes food and makes bread.....which is then stored as food. Why is it a good thing to build this building? Does bread do something different? I also have NO idea what norias and the other water systems do, because they don't say in the description, and I'm not wasting time/resources building something without knowing what it does/why I should.
- While the advisors were a fun idea, they feel almost useless. The city advisor is kind of okay, but I have only heard from the agriculture advisor if I was running out of food (or places to put food), and I don't think the military advisor has said a single thing. I would expect advisors to be guides, and they don't guide you; they seem to be there mostly to tell you inform you you've done something wrong after you've done it, when it's already clear. Their messages could pop up in the message feed, and it'd be just the same, and more convenient, because I wouldn't have to look back to my keep to see their message.

There are a lot of really cool concepts in this game, hitting enemies knocks them back, and by pushing enemies around cleverly you can deal extra damage or instantly kill them by knocking them into the water.
Standing units next to eachother lets you form walls. Linked units can't be pushed or be crossed or shot over by enemy archers, making formation important.

I could just keep going, just trust me this game is worth checking out.
Furthermore it has the best cross platform system I've ever seen. Not only is there online play across all platforms but your profile and save file carries over too. So I can play this game with my phone on the bus, and continue the campain at home on my PC.

Reaching higher levels gives access to better equipment. There are several different match types and a strong presence of permadeath always lurking, done really nicely.
- The combat is awesome, it almost tastes like sweat and blood. It's absolutely the best combat system I've ever tried.
- But be warned, the learning curve is steep. Learning to use the space key for realigning the cam is one of the key things, and it can be a bit unintuitive for a regular gamer. For me it took around 3 hours to get a grip on it.
- Watching youtube tutorials can be really helpful.
- Getting to the master level requires decent amount of grinding, but I enjoyed it a lot.
