The game has great combats but there's also many weaknesses in the design of the global management mainly, plus many design choices of the global management that I don't like.
The main negative points that are more or less objectives:
- The UI looks cool and is ok for combats, but overall it is rather weak on many points because of a bad "ease of use" design, like bizarre cumbersome lists, inability to check keeps during events or during some other actions, lack of switch tool like see next hero detail or see next keep detail, many more. You'll get more or less used to it, but it's still a rather weak point except in combat where it could be improved but it is ok overall.
- There's a lot of random spread into the global management but they are too much pure random, much more procedurally generated random could only be much better.
- There's too many rules or effects not explained, it's a design choice of the game copying a bad design element of old classic roguelike, it's still a bad design even if some old classics used it.
- The strategy layer coming from the general management is rather thin. It's more a management game than a strategy game, few strategic choices, not much opportunities to setup plans and adapt plans. The game is much more about series of micro decisions. To be clear new xcom is a bit better on this but not good either.
But for me the weakest points of the game are design choices that some other type of players could enjoy, the main points are:
- The general management is designed with a spirit of high negativity, it's copying a design approach of old classic roguelike. It's not a matter of difficulty, it's a matter of being negative. For example you have to bother with paralytic, asthmatic, mostly blind, drunk, sterile, nervous heroes is just pointless and highly unpleasant for me. It's honestly my main grip against the game, and without this I'd probably vote thumb up, perhaps.
- Mixed classes are by themselves a good design but how you get heroes classes linked to keeps marriages is generating a high lost of control of classes used, and I don't like at all this. That destroys the ability to do thematic replays based on a choice of a set of classes. That point is also a major reason why I am overall more negative than positive about the game.
- There's many events along a campaign play, the problem is your choice will be random until you know the answers. The events are a good idea but I don't like at all to have to do random choices, and it's infuriating when it leads to a huge penalty and a smash in your face.
- Too much random in the global management gameplay, that's tedious for me.
For the sake of balance, I should add that the game has also good and even great points:
- The combats are very interesting with both depth and tactical diversity at your disposition. And don't listen players complaining Hunters are only valid or that the game has no tactical depth, it's just they don't know play the game.
- Despite there's only a relative random generation of combats areas, it's still working rather well and don't feel repetitive. It could be better but overall it's a good point.
- The aesthetic choice of the game could seem bizarre at first, but it works very well, it looks rather nice once you admit the approach, and such aesthetic will never look old. On that aspect the UI is successful too and has a nice and marking look. It's too bad that the "ease of use" of the UI isn't as good.
- The events are a good idea to setup a story mood along a play, and that works rather well, too bad that the choices you have to do for those events are too much random until you know the events/choices/consequences.
Overall only players that like a lot either pure random and negativity spirit, either squad combats, should try this game. Other should apply a lot of caution. Myself I'm in second category and don't really regret my buy, but it's definitely for me a highly irritating and relatively frustrating game.

This is the tale of Chris "Red Hands" Antony.
Red Hands didn't come from a large house, and was an only child. He quickly proved himself a great hunter, and could have easily solo'ed some missions if he wanted. After leading my army for over 40 years, I built a training school, the first of its kind, and retired Red Hands from battle to become a teacher who would soon influence the rest of the nation with his high level and favorable traits. Within a year, news had spread of his new school, and it was then attacked by a large group of monsters with the intention of trying to kill the teacher who had killed so many of their own. I, as King, launched a rescue party to go in and kill the monsters, and Red Hands barely survived, getting down to 1hp at one point in the battle. Several months after the attack, Red Hands came to me and told me of a love child he, which under the law was illegal without the consent of the King. I decided to show mercy on Red Hands, as he was the most famous warrior in all the land. I decided to exhile one parent, and let one live, but I would let the child choose which. The baby girl chose Red Hands, and he had to watch as his lover was escorted away to be exhiled. Unfortunately, the child inherited all its atributes from the mother, and was predestined to be a terrible warrior. Red Hands taught for 12 more years without issue, and died months before his only child old enough to fight in battle.
While Red Hands house will probably never rise to power, and more likely will die out when his daughter is married, Chris "Red Hands" Antony will always be remembered as the best warrior these lands have ever seen.

A pretty good entry in the city builder genre.  However, don't get this game if you are expecting 40+ hours of enjoyment from it.  My "hours played" (approximately 6 hours) represents the amount of time it took (less ~30 minutes to learn the basics) to fill an entire map with structures, build at least one of every structure in the game, and fend off dozens of attacks by dragons and vikings.  At this point, I have seen everything that the current version has to offer and I have no desire to keep playing.  I think that this is acceptable value for the price, but you might disagree.
- An option to adjust the map size, including maps much larger than the default map.
- This could be an oversight on my part (then again, the fact that I could not figure this out after six hours indicates that the system, if it exists at all, is neither intuitive nor obvious), but I could not get citizens to occupy specific buildings with any consistency.  This issue poses problems when your kingdom gets attacked, because your defensive structures sit idle if no citizens are operating them.
Even so, rebuilding after an attack was never an issue.  I think that any increases in the difficulty or frequency of attacks must come with similar improvements in your ability to defend the kingdom.
: Citizens do not want to die, and don't want their homes destroyed.  When an attack is detected, citizens automatically stop their current activity and move to the nearest tower or barracks.
Alternatively, add an option to give each structure "priority" (e.g., high, medium, low).  High priority structures would then attract workers before other structures.
- Mod support via Steam Workshop adds a lot of value for me.  I would be much more likely to continue playing if there was an active modding community working to make new buildings and map options.

In a few words…Fresh, Unique, Challenging, Fun.
Exanima stands high above any other iso rpg I have played. I’m not a reviewer by any means but a job well done deserves mention.
Firstly, be prepared to spend some time learning the game, there are game modes that cater to this.
Once you get acquainted with the controls the fun really begins. Every hit is registered on the body part it strikes, you can see your opponents head snap sideways or their sword react to blocking a blow. On a very strong hit, their knees actually buckle. Speed and power can be added to your attacks with certain mouse movement as well as stepping into attacks.
Some notes on combat. There is a magic formula of audio feedback and character movement/reaction that makes things feel very organic. You can intuitively tell the difference between a hard hit and a glancing hit. Combat is unrelenting and intense, especially when you are down on health and can’t afford to take another hit.
The dungeons are very dark, and well designed the one torch you get is your friend. Things are laid out with very distinct areas; workshops, living quarters, taverns etc. all of which are meticulously laid out and eerily vacant. Exploring the levels takes time but you are rewarded with finding items which otherwise may be missed.
Despite being early access, the game runs very smoothly and has a polished look. I applaud the Devs for perfecting the system over adding content.
Exanima will not hold your hand, it’s meant to be a challenge, but the greater the challenge the greater the satisfaction when you come out the other side.

After watching the trailer for this game I was instantly interested.  It had something that I just had to try out for myself!
I'll admit that I can see a lot of people being turned off by the game mechanics, but for someone that doesn't mind taking the time to get to know the game, it's been a fun ride so far.  You'll notice right away that your character moves like a drunk sloth at times and the combat can be a bit clunky, BUT once you get it down, it's actually a lot of fun and takes a bit of skill to get good at.
Exploring the dungeon and taking your time searching around is where this game shines.  The game is rogue-like in a sense, and if you're lucky enough to survive a "knockout", you'll have a second chance to pick yourself back up and tread lightly though the dungeon again (with what is left of your health).  The game also has an arena mode where you can fight and hire other characters to fight for you and it adds a bit more content for you to sink your teeth into as well.
All and all, If the trailer has you wondering what this game is all about, and you don't  mind risking your cash on an EA title, then give it a go!!
***UPDATE***
After doing a little more poking around, I've discovered that this game is actually a prelude to another game the devs are working on called 'Sui Generis'.  Examina takes place 20 years before the events of SG.  The only difference is this game is limited to the underworld dungeons of SG. Exanima is its own full game and should not be avoided because of SG.  SG looks even more amazing than Exanima and far more ambitious too!

This game is quite amazing and unique, also hilarious if you know what to do.
You start off fumbling like an idiot until you learn the weird somewhat complicated controls, you spend a few hours getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥as you flail your your little noodly arms at all the zombie people, giving them hugs as they slide their weapons into your flesh.
After a while you start to learn how to use your legs, you're able to keep a safe distance now but still manage to keep yourself within range of the enemy for you to rush in and attack, but oh no, all your blows are being blocked, you must learn how to use those puny limp little arms of yours. You rush in and do an overhead swing, they block and try to swing, you back away. You use your small metal spike and do an alt attack while rushing, you get them in the gut right as they get ready to swing again, there blow is stopped by the side of your jiggly body as you press your spike in. You freak out as they continue to try and swing, your limbs are entangled now, it almost looks sensual as the enemy writhes about between your legs, eventually they are on the floor unable to get up for a moment, you manage to step away and remember the game has a crouch function, you crouch over him and repeatedly stab him in the eye with your spike.
You have just sodomized and brutally killed a man carrying a bedpan, congrats.
You steal his clothes and equip his bedpan, and continue on.
Next you see a person with their back to you, they are carrying a two handed sword that can obviously ruin your day.
Next to that man you see a bucket, you remember you can move things around so you pick up the bucket and adjust it so it falls on his head. He doesn't care, you move past him and get startled as he begins to move, instead of attacking he instead bugs out as the bucket falls through him, removing his hair and trapping his arms, he starts flying around the room with the bucket wrapped around his waist, his sword still in hand, he flys by and kicks you in the head, knocking you down. Amused and terrified you try to get up and leave, but no, the bucket decides that you aren't going anywhere and it throws itself at you, slamming you into the door, your hand gets jammed in the door but you take no damage.
The bucket finally stops flinging the man around, instead spinning him on the ground behind you, getting closer, the blade still in the mans hand knicks your leg, you realise you're absolutely screwed, watch in horror as a spinning man with a bucket around him slashes at your legs until you bleed to death.
Fun game, extremely unique, get it in Early Access while you can still turn into a breakdancer using a bucket.
It's a rare glitch but it works, just drop a bucket on your head.

Exanima is doing to top-down isometric dungeon crawlers what Demon Souls did to third person action/rpgs, i got from it the same raw feeling of danger and excitment i got when i first played Demon's Souls.
And like DS this game is unforgiving and will not hesitate to crush you and kill you in the most humiliating and brutal ways but you will learn something new with every death, there is little hand holding here and the learning curve is pretty steep, but all that makes it really really rewarding, even killing a single foe here feels like a grand victory of epic proportions, you made it ... You survived ... And the other guy is lying bloodied on the floor, pat yourself on the back and eat a cookie, you have done it and survived another brutal fight (cause here when a character dies here they die for good, no coming back from a 10 kg sledge hammer meeting your skull at high speed).
Also note two important things, first is that this is still a work in progress early access game so expect some bugs (quite rare though) and also that its story mode is still incomplete (though i could barely survive the first area till now and there are three of them as far as i know), but it is playble and quite polished showing the serious effort the devs put into it.
Second is that it's a physics based game, your character's body, your enemie's and the enviroment objects are all physics enabled, and it's not just rag-doll physics .. You and everything around you are under the influence of physics all the time ... This dramatically changes how combat plays out and generally how you traverse the enviroment, running from an angry hammer-wielding dude that can bash your skull and kill you with a single well placed hit to your face .. See that chair .. If this was a normal game you would probably tear right through it or push it aside, but here it can be quite dangerous,this chair can really trip you over and get you killed in the most humiliating way possible.
Cause that dude with the hammer will be more than happy to smash your head on the floor before you can even get up, so next time you see a chair while running from angry dudes with hammers make sure to avoid tripping over it, and maybe take a sec to push it in their way, maybe they will fall over and give you a chance to take them out while avoiding their hammer getting introduced to your poor face (usually a very brief, loud and bloody introduction that ends with you dead on the floor), i mean who who would have thought a chair could make such difference in a fight (unless you are into bar brawls), it does here in Exanima, so mind your enviroment and use it to your advantage, got an angry mob chasing you with cleavers and axes, run into a two door room/hallway then close the door behind you quickly and bar it with chairs, ladders and wooden planks, and always beware the angry dudes (or dudettes) with hammers.
And did mention i love the character models and character creation here, there are both male and female characters available and a very nifty body type modifying graph (that i wish all RPGs had) along with few hair types and realistic hair and skin colors to pick from, also the gear equipping system is neat and realistic (you can wear up to three layers of clothes/armor and they all offer varying types and degrees of protection from the various types of damage in the game (slash, blunt and pierce damage), not to mention it's quite an accurate depiction of medieval armor and your chatacter will look pretty rad decked in realistic full plate armor after starting out with nothing but rags (and i'm yet to get there but the Arena mode allows you to try the look of items before you buy them, and the high-end items cost a lot of gold, which you earn by winning arena fights), one day you sweet full plate helmet, one day you will be mine, hahahaha ... ahm.. Never mind that, i just got a little excited!
Long story short it's a game for those who want something creative, exciting and challenging, something that simulates the look and ferl of medieval combat pretty damn well, it's all for you if don't mind it having a steep learning curve.
If you want to get instant gratification, empowerment and to just obliterate dozens of enemies per minute steer clear of Exanima, go play other isometric hack & slash dungeon crawlers like Diablo 3 or Grimdawn (which are damn fine and i play them too, but they are very different from Exanima), these games unlike Exanima don't punish and
Kill you for flailing your weapon around, they encourage you to do so and make it enjoyable, but Exanima's methodical slow paced phyiscs enabled combat this just gets you killed, it surely isn't for everyone but if you can get into it and learn its innerworkings it can be extremely rewarding way beyond any of those other games in the genre.

Orcs must die 2 is the sequel to the original orcs must die (unsuprisingly), and is more or less the exact same game with new levels, a new character, minor improvements and just more content in general.
There isn't much to ruin really, plot wise, whether you've beaten the original or not. At the end of the first game, your hero, the apprentice warmage, decides to close all the rifts that join the human world and the orc world, thus cutting off all magic for them both. Jump cut to the future where the rifts are now opening again and the main antagonist from the first game, who is basically a sterotypical evil witch, manages to get through and along with the warmage from the first game, must work together to stem the tide of the orc horde and to figure out why the rifts are opening again.
The gameplay from the first game hasn't changed all that much except for a few minor differences, additional traps were added, as well as trinkets and an entirely new class which has different traps, equipment and is much more focused on spells than the warmage. There are also some subtle changes, like certain weapons now costing mana to use when they didn't require any before, and some new enemy types which weren't present in the original game.
Visually speaking, it hasn't really changed much from the original, nor have the music scores, its still very cartoonish and light hearted, with the music still being memorable.
Overall, orcs must die two is just the original game but with far more content and a bucket load of DLC that are all worth the price. If you were a fan of the original game, you'll love this as well, But if you don't want to bother with the original because some of the minor gameplay issues bothered you, a number of the original maps from the first game are also up for grabs.

The Super Mario Bros. and Anchorman quotes made sense in the context of the story, but the references really got out of hand when one of the characters quoted lyrics from Poison's "Every Rose has its thorns" for no reason (something like this happens at least once per cutscene). But the gameplay is 100% solid. You have multiple viable commands to give your units every turn, and the pacing of aggression versus gaining strength almost always presents a few gripping decision points per turn. This game is absolutely worth the $5 price tag.

Solforge is a free to play online collectible card game, made by Stoneblade Entertainment who are essentially a super team of Magic the Gathering veterans who joined up with the godfather of tcgs Richard Garfield to make this product.
Solforge is perfect for anyone who loves to play tcgs, but hasn't the time or money to do that anymore, the rules are simple, but the longer you play it the more you will discover the deep strategies this game inherents. The simple ruleset also makes this game great for tcg starters who can grasp the rules very quickly.
Basically there are 5 lanes and each turn you may play two cards are turn, creatures attack every turn (even in the opponents) and will battle either creatures on the opposing lane or hit the opponent directly. Both players have 100 lifes and your goal is to bring your opponent to 0. Now here comes the clue of the game: There is no resource system like Magic's mana system you just play two cards every turn, but every card has three different levels and cards level as they get played, coming back much stronger later in the game. So you have cards which are good on lvl 1 but might not be good to play because they level badly and there are other cards who do next to nothing on level 1 but might be gigantic later on. The leveling makes for interesting decisions, because you always have to consider if you can allow to level a stronger card or if you want to get ahead on board.
If you want to play the game for free you can easily do it, Solforge has a front loaded reward system where you don't need to grind for hours to get your stuff. And you can even draft which is a ton of fun and allows to get many new cards.
Since Solforge is currently in open beta there are more features to come: A crafting system, set 2 and a single player campaign are all down the line. The game is also available for Iphone and Ipad and will support Android devices on one point.
I would recommend this game for anyone who loves tcgs, because this is in my honest opinion the best one you can play on your computer (except maybe magic online, but it is a pain to play with it and is ridiculous expensive) but also for anyone else who is interested in this genre, this game is a good starting point for it.
An excellent digital card game with one of the best draft environments I've ever seen.
If you like Ascension or MTG - give this new style a try!

A very old-school, action battle game that was definitely made in the '90's, Diib's Dilemma is an RPG about discovery rather than exploration.
The meat of the game is to survive through increasing levels of difficulty by upgrading the spells in your spell book with elements found battling in the levels.  Unlike other games of this type there are no maps to explore, instead each level will be the same-sized, square, isometric grid (presumably one floor of Diib's Dilemma Tower) which you then have to defeat all the monsters of the current level in order to progress.  You have a limited number of spell types to take into battle, 2 at the start of the game, and you must be able to cast spells to defeat monsters, and then dodge enemies as your spells slowly recharge.
Your character does not have levels or stats that increase as the game progresses, just the spells in his book.  At first there are 4 spells to choose from including attack spells, a trap and a heal spell.  After you have collected some of the 4 elements found defeating monsters, you can start creating newer and more powerful spells.  The real fun and strategy of the game is to experiment with different spell combos, and to discover new spells as you build up your spell book roster.  But be warned, this game has an old-school difficulty to it, traps you lay will be invisible once you have set them, and if you are the first to walk through the square then you will spring the trap and take the damage.  Also, many monsters require several hits to defeat and there are no shown lifebars, plus the mosnsters move all over, so it gets hard to keep track of which ones you have weakened and which you have not.  But all of that is designed to keep the strategy of the game interesting as there is not much variety to each level other than monsters types and the spells you choose.
This is an old-school game and it's graphics and audio lack the polish that simple games of today have.  The game doesn't even utilize the mouse, this is a keyboard game only which uses the arrow keys and the number keys in order to play.  And there are almost no options other than turning sound and/or music on and off.  However, given the fact that this game was made in the 90's and the game's low price point, I'm willing to overlook those points.  The overall movement of both your character and the monsters has a slight delay to it, making dodging and moving through the enemies a bit of a prediction game but I feel the quirky movement actually adds to the strategy and difficulty of the game in an interesting way.
Another point to mention is that this is a survival game more than a story driven RPG.  You are expected to die, and you will die and you accumulate a score as you play so that when you die you will have a top score chart to keep track of your best playthroughs.  This is not a global leaderboard but a personal top score chart.  And while you can save your progress, there is something to keep in mind:  The save files only keep track of your current tower level, the elements you have earned, and the spells you have purchased.   If you exit the game or die your score will be set to zero when you load up your save file and your currently selected spells will be reset to the basic fire spell, so keep that in mind when choosing to exit the game if you have worked up a nice score.
All in all, the age of the game shows in its graphics, sound, and play quality, but it has a unique strategy and style to it, which makes it an interesting game to play, even today.  It's super cheap and a little different than most games out there, so I recommend trying this game out if you don't mind playing older games and want a challenging game to play.

Before reading, I want to note: I was given a review copy of Massive Chalice by Double Fine for the publication I write for, Gamemoir. This disclosure notice is also at the beginning of the video posted below.
--
Massive Chalice is an interesting game. The premise itself is pretty straightforward - take Firaxis XCOM's streamlined combat mechanics, mix it in with a simple base building system, add in a hereditary bloodline for your heroes, and kill everyone with Old Age.
Everything Massive Chalice sets out to do is done well. The narrators are hilarious, the base building is well balanced, and combat has a nice mixture of classes to choose from. But I think Massive Chalice suffers from its own success - it's a very simple game that isn't trying to introduce the player to any risky mechanics, or complex strategy. Even on Brutal mode, you won't be biting your nails. Once you get the strategy and mechanics down in an hour or so, it's smooth sailing.
If you're looking for a game as complex as XCOM, Xenonauts, Jagged Alliance, or Crusader Kings II, I don't think you'll enjoy this title. There's not as much depth as any of those games. However, if you're looking to scratch that tactical turn-based strategy itch - I still recommend Massive Chalice. It might not be perfect, but it's still fun.
tl;dr - Do you like Double Fine humor? Do you enjoy simple, ease-of-use tactical gameplay? Then I suggest giving Massive Chalice a go, preferably during a Steam sale.

Your kingdom is dying. The Cadence - a pestilence, an army of monsters, an evil slime mold - is closing in around you. And the only thing you can do is trust in the wisdom of two disembodied advisers talking to you out of a large cup/fountain. They're telling you that the Cadence can be beat. It'll only take three hundred years and men and women of noble blood to fight the good fight.
You'll see families turn into dynasties, the clumsy 'slow learner' turn into Lydia 'the Rose' Kendrick, your most formidable alchemist, and all the while, the rotting of your nation will continue. The outer regions will fall and heroes will die. All to the accompaniment of a soundtrack that's appropriately mournful, graphics that are appropriately understated (though I will admit a little more variety in the character models would've gone a long way) and surprisingly engaging voice work.
Massive Chalice isn't perfect, and I don't think it holds up well to multiple playthroughs. But as someone who's not particularly good at tactics games, and whose poor decisions early on made even a 'normal' difficulty game really harrowing around the year 150, this game's tone, aesthetic and the actual difficulties I was facing came together in a super memorable way.

There is a lot of cool stuff about Massive Chalice. For example, the family system; being able to marry off heroes from differing families to create different classes and even more powerful heroes makes for an interesting time... be careful though, you might end up with a single bloodline of only Hunters if you're not careful. It's also pretty cool to watch the lives of your heroes from the day they are born, to the day they go to jail, to the day they die... be prepared, however, you're going to see a lot of birth and death in this game.To add on, beautiful graphics, great voice acting from the two advisors within the chalice itself and a hypnotic and somber soundtrack that really immerses you in this soon to be destroyed world. Then there is the badstuff... well, the bad thing, really.
That being, the combat system. Combat in the game can pretty much boil down to a couple of different enemy types that if allowed to close in, will absolutely ravage your heroes. While this isn't a bad thing, the combat itself is just tedious... and fighting battles isn't half as interesting as what's going on during your forays on the Campaign Map. Truly, I'd be okay with just autoresolving the battles so I can delve further into the lives of my short-lived heroes rather than manually fight every single battle against the Cadence.
All in all, I definitely recommend this game. For 20 bucks? I'd say that's a damn good price.

Double Fine has created a game that is a combination of XCOM-style tactics games, and Game of Thrones-style bloodlines system.  The game switches between those two parts throughout the game as you are constantly trying to ward off “The Cadence” and keep your several families’ bloodlines alive and ever growing. The Cadence is a hoard of decay that has surrounded your kingdom. They will attack sections of your land a few times every decade. And most of the times they attack, you have to pick only one section to save. The other sections will then be afflicted by the enemy.  The different types of enemies represent different effects of time on the mind or body.  Some enemies make your heroes forget their combat experience. Others might add five years to a hero’s age with every attack.  I’ve even had heroes die of old age in battle because of this!
Massive Chalice spans a timeline of 300 years.  As an immortal omnipresent ruler, you will watch generations upon generations of your people live and die in battle or of old age.  You will research armor, weapons, and accessories for your combat team, “The Vanguard.”  You can also construct various buildings for things like housing families or to speed up the leveling of your trainees. All of your research and building takes years to complete.  You have to choose wisely because time is always afflicting your heroes with age.  When they get old, they are less effective in combat and become less fertile.  This can get out of control if all of a sudden you’re trying to defend your kingdom with white-haired, frail heroes having traits like Puny, Nearsighted, and Arthritis.  You also need to pair the right heroes together at a good time inside a Keep.  This will allow them to produce children for the future.
The art in Massive Chalice is a bit hard to enjoy.  Some parts of the game look beautiful, like the vibrant environments when you’re in combat.  But the basic models of the heroes still look unpolished.  A lot of the game still has a placeholder look.  There might have been some compromises Double Fine had to make with their Kickstarter money.  It’s not an ugly game by any means.  But it also doesn’t pop at all.  The music in the game however, is really great.  There’s some well-fitting drums and string instruments in the soundtrack that kept me in the moment during combat.

Juggling the two focuses, combat and bloodlines, in Massive Chalice is what makes it hard to put down.  Watching your research timers tick down to completion, leveling up your heroes in combat, passing down family relics to future generations, and trying to perfect the genetics of your houses is quite unique.  Massive Chalice offers a very different take on the turn-based strategy genre by making you have to really think about the effects of time.

Battle Tips:
+ Melee units (Caber) can knock back and damage to avoid corrosion
+ AOE units (Alchemists) can do 2 shots/turn at level 2
+ Range units (Hunters) can stealth for free, unlimited
Unique to Game:
In this game you are leveling the “Keep” or Bloodline, not the heroes.  In general, for any game, the player’s heroes need to gain stats at the same rate the monsters do.  If the player’s stats lag, the game is too hard, if the player’s stats leap ahead of the monsters, the game is too easy.  This game works on the same balancing concept except that instead of leveling the heroes, you are leveling the Keep.  Heroes get married and produce children in the Keep that inherit some of the stats from the Keep.
There are about 30 battles in a game, approximately 1 every 10 years.  The average hero can fight from age 16 till his death around age 65 – at most 6 battles.  Then he (and his personal stats) are lost forever and a new hero takes his place.
The game is about using the hero’s temporary life span to contribute to the improved stats of the Keep/Bloodline fast enough to keep up with the monster’s increase in their stats.  If you can do this really well, you should set the game to Brutal, which makes the monster’s stats better quicker and your stats go up slower.  If you are having trouble keeping up with the monsters, you reduce the difficulty to Hard or Normal.
Improving Keep Stats:
This is the fun of the game, I've been playing about 3 days and my longest game is 106 years, so I'm still just getting going, but here's what I've learned early on:
+ If a hero fights in a lot of battles during his life (4+), he has a chance to produce a relic.  This relic in the form of a weapon etc. is passed on from one hero to one other hero and itself levels.
+ Heroes that marry have traits and personalities that can pass on to the kids.  At the beginning of the game most of your heroes have really bad traits, but by carefully selecting the heroes to marry, you slowly select for only the good traits, and the bad traits fall away.
+ When you build a crucible(s) you can make your highest level heroes a Standard, and then all the heroes that are born (ages 0-15) get a yearly experience boost based on the Standard’s level.  That way your new heroes start at a higher level.
+ And of course, Research can boost stats
+ Use your heroes with the best stats for marriage. Almost any hero can win the first few battles, so it's better to invest heroes with good traits in a marriage.
Graphics are good.  Camera controls are good.  Game seems crash proof.  The AI is not the best.  This is not the best turn-based battle game. The fun in this game is learning how to increase your stats even though your heroes keep dying off.
The rare gem you should definitly try if you enjoy tactical games and playing god of your little world.

As a long term fan of the Broken Sword series, "Broken Sword 5 - The Serpent's Curse" is both a lovely trip down memory lane and a mostly successful adventure in its own right.
Seeing the return of George and Nico to a 2D adventure is a very welcome thing, the backgrounds are all beautiful throughout the entire game and I would look forward to each new location to see what it would look like, just as equally to continue the story. The 3D model based sprites used in the game while not a perfect fit (sometimes appearing to be out of perspective with environments or simply standing out too much) do a great job of conveying the colourful and exciting world the game inhabits. I personally would love to see a return to 2D hand animated characters, but it is obviously something that it's too expensive for a game created through kickstarter and that's understandable.
The story for the most part is a success, an interesting and sometimes mysterious adventure into another hidden powerful religious artefact although at points it feels predictable and formulaic with the rest of the series, especially in the second episode which sadly to me felt a little padded and included some odd/unbelievable decision making from some characters and an ending that can sadly only be described as a bit lazy and pandering.
The music as always is spectacular and brought me right back to what I loved about the series within seconds of booting up the game.
Overall I would say this game is a success however and I really can't wait to see what's next for George and Nico. Hopefully a little less reliance on nostalgia but bring on Broken Sword 6! I'm ready!

Not since "Hitman: Blood Money" have I played a game in the genre that just felt so perfect in terms of what it offers. However, that's not to say it was without flaws though, because there were definitely some things that were less than stellar, and I did run into a few bugs here and there with getting stuck in doors when operating them, forcing me to reload. Luckily it only happened a handful of times throughout the game, and since there are no save restrictions (there's even a quick save), it didn't take much time to get back to where I was, which made it, at worst, a minor annoyance.
You play the role of a Russian KGB agent, who is sent on all types of missions ranging from either capturing or assassinating German officers, performing acts of espionage, rescuing allies, to even blowing up places of strategic importance.
The game is split up into 10 missions, each lasting anywhere from around 45 minutes to 2 hours depending on the difficulty setting, and style of play. There's a great amount of mission variety, making sure you never get too comfortable with a certain type or style of environment. The missions, while appearing quite linear are very open-ended in how you go about achieving your goals, and it's never about just meeting one objective either. In fact there are always several ways to succeed.
To give an example of this, one mission has you infiltrating an internment camp where your overall objective is to rescue a friendly agent. You have no idea where in the camp he is though, so the first order of business is to obtain that knowledge. To do that you need to go to the officer quarters in the middle of the camp, which is something you can't just walk into wearing your Russian uniform, or carrying your Russian made weapons and backpack, as you'd just get shot on sight. So you stalk a patrol to a quiet place, where after having disposed of them, you slip into one of their uniforms.
However you still can't just stroll right in, because there are certain types of German personnel who can identify you as not being one of theirs, and this will once again get you shot on sight, so after finding a weak spot in the fence surrounding the base somewhere, you cut a hole giving you access to the base itself. Once inside, you quickly locate the officer barracks, only to find a guard denying you entrance, telling you that someone of your rank has nothing to do inside. This means you need to find an officer and acquire his uniform in order to gain access, which is easier said than done. Once you've done that though, you're then able to access the officer barracks where you can find the correct papers, meaning you now know the agent's location. From here there are several ways to rescue him. One way is to stay in the officer uniform and obtain some access papers that'll allow you to escort the prisoner to the exercise yard, and go from there. Alternatively you can acquire a doctor's uniform, enabling you to escort the prisoner to the medical station, and go from there. You can of course also try to just kill everyone in the camp who gets in your way without getting caught in the act. However you choose to go about it, each way presents its own obstacles, which makes for an often very tense and always interesting game session.
When a mission is completed, you're graded on your efforts by use of a scoring system. Did you take your time, and chose to subdue the least amount of enemies using only non lethal methods such as chloroform, or were you pressed for time and chose to not leave anyone breathing along the way? Furthermore, were you able to hide the bodies well enough so that they weren't discovered later on? Were you noticed, and if so, did you manage to kill the enemies before they could rush off to sound the alarm?
All these things, and more, end up giving you a final score alongside information about how long it took you to complete the mission, though in truth it's all a bit irrelevant, and is really just for personal enjoyment, since as long as you complete the mission in any way, you'll still progress to the next one. There's no gear to purchase or leveling to be done.
The game is well worth your time, though keep in mind that it was released in 2007, so adjust your expectations accordingly. However, if you're the type of gamer who can look past dated graphics and some issues, I'd very much recommend it, assuming you're a fan of the genre.

I played through this game after completing the first part in the series and I have to say that I am somewhat disapointed with the game in several ways that I will list down below.
1) In the original game the crossbow was your bread and butter, the game was really a blend of true TPS and TD but I feel like actual marksmanship has been removed from the game. Projectiles fly off in random directions unless a special focus has been met making the use of the crossbow highly impractical compared to the first game.
2) Throughout the game you are reminded that you need to farm skulls in endless mode in order to beef up your traps so you can proceed in the campaign. Granted that it is still possible to complete the campaign levels without dowing this, if you want to play the game solo then it is impossible to get perfect scores in certain levels without farming up a bit.
3) The heavy emphasis on coop play shows in the level designs, while most stages are perfectly doable on your own it is sometimes extremely difficult to work around in later stages.
4) The original game had Weavers, certain skill trees you could use in a stage to enhance certain aspect of your character or traps, this has been completly removed from the game in favor of upgrading individual traps and weapons using skulls.
5) Last but certainly not least: This game has a terrible amount of bugs. It crashes frequently upon completing stages giving you the strange state where you have unlocked the next stage but have no registered high score. While playing coop (something this game has seemingly been designed around) the game has even more oppertunities to crash making it really frustrating when you have finally gotton to one of those later waves in a stage only to see your work amount to nothing.
Now for nuance it seems like that game has a somewhat more involved story line that still has a big open ending and playing as the new character class was quite an enjoyable experience.
My final verdict is that if you are really looking for a game that you can casually play with friends during LAN events or get togethers that this game can be a nice fix. If you haven't played this series before and are more inclined to play solo anyway I highly recommend to get part 1 instead. If you have already bought and or played part 1 then I am not really comfortable really recommending this one.
I hope the devs get around to fixing some of the bugs in this game to make it a more stable experience.  Until then the game has a lot of potential but sadly fails to deliver.

Cons:

This is a fun game to play, and it's easy to pick up the rules and jump right in.  For a casual gamer like myself, that is a big plus.  The mechanics of "leveling" a card were new to me at first and took a little bit of time to get the hang of, but the best times I've had are figuring out good combos to play.  I played M:tG years and years ago, and at first I tried to approach SolForge like that, but I was not very successful.  I like that there are a bunch of powerful cards that you can work towards and hope that they turn up in a booster, but the ability to purchase basic booster packs using silver you win in game is a much easier way to start growing your collection.  I don't like that you can't trade cards (hopefully that get implemented in some fashion, someday down the road), and all the tournaments that I have entered were filled with very powerful decks (so I lost almost every time), but overall, this game is a great way to spend 15-30 minutes at a  time.  It's still in beta right now, and they tweak the cards when trying new game balances, but it is very polished and I have only had one or two instances where something buggy happened.  Lag is sometimes an issue too, but that might be my local connection more so than anything in the game itself.  Give SolForge a try, it is worth it.

First, let me make clear that this game does unfortunately not feature any literal butlers.
Now with the most pressing question answered, quick spoiler-free review:

The plot mainly revolves around a murder mystery. You try to make sense of clues and interrogate suspects.
It's all pretty well constructed overall. The pacing can be a bit slow in the beginning, however.
There is a defined theme in this story, that is embodied by the detective, and which the protagonist is confronted with.
With that, it does set itself apart a little from being 'just' a mystery. I do think there was more potential that wasn't done to explore it here, but overall it's implemented well.

The titular detective arguably steals the show, which does mean some others get a little less time to shine. Still, a surprising amount of backstory is explored with some characters (arguably too much in some cases). They can still end up rather forgettable in comparison though.
What about our protagonist Gilligan? He also gets some development over the course of the story, and does have one or two really good moments. I've seen worse.

What you see in the screen above is what you get, pretty much. Good sprites, filtered backgrounds. It's usually possible to tell what you're looking at and visualize the scene.
There are some CGs to change it up here and there. They are not terribly detailed but still nice to look at.
The sound direction is pretty atmospheric and always fitting. The tracks themselves are mostly simple in quality, but a lot of them have catchy melodies.
Sound effects are also present and well-used to add a nice little touch here and there.
Heh, well it's mostly a kinetic novel. In other words, you just read through the whole thing by clicking.
There is a detailed journal that gets frequently updated with clues that you can read to try and figure things out yourself, which *is* very helpful to stay on top of things. (or if you just like the hunt for all that little extra information).
But yeah, you do not get to directly influence anything beyond choosing the order in which you read things at some point, so no
gameplay.
Well done for what it is.
No harm to give it a try if you like murder mysteries. It's free, after all.
Might seem a little slow in the beginning, but it's actually not terribly long.
You can probably read through it in a couple hours.

I just managed to complete the game, and the direction the game was taking toward the end of the game left me mostly dissatisfied. I think that this is a fantastic puzzler, and a great U-turn back toward what makes (made?) the Broken Sword series so good back in the day. However, when coming toward the final act of part two (roughly 80% into the game) you are faced with an extremely taxing puzzle that slows the pacing of the game down to a crawl. Upon completing this puzzle you are then faced with a situation where your antagonist miraculously knows off-hand all the information that you just toiled away to figure out, from the remains of a person who (literally) took the secret information to his grave. This scenario had me so irate that I began to pay attention to the flaws in the game: the way that characters turn their entire morality upside-down with little effort, the lacklustre voice acting from the supporting cast, the crutch of returning characters from the first two games in the series that the game leaned upon the entire time, and finally the extremely anti-climactic ending that isn't without its fair helping of cheese.
I feel that Part one is fantastic: the puzzles are exciting and the pacing of the story is well maintained. I only felt aggrieved toward the end when the dialogue practically vomited out all the loose ends that needed to be resolved in Part 2 (back when this title was split) like a cat regurgitating hairballs. It was poor writing and it left a bad taste in my mouth. Part 2 felt very rushed in comparison; I'm not sure what deadline the team were under, but the story was leaping from location to location at an uncomfortable pace and the puzzles became less about solving riddles and using logic and more of the classic point-and-click trope of "try combining all your items in your inventory and see what♥♥♥♥♥♥sticks this time".
Despite all that I will recommend this game to lovers of the point-and-click adventure genre. It has its great moments, but is let down by the pacing and disappointing conclusion. At times it really does remind you that it is a Broken Sword game, but when you try and compare it to the original and its first sequel, it sadly falls by the wayside. Broken Sword 5 takes bronze in the series.

PROS:
- Basically infinite exploration
- Even the loot and the weapons are randomized, so no weapon is the same
- Lots of mod support
- Great variety in gear and races
- Mechs
CONS:
- Planets feel all the same, but retextured
- Haves a quest line forced on you
- Poor design choices, like techs or not being able to beam up deep underground
- Loot feels extremely underwhelming, especially the guns
- Combat is just not fun
- Exploration isn't rewarded since loot is underwhelming, loot from quests included
- Scan quests. ♥♥♥♥ing scan quests.
Overall, the game is a great idea horribly executed. Combat is underwhelming, loot is underwhelming, exploration is underwhelming, rewards are underwhelming. The game is just not fun.
It started well, a space exploration sandbox game, but the game now haves this boring quest line you have to do to unlock certain things, and it would be fine if the quests weren't horribly unfun.
Poor design choices, like not being able to use more than one tech at a time, or even equip more than one tech at a time. What's the point of unlocking them all if I can only use one? And it's not even a progression, you can unlock any of them at any given time, if you have the tech cards necessary for it. Only a few of them are even useful.
Digging deep rewards you with better ores, aswell as some cores to make bombs. But then you have to jump your way up all over again, which is slow, since you can't beam to your ship from the underground.
Scan quests are basically going to a specific type of planet and HOPE TO GOD they have the things you need to scan, else you'll be here for a week trying to find a damn planet with the right items to scan so you can progress. And they might even repeat the same items too, so even if you find two planets with the villages or dungeons from the race you need to scan, you will still be out of luck since you can't scan the same thing twice.
Game feels extremely empty as planets have barely nothing for you to explore. You beam to a planet, mine the ores, and get out. There's really nothing else to do there. Maybe you'll find a village with some merchant selling good stuff and getting some quests to upgrade your ship, but that's it. And that's a very solid maybe, because you might aswell find nothing.
I really can't recommend this game for anyone who wants to have fun. I might've recommended it a couple of years or so ago, but now? Game is horrible.

In many other games that I have played, I would have liked to download mods, but it was usually a very long and tedious task. Therefore by having such and easy system of downloading mods, I kept playing Starbound far past completeing the initial story. Aside form mods, the gameplay was usually smooth, (unless you were playing with friends or on a server. The game could lag quite severly sometimes) and it was easy to get a hang of the game. One of the main parts for me was probably the amount of customization. Sure it may not actually be insane customization where you can change every single aspect of your characters body and features, but still I liked it. When games have customization features for about every part of your character, sometimes it can get a little wacky and look weird. Starbound on the other hand, kept the customization simple to the point were you can make your character just unique enough for you. Luckily there wasn't too much customization, since I have a weird thing for games with character customizations, I can literally spend probably hours on end just making a character.
Like I said earlier this is one of my most favorite games. I don't really care what other people think about there being a shallow plot, or bosses being too easy. This game is a lot of fun for me and had many aspects of games that I love. I really have to applaud the developers for being able to make a game that made me write this much!

I just completed the game (Normal Iron mode) and wanted to share my thoughts.
The game is often compared to X-COM for its tactical component and therefore criticized for having less depth in this segment.
I would say this:
- It is less deep (big difference is overwatch), but still deep enough to enjoy.
- It is faster! You will handle many encounters upon finishing the game (around 30), so it is a good thing.
- The tactical maps are not too varied and rather small. But in the end, it helps making the combat resolution faster as you don't have to seek enemies everywhere.
This fast pace suits the game as it focuses on managing generation of heroes.  You want to see how generations evolve and not linger for hours in tactical and wait hours in the management part of the game. So, I think it is sound design here. This is what will make you love or hate the game. You have to consider if it works for you or not if you hesitate purchasing.
I still felt attached to some of my heroes (not for so long, at best you play 4 times with them). The fact that they are not long-lived makes it so that you are not punished hard when you lose one. And there is always the next hero to be fond of.
The setting/theme of the game is original (never seen elsewhere monsters), the chalice, the generations of heroes makes for a new experience, never played before game. In this day and age of sequels/clones, it was a good surprise.
Graphics: Atypical but very clean and I liked them. I loved the fact that the armors/weapons get different looks when research advances. It shows care for details.
Music is also very good. The voices are superb.
The controls are very well done.
The game is really balanced in my opinion. Funnily, I read most people use hunters. I used my alchemists (brewtalists to be exact) so there is more than one way to play  the game. This is positive obviously. Some research options on the weapons open tactics as the abilities offered by the different classes.
Is there anything not to like? Well, for me: not really. I just have some regrets though:
Sometimes, it is a bit difficult to understand exactly how stats and traits are propagated. Granted, part of the fun is maybe to figure that out.
I wished there were better ways to track heroes in the different blood lines. There is a small family tree, but would have liked an overview.
I sometimes wished there was the (optional) possibility to customize heroes/Houses. But the Houses out of the box are already very enjoyable.
I somehow, want more... So many heroes were 'lost'. You can assign them to research, training, combat or breeding. I wished there were just more to it (more options), more events, leaderboards of heroes and so on...
I do realize though that more features could work against the design of a fast paced game with constant choices.
Relics were a brilliant idea to have some cross generations element, I wished for more. More logs/relations between heroes.
Congratulations to the developers, this is a very unique, well designed, well executed and beautiful game.
I will finish with a last comparison with X-COM :the price. Price tags at release were very different. I would dare to say that quality/price, they are a close match, or maybe even Massive Chalice is the winner there.

A fun arena brawler with a unique, physics based combat engine. While certainly a proof of concept for their next game (Sui Generis, in fact) this still stands as a great deal of enjoyment in a small package. Exanima is an isometric, combat focused "RPG" with a loosely tied-in skill/trait system with two distinct modes. The first is a Souls style story mode, right now with only one dungeon, in which you will run screaming from mobs of zombies/ghouls in order to collect the minimal pieces of a very particular story. However, there is no saving, map, minimap, or smart cursor for navigating the samey dungeons with means a monumental amount of your time will be spent backtracking and irritated. Story Mode is my least favorite of the two, and truly, this game could do well to lose it entirely to focus on the enjoyable part -- Arena
In Arena Mode you make a persistent character and go through numerous challenges for a monetary reward, which you use to recruit new "gladiators" so to speak -- a party rotation of sorts is nescessary in exanima because damage is almost entirely permanent unless your armor suffices. You can buy gear, recruit people, and take on more challenging missions with a truly fantastic AI to fight against. The devs promise ranged and magical combat, and base building, next.
The reason why you're reading this review and looking to buy this is for the combat. Well, it's great! ...But sluggish. Every weapon is cut and slashed like it weights 20lbs, and armor does little to nothing to affect how fast/slowly you move. There is no stamina either, which means every battle is a challenge to simply out finesse, parry, and execute your opponent. Fights can be over in seconds or ten minutes depending on gear, and every animation is procedurally generated. I have had my billhook get stuck in an opponents shield, only to be pushed to the floor, stepped on, and overhead swung to death by a mace.
If you swing left to right and they parry, your sword will be deflected and spark off the floor, but you can duck their incoming riposte and follow through with a lunge. You've never played anything like it. Exanima is the proof of concept and tech demo for their next game, a true RPG, but provides a ton of fun through an ever expanding arena brawler mode.

I don't understand the hatred for this game.
Double FIne did that debacle for DF-9 so don't buy from them! It's an X-COM lite with worse strategy and tactical layer -- go get Klei's Invisible Inc instead! The artwork sucks -- what is this boxy polygon artwork thing? It's got no theme and I can't customize characters and they die too fast!
So goes all the complaints.
First off, I have to state I'm not Double Fine's typical customer -- I typically don't play anything in the adventure genre. Secondly, I love this game so far, and it's as good and interesting as XCOM and Invisible Inc (which is also brilliant).
Why?
Because the game is a great mechanically - the strategic and tactical layer intersect in really interesting ways. Particularly on higher difficulties and later in the game, small choices can have serious repercussions.
For example, choose that "passionless" old vanguard for your crucible to pass on his experience and you will affect the kingdom's fertility bloodlines further down the road. Don't choose him and you might get outmatched by the Cadence levels. Spend time researching things you don't need and you will get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked on harder levels.
You need to have enough bloodlines, enough technology (weapons and items), hopefully pass down enough relics, have enough vanguard experience to do well. Mechanically, it is a really interesting game.
It took me some time to really get and love this game, which I guess is its biggest flaw. At first I thought it was a tad easy mid-game and there were not many options and hunters/alchemists were the best way to go. Suffice to say I was wrong and the late game really shines: Interesting valid tactical skills, difficult battles, difficult strategic decisions that have you second guessing yourself.
Forward to later, after rebooting the game several times running on hard, all the classes are interesting, with interesting skills. Caberjacks are by no means useless. As a crowd control class, they really shine later in the game.
To charge that the game has no depth because it has no overwatch, or cover doesn't cut it. It is different, and as a big lover of tactical games like XCOM and Invisible Inc, I will state that this game is good, just different. Another game to compare this to is King of Dragon Pass (the random events at least), which adds another unusual flavour to the game.
In summary, I guess the hatred for this game is because of expectations. It doesn't feel like a Double Fine game at all.
There is not much story or exposition, but as a strategic/tactical hybrid, this game is different, and a really good different: I've been enjoying it quite a bit.

This game is a lot of fun. It is not, however, a deep strategy masterpiece. Really, this game is Oregon Trail set within the Game of Thrones series.
You are an immortal king, bound to a Massive talking cup. You make choices on which houses to breed, where to guide research, and who to send into battle. Instead of traveling a trail from Missouri to Oregon, you're watching the impact of your decisions as you travel a timeline from the present to the future.
Instead of shooting bears with a green pixel, you have a battle system consisting of a fun light-tactics RPG format. There is a lot of similarity to recent titles like X-Com, Shadowrun, or Banner Saga.
I beat the game in about 15 hours, and had a lot of fun with it while I did. There is some fair replay value to see how some of my decisions could have panned out differently, but you're likely to take a break and come back to it later.
Not as thematicall engrossing as XCOM, but the gameplay is well-balanced and fun.

I had some fun playing with Massive Chalice when I first installed it. The bloodline ideas, Game of Thrones/Birthright vibes and X-Com style game play were engaging and the graphics, audio and interface were good enough to keep me in the game. Unfortunately, the more I played the more the veneer of an interactive world fell away and I was left with a puzzle game; moving the pegs, filling the holes and becoming painfully aware of the fact that it was all about figuring out the underlying equations. I know this is the essential reality of all single-person computer games and if I’m playing a game with no pretense of creating a living environment, that’s fine. But Massive Chalice does have pretenses and they just do not stand the test of time.
There’s real potential for a good game here especially in the concepts and with a bigger playing field, more randomness and most of all a greater sense of a living, breathing world, this could have been an outstanding title. When it comes to a thumbs up or thumbs down on Steam, I generally go by value for price. As the game stands right now at full price it’s about ten dollars short.

The Haunted Hells Reach is a third person action horror cooperative game. The goal is to liberate cursed places and survive the assault from the minions of Hell.
Four game modes are offered: Survival, Battle, Demonizer and Inferno. Each mode can be played on any of The Haunted’s eight maps.
Survival simply makes you keep fighting until you die, which is not a particularly engaging objective, while Battle and Demonizer are The Haunted’s efforts at player-versus-player modes. In Inferno, which is the best mode of the game, four players must survive four waves of enemies that increase in number and power over time before fighting Abaddon, a huge boss monster in a separate Hell level.
The player is equiped with a handgun, shotgun, machine gun and knife. You will unlock upgrades to these as you kill.
The game has also a deep melee system that gives the player an easy way out when surrounded by undead.
Unfortunately, networking issues can make locating or connecting to someone’s game difficult. The biggest problem of The Haunted Hells Reach is that joining a game forces you to wait until the next wave of enemies, which can sometimes be 10+ minutes until you can finally play.
in my opinion, if you are seeking a new, unique team-based game to play with some friends, The Haunted Hells Reach is a worthy choice.

This isn't for the faint of heart, or those easily frustrated, but if you're persistient enough it's a great stealth game and well worth a buy.
The game is set in the context of an interrogation by a Russian intelligence officer of the protagonist, Sermion Strogov, as he recalls several missions he was involved in during WW2, in various different countries and with different goals. That isn't a spoiler, as the story is completely worthless and adds virtually nothing to the experience, it's just there to provide context. Your average Call of Duty game is more story-focused, so don't get this if you're looking for a deep, intriuging narrative experience.
The level design and stealth system are both great. Levels are fairly varied, though a few missions are quite similar to one another. Trial and error is crucial - this is a very hard game, and you will die, or be discovered, or fail, a lot. Constantly dropping saves before doing anything risky at all is strongly advised - it is not a pleseant experience to have to reload back 5 minutes because you messed up avoiding a single guard.
The health system is BRUTAL - no regenerating health or bullet sponge hero here. Strogov will die extremely quickly under fire, and there is no cover system so being discovered is essentialy a death sentence. Trying to just shoot everyone is pointless - you'll just die over and over again.
The graphics still stand up in 2016 - it looks dated, but not awful.
The controls are fairly bog-standard, and as someone who is primarily a console gamer I found them surprisingly good. However, you have to constantly correct Strogov's movement - for some reason, he walks diagonally by default.
There are a few irritating animation glitches, but nothing gamebreaking and certainly not what other reviewers are sugguesting.
Whether or not you get enjoyment out of this is basically down to how much failure you're willing to put up with. Just use your head, think what the logical solution is and you'll fail slightly less.

Quite the addictive Tower Defense esque game. I am writing tower defense esque, because you are not exactly fighting waves of enemies, but instead you are fighting waves of goo. The goo is generated by one or more spawner on a topographic map. The spawner acts as well for the liquid goo that is starting to slowly spread from its origin and you are tasked with destroying the spawner.
In order to destroy the spawner you have to build an infrastructure that can fuel and provide your military forces (Towers) the necessary energy to stem the tide of the goo. You start from your own base/spaceship and extend from there, building collectors and relay stations in order to gather and transport energy to the guns. The guns once build have to be provided with energy in order to shoot. If the goo touches the base of the installation, the installation gets destroyed.
As mentioned before, you are fighting on a tophographic map, which means every map has several layers and you can for example use the high advantage of a plateau in order to attack the goo beneath it. The goo, behaving like a liquid has to fill the entire level, before it can advance in height, which can be used by the player via terraforming the level.
A quite addicting little game. Although, little might be a bit confusing. There seem to be at least 250 levels in the game, and for the hardcore, there are time attack leaderboards.

ШП is a challenging and unique puzzle game containing three different puzzles where you click on seemingly random buttons laid throughout an interface in order to solve the puzzle. In order to solve the puzzles, you must experiment with the various buttons and figure out the function each button serves and how you can utilize it to progress. There are not many aspects I can talk about due to the lack of content, so I will discuss the gameplay and the aesthetic design.
During my time playing this game, I often found myself confused. This is due to the sheer difficulty the puzzles offer, as the puzzles present an interface with various buttons scattered over the window with either nothing written on them or labels that seemed to not make any sense. This great level of difficulty and vagueness means that this is not a game for everyone or the general public, so I would suggest making easier puzzles that gradually lead to harder and more impossible puzzles so that the players can get the hang of the game. The seeming randomness of the buttons on the interface further makes the puzzles difficult and confusing. Nevertheless, puzzle solvers may enjoy this game if they like to experiment with puzzles and use logical steps to solve the puzzles. I also like the challenge the puzzles present and uniqueness of the game. It’s not often that I would come across a puzzle where players would mainly experiment and make use of ambiguous clues in order to solve it.
For a game containing interface-based puzzles, I find the old Windows theme highly appropriate. However, this comes at a cost of lowering appeal. Additionally, the randomness of the buttons on the interface does not make it appealing; rather, it makes it seem like a jumbled up mess of a game. I suggest at least making the game appear a bit more refined.
To conclude, ШП is a unique but hard and vague puzzle game that will not appeal to most players; however, there is room for improvement on consumer appeal. As of its current state, I only recommend this to puzzle solvers who enjoy challenging themselves. For its three puzzles, the game is worth its price.

Minimalism. The word that could better describe this puzzle game. Besides difficult. And unusual.
ШП (read Ship) is an "out of standards" puzzle game. What does it mean? It doesn't mean it follows other ways to make a game. It means it takes away every standard leaving just the essence. ШП presents itself as a classic OS window with buttons, scroll bars, checkboxes and text fields. The purpose is to obtain a result (which should be the closure of the game itself... CLICKING ON THE RED X DOESN'T COUNT!) through a precise sequence and combination of actions. Each single action gets a consequence and the order is very important and hidden in the appearently nonsense messages and popup windows generated along the process. One of the most specific aspects of the game lies in these messages. All texts and messages appear to be totally nonsense... At first sight. But they actully hide clues and references for the required actions to do in order to complete the game. Hence gameplay consists in understanding exactly what each action really do and interpreting the weird messages appearing on screen.
ШП Doesn't explain you anything. All you need to understand what the game is about has already been written in its steam page (making the first half of this review quite useless). Once the game starts you're directly at work. So no classic explanation, examples, or what we could call introductive tutorial. The game requires the player to adapt to such an unusual lack of context that represent an increase of difficulty over any common game. There's no progressive growth in the game, where you start with something simple and at hand to get how all mechanics works to then get to increasingly difficult situations. It's like you want to break a pile of bricks with a fist. Some people are trained and can do that, but most of people are not and should start with something easier and then proceed to something harder until they're strong enough to break that pile.
And this is how ШП could feel like. Are you a smart mind used to riddles, patiend and analytic enough to invest your time in these riddles? This is your game and will surely test your skills. Are you a casual gamer, someone that likes action games, or stories, or adventures, or point & click adventures? You won't find much for you in this game, and the problem is that the second group makes the most of the mass (which I am part of), hence this is the reason I do not recommend this game.

From the Depths is a complex but wonderful game that possesses a plethora of blocks to choose from when it comes to designing and building your own unique ships, airships, submarines, helicopters, propeller-driven planes, jets, space ships, satellites, gliders, cannons, missiles, the housings of said cannons and missiles, land vehicles including tanks, half-tracks, anything with wheels, and anything without wheels (<yes, hovercraft too). ... I suppose it still needs train 'tracks' but you can also build "trains" too.
The scope of what you can build in this game (and put it to use) is really unlimited as compared to many other building block titles.
In addition, there are campaigns that you can do that allow you to test your designs against NPC factions and over a rather large game world as well. Depending on your world settings, this means that you may have to take logistics into account with regards to providing supply-lines for transporting repair material and ammunition in order maintain your forces far from your base. <this means supply ships/aircraft etc.
A "Small" list of things that you will need to consider when designing:
-Material type and defense/response to incomming fire. (Spalling (aka fragmenting) and armor penetrating rounds behave differently to different materials and angles of armor)
-Bulkheads and interior spacing. (It's not always needed, or viable for small designs, but it certainly helps keep a ship afloat)
-Center of Mass. (very important when creating aircraft; especially helicopters)
-Drag (the actual blocks you place on the front of your craft actually matters as having a flat face will make it slow down due to water/air resistance).
-Target Detection (there are blocks dedicated to detecting a target and some are better at, specifically designed to, detecting certain things)
-Target Tracking (there are blocks that are dedicated to keeping track of those targets and they provide various levels of aiming accuracy)
-Defensive Armaments such as Flak, Anti-missile missiles, CWIS, lasers, and Flares. (Because you will be getting shot at with missiles often)
-Offensive Armaments. (Because this is a combat-oriented game)
-And last, but most certainly not least, is the AI and control blocks (This one will have you cursing some times but its so damn gratifying when everything comes together)
Now the trade-off for all of that...
-The game is difficult to learn obviously as the amount of different blocks that are provided (that allow you build all of those previously mentioned things) interact together in many, numerious ways. This is not a game where you simply place a single block and that single block does everything for you. You will need to use many different blocks if you are going to create a functional design.
-The game uses "real-world" physics (to a degree) with regards to drag, center of mass, and certain blocks mimic real-world counterparts. This means that you must take into consideration many design problems that exist in the real world; meaning that some level of engineering and fluid dynamics should be understood (or can greatly help you when trying to build something). <simply having a basic understanding of  "Center of Mass" will help you when building helicopters and other such aircraft but so too is knowing that wings provide lift and that lift is applied at the wing rather than center of mass.
-The Tutorials are... not overly helpful. Sorry Devs; it helps, but that tutorial needs some TLC. You will be watching Youtube for the majority of your learning process and more than likely refreshing your mind with the tutorials/examples provided. Hint: Some things actually need to be oriented in a specific way in order to connect to certain things.
-The more complex you create your designs the harder it is for the AI to pilot/command the thing you build. The AI is simple and there are ways to get it to work with complex builds. But this generally requires some level of programming (to which i have zero skill in). But they do provide simple "control blocks" that can allow you, yourself to work around some of these problems and setup actions based upon what your craft is doing (or suppose to be doing) at a given time.
Other than that, the game is not the prettiest out there. It does not let you deform the terrain (did once but was removed for performance reasons I think). And it's not something that you can expect to pick up on in one day or perhaps even a week.
But when it comes to building and creating your own personal army, navy, or airforce and the weapons that they use, there is no comparison. In addition, the Devs continue to add more and more to it so it still has some work to be done which is nothing but good news for those of us who like more to work with.
