This remaster is probably the best version of the game so far, though I've never played any Turok game prior to this one. I do question why the
is kept here and has to be kept on since I'm pretty sure most people's computers can run this remastered but still age-old game. There's an "Extended Draw Distance" option but that only lets you view a little further ahead. I've only seen a couple of enemies actually fire at me from beyond the fog so I don't see much reason to at least not have the option to remove that. At the very least the fog along with the graphics gives it that 90s feel.
A training mode of sorts is available that pretty much teaches you the how-tos of the game.
There's a prologue which after that's cleared you'll reach The Hub which is just an interactive level select area. There are 8 pretty long levels to go through with only 4 bosses in those 8 levels and the final boss only a minute after the 3rd's been defeated.
Within each level there are 3 keys to collect for unlocking later levels, usually the next one after the current. The 7th level only has 2 and the 8th has none. While they're generally not hard to find, it's possible to actually miss a key as you play so if you exited the area or the level doesn't permit you to backtrack to find the missing key you'll have to exit the level from the end and re-enter from the beginning so you can do a proper search through. There's a "Keys" list in the pause menu that allow you to see which specific key you've acquired so you can pretty much determine which ones you've missed. Most of the levels are linear somewhat but they generally have plenty of side routes to sidetrack yourself to as well as secret rooms for useful items or otherwise.
As most FPS bosses go their fights aren't very impressive as they're mainly just run & shoot but the idea of fighting one here is a benefit in itself as it's a nice change of pace from the usual levels. Plus, concepts like fighting a cyborg t-rex is always a really cool thing to think about.
There's a dynamic map you can view that's really more of an outline of what you've explored. It starts to fill as you go through places you haven't gone to yet but as far as I know you can't zoom out and can only look at parts of the map that's around your location.
Except for the 8th level's case you can revisit each level again although everything you've picked up and done will stay that way. In a way, ammo and such throughout the game are actually limited and you can't conventionally "resupply" yourself but the game's
enough to
enough to get you through, at least on Hard Difficulty and lower. However this can also mean that the fun in using preferred weapons can vanish fast especially when tougher & bullet-spongier enemies start to come in and it doesn't help that the amount of ammo you can carry for every weapon is, to me, really small even if there are loads of weapons to find & carry. Some weapons use the same ammo and two of the weapons have explosive ammo that apparently if you pick them up for said weapon you can't switch to using their regular ammo until you deplete the explosives first; the damage they deal is significantly higher but it just makes for BS reasons to conserve. You've got a knife and you can circle most enemies while slashing them until they die but that just takes too long.
The game uses a lives system though they're plentiful enough and there are a small number of places in each level you can save your game to. Dying respawns you to the nearest save point or checkpoint and a Game Over obviously means you'd just have to load from a save file.
There are various health items to pick up as well as overhealing ones and armor that replaces your health completely until the armor itself is gone. The armor here doesn't act like your health at all. The number the armor will represent will indicate how many number of hits it can take from anything before the armor disappears. While you've got armor equipped you can continue to heal and overheal until the maximum you can overheal is reached, which is 250. If somehow you die say from falling to a bottomless pit then obviously the overheal and armor vanish and you respawn with the default max, 100.
Plenty of neat platforming sections in here with many of the platforms almost impossibly smaller than one another. Of course plenty of these sections will have dangerous falls and few with bottomless pits as well as enemies firing at you as you jump from surface to surface. Ironically there's no fall-damage so jumping from any height to a surface below that's designed to be walked on won't hurt unless it's lava or some other hazardous surface. Even those don't do a whole lot of damage unless you're keen on staying there.
It's a remastered game suited and polished for modern PCs while still retaining its 90s game design charm with even a cheat menu being available. The levels can feel pretty lengthy and can get tedious since you're generally doing the same key searching over and over again only in different environments, but I do think the gameplay itself is solid with how fast & tense it can get. It takes a little around an hour to beat a level so the game can probably be finished in around 8, even while trying to find secrets along the way.

This really surpassed all of my expectations. I remember growing up with this game - my parents wouldn't have it in our house, but I'd play it all night with my best friend when I'd sleep over at his place - and I only went into it expecting to get a nice nostalgia boost. It is, however, much, much better than I remember it being. Due to this excellent port, the ability to finally play the game with proper keyboard/mouse support, and excellent customization options for both the graphics and gameplay (setting the difficulty to 'hardcore' is very challenging), this version of Turok feels like the definitive version of Turok. It does not feel like an N64 game exactly - it feels like an N64 game reimagined and remastered perfectly for PC. Flying through the labyrinthian levels and blowing away tons of creatures feels nearly as responsive and fluid as it does in classic iD software games like DooM and Quake, and the weapons are cool and fun to shoot.
It's a steal when it's on sale, but now, having played it, I could recommend this game for its full $20 asking price - even if the developers never get around to finishing and releasing the SDK. That's right, there is/was an SDK in development for this game. Heres to hoping it sees the light of day.

It is true when people compare it to World War 2 Hitman. For example, most dead NPC's uniforms can be stolen and worn. Be warned though: This game is hard! I don't play many stealth games, but even on the lowest difficulty, the enemy's suspicion meter seems to increase very quickly and easily. One thing that makes stealth hard is that silent takedowns are hard to perform. When you crouch run behind the enemy to complete a takedown, their suspicion raises to full almost instantly. If you screw up here, the guard will turn around and quickly unload a mag and kill you. Another thing, which I have yet to see in another stealth game, is that when you are disguised and walk into a guard's "cone of vision", their cone of vision will follow you for a time because they are watching you, which could lead to the suspicion meter growing. Also, even when disguised, like in hitman, higher ranked NPC's will get suspicious of you faster.
So far, I have not completely finished any level stealthily, as I'm not very patient. Instead, I use more of a run-and-gun playstyle with a small mix of stealth. So far there have not been any stealth requirement levels, but I expect one might come up. One thing to note if you plan on run and gunning is that the guns are realistic in terms of recoil. Holding down the trigger for more than 2 seconds will send your sights flying upwards, so you will find yourself clicking your left mouse button for every shot to be accurate, even on smgs.
One con that I have noticed is that on multiple occasions, I would stealth kill one guard, and then the body gets found. Normal, right? Well, if there are five or six guards nearby, and they all see the body, they will run to it and start searching nearby. This system makes it so that at times, one body will make multiple guards clump around it and make easy targets of themselves. A couple of times, I've thrown a grenade at these groups and gotten multiple easy kills.
Another problem is that if you camp in a one enterance area and hold your crosshairs on the door, wave after wave of guards will come running through the door idiotically, and run right into your spray. The only way they can prevent this, is if they see you, they will sometimes throw a grenade at you (Instant death, no matter how much health). The problem with this is if you are camping a door, you will most likely spray them down before they have time to throw a grenade. Because of this exploit, after several camping sessions, the door way would literally have a heap of 10 to 15 corpses.
Another complaint I have is that when driving cars, going reverse will make the camera akwardly look down, then back. Also if you are reversing, the camera gets locked looking backwards, meaning that you cannot look in fromt of you while reversing, and vice-versa (this mechanic gets really annoying specially when you are trying to escape guards and can't look at them unless you are driving towards them.
Also, if you are worried about content, you don't have to. At the time of me typing this, I have run-and-gunned my way through 3 missions in 9 hours (though I did make it my mission to kill all the nazis on all of those maps, even the ones that were out of the way) Plus, these levels are highly replayable, as you can choose your loadout at the start. You can choose any combination of equiptment you want through a weight system.
Because of the difficulty in stealth, health system (no regen and only one full health medkit-sometimes none-per level) and shooting mechanics, this game really is hardcore stealth-action.
For me, Death to Spies is a steal a $10 for any stealth, action, or WW2 fan!
Oh, and also, lots of people say their game is buggy beyond playability, but I haven't experienced any game-breaking bugs yet. (I'm playing on a windows 10, i7 Laptop with Intel graphics)

Cons:
* 3D Character-models and lazy animations. (There are severall glitches due the mix of 3D-models and 2D-Backgrounds)

I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a challenge but more casual gamers might want to steer clear of the campaign.

I've been longing to create a review for this game for quite a while now, and so instead of waiting more and more, I'll write it now.
Because of my laziness, I'll be making this a con/pros review, explaining different parts a little more than just two words.
PROS
- Very high replayability (No matter how many times I go back to this game, I always find myself enjoying it as much as I have in a previous playthrough)
- Compelling exploration (Almost everytime I land on a planet, I find myself discovering things I may have never seen before even after so many hours, both unique items or structures)
- Character ability addons (As you progress through the game, more and more abilities are revealed to you allowing you to modify your character to traverse better depending on your play style)
- Infinite planets (You'll never run out of planets to explore since the planets are basically infinite)
- Many planet types, biomes and sizes (There's a huge amount of unique biomes you will run into when going through several planets, and the planet types add more atmosphere to it whether it'd be a planet mostly made up of water, or a planet with mass plantation for a more jungle-esque atmosphere. Planets also have different sizes, some being huge whereas some could be small)
- Beautiful soundtrack (Every soundtrack in this game seems to fit wherever you hear it, the day themes, the night themes, and even the boss battle themes)
- Great community (The community seems very nice on most of the forums I've visited, or even ingame. Members of the community even show off coordinates for unique planets or interesting things they've found in their playthrough, which means if you ever need a specific structure or item, there's almost always coordinates for a planet that has what you need provided by the community itself)
- Amazing modding community and support (There are some very game changing or game improving mods out there which you can also mix and match with other mods. If you're looking for a sandbox experience with a lot of modding compatibility, this game is very good at doing that)
- Great multiplayer (You can create a server for you and your friends without having to port forward or use other software to connect. On top of this, connection doesn't seem to be too big of an issue since I almost never notice anyone having bad ping or connection overall)
- Randomly generated gear (Weapons you find in chests or from enemy drops always use randomly generated stats unless they're unique weapons)
- Quests and side quests (The game has a lot of side quests along with the main quests. Each of these quests are rewarding in some way, some giving out bigger rewards and some smaller rewards)
CONS
- Limited story (Although the game itself has a main story, it isn't exactly the best. The story feels a little rushed and lacks depth, always feeling very straight forward or even a little random at some points. Along with this, some of the objectives you go through to continue the story feels like they're copy paste, meaning one objective feels like another objective you've already done just slightly changed. This game isn't very well suited for people looking for an interesting story)
- Some modding issues (The game will often crash if two mods don't go well together, especially if they're both changing a feature at the same time. This can however be avoided as long as you don't subscribe to mods that aren't compatible with another mod or the version of your game)
- Slow progression at the start (New players will often find themselves progressing very slowly at the start, and even players who are returning to the game may experience that the progression is quite slow at the start. The game requires you to go through a couple of chores at the start before you can do much)
- Repetitive combat (Although combat can feel somewhat satisfying almost always, you'll realise that the combat is very repetitive mostly when it comes to melee weaponry. There aren't very many "special" attacks for melee weaponry or ranged weaponry, meaning you mostly just have to spam your left click on a target)
- Re-used enemy sprites, or enemies in general (Every now and then when you start exploring a planet, some of the enemies you see have already appeared on a previous planet, and this seems to happen frequently with planet wildlife)
That's about all I can think of in my 270+ hours I've put into this game.
In conclusion, the game is amazing if you really like exploration, amazing community, sandbox-esque games, RNG type stuff, character development, and overall a game to come back to over and over again rather than a game heavily based on story and non-RNG elements.

It pains me to put a 'not recommended' mark here. (Also was not an early access contributor).
The game starts out with a brilliant concept, beautiful visuals and atmosphere.
It quickly turns into jumping puzzles. Then more jumping puzzles, then vaguely timed jumping puzzles. Then jumping puzzles in the dark with no clear path, leading to keyboard-snapping frustration.
I approached this expecting an exploration/story/adventure game, in the same vein as Dear Esther. The first hour or so of that game is exactly that, until it jumps off the rails and becomes Slender with jumping puzzles.
The one thing that kept me on task to finish the game were the visuals, straight out of 60-70's era sci-fi, beautiful and eerie. Come for the visuals, leave before the jumping puzzles make you kick the wall.

The trailer sold me. It seemed like a really cool idea and I really wanted to like it.
The atmosphere, the music, and the setup of the story is fantastic. However, after an hour into the game I came to following conclusions:
- You walk. A lot. It's a complete walking simulator with big giant set pieces that set up the isolation that you're supposed to feel. It works, but most of the time I played it I was walking instead of looking around trying to get the story going.
- It's very linear. The game is on rails and you can tell that you can't go to certain areas. The terrain luckily blocks you from going anywhere that the story doesn't want you to and it got old pretty fast.
- The jumping is hugely awkward. You also jump a whole lot as well. There were plenty of times where the jumping wasn't accurate and I feel off the many platform rocks because I jumped too short or too far. You try and angle the camera to give you the best shot but you never know if you're going to stick a landing. This is especially frustrating if you fall off at the end of one of many jumping sequences and you have to traverse to the beginning of the area because the scenes are so big.
- The Mystery of the story seemed to be solved within the first minute and a new mystery popped up in order to replace it but by this time you don't care. If the first mystery was stretched out instead of given away for such a cliche second one, I'd much prefer that set up.
What ultimately caused me to stop playing the game was one such jumping sequence where I over jumped a ledge in the dark and fell to my death. Normally not a big deal but when I respawned, I was in the middle of a rock and unable to move. A Menu selection of to my last checkpoint did nothing to ease my problem so I restarted the game. When I reached a story/plot note that autocollects in your PDA, it registered but I fould the rest of the story notes blank. I didn't have the motivation to go on without my earlier story notes.
Is that semi-petty that I'm stopping after a glitch in the game? Maybe. But it had lost most of my attention with the issues that plagued it in the first place.
I really wanted to like it, but there's too many games in my library and not enough time in the day to continue with this game. The game does try, but it didn't work for me.

This atmospheric puzzle platformer was an enchanting experience, mixed in with a subtle and absolutely sublime soundtrack. The narrative and method of telling the story kept me completely engrossed in the game, and left me pressing on until the eventual and rewarding end.
Only two puzzles out of the many actually had me stumped. I'll say this, I'm terrible at puzzle games, and this game does not hold your hand, however the puzzles become fairly intuitive as you press on. But beware the 'forest'.
The platforming and controls were quite solid, and one unique thing to note was the characters 'building up speed' as you continued to hold the directional button. Which is a mechanic you should familiarize yourself with, as it becomes important in a few of the platforming portions. There were maybe 3 platforming sections that irritated me, mostly because I didn't know which way to go, but one in particular was due to my inability to time my jumps. I don't fault the game for this at all.
If you have 4-5 hours that you want to spend having a unique and pleasing experience? Then buy this game.

Oh boy, I might be blinded by nostalgia on this one, because this was one of the first FPS games I played, and to this day, still one of my favourites.
Turok: Dinosaur Hunter is a FPS where you play as Tal Set, a badass native american with weapons ranging from a simple knife, to an explosive bow, to shotguns and rifles, alien weapons, a ♥♥♥♥ing fusion cannon akin of the BFG 9000, and even an ancient weapon with power to destroy the Lost Land, place where the game takes place.
You are trying to stop the Campaigner, an evil cyborg that wants to gather all the pieces of the Chronoscepter (Which you're trying to get) so he can fuse it with a weapon in his fortress to harness it's power and rule over the Lost Land. The Lost Land is some kind of weird place, where you'll find endless pits, jungles, ruins, ancient cities, robot fortresses, and all kinds of stuff like that. It's denizens are poachers, soldiers, dinosaurs, giant worms, killer plants, giant bugs, ape like reptile beasts, demons, aliens, natives, hell, all kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥is against you in this game. No regenerating lives, in game save points, so you can't abuse quick saves, and limited lives, quite old school.
Now, I played this game back then using the N64 controller, and I was never really a fan of using a joystick in shooters. (Haters gonna hate)
In my opinion, the shooting was kinda hard, and the platforming was a nightmare at time. Yes, I blame this game for my fear of heights, because some of those jumps are merciless, and if you miss, you plummet down the abyss.
Now, this port feels amazing. Even if the graphics are kinda dated, because it was an N64 game, they gave it a few improvements, like water reflections, sun rays, and stuff like that. And I still managed to keep a smooth 60 FPS no mater how much♥♥♥♥♥♥was moving in my screen. Now, the controls are beautiful. Being able to play this game with a mouse and keyboard made those jumps way easier, and shooting feels way better now. I was able to pull incredibly accurate shots over long distances, something that was quite hard on the N64.
The soundtrack is amazing, still one of my favorites from that era after all of these years. This game is sort of linear, mostly on the first and last levels, but it still forces you to explore every nook and cranny of the map, looking for keys for the next level or Chronoscepter pieces.
The only thing I would kinda dislike about this game is that it's rather short. That, and the base price is kinda high, so I'd recommend waiting for a sale. But yes, maybe it's the nostalgia googles, but I really recommend this game.

The story goes in the style of previous games. It includes all the things Broken Sword is known for - murder, mystery, conspiracy, supernatural elements and goats. A straight port of a classic Nintendo 64 game for the new generation.
Everything you remember about this landmark FPS (Next to of course Goldeneye & Perfect Dark) is included.
The graphics have been slighty bumped up from the original version and the fog has been toned down signifcantly.
But the rest of the gameplay remains the same, running at a solid framerate.
Some gamers might think the original Turok has aged poorly, But this PC port does the game justice.
It's an early example of how far we came when it comes to 3D gaming and how much shooters have changed in nearly 20 years.

SolForge is a great CCG in the vein of Magic: The Gathering.  Unlike Magic, SolForge is much faster and easier to understand (although it still has quite a bit of strategic elements).  Also, SolForge is well adapted to digital play, compared to many CCGs that are really only "paper-based" games.  SolForge's uniqueness is in how it upgrades your cards as you play them, so your Level 1 card becomes stronger (Level 2) the next time you play it in the game.  It's quite a lot of fun to try and turn your small "squires" into giant "Knights" as you play.  The price to play is a bit high, in that you need to buy a starter and if you want more cards, you will need to acquire more boosters.  You can earn some boosters by playing each day and earning in-game currency (silver) to purchase more packs, but it is a slow process.   It is still in Beta design, but I think it's going to a great game once it's totally completed.  Both constructed and booster drafts have recently been introduced and are a LOT of fun.  Originally a dream on Kickstarter, SolForge has become a really fun and enjoyable reality!

What it was, way back:
Fun free to play game.
Excellent tutorial, easy to get into. After a few hours I was playing on hard against the computer, which is just right for me (I lose, I win, I groan at missing the obvious move after ending my turn, I am happy when I manage to turn the table from a bad start,...).
Gameplay: You play creature or spell cards against an opponent, taking turns. Creatures have attack and health, and some have nifty special abilities. That and the spells is what makes this so fun and always different every game. Do you play a spell that gives one of your own creatures +3 attack, stolen from a creature the opponent has, or do you play a creature that can hit anyone with its attack on the next turn? Playing a card also means it's better next time you are dealt it (each has 3 levels), look to the future! You only get 5 cards to pick from every turn (exceptions may come with new, non-starter deck cards).
The game is also very nice at asking you to confirm stuff that isn't really good for you.
You start with 2 decks of 30 cards each, of which you can use either, or a combination you make yourself from the cards in them. To start with the opponent is the computer on easy, normal, or hard, whose decks you can also decide.
I eventually caved in and signed up on their site for the rewards you can get. (For logging in, winning 1 game, and winning 3 games, once every 24h.) And I already got some nifty new cards to use and in-game currency to buy moar cards, all for free!
This also enables me to make my own decks, with said nifty new cards! Only restriction is that you can combine only 2 of the 4 different groups of cards (kinda robots, elements, undead, and nature) per deck. But you can make more than the obvious 6 different combos, with all the cards you soon pile up!
There is the option to use real money, but from what I can see and read in discussions, everything can be had without that.
And  I'd like to play with friends (you need to sign up too, for that). I'm too much of  a coward to play with random strangers yet (also an option when you're logged in).
Plus there's tournaments for folks who are into that!

A few things that I like about this game
The movement system: Skulls of the shogun, rather than having a traditional hexagon/square tile system, allows you to freely move your units within a movement range circle that shrinks as you move.
Combat: This game doesn't over complicate the combat system by having a million different rules and exceptions, the combat system is pretty basic (3 main types of units with several unique spell caster units and a general) while still leaving room for a lot of strategy
Orders: Every turn you can order a maximum of 5 units, which I really like because it involves more strategy, neither you or your opponent can utilize their entire army at once, it forces the player to make smart decisions
The story/campaign: You take the role of the recently deceased Akomoto, a general in feudal Japan, who reveling in his greatest triumph, was stabbed in the back by your former second in command and sent to the land of the dead. Your second in command, who also died shortly after killing you, and has convinced everyone that HE is the great general and taken your rightful place in the paradise of the afterworld, you quickly organize a rebellion in an effort to take back your name and get revenge on the coward who stabbed you in the back. Long story short, the story is funny and entertaining while allowing for some interesting game mechanics
Easy to pick up: This point is really important for me, the game is easy to learn (goes back to not being overly complicated) and fun to play if you don't have a ton of time. Looking at a similar game, like Civ, once you start a game it takes a long time to finish. Skulls of the Shogun has fast paced gameplay that you can get into in only a few minutes, while still being difficult enough to give you an enjoyable challenge.
Overall I really like the game, and I think just completing the campaign, should last you around 20+ hours, I would highly recommend it for a pretty unique strategy game focused more on combat/tactics than other turn based strategy games that require you to build up an army first.

Pitiri is a short entertaining adventure platformer that you can quickly beat.

The music I actually listened to (Most of the time, I turn off the sounds, play the game, and watch Netflix... not this time), and it was great.

Oh, and the game DOES have trading cards, even though the store page doesn't list them. 3 card drops. Devs never updated it?

I struggled a bit with controls and, at times, I was confused about what should I do next, but since the puzzles weren't time-constrained and I wasn't surrounded by enemies or traps (like in Limbo, for example), I gave myself into the exploration of the game's beautiful dream-like world.
There were also some lovely, naive dialogues with a good dose of irony that made me smile. So, that and music and art created a nice overall impression.
Pitiri is a lovely game suitable both for adults and children. It inspired me and showed me a lot of good things that could be done with its engine. And I'm glad that I have another game to offer to my little goddaughter.

I've bought and played all variants of Creeper World, and this is the best one yet.
It's very good at scratching the strategy, RTS, tower-defense itch.
However, the nature of the enemy in most levels, essentially a corrosive liquid, combined with periodic balistic strikes, means that once you have built up your initial defense, you are effectively safe and need only expand your defensive line until you eliminate enemy towers/units. (Yes, I know there are other enemy-types besides the two mentioned above, but none that show up mid-game or late-game, to create dynamic havoc in your carefully laid plans.)
There IS the concept of pre-existing barriers that corrode, giving a timed threat-release, but these are rarely employed to anything like the full potential of providing a mid-game threat. Even if they did, there is nothing that provides a late-game threat or reversal of fortunes, no increasing flood of more powerful foes, etc. There is no ramping up of the initial threat which might turn the tide if you don't deploy for it. Really, the only way to lose a game at the mid-point or toward the end is user error, like uncovering a flank with anti-missle defenses and having an attack get through to the rear. Even then, if it doesn't cut off significant supply lines, which can easily be made redundant, then the front-line may not be affected at all by the misfortune.
But then... you can download fiendish levels that are user-made to solve that problem to a degree.

Lifeless Planet is a peculiar game. On one hand it has that endemic lack of tact in the writing that indie games seem to all share and the production values (for the most part) are sorely lacking at times, but I still found myself playing through it and enjoying it. "Just one more level" was a frequently thought of phrase while playing the game and the source of it was wanting to have closure on the game's narrative.
There's nothing but walking around, platforming and a few simple puzzles (obstacles would be a better description of the puzzles really) and it works for the most part. It is almost woefully simple and linear but the story and a few of the enviroments, though plain, makes Lifeless Planet an oddly engrossing and pretty game. I was disappointed at the rather weak visual design but it still fulfilled my urge of walking on an alien planet in a videogame; I just wished it was better realized.
The music is good but I felt that it tried too hard to be the source of emotion instead of complementing the game, which brings me to a point that nagged me for most of the game. The game, though it tried, didn't really succeed when it tried to be meaningful. Sure there were a few moments that piqued my interest but I felt it was too vague and/or lacked tact when it tried to say something about the situation and the protagonist's motivations. What the story does well enough is that it hooked me into wanting to know more about it, thus pushing me into playing for longer sessions that I wouldn't have otherwise. In another note, the atmosphere was surprisingly good. While I won't call it a horror game, it did an ok job of setting the right amount of tension you'd expect in the same situation. Again, I just wish it was better realized but it still did the job.
In the end, I can recommend the game to people that can look over the plainness and low budget of the game but that think it'd be interesting to explore a planet. While I wouldn't pay full price for it (got it during Steam's Summer Adventure 2014 Sale) it's still a solid and interesting enough of a game for that very specific niche of players.

It's always annoying when technical issues get in the way of enjoyment of a game. I'm doing this to compliment or complain about design decisions, not coding errors. Where's the fun in pointing out that someone forgot to add a colon somewhere in the thousands of lines of text that make up the framework of a game? Still, sometimes games are so badly compromised that it must be mentioned. Clockwork Man: The Hidden World is one such game. It tells the story of Miranda, a young scientist bent of uncovering the secret behind her parents' disappearance nearly a decade earlier. She'll travel to Thule with the help of her clockwork robot sidekick - a small golden droid who speaks entirely in bleeps and bloops, turning him into a sort of combination C-3P0 and R2D2.
Sadly, this journey is hampered by both design errors and technical gaffs, which I'll detail as we move through the... Hidden Object Criteria!
Criteria 1: To what degree do the puzzle screens look like a thrift store vomited on my monitor?
Oh, it's bad. Extremely bad. While the game tries to keep the items true to the steampunk Victorian setting, there is no excuse for how absolutely covered in garbage the game's screens are. One particularly dire example gives a quaint Irish cottage the character of a trash yard, with empty pots, furniture, and bits of food scattered over every concievable surface. Then there are rampant cases of size-cheating - in one case I was asked to look for a pocket knife which was hidden in the spokes of a wagon wheel, making it something along the lines of eighteen inches big. This is all made worse by the developers' decision to include 'scrolling' hidden object screens, in which the player is forced to scroll the screen up/down or left/right to find all the items. I'm baffled by this choice, since it takes the baseline concept of hidden object games - put 20 items on a screen and have the player look for them - and increases the amount of trash-covered space they have to look through by threefold. Absurdly, this massively increased difficulty is accompanied by one of the slowest-to-recharge hint buttons I've ever encountered. Also, during once stretch of playing the game the hint button glitched out on me and flat-out refused to recharge, stranding me alone with some of the most annoying difficult hidden object scenes ever.
Criteria 2: Are the searches justified by the premise/story?
Absolutely not. This is classic 'find a load of nonsense, get one useful item' design. Occasionally the game offers some meagre justification, such as 'clean up all the bottles in this yard' or 'help me find all the food I've squirrelled away', but by and large there's no rationalization given for any of Miranda's searches.
Criteria 3: How well do the various puzzles and object searches meld together to form a coherent whole?
It's a compelling enough narrative - villains are on their way to Thule, where Miranda's parents were last seen, and she's got to go along to stop said conspirators from ruining that paradise undisturbed by history. The journey isn't structured particularly well, opening with Miranda exploring a mine, then flashing back to an extended sequence of searching through offices and attics a few weeks earlier. The developers are trying to use the cinematic device of starting with the action and then zipping back to tell the story, but the mine exploration isn't notably more thrilling than searching for old documents and artifacts hidden in a house - this is a hidden object adventure, after all, and the 'thrilling' scale is only ever going to get so high. While the hidden object puzzles don't usually make the most sense, at least the puzzles hit in nicely with the setting. Repairing a submarine and unlocking alien technology seem like the kind of things that could be solved with clever puzzle design, and they are - but the lack of a skip button could prove terribly frustrating to players looking to just enjoy a pleasant story and some object hunting.
Clockwork Man: The Hidden World has too many missteps to easily recommend. The HOSs are needlessly complicated - beyond their sheer size, they also feature parallax scrolling, meaning that different planes of the background move at different speeds, covering items at different times. Good luck finding a snake when it's only visible for a few degrees halfway to the right edge of the level! Glitches in the hint system mean that sections of the game drag on  far longer than they're welcome, and sometimes the music gets stuck, and continues playing a single set of atmospheric effects in every screen. It's a mess, and the story just isn't good enough to be worth slogging through to experience all of it.

It's better than the first game, but that's not saying much. The first one was absolutely terrible, while this one is merely awful.
The hidden object scenes very inconsistent in difficulty. Most of the objects are glaringly obvious but there's often one or two that are tiny and blend with the background, making them almost impossible to see. This is only made worse by the low resolution. The difficulty progression is also way off; many of the early scenes are far more difficult than ones later in the game. The items in the scenes are quite boring and the player is often required to find multiples of the same object. Some objects are mislabelled, quite badly so in some cases.
The puzzles are for the most part pathetically easy, although, again, some are much harder. And again, this seems to have nothing to do with progression through the game; some are just randomly hard for no apparent reason. Some puzzles lack context, meaning that the only way to solve them is to randomly try things until something works or just wait for the hint bar to charge.
The story is fairly bad, although well acted, and the ending is just rubbish. Perhaps the most annoying thing about it is that it has nothing to do with the story of the first game and in no way addresses the cliffhanger ending from the first. I thought that perhaps it would tie in later on, but nope, it's like the devs just forgot the first game exists. Which in all honesty I can't blame them for since the first game is so atrocious.
Apart from the gameplay itself there are numerous other problems with this game. There are instances where puzzle elements appear almost completely off screen; and by almost completely I mean that only a single pixel is visible. Some objects in the hidden object scenes are behind parts of the interface and so are not visible at all. The click detection is frequently so picky that it refuses to acknowledge that the player has clicked on an object unless the exact couple of pixels that it is happy with are clicked, leading to a great deal of wasted time looking for objects I had already found and clicked on a few times. Also the sound is somewhat bugged. I found numerous instances where lines of dialogue did not play, and at one point the ambient sound in one scene got stuck in a loop and continued to play in every other scene after that.
Having played many HOGs I feel I have a good basis for comparison and I would have to say that this one is not worth it. Not even if it were free. There are many other HOGs that are far better and much more deserving of your time.

I actually have a lot to say about this game. I was initially hesitant on my purchase, as it wouldn't be the first time Early Access has f**ked me. But hey, it was on sale for $10 and I've grown pretty tired of shooting things in the face. Looked like a neat little dungeon crawler. Nothing overly ambitious, but charming at best, I thought. A friend of mine was playing it, so I inquired, and did some market research, as I do before buying a game (#protip). He lamented how the game was "different", mentioning that everything was physics. Well, a lot of games have physics, ... Anyway, I bought it.
Good God, did I not expect what this game was. The store page has a disclaimer on what you're getting. There are videos / etc of the movement / battle mechanics. Now, I may just be numbed out from all the shooters, rpgs, etc, but this game IS different. I got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me within the first 4 minutes. Frantically clicking away, trying to kill one guy, only to be bested time and time again. This is where I'd normally click 'refund' and say f**k this s**t for life. But this game is crack, so I spent, literally, six hours in the games practice mode to learn the controls. This game makes you relearn how to ride a damn bike, and that there is what I'd call innovative. A lot of games make that claim, but they're f**king liars. Exanima doesn't even match a genre of game out there, because it's like 12. Sort of like a rouge-like, isometric, action RPG, dungeon crawler, strategy, rage-educing, panic-simulator. Or, If Dark Souls, Diablo II, and QWOP had a baby, decided they weren't responsible parents, aborted, and let Satan make a game out of the after [un]birth. And I love it.
This has to be one of my new favorite games, as the time I've invested in it has ultimately given me a sense of satisfaction. I feel as if my character is an extension of myself, which feels weird to say, but it's like you [your character] is alone in this world, and you have no idea where you are, why you're there, or what to do. Before I said it's easy to get lost, but it's that sense of 'I'm lost' that you as the player feel, and have to imagine your character would feel very much the same. Those foot steps you hear ahead could mean death, and you might be afraid to move forward, or panic try to escape. It's almost serendipitous. Not many games have the power to evoke a real world emotional response, and it's really quite thrilling. For a beta, and essentially a prequel for anther project, Sui Generis, Exanima is really shaping up to be an amazing game. Challenging, but nonetheless a great piece of work. Bravo Bare Mettle.
It's also worth mentioning that the latest update (0.6.2.0 at time of writing) really cleans up the combat, and has overall improved the experience. The new 'k.o.' feature is nice, but doesnt always save you, but at least you can -try- to save yourself.
I'd recommend this to anyone who likes a challenge and/or is bored of convention, by the numbers RPGs. Also to single moms who have enough stress in life, so why not add video game perma-death anxiety on top of  it.
-Arena- [short ver.]
I initially didn't say much about the games 'Arena' mode, as, well, I forgot to. As follows:
As much as I like to praise the ambition of the core game, Arena in itself is a little busted. It's a beta, yeah, I know. The fighting mechanics are identical to the main game, and perma-death is still in play. You can regain heath after a victory, or hire / recruit a new contender to fight while your main character is on the mend. That's a lovely feature, and adds some mercy to an extent. You wont always win, but you don't always have to die. All in all, it's just a fun sort-of mini game, and can be quite addictive. For blood and glory.
Pro~
+ It has the addictive qualities of heroin. Except if you die, you want revenge instead of an ambulance.
+ While simple in it's own right, the music is atmospheric and really enhances the mood of the game
+ Each fight is unpredictable, and victory is satisfying every time.
+ There isn't an over complicated story, and the little bit you get makes you piece it together. It works.
+ The physics (that word again) allow almost total interaction with the world.
+ The layered armor system is great, and uses practical equipment. 'Metal thongs' need not apply.
+ Sticking to a favored weapon, and honing you skills is almost magical.
+ Arena is fun, and just as rewarding when you axe a guy.
Neut~
= The learning curve for combat is pretty steep. But once you learn it, you love it.
= The control scheme takes a bit to get a handle on. Longer to be competent at. Longer so to use effectively.
= Cheap deaths are going to happen, but it's all relative. 'Get good' actually applies here.
= The skill system is while unfinished, is simplistic, and easy to use. Killing a guy wont make you better at alchemy.
= The free-form inventory is based on weight, not square slots, like Diablo /etc. But can easily be cluttered.
= Arena is still janky, but fuctions well enough. Hope to see MP added >:D
Con~
- VERY easy to get lost. Especially when  looking for a locked door that you probably have the wrong key for.
- No map, or even a mechanic to orient yourself, aside from a compass. Which only helps in minimal terms.
- Some of the 'puzzles' border on tedium, and aren't really fun or necessary to solve.
- The Arena store is needlessly expensive. You likely die before saving up for anything good.
TL;DR -
For a develpoment title, what you see is what you get. If you read the above, then you can decide if it's worth your time, money, and tears. It's risky to try something new in gaming, but Bare Mettle is nailing it. Color me impressed.

I bought
on January 2014 and have 116 hours logged on Steam. I played 4 different characters in 4 different versions of the game. I desperately wanted to like it. The game superficially has every feature I would've wanted from 2D big open sandbox: actual farming, a single-tool-to-harvest-them-all, space theme, starship to quickly get to completely different areas, infinite world with planet's map looping on themselves, shotguns. And yet, the feelings I feel when I play it are frustration and stress.
The game is a fractal of baffling design decisions. Tiny little interlocking things, spread from UI through encounter design and technology tree to game mechanics, come together to bloom into what seems like a diabolical exercise in passive-aggressive sadism.
You can see it when you learn that dropping down through several platforms causes you fall damage. Or when the game ALWAYS returns you to your ship when you load the game, regardless of whether you were exploring a complex cave system or just checked a checkpoint 90% into an instanced mission. Or how items in Tier 1 require you to craft
intermediary products from
basic materials. Or how that one boss fight begins with your character having to drop down from
to take fall damage. Or how many, many, many factors force you to do insane inventory juggling. Or how you can't ever hide that annoying starting pet. Or how the bats in the entrance tutorial dungeon stunlock you to death if you try to fight with an axe or a hammer. Or how HUD buttons do not have any tooltips, despite the game having loads of tooltips. Or how the prevalence of automatic fire that you can't really evade forces you to choose between interesting two-handed weapons coupled with constant switching to healing items, and bland one-handed weapons with shield. Or how you have to constantly plock down hundreds of torches or switch between flashlight and your weapons, because all personal light sources are way up in the tech tree and come with enormously high opportunity costs. Or how you have to either constantly use healing items or constantly put down sleeping bag to deal with tiny bits of damage.
I tried to mod out everything I didn't like, but 27 mods in and I'm still left with a game that's just frustration and stress.
I just... I just can't take it anymore.

I would 100% reccommend this game to anyone who has the patience for it. This game takes a LOOOOONG time to learn, but after you finish the hours of tutorials the game provides and learn your way around the build menu, the game is actually really streamlined. One thing that makes this game so great is its level of detail. Every weapon system can be completely unique, especially with the shell and missile customization menus. And while the many hours of building and testing your designs can be boring and frustrating, there is a great satisfaction when you watch your design tear apart another vehicle, actually working the way you wanted it to. One other thing that makes this game great is the campaigns that are available. The Neter campaign is great, as resources are in abundance and larger, more expensive craft are encouraged. The Glao campaign is the opposite, with very few resources and encouraging cheaper builds. These campaigns challenge players to think differently and creatively.
Overall, while it does require a player with LOTS of patience and the learning curve might as well be a brick wall, this game is a great game with only a few minor bugs.

Warning, this game holds a lot of Nostalgia for me, as this was my second most played game on my N64 back in the day. (Turok 2 being my most played.) *I still own my copies and they still work.
Turok Dinosaur Hunter was, in my mind, one of the BEST FPS games on the N64. Some would argue that 007 Goldeneye and Perfect Dark were better, but Turok was basically the QUAKE/DOOM of the N64. Fast paced and total devastation to your enemies, which is why I hale this better than 007 and Perfect Dark. The quickness and speed to it and the feel of the weapons made it more fun to me than the others.
It may have only taken me 6 hours to beat this (on Hardcore), but as this game is burned into my memory from playing it so much on the N64, it was easy for me to remember were everything is. I already knew where all the secrets were, all the weapon locations, ultra health, tech armor, keys, etc so I was able to really rush through the game. The game is near identical to the original version, minus the first level.
Close to the beginning of the first level, on your way to get the second key, they had changed an area completely. It had made me stop and think, how much more did they change/add? Well sadly nothing major that really stands out other than that one spot. Some areas were slightly changed here and there, but you honestly would never noticed them unless you were paying real close attention.
The game consists of traversing 8 levels, of which you run, jump, climb, swim, and shoot everything in sight. Collect 14 weapons to destroy your enemies, and kill the bosses. Exploring the maps to find the level keys, as well as secrets for more weapons/ammo/powerups.
All the original enemies are still there. All 14 destructive weapons are still there. The music that is engraved into my skull is still there. The same sounds, textures, it's all the original stuff! (Some fan made mods add some HD textures, which is awesome!) Some people may not like it that it looks outdated, but this is NOT a remaster/reboot. This is just a "upgrade" to make it work on PCs. No new content was really added into it, and nothing has really changed... But honestly they didn't need to change anything!
The plus side is since they smoothed out the graphical settings, it can pretty much run on anything. I boot the game up and it already selected my resolution of 1920x1080 60Hz borderless window, and runs at a smooth 60FPS. This has everything from FXAA Antialiasing, Bloom, Light Scatter, Occlusion Queries, a new water texture with new refractions and reflections system, and a freaking FOV setting!
FOV settings has a few choices. 47.5 (which I think was the original N64 FOV, which makes the game unplayable at this day in age, terrible motion sickness,) 74.0 (your standard console FOV,) 90.0, 110.0 (which is what I played at,) and 120.0.
Another addition to the settings adding a crosshair (which I didn't use), changing the "weapon bobbing" settings, being able to change ALL control imputes, as well as using "Extended Draw Distance" which can greatly change on how the game plays. With the extended draw distance you can see so much more of the world. Hell I didn't even know certain places had roofs on them! Since of the addition of the extended draw distance, the enemies have also been tweaked. They have been made to work with the extended draw distance so they would shoot you from a distance like you would as well, making it fair. This ALSO causes some enemies to shoot you from parts of the map that you would be going to later. It's not a major problem, but can be slightly annoying. If you really want the "Retro" feel on how it played on the N64, turn off the extended draw distance. It gives the game a different feel to it.
All the little tricks/glitches that I used/abused back on the N64 still work in this game, which is great. The strafe running, the platform shortcuts, the quicker way to get down long flights of stairs. The only sad thing is, back in the original versions, you were able to blow up people off the edges and make them fall into the abyss just because it's funny (to understand what I mean, look at the last screenshot on the store page)... Well they took that out.  Now when you try to fling an enemy off into the abyss, there is like an invisible wall that stops them and keeps them on the platform. It's not a major problem, just sad that I could not do that anymore.
From the little problems, it doesn't affect the game. It's still the great game that I grew up playing, and was nice to run down memory lane while murdering everything in sight. This game still a blast to play, and I will always recommend this to everyone to give it a try!
EDIT: There has been a new update that added a Level Editor and Steam Workshop support! Like, WHAT?!?! That is awesome as F*CK!
I've attempted my own hand at the editor, but it seems to be broken for me. Devs are still working on improving and adding more features to it in the future.

Set in ancient japan the skulls of the shogun beckons the player to take hold of a shogun backstabbed by one of his subordinates during a battle aiming to seek revenge after being reincarnated in the afterlife.  The gameplay consists of a relatively simple but unique turned-based combat system where the player and the AI each take turns commanding their units in a round to either move, attack, or perform other actions until they run out of moves (5 per side).  The player wins if he/she can kill all of enemy units or the enemy general, but must protect his/her own general in the process.   Three types of basic units are available from start including infantry, cavalry, and archer where they can be utilised to work together for maximum effect in a scenario.   Multiple strategies come into play during each scenario which is unique in their own way such as preventing enemy units from counterattacking when they are being attacked, or positioning one's units properly before the end of a round to minimise the damage received during AI's turn--can be accomplished by either running out of enemy's  movement range or hide in a bush which can grant a 20% chance for an attack to miss.  The gameplay can become stale were it not for golden skulls challenges and the succinct degree of humour present in the game which, surprisingly, can be quite amusing and definitely goes a long way in making the gameplay experience more satisfying.  There are also xp for levelling up and emblems you receive at end of each scenario depending on your performance but otherwise they do not have a direct impact on your gameplay, if at all, whether you are level 1 or 10 you do not possess any distinct advantage whatsoever aside from having bestowed a different title each level.  The emblems are purely for asthetic purposes to show off your dedication or time committed to the game, notwithstanding the amount of repetitive grinding just to be able to collect all the rare/very rare emblems either through gameplay or combining them to hopefully obtain the ones you want and then upgrading all or most of them to Gold rank.
There is a multiplayer component in addition to the single-player campaign as well.  However, the matchmaking lobby is usually empty majority of times and hence one would have to encompass a gross amount of patience in order to possibly find a mattch courtesy of the ability of the game to continuously search for opponents in the background whilst you wreak havoc in traditional campaign mode or casually browse through the leaderboards and emblems you have amassed.  Despite the near non-existence of an online community, I find the single-player campaign infinitely enjoyable on its own and that alone is enough to make this game remarkably innovative and is a refreshing change from the traditional, stagnant TBS mechanisms

In my opinion, Creeper World 3 is more carefully crafted and more well-made than most big-budget games out there today, it truly is a show of how it isn't the budget that matters, it is simply how the game ends up being upon release.
How was it on release? It was pretty good, having had it about a month after it was released on the Knucklecraker site, it was later released on Steam, and due to the Developer beign a really awesome person, Virgil allowed all previous owners of the game, to get a free steam key, since they'd already bought the game.
So okay, I'm keepnig this one short.
The game is basically a Tower Defense/Real-Time Strategy hybrid, where the enemy is not identical to you in any possible form. Your enemy is (as the store page itself says) a fluid-like substance that flows over the transformable terrain. This substance acts exactly like water, only if it touches your stuff, it either outright destroys it immediately (non weapon/titan units) or it slowly melts away at it (Weapons and titans).
The substance flows from emitters, which you need to fight towards, and destroy them using Nullifiers, doing this as you go from world to world, saving them all from the Blue Tide named Creeper.
Pros:
- The Story is well-written honestly, keeping you guessing, even after you've beaten the story.
- Unlike previous entries, you can use Titans, which are like superweapons, and they are awesome!
- Also unlike previous entires, there are three endings insted of only one.
- Each Story mission has many ways of beating it, there are those "Per map strategy that always wins" but no single strategy will get you a victory on every map.
- The Environment actually means something in the game, allowing you to create fortresses for defense using terraforming, or for offense to get an easier shot at something, or even boxing in an emmitter.
- The Soundtrack is by far the best I've ever fonud in the game. It perfectly fits the game's underlying post-apocalyptic setting set in the far future.
- There are no bugs that are atleast in-game. It's never crashed, it's never frozen without external conflicts, it doesn't even have glitches.
- You can make the Creeper any color if blue doesn't work. Red, Black, White, Purple... if it exists as a color, you can do it pretty much. Also works for anti-creeper too.
- Literally thousands of levels to play after the story, with levels made by testers and part of the dev team like MadMag, the artist behind the game, or Virgil, all made with the game's own random map generator, the DMD, Dial Map Device.
- Has the most impossible level ever put on a strategy game, Jovincoting, a map so hard, absolutely nobody has ever beaten it. This game has technically been out for about a couple years now. Or almost.
- Strategy mostly consists of neat tricks you pick up along the way than actual builds as following a build will slow you down in almost every possible case, due to how maps are all different.
- The Game has a map editor with it's own scripting language, using it can allow you to change the game form what it is, to a top down shooter (Credits mission), or even a game where you play as the creeper against AI-controlled enemy command nodes.
Cons
- The map selection music will often content ID youtube videos showing it.
- I literally cannot think of anymore Cons. I've been trying to for the last two days.
All of this and even more is only 17 dollars CDN, probly 15 US. Just get it, this game is basically one of the best, most underappreciated titles on the market today. A must buy for anyone who likes a good strategy game.

This is a review for both "Clockwork Man" and "Clockwork Man: The Hidden World" since I played them back to back and they share the same lead character. Actually, I've played both these games many times on a different PC before I got into Steam. So my playtimes you see for each will probably be less than a normal playthrough since I can whiz through the games by now. We'll start with game #1:
Pros:
- Nice graphics and good character designs. The main girl, Miranda (YAY, she has my name!), is quite lovely.
- The voice acting is also good, for the most part. I really like who they chose for Miranda. Some of the others can be a bit cheesy but it is amusing rather than irritating.
- Interesting story.
- Both games have a very neat hidden object feature. Scrolling and zooming. Not every scene but many allow you to move around the area. Some items are sneakily hidden behind others but just one click to the left or right will reveal them.
- Both games also have an interesting hint system. You travel around with a little robot man and he'll help you locate those tough to find objects. He starts out with the ability to just tell you where a random something is. Then a little into the story, he learns how to give you an item's silhouette (which is the hint I prefer if I'm stuck). Further in the story, he gets other abilities. Like briefly highlighting each metal object on your HO list.
- In both games, the music isn't spectacular but it's pleasant to listen to. Actually, in #2 there are a couple places with very lovely melodies.
- When you beat each game, Freeplay opens up. This gives you random hidden object areas. Good for if you're in that "I have a craving to find stuff" mood.
Cons:
- Neither game is connected to Steam while you're playing. So you won't be able to chat with friends or take steam screenshots.
- Unfortunately, both games have issues when it comes to clicking on items. You'll find you need to be very precise and occasionally you'll need to click more than once or try clicking on a different part of the object. It doesn't happen TOO often or else I wouldn't be able to recommend these games.
- Both games are short. Boo.
Now I'll list the differences in Clockwork Man: The Hidden World:
- The length is longer. Because of the higher difficulty, possibly much longer.
- This game has a journal where Miranda records her adventures and anything of note. You WILL need to use this journal to solve quite a few puzzles.
- There are many more puzzles in #2 and some of them are downright devious. There are no skip options either. Also, it's easy to miss things that you need in some scenes so you might get stuck for awhile. I love this game but it IS a bit aggravating sometimes. Those who enjoy a challenge will have fun. :D
- The story has no tie-ins with the first game. The Hidden World's plot is much more involved than #1 and, in my opinion, fascinating.
- The voice acting, again in my opinion, is better than the first game. (Miranda is still the same, which is good!)
- Maybe it's my imagination but it seems the graphics are better in #2, though I'm pretty sure they used the same game engine.
- When you finish the game, you can rewatch any of the cutscenes.
So in closing, I really enjoy both these games so I'm definitely recommending them to hidden object and puzzle fans. But, because of their short length, you should wait and grab them when they're on sale.
Important Note! The games might not load up for you, which is an issue I had. Right click on the Clockwork Man title, click on Properties, click on Local Files, click on Browse Local Files (which will bring up your program files for the games), right click on the Clockwork Man title again, click on Troubleshoot Compatibility, and finally click on Try recommended settings. I did that for each game and then they worked just fine.

A very simple little game, balloons rise from the bottom of the screen and float towards the top, bursting if they touch the top of the screen with the aim of the game to burst the balloons before they do so.
There are 4 different coloured ballons (red, green, yellow and blue) and in order to get a high score you must pop ballons of the same colour repeatedly. (EG bursting your first red nets 10 points, the second red in a row 20, then 30, then 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100 with each red their after giving 100 points).
Each balloon has a peice of string dangling from underneath it and this can be used to pull balloons down to give you further time to continue popping balloons of the same colour and thus far this all sounds jolly good casual fun, the problem is, it isn't.
The game was clearly made for mobile devices (Android/iOS) as the instructions on the first level tell you to line ballons up and swipe them to pop them, in the PC/Steam version of this game it only registers mouse clicks. As such you have to tap balloons to pop them or click and drag to move the balloon string, the result being you have the reactions of a house fly when moving your mouse to stay on top of things.
I'm sure as a free to play game supported by adverts on mobile devices this is a fair enough game, on the PC getting 3 stars beyond level 10 is something only hardened gamers will likely achive and given the lack of achievements to show off such feats I doubt few of those will waste their time.
As EnsenaSoft games go it's not that bad a game, it's just that it's more befiting as a browser game supported by ads and it's clear that no recalibration has been done to compensate for the fact you are using a mouse rather than a finger to control the game.
The game mechanics are poor and I just can't immerse myself into it. It's a shame because there seems to be a lot of good ideas.

I can't help but compare Death to Spies and Hitman: Blood Money as both have a lot of similar mechanics and  gameplay aspects.
So for those who've played Hitman: BM, it's the same except:
* With Nazis
* More confusing
* Harder
* Way more restrictive (mission failure conditions more cohercitive)
* Larger, more open maps in general with more enemies
* Yet less ways to complete a mission
For those who haven't played Blood Money (a game I strongly recommend)
This game is about completing a mission, using of stealth and disguise, the latter being extensively important as the sheer number of enemies and some mission conditions (as well as the limited ammunition and firepower) make it impractical if not impossible to complete a mission by gunning your way through.
So you have to wait for the correct enemy to get in a spot where you can take him down stealthly and steal their uniform to infiltrate enemy zones.
If it's great on paper, it doesn't work very well in-game as weapons accuracy, enemies' detection and permitted actions/zones are sources of frustration.
Sometimes, you're dead on target and your shot will miss, alerting the enemy that will probably sound the alarm, run away or alert his friends. Some enemies will just simply detect you (or not) depending on how the game feel. An enemy will be deaf and won't hear you breathing down his neck, or won't see you in his peripheral vision depsite you being in plain light, very visible. The very same enemy can detect you someties if you're out of his range (marked on the map), on a different elevation than him (you're uphill, he's downhill) and laying down in the grass with a camouflage suit.
And even when you finally get a disguise, you're not out of trouble and will continiously be frustrated by the way the disguise system works.
Once again, if it is good in theory, its application ruins it.
Basically, when you are disguised you are authorized to be in certain area or perform certain action (an outer patrol isn't authorized in buildings), you won't fool commanding officers that are directly related to the disguise you're wearing (ex: the chief for outer patrols will spot you in an outer patrol uniform but the chief for inner patrols won't) and you need to carry the standard issue guns related to your uniform (while wearing a german guard uniform, wielding a Tokarev will get you spotted but an MP40 won't)
I told you, it seems really interesting on paper.
But in-game, while the interface will pop a message when equiping a weapon that doesn't fit the uniform, there's little to none indicator to what zones or actions are restricted to the uniform you just stole as most uniforms you can steal are by definition those of soldiers in secluded area and thus were not interacting or meeting other soldiers. How can you know if you can enter a building with your current uniform? The guard will tell you that you can't enter. If there's no guard, you enter and meet someone inside? They'll shoot you, no question asked. Same goes for most interactions.
This makes the whole inflitration more based on trial and error rather than on observation.
In brief, Death to Spies could have been so good, but ended up falling short on most of features.
A waste of potential: 44/100

The obvious comparison to make with Death to Spies is Blood Money.
Blood Money was an open sandbox, filled with various approaches and methods of killing that the developers had meticulously thought of and catered to. The player had the choice of experimenting, replaying, experimenting again, and treat it as a puzzle with many solutions. Blood Money and it's players enjoyed the fact that the developers gave it loving attention to detail.
16 hours is not enough to fully explore Death to Spies but the initial impression I had of the game was less of an open sandbox to experiment in but a tough, and sometimes very tough, puzzle to crack with one optimal solution. If there's a noticeable difference at first, it's that unlike Blood Money, the missions are not set up at all for you to win through violence easily. In Blood Money, it's quite easy to kill everyone. In Death to Spies, unless you've got a handy doorway or corridor to abuse bot AI, you'll die in combat quite easily. A realistic number of guards patrol overlapping routes, often in groups of three or more. Towers will sometimes overlook these guards and static guards will sometimes place an additional layer of observation over roaming patrols. The guards will number in the dozens, far more than anything Blood Money will throw at you. Your weapons are also far less robust than the ones found in Hitman- there is no dual silenced pistol for you to mow down enemies while laughing- the best you get for handguns is a silenced revolver, and ammo is always scarce. Careful planning, observation, a bucketload of patience and good aiming skills, however, will get you far.
The joy then, is to be found in seeing the minimap show a chunk of black dots instead of green ones, showing a successful penetration and exploitation of the whirling tango of green and red triangles. There's satisfaction to be found in finally finding a section of the map where the guards seem to lose sight of each other for just a bit, when you can violently ruin their day to make a gap in their patrol routes which you can use to sneak in further. The rest of the game after this is finding an officer's uniform to blend in and that's still filled with danger and close calls, as some NPCs won't be fooled by the disguise and will happily alert the dozens of armed guards next to you about your Russian heritage.
It's worth noting that like Hitman, Death to Spies has also received attention to detail, only if it's been mostly apparent in the 16 hours I've played so far that the devs made a commendable effort to make the game look good even in 2015. Functional mirrors get an honourable mention here, as some modern triple AAA games still fail to have these. Sadly, there are also a few issues and bugs which do sour the experience, like issues with the camera bugging out temporarily, being stuck, bots being stuck and a few oddities like dropping a stunned person from your shoulders killing the person and unfortunately being the last diplomat you were allowed to kill before a diplomatic scandal happened.
The audio is ok, although the dubbed translations are horrendous though tolerable (skippable). Expect nothing from ingame conversations or the like either.
Level wise, the game does take you to quite a few different places and setpieces, which keeps things fresh enough to stop the 'get officers uniform- avoid red triangle' formula from becoming stale.
For a dollar, this game was more than worth it. Gonna say that Death to Spies has less replayability than Hitman but if you want something Hitman like while waiting for the new one to come out, you should have bought it during the stealth sale it was pretty damn cheap.

On the one hand, Massive Chalice uses squad based combat similar to XCOM. On the other, you breed new heroes by arranging marriages (kind of like Crusader Kings 2). The traits of the parents, good or bad, can pass on to the children. Producing children is vital because in-game time passes quickly. Battles occur about every 10 years, thus your combat squad composition changes nearly every fight as heroes die naturally.
Overall, I think it's a decent strategy game for different types of personality. If you are the micromanaging type, you can spend a lot of time looking at character sheets to optimize marriages and squad selection. If you are a casual player, the game is forgiving and does not have a lot of complexity. There are only a dozen or so enemy units which get tougher.
The art style may not be for everyone. The game sort of looks like if you turned the graphic settings to the lowest, giving everything a slightly geometric, block-like quality. This is by design, makes it unique but I can see it turning some people off. However, the use of color is amazing and to me, made the game visually memorable.

In 1997, Acclaim published a game for the Nintendo 64 and PC: a game called, Turok by Iguana Entertainment. It was a first person shooter based on the comic book of the same name. Set in a world with roaming dinosaurs, creatures, and evil tribesmen. Your character, Turok, is tasked with the simple job of stopping the world falling into the hands of evil. Evil that have, in their power, a weapon that’s as ancient as themselves. Pretty vague blurb eh?
Despite that Turok was a ground-breaking game, taking the player from corridor shooters such as, DOOM, and throwing them into a vastly more open world. It set a standard which made the series a household name, and changed the way level design worked for years to come.
In 2015, Night Dive Studios released a remaster. Unlike what normally comes to mind when you think of remasters, Night Dive’s work was more of a service, than bodywork. There was no super high rez textures, anti-alias tinkering, or insertion of HDR  sun-rays peering through tree tops. Oh no, this keeps its roots pure, it celebrates the graphical style and standards that the original carried back in the 90’s and, it even kept the controls as simple as the original.
It looks like the exact same game, but with a resolution, and smoothing fix, it feels like I’m back in my living room on my N64 as a child. Element which would need tweaking as to accommodate the changes in screen resolutions have clearly been prioritised;the HUD looks smoother, sharper than it used too; the overall game brightness is tweaked, brighter, with more vivid colours than the game could manage on it’s initial outing; the frame rate is smoothed, balanced throughout. All this combined with the slightly tweaked textures also come together to keep the game fast, flowing, and as easy to pick up and play as before. which helps with the game’s fast paced shoot outs, and the textures look a touch more detailed giving the world a little more character.

There's something to be said for "big" twists being a lot harder to pull off than they're given credit for.
It's easy to see them as easy narrative devices to attempt to shock the audience into thinking something is smarter than it may actually be by completely disproving what they thought to be true and being a convenient focus point to write towards. But that's only because they're so often done poorly or telegraphed so well that they're no longer fit to be called twists at all. Pitiri 1977 goes in a somewhat different but no less flawed direction and simply writes its entire plot as a series of twists.
Every event save the mundane and far too long encounters with random robots is setup as something that's intended to be revelatory, but comes off as dull and meaningless. There's so little in the way of word building or character that a narrative almost doesn't exist until it wants to be in your face trying to blow your mind, when all I wanted was for it to go away and quit pretending it was so much more interesting than it was. The tonal differences in its writing also makes it hard to feel even the smallest bit connected to the world you're in, full of references that fall flat and the running joke that everything just reminds your character of a sci-fi movie they saw which was tiring the first time I heard it.
There's also the issue of how badly gameplay mechanics are attempted to be integrated into the game, gaining items at access point inexplicably placed around the ship for who knows what reason and solving bizarre puzzles that border on complete incomprehensibility. It's definitely a video game and it wants you to know, but it's also a pretty rubbish one, clunky and tedious with no sense of pacing and some really weird technical issues.
I wasn't sure what to make of Pitiri 1977 for most of the hour I spent with it, but there's very little to make anything out of that isn't immediately forgettable in all its monotonous glory. It's an odd experience with no direction that somehow manages to feel at least three times as long as it is, which I guess is its one saving grace: that it's over before it becomes truly exhausting, though it's a close call at that.

Pitiri 1977 is a fun, little platform game that mashes together the love for retro gaming, scifi and metroid.

All the art assets have been hand-drawn and put into the game, the animation reminds me of some of the cartoons I watched growing up, and there's just a sense of 'Child's Dream' to it all. It might not be for all, but it worked for me; mixed together with the soundtrack and the sci-fi references, I found myself smiling.
The controls are very basic, and exclusively use the keyboard's arrow keys for movement. So at times it can feel a little 'old school' by nature (and maybe by design). There are no option settings too, so you'll have to make do with the default volume levels (or change them in your control panel setup if too loud).
Once you complete the game you get to unlock Sandbox mode, which allows you to create your own levels - so I look forward to those in the future.
