SolForge is a very interesting digital CCG.  Those familiar with CCGs such as Magic might be skeptical about the lack of an explicit resource system, but the game manages beautifully without lands to pay for your cards.  The idea that you can play any card in your hand is incredibly empowering, but the knowledge that the cards you don't play will be discarded makes for agonizing decisions.  Each turn is a difficult balance between playing for short-term needs and long-term strategy.
Cards can be bought with real money, but they're also handed out quite generously through simple play rewards.  One can earn the play rewards by beating the AI, and AI difficulty can be set to make the rewards trivial to obtain.  A downside is that there's nothing that can be done with duplicate cards, but I hardly find this to be a significant fault given how quickly it's possible to build a collection.
Speaking of the AI, I'd never have put as much time into the game as I have if the AI wasn't interesting to play.  The Hard AI poses a reasonable challenge, and is great for quickly testing out deck strength.  Humans will always pose a better challenge, but the AI is good enough to making beating up on it fun, and if I can't beat it consistently then I know my deck needs work.
I highly recommend SolForge.  It's a fresh design in a world where so many games are simply tweaked clones of those that came before.  It's fun, it's challenging, and it's free to try.  What more can you ask for?

SolForge is an interesting take on the digital card genre. It's a fairly simplistic card game, but with a suprising amount of depth / theorycrafting to your decks once you've unlocked some cards. It has the unique aspect of your cards levelling up as you play them; adding a depth of strategy that other card games haven't really explored. Not only do you have to think about what card to play right now, in order to damage your opponent, or save yourself from damage, but you also have to think about the future - and which cards you'll want then and how your deck will evolve compared to their deck.
The starter decks are playable, but I would strongly advise you to buy some packs (you can use silver which you can get from logging on daily and from winning matches) and get a custom deck going. You will get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked taking your cheap/free decks into PvP, but you can win your silver rewards playing against the AI - which is beatable on all difficulties with the starter decks, although the higher difficulties will be a challenge. If you do use real money to purchase packs, you will have a higher chance of getting the best cards, ultimately people should remember that card games are about spending money and RNG, but overall this is very playable as a free player too.
One of the big advantages of this game right now to me is that the Ipad app is extremely fluid and responsive. You can play untimed games with friends and the push notifications are accurate - meaning if you have a lazy day with 5 minutes to spare here and there, you can have a good duel with your friend from anywhere. (Untimed) games save despite the application being shut down; and you can start a game on the ipad and continue it on the PC, or have the game running in two locations at once if you so desire. A lot of digital card games right now have promised this sort of cross platform interactivity, but few have competently provided it yet. The android app is sadly not out yet so I can't comment on that - but they have said there'll be one in the future.
I'm pretty happy with it overall and would recommend.

I whole-heartedly recommend this game. Fair warning: you will become addicted to it, and rack up 20 hours playing it in a  single week. I've played it over 10 hours in two *days*.
The trailer, pictures, and even description on CW3's store page fail to do the game justice. It's RTS only in that you can place and move units while the timer is running. It's TD only in that your units only fire while sitting still, and half of your units can't move once placed. Allow me to paint you a different picture of this game. The creeper is like water that bubbles up from the ground, and you can't touch the water...because you're a cat with a lot of really cool turrets. Each of your turrets does something different. Half of your turrets aren't offensive devices; they're used to set up the infrastructure of your base, collecting resources, etc. Your energy recharges continuously, but your base can output more energy than it collects, and will eventually reach equillibrium with your input. When you start to net energy income, do you build more energy collectors, or new weapons? Eventually, you can terraform the map at large energy output, but you don't need the terraformers on constantly. Want a turret at a different location to combat the creeper? Your offensive turrets can fly. to new locations, but if your infrastructure hasn't caught up to the front, their ammo stores will drain rapidly.
Each map is essentially a series of multi-step problems that can be solved in a variety of ways, especially as you unlock more turrets. Early in the game, it's pretty obvious what tactics the map maker had in mind, promarily because you haven't yet uinlocked all of the turrets. But not even half-way through the initial campaign, you come to understand the myriad paths you can take to solve each particular step of a problem. Terraforming is a big part of this: because you can literally change the shape of the map, setting up infrastructure one way opens up different solutions down the road.
The two extremes of the spectrum of CW3 players are probably Speed Runners <----> Slow and Steady. I'm the latter right now, which is one of the reasons missions take me so long: I spend more than half the run-time with the timer paused. But you've got to be careful while paused: queue up too many turrets, and your production rapidly outpaces your income, slowing your entire system. The game doesn't punish you for being either kind of player--on most levels, your resources don't dwindle over time, so you could play a single map for hours in a trenchy-style of building one row of turrets just in front of your previous row. The game *does* punish you for not paying attention--being fast is definitely doable if your minimalistic solution has all of the right components.
CW3 is a phenomenal example of the adage: gamers prefer good mechanics to good graphics. But don't let the 2D simplistic art scheme fool you. Not only are the mechanics solid, the performance stellar, but the interface is also straight-forward, and the controls seem pretty intuitive. Left-click to select, right-click-hold to move around the map. Zoom in/out with mouse wheel. Escape to un-select or exit out of a selection. The visuals and animations tell you what you need to know, and if something isn't working like you expected, it's pretty easy to figure out why.
I wouldn't say it's a difficult game in the initial campaign, but it *is* intense regardless of your strategy. There appear to be scads of maps that the community has created that will test your skills, as will the Challenge section by the developers, *and* the custom-level editor is built right into the frakking game.

This is a gem of a strategy game. It's a RTS Tower defense-esque game, this might not sound like a good idea, but it works beautifully. There are two main mechanics that I will address:
1. The Creeper. This is your enemy, it's a liquid entity that creeps forward from spawners, slowly covering more and more of the stage. You need to build towers to fight it back, and in turn advance farther along the stage yourself. Creeper would be very difficult to deal with if it didn't obey the laws of physics. Basically, in order for creeper to overflow onto a higher level of terrain, it has to have nowhere else to go on its current level. This leads to some fairly interesting placements, like a very powerful spawner at the bottom of a deep crater. There are plenty of other enemies too, runners and digitalis namely. Runners just run along digitalis and need to be destroyed with sniper towers, they can't directly destroy your towers, but can stun them long enough for creeper to overflow onto them. Digitalis is a kind of grid-like enemy that conducts creeper and prevents towers from being built, trust me, it's more difficult than it sounds.
2. The Network. This game has parallels to a tower defense game, but calling it one doesn't do it justice. The biggest conventional differences being: Towers are networked, they have to be connected to your base to function; Towers can be moved freely, even off the network, albeit with limited ammo; towers use energy, constantly.
The biggest difference as I stated is the network. You have to build collectors and relays between towers to provide pathways for the "packets" of which there are three types, ammo, construction, and totem. This means you can't just build towers in the most strategic spots right away, you have to build out to them, often fighting tooth and nail to get to them. Additionally, these packets cost energy, which is distributed evenly between the active types of packets, energy is obtained through collectors, which collect energy across an area, and reactors. Collectors gain no benefit from overlapping area and should be spread out, they are also one of the main staples in your network of towers. If you get too ambitious with your expansion, you'll enter energy starvation, where packets are produced less efficiently and you run the risk of your blasters running out of ammo and the line being pushed back.
Between the campaign mode and the hundreds of other levels in the game + fan made ones, you could get hundreds of hours out of this game (I didn't because I just played creeper world 1 and 2 before it and was done after the campaign). Having played all three games, this is the best.
Even at full price, I think you'll get your money's worth, this is a difficult game, you will need to think strategically and act quickly. It's a refreshing change of pace from most RTS and tower defense games in my opinion.

Playing TD's as a youngun, who recently discovered the wonders of the internet, were absolutely incredible times. But I always got a bit tired of the repetative movement of putting down another tower, upgrading them blah blah blah.... and then just leaving the game to run it's course, throwing wave after wave of enemies until your computer began to stutter and lag behind as it was somehow managing to cope with an incredible array of pixals being thrown into your eyeballs. I am mainly talking about the infamous Bloons TD, which will always remain my favourite TD, although there are others. However, this game is a little different in that respect.
I like to think of it as a combination of a TD and RTS, in the sense that The Creeper, some blue liquid thing, is not stuck on rails and just has to get from A to B as it floats down a path ignoring all defences on its journey, it is instead open to go where it pleases, only limited by the geography of the landscape. The RTS element in the game is the fact that you build up cannons to protect your 'base' and resource collectors. They take time to build and must be placed strategically in order to maximise the efficiency of your defence and keep The Creeper at bay. After that, you must push forward and move your defences forward even more. But they can get delinked from getting resources, so extenders are put in place. On large maps, it can be very rewarding seeing a huge web of links and seeing your packages of Anti-Creeper and firepower flowing down these pathways.
In later missions, more enemies arise and give even more things to think about when planning out defences, but don't worry. A reasonably nice variety in defence types can help with that. But you'll have to play it in order to find out what.

I really wanted to like Omerta. It seemed like one of those instant bestsellers popping out of nowhere. After having played it for quite a while though, I cannot recommend it. You play as an italian (surprise eh) immigrant looking to make a fortune in the U.S.. Most of your actions are performed on a top-down map in real time. You can rent premises, establish some businesses like illegal breweries, boxing rings and pizzerias (yup) and they will generate money and ressources, which can be sold for even more money. You have a selection of gang-members at your disposal who will carry out your orders, like gathering information or eliminating a rival casino. This has all been done before, I remember playing Gangsters 2 by EIDOS and having a lot more fun. My main problem is that missions are way too short and as soon as you finish one, you start another one with all your achievements gone, from scratch. There is no continuity apart from who your gang-members are. You cannot have custom members either, as all of them come with preset backgrounds, portaits and loadouts. Additionally, they threw in a XCOM'esque turn-based-combat system for some special missions. While being an interesting addition, it just does not work that well and, again, other games have done it better. The multiplayer is a joke. You would expect to be able to play a big campaign in a vibrant city with multiple people, but all there is is 1on1 turn-based-combat matches, or Coop against the AI. No big Mafia-empire simulator to have hours of fun in, no intriguing scheme-play between you and your friends... just some rushed, copied gameplay definitely not worth full price.

Your shogun utilizes another unit type - one that depends on the landscape of the map - the monk. Your units will fight to capture valuable mink shrines that will then summon whichever spirit inahbits it: fox, salamander, crow, or tanuki. Skulls of the Shogun is a turn based strategy game with a surprising amount of tactical depth. Units are varied - samurai, cavalry, archers and four types of magic using monks - all with different strengths and weaknesses. Positioning of units is important, because they can counter attack in certain situations, and can also be knocked off ledges for an instant kill. Eating the skulls of dead enemies regains health and increases max health, while controlling rice gardens and shrines lets you summon extra units. The game is challenging, because on most levels you are outnumbered and surrounded, but at the same time well balanced, because each side can only move 5 units per turn. However, any unit that eats three skulls unlocks an extra attack per turn. The game has a wacky sense of humour, particularly with its amusing text only dialogue and animation style. The singleplayer campaign is quite long and very stable. Definitely worth checking out.

I haven't beaten this game yet. It's sort-of Roguelike, very tricky, but pretty fun.
You make a weak peon and subject them to the horrific trials of you trying to figure out how to play, getting beaten up by goons and tripping over beds and boxes, occasionally getting a meager kit together and then dying shortly after.
Exanima sort of plays like Baldur's Gate or something, but the game is a bit more bleak. A little like Dark Souls in tone. The combat is really the highlight of the game, because it's one of the most unique features. It's strongly physics-based and each character has a system of balance and musculature.
You have a couple of basic attacks, which doesn't sound like a lot, but there is a lot of skill in just how well you execute them. The weapons have very precise damage zones, and won't work well if you get the attack wrong. For example, a polearm with a hook on the end has to hit with the hook. Otherwise you will hit the enemy with the handle and it won't do anything. The fights are often different and unique, and occasionally you can stumble on something and fall over in a fight, letting your enemy clobber you easily. Despite having only some basic swings, fights feel very free-form, and often extremely chaotic. Sometimes things go wrong and you get punished.
The levels are big, and fairly difficult. I had to watch some youtube videos to figure out what I was supposed to do. The game basically doesn't hold your hand at all. It offers a one-time warning of its difficulty.
So I guess it won't be for everyone, but it's a pretty original game in my opinion, definitely worth playing for fans of the dungeon-crawl genre.

I'll tell you the bad things about this game.
Combat:
The combat is a little bit clumsy. There may be some combo for certain weapons, but those combos get very repetitive after a while. You can only direct your attacks for some weapons.
Firearms in this game use your "energy", rather than ammo. If you like to shoot things like me, you might get turned off by this.
The weapons are randomly generated. You can find weapons of all shapes and sizes. Weapons can come with "specials", such as a grenade launcher or a flashlight. What I don't like about the "random aspect" is that there is no upgrading. This may be nitpicking, but I really hate ugly weapons. When I find a good looking gun, I want to upgrade it. Customization isn't really there. You just have to scour planets and hope to get a gun that suits your needs. You can circumvent the lack of ingame customization with admin mode.
Also, where are the bosses outside of stories? I wouldn't mind killing hordes of demon space wasps and their queen.
Exploration, Questing, and Story:
There isn't too much variety when you find settlements. Once you explore all of the current "settlements", you'll find that there isn't much in terms of variety. Where are the HUMAN cities? Surely planets other than Earth would have human cities. Where are the docking bays? People get to places somehow. What about randomly generated battlefields? What about massive gypsie camps? What about random derelict space vessels that contain enemies? There are lots of things that can be added here. The planets themselves have quite a bit of variety at first, but it would be nice if the developers continued to push the variety.
I think the story is like moldy bread. It's just awful. There is almost no character development. There's not much to tell about the story because it's quite plain. Don't buy this game if you're in it for the story. I know the Novakids are a "new" species, but where is their involvement Are they just that mundane?
Questing feels inadequate. You complete menial tasks for people, only to be given a goodie bag. These goodie bags, more than not, contain nothing but garbage that you'll sell later.
All of that said, I think the game is worth buying. The game is beautiful and simple.

Turok is a fast-paced first person shooter in which you play as Turok, a time-traveling Native American man who's after a mysterious bad guy named the Campaigner, who is trying to screw over time or something. Beyond this, we don't get much story, the game instead relies on its gameplay.
Turok plays a lot like Quake or Unreal tournament, except the levels have a lot more verticality. Levels are very long and require a lot of platforming, usually not requiring much precision-jumping. You get a large arsenal of weapons including some interesting ones like the bow which shoots explosive blue arrows. You'll also get your typical shotguns and machine guns, which are good as well. You'll face off against dinosaurs, cyborgs, and alien-like monsters, all of which are fun to fight.
One of the main differences between Turok and other FPS games is that Turoks levels require that you find a certain number of keycards in order to unlock more levels. The problem with this is that the keys are very well hidden and often frustrating to find when you have to backtrack to old areas and face the same enemies again who respawn after a few minutes.
Besides this one complaint, I don't have anything else bad to say about Turok, other than the game is quite dated graphically, so that might turn off some players. The game is fast, fun, and surprisingly holds up well and stands toe to toe with Quake in my opinion.
Pick Turok up on sale and you're sure to have a good time.

For anyone that has been following me on Youtube for the past few months, you probably noticed that my focus is on digital TCGs. And SolForge has been one of the most commonly played games. Currently I am sitting at over 150 hours played (though some of that may or may not have involved accidentally leaving the game on overnight a few times) and I have played countless hands. The style of this game is what I would call a lane game (as opposed to a MTG-like or a board game like game like Faeria).
First of all it is free to play. The game comes with 2 precon decks that are not in your card pool as far as I know (meaning that those 4 legendaries between the 2 decks you do not own). The prizes currently are fast to earn. Every day at midnight pacific time it resets. You get bonuses for loggin in, first win and 3rd win. The prizes are silver (free to play currency which can be used to buy play mats, the smallest booster pack, and deck slots), and randomized prizes which currently only includes cards or packs.
The pacing of this game is the most enjoyable I have ever played. It is easy to play a 5-10 minute hand and just as easy to lose yourself for hours at a time. The basic gameplay is so simple that I think my cat could learn it. But the strategy does present itself if you give the game a chance. Leveling up is the resource in this game and you need to play the right cards at the right time to progress your deck properly. There is still plenty of luck... but trust me. It is less than you think there is the first time you play a hand.
Plans for the future include: booster drafting and in game tournaments (coming in next patch that will be "soon").
A new 20 card psuedo expansion which will be added to the current set. Save your silver to buy those new packs but don't be afraid to open any packs as old ones will not have new cards.
Graphical and UI upgrades.
And most importantly some form of trading and crafting.
If you are not in this game for the long haul now is the time to warn potential players. The pack system is currently very frustrating. You can only get the 3 card pack for free now. I recently opened 110 of these packs and only got 2 legendary cards. Premium packs guarantee 1 legendary card. But they cost $10. And there is no way to guarantee getting the legendary you want unless they are in one of the faction starter decks. Legendary cards aren't necessarily always better. But they add depth to decks and make certain strategies work better (or make SOME viable since they do not work without specific cards). Between the fact that there is CURRENTLY no trading or in game card crafting, it can be very frustrating for new players. Or even players like me. I Kickstarted this game. I used my store credit to buy 1 of each starter pack and 145 of the middle sized booster packs. And there are still numerous legendary cards that I have 0 copies of.
This game is good enough that I recommend it to anyone that loves lane based CCGs. But I want to say. If you are easily frustrated by RNG with packs. If MMDoC made you flip tables because of the lack of trading. I recommend just doing your daily bonuses against the AI, playing occasionally with your friends, and waiting until trading is implemented in game. If you have the patience to slowly build a decent card pool, then go for it!  Otherwie just remember that beta is beta and SBE is still a small company. And there are plenty of CCGs out there right now while you wait for Kibler, Justin, and the rest of the team to continue developing SolForge.

After playing through the full (post early access) release, the verdict is in and I can confidently say that Skulls of the Shogun is a winner. This quirky turn-based strategy game seems simple at first, but there are actually some surprisingly deep levels of nuance and complexity beneath the surface. You play as a Japanese swordsman General who is trying to reclaim his stolen identity in the afterlife. The art style is very unique and really well done. The cast of characters and story are also very cool. The dialogue, in particular, is a highlight. I wasn't expecting much from that aspect of a seemingly simple strategy game, but I was pleasantly surprised at how funny and entertaining it was.
So the aesthetic portions of the game are definitely good, but what of the actual gameplay, you ask? In short, it's pretty damn good. Gameplay is turn based, but on each turn you have 5 "orders" that can be performed. Your team is comprised of various types of units (warriors, cavalry, archers), each of which has their own strengths and weaknesses. Instead of moving on tiles like other strategy games, the actions in this game are more free-roaming. Units are able to move anywhere they want, within a certain radius, and are also able to continue moving after performing an action, which adds to the level of strategy involved. One of your main goals is to eat the skulls of defeated opponents, which restores health. However, if a unit is able to eat 3 skulls, they transform into a Demon, which enables them to perform 2 actions per turn, which is a huge advantage. Gameplay becomes a delicate balancing act of attacking, positioning and staying alive long enough to power up.
Outside of these main elements, there are a number of other nuances (summoning monks with special powers, forming spirit walls, environmental hazards, deciding when to bring your general into battle, and more) that add many layers of complexity to the basic strategy. Every level seems to provide some new elements to learn or deal with, and this keeps the main campaign fresh from start to finish. There's no padding at all. The main campaign lasts several hours (more if you play on a higher difficulty or attempt to complete the set of special goals for each level) and is worth the price of admission alone. In addition, the game also features online, local and asynchronous multiplayer matches. So there is plenty of content here for both casual and competitive types.
All in all, this game is solid and brings some really cool twists to the turn-based strategy genre. If you are into that type of thing, pick this one up. And if not, well, this could be the game that makes you a fan. Check it out.

***UPDATED***
POST RELEASE REVIEW:
I've played this game in early access, decided that I don't like it at current state, but was sure that it had much potential and release will change a lot. And it didn't.
While Double Fine has added class shuffling and improved graphics a bit, game's main disadvantages (in my eyes) are still there - the HUGE dependance on luck factor, lack of depth in battle missions and unappealing maps and models.
I officially regret that I have backed this game up on Kickstarter. This will be a lesson to me, not to back concepts that has nothing to show but idea. Ideas can be great, but bad realisation can ruin any great idea. I hope you will learn from my mistake.
ORIGINAL PRE-RELEASE REVIEW:
Now a little bit more detailes:
My main complaint is luck factor. There is a LOT about luck in this game, from the begining, traits of your heroes are random and while it's not difficult at first to play with idiots, drunkards and slowpokes, the biggest problem is that you have to apoint one of these genetic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to start a bloodline, meaning he/she will pass down all the bad traits and habbits across generations for at least 50 years or so. Then you have random events - they can cripple your only good heroes or even kill them. Good choices are not even remotely as rewarding. Defend missions may have♥♥♥♥♥♥for reward, and if you are unlucky, the same zones will be attacked and eventually regardless of what you do, you will start to loose land and buildings that you have puted so much time to build.
And finally luck on the battlefield is a huge factor - starting from position (you can start with all heroes being surrounded) and finishing with misses. Even the veterans can miss, especially if they were bred by genetic trash you had to put up with at the begining of the game. And while it's not always lethal, with each hero you loose, your macro economy will get cripled a lot.
The only existing remedy to this is load after each huge fail, but that is a gameplay killer for me. Now don't get me wrong - I'm not saying the game is too hard or impossible. It's just frustrating.
Also there is very little depth in the whole mechanics, but I really hope that it's just the matter of time. Basically, you don't have to be a smart strategist to play this game as long as you have good heroes, simply because all correct things to do are obvious and there isn't a lot of things you need to do but wait.
Combined with luck factor this is really bad, because it's the depth and smart unobvious choices that are supposed to balance bad luck you have to face with, and this game doesn't have the any of that.
The final problem I see in this game is it's graphics - while it does have certain unique style to it, the models are so poor on polygons, I don't understad why have developers made this in 3D - the game obciously could have been 2D with MUCH more appeal. I'm sad to say this, but heroes models look ugly, Double Fine have been cuting budget to 3D modelers waaay too much. Now this problem isn't big for me, the good gameplay always comes first, but it's certainly a letdown.
Heroes are the only (except for the Challice) alive characters in this game that you can see, but being faceless and almost featureless makes them very hard to think of as characters, instead of skill sets.

As a fan of XCOM I was very exited when this game got funded on kickstarter, I only realised a few days ago that the game was actually available for download. I've played the crap out of it over the last few days and I've got to say for the most part I've really enjoyed it.
The presentation and style of the game is great, it looks beautiful and has a quirky sense of humor. The character classes are distinct but lacking, as there are only three. Caberjack (melee), Hunter (ranged), and Alchemist (mix of both), although this is set to change with an upcoming patch which will allow players to mix classes. The gameplay is fun, although it did begin to feel a little repetitive by the end of the game. I really enjoyed the bloodlines aspect of the game which gave you the chance to marry different heroes with the hope of creating offspring with the best traits of their parents (this was a little tricky but very enjoyable when done right). If your heroes went through several grueling battles and distinguished themselves there was the chance that their weapon would become an heirloom, basically a special weapon that leveled up over the campaign.
One of my favourite moments in the game came when a young alchemist named Seargent Ra became my first level 6 character after two battles. With his amazing stats I decided to name Seargent as the next reagent of the house Ra, now Standard had the ‘bountiful’ trait, allowing him to basically have kids in litters. The guy ended up having nine kids and established the Ra lineage as the dominant family in my game. That wasn’t enough for Seargent, when the magnificent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ died he left his weapon behind which became the first heirloom in my game. Two of his ancestors fought in my final battle many generations later, one of them carrying his weapon, the ‘Inevitable’. This is exactly why I bought this game, I wanted a story behind my heroes, I wanted to feel this connection to the characters. The main issue I had that it did get repetitive by end game and I didn’t have as much of a connection with the heroes as I originally did. However I still enjoyed the experience.
On the whole this is still very much a work in progress but I’ve really enjoyed it so far.

My review of Solforge used to be longer, and sort of confusing. That, and my impression of the game has changed quite a bit, so I decided to delete the old review.
The core mechanic of Solforge, card leveling, is incredibly unique, to the point that a lot of people won't grasp how it affects deckbuilding and gameplay for a very long time.
While SolForge seems like it doesn't have much strategy, it is actually incredibly deep, and every turn has very intricate decisions. You have to balance the desire to not fall behind on the board with leveling the cards that are going to help you win later. Using your life as a resource is imperitive when you are behind, and choices such as choosing the correct empty lane to put a creature into can be incredibly important. Tight play is rewarded very well in SolForge.
Deckbuilding is also incredibly deep. You see your entire deck every game, which allows for narrow but powerful cards to be included in decks. When building, you have to plan the entire arc you want to follow in game. Do you plan to play very aggressively with powerful level 2 cards, or do you fill your deck with insane level 3 creatures, and build the rest of the deck to buy you time to get them out?
The leveling mechanic makes drafting SolForge incredible. Every game I play with draft decks feels unique, since different cards get leveled, based on what my opponent was playing.
In short, in a lot of ways, SolForge is too clever for its own good. The game's design is super simple, but the leveling mechanic has a ripple effect on strategy. I have so much fun brewing decks every day.

Original Review:
Keeping in mind that this is an early access review (although when it is this short I have trouble calling it a review), I can not currently recommend CDF Ghostship.  The game seems like it will be really cool when some more work is put into it, but at the moment there are things that make it too frustrating for me.
Shooting can be painful.
I know, it is Early Access.  I get that.  I'm a game developer, I know what it is like.  That said, I'm also a gamer.
Any other problem I could mention with it is no big deal to me at the moment so I will leave it at that.  The bottom line here is that it is playable, but if you are short on cash I would wait.
One other thing to note is that while the game does support side by side 3D (Oculus Rift), the UI is NOT built for it and the guns float right in front of your face not only making you uncomfortable but also blocking much of your vision.  It is not playable with the Rift.

It is a mix between the good old System Shock 2, Dead Space, Doom and even at times, Alien: Isolation. As of now, you can only play as one character in the story mode until the marine releases down the line. So, you are a pilot that has boarded a ship where some nasties are running around, waiting to be exterminated!
The difference here from Ghostship Aftermath is you seem to be alone in this game, contrary to Aftermath where you could have directives from your partner then the AI or not at all! Well, maybe that changes later?
Aside of the story mode, the game offers an onslaught mode which can be appealing to horde mode lovers! The skirmish mode is fun but get's repetitive eventually! Challenge mode tests your skills in the game but I didn't liked that mode much, especially since the controls aren't that responsive in this game, just like the previous title Aftermath. When being stuck in items on the floor and hinders your movements, that irritates me A LOT!
The last game mode, simulation, is quite cool indeed. You get to explore the ship from a choice of fixed scenarios or you can simply roam the ship, map the areas in your mind. I was surprised to see a few enemies though!
I'll sum up the pros and cons so you can get a better overview and decide for yourself whether or not to get this game.
+Solid Atmosphere (similar to Ghostship Aftermath and also, reminds me of System Shock 2).
+Various Game Modes (Story, Skirmish, Challenge, Onslaught and the best in my opinion; Exploration).
+Decent Replayability.
+Infinity ammo for some weapons but takes time to recharge.
*On GhostShip Aftermath, the game offered different playthroughs but here in CDF Ghostship, the startup and miway through the story mode seemed to spawn the same elements around. Maybe it changes near the end or with the second character? Sadly, I can't put this on the PRO yet since that part is incomplete.
+Predictable Story but how can you be original when something that has gone wrong in a ship or space station happens yet again?
+Controls are improved from GhostShip Aftermath. Aiming works most of the time!
-Price is steep for the game. I do recall buying it in December 2014 and the price was around 10$ but now, 22$ the game asks.
-Many technical glitches. Granted the game is in BETA and Early Access so it can be understandable. It is more serviceable than GhostShip Aftermath though! But I keep getting stuck on ground items that hinders backtracking when enemies are rushing in my face. Very annoying!
-The running speed is not long enough. Is your character in such a bad health or something? Can't run more than FIVE SECONDS?!? Weak!
-Cannot remap or just see the controls while in pause? WHY!
-Weak graphical settings (Limited graphical options. Only three resolutions available. No eye candy as you are used to in any modern games. Can't even change game settings when in-game.
-Visually and animation speaking, it is very lackluster. I know this is a BETA INDIE game and its easy to pick negatively at the graphics. Still, I've seen indie games with better visuals and CDF Ghostship looks like it was made back in 2004.
-Auto save only. Can't save the game manually.
-Zombie/worm-slug-spider sound glitch that can still be heard after you killed the monster. Only way to make it stop was to quit and reload the game. (That was present on Aftermath and is occuring here as well). Very irritating!
-Same enemies throughout the whole game. Same twitchy movements and even walk/crawl through walls.
CDF Ghostship is a much more improved "GhostShip Aftermath". The game still has many faults but with its beta & early access phase, it can only improve upon before the full release. Like Aftermath, CDF has a good concept and some very good ideas. However, many things hold it back. It is still a commendable work the developer(s) [unsure if Shaun is alone in this or not like Aftermath] did on this project and hopefully the dev(s) can only improve before the full release.
-Glitches/bugs,
-Controls,
-Adding options in the pause menu,
-Increase the running time,
-Modern visuals.
I recommend to wait on this title before the launch. With the inconsistencies, glitches and bugs, you would be better to wait until the game is out of early access at least. Besides, I find the 22$ price tag steep for what you get here. I'd say that my best recommendation would be to play System Shock 2 and/or Alien: Isolation until this game is ready.
But, you always get it now and see for yourself how the development progress though! I can honestly say that CDF is much improved from GhostShip Aftermath. So get CDF on a sale and give it a shot!
6.0 / 10
PS. Just like GhostShip Aftermath review, I do not own any VR equipment at the moment so I cannot comment on that matter here. HOWEVER, I imagine playing this game in Oculus should enhance the experience considerably.

Wow, so Brian Kibler (Magic The Gathering Pro) designed his own card game, I'll bet it's ROCK solid eh?
Nope.
This game is literally 99% luck, there's no trading between players, rarer cards absolutely decimate cards that are less rare (eventually you'll get an all-rare deck) and you will lose games because they drew Level 3 cards and you drew Level 1 cards.
Now let me explain, the fundamental mechanic here is when a card is played it goes back into your deck, but it levels up. As a card levels up it gets better. You can play two cards per turn and discard the remainder (so they go into your deck but don't level up) while drawing 5 cards at the start of your turn.
What does this mean?
You can't hold cards until they're strategically useful, you just have to play what you got.
Mid game is dominated by level 2 and level 3 cards as neither player will have access to them.
Late game is entirely dominated by level 3 cards and the loser is often whoever has less rare cards available to them.
The limit of cards played per turn makes cards that grow in power amazingly good, or cards that can deal with multiple cards.
This means that with the correct combination of spells it's easy to quickly create a giant creature that's unkillable and will win you the game.
Of course with the correct combination of spells it's easy to dismantle that strategy but c'est la vie.
So is this game fun? Definitely, the mechanics are fun.
Is this game worth money? Definitely not. While the mechanics are fun and interesting they don't really reward skillful play, many games will be lost to simply drawing level 1 and level 2 cards when the opponent plays two level 3 cards and then two more the following turn.
Worth a bit of fun if you don't care about winning/losing for no apparent reason.

Turok is a first person shooter that ends up feeling kind of like Doom.  I really enjoyed it as a kid, having owned it on the N64, but I don't think it has held up as well as some other games.
Level design is often just big rooms or hallways with enemies thrown around.  Some levels in the mid to late game are cool, but early levels are kind of dull and the last couple levels throw a lot of mazes at you.  Some of the keys you need are easy to miss and the game doesn't give any indication of whether you've passed a key or if it's still further up.  (I was missing level 3 key 3 and spent a long time searching for it because I didn't realize the level end portal teleported you to a boss instead of the hub.)
There is a good variety of weapons, although many share ammo and some are only upgrades of lesser guns.  Most of the enemies don't feel very distinct, many are reskinned or feel the same.  As the game goes on, enemies get more health, so it's easier and quicker to just run past everything and kill only enemies that are triggers.
If you played it back in the day and loved it, it is probably worth picking up. If you have never played it, I recommend getting it if you like Doom games or if you really like old 3D action platformers.  I finished it in less than 6 hours, so keep that in mind.  This version adds a lot of convenient graphical and gameplay options that helps bring Turok up to modern fps standards, but if you still have an old copy you might be better off just playing that.

Yeah this is a difficult one.  It's going to be tough for some people to appreciate this one, and I had a heck of a time diving into it.  I read a ton of positive reviews, watched some videos, and got really excited about this game.  Offered as something different, it is the most unique combat experience which I've ever partaken, and the learning curve is steep.
At first, the combat feels like you're driving a tank; trying to steer the camera, aim your weapon's swing direction and position your character all at the same time and it's near impossible to land any kind of powerful or accurate blow on an enemy.  I recommend diving right into the arena to get a handle on the battle mechanix.
One thing that people will enjoy is that it is visceral and much more than simply smashing the left click button to melee hordes of baddies, although I've had to suffer through not even being able to land a single blow on one guy standing right in front of me.  I grimmace at the thought of my first encounters - it was like two tired boxers just clinging to other falling over themselves in a punchdrunk haze.
You may want to hold out on this game for now if you need to jump into a game and be good at it and kill everything, this isnt' for you.  If you want to take a bit of time rummaging through rooms and using a keen eye to pick up items for survival and plot points, all while being weary of what's behind that next door, you may be in for a treat.  Be warned, and tread carefully.

Surprisingly good game series and it's growing in quality, complexity, polish and number of titles. It's actually real time strategy rather than tower defense -- much more dynamic and fun.
The creeper is the enemy; there are structures on the map which will produce waves of creeper, which are hazardous to your units. Some structures will launch creeper artillery into the middle of your infrastructure. You use weapons to defend yourself and push the creeper back. Towards that end, you must acquire and manage your resources. Your objective is to destroy enemy offensive structures and the score is determined by how fast you can do it.
The high variety of maps presents a unique challenge every time. You can play it safe and ensure victory at lower scores, but the real challenge comes when you strain yourself and your units to win as fast as possible.

Short version: It's fun. It's hard. It's relatively bug-free.
MC seeks to address a lot of the issues with squad-based tactics games like X-COM, primarily by making character death less of an issue. The fact that even your best warriors will eventually die of old age means that losing a few in battle doesn't NECCESARILY require a restart of the entire mission. Heck, if they die in battle they might turn into a magical weapon for your other warriors to use.
That being said, there are issues, though most of them just come with the territory in this type of game. There are a lot of things to research and build, and all of them take a long time. If things start going badly for you, don't expect them to stop. Sure, you have a crucible to train your new recruits, but without someone to staff it, it does no good. If you find yourself low in units and your birthrate isn't good, you can go scour for new recruits, but it takes years.

Just a short review of the game as it's in Early Access December 2014. I've tried two playthroughs by now.  The first went haywire so I restarted, the second I made it to Year 300 (end game). I think there's a bit of a learning curve still :)
Anyway, I really, really like the game. It reminds me of a hybrid between XCOM (new one) and The Last Federation. The XCOM part is somewhat simpler in regard to the combat, yet it has its own flavor and you have some pretty clever things you can pull off with the different classes, equipment and skills. As to the Kingdom/Base Management it's two widely different beasts. Where XCOM had a lot of smaller research paths and many types of equipment there are fewer in Massice Chalice, so every choice counts - and smacks - like a b*tch.
If I had to pick one great feature of the Kingdom Management it's the breeding for various traits in the regents' children. It makes a heck of a difference. If you marry two regents with bad traits your resulting heroes will be so pathethic it's painful.
Right now it's not just playable but also enjoyable. I don't know for sure if there's just a lot more learning to do for me or if there are genuine imbalances in the game. I miss the feeling of late game XCON where you're very powerful and just kill scores of enemies. Actually, the second game I'm not sure I'll actually be able to complete, and I got this nagging feeling that maybe, just maybe, I shouldn't have paired that decent regent with that too young, unknown spouse.
Perhaps with the right bloodline with the right traits and personality ...

This is already a pretty complete game, and worth the purchase.
The combat is X-Com style, but a good portion of your troops will be melee, so cover is less of a deal. It's mostly about staying outside of the attack range of enemies, and ganging up on them one at a time. (By the end of the game you can sometimes eliminate one enemy per soldier per game though).  The soldier classes are pretty fun, especially the caberjack, which can push and stun enemies. If enemies are stacked in a line, he can even stun more than one. He synergizes well with the alchemist, who can drop some bombs on the enemies he's shoved together. The hunter is a little less impressive, but it's excellent to have one on the team due to the stealth abilities they get from the start. I understand DF is also working adding some hybrid classes.
The strategic game has a pretty steep learning curve. Your soldiers will maybe get 4 combats in over the course of their lifetimes, and so you need to build a dynasty. It's a mix of ensuring fertility (many offspring), experience (new soldier experience depends on regent at keep and standards at crucibles), and positive traits (a bit of eugenics between experienced regents and desirable mates). Now that I have that out of the way you may notice how I still recommend it. And that's because I want to emphasize that the game is still fun, just VERY VERY frustrating.The game is very fun and could be very addictive... once they fix the issue of difficulty and others. Think of the game like Xcom if it met with Game of Thrones, with the idea of making families out of heroes that will produce offsprings. On paper this is fantastic and for the most part the execution is more than decent enough when you consider the budget. The mechanics of choosing X or Y is not as punshing as XCom where the latter makes you feel like you just ruined the lives of millions  if you choose one continent over the other. Some complaints I have right now that will make me stop playing the game for now in hopes they'll be addressed:
1. Right now how far you get in the game is EXTREMELY dependent on how lucky you are with your initial role of heroes, ages, and classes. For example I just rolled a game where I had like 4 melees and 1 archer. I then made the highest ranked melee into the regent and gave her a partner to produce babies. By the time I built my second keep to get a new regent, I only had one Archer at a decent level, and once I put that one as a regent to give me high level archers I was basically F'ed because I had no other archers for battles, so now I need to fight battles with nothing but melee and alchemists. Which is extremely hard once you hit level 40.
So the issue at hand is that the regent/lineage system needs rework. Having to wait 15 years minimum for your next generation of a specific class is horrible. You don't get enough heroes.
2. Heroes don't level up unless you bring them with you to battles and use them to kill enemies. It's fine by itself if you were given higher level heroes, but you tend to be given low level heroes.
3. Bulwarks or w/e they're called are broken. So is whatever system that decides how many enemies you gotta fight at a time. I'm in year 40 and I got a map with bulkwarks in groups of 2 and I had to fight like 10 with nothing but melees and one archer. This was a pain, but then like three more appeared. If you're gonna have these guys gain a shield after an attack at least don't make it where damage goes down to 1. Or lower their base damage, because 5-7 per hit is ridiculous.

Starbound... oh where to begin?
i'll start by Saying sorry for my poor grammer or spelling. now onto the review.
First of all its basically a 2d side scrolling minecraft with lots of combat and space travel. it has come a very long way from when i first purchased it. and i have played nearly every itteration of it. in the early days there was no story line. just the game sort of like minecraft you survived and dug, flew around space alot. and explored.
BUT
the improvements the guys and gals down at chucklefish have for lack of a better pun made the game boundless.
@ the time of writing this the current pros and cons are....
PROS
-7 races to choose from each with there own race style as well as ship desgin.
-Plethera of randomly generated weapons via chests and enemy kills
-tons of crafting recipes
-so much variety with materials and decorations
-the universe coords use the usual X and Y setup + and - and the number stream can be up to 9 long for each, each 5x5 coord grid has at least a minimum of 30+ systems and each system can have anywhere from 1-6 or 7 planets, usually all explorable.
-Space stations you can make yourself and go to NPC ones
-Spacial anomalies usually hostile but the threat level varies from minimul to extreme and a handful of labels in between
-the number of locations you cannot alter and or harvest for every little block are small. i rarely encounter them short of quests
-NPC's generate random quests. they become repetative after like 10 of them, but depending on the planet the dificulty changes, as well as the rewards
-After enough quests some NPCs can be hired for your crew. i believe every 2 crew members up to 10 grant you a ship upgrade, allowing you more space on your ship.
-There is multiplayer,  so you and your friends can control a sector. though with the vastness of space you may never run into people.
CONS
-It's Hard when you start out, and there really is no Supreme endgame gear. Just top tier. but you still take damage pretty easily.
-Online populace is touch and go. you get random party invites and even people who seem cool still steal your stuff out of your ship.
-Playing alone is well lonely, you of course want some people to Gawk and clap at your creations.
-Repetative feeling surfaces alot, and creatures of the same archetype can be found on most planets, even though they are on the other side of the universe.

You are a Soviet counterintelligence agent reliving his memories of sabotage / assassination assignments for SMERSH through flashbacks during an interrogation. The storyline is scattered, as it features select important missions from the spy's CV. Each mission is thus standalone and the main character remains the mysterious strong & silent type. The graphics and controls remind me a lot of Mafia 1 and Max Payne 1 and 2. The shooting accuracy is very messy (not smooth). The game is undemanding and runs smoothly even on older / weaker rigs. Despite it being set in WWII, you won't get that "nazi bashing" feel you get with most games set in that era. DTS is a long enough (will take you 10-12 hours to comlete), stealth-oriented game, so you get lots of rewards for acting qietly - infiltrating enemy compounds, silently disposing of bodies and walking around in enemy uniforms, for the obtainment of which you get a rich array of tools (strangling cord, cloroform, poison, throwing knives, silenced weapons, distraction tools and opportunities, whistling, etc) and you get a rating for your work at the end of each mission.
A lot of people and gaming magazines claim the game is overly difficult, and it is not due to the quality of AI. As a matter of fact, the game is difficult mostly due to their quantity. Some missions are literally spammed with civvies and soldiers (who are immune to spatial awareness) to the point where you can't reach your objective on time. Don't get me wrong, even on the easy difficulty, the AI has excellent sight, hearing and identifying capabilities. The higher up you go in uniform, the less suspicion you arouse. Enemies will also recognize foreign weapons and backpacks. Trigger an alarm and you'll have to redo a whole section. Save, save, save. I normally have around 7-10 saves per mission and each mission is about an hour long, mostly because of unknown variables, such as random civvies / soldiers walking in, or you walking in on an uncomfortable set of enemies. You'll spend a lot of time scheming and waiting for an opportunity to strike and hide a body, or a window to run past a diplomat, pick his safe and replace his documents. Compared to other stealth games like Splinter Cell, Death to Spies is more "wooden" and realistic in terms of the human limitations your character has - get in trouble once and it's over. He can't even climb stuff other than ladders. He's just a regular guy, and that makes fooling an entire enemy base such a rewarding experience.

An improvement in every possible way
AVGN II is, obviously, the sequel to the successful AVGNA. The story is essentially the same except you are not pulled into a video game and the levels end when you step on a detonator and blow them up. The only thing missing from the sequel is the ability to resue and play as multiple unlockable characters but don't concern yourself with that as every other aspect of the game has been improved, expanded, and polished.
You only play as the nerd this time around but, as with the prequel, he is so well-rounded and capable of getting the job done just fine. In exchange, you'll eventually run into various powerups that'll transform you from versatile nerd to video game assassin. In true parody fashion, the stages are expanded into a map format and are split into various zones which can be completed in any order. Even better, the stages are far superior than its predecessor in the sense that you can replay various stages with your powerups to find secrets and extra pathways. The powerups are useful to obtain to help along with your adventure and are no longer situational gimmicks. The music and controls are top-notch and the ending is satisfactory both as a tribute to the games of the era and to the game itself. With multiple modes to play, items to collect, and levels to perfect, you have hours of entertainment to keep you occupied. Every aspect of this game comes together in perfect harmony and does a fantastic job in paying tribute to the nerd and the genre.

Got this game when first released into early access .Back then it had  very little story content and  a few ideas that really needed fleshing out  a bit . Key bindings  back then were  non  existant  and the game would be ok  provided  you were right handed .There was no inventory as such  and  Video resolutions  were as rare as hens teeth, while  the graphics  left some margins for improvements.
Since its release into EA however the Dev has worked hard on the game and improved it with a steady stream of updates.We now have an inventory,bindable keys, many more resolutions and graphics that can be turned up or down according to your rig.The storyline  is now completed with three variations on the endings.You can play at your own level and pace with three difficulty levels ranging from Easy through normal to nightmare.The dev does not spoon feed you and finding information  to move  the game forward  requires  you to explore the ghostship seeking out clues, weapons and goodies.There to stop you doing this are a  raging bunch of  alien monsters and mutant infected crew members and you will certainly die a few times before getting into the swing of it.
Although some of the battles can be very intense with seemingly endless streams of aliens  coming at you ,there is an auto  save point at the last airlock you passed through, in all the  difficulty modes.The few ideas that needed fleshing out a bit have now become completed versions  in Onslaught mode,Challenge mode,skirmish mode  and Simulation. All these modes have 4 or 5 variations within  each of them so there is plenty to get your teeth into  for the majority of gamers.I would  recommend this game to those that enjoy a challenge and having to use their powers of observation and deduction. They must be prepared  however  for  the many jump scares  that  are sometimes just  around the corner on  this  CDF Ghostship?

Would I recommend Lifeless Planet? Yeah, kind of.
Would I play it again? Nope.
The game was, to a degree, fun. It had an interesting storyline, and some nice visuals. There was an interesting concept to boot. However, I feel like the game still isn't... finished.
The graphics aren't the best, but they're definitely acceptable, and they get the job done.
The gameplay is simple and makes it feel more like a visual novel. To put it simply, the game is a corridor; a simple hallway you walk through. Sure, there are some neat tiles here and there, and occassionally there's something you might need to step over. As much of a corridor that it is, it's a big one; both wide and long.
If you enjoy the occassional narrative, give it a try. Don't expect it to blow you away.
Over all, despite the game having been officially released recently after having been in open beta, the game still feels very much like it's in that beta stage.
While I would recommend this game, I'm going to have to go with the Ice Cream formula: With the money I spent on this game, would I have had more fun spending that money on ice cream and/or hookers?
At some points, the answer is yes. At other points, no.
To put it simply, the game was a mixed experience, and I would recommend getting it again... at least, if it ever goes on sale at a fair discount.

From the Depths is a sandbox strategy building game, which puts it into a nice niche. There are only few games that play comparably to this game and all that do, don't do it as good (I'm primarily talking about games like Besiege).
Now to the main review topics:
Graphics:
The game is not having any specialities here. It has a neat comic-like artstyle, which benefits from the graphical restrictions and gives the game a nice individual touch. The game runs very smoothely on the lowest graphic settings, which enables even the most tomato PC to handle the game. However, when using larger (or more) creations in the game, it all gets resource heavier, up until the point where even the strongest PC's fall on their knees. The game is poorly optimized. People who are going to expect amazing graphics and AAA performance are going to get let down a bit here.
Tutorial and game depth:
The tutorial is made very well in this game. You are not forced to do one, you can decide whether to do it or not. That is a huge + for the game, because many developers these days simply go the route of "do this. do that." they force you down a linear path and From the Depths get's it right. After being put into the game, you get a tutorial-completion-meter, which displays your development in a huge list of all sorts of small, compact and insightful tutorials. For completing a tutorial you get rewarded with experience, which you can use to give yourself useful abilities in the game, like consuming less fuel per vehicle and things like that, but nothing gamebraking. The tutorials tells you anything you need to know about the game mechanics and equips you with the skills you need in order to be successful in the campain mode.
Enough said about the tutorial, let me lose some words about the depth of the game.
There are a crap ton of mechanics you need to understand and take into account if you want to succeed in the campain very far. The game has aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, armor models, radar detection models and all sorts of other goodies. There is nothing like a super weapon, since anything can get countered, some weapon systems easier, others trickier. You can build whatever you like, there is no "right" way and making the basic components of your vehicle work, is easy. The tricky part is, to make them as effective as possible. The game has a very steep learning curve, which may seem intimidating to rookies, but you learn over time and succeed. You can tweak a campain's difficulty by regulating the enemy's growth factor and the recource they're given. But you can also tweak the difficulty by using the game mechanics right. That are the treats that Dark Souls is having success with! For example by using a special type of shell in a specific way, you can counter an enemy faction completely. So there is an artificial difficulty and a set difficulty.
Gameplay:
You can choose between 4 different campains in which you have to reign supreme over the world of Neter. In the game you get recources, with which you can  build vehicles and structures from building blocks and components similar to Robocraft, or Minecraft. You can make use of different engine types (electric, fuel and steam), weapon systems (cannons, missiles and energy weapons like lasers) and propulsions (wheels, jet engines, hydrofoils, etc.). All of them can be combinated freely without any restrictions, you can build your crafts the way you like! Want a car with lasers and missiles? No problem. You can build anything from tanks to spacecrafts, from submarines to weaponized sleds.
Facit:
20 bucks is a great deal for this amazing game! Get it, it will give you hundreds of hours of joy! Just don't forget to git gud, m8.
Building is very time consuming but really fun. Still waiting for improvements for land mechanics and more blocks.

From the Depths is a game you don't see much of. It has its similarities with other "freeform" vehicle building games, utilizing voxels, but ultimately it's so much more than that. Development is admittedly a little slow, the game already gives you plenty to work with, and while the initial learning curve is quite steep, if you can push past that, you'll quickly find it well worth the purchase cost, especially in the full freedom it grants you to build using quite a number of components: whether it be for a military campaign that can be played like an RTS or a personal combat simulator, or simply a building platform, the game has a little of something for everyone, and I highly recommend it for anyone who can enjoy a game with a bit of complexity.

Tournament play was introduced just before christmas 2013, and offers additional chances for new cards, and another way to play against equal powered decks (draft tournament). Due to daily rewards, one can play maybe one draft tournament per week for free. Winning enough matches in them will provide additional tickets, allowing even more drafts without paying anything.
Online play tries to match players against roughly equal skills/cards, so the games should be relatively close ones. And remember, due to game mechanics, it is quite possible to win even after being 100-10 behind, so know and trust your cards and decks.
If you enjoy the game play, then there is a lot of fun to be had for free. If, on the other hand, you can't resist the urge to get all the legendaries, then prepare to pay. While legendaries have their place in decks, they are not required, and certainly do not guarantee a victory. Knowing the strengths and weaknesses of all cards is more valuable, so just playing with any deck against the AI will help you improve. Playing against other people allows you to see how cards you don't yet have might work, and allows for differing play styles from the AI.
If you like Card Games...this game is really worth exploring. Deck Building capabilities feature alone sets this apart.

Alright. Giving credit where it's due, Massive Chalice is a pretty ambitious game. It takes the best qualities of XCOM: the R&D aspect, the top-down tactical combat system, and that fun little dance on the knife's edge as you try to level up your favorite character while avoiding that permadeath. All those qualities and throw it in with elements of a fantasy kingdom simulator with the whole 'kingdom in peril by a mysterious corruption that taints the land' plotline and the system of marrying off your heroes to produce heirs to continue your war on this corruption. All those things are great. Also? The Cadence enemies? Pretty sick designs and it totally showcases the unnatural corruption feel of what the Cadence is all about.
All those things are what makes Massive Chalice a pretty interesting game to check out... But not for thirty dollars.
The eugenics system feels like it creates a funnel where eventually you want to marry off all your heroes together to create better heirs with the right traits and personality and the right stats. (Hard enough as it is to find the right hero with the right traits and personality to marry off at the right time, but that's another thing.) Eventually the relationships between your later-gen heroes become incestous as in order to preserve the genes you want, you'll have to start marrying off cousins togeher. Which is something wrong that I can't seem to wrap my head around.
Continuing on the subject of the eugenics system, let's talk about the bloodline relics. I haven't found the right pattern to create a relic reliably yet, but it seems to come from either the number of enemies you kill and the number of missions you do. Either way, trying to build a relic is frustrating as the Cadence attacks are infrequent through one hero's lifetime. It basically creates a weapon based on the stats of the hero's weapon that you can level up with the heroes that come afterwards. In the period of time you can level the relic, you can pretty much research the next tier of weapons and it would generally surpass the relic.
Last thing I want to talk about are the Cadence Pawns, I have already acknowledged that the Pawns are pretty sick looking but then there's their performance in combat. You see, each of the Pawns have a special ability. Cradles have the ability to spawn more pawns to throw at you; wrinklers can age your heroes with an attack; Lapses can effectively drain your HP... You get the picture. Now my problem with the Pawns are that they are one-trick ponies. They have their little special ability and then the rest of their movesets are routine for every one of them. It makes combat monotonous and repetitive after a while and that's just a bummer.
To recap. Cool and ambitious project, but it falls short of expectations. Nonetheless, it can't be called an XCOM clone because it does take a unique approach to the genre and I do hope that it can straighten itself out when it comes out of Early Access.

I don't understand some of the negative reviews, every game has faults. But especially here the good outweighs the bad.
Good:
A great Tactical Turn Based RPG/Breeding Simulator. Aside from units seemingly not having "Facing". I'm not always doing the same thing with my capital either so far, a few times I've researched more pools of heroes to have more people to breed due to an irritating loss due to a few mistakes in combat facing a new type of enemy. This one time one of my forts was empty, so I set a 1 year old as the regent and married him to a 3 year old girl because I was low on choices (despite not knowing how likely they would be to breed). Then they had babies twice right away at ages 16 and 17. I was like "Success!". I feel the game gives you "enough" choice. For example, I had the choice of defending an area with no blight but I would get more XP for killing stuff, whereas the other place already had blight but I would only get a baby girl for defending it. It would be more risky to let the blight spread where it is already, but more rewarding for my heroes to take the non-blighted land.
Not Good or Bad:
Some people complain about the graphical style, saying it has "Bad graphics". At first it was jarring for me. But as I played about an hour into it, the style just works. It reminds me of some of the art in Civ, just in 3-D. As your heroes age, it shows in their faces. This simplified style works wonders here, as you can tell they are older just by looking at their faces. The style remains consistant throughout the game and works well in most if not all areas. It also gives it more of a painted fantasy storybook look. I wouldn't change it, but adding some new particles or lightning might further boost the look.
Things I would improve:
Free equipments. I think the research time should be cut and you should have to "build" equipments consuming monster parts. If you lose a group out in the field you lost those equips, if you lost one dude out in the field, but you won, you get his equips back. It just bugs me a little that once you research something, you immidiately get 100+ free items through the course of the game.
Bad:
Crucibles are too hard. There are ways of dealing with every enemy and situation in the game (so far) that I've found out by using each class's different skills (Clobberjacks for stunning things at right times, bombing enemies from around structures, using the hunter to scout ahead a bit, etc). Except for Crucibles. They seem to outrange you, and not only that they can kill any ranged person in one shot because they do like 14+ damage. If you use both actions in your turn and "ran" into the sight of one, you are dead as soon as it's their turn. Even Clobberjacks like level 5 with the second teir armor seem to go down to like 1/3rd hp. Since they are ranged it is sometimes hard if not impossible to get to them in time to stun them too. You either catch them around a corner and stun/bomb/kill before it's their turn, or you get unlucky and have to fight them in the open. I found on a level where there are more than 2 Crucibles, I should always expect to lose a guy. Even the brute kockback teleporting fist dude can be dealt with, but these crucibles...

There have been many iterations of
over the last 20 years, so first let's be clear about what exactly you're getting in this version of the game: this is a
edition of the first game in the series,
, originally released on the Nintendo 64 in 1997.  This is not to be confused with a reimagining or a remake; Night Dive Studios' mission was to clean up, repackage, and preserve the original game, and in this modest but noble goal they have succeeded.
is a faithful reproduction of the retro classic, which includes all of the charming glitches from the original but none of the technical flaws.  The game is optimized for modern platforms and has never looked better on an HD display.  Minor graphical touch-ups have been added, although they are very subtle.  All in all, this is now the definitive version of the game.
There are three major elements to
gameplay: combat, platforming, and exploration.
Combat moves at a fast clip, as most areas of the game feature at least one respawn wave of enemies who will flank you if you backpedal from the enemies which lie ahead of you.  The enemy respawns are sometimes quick and occasionally relentless, but it never feels unfair since there are clear audio/visual cues associated with the spawn-in.  Adding to the frenetic pace is a very quick character movement speed.  Enemies can close distance in seconds and the player-character is equally agile and responsive.
The gunplay itself focuses on the player amassing an arsenal of weapons (found through exploration) and then frequently switching through the inventory wheel to pick the right tool for the job.  Unlike many modern First Person Shooters,
places no limit on the number of weapons that can be in the player's possession at any given time.  Additionally, unlike many of its contemporaries,
does not reset the player's inventory after each mission.  As a result, there's a continuous sense of character progression / growing strength.  Yet, the game also manages to gradually become more challenging as spongier, heavier-hitting enemies are introduced later in the game.  Gunplay in
is just as much about being accurate as it is about managing and conserving ammo; if you use too many rockets on the middle-tier enemies, you won't have them when you really need them to deal with the bigger baddies.
Platforming in
can be a particularly vexing mechanic, especially for newcomers.  If you haven't done a lot of platforming from a first-person perspective, get ready to learn the hard way.  Missing a jump usually means instant-death, and there is a whole lot of unskippable jumping in this game.  Not even cheat codes can help you get past these segments, so it's a skill you must be committed to mastering if you plan to play the game to completion.
Exploration is a large part of the game, and it's one of the most-rewarding.
level design is smarter than meets the eye, often employing subtle environmental clues to lead the player in unexpected directions.  Some levels are more linear than others, but all of the game's eight major regions are full of secret areas off the beaten path.  Diligent exploration is rewarded with upgraded-ammo, extra life tokens, keys to open new levels, and early access to more-powerful weapons.  The trickiest and most-rewarding collectables of all are the hidden pieces of the game's ultimate weapon: The Chronosceptor.  It should also be noted that, while some of the mandatory pickups (namely: level keys) are easy to miss, backtracking hardly takes any time thanks to the extremely fast player movement speed.
was originally released towards the beginning of the N64's lifecycle when 3D gaming was still relatively new to the masses.
was one of the better-looking 3D games of its time, but to virgin eyes I imagine that it must look really rough around its sharp, polygonal edges.  Luckily, Night Dive Studios has cleaned up some of the original game's glaring technical flaws.  Most apparent among them are the oppressive fog and draw distance.  If you remember the N64 game fondly then you'll definitely appreciate how much easier it is to see where you're going in the remastered version.  No longer does the fog hide enemies standing five feet in front of your face.  However, Night Dive has tastefully decided not to eliminate the fog completely, preserving the some of the mysterious, haunting aesthetic of the original without compromising playability.
True to the original, the music is serviceable enough but doesn't stand out.  It's thematically appropriate but not very interesting.  There's a lot of minimalist, primitive-sounding percussion, but the music loops too frequently and conspicuously to effectively blend into a subtle, immersive, atmospheric texture.  The sound effects are actually rather humorous at times, which breaks the mood a little but is generally joyful.
This is a solid game.  And the remaster-- price not considered in this review-- doesn't come across as a simple cash-grab, in my opinion.  True, very little has been added to the game.  But Night Dive Studios has made too many considerate, tasteful decisions for me to be cynical about it.

Very fun game, but keep in mind it can be very frustrating. I keep coming back to the arena mode, and I haven't tried to play the story mode in weeks. Even without the story this game is great. If games with physics based combat are your thing, this game is basically the most complex you can get, melee combat wise.

It's a remarkably fun game solely by virtue of it's combat system.  To the uninitiated, it controls rather awkwardly, with everyone essentially being a ragdoll animated by physics.  Once you get into the swing of things, however, you tend to find that this is about as skill-based as an action melee game can get.  Hits and misses are entirely physics-based.  You have to work with your movements, build up momentum properly, time everything just right, down to a shuffling of the feet or a swing of your weapon.  You can win any fight as long as you know what you're doing.
It's all based around realism while still being balanced.  Blades don't require as much force and have a greater contact area for doing damage generally, while blunt instruments are the opposite.  Armor will protect better against blades, reducing it to less-lethal blunt damage, while maces and morningstars will bully your tin can until you're nothing but tomato soup inside.
Once you get good at it, nothing can really compare to smashing someone's stupid face in with a mallet, or even a cleaver.  It's all very satisfying, as many others would testify.
The arena mode sates my need for progression, and I look forward to seeing how the game develops.
