I want to make this very clear before I properly start this review: I have put this as "Not Recommended" as it is definitely
recommended for the average gamer - for most, it will be too frustrating and infuriating to last much longer than an hour. However, if you are a big stealth fan like myself, then you will get some enjoyment out of this game. That enjoyment is limited though, and I'll explain.
If you've played the Hitman series, Death to Spies should instantly remind you of it. You're walking around open areas with multiple paths and disguises are a vital aspect of the gameplay. The difference is that Hitman does it a lot better. The disguise system in this game is a strange beast - you can wear multiple disguises in each level, usually 2 or 3, and usually one will be "better" than the other - as in, there will be less "red" enemies who are able to see through your disguise. The whole thing doesn't really make sense - some enemies, for whatever unexplained reason, know you're a spy. I've completed the game from start to finish and I still don't really get it.
This game is also mercilessly difficult and frustrating. I won't say "challenging" - because that implies you have to think deeply and strategically about what you're actually doing. Most of the time, you'll have quick save and quick load at the ready, doing things in hope rather than guile and seeing if they actually work. The game leaves you very little hints or clues about how to achieve your objectives, which I know some will love as they hate the idea of "hand-holding", but it isn't a black-and-white concept - there is a middle ground where the game can both help you out and you can think for yourself how to solve situations. Other stealth games like Splinter Cell and Metal Gear Solid get that middle ground, while this unfortunately doesn't. People who dislike stealth games often criticise popular titles in the genre for being trial and error games - and yet, as a stealth fan who's played most games in the genre, I found this overly trial and error based. I don't think I've ever looked at a walkthrough as much as I did on this game as often I was left wondering how I was actually supposed to complete my objectives.
Just to add insult to injury, the game is rife with bugs and glitches. You'll find yourself getting stuck in walls and tiny unexitable areas. You might experience a glitch where the camera is in a completely opposite direction to where your character is moving. Oh yeah, and the music in the intros is incredibly loud, so you've got that to enjoy whenever you launch the game.
One area where Death to Spies does deserve credit is the map design - these maps are unusually large for stealth games and is a great change from dark, linear areas in many stealth games. However, there's nothing to do in these areas - if you want to complete the missions, there's always some linear path that is by far the simplest way to complete the missions. The game makes it far too difficult for you to actually use these open areas so you can complete a mission a different way from someone else.
Despite all these issues, I still had fun with Death to Spies, and other stealth fans will feel the same. Credit has to go to the developers, as you can see they tried - the poor English grammar due to the game being a low-budget Russian title adds to the appeal a little. Unfortunately, the game is just plagued with too many flawed gameplay mechanics to make it enjoyable for the general gaming populace - and it's that which kills it.

This gets a tentative recommendation, though in my opinion, this is a $10 game, not a $20 one.  Wait for it to go on sale, then buy it.
*Spoiler Free Review*
This is firmly an adventure game, and it uses its horror well.  You never have a way to fight back against the dangers of the planet, which works in the game's favor.  I was on edge the whole time, examining my path carefully to avoid dying horribly.  The game does host invisible walls, but with one or two exceptions, I never encountered them, focused on not being killed by the enemies lurking about.  To further play up the horror, you occasionally hallucinate through the game, which left me frequently wondering if what I just saw was real.
The mystery of the first half of the game was phenomenal, as was the revelation of the planet's history, but this actually wound up working against the game.  The ending left me unsatisfied, and the twist revealed by the final document was disappointing.  I felt that it verged on pulling the game from Sci-fi to Fantasy, and after all that build up, it was a real let down.
As you travel, there are set points where your jetpack fuel will run out (limiting you to just one boost, down from seven), as will your oxygen.  The oxygen is done to show passage of time, as well as to play into the story, and the jetpack fuel is done to present new platforming challenges, but both came off as contrived and pulled me out of the experience each time it happened.
The controls work well on keyboard or controller, though a little bit more air maneuverability would have been nice.  Most of the puzzles are just a matter of finding the right object to drop into a hole, and the rest are figuring out a button sequence, but that's fine.  This isn't a puzzle game foremost, this is an exploration game.  The fact that the dev managed to make a linear exploration game not feel linear speaks volumes to his skill.
The graphics leave much to be desired, but so long as you're looking at the surroundings, it works fine.  It's when you're looking at a facial expression that it becomes jarring.  Faces here always seem to be either neutral expression or vaguely malevolent, which makes the protagonist's description of what they were supposed to be expressing seem canned and insincere.
I didn't get attached to the characters at all, and I can't help but think that had the protagonist's personal story been left out and the player been left to project on the character, the game would have been improved.  Without spoiling anything not already spoiled in the description, the mysterious woman had little personality.  Several scenes were thrown in to make me feel for her, and while one or two did make me feel horrified or confused as intended, I never managed an attachment.
The level design is done quite well, though the transitions need a LOT of work.  Frequently a new level would start, I'd turn around and sit there wondering how in the hell I got here.  A few levels also felt that they were put in just to have them.  The fire level, or the hot springs level, for example.  The level in the volcanic area in particular was frustrating, as the game became one of guess and check to figure out which ledges were safe to land on, and which would kill you instantly.  A few times there were even invisible walls mid-air that would do the same.  Fortunately, the death system is done very well, or I likely would have stopped there in frustration.
Overall, this is a good game, and it made me stay up far later than I should have to finish it.  A good story until the end, and I look forward to see more of the Dev's work in the future.  However, between the graphics, short run time (I finished it in ~4.5 hours), and lack of replayability, I don't feel it was worth the price of admission.

A honest review for 'From The Depths'
Computer: Macbook Air (early 2015) w/ 4GB ram
(also the game runs fine)
In this review, I will try my best to write a review of this game in the least bias way possible, even though this is without a doubt my favourite game.
First, Let's start with the most obvious con that you will see in almost every review; the learning curve. This game requires an immense amount of dedication, the tutorials are alright but they barely help at all. I, personally, bought this game after watching a youtuber named 'Lathland' complete multiple series so I started with a decent amount of knowledge. If you are a fast learner you will find it will take at least 50 hours to build a small boat only to find out that it is not big enough to house all the vital components you need. after 100 hours you will be familiar with the basics of the game but that is when the user experience deviates for each player; some will uninstall the game due to the difficulty and them getting their souls crushed after getting obliterated in the campaign. and the rest will keep messing around in designer mode and keep getting better.
(Disclaimer: This is where the non-bias part of my review ends everything beyond this point is my experience and may not be the same for you.)
The reason why this game is my personal favourite is that it is one of those games where you can be thousands of hours into it and still be learning new things. I have made plenty of vehicles in my time playing this game; each one better than the last. I believe early access reviews should focus on two parts:
-Is the game worth buying at this time?
and
-How does the games potential look?
At this time, January 9th 2015, both of these questions hold up pretty well with exanima. I won't bother to explain what the description already says, but I will elaborate on how it plays out.
The games physics engine has a huge amount of effort poured into it, even at this early stage. The strikes you do can land with a crushing thump, or maybe just a light scrape, depending on how you angle your hits and how hard your strike hits. It turns into a very challenging fighting mechanic that rewards careful tactics and good swordsmanship.
However, it should be mentioned that at the current time, everyone is drunk. Yes, even the skeletons. Essentially theres two types of stances. Normal movement stance, and fighting stance. Movement stance is fine for the most part. Feels a little funky due to the nature of physics and such, but overall very responsive.
And then theres fighting stance. The character readies his weapons, widens his stance, and slowly crab-walks towards his foes with determination. To say the least, it feels a little funny switching between these two modes, and the crabwalk feels a bit unresponsive at times (once again, due to physics. It makes sense when you analyze the movement). However, it does the job well enough.
Once you get the hang of these, it works. Most of the time, quite well. But even though its mechanically smooth, it feels a bit clunky just due to the very nature of the beast. Expect to die a few times while your getting used to it.
The combat is very very satisfying. As mentioned before, depending on how you strike a target, or a target strikes you, changes the amount of damage done. Since parrying happens quite often, landing those satisfying blows is just too much fun. Its the delicious crunchy reward after being hammered blow after blow and barely fending them off every time.
The story at this stage has a little bit of love too poured into it. Its told in dark-souls style, where little fragments of parchment lore are scattered throughout the level, and by reading parchment after parchment you begin to piece together a rough idea of whats happening. So far, it needs quite a bit of work and a little more substance: I've read most of the accessible parchments and I still have no idea whats going on. But, its intriguing, and leaves me searching around for more.
On whats apparently considered a good run, I completed the current storymode at around 8-10 hours. If you were to speedrun it, I'd probably say it could be completed in less than 2. Exanima has the mindset where levels could be completed very fast if you know where everything is, but most of the fun comes from exploring the various rooms, finding new story fragments, gear, and areas.
With all that in mind, exanima is a unique experience. Many games say they have physics, but nothing implements the idea so thoroughly as exanima. It permeates its every fiber and decision it makes.
For that, I'd say its well worth the asking price at the moment for 15 dollars, and its potential is astounding. I'll be watching this game closely as it comes out with updates, and I'd recommend for anyone else who wants to try a truly unique RPG experience.

I want to preface this by saying that I've met James Rolfe a few times. He's an awesome guy and I've been supporting him in every way I can over the years.
So, that being said, I am very happy with AVGN II. I really liked the first game and I really like this one. Is it exactly the same as the first? No. A few things were changed here and there, some for the better, some of the worse, but nothing makes the game unfun.
If you haven't played the first, don't worry. There's no connecting story between the two so you can jump right in.
AVGN II is an action platformer, just like the first. You shoot enemies and dodge obstacles. It's as simple as that. So what makes this different from the first game? Well, to begin with, there's a world map like Super Mario 3 (unlike the first that had you choose zones like Mega Man.) This doesn't add or detract any difficulty from the game, but it's a difference. As far as actual gameplay, it all remains largely unchanged. Things that are different are fine tweaks like being able to wall hike, hold a diagonal aim, collect upgrades that stay with you from level to level: things like that.
One thing that was changed that I'm not super big on is the decrease in difficulty. Levels tend to be shorter and far less difficult than in the first. But there is some nice variety in the way of auto-scrollers thrown in for good measure, so that's cool.
And the burning question: is the game funny? Well, one of the stages was called Hang Dong '97. No shame, I laughed out loud. If that kind of humor is your thing, you're in for some laughs.
Overall, I was very happy with AVGN II. I beat it much more quickly than I did the first, and while I feel some of the stages were a little too short with a decrease in difficulty, I still had a fun time. Buy this and keep the Nerd going.

Been a fan of point and clickers for as long as I can remember and been a long time fan for BS. When I saw it out for sale, I couldnt resist. We are greeted by pretty new graphics, yet familiar faces and voices with a story that seems promising.
If you are new to the series then I would suggest getting the triple pack of 123 together, however, if you are familiar with the series and want intrigue adventure and fun, well, so far, BS5 has the potential to 'deliver' but right now, it doesnt. The locations you visit are few, the puzzles are easy, straight forward, almost idiot proof (prompts and hints are too readily available too), humour is few and far between, or simply not funny and you only get a few hours worth of game play.
Though we are promised a new chapter early in the new year, the first part of the game simply seems like a prolouge, does that mean after the next chapter they will start charging for the follow ons as DLC?
BS5 promises a lot but has delivered very little... so far... all it has done is set out a mountain of promises and I really hope it doesnt break them.
If you are a die hard fan, then you will likely jump on this game regardless, however, right now it isn't complete, feels far from it, feels unengaging and plays more like a Japanese animated novel where you simply click the screen repeatedly and make a few choices now and then, with that in mind, they may as well had turned the whole broken sword franchise into an animation, at least it would have removed the 'chore/bore' from the game. There are no random choices with consequence, no alternate ways to solve puzzles.
Right now I hope it gets better, I will always hold broken sword with eager eyes to 'reinvigorate' the genre again, but with games such as 'The Walking Dead' out there, there will be many people disappointed with this game.
If you are a die hard fan, look into it, they may pull something out of the hat yet, but if you are new to the series, AVOID AVOID AVOID play the first and second game then maybe follow on.
P.S. hurry up and get BS4 on Steam already Valve!!

This game is catergorized as an "explolration" title, and while there is a little bit in the sense of looking around for minerals, it is actually a very linear game. That said, it doesn't detract from what the game is. It's about 4 hours long and is incredibly atmospheric.
It is basically a "follow a path and do a few jump puzzles sequences" game. Every now and then there is a small puzzle to get through. There isn't a ton to it, but what is there is just fantastic. You will want to play this game for the atmosphere alone. The music is really great and fitting. The story is somewhat interesting. Interesting enough to pay attention to it. And though the name of the game isn't really acurate, it does still give a sense of loneliness.
The one thing I don't like is the achievements. A few of them are "do such and such on your first play through". If you don't look at the achievements before playing the game, you will have no clue that you need to accomplish these things on your first playthrough, and so after you screw up once on your first playthrough, you can never get the achievement then? That's not cool. "Don't die on your first playthrough." You die once, you can never get the achievement? That's just dumb.
But that's an incredibly small gripe that doesn't actually have anything to do with the gameplay. Overall a very solid atmospheric game that I really enjoyed.

An interesting take on the tower defense genre.  In a lot of ways it plays a lot more like a conventional RTS, with interesting resource management, movable units, and requiring the player to offensively attack enemy structures, rather than sitting back and waiting.   Instead of fighting discrete enemies, you battle back a flow of liquid-like creeper.  Most levels have multiple viable strategies to beat them, giving the player a lot of decisions on how to tackle a level.
The game features a massive amount of content, with a lengthy, well written campaign, along with nearly infinite player created and procedurally generated levels.

If you are looking for a combat strategy game and you have fun with tactics and you like to continue playing a game for ever (custom maps), then this game is for you!
The whole gameplay is just perfect. The interface is easy to use and very effective, the maps in the game advance in difficulty to adjust the players progress.
Don't be fooled by the simple graphics! On the pictures it doesn't seem that good, but once you play, the graphics make absolute sense. With the graphic style the Devs chose, they have made it very easy to control all of the map.
I like the story, even though it is cheese. It does add to the whole experience.
So far I had no crash and didn't find any bugs! So the Devs have done a great job in programing.
I highly recommend this game to any strategy gamer out there!

Early Access Review: I don't see how this game can change a whole lot to make a vast improvement, which it really needs. If you've ever played X-COM, it's hard to play a dumbed down version of that. Massive Chalice has some really awesome concepts that work better on paper. You get to create several generations of blood and name that will go on for as long as you can keep them alive. They may have some weaknesses and strengths, and many of these can carry on for a couple hundred years. This can be alcoholism, higher HP, lower evasion, better aging, lower lifespan, better stealth, etc. The list goes on and I probably only got to play with a third of what's out there. The important thing is, once you find a strong bloodline, you stick with it and make it stronger. Sounds pretty cool, right?
Well, unfortunately, there's not a whole lot else here. As time goes on, your birthing choices mean less and less and eventually you just want to get the game over with. The combat is challenging, but not complicated enough. You only have so much to work with, and it's not even 1/10th as intricate as X-COM. There's some fun concepts here like trying to plan your means of attack and stealthing in unseen on a group of 10 enemies. But it all starts to become fodder to a point. You get to saying "here we go again..." and finish it like you had the other 20 battles before it. So I just don't see how this game can be greatly improved on full release. I completed it with an emptiness to fill and hope the best for it. Unfortunately, it wasn't enough for me. I recommend getting this on a massive sale if you REALLY need to play this type of game.

It is very different from your average WWII game which there's a lot of shooting.  This game involves careful planning and stealth.  You will find yourself dead very quickly if you start shooting.  I will discuss this game under these heading:
LEVELS: There are 10 levels in total.  Most of them take at least 1 hour to complete.  The levels include; a German concentration camp, a British hotel, an American military base and a German military school.  A detailed tutorial mission can be done at the start of the game.
DISGUISES: Disguises are an important element of this game.  Most levels you start off in Soviet military camouflage clothes.  German soldiers will immediately start shooting at you until you get a disguise.  There are different disguises available.  A German soldier is the most basic disguise.  Most German soldiers will not bother you but higher ranks may see through your disguise.  Some levels require you to get officer's uniforms, staff's clothes (e.g. a chef) or a worker's clothes.
WEAPONS: Before you start each level you can fully customise your equipment.  You can carry a shoulder, side and a knife weapon.  Main weapons include MP40s, MP44s and Stens.  Many pistols are also available.  The silenced pistol is he most useful.  Knifes can be carried - they can be used at close range or thrown.  For silent kills you are equipped with a choke cord and chloroform.  You can also punch people, although this is nosier.
VEHICLES: Vehicles can be driven in some missions.  Trucks, motorbikes and cars can be driven.
UI: You can swap between a main map and a mini-map.  You can use the + and - keys to zoom in and out.  The AI are shown as green, yellow, red and grey icons; green meaning no suspicion of you, yellow - vary (don't stay around these guys too long!), red - alert, usually if they see you they will raise the alarm and grey - civilians.  A suspicion meter appears at the top of the screen when guards are suspicious of you.  If this fills the alarm will be raised.
AI: There are many different types/appearances of AI people, though they aren't great.  Once you start shooting they tend to run around crazily until they compose themselves.  Mostly they're OK though.
Sound: The sound is good in this game.  German music can be heard coming from gramophones and the environmental sound are good.  The AI are pretty wordless.  This is improved in the sequel Moment of Truth (they say
to you if you're dressed as an officer!)
OTHER: You can pick locks, spy through keyholes, sabotage functions to distract attention away and more.

Sadly the controls are impossibly cumbersome, I know there's a school of thought which asserts intentionally obtuse, fumbling controls lends to the experience, but from classic horror titles, to Condemned, to this, I've just never had an appreciation for that approach.
I suppose if you even had strafing the game would be too easy, and thus not a Roguelike experience, but I just can't appreciate fighting to turn and dying as a result.

Though a cool example of physics based sword fighting in the vein of games like Blade Symphony, Exanima isn't truly about sword fights. Nor is it about the survival horror setting that will have you running from permadeath-inducing monsters. Sadly, what Exanima is really about is enduring an absolutly unforgivable control system that will see you stumbling drunkenly around the room.
Exanima's loose, inscrutable controls feel like trying to work a puppet-on-strings. The in-game camera is controlled by mouse-- but so too are your character's feet and arms, forcing you to choose between running, swinging and looking the right way. And when you do manage to do all three of those things, your attacks will send you spiraling out of control, your back to the enemy and your progress about to be deleted.
Exanima controls, in many ways, just like Surgeon Simulator. And though there are certainly Surgeon Simulator aces out there, nobody would tout the game as a serious simulation of an operating room. Yet Examina takes itself
seriously- and punishes you gravely for each nose dive your character chooses to take on your behalf.

Long and numerous discussions with the developer by myself and others have seen us spurned for merely suggesting that there was a problem. The developer finds that controlling the camera, your feet, and your hands with only the mouse is cutting edge (rather than confusing) and artistic (rather than obtuse). This method of control isn't going anywhere. And while it remains, your character in game won't be going anywhere either.

Basically, a very good concept in development here. When you first start out playing the game, when you have no idea what you're doing, it'll seem like all it is capable of is drunken fighting, but that is only because you have literally no idea how to play it. A few tips on the game in general:
1) Spend a while in the arena before you leap into the campaign, or how far they've gotten into designing it. You start out with either a spiked board or a rail-road nail essentially and whatever clothing you've chose to equip, so you best know how to fight.
2) Only is combat movement while in combat. Combat movement was not made for running across the room. It's why right-clicking while in combat mode gives you a dash feature; so you can actually move about.
Aaaaand some tips on the combat:
1) Footwork is important in this game. How it works out in combat is tapping will move you in slight incriments, while holding the key down will send you lunging in that direction. This is why it's so awkward to try and move long distances in combat mode: you're literally lunging everywhere. If you want to get in past an enemies guard, a good way to do such is sidestep them while they're in swing. Another good way is to let them swing, backstep, and then lunge in with your own attack in quick succession. You'll never get hit and, depending on weapon, possibly be able to get a couple good swings in.
2) Parry. Parry lots. This game does quite well in providing a realistic combat system. To take advantage of it, pay attention to the position of your enemy's weapon and your own. If you're in a guard state and hit attack just as you're blocking, your character will transfer it into a hard block into a redirecting block, followed by a quick parry. If you don't get the redirect, you can still parry to an extent, as your character will still be able to get a quick slash in, depending on the circumstance. Each weapon and combination will have its own set of distinct movement, so be in consideration of that. Even things such as which shield you use matter. The rectangular parrying shield, for instance, when you block an overhand strike with it, the parry will be an upper-cutting slash to the opponents abdomen, wheras if you are using a single weapon, the pary for the same sitation will be a flat-blade hard-counter transfered via a circular swipe into the opponents now non-guarded side.
3) Weapon choice matters. Each weapon will have an area that they excel at. Short, light, weapons, such as any of the arming swords (especially them, considering their speed of strike) will excel in slashing at an opponents legs in exchanges, as well as getting quick horizontal swipes  across the abdomen (it's possible to combo multiple slashes in one parry with the arming swords), while polearms will generally do well with striking an opponent's upper body and sides, circumventing the opponents guard with their reach to hit them along the side, the arm, or in the head and neck. I can't speak for heavy one-handed items as, well, clubs, maces, etc. has never had much appeal to me.
4) About good weapons for beginners to the game in arena: I would personally recommend starting out with just the arming sword if this is your first time playing the game. It is very swift, you don't have to worry about yellow damage that you accumulate with a shield due to the hard-blocking nature of a shield versus the parrying of the arming sword, and you will learn good footwork with it. Alternatively, picking the longsword will do fine as well, as it shares the swiftness of the parrying sword, can guard quite well, but also has the superior reach of polearms and can strike along the entire length of the blade so you don't have to worry about maintaining your distance as much as you do with a polearm to avoid striking people with the shaft versus the actual weapon head. I'd recommend picking up the upgrades that you find along the beginner arena, as the upgrade to the arming sword strikes better, being better balanced, while the greatsword has better reach than the starter longsword. You will, eventually, however, when you go into the expert arena, pick up some skills with polearms and definitely the maul. When you start fighting people in full plate, your swords do very, very, little to them, and the maul is the heaviest hitting thing you can get, being a giant hammer. However, because of that, it's stupidly slow and ungainly, so use wisely.
That is a bit of an overview, I may end up going further in-depth, writing a guide and such for the game.

Lifeless planet? More like lifeless game. This hunk of crap should be priced at no more than $1. In fact, they should be paying YOU to play this repetative, ugly, boring "game". If you like long walks in uninteresting deserts, then this game is for you. It even has a plant species that will kill you if you go off the designated path. Everything is so "mysterious", so naturally you just keep pushing on down the track instead of stopping to do any REAL investigating. From the beginning you can tell that not a whole lot of thought was put into this game. Your team of three astronauts crash lands in a tiny little pod, the kind that drop people from the space station. So how the hell were any of the characters supposed to get off the planet?? It's obviously a suicide mission, but they never touch on that. And you wake up magically outside your craft and in your boring, inept suit, your teammates long gone. Who were they? Why did they leave? Meh, it's not important. Naturally the first thing you should do is split up when landing on an alien planet you believe harbors life. And you randomly run out of oxygen, but only when you're nearby a convenient oxygen dump. Simply go near it and you're good. What's the point of this  little exercise? Not a damn thing. Oh, and you can collect little rock samples, which is neat because you're character is a geologist. A geologist that gets sent to an alien planet presumably because it has alien life on it. Smart. As you stumble down the track (which you cannot deviate from), you quickly come across one of your crew, bleeding in a barn. The crewmember doesn't speak, you don't say their name (they're just "buddy" to you) and then they get sucked into the ground and your character is like "huh... better press on then. Gee wiz this place is strange." Oh, and did I mention the barn is guarded by a sentient tornado? You can outwalk it, so you never need deal with it, and it never gets mentioned in the game, so it really doesn't matter. After meaningless exercises in jumping and jet packing along most perilous and haphazard trails, all in an effort to chase down some Russian-alien hybrid girl (with rendering from 2005, even with the graphics jacked up to "fantastic" level). The story comes to an abrupt end when you come to the second big alien door with buttons that are just too high, which require the use of a super-exciting robot arm. The first door opens easily enough, but the second door features nothing but broken buttons that you can't press, leaving you stuck. Think there's a way around it? Nope. There's invisible walls guarding the only way around. Think there's something else you should do? Nope, there's absolutely nothing else going on, except some huge structure that you can't access due to a broken lift. Think you can save right there and load it up later when you've calmed down? Nope, you're starting all the way at the beginning of the level so you get to go through the meaningless trails once more. Hope you like walking, jumping, and jet packing (but only a little bit, because your suit is♥♥♥♥♥♥, because that's all you're going to be doing.

This is an amazing game buy for the last year and a half there has been a bug that allows you to get unlimted money easily.  Here is how.  Make any ship, even if it's just one block and then attach and RTG to it.  Then delete the RTG so you get the full money cost back.  Then go to the ship in the tactical map view and click retrofit.  It will repair the RTG but for half it's cost.  Then you can delete the RTG again and get the full price back.  So a 5000 cost RTG costs you 250 money to repair, and then you sell if for 5000 every time.  With this bug you can obviously win since the only thing holding you back in this game is your money.  Since I know about the bug it's just too game breaking for me.  I love using RTGs and have them in every single vehical I use and I don't like using the fuel engines or steam engines.  So anytime I load up one of my vehicals I'm technically cheating because  when you load a vehical it makes you pay the repair cost for the RTG, not the full price.  The bug has existed since january 2016 and is still not fixed in november 2017 and will probably never be fixed.  This is a great game for building cool stuff and watching it blow up, but if you are looking for a sandbox resource game it's broken.  I'd reccomend skipping this game.

I really want to like this game, but so far it's not nearly as good as the original. My main problem is the controls feel really floaty and imprecise compared to the original, and the hitboxes are noticeably bad. While the original game had a lot of insta kill obstacles, it felt very fair when you got hit like it was your fault, everything moved in a clear pattern. In this game the difficulty is not only less rewarding, but instead of carefully placing obstacles it feels like they remove the insta-kill elements and create difficulty by just throwing a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥at you. The game's movement is NOT right to be able to dodge bullet hell levels of stuff they try to throw at you.
I know I only have 0.6 hours in this game, but I'm already 1/4th of the way done with all the hub world levels. Levels are extremely short and checkpoints are placed way too close together, often to the point where on normal you can just walk through and get hit by everything in your path and still make it to the next checkpoint. The level design is really inconsistent as well, some levels have been alright but otherse have been just boring and frustrating.
The music is also worse than the original so far, but that's hard to say since there's only been a couple of original tracks! The rest of the music is ripped straight from the original.
The only real improvement from the first game is the bosses and even then they're not great compared to other games of this genre. Also, the game looks aesthetically better, less like a pixel flash game and more like an SNES game which is far more appropriate, but even then it still fails to truly capture an old school aesthetic and comes off as a pixel indie game, just a slightly better looking one than the original. They take a step backwards with the aesthetics as well though, as a lot of the levels have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ filters over them that just make things harder to see, like the black and white filter on the Halloween themed levels.
The original felt like a tribute to AVGN that harkened back on NES era level design borrowing from games like Mega Man and Castlevania. This game just feels like a really bad mega man fan game. I'd stay away unless you're a really really huge fan of the Nerd, I'm a huge fan myself and I'm still highly considering requesting a refund.

This game has me spending way too much time than what I should be (in a good way). Once I start playing I have difficulty turning it off as there is always "one-more event" that I begin counting down to and the battles are engaging and well designed.
I really enjoy the "recruitment" process of marrying off your heroes and having them found dynasties to continue producing heirs and playable heroes. It's a great twist on how heroes are usually recruited, especially with the ability to breed for particular traits.
It's great how much the game is actually affected by this mechanic, as you need to decide when to essentially "retire" heroes in order to benefit from their strengths in future generations, without them dying before their time.
It would be good to see one or two new classes be brought into the fray, there would obviously be alot of work required to maintain the excellent balance that already exists, however the addition of extra classes would prevent it from getting stale too quickly.
I also enjoy the random events that require decisions to be made and years later the full repercussions of these events are revealed, for good or bad, it really makes you take the time to think on your choices, as you can't simply save / load a file to rethink your decision.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good turn-based strategy with roguelike elements, a gameplay and difficulty similar to the likes of X-Com, however it is certainly by no means an X-Com clone.
If you like older style games that are notoriously difficult, this is the game for you.

The game is still early access at time of review.  I've completed my first playthrough in ~15-18 hours, I believe.
Overall, I really like this game because it provides consistently difficult choices which are only going to last a short while before you have to make even more. I should have restarted once I got the hang of everything because you're semi-pigeonholed once you're up and running with the initial choices - however I won and it was fun seeing how far I could get and seeing what I can do with it all.
There's a really big timeline which I believe is ~300 years. The ultimate goal is to hold off the monsters for 300 years until the Chalice can do something epic and cleanse the monsters (the Cadence) forever(?).
Any time you need a building/research/item for your people/weapon/armor to be made you can only pick 1 of those things. Often research takes anywhere from 5-20 years and you cannot research anything else during that time. You can only hit the "fastforward" button on the timeline and hope nothing bad goes down. Once something occurs the game pauses and you can deal with it, whether it's research or an attack on your lands.
You've got heroes from different houses and you appoint a male and female regent & partner so they can create offspring. The templates of their traits and tendencies for stats come together and create children that are then trained to be fighters. Your characters are constantly dying from battle but more often from old age, and you have to continually supply new ones to keep things running smoothly. The big battle here is to make sure you appoint people who are very fertile with good stats so you can supply enough for upkeep. You can sacrifice 7 years to recruit new heroes. Deaths of any kind are permanent in here. It's actually a tad depressing, because I actually found Brad Muir (Thed esigner) as a character and watched him grow old and die.
The combat itself is very reminiscent to a partially simplified XCOM which is not a bad thing at all. It provides challenge from the get-go, with enemies that you absolutely do not want to get close (they'll explode, they reduce your XP on hit, or their melee makes you 5 years older every swing), enemies that keep their distance and snipe, or enemies that create other enemies and you're in a mad dash to kill them so the flow of creatures stops.
You can save and load throughout your timeline so there's no real pressure if you make a terrible mistake - you can load an older save you'll get an entirely different scenario all together. This is a bit of a player crutch but it's not unwelcomed since I'm 7 hours in and I'm still not through the whole timeline..
The art is cool and the UI is fairly basic in a good way. All you really see is the damage spread you'll do and the amount of HP left on the creature. Moving and attacking are fairly simple.
Characters in your ranks gain abilities as they level, each one being a "one or the other" choice down the chain. I've never gotten down the entire chain before dying of old age, so I don't know what some of them do.
The classes are hunter (ranged stealth DEX), caberjack (melee, knockback tank STR), and alchemist (mid-ranged finite amount of bombs being thrown --- honestly this class seems to be a bit weak, I can't find anything very good about it. INT).
You deploy up to 5 at a time, and really, less than 5 heroes is often going to be a tough challenge.
I just bring hunters and caberjacks due to the types of enemies I've been encountering. I generally don't want them anywhere near me so I just try to snipe them all before they close any ground. I also like using the hunters to go invisible and scout out the territory so I know how I want to set up.  You can lead enemies into traps if you just set up your hunters and have the caberjack as bait.
So yeah, totally pleased with my purchase on this one. It's got its kinks, especially if you've appointed characters of different ages offset in such a way that it'll keep stopping you and asking you to appoint people to thrones or roles. Stop, transition animation into building, click on a guy from a list, exit from menu, fastforward on timeline (repeat x5). The kinks, though, especially for an Early Access title are very small and the overall thing has felt solid.
And yeah, the art is solid and simple. The environments have breakables/exploding stuff/hazards. It looks good.

This game takes A LOT of "inspiration" from Firaxis XCOM but that is not necessarily a bad thing. The level of strategic choices seems a bit shallow and the battles are a lot less fun than in XCOM but the hero breeding system and the long term kingdom management aspects are interesting enough to keep me going. Details:

This game takes two of my favorite games Crusader Kings II and XCOM and mashes them together in a way that fixes some of the glaring flaws in XCOMs design.
This game takes place over Hundreds of years and you are managing a nation and stable of heroes across multiple generations. Through out the game you will build keeps to further bloodlines, crucibles for training and Sagewrights guild for research.
You will also engage in some genetic engineering through selective pairing to get the best possible heroes.
The heroes you pair do a few things. 1. They have a chance to pass along some of their traits (positive and negative) to their kids. 2. They pass along some of their XP. This alone fixes the massive flaw in XCOM, by the midgame of XCOM any new recruit you get is useless to you. Now your new recruits are able to scale in power as the game progresses.
The other big flaw involves "losing" a battle. While there is no "ironman" mode that I can see, I play with it self imposed on myself. In XCOM ironman mode, a team wipe is essentially a loss state. You likely have no team of soldiers that can adequately replace a team that fought something tough enough to get wiped by. In MC, a team wipe hurts, you spread more "corruption" (Panic) and obviously you lost your heroes, BUT it is not a game over scenario as you have a team to fight with comeing through the ranks (at least you should) infact, losing members of your team can result in the creation of a "Relic", a weapon that it bound to the bloodline of the hero, can critical strike, and grows stronger as you use it.
The game is a blast to manage if you love XCOM and CKII. It is still unfinished at this time, the only feature that I can tell is missing is hybrid classes, but the game plays great without it right now. If there was one thing I would add to this game it would be an active/reactive combat system like Gladius, but that is just me being wishful for Gladius II...
The actual tactical battles are cleverly done with some cool maps and the different types of enemies add some good depth to the combat, certain enemies need to be approached the right way or they can really cause problems at different points in the game. Lapses in the late game are nasty, wrinklers in the mid game, Bulwarks in the early game. They all attack very differently (especially in the case of Lapses and Wrinklers) and in ways that are thematically appropriate (messing with time) and not simply a case of one just hitting harder. The one knock I do have is once the 5-6 different enemies are rolled out it kinda stops, eventually they all become "advanced" versions of the same thing, no reskins, no different mechanics. That is an area for improvement as the game moves to launch.
There is no difficulty setting I can see, but the games difficulty is more than adequate, however as you get a bit more familiar with the items you can equip, you can use the imformation about the types of enemies you are facing to give your guys a leg up. In future playthroughs I am going to try and not look at that information before battles as the game got a lot easier once I started really looking at the types of enemies I would face pre-battle.
One successful playthrough (3rd try) took me about 25 hours and it already has great replay value in the randomness of it's design. As it sits right now it is worth the price of admission and this game will only improve as it gets closer to launch.
The short version is that this game took XCOM and made it better in almost every way, even in it's presently unfinished state.

Examina is a game I want so badly to like, but I just can't do to the multiple issues I have with the game. Before we continue, remember that this game is in early access, so any problems I mention can be fixed or improved on. Also, this is my opinion. This means some aspects of the game I list as a problem may be a positve to someone else. Anyway, let's continue.
Examina is a Isometric RPG Dungeon crawler where the objective is to explore a dungeon to get better gear so you can survive against the ruthless and deadly enemies. The games combat is entirely physics base, so the way your character is animated when moving, attacking, reacting to hits and everything else is done by the physics engine, and so are the enemies and the props (of course). Let's get the combat out of the way. I love it. It is a brilliant way of breathing new live into the genre. What it is, is that when you are up against an enemy, you go into a attack mode, which allows you to swing your weapon and block. You block by hitting the enemy's weapon with yours, making the enemy's weapon lose momentom and not hit you. This, of course, prevents you from taking damage, though even if you do block, sometimes you will still be clipped and take a small amount of damage. You attack by holding the left mouse button to hold your weapon up and you move your mouse to swing it (there are other ways to attack, but that's how I usually attacked). Base on you weapon's stats, the amount of momentom your weapon has, where you hit, and the armor the enemy is wearing will determine the amount of damage you will deal. My descripton of the combat is extremly simplified and it much more complex than how I have descripted it.
This game is also brutually difficult and is NOT begginer friendly (heck, I don't remember if there is even a tutorial). I don't find this to be a positive or a negitive. I'm fine with it being brutually difficult, but it's the fact that you aren't even told the controls is pretty annoying, and as a result, prevented me from getting into the games combat fully, as I didn't even know the basics of combat. One of my favorite games of all time, Dark Souls, is known for being extremely difficult, and yet that game told you how to attack, defend yourself, how to manage your inventory, and how some mechanics works like how resting at a bondfire may refill your estus flask (a healing item), but it revives every enemy on the map except mini bosses and bosses. I wish this game would just explain the basics and players can find out the advanced tactics and mechanics on there own.
The level design is pretty good. Nothing really special about it, so not much to talk about.
There are two modes. The first one which I believe is called adventure, and the second on called arena. Adventure is where you explore a dungeon to get better gear so you can face the enemies ahead. Arena is my favorite mode, it's where you go up a enemy 1v1 in a small arena. If you defeat the enemy, you get the chance to loot the enemy and go onto the next stage. This continues intill you die I believe. The AI and the equipment they have gets better and better the more you progress. It's brilliant, and it is fun if you enjoy the way the game controls and how the combat system works.
The AI is brilliant...     during combat, but outside of combat, they can be really dumb. The enemies are set on a predetermined path, and if they aren't, they will just stand there, and do nothing. Another problem with the AI, and this also affects the AI during combat, is the fact that they CAN'T OPEN DOORS. If the door is completly shut, they can't get through.
The game looks pretty good. The textures appear to be high res and the lighting is quite good. The dark and creepy art direction is brilliant and the atmosphere is just perfect as it set's the mood brilliantly about the dangers you will be facing. Not much else to say again, so let's move on.
Now let's get to the main problem of the game and why I don't recommend you pick it up yet is the controls. I would love to play and experiment with the games combat if it weren't for the fact that the game controls like♥♥♥♥♥♥and are extremely confusing. You feel like a tank. I know they're trying to focus on the fact that you are heavy, but it is not needed to the extent this game goes to. Half of the time I just walk strait into the enemy, preventing us both from swinging our weapons. I just want there to be a lock on system, since the game focuses on 1v1, where you press A and D to circle around your opponent, and W and S you move closer and futher from you opponent. But instead, it feels like I'm controlling a character from Resident Evil 1. I hope they do add a lock on system. If there is one already in the game, I can't find it. This problem breaks the game for me
Here is a short list on what I like, what I was indifferent to, and what I disliked
Pros:
+Combat
+Graphics
+atmosphere and art direction
+level design
+Enemy AI during combat
+Arena
Indifferent:
+/- The game not telling you anything, including how to play.
+/- The enemy AI outside of combat.
Dislikes:
- The Controls
- Enemy AI doesn't know how to open doors.
Overall, I want to love this game, I really do, but the awful controls in my opinion just destroy this game for me.

The Graveyard is a third person action adventure horror game with rogue-like elements (when your character dies the game continues). You play as a three-legged elderly woman exploring robust and realistic looking graveyard. Along the way you will encounter birds, a stone wall, stone tombstones, foliage and more until you get to the final boss, a standard sized park bench.  What happens next will leave you breathless.
Controls: 3/10
Resident Evil style controls with up and down moving forward and backward while left and right are used to turn. Grandma is as slow as a tank but without the bonus of destroying everything in her path. And when she finally does destroy the only thing she can, there is no way to quit the game after your victory. Also, there is no controller support.
Graphics: 7/10
Some nice chiaroscuro in a beautifully rendered locale. Grandma's thick saggy jowls are a bit outdated, but you can imagine what she might have looked like 60 years ago.
Sound: 6/10
Pleasant sounds of a park; not even grandma's death get in their way. Or did you not play the full version?
Music: 5/10
All that setup just to get me to listen to a song by some guy named Gerry De Mol. He also has a song called "Doof Me" that you can check out on youtube.
Camera: 4/10
Assuming this was an open world graveyard game, I tried taking grandma down a side path in the cemetery to give her a little more time in this world and see if I could get any power-ups before facing the final boss. The camera didn't follow her movements and she disappeared. Having little value for my own time left on this planet, I tried to turn her around and have her walk back without seeing her movements (instead of just having her walk backwards) and ended up losing even more of my own life to this game. Now that I think about it, I never actually tried to walk backwards in The Graveyard, but I wouldn't be surprised if the programmers left that function out since time only moves forward.
Final Thoughts:
**Spoiler** If grandma doesn't die in the demo then isn't the promise of eternal life free? If you pay for things, you die; and please listen to Gery De Mol: that's the real message here.
The creators really should have added a 2x speed option for those of us who would have preferred a painless death.
If you want to experience a graveyard on a nice day, go to a graveyard. If you want to see death up close, spend your $5 on a bus ticket to a retirement home. If you want to hole yourself up into a virtual solitude, put a blanket over your head, grab a bowl of popcorn and enjoy the final cutscene of The Graveyard. It will bring you closer to death.

I've always had a thing for RTS and Tower Defense games, and so when I first found Creeper World on Kongregate, I was overjoyed. There were many different versions available freely there. Recently, I decided to purchase the third installment to see how it was.
There is much to love about this game. The game follows more or less the same rules throughout, but the final two story missions are definite game changers. I've seen many complain about losing on the second to last mission due to time constraints - I myself lost the first time around, but with a little advice I figured out how to beat it. The consistency of the gameplay can make things a little drab if you play too much, but if you enjoy one level, you're likely to enjoy a whole lot more - and there are a whole lot more. There's an practically endless array of levels once you beat most of the story. You can binge play or play a game every once in a while - either way, it will take you a long time to run out of official maps, and you'll never run out of custom ones. The game isn't all too challenging if you remember to pause frequently and keep tabs on the Creeper and your resources, but there are more difficult levels available if that's what you're looking for. The graphics are solid - nothing incredible, but well-done nonetheless.

Each level in the campaign introduces a new unit or a new mechanic or just has some kind of unique property to make it interesting which is really the key to any decent RTS campaign. After you 'finish' the main story there is a bounty of user designed maps, wacky beta tester maps and 2 'sectors' of conventional maps with a specific goal in mind, not to mention the ability to design your own maps. Not only is the replay potential limitless it's also really good content in its own right, some of the use made maps are really fun and if you beat it in the fastest time you get to 'claim' it as your own.
If you're into oldschool RTS like red alert 2, starcraft or the aforementioned TA this the ultimate indie game, you wont get a better experience for your money.  I honestly can't believe this was developped by one guy given the amount of content squeezed in and the elegance of the design.

Very short mod. As others have said, the English used in this mod isn't particularly good, but it is good enough to understand. The basic plot of the mod is that you are some sort of... Black Mesa scientist? You are sent to a different universe to obtain some sort of crystal. The signifigance of this crystal is never elaborated on, you just know you need to get it.
You start out on one end of the ship. You need to assume the crystal is located on the other side (because that's the only place to go) and walk there. On the way you will meet a few of the Half-Life Aliens and Zombies. Reaching the other side is very easy, with one of the only challenging parts being with the 3 Turrets guarding the door to the other side, and this is still easy. You need to ascend the ship at this point, pushing boxes and crouch jumping often. Eventually, you make it to a man. He greets you with "Stop, don't kill me" or something. He then walks (Very slowly, every turn takes about a second or two each, and he turns quite a bit) to a cargo hull release or something like that. He opens it, and a short cutscene will play, showing you that the crystal was back at the spawn after all, you just walked over it!
Reaching the original side again is a much more challenging experience, as there are many more Hostile NPCs that will attack you. If you are quick enough, you can completely bypass combat if you wish by running. Yes, that's right, running. Try as they might, the NPC's cannot harm you very much as long as you keep a brisk pace. Once you reach the original side once again, jump in the seemingly bottomless pit of a cargo hull and wait for the loading screen. You will be brought to another cutscene, afterwards you will need to fight the final boss.
I'm not sure if the soundtrack to this mod is original or not, but it is a bit loud for my taste. I needed to decrease the volume quite a bit to have a bearable volume (keep in mind, I do have some pretty loud speakers). Some of the soundtrack is a little bit annoying, but nothing too bad.
In all, I would recommend this if you have a bit of time to spare, it's a REALLY short mod unless you take time to inspect  EVERYTHING. It has many flaws but is a good timekiller.

I have played hundreds of games in my life. Death to Spies is, without question, the absolute worst of these games.
I say this with no sense of hyperbole. This game fails to implement even the most basic move and shoot gameplay elements competently.
I challenge anyone to finish the tutorial without quitting in a fit of range. It's the basic "shoot these types of weapons and then throw some grenades" military game tutorial with a few additional quirks. First, the way your avatar is facing and moving has only a tangential relationship to where the mouse is pointing. Second, once you get into the indoor firing range, there are invisible and intermittent impediments to your movement that have you running in place for seconds at a time. Finally, should you manage to actually pick up and fire a gun (no small feat), you can move your cursor over the target, press the fire button, all while your avatar is visibly firiing a gun at a 90 degree angle from said targets.
There are other niggling things that I could go on about: there's the fact that Russian characters in a Russian-made game speak in stilted American accents. There's the poor-man's Hitman inventory system, and the way that the whole map is alerted if one lone soldier spots you. But all of this pales in comparison to the fact that the TUTORIAL IS THE SINGLE MOST ONEROUS GAMING EXPERIENCE I HAVE EVER SUFFERED THROUGH.
Nobody ever playtested this game. Nobody should have ever released this game. I would say it is funny, but I paid fractions of a dollar for this game, I invested almost an entire hour of my life into this, so I will just say do not play this game. If you do, please make a video of your tutorial experience and send it to me.

This was played on Windows 7 Home Premium SP1 x64. While the premise sounds interesting, the game is filled with game breaking bugs. Players will often find the camera's direction desynchronizing with the character's direction. It can get so bad that the camera may be 90 degrees away from the character's direction, resulting in the character running to the left of the screen when you press the up arrow key. The other game breaking bug that I encountered was the character getting stuck for no reason within any interior location. You'll also find AI walking into walls(not following their pathing) and moving away from their designated paths, causing missions to be incompletable. I would not recommend this game to anyone.

I haven't finished the game yet, but I sincerely doubt the ending of the game is going to fix any of its issues. First of all, the premise is actually quite interesting. You crash land on a planet that is supposed to be full of vibrant life and oxygen levels close to Earth's, but instead you get a barren wasteland with no air. Right off the bat, you discover a deserted Russian colony, which should not be possible, as you're the first people landing on this planet after a 15 year journey. As story settings go, this one is pretty damn solid. The only problem is, the characters suck. Straight away, the main character is bombarded with situations both deadly and bizzare and 90% of the time he won't even bat an eyelash. For somebody who saw his crew die violently in front of him, he is pretty damn composed and that screws with immersion so bad! You're supposed to empathise with the guy you're playing, but most of the time I just wonder what the hell is wrong with him. If the game was trying to put all its chips on atmosphere and playing experience, the complete lack of emotion really kills it. The secondary character, who you follow for the entire game, is just as uninteresting, except she speaks in Russian.
In terms of gameplay, there are no new or exciting elements in Lifeless Planet. For most of the game, you're just jumping around. I wouldn't really call the obstacles in front of you puzzles, since they are entirely too simple. You just move from spot A to spot B, jump over some cliffs and enjoy the scenery. Skill is not really a factor in this one - if you happen to die to something, you just make a mental note of it and any sense of danger is gone. You also get get a robotic hand at some point, but that fails to inject even the smallest bit of fun. Without a single mechanic to pull you into the game, it gets boring VERY fast. Lifeless Planet is not worth the asking price of $20.

Massive chalice? It might as well be called "Massive Time Sink", but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Like similar games in the tactical campaign genre, this one involves a lot of careful planning and unnecessary soldier deaths.
The thing that sets it apart, however, is the breeding system, where family lines continue on through the ages, passing down training and useful traits. While these bloodlines are kept mostly safe in keeps, it's possible through poor luck or poorer planning to lose one entirely-- which keeps things interesting.
Basically, if you enjoy short rounds of tactical combat spread over prolonged strategic campaigns, this is an excellent game. It's strongest when you're making interesting decisions, and the random events keep things lively, but it's not as fun when you've made a fatal mistake but still have an hour of gameplay before the inevitable loss claims you.

It's really made for power gamers. There are a ton of variables you need to master in order to win, and the game is stacked firmly against you in every way in regards to the amount of enemies, their powers, your limitations, etc... Also, there's too much random stuff happening (heroes dying, especially) for you to get a real grasp on what's going on.
If you're spending 40 hours per week gaming and don't mind running a spreadsheet to keep track of what's going on (what regent has what powers, family trees, and so on), then you can probably, eventually, get somewhere with this game. For me, I'm a few days in and I'm done with it. Here's what I think it needs to make it better:
a. Variable difficulty settings. Seriously. Spending five hours trying to manipulate bloodlines before getting decimated by an onslaught isn't fun.
b. More items to research to improve your heroes. You shouldn't have to kill three missions worth of something to then research better weapons. Or anything else to level the field. The monsters with level drain and nearly perfect ranged accuracy who show up from level one need to be fought with something better than a puny hunter with 28% accuracy.
c. Less stuff to keep track of. Is there a reason that I'm made aware of babies, trainees, and heroes? I can't tell if this is necessary to know or not in any practical sense. I either have enough heroes when I'm attacked or I don't. Do I need to know how many heroes I'll have in 15 more years? Why am I shown infertile partner choices when a keep needs a regent? Why is it sometimes a fertile partner and a fertile regent can't have children?
d. More ways to keep your heroes alive longer. Is there some sort of immortality mechanism later? I don't know because I've never made it that far, nor do I intend to.
In all, unless your idea of a good time is studying a game for hours, taking a lot of notes, and doing a little bit of finite math in the bargain, then buying this game probably isn't a good idea. I certainly wouldn't have bought it had I known it was like so.

Original Review:
I backed this game due to interesting core ideas. But the ideas didn't produce a worthy end result. Do not buy this game if you want or expect an interesting strategical or tactical challenge. The options you have are extremely reduced, flat and boring. (3 classes, extremely simple or no skill choices, extremely bland upgrades etc.) The game can be difficult, but mostly because you have so few factors you can influence or strategy routes you can take, which is the BAD kind of difficult.
The biggest atrocity within this product is the straight, shortsighted copy of the (bad) 'activation' mechanic of XCOM: Enemy Unknown as soon as Line of Sight is established. The battles are supposed to feel like a wave of demons attacking one of your provinces. In a blatant failure of design, enemies are just standing around, akin to braindead animals standing around in a forest. (If you use the close combat class a lot, it's often impossible to avoid activating multiple groups at the same time, just by approaching an enemy, while the ranged class allows you to easily snipe them from afar).
The one interesting aspect of the game, the management of families, is still interesting, but as far as I know can be exploited as soon as you understand how the system works.
I was simple not able to stick around for later stages of the game. It was just such a MASSIVE FAILURE.

Fun game, however right now it's a little frustrating. It crashes on me pretty much every play through. Sometimes it crashes hard where my monitor goes black and I need to reboot.
As far as gameplay, there isn't really much depth here at all. It's fairly X-COM like with the combat. I like turn-based combat,so I'm a fan of that. In the world view where you're not fighting, that's where the game is super basic. It's got some research tree component to it, and a few other things, but there isn't a lot here. I'd say it'd be worth it for $20.
However, that all said, despite that it is lacking in depth, I find that I'm still somewhat hooked to it (but I've only been playing for about a week.. not sure how long that will last).
If you like turn based strategy this is a great twist on the genre. Some fun innovations so far and really glad I backed this early. Feels like the devs are big fans of the genre.

It is pretty rare that I write a review for games, but this game struck a particular chord with me, so here I am.
Let me start by saying that I love these kinds of games. On top of that it isn't a "sit and wait 24 hours or buy gems" BS game makes it more appealing. The first 30 minutes were awesome, I was super excited for it.
Then I started to actually examine it.
Lets start with the Pros:
- Good art style, its not graphically amazing, but for what it is it does a good job.
- Excellent basics
- Easy to pick up
- Straightforward
Cons:
- There really isn't a good balance between "I want to build a city I don't have to defend" and "I will have to constantly rebuild everything". This to me is the biggest issue. My first playthough I played on the normal difficulty. I got freaking destroyed by the vikings the first time they came. I thought, "hmm, must not have been prepared". So I got prepared. I got some heroes, completely worthless. I built some walls, completely worthless. I trained some troops, again, worthless. Lost half my walls and a quarter of my city burned down. Nothing I could do. Ok I thought, I'll just play the easy mode. Well playing with no enemies gets boring EXTREMELY quickly because there are only a handful of buildings. Eventually you've finished it. Not to mention the vikings only get worse as you get bigger. WHICH MAKES NO SENSE. I have literally yet to fend off a viking invasion. I had walls 5 high covered in ballista, and they send 6 ogres at me to just absolutely demolish them. The Heroes are a complete joke. So slow and can't even go 80% of the places the vikings are. It makes playing normal difficulty miserable, and the easy difficulty boring af.
- The macro gets to be completely tedious. There is no way to drag and select things to remove. This is so obnoxious when you have to press every individual tile to remove a forest. There is no good way to swap around your workers. You have to press and click on each individual thing to close or open it.
- The game begins to lag at around 500 people. Maybe its just my computer, but I can run Witcher 3 on Ultra no issues, this game should not give me problems.
- Some things are just dumb, like a Manor not getting charcoal when there is a market with charcoal across the street. Or food going rotten because people aren't smart enough to transfer food from the full Granaries. People dying of the plague simply because no one goes to the hospital.
- When I hear the direction the game dev's are going with it, VR and Stream support, I am even more upset. You need better macro mechanics first. It needs to be easier to transfer people from foresters to archer towers or farms to quarries. I should be able to press and drag on the road to continually place it, thats basic mechanics for these types of games.
My biggest problem is a game like this should be enjoyable. You should be able to reach a point you can defend your city. Maybe some people enjoy a constant challenge, but I would rather have some satisfaction. It never feels like you really win. I have killed two dragons in 10 hours of play, never once defeated the vikings. Once you've built all the buildings, there really isn't anything left to enjoy. You will literally just be fighting to survive, and its not like a survival game where that would be fun, its a city builder game where it is just tedious and annoying.
Please, make the combat winnable and actually interesting rather than just watching your city get absolutely destroyed every time.
Please, add some better macros to the game, like an ability to quickly close or open all of one type of industry or employ.
Please, add more buildings and depth to the game.
Please, make smarter civillians that won't lag out the game. Because the ones right now aren't even smart enough to walk across the street and it makes my game lag.
I greatly appreciate what this game stands for, and I got my money's worth, but it has so much potential to be so much more.

Having back this on Kickstater I thought it only fair to give it a review after having completed this (first part) of the game.
First and foremost it is great to see the game go back to its original format, the background detail is fantastic with little tidbits thrown in there for you to spot and have a giggle over. The characters look awesome and the animation is brilliant, not to mention the voice acting and delivery of the script.
There's no need to have played any of the other games as this stands alone with its own story which is engrossing enough to keep you wanting to find out what happens next. For old school players that did play the first 2 particularly there are lots of nostalgic references thrown around and characters that we know and love.
For those that are being highly critical of the game I do admit the puzzle solving does seem to have gotten easier but wether that's by design or we have just got used to how revolution puts together puzzles is another thing. Though I played through with hints switched off there were plenty of verbal queues that helped lead you to the solution and I do feel that made things a tad too easy. On the flip side I think it helped the pacing of the game and story and I'm sure a lot of people would be thankful for not spending hours smashing your head against a wall trying to figure something out.
I also agree that the game feels a little short but again I would have to go back to the originals which I know very well and play through without struggle for comparison to see just how long they were when you weren't wracking your brain trying to figure out how to get past a security gate. That said where the game currently leaves off for part 2 was satisfying in a "next week on..." kind of way.
All in all do I think the game is worth its asking price? I think after the second part of the game is released it will be worth its weight in gold but I wouldn't let that deter you for purchasing now. The time I spent with game was enjoyable, funny and engaging and I expect the second half of the game to give me more of that with a satisfying conclusion. I would recommend this to any fan of point and click adventures or anyone wanting to try out their first one. If you like it go back and play the first 2 as well.

Lifeless Planet has a creative storyline. The load speed of the game is amazing, all the while requiring little from the hardware. A frequent example of this is the jet pack charge-once it is depleted you know that all upcoming jumps will be small, removing a level of unknown from the player.
Character development is crucial for the player to become immersed in the reality of this game.  Too much time is spent on the technology development, and too little on Aelita.  You have the opportunity to develop a sense of sympathy for the planet, but very little for Aletia.  It would have been endearing to see the two parallel each other.  There are also small glitches with the PDA and claw.  I hope to see more games in the future from this developer.  On a scale of 1 to 5, with 5 being the highest rating, I would give it a 3.5.

Crazy difficult WW2 stealth game. Plays like a cross between "Hitman" and the old "Commandos" games, but it also has some unique twists on the genre that make it stand out. The missions are nicely varied, complex, and are refreshingly light on the hand holding. Often times you are dumped in a field outside of a city with nothing but a map, leaving you to tackle objectives as you wish. Likewise, while it's not quite the ultra realistic stealth game I've always been dreaming of, there are some nice nods to reality here and there (for example, you can't wear uniforms if you've bloodied them and guards will sometimes recognize you regardless of your disguise). Of course it does have the silly "choke dude for 2 seconds, dude sleeps for hours" mechanic, but there are also dozens of more realistic ways to take people out as well, so it's optional.
The writing is dry, production values are low, and it has some bugs, but it's worth a try if you want stealth that's a bit more demanding.
