I desperately wanted to give this a No, given that it's comming from the company that lost any possible claim of credibility with Early Access games, but I just can't.
I was a big DF fan, for the games they had done before, and for keep on innovating on their smaller Amnesia'ed games. I even went personaly to their offices and gave Tim a framed
, and got The Art of Brutal Legend signed by the team, and a Brutal Legend box signed by Tim, so you could say I was a "fan-boy". But I didn't much care for Broken Age, as I think it devolved the genre rather than evolve it - I'm sure the next logical step is to keep bringing the number of interactions down, so it will go from one to zero, and the game will just play by itself...
But then the DF-9 fiasco brought down my fan-boydom overnight. I understand the logic they were working on, but a lot of people today simply no longer buy Early Access games, and were waiting for the game to come out. I was one of those people, and now they'll never see that money. So I believe that any loss they would incur now during development would be made up after relase, but now not only did they severely hurt their prospects with any future Early Access games (and Kickstarters too, I'm sure), they've managed to further distance most players from Early Access titles (which I'm not overly concerned as a player, but as a developer with an Early Access title on Steam myself, this affects me personaly, so color me biased...).
That said, this game is VERY good and deserves your attention. The art style oozes personality, and the strategy layer that takes place between missions is very deep and engaging. If you get too attached to your fighters you will be disappointed, as if they don't die in the battlefield, they'll die of old age. But that's a good thing and not a bad thing like some reviews here state - you can't possibly be interested in a game for it's multi-generational layer, and then complain that your squad is not made of Methuselahs that live 500 years. Fighter recycling is at the very core of the game here.
Another great thing is that you'll have some very tough decisions regarding were you allocate each of your peoples. They can be fighting, but they can also be assigned as:
- Regents and their partners make new heroes and pass their traits on.
- Scholars decrease building and 'science' time
- Defaults give XP and other bonuses to heroes.
(I don't think these are the proper names, but that's the gist of it)
You want your best people on these roles in order to keep improving and have better heroes in the future, but you want your best heroes in your squad to fight the missions and not get slaughtered.
The tactical battles are good but not great. Yes, X-Com is a better game on this regard, and if this is all your care in a game of this type, then by all means, install the Long War mod and avoid this game. I for one like to have a deeper strategy layer, and I think Massive Chalice beats X-Com in that regard. Given this game's budget compared to X-Com's, I think 1-for-1 is pretty darn good. Is it an inferior X-Com clone? Most certainly not, as it does a LOT of things differently, both in the tactical battles (even if I personally don't like them), and specially on the strategy layer.
My two biggest complains with it so far:
1. This game requires a decent ammount of min-maxing to make good decisions on the things I mentioned earlier. This is not a bad thing on itself, I enjoy min-maxing games, but it does lack features that allow you to min-max efficiently, like robust tools to sort, filter and compare heroes stats and traits.
2. Alchemists frequently do something like this:
I'm waiting for the official release to keep playing more, specially due to my first issue there. That said, if the worst came to happen and the developer just walked away today (it's certainly not a far-fetched idea...), I think the game already delivers it's full price in entertainment value as it is. That's why it gets a Yes from me, no matter how much I wanted to not like it.

This is just an initial review for the 7.2 hours I've managed to put into the game so far (year 150) so please keep that in mind.
I feel that Massive Chalice wants to be more than just a tactics game, more than just an empire game. Where the game is now, however, it's not /quite/ there - but it more than easily has that potential. The attacks on your kingdom force you to truly build up a team of heroes that rival the forces of the Cadence, while at the same time making you choose which of those heroes will carry on a bloodline, teach trainees, and who will carry on the research. The balancing act is, by itself, a game that put me to a bit of a challenge, at first.
As I said, I feel that this game wants to do two things at once, which is fine. But in the wise, immortal words of Ron Swanson; "Never half♥♥♥♥♥two things, whole♥♥♥♥♥one thing." My first playthrough (which ended up with me having zero hunters and no idea how to get out of that bind) was a complete flop - But it frustrated me in a way that I /wanted/ to find out how to remedy that situation. So, I started anew and quickly built up three keeps, stocking them each with one of the classes, figuring this would keep my army strong with new recruits and my sagewrights pouring in.
How wrong I was. Quickly, it became apparent that I had partnered with each of my regents, Queenmakers. My female population boomed! That wouldn't have been an issue if most of my males had survived past the Regent's deaths (I've only had one hero die on the battlefield, so far, my regents just refused to die). As it was, I struggled to balance out my kingdom. It was wonderful and challenging just enough because you cannot replace regents, you cannot pull back your sagewrights. But now, in year 150, I've found that simply bolstering your ranks with new recruits from the research/build option, that's never an issue.
But it should be! And while, yes, I should be able to recharge my kingdom with new blood, I find that I'm able to do so easily and without effort because of this; There's simply not enough to build/research that I can't spare 15 years to recruit three times in a row. And this leads me to my next point...
The combat is fantastic! I love when the Cadence get the balls to move into my territory and the balancing act of which territory will get an extra corruption. Now, being in Early Access I understand the sameness over and over, but each battle I try to go into with a fresh perspective because the enemy types aren't always the same. However I've come to realize that currently, hunters are extremely powerful. Not because they're overpowered, but because Alchemists and Caberjacks just aren't up to snuff yet.
The Alchemist does have a nice aoe attack, but it pales in comparison to a hunter because of the lack of vials. And while they're "weak" physically, most of mine do actually punch things pretty hard - so they're not totally useless after they've blown their load all over the field, but I just feel like having the hunter would do more for me. Caberjacks, on the other hand, hit like Optimus Prime and if you equip them in the Bulwark armor they're actually fairly tough tanks. But they lack the range of their hunter counterpart and still have the same HP pool on most heroes.
Now, I know these things can be breeded out through genetics of your bloodlines, and that's fine. I just don't feel like the other two classes are quite up to par just yet - which is terrible because it caused me to build another two keeps for more hunters and another for Caberjacks (as a just in case) but I completely disregard my alchemist line except for Sagewrights. Which, in a weird way actually works out well because I've bred them to be intuitive and that helps research times. Except, I'm out of things to research.
So, in closing, Massive Chalice has great potential and while it is still in Early Access, it's the perfect time to get this kind of feedback in for the developers to look at. Again, only halfway through my (second) playthrough and I can see replayability being a thing, because I want to know how some of those random events turn out in other ways. If you're on the fence about this game, I highly recommend it, especially if Double Fine can keep up the work.

Heyyo, I was a Massive Chalice
. :)
Double Fine has delivered on their promises of Massive Chalice. It's turn-based strategy, permadeath, bloodlines, relics and strategy where you play as a ruler who is immortal and guides his people in a war that spans 300 years.
So as a ruler? You get chalise-attuned heroes which means not just any pesant can join your ranks. You can aquire them from mating your heroes in keeps via bloodlines which at random of a hero death may lead to a bloodline-tied relic, an extra-strong piece of equipment that gains effectiveness as the hero it is equipped to gains experience... So you're constantly balancing researching new technologies, building keeps/sage towers or Crucibles (for boosting experience points of your heroes per day by dedicated a hero as a Standard Bearer). Plus? You can't forget about random events... oh yes, they are random, interesting and both rewarding or dangerous. ;)
I'm only on my first playthrough and have made some bad choices and have been paying for them... but it has taught me that no two playthroughs are the same and this game is definitely a gem. I definitely intend to do more playthroughs after waiting for a few patches and changes to the game.
Right now? It's on patch 0.85 and is pretty fun. There is a few balance issues with the game... namely Hunters (the archerer class) is overpowered compared to the other classes. I found using 4 Hunters and 1 Alchemist (a potion-based warriror/mage class... thingy or something lol) was the most efficient team of heroes to use in combat. Mainly because the Caberjack (melee warrior class) has several disadvantages due to the unique properties of the Cadence (the evil forces of the game). For example, Wrinklers are an enemy type that does melee damage and causes aging effects if they hit you... but with a team of Hunters and Alchemist? You can usually take them out before they get close to you... Lapse's are an enemy that cause your characters to lose their memories (experience points in this case) and when they die? They explode and cause minor damage to anyone nearby but also there's a risk of getting stunned... Rupture's are suicide units and wether they die or kamikazi? They explode and do minor damage but lower armor effectiveness (called armor corruption). All three of these enemy types can be easily dispatched from a safe distance. Debateable? But you can research and equip Wünderpants to negate the aging and memory-loss attacks of the Wrinklers and Lapsers... but it takes up the only item slot they get which means no health potions or Max HP buffs and they can still damage you or stun you... so once again, better from a safe distance. Plus, if they get close? Alchemists are decent melee units... so I always sent any camberjacks I recruited to the Sage Tower (helps lower research time) or as a regent's partner for breeding.
So yeah... Massive Chalice is a darn fun game, but it does need a little patch refining to especially make Camberjacks more effective... they need a bigger healthpoint pool and dare I say more than one inventory slot for acessories out of the gate. Upgraded? Camberjacks are pretty handy... but they usually have an average Hitpoint pool just like the other classes and that's not good when they're supposed to be in the front lines taking abuse.. and abuse they shall take.

A EA review after a single playthrough (next to several failed attempts) which took just under 20 hours.
Let's clear up things right away:
-The game is titled Early Access, but according to the developer it's pretty much finished content-wise and they mainly intend to do open beta testing (in EA) and bugfixing, as well as UI improvements now.
-Despite some... questionable history of this game's dev regarding other Early Access games, this one is fairly playable, so there's no threat of it being stopped before release.
Now, on to the actual game. Imagine a crossover of a light dynasty-simulation, some light text-RPG, and a light turn-based tactical game. Yes, it's actually not very deep in any of it's components. And whilst the concept of mixing those is quite good (and the prime reason why I got this game), but it clearly has weak points.
Effectively, the game comes down to managing your heroes and nation on a strategic view (not unlike managing your base in XCOM) and managing a crew of five heroes in a tactical turn-based battle, which is both affected by your strategical decisions and does affect your strategical situation.
However, whilst the whole "breed your heroes to genetically engineer the next clan of super-warriors" is very interesting and the various mechanics like tutoring, personalities and inheritable 'relic' weapons definitely add onto that, the system still feels a tad flat when it comes to content. Most traits are just "+X of stat Y" (or, in negative form, the opposite). Personalities often are similar, albeit here we see some more interesting concepts, like boosts when sticking to the group, or opposed a buff when a hero is alone. But, across my entire gameplay, I felt like ignoring those traits was a good bet, given their actual impact was minimal compared to the additional movement it would have required to actually set up their situations. In the end it really came down to just breed "whoever is the most fertile and has the most positive traits" of the right class and then let RNG throw something useful at you. Across my entire game I tried to specifically create distinct classes (f.e. long-sight, high-dexteriy rangers and quick, extra-strength warriors) but somehow ended up with a wild mix of traits and 'Quick learner' on pretty much everyone. Which apparently was enough to beat the game with ease.
Because, yeah, it took some failed starts, but that was mostly because the game does a rather bad job at explaining things to you. So, effectively you play, mess up horribly, are forced to restart, repeat a few times, until you grasp the basics. And then the same problem as XCOM kicks in: Past a certain point, you are either already dead or so absurdly strong that the tactical battles become tedious and uneventful.
Which brings us to the second part of the game, the tactical battles.
Rudamentary movement system with an occasionally clunky UI and initially confusing controls. Likewise goes for the 'cover' system and the AI. At some point you get into it, and it's not bad in itself, but again, casual players would probably need a tad more help early on.
A big problem, in my oppinion, is the complete lack of a time limit and the fact you start with free stealth scouts (think of Mimetic Skin of XCOM) from the start of the game. It's trivial to sneak around, wait until a single enemy wanders off, then alphastrike him down. Rinse and repeat, unless you mess up it's not uncommon to end missions without even taking damage. This only gets worse as the game progresses (as mentioned) and your characters become more and more versatile and accurate (because, really, the only times where you take relevant damage is either because you make a big missplay or all 3 90% attacks miss).
Shortly summarized, the game really needs some more balance tweaking, both in between little details like classes and weapons, as well as difficulty wise. Which is already on the list of the devs, according to the last info I read.
And then there are a handful of bugs and weird design issues. F.e. hitting a group of Bulwarks with an acid vial of an alchemist. Bulwarks will form a layer of armor whenever they take damage, reducing all further damage in the same turn to 1. The problem is, that each hit bulwark will perform the 3-second 'IMA GROWING ARMORE!' animation SEQUENTIALLY. And then, once their turn starts, the armor will break, they take acid damage and the animation will PLAY AGAIN. There are other occasions where the game puts in dumb pauses (even within your own turn's movement) to point you at any kind of buff triggering or disappearing. Which definitely takes time and becomes annoying later in the game.
As well, there are a few skills with issues, f.e. Flarrow not actually triggering the blinding explosion, or not revealing the map (or sometimes neither of both).
But I'll assume that will be patched at some point.
Now, would I recommend this game?
Nnnnnnot sure. I got 20 hours out of it, but I got to say that I doubt I'll play the game again. Simply because the only 'fun' laid in figuring how the shallow, obfuscated gameplay mechanics work. It was a real drag to play through the last couple decades of the game, simply because one fight was as simple and boring as the next, all further research was legitly pointless... you get the point.

Personally, I think Kingdoms and Castles successfully delivers a city management experience with the theme of a medieval Hamlet to City progression.
However, this game doesn't appeal to me in the sense that I feel it is sort of lacking. I'm unsure what specifically, but its just not a game I can see myself plunging hours into, which is what I look for in a game (Granted, that may not be what others are looking for, also). The art style is somewhat charming and simple, and I like what they've done with it. The mechanics are rather basic (Although slightly confusing at times), and short term aims are displayed through ingame help.
What I didn't like, however, is the game's tendency to not explain things until after you've done them. For example, diving into the game, I didn't realise I would need stone for a well, essential in increasing villager life quality, so I placed my initial keep far from any usable stone (Which was something that threw me off, darker stone is unusable), so had to build roads to the other side of the map in order to actually get the stone. The happiness mechanic also confused me, as, despite having numerous happiness-generating buildings across my city, none of the villager homes were ever at sufficient happiness despite having checked all the building requirements (The city advisor kept saying I didn't have enough libraries or churches, despite having multiple of each throughout the city, getting the boarders and areas of effect right). I am unsure exactly how the game calculates random events, as at one point, around the beginning of my playthrough, a farm randomly set on fire and it spread to the others around it, destroying them, and set me back quite a bit, so that broke the realism for me and made it harder to recover that early in the game. Finally, a little feature I feel would be useful would be the inclusion of an arrow to direct the front of the building, as at numerous points I placed a building with a 1x2 area lengthways along a small alley (If you'd call it that), and was consequently unsure if it was accomplishing anything. Speaking of which, there is a lack of information in a lot of areas, yes the advisors give you pointers, but a lot of the time I was just unsure if what I was doing was right. Some people like that learning through experience part in a game, but I personally feel like I'm doing something wrong.
There were also a few minor bugs, such as charcoal piles not being accessible to different houses despite the fact they should've been, the food collectors not using granaries right beside them, and instead going to one on the other side of my city, but being unable to get there in time before winter came and took the food in transit.
Overall, though, I can see why this game is quite popular at the moment, and I'd say it does the job of being a city builder, accompanied with a charming art style and an appropriately-executed theme. I do recommend this game, but I stress that it didn't appeal to me in the ways that I was hoping.

Exanima's biggest virtue is the physics based combat system, but besides that there's a huge amount of detail went into pretty much everything and the overall quality of the game is top notch, especially for a $15 indie game.
+Challenging roguelike gameplay
+Everything is physics based
+Unique combat system; once you get the hang of it it's really satisfying
+Detailed armour system: Not the usual helmet / chest piece / gloves / boots system, my character currently wears 11 pieces of armour from top to bottom (don't know what's the max number you can wear), and a piece of armour only protects the part of your body that it actually covers
+Large dungeons to explore, find secrets and hidden loot
+Dark, creepy atmosphere
+Pretty graphics and lighting, the sound effects are great, too
+Complex enemy AI
+Runs very well
+/-Story: you wake up in a dungeon with no explanation whatsoever, you have to find clues to piece it together for yourself and unravel the mystery (it's a huge positive in my book, but I know some people prefer a more direct narrative)
+/-You have to spend some time on practicing the physics based combat or you won't be able to defeat the first enemy you meet (by no means a negative either)
-(As most of the negative reviews pointed out) the controls need some getting used to, the camera controls/movement could be improved a bit

It's a pretty competent Terraria kind of game. Years ago, when this game first got popular, it was pretty lacking, but now that it's been fully developed and released it's quite amazing. It plays quite similarly to Terraria, having similar mining and fighting mechanics, but is more focused on quests and exploration than mining (for the most part).
The greatest strength of the game, however, is certainly its ability to make you feel cool in whatever way you want: there are seven different races, each offering a different aesthetic for you and your ship as well as a different personality for your character and the NPCs you meet. Whether you like dystopian super smart ape-men, tribalistic plant people, aztec birds, rootin' tootin' gunslingin' star people, or japanese fish people, at least one race has something for everyone to enjoy.
Another fun part of Starbound is the silly little things in the game, like the ability to find and play musical instruments and have everyone else be subjected to hearing the music you play. Playing dress-up is lots of fun too with lots of really cool looking accessories and character choices.
Overall, Starbound is a great pick for anyone who likes to explore in games - having an entire universe of semirandom planets to explore is mindblowing, especially when you have to tell your friends your exact spatial coordinates to allow them to travel lightyears to get to you so that you can rickroll them with an accordion.

Starbound is pretty darn good.
First of all, the Starbound universe is massive. It's procedurally generated, so each planet is different. As a new player, this sense of exploration and wonder is amazing, to the point of being overwhelming. There are so many planet types, dungeons, villages, and biomes, that it seems infinite. Add the extras of NPC space stations and ships, as well as "cosmic anomalies," and it will take a long time to become bored of the universe. That said, boredom did eventually set in. I began to find the large, but still limited, amount of biomes tiring. However, despite my travels across the galaxy, there is still loads of content still waiting for me to discover.
Next, the levels of progression. At first, Starbound is harsh. You are dropped onto a planet with nothing but a weak sword, some food, and some bandages. All of a sudden, there are monsters, which can be pretty tough in the early game. Needless to say, you'll die. A lot. However, soon you craft an anvil, and start making armor. The basic enemies stop being so much of a threat. As you continue to get stronger gear, you must travel to more dangerous planets, some of which can be really difficult. The game keeps you on your toes, always trying to upgrade your armor or weapons. It may be difficult to hunt down all of the materials, but there is nothing as satisfying as finally crafted your final set of endgame items.
Finally, I would like to praise the open-endedness. In Starbound, there is very little that you MUST do. Aside from the introductory stroy missions, hte way the game goes is completely up to the player. You can choose to be a builder, collecting blocks and furniture to create structures of epic proportions. You can min/max the game, farming pixels (the in-game currency) through any way possible, all while being the most efficient resource gatherer. You can be a fighter, levelling up your gear for the most powerful gear. Even within combat, there are many choices. You can fight with: A broadsword, a shield, a pistol, an automatic rifle, a grenade launcher, a spear, an axe, a hammer, or with any of the many legendary unique weapons. Or you could even venture into the world of custom items, but that's a whole other story. My point is, there is no correct way to play Starbound, and it can be as deep as you let it.
There are a plethora of other strengths (and flaws) of the game, but I'm going to end after this. Just remember, the game is great, but nothing is without at least a few downfalls. Even so, for $15, I'd highly suggest giving Starbound a try.

Player also doesn't really need to climb much as the jet pack seems more powerful to start with and is powered up much more quickly. This is one game i went into wanting to like and trust me when i say i did,i "REALLY DID".
The graphics really suit this game and do a good job of portraying the lifeless nature of a barren planet devoid of all life and the vistas and sites you will see in game would not look out of place in a full blown sci-fi film (hope someone takes note as this would make one of the best sci-fi films ever),the sound does a really good job of putting you in the position of being the astronaut stuck on the lifeless planet with the weird sound effects and music that you hear at times doing all they can to portray that lifeless feeling of loneliness the game is aiming for.
The story is really entertaining and very mysterious (and pure sci-fi gold) and at times lost me a little (but in the best of ways),lets just say you are on a mission from which there is no return to a planet that could sustain life,you have lost all contact with the other crew members you came down to the planet with,so alone you then discover that you dont have enough oxygen in your tank and so you wander of to find some (and the other crew members) as your tank only holds so much and it has run out (right at the start of the game-HELL thats considerate) and this game play mechanic comes into play a few times through the game and some of these times it can be quite nerve wracking as you wonder if you will find that next oxygen tank to get your levels back upto normal (they are usually somewhere near but can be a pain to find as you run out of that life sustaining O2).
As you play you come across various puzzles that need solving for you to progress and most of the time these are quite easy to solve (some of them stumped me quite a bit though i must admit),and this is where the robotic arm comes into its own.
This device offers you the chance to reach out of place switches and also reach those heavy out of place item's you just wouldent get to without it,which in turn then leads to the robotic arm then helping to solve that puzzle that has been getting on your nerves for the last 30 minutes.
Your booster pack also plays a huge part in the game and without it you just wouldent get past those really hard platforming areas to get access to the next area and therefore uncover more of the mystery that this planet holds.Your booster only has a limited boost capability (normally just one charge) and can only boost you once so in some of the situations you find yourself in you need to go and find the special tank that provides you with those extra charge's you need,so instead of one boost charge you can have upto between 4 or 6 which really helps out with those hard to do areas that without these extra charges you just would not over come.
Lets get back to the story (dont worry wont give anything away),the script that accompanies the game as you play is one that kept me fully hooked and i must admit that i havent come across such good writing in a game in a long time,as it turns and twists its way right up until one of the best and most satisfying endings it has been my privalige to play through to get to in what seems like a life time of playing games.
In summing up this game would you enjoy it well answer the following questions and make your own mind up--
1 - Would you like to play a game unlike anything you have played before and which also has one of the best and most engrossing storylines any game has had in quite some time ??
2 - Are you a huge SCI-FI game fan who is looking for that something different and unlike any other SCI-FI game you have ever played ????
If you answer yes to both of the above what are you waiting for buy this game now,and if not then you will be missing out on not just one of the best sci-fi games ever made,but in this reveiwers humble opinion one of the best games that the medium has seen in quite some time.

Turok definatly looks like its from 1997, but that older look just adds to the charm of the game. If you like older, Doom style games, you'll most likely enjoy Turok.
The story of Turok is very simple. You are Turok, and you hunt dinosaurs. The game starts you off right into the action with very little context on what is actually going on. This could annoy some people, but it doesn't pull away from the immersion at all. Although this lack of story can make the latter half of the game make little to no sense storywise.
Turok has a very fast movement speed which is a nice change from the sluggish sharpshooters from today. This makes the game playable at any pace you would like, whether you want to speed through or explore the levels.
When it comes to the levels themselves, many of them are fairly forgettable in design, but some have a genuinly interesting theme and layout. Either way, they are all fun to explore, with tons of secrets in every level.
The combat is responsive, and very satisfying with a large variety of weapons to find and use. As an added bonus, none of the weapons feel redundant or outshined by others (with the exception of a few), which allows a lot more options when you're tackling either a boss, a particularly beefy mob, or your average joe of an enemy. Turok also does a good job when it comes to ammunition drops, which seems like a weird thing to think about, but it manages to sit on a fine line, where i needed to be mindful of my ammo, but at the same time I didn't feel the need to be overly conservative with the weapons that I used.
While you will be seeing some of the same mobs a lot, there is a nice variety of enemies that keeps the combat from getting too stale and repetative, especially in the last few levels.
One problem I had with the game however, was that I wasn't %100 certain on what I was actually supposed to be doing. The game does a pretty poor job of telling you what you need to do in the beginning, and you can easily get lost on the first level. If you can get past this however, then it should be easy to figure out what you need to be doing for the rest of the game.
If you have played a lot of games like doom, then you will not be disappointed with Turok. If you are new to this style of gameplay, then Turok is an excellent introduction to other games like it. While Turok is not necessarily an innovative game, it is a fun one that does what it does well and is definatly worth the $20.

Mostly, Acclaim and Iguana Entertainment have made it more gameplay and goal heavy. Though the controls may be more simple, but overall, there are things that are enjoyable about it. Like for example, when I play through it, I got a slight sense of what the story was behind it. That was what made the first game so great. I notice that Iguana Entertainment has attempted to put together a story for the later series like Turok Evolution, as well as Vexx which was a platformer I personally enjoyed and wish Nightdive would bring that out on the Market. Just like it's prequel, Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures, AVGN 2: ASSimilation is inspired by classic NES and SNES era platformers and sidescrollers. Unlike the previous game, this one has more playable levels and collectibles that you can find for 100% completion such as the Nerd's gear and NES cartridges that spell out NERD (akin to Star Coins in the New Super Mario Bros. series). The game is split into 5 worlds with 3 levels plus a boss level per area. Unlike the previous game, you can't play as different characters (BS Man, MotherF*cker Mike, and Guitar Guy), but you can find the Nerd's equipment scattered across the levels.  The Nerd's gear allow for permanent power-ups similar to upgrades in Mega Man and Metroid games. You can get a more powerful version of your starting weapon, a cape that allows your to glide in the air, shoes that allow for wall sliding and jumping, and all that. The levels reference AVGN obviously, with levels based off of the games he's reviewed such as TMNT, Hong Kong '97, and Castlevania 2. There are a lot other references too, such as the Nostalgia Critic serving a similar role to Proto Man in Mega Man 3, Cinemassacre's Monster Madness, James Rolfe's other series Board James, and the AVGN movie just to name a few. The music is amazing, being mostly chiptune tracks akin to 8 and 16 bit themes. The difficulty is much more lenient than AVGN Adventures and it only took me around 6 to 7 hours to beat the game on Normal mode. Overall, if you're a fan of the AVGN and retro platformers and sidescrollers, buy this game.

The Graveyard is a very short "interactive art" game in which you walk through a graveyard as an old woman, sit on a bench, and listen to a song.
The controls are simple, but the woman's movement is very slow. You are unable to explore the graveyard because invisible walls block all paths except the one between the gate and the bench. The camera only faces one way, so the character can be obscured by a grave if you try leaving the main path, making it unapparent that you are futilely shuffling into an invisible wall.
The game is intended to be atmospheric, but making the movement slow and the graphics being entirely greyscale does not achieve the intended effect. The graphics and audio are lacking, and while the song is interesting, it feels out of place.
SPOILERS:

SPOILER ALERT:
Old lady walks around.
She might die.
Game over.

If you watch the video above, that's the absolute entirety of the game, sound and all. You walk (slowly) to a bench, turn around and sit down, then contemplate life while listening to a song. It actually even has something extra in the video, as after three full playthroughs, my old lady never stayed alive long enough to get up off the bench and walk out of the graveyard. Coincidentally, this is what you need to do in order to actually exit the game via the game controls, meaning I needed to exit via keyboard shortcuts every time. I guess when they say the full version includes the chance of death, they really mean that there's a very small chance of living. I can't stand playing any more to see how many attempts it takes. In any case, as much as I actually tend to enjoy the "art" games, this really has nothing worthwhile to it. Of course, having gotten it in a bundle with other games I actually wanted, I really don't care, but if you are thinking of spending money on this, go watch paint dry for five minutes instead. You'll have almost as worthwhile of an experience. I will give them this, in that the game description is quite accurate, though "explorable" and "walk around" are stretching things a lot. I was expecting to actually be able to, I don't know, maybe walk around and explore the graveyard on my way to the bench.

The comparison that it's terraria in space holds pretty well, but there's just something about it that makes it feel even better.
It's less boss oriented and more sandbox. Instead of just one world you have virtually infinite planets that you can link together and teleport between, with your ship serving as an intermediate space which you can also expand and build on (although not to the same extent as the planets). If you find yourself visiting a planet frequently enough and you have the resources (and trust me, it's not cheap), you can even place a teleporter so you don't have to beam to your ship, although beware that you won't be able to remove it thereafter without destroying it.
That's not to say there are not bosses and interesting combat mechanics; there are. It's just not what you may be used to. For instance, weapons are either one-handed or two-handed, depending on whether they have a built-in secondary ability, so one-handed weapons tend to be more flexible, whereas two-handed weapons are generally more powerful. The ranged weapons use energy in much the same way as terraria's magic weapons use mana, but unlike terraria, pretty much all armor offers boosts to your energy capacity.
Bosses are also different, but not so much in combat as in how you encounter them. Unlike terraria, you don't just summon a boss by using an item, but rather you must complete a sort of dungeon that resets if everyone in it dies, much like a party wipe in an instanced encounters in games like WoW. There will usually be a checkpoint before the boss though, so you can keep trying as long as you have resources to keep trying. (It's also easy enough to spawn in items if you get desperate, although obviously that's considered cheating. I may or may not have done this to get through my first encounters with bosses 2, 3 and 4, but in my defense I have a spinal cord injury so the fact I'm able to play at all is a testament to modern technology...)
All in all, whether you see this as a new twist on the general concept of terraria or a game of its own is irrelevant. It is a VERY good game and I've barely played anything else since I bought it. 9.8/10

The reality is that this is an old-school style dungeon crawler that places emphasis on survival rather than running around and popping loot-balloons masquerading as enemies. While my playclock there is probably half again what I have actually played, I have played a lot of this game. I have a few top 10 high scores (look for Seika), I've completed the story, and whole heck of a lot of missions in Tormented Space area (hard mode), so I have quite a bit of familiarity with the game.
Pros:
-A unique take on strategy that generally emphasizes resource and space management more than managing unit tactics, and the enemy is a rather literal tide rather than a more discreet set of units
-Huge array of playable content, with a wide variety of maps.
-Once you clear the main campaign, there are three main modes of pre-constructed maps. Prospector Zone has literally hundreds if not thousands of hours of content, Tormented Space exists for a good challenge, and Alpha Sector has some interesting and often difficult custom maps.
Cons:
-There is little to no AI to speak of. Certain types of enemies are capable of either roaming around randomly, and another will target random sections of your grid, but otherwise, the enemy will follow a strict pattern every map. Except for speed running, there is little point to replaying a map.
-Music will get repetitive.There is a mute button for a reason.
-Once you clear the main campaign, there are three modes. Prospector Zone is where much of the game's content lies, but the (generally) lower difficulty and lack of custom scripting means that most of these maps will get boring and repetitive. Tormented Space is not always the best tested: Some maps will feel almost as easy as the tutorial, while others are quite literally impossible without cheating (there is a thread on the Knuckle Cracker Forum dedicated to which maps are super difficult, which are insanely difficult [often requiring odd tricks in order to even stand a chance], which are possibly impossible, and which are undeniably impossible). If I have any complaint about Alpha Sector, it is that many of these maps were designed by some of the best players to be at their level, so it can be hard to make progress through those missions.
The game can feel repetitive, particularly playing too much in too short a time, but the game has kept me hooked. I would recommend playing this game to anyone who enjoys puzzles and strategy, or who likes playing unique games.

I am a fan of the Broken Sword series ever since I was 10 and as such, I couldn't help feel very excited about the news of a fifth installment and of course I backed the kickstarter campaign. In this respect though, I am somewhat disappointed with the end product.
My first gripe is, of course, that this is actually not the end product - this is supposed to be just half of it. If you're new to the franchise DO NOT buy this game until you've played BS 1,2, and 3 (I don't believe 4 is in Steam) - it is much, much, much more value for money.
Of course, I read the update saying that there will be another episode in January (free for me, yay!), but when I saw that I have completed nearly half of the game, I thought that it was half of this episode - and it feels this way! this game is just so short, I was a bit dismayed even when I was thinking I did 1/4 of the story, not half of it! SPOILER ALLERT! BS5, as it is right now, is really just a murder investigation. I cannot help but compare it to the original Broken Sword, where the story just began as a murder investigation, but unfolded to be about much more! This time, it felt as if I was jumping down the rabbit whole... to find it painfuly shallow! I really hope that the second episode speeds up the pace and present and reveal more secrets for us to solve!
Finally, I really hope that there will be more locations in the second episode - in this one there were only five locations for us to explore. Again, a comparison to the original Broken Sword does not make the Serpent's Curse look too good. I can only assume - and hope - that we will be given more than just Paris, Spain and the promissed in the kickstarter campaing Middle Eastern/North African location (these are a must, of course!).
Finally, the reason I compare this game so much with the first one in the series is because the Serpent's Curse is made as mainly fan-service to the die-hard fans. 1 of the frequented locations in the game (that is, 20% of all of them) is an old one and a large portion of the characters are from the previous games. Nothing wrong with bringing old characters back, but the new ones are so few!
As a conclusion, you'll see that it says on Steam that I'm recommending this game. While this is true, it applies only to people who have played the previous installments - it is, after all, a Broken Sword game and the story looks promissing, so I am having high hopes for the second episode. But if you've never played any of the previous games - please, do, before bying this one! The story stands alone, you are not going to miss anything - however BS5 just does not provide as much value for money.

I was one of the privelaged few who got to play Turok: Dinosaur Hunter when it was first released on Nintendo 64 back in 1997. It was one of the games that attracted us to Nintendo's quirky, but unique new system. While some preferred Goldeneye or Doom 64, Turok was still a strong competitor in the FPS genre and spawned a few successful sequels until plummeting into mediocrity. The controls took time to get used to, but the gameplay was fast paced and bloody, and it even managed to please longtime fans of the comic book.
Night Dive's re-release is like plugging in a 20 year old system again. Your memories begin flooding back and the first few minutes are glorious, but then the nostalgia glasses wear off and you realize just how far games have come. Turok is not a bad game in any way, it's just very, very dated. I love classic FPS games. Doom 2 and Blood still get playtime for me after all these years. Turok just has nothing that keeps it fresh after almost two decades.
I have no problem with the graphics, and applaud Night Dive for leaving the original design untouched. They even kept old glitches intact on purpose and, in a recent update, implemented the original N64 sound effects. Visuals and sound are still great. It's the gameplay that hurts. While playing on a mouse and keyboard is superior to the goofy N64 controller, and Turok moves pretty smoothly, some of the platforming in the game is near impossible. Some of the jumps you are asked to perform happen only by miracle, and sometimes just looking at a platform the wrong way can cause you to fall through it. The weapons are fun, but some don't seem to do anything or cause any varying degrees of damage, and just feel like they were put there to look cool. If you are lucky enough to assemble the Chronoscepter, good luck getting a hit in with it.
My biggest complaint is that the levels are TOO DAMN LONG. Level 8 wins the award for the longest, most excruciating level in video game history. It's neat that the levels are so open and there are multiple paths, but good god the last level takes almost two hours to complete! It begins to feel tedious after a while and you stop enjoying the game and just wish for the level to be over. Also, enemies respawn, making the levels EVEN LONGER when you have to clear the same corridors multiple times.
Turok is not a terrible game. If you have played it before and it's cheap, go ahead and relive some memories. Just be ready to cringe. It's very hard to recommend Turok to those who have never played it because it is so dated, but if you enjoy games of old and want a field trip back to when FPS games were still in their infancy, it's worth a look.

Like the Son of Stone himself, Turok is a game from another time and place - the Lost World of the '90s where TV was  somewhat watchable, movies were occasionally okay, and games were (usually) shipped done.
Turok is a hardened Saquin warrior with a mystic lineage and a champion's spirit. He is the inheritor of a familial mantle that both compels and empowers him to -- well, you know what. None of that is actually important right now, because it's hardly mentioned in the game. And that's for the better, really. The comic books that inspired the game were absolutely all over the place in terms of tone and setting, as seems to be the standard for the medium.
Suffice it to say, you play the role of an awesome Native American warrior who handles ultra high-tech future weapons just as well as he does the bows and knives of his heritage. You travel the Lost Land - a realm parallel to our own in which time has no conventional meaning, and creatures and technologies from countless other universes coexist - in a quest to assemble a forbidden superweapon and use it to take down the evil Campaigner. The Campaigner is like a cybernetic Genghis Khan, only worse, and he's raised a bloodthirsty army to wreak havoc upon the Lost Land and beyond.
Turok was a technological marvel in its time. It's got wide-open spaces like Unreal and it sports the fast-and-furious run-and-gun of Quake, and it blends the best of those two games together. The result remains unique still today because nothing else out there plays quite like Turok does. It's not your typical shooter. Turok requires an adventurer's touch, as the game is just as much about exploring massive, mysterious hand-built environments as it is shooting velociraptors in the face with explosive arrows.
Therein lies the problem most modern gamers are likely to encounter playing this game. Turok is linear to a point, but the action takes place in fairly large, often vertical, outdoor areas, and it's easy to get lost if you don't pay attention. The game doesn't lead you around with big glowing waypoints, either, and uncovering the sprawling environs' many secrets is crucial to getting through the game without cheating. The game utilizes an atypical hub system that links all its levels together. Teleporters to the various lands are opened using keys Turok must uncover along the way. You'll need to find the keys that are scattered throughout the levels in order to proceed through the game.
If you lack the patience to explore - and you like your games on a leash - then you should know up front that Turok is probably not for you. But if you're anything like me, you're sick of modern shooters and their over-reliance on scripted set-pieces. I find Turok's open-ended, "archaic" approach to be a breath of fresh air so many years after playing it last. Exploring the world and finding a well-hidden secret brings a real, palpable sense of accomplishment, the kind of breath-stealing "eureka!" moment that very few recent titles manage to evoke even once.
The various levels are varied and interesting, and are underscored with an abundance of ambient sound effects and a truly bizarre drums-and-synths soundtrack that stands out on its own and is instantly recognizable. Though it began life as an early N64 game, Turok has atmosphere in spades. Its enemy design can only be described as eclectic. Velociraptors with cybernetic gun arms are awesome. Insectoid aliens with plasma rifles? Those are great, too. Sometimes, their armor malfunctions when you kill them, and they struggle against their inevitable explosive demise. Even better. Killer plants, overgrown bugs, armor-clad mercenaries with pulse rifles and tank-top wearing grunts with machetes - your opponents are always varied and never boring.
The entire experience has a hand-crafted feel, and everything is in its proper place. Though a shooter at heart, the feeling of adventuring in a bizarre otherworld is prevalent throughout, and the architecture occasionally reminds me of adventure games like Myst. Perhaps the rooftop village just reminds me of the Channelwood Age or something.
It's not all exploration, though. The action is fast and fluid with mouse and keyboard controls, and is super-responsive. It's a blast to blast away while staying on the move. Turok plodded a bit with the flaky N64 controller, but now the game is blazing-fast like Quake on the PC and somehow the game manages to handle the player's faster input very well. Especially if you bump things up to Hard - the setting has obviously been tweaked to be *quite* difficult in order to compensate for the player's better aim. Things get very tough, very fast on Hard, though easy and normal are just as I remembered them back in the day.
There's a respectable arsenal of exotic weaponry, which Turok literally stores in his magical Bag of Holding. No weapon swapping here. When I was a kid, my circle of friends derived much amusement from the over-the-top excess of some of the later weapons, what with their elaborate folding/unfolding deployment animations and sound effects. Whenever we thought of crazy, overblown weapons or machines, we thought of Turok and laughed. One of those weapons is essentially a portable nuke, and really has to be seen to be believed. Oh, boy, did that ever rock our worlds back then. Watching it blow over trees was exquisite. And of course there's a minigun, which you can unleash into the brush to reenact everyone's favorite scene in the Predator movie. And the ridiculousness of the more advanced weaponry actually serves to make the conventional all the more compelling somehow. Running around with an AK47 and blasting human commandos in the face keeps things feeling real, know what I'm sayin'?
This is a source port of the PC original by Samual Villareal. If you're a Doomer like me, the name will be familiar. If you're not, suffice it to say that the man is well-appreciated for his work on other source ports, and his involvement in the Doom community. Turok runs wonderfully well on modern PCs, and features some nice, subtle visual improvements that fit in perfectly with the style of the graphics. No ridiculous bloom or lens flares or anything like that - what's here is good enough to highlight that Turok never really looked that bad to begin with. Honestly, I'm surprised just how well it holds up, though the reflective water and atmospheric lighting really does add to the atmosphere. In high resolutions with anti-aliasing, it's a treat to look at. With about 500% of the colors present in Battlefield 4, my eyes almost couldn't handle all the sensory information.
So is it worth your time and money? Yes, absolutely. There's plenty to see and shoot in Turok's eye-catching, lovingly hand-crafted world, and I couldn't be happier with my purchase. And yes, I bought this game years after completing the original multiple times. It stuck with me, certainly. I'm beyond excited for Night Dive's rerelease of Turok 2. As much as I love the original, the sequel is even better. They're noticeably different, though, in terms of style and execution. I highly recommend anyone to get both.

This is not a carbon copy of XCOM, it's more like inspired by XCOM, as well as much more difficult. The main thing this game has in common with XCOM is the combat mechanics and permadeath and these are not bad game mechanics so I believe it's acceptable. Every choice matters and your soldiers (named Heroes) WILL die and you will have to accept this. I love this game but not because of its combat, (which is very light strategy and needs some fine tuning to be satisfactory) but because of everything outside of combat. You rule a kingdom and control when time starts and stops. Time means everything in this game, as well as the age, experience, fertility, and traits of your heroes. Even some enemy designs revolve around these subjects, a type of enemy can cause you to lose experience, or make you older by 5 to 10 years, or even make you sterile. Your people WILL die on the battle field. Accept it. The artstyle is fantastic and the gameplay outside of combat is very intriguing and interesting. Now for the enemy types, the only thing I have a problem with is how powerful the enemies are. I don't mind a challenge but I believe some tweaks would improve their combat mechanics, such as for example, the Lapses who when hit a hero they drain experience, the amount of experience should dialed down. Also the variability of hit success can be infuriating at times, (f.e. 87% chance to land a successful hit and misses can be very  frustrating.) This game is a work in progress for sure, however despite it's flaws it is well worth the price and extremely fun, satisfying, and very challenging. 9.5/10! In case you don't think this review is helpful because I may be confusing in how I feel about this game, it's worth the money if you enjoy strategy games like XCOM. If you don't enjoy those types of games then you won't enjoy this one. Simple as that. For thirty bucks though this is worth it.

THIS IS A BETA REVIEW.
I've played about 2 hours of the game (30 years of the 300 year timeline). So far, I like the game, and I see potential for continued improvement before the final release.
The game does play like a fantasy X-COM in a lot of ways, but I was also reminded of the random good and bad traits from Rogue Legacy. These affect your strategic choices because many can be transmitted genetically (so be careful who you choose to found bloodlines) or socially (so be careful who you appoint as trainers). I also feel losing a valuable soldier hurts less in Massive Chalice than in X-COM, because all your soldiers are going to age and die anyway. It's a neat twist.
WHAT I LIKE:
- the graphics are charming; I like the style
- the choices on the strategic planning map are challenging and I feel there are probably multiple good (no "best") choices
WHAT I'D LIKE TO SEE CHANGED:
- unit variety I'd like more than three classes, and some way to "blend" abilities of different classes (e.g., one parent's an alchemist and the other's a hunter, so the kids they raise are a little bit of each)
- silly catchphrases make me roll my eyes a bit; maybe the "serious mode vs. silly mode" setting (I forget what it's actually called) isn't implemented yet?
- eventually, I'd like to see an option to let the timeline extend beyond 300 years
Anyway, I've enjoyed what I've played of Massive Chalice so far, and will be on the look out for future updates.

I now finished the game so here is my point of view:
- Very good game, fun to play in both the management phase and combat phase. It's definitely worth buying and playing, expect a 10 hours run if like me your first game goes well.
- Story could be a little more explained, I wasn't always sure what was the clear goal, even if you have no choice but to go toward it. I learned when it was going to end mid-game, but I think there should be a better build-up to it.
- The game could use stuff like 1-2 more classes maybe and some more traits for heroes. Relics are good, but eventually all look alike, could have some special bonuses to attached to each one.
- The game NEEDS a tutorial... I had no idea that relic had to be equipped, how everything affect everything, lineage (ended up having 3 keeps of the same family), etc... You can figure everything as you play, but might discourage some people.
- Loved the end game fight, but I would have love some more "explanations" on special stuff happening on both side. Don't get me wrong, it's super cool, but I felt like it was coming out of nowhere.
- Other game mode (only auto-save, higher difficulty, etc...). Options could give a lot more lasting appeal to the game.
I'll be sure to play again when the game is completed, but it already felt like a completed game to me. It can only get better with updates I think.

As of v0.85:
Massive Chalice is a curious mix of XCOM and Banner Saga mechanics with just enough unique innovations to make it stand out.
If you enjoy good turn-based strategy combat and survival resource management - this game is probably for you.
Not only you have to fend off Cadence in pretty hard battles, you also need to manage your heroes bloodlines.
Since your heroes are going to age and die eventually, there must be someone to take their place. Like their children.
Dead heroes can pass unique artifacts to their children, which can be very powerful on a field.
Older and more experienced heroes can be used to teach younger ones, as well as to speed your research up.
All of that adds up to a pretty nice and unique gameplay experience.
And there's not too much of a downsides either - game is very well balanced, has quite a lot of content and feels solid overall.
It does still have a few bugs and performance issues, but I guess that was the reason for going Early Access here.

This game was fun-ish while it lasted, but the late game, once you get there, is completely boring and repetitive. It becomes increasingly less challenging and eventually I just quit. Enemies are boring, poorly conceived, have no life bars to denote how much damage you're doing, don't change as time progresses (once you get the giant, that's the last new enemy), and combat itself is painfully bad. Your own armies will let the enemy walk right passed them if they don't pass through your space, will not chase an enemy that doesn't stop to fight you, and there is only one unit type in the game and a max of 3 different groups of units. Whoever programmed the combat mechanics in this game did a very, very, very bad job. It's easily one of the worst combat systems I've seen in a strategy game, ever.
Games like Factorio, Cities: Skylines, and Banished all of have deep late game organization potential. They all have massive maps to spread out into. They all have modding and variety. There is, again, no late game in this. You have such a limited amount of space that you basically get capped out and can do some optimizing, but that's not really fun because of how limited the map is.
This game is a solid 5/10. It's cheap and easy to get the hang of, but once you beat it, there's honestly no reason to ever play it again.
For $10, I would save your money and spend $20 on Factorio or Banished. WAY more bang for your buck.

From the Depths is the logical progression of a childhood interest in legos and war machines.
The games initial startup and learning curve is a little difficult to master, but very rewarding once you get the hang of it. Construction is fun and time consuming but very rewarding.
The campaign constantly challenges you. Each ship you design may be good against a few ships, but will struggle against a wide variety of enemies with different armor styles and weapon styles.
Similar to reality, a good design is upgradable and can be developed to fight increasingly difficult foes. It is up to you to decide how you go about this. Add more armor but sacrafice speed? Add shields but develop a more powerful and efficent engine to compensate for the increased power consumption? Overhaul the weapons with longer shells, barrels, or different shell types? All of this will make your basic design stronger but also more expensive and complex. You may hit a point where you reach the final development of your carefully nurtured design. Thankfully, you don’t need to have played either of the previous games to enjoy Creeper World 3, as it has a mostly self-contained plot.
There’s no getting around it: the game looks ugly. The graphics are utterly functional, and that’s it. But this ugly duckling has a supernova of elegant swans that explode from its superdense core the moment you start playing. Arc Eternal follows a well-written science-fiction plot as you fight an enigmatic foe known only as “Creeper”.You can place turrets, mortar launchers, build bombers, cannons, and terraform the terrain to redirect the Creeper’s endless flow, provided you have the resource generating capacity to sustain it all. By the end of a mission, the sheer scope of your network of energy-producing Collectors can be impressive.
The campaign is lengthily with many unique map elements. There’s a huge amount of side-missions and bonus content if you’re up for it, and the Dial-a-Map Device can generate infinite random missions.  Creeper World 3 is impressive where it truly counts.

is a traditional side-scrolling platformer, and the sequel to The Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures. I'm a big fan of the Nerd and I thoroughly enjoyed both games, so this is going to be a bit of a longer review:
- It's basically a different version (I'd call it an enhancement) of the original game. The same basic goal remains: The Nerd must once again rid himself of the horrible game he's found himself in, and save his world. Just like the first game, the story isn't complicated or important, and only serves as a vehicle for the Nerd's adventure to have a purpose, much like in some of the AVGN episodes.
- Is mostly the same as the first game, but with some tweaks and improvements. The Nerd can now wall jump and collect hidden upgrades to aid in his adventure, much like in the Mega Man X series of games. Another major change is that rather than having eight big stages and then the final stage, there's the tutorial stage, followed by five areas, each containing three smaller stages (which are unlocked in sequence) and a boss battle. It's similar to the first Sonic the Hedgehog, which had six Zones each with three Acts, and a Final Zone. You still get to pick which stage you want to tackle, and you can move from one area to the next before beating the boss of either. Some may prefer the first game's layout, but I thought this one was better because it caters to players who only want to play a little part of the game at a time, and don't want to be overwhelmed by one big stage they can't tackle yet. I do wish there was maybe one more area, but five areas plus the last stage isn't terrible.
Arguably the biggest change is the difficulty; the original game was very tough and at various points quite unforgiving (ESPECIALLY the final stage). This game isn't
punishing, but it's still far from a walk in the park, especially if you wish to tackle the higher difficulties. Some people complain about the overall difficulty of both games, but I don't quite understand; not only is there an Easy mode (which games in the '80s, as well as my early childhood of the 90s - early 2000s typically didn't have), but one shouldn't expect a game based off the AVGN to not be infuriating at points. This game's difficulty is much more balanced and even the final stage isn't too bad once you get the feel for it. You even get your lives replenished when you exit a stage, so there's no beating a level and then being short on lives for the next one. You can even quit a level if you're stuck, with no penalty other than having to start from the beginning the next time you play that level.
- The controls are basic but do what they're supposed to. They feel fluid and I never had a problem running, jumping or shooting when I wanted to. I played on a keyboard as well.
- Again, similar to the design of the first game. They graphics are very colorful, pixelated and go a long way in making you feel like you're playing as the Nerd. The sound effects are good, and the soundtrack is just as great as the first AVGN game. I could listen to the Security Breach theme for hours.
- Probably the weakest link in the game for me. For the most part, the game runs great, but there are a few instances where there's so much stuff on the screen that you may experience significant stuttering or frame drops. This is most apparent on the Raw Fish Rampage stage, and since that stage auto-scrolls, this issue makes beating it in one shot considerably harder (and that stage is a hassle to begin with). Frame drops can sometimes be even when the game normally ran well just a while before.
Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game, even more than I did the first; it felt like an overall improvement of an already very good game. The many references to the series of videos and movies made me feel like I was playing as the Nerd in his prime. If you're a fan of the Nerd, or you like very challenging platformers and don't mind the potential rage factor, this game is probably for you. I'd rather superglue my a--hole shut than not have this game in my library.

I don't expect the developers to literally walk players through the entire process available.
The ability to place multiple links can be almost a nuisance at times, especially when you want something to be locked while doing something else. For example, playing a music link while placing other links. Any link you place is "selected," thus stopping the music as previously selected.
There doesn't seem to be much base content, but with the additions possible through the steam workshop the possibilities are endless. There also doesn't seem to be any type of leveling or unlocking system for your available props, but again I refer to my previous statement.
I don't have much else to add. As the description says, this is really just a 3D desktop program, allowing you to link to your other programs. I'm not giving this game a bad review, I'm only giving a bad review because someone who doesn't do their homework probably doesn't want this.

This review contains minor spoilers and self opinions!
When I first played Turok on the N64 in 1996 it was just ground breaking. Reading about the Remake and finding Turok on Steam 20 later is just awesome. I guess there are a lot of people who wrote already glorifying notes, hence I'll pinpoint out the differences.
1996 vs. 2016:
better graphics: I'm sure there is an overview concerning the graphical enhancements (water, AAFX, fog, etc). The developers didn't enhance the graphics to much. Hence Turok kept its look and feel. For example the fog – originally designed to save comping-power – wasn't removed. But the player is provided with the option to reduce. Hence he still can enjoy the original games atmosphere.
more accurate controls: the PC Version in 1996 felt like a N64 port. Setting up the controls took some time and usually ended up in a half baked configuration – Uhm... jeah I cyn play with this, but I could be better. The remake controls are WASD-Style and work precicely.
aiming: opposing to the 1996 version the Player now can turn the crosshair on :)
the “mortal wound”: in the current version it drops very rarely, but this doesn't matter because this item was originally designed to increase the auto-aim-accuracy.
Violence and blood-settings: opposing to the games PC Version in 1996 the current Version allows the player to chose red, green or “no blood”. Especially the German Players might be happy to notice, since the German Version was cut by removing Skins and blood effects to match the youth protection requirements.
I hope that Turok 2 will be remade soon and that the Developers port the bugfix concerning the Tranquilizer Gun.

This is a game worth playing for anyone who thrives on creative projects between adventures, and collaborative ones among friends. It's something that has intrigued me since the early beta, never failing to inspire my return. Even unmodded the game offers a solid blend of story, exploration, building/decorating, and character customization. The game offers just enough survival elements (somewhat optional), a plot with NPCs and quests, plenty of loot, tech abilities and upgrades, extensive cooking recipes, and the freedom to build almost anywhere. The world is vibrant and the graphics, controls and art style are very polished. I recommend this game to anyone who loves to build and explore planets above and below, and even more if there are cooperative friends.

First off, this is in early access, and I backed the Kickstarter at the time so take that for what it's worth.
Massive Chalice is a turn-based tactical game in the same vein as, but on a smaller scale than, X-Com.  Where it differs is in the meta-game; rather than building a base and managing resources, you're managing the family trees of your squad.  You do still research equipment and choose buildings for the different regions in the kingdom, but it's a more limited set of choices than you may be used to.  The overall aim of the game is to survive as a kingdom under threat, until the titular Massive Chalice is able to purge the threat from your lands forever.
The heroes that make up your squad (up to 5 at a time) are born, they age, gain experience and abilities, and die.  They will die a lot, and saving and reloading when a mission goes poorly won't save them.  The timeline that you are trying to survive through means that even if everything goes according to plan, your heroes will still eventually succumb to old age.  The trick is to ensure you have enough new heroes being born (with beneficial heriditary traits) to replace them.
On a functional level, the game looks and sounds beautiful.  The art design is outstanding, and I wouldn't be surprised to see it win some awards at the end of the year.  It is still in Beta, but I've not experienced any game-breaking bugs.
I've followed the development of the game throughout the process, from concept art to playing it on Steam, thanks to DoubleFine's excellent TeamStreams.  I understand why certain decisions have been made, and while there are some tweaks I'd like to see to the balancing, overall the game is challenging, fun, pretty, and a triumph for open game development that I hope more developers learn from in the future.  :D

A little gem of a game. Basically a proof of concept for its upcoming older sibling, Sui Generis. A dungeon crawler with a highly nuanced, physically simulated combat system - which at the time of this writing comes with a difficult and interesting (if unfinished) campaign and an incredibly addictive Arena mode (recently expanded upon in an update) for you to practice your fighting skills in. And practice you must: The selling point of Exanima is its frankly brilliant combat system, which is all about influencing your character's basic set of animations at key moments in order to procedurally generate the unique actions the situation calls for. It will take you, at the very least, a couple of hours to get used to how it all works (and the game's camera system), but the reward is well worth it. The developers have spent the past couple of years not only working on content (such as weapons and new floors for the campaign dungeon), but also polishing the combat system and the underlying details of its simulation. And their efforts show  - Bare Mettle has achieved something undeniably unique here. It currently has a a bit of a dearth of content (if highly replayable), but I would nonetheless suggest you pick up this game even in its current state. Mechanically speaking, what's in there is already quite impressive, and will give you a relatively clear view of the roadmap towards the full version.

This is not a traditional tower defense game.  You don't build mazes.  You don't upgrade towers.  There are no units to attack.  Yet, it contains a lot of the same mechanics as TD games:  you build towers which attack for you;  you decide whether to spend or invest resources; you strategically place towers at the right places and times.  Thus, I don't feel uncomfortable categorizing this in the Tower Defense genre.
The game goes like this:  you expand your base to earn resources.  The larger the surface-area of your base, the more resources-per-second you earn.  Meanwhile, the "enemy" is simply a geyser of fluid
which spreads out in all directions.  If the fluid touches a tower, that tower dies.  You use your towers to push back the fluid, so you can get close enough to destroy the geyser(s).
On paper, it sounds stupid.  But then again, I would have said the same thing about TD games at first, and now they are my favorite genre.
In reality, this is a
game.  The game constantly introduces new gameplay-elements throughout the campaign, keeping it fresh and unrepetitive.  The levels are never too easy, but also never too hard
.  And after beating the campaign, the game opens up hundreds of levels created by the developer, his friends, beta testers, etc. giving this game immense replayability.
I've played
of TD games, and this is one of my top 3 TD games of all time
.  If you enjoy TD games, I personally guarantee you will enjoy this game. 10/10

A good game, but with issues in its "packaging".
I knew the series from the previous Flash chapters. The developer did a good job adding enough elements to this episode to keep the gameplay interesting throughout the campaign.
It's an interesting strategy game, where you know how the enemy will behave from the start (since it follows fluid physics) and yet every map requires you to think about how to approach it with the land provided and the techs unlocked. The gameplay is solid, it is decently challenging for a first walkthrough (yet nothing a player with any experience in the genre will not be able to tackle) and offers a chance for speedrunning/score attack replays of existing maps. Apart from the campaign (which took me somewhere between 8 and 10 hours at a leisurly pace), the game has a couple extra modes with different objectives, for even more longevity.
The problems I have with the game are mostly outside of the gameplay itself. The game asks for a relatively high price tag for a series evolved from a Flash game, but does it add enough to make it reasonable? In my eyes, it doesn't.
The storyline is ridiculous, it pretty much revolves for the entire campaign around the idea of "I lost my memory, what's all of this?". You could skip every dialogue in the game and not miss anything relevant. The only campaign progression is the gradual introduction of more buildings and techs.
Which leads to the second point: after you unlock everything and you figure out which approach works best for you, most of the extra modes are more of the same. Which is good if you want to play more on different maps, but it lacks the tailored scenarios of the campaign. Still, it's good to come back from time to time for a map or two and have a large selection of unexplored locations.
The graphics haven't improved in a relevant way compared to the Flash chapters. The soundtrack is very limited and you will get bored of the few track really fast.
All things considered it's still a game I'd pick up, but at a sensible discount, since it's reasonably fun to play for a while but lacks the added value to justify the price point.

I have played ANNO 1440, and have read a lot of the not recommended reviews about ANNO 2205.
I agree that they are two games, 2205 advanced in some aspects, but lacks in some other provided by 1440.
First off there is multiplayer in 1440, I don't see that can be implemented in 2205. The reason is that 1440 is more of an RTS, 2205 has shifted quite heavily towards a city builder / management game.
2205 does try to bring back some elements of it by having invasion into your territories, disrupting your production and trade and sort of economically force you to go to a war, but of course, combat is quite a joke compared to 1440, but I would also say the same thing comparing ANNO to actual RTS.
On the management side, the economic tree was quite deeply developed compared to 1440, 20 hours into the game, I have yet to fully develope the entire tree. The supply and demands of goods from different regions are so intricately linked, that it is not a simply "plop down several buildings and your are good to go to combat" 1440 mode, going back and forth and back and forth between regions and trade routes, it actually get you to start thinking.
And speaking of going back and forth between screens, Windows 7 does have memory leakage problem with it, but my 16GB rig survived 6 hours of gameplay, RAM only built up to 8GB.
Some may complain that 2205 involves so much waiting for credits, I will say the same thing for 1440 waiting for siege.
Some complains about how easy the game is because when you go broke, game just gives you more money. Just turn on the difficulty settings, you can easily get♥♥♥♥♥beaten, and same as other ANNO, you can turn aspects of game you like or dislike on or off.
All in All, 2205 is not 1440, they are different, 2205 is more of a management game, I like to look at it that way, and enjoy it that way, the DLC does add even more to it. Don't let the previous installment of ANNO elude you, or if you are die hard fans of previous ANNO and only enjoy their style, you might really want to just skip this title.
