This is far worse than the first game.
This feels like Ubisoft just dumping out a sequel because the first was well recieved.  All the assets look identical, I can't find anything that looks new.
Issues I have:
1. Grabbing now Sucks:
First and foremost the main mechanic in the game, grabbing surfaces, is broken now.  Often times your hands are in range of a surface and you hold grab and it just doesn't grab. Othertimes it lets go while climbing vertical or upsidedown surfaces. This makes all of the navigation frustrating and failure prone.
2. Big world thats confusingly similar:
The world seems much bigger, which would be good.  But it all looks the same, I find I can't tell where things are and navigation is difficult.  I'll lose track of certain floating islands just by turning my camera 180 degrees.
3. Purposeful ability cuts to draw out the game:
The main character gets a jetpack right away, which theoretically should be liberating.  After playing the first it's nice to begin with that.  But they cut the main characters jump height practically in half. And the jetpack can hardly keep  altitude while it goes off.  It seems like they intentionally made it awful so that you have something to upgrade into.  But because of that, the hours and hours of gameplay without it just suck.  Can't make jumps, can't naviagte the world well. Also it feels like the character doesn't gain as much speed, so jumping is stunted and movement feels slower, yet somehow less responsive (maybe be connected to bad physics)
4. Physics are far more volatile:
Many times, I will jump and suddenly go way further for no appearent reason. Or I'll try to slow down for a descent with the jetpack, and still end up skipping off the ground and flying off an island.  There are a type of flipper plant, that automatically winds up when you stand on it, and flings you great distances. But the slide  off of it really easily, and it makes experimenting with flinging objects nearly impossible. It also makes it nearly impossible to reliabley get a good fling. And often times, if you dont slide off and you line up just right, you will just clip through it anyway and not go anywhere.  In general, traction in the game is too low. Sometimes you gain speed really well, but most of the time you just slide all over the place.
Over all this is just a really sloppy, unsatisfying platformier.  And it's disappointing because the first game nailed a lot.  I don't know if they tampered with the formula, or just didn't test this game much.  But it's very disappointing.

I have mixed feelings about this game.
The original mechanics are still there, with some modifications. the procedural animation is still endearingly clumsy, and there are still plenty of plants with interesting functions. The art style remains unusual and beautiful (with a buggy, stripy shadow here and there). The new, more open world is fun to traverse, and the new ability to grow and remove plants is fun to use. However, this game has lost a lot of what made the first one so special, and nearly all of that can be attributed to one thing.
P.O.D.
P.O.D is a drone with no interesting character traits, as far as I can tell; he just says things like "With this jetpack, you can fly, sort of, but not like me," and "New floraform. Scan for info." He gives you the ability to see basically the entire planet and zoom in and out, eliminating much of the adventurous intrige of Grow Home. He also points out new plants whenever one comes on screen, and, as mentioned before, instructs you to scan them. Now, instead of the feeling of joyful discovery I got when I noticed a new lifeform, I get massive square icon and a bright blue notification on the side of my screen, telling me that yes, indeed, there's a new plant there that I haven't seen before and I should scan it. There are bright blue square icons everywhere, by the way, and they can just buzz right off.
What bothers me most about P.O.D., though, is that he essentially eliminates any reason for B.U.D. to be there. He can see basically everything and is fully capable of lifting the spaceship pieces you need by himself. There are "P.O.D challenges," which P.O.D. claims helps him learn things, but there's absolutely no reason he couldn't just fly down there himself. These challenges also have arbitrary time limits that make absolutely no sense if these challenges are really just supposed to help with gathering information. Essentially, I've spent what I've played of the game so far feebly pretending to matter while knowing full well that I essentially serve no purpose.
I'm recommending this game because it's only ten dollars, which I suppose is worth it for the pleasant open world and the nice platforming mechanics. However, I do have a lingering sense of disappointment. In Grow Home, I played through the game as M.O.M. provided me the comfort of knowing that I was not alone. In Grow Up, I'm playing the game wishing to be left alone.

It's like, basically just more Grow Home. A few great mechanical improvements - the air brakes are a lifesaver, the jetpack feels more powerful, and the hang glider is just a much better implementation of the leaf. The larger game area means that collectibles are a lot more spread out but in return pod challenges are added to make some of the other landmasses a bit more meaningful and give the game a bit more of a platforming focus. Before I start, I'll note that this review does have a few very minor spoilers. None of them refer to the story, all to locations you visit in the game.
I'm going to say outright that I believe this game is truly worth your time, despite the fact that I, personally, was not as interested in the story as I should have been. This is entirely my own personal preferences of storytelling, yet despite this, Lifeless Planet is a solid game.
I purchased Lifeless Planet during the Early Access period and was quite interested in the plot of the game: as an American astronaut, you are traveling to a planet far, far from home. A one-way trip, in fact. Yet, somehow, there was human life already on this planet.
Don't let the tag "walking simulator" put you off. Sure, there's a lot of walking. However, in addition, there are puzzle elements (quite simple, though at times a bit hard to detect as other elements not involved with the puzzle would catch me off-guard) as well as multiple stages of platforming that were for the most part enjoyable. There are also multiple occasions where you could die, as well as fail.
The game does have an air of an indie title to it, especially with the developer's constant changing and fixing of the game even after release. It's a sign of a great developer when they are willing to listen to glitches and bugs and actively interact with the fans to fix the problems. Kudos to you!
There are a few bits of the game that reflect in a bit of an unpolished experience, however. Mainly this is in consistency. At a certain point in the game, you realize a certain plant in the game will kill you when approached. However, a bit later in the game, there is a plant in the shape of a flower that can be jumped upon. Gamers would assume that these objects should be avoided due to past experiences, and I spent a long while trying to find alternate routes around the flower, only to find I could hop right on for a bit.
Additionally, areas in the game considered "safe" at times are not, and can kill you without much warning. A lava portion later in the game gave me a slightly frustrating amount of deaths, as I was incapable of knowing where I was allowed to go without bursting in flames. Certain areas lacking plant life would stab and maim me before I knew why. At other points, canyons and craters that I thought unaccessible were capable of being traveled upon, despite dying several times attempting to navigate previous large holes. If you go for achievements, know that doing so requires a lot of effort for several of them. They truly are "achievements".
HOWEVER, the game is sound. The voice acting is terrific, particularly by our main astronaut. Russian voiceovers are realistic and well-done (though they do clash when reading English text-logs). As someone who does voice-acting, I found this area particularly strong, and I congratulate those involved. On top of this, the game does what it says it does. It tells a story. An engaging, interesting story.
Sure, there is a lot that could be looked into gameplay-wise, but for the most part, I doubt you're focusing on that. You're focusing on the tale it has to tell. You need to have a mindset of "I'm going to walk around quite a bit with some platforming, while listening to a story." There are long distances in this game. Long, barren distances. You need to get immersed to enjoy it. When you do, however, you truly experience a memorable game.
Take a look into it! Perhaps it was not my cup of tea, but what I DO know is that I'm not the "almighty lord of good taste". You're in for an interesting experience, and it's definitely one of the most original ideas I've seen for a game in many months.

The music is nice, but I didn't find it to be deeply immersive like many reviewers seem to. The player character responds to the controls in a very jerky way and interesting moments are always going into cutscenes and doing other jarring things that really take you out of the experience.
If you're super bored or super high this might still be a worthwhile play for you, but if you're like me you'll find yourself just running through a lot of "this path only" monotony hoping to find another shred of plot .

A wonderful entry to the series, it is the closes thing to the original Broken Sword (not only the best game in the series but also one of the best point-and-click adventures ever made).
The game is wonderful in almost every aspect. I'm really happy to see extremely detailed 2D backgrounds. In my opinion, this is the only right way to do classic adventure games. I haven't ever seen any 3D backgrounds that could rival the 2D ones. The voice acting and the music are of the best quality too.
The only disappointing thing is the characters. They are not in 2D, sadly, and look even worse than 2D characters featured 17 years ago in the original game! Well, the character models are actually made in 3D and then pre-rendered and put into 2D frames, they are not processed in real time. Nonetheless, they are much-much worse than authentic 2D models. A good example of how the 3D characters ruin the whole feel of the game is the introduction movie. The intro clearly takes cue from the first game in the series but looks worse than the original 17-year-old movie, even if you put them side by side now. Only because of those 3D models which stand out too much and not in a good way.
Other than the 3D models, I couldn't find anything I didn't like about the game. It's absolutely gorgeous. I was one of the backers behind it and I wouldn't hesitate to back any of Revolution's other games.

- Knight's Dungeon: you have 1 or 2 knights and need to move around all the squares of the custom board one and only one time.
The game offers a good amount of hours for the price.

Yes, Anno 2205 is not like the other previous parts, especially not like those taking place in the past. As a former Anno-Player, you may used to build and manage your city/town in one sector, supply it with ressources, goods and services in order to make your people happy, therefore wealthy and finally increase your income. The new twist in Anno 2205 is, you still do the same (sort of) but on a larger scale. You act more like a CEO of a large international (spoiler: interstellar) company, managing many cities in different sectors. You do not set up routes to transfer goods from one isle to another, this is done automatically within a sector. BUT, you still do it from one sector to another. You don't care anymore wether there are 100 Units Fish in your storage or 150 (you still do, but not in the first place), you just care "Is there more fish-production than fish-consumption?". And this is exactly what Anno now tells you, it shows you now in a new windows the production-consumption-balance of each product. Basically what you may have done in all other Anno-Games: You calculated in the background (on a piece of paper, in an excel-sheet, using a calc-tool) how many fishing-facilities do I need to feed 500 people? Then you build that much facilities and watch the amount of fish in your storage going up. Fine. In Anno 2205 each factory tells you directly in your face "Dude, I need 4 Units/min of Ressource X and I'll give you 2 Units/min of product Y".
So you can decice that you e.g. need two factories, therefore 8 Units/min of Ressource X, which can be covered by the 10 Units/min output of that mining industry in the arctic sector.
And this is how you gonna spend many hours of finding balance of each ressource, product, energy and work-capacity (= Humans), slowly steadyly growing your company, facing some random challenges while trying to populate and dominate each and every sector, outperforming the "Big-Five" (= 5 AI opponents) either in production or economics and ultimately... well, I don't know the ultimate goal of Anno. Choose yourself, there is a lot to do.
Oh, and yes, the fighting system changed. As for me, I used to beat the previous Anno-Enemys barely by fighting, so a change in the fighting system does not really matter for me. Instead of building and financing a huge armada of battle-ships, establishing escorting routes to fight back pirates and stuff, now you got a (one!) fleet of several ship-types. You need to care for them, upgrade and repair, as it becomes pretty expensive to replace a single ship once destroyed. Also, since there are no other (permanent) hostile players in your sector, you have to send your fleet to remote sectors to fight mission- or project-relevant battles. Imagine Warhammer 40k:DoW 2 ... with ships...
Some other reviews say, there is no sense in playing Anno 2205 a second time once finished. Partially true. The locations for every harbours are fixed, no big chance of "re-designing" your city in the second round. Same for each mining site and coast-based factories, all map-designs are fixed (not auto-generated). You cannot choose the AI-players, cannot choose the villains. And of course, all missions and projects will be the same. But still... For example, in case you play Factorio you know that starting a new factory still has something satisfying even though you already know whats coming next. Optimizing here, finding better solutions there. Maybe Anno 2205 will not provide the same satisfaction as Factorio the second time, but it's possible that you may find something new.

Creeper World 3 is one of those funny little games that don't quite fit any established genre.
It's broadly speaking an RTS, but it doesn't really play like any other RTS on the market. It also has some tower defense elements to it, but again, it's quite different from any "true" tower defense game.
Like a TD, it's a game about fighting a relentless enemy that keeps coming at you along predictable paths.
Like a regular RTS, you build structures to harvest resources, and your towers can move around (this is
important on many levels) once they're built.
Your enemy is a liquid with no ability to react to your activities. It simply spreads from emitters and flows downhill, forming pools that eventually overflow and flood the map. There's no enemy AI worth mentioning. And it's still surprisingly challenging, because there's a
of the stuff, and your resources can be quite limited. You'll have to make careful decisions about where to build something and
because running out of power at the wrong time can cause your entire line of defense to collapse in a real hurry.
It's a very simple concept, with only a few types of unit, a very straightforward upgrade system and extremely barebones presentation...and it adds up to a highly addictive game with surprising depth once you get into the tougher maps.
All in all, I can definitely recommend this.

The biggest complaint people had with the first game was that it was simply too difficult.
The original game had nine sprawling levels, each capped off with a challenging boss. This one breaks each level into small segments, and in between your life count gets refilled to 20. In the original if you started a level with 4 or less lives you'd just intentionally die to reset your life counter.
Cameos in this game aren't worked in as playable characers/items. Instead they're enemies and stage props. A couple characters and even famously bad games excluded from the previous game make their debut here. It's great that they included content the first game missed.
However, the game feels a little bit too reserved. The unfair, pixel-perfect difficulty from the first game demanded a nearly surgical precision. In this game there isn't much challenge, even in finding the K O N G letters in each level. There's no suspense and nearly zero tension. Nowhere is that more apparent than the final boss I killed in one attempt. How many times did you die to Fred Fuchs in the prequel? There's no comparison.
This game bears a lot of simlarities to the first. Pixelated gore, over the top explosions, homages to bad games, the humorous ire of a protagonist who hates his own game. Even so, this game left a much smaller impact. I left the first game feeling accomplished. This one just made me feel hollow in comparison.

Isometric dungeon crawler meets Die by the Sword with GTAV style physics based locomotion.
- Game looks modern and runs well.
- Euphoria-like animation engine allows for natural character movements.
- Darkness in dungeons is pitch black and the torches show off the game's lighting.
- Custom male/female PC with variable height, weight/build, skin tone, hairstyle, and voice.
- Tense and tactical combat.
- Very high learning curve for combat...expect to practice for hours. Some may interpret this as a "Pro".
- Lack of or too subtle enemy feedback upon taking damage from blunt weapons makes early encounters frustrating.
This appears to be an interim game to help build up some interest and funding for Bare Mettle's main game, a full RPG experience (using the combat from Exanima) so if you want to support the developer, this is the best way. If you're looking for a complete game, as with most "early access" titles, it probably won't be that for some time. If you don't mind trying something new in a sea of clones and me-too games and are predisposed towards fantasy settings, exploration, rogue-likes, and difficult titles such as the Dark Souls series of games, you should strongly consider picking this one up.
After putting another three hours into the game, mostly in Arena mode (1v1 combat vs progressively more challenging AI characters), I've decided to update the review for a bit more clarity and to reword some lines. I removed "Diablo" as a descriptor and replaced it with "Isometric dungeon crawler" as the game, aside from the perspective, bears almost no resemblance, in terms of gameplay, to Diablo at all. Also added a bit more to the "Is It For You" section.
(Review based on eight hours of Early Access version 0.6 gameplay.)

Exanima (Prelude to the game ''Sui Generis'') is a 3D isometric low fantasy RPG that propels you into a physic based combat system. The game is developped by a small indie studio called ''Bare Mettle Entertainment''. Surprisingly, for an early access game, Exanima shows great polish and a certain love for well crafted details. If you like realism in a game's world, this title will surely provide what you need. Though... let's make things clear.
This game ain't for the average gamer and even though you're a RPG veteran, Exanima will challenge you and most likely punish you
. The learning curve (which is not a small one) lies in the controls, especially in the combat. Your regular ''Strenght'' - ''Agility'' - ''Constitution'' (...) stats aren't to be found in this game. It's all about your skills with the mouse and keys and the amount of practice you've got, like the devs said in their Kickstarter video ''It's a case of easy to learn but difficult to master''. Be ready to dedicate a couple hours just in understanding the mechanics. Also, If you don't like dying often, this game is not for you, it's hard... very hard. Don't get me wrong, this playstyle is quite refreshing, it's something new, done well. Once you get a grasp of how it works, every battle becomes personal and winning them is satisfying and rewarding. I highly recommend that you get some experience in the arena mode (at least beat the novice one) before jumping in the adventure. As for character advancement, there isn't any level system but there's global experience bar that allows the player to learn different perks (Moving faster with heavy armor, rapid hit after a parry, better parrying...). The good thing is that these remains even after the death of your character.
If you like a low fantasy, dark and gloomy medieval atmosphere, you'll certainly enjoy Exanima. In this underworld dungeon, the immersion is complete and as you advance and get experience you'll slowly feel less like a lowly peasant and more like a courageous (or insane) knight. You can see that the devs understand the importance of details. The environment is believable and never breaks your immersion and the physics (applied to every object) helps to that a lot. Lights and shadows are superb and an important part of the gameplay. Also you have a ton of medival style gear to chose from that you can loot from various chests (This loot is, btw, randomly generated, hell yeah). You will always be on edge, not knowin' what lurks beyond this or that door. It's a game that will have your heart pumping abnormally fast and often, too often. There's also a backstory and lore that you can read by finding random scrolls and books in the dungeon, it's nothing too original but enough to keep you interested. Of course right now there isn't too much content, you can only explore 4 levels of the underworld but let's remind everyone that we're talking about an early access and according to their website, the devs are planning on adding more content.
It's a great game and I do recommend it, but no game's perfect... There's really three major complaints that I have with Exanima. First of all, this game is a tad too punishing for your average gamer. I mean aside for the ''Early Checkpoints'' that you can activate through the option menu, there really isn't any save system. That means, if you die... well you die. You have to either start over or reload to your nearest checkpoint (which is usually at every new dungeon level). So the repetition can get on your nerves pretty fast. I understand that the devs did this on purpose and that the game is also meant to be a ''Survival'' one, but giving the players the option to chose would, in my humble opinion, be the best. I mean, give me that little box in the option menu ''Hardcore'' ON or OFF. That way you don't step on anyone's fun, not the hardcore gamers nor the average ones. The second deal is with the physics engine which sometimes goes ''nuts'', of course this is an early access game that is still in development, and of course all physics engines have their problems. The deal is that in a game that is as punishing as Exanima, dying because your character (Holds Breath) Exploded, disapeared through the floor, got stuck in a door, table, chair, chest, corpse... Well that's quite frustrating (especially with no option to save whenever you like). My last complaint is with the very small variety of enemies you'll find during your playthrough (Yes I know it's an early access, I said it before). It's just that I would like to see different stuff for an already 4 level dungeon, maybe undead knights in full plates, wild or zombie animals, spirits... I don't know, just more variety, doesn't matter what it is. Of course all of this isn't that bad, not enough to spoil my fun in any case, but these are definitely issues that could be attended.
Even with it's flaws, Exanima still is a great, unique game that shows a lot of potential. The combat is fun, the atmosphere is there, the loot is amazing and there's already plenty of hours to spend on this early access title. In it's current state, I would recommend it mainly to ''Hardcore'' gamers who don't mind a big learning curve, repetition, punishment and numerous bloody deaths.

New Broken Sword is good game, all adventure fans will enjoy it for sure (and it doesn't matter if this is your first or fifth game of the series). Characters are really fleshed out and every one of them has memorable personality unlike many other games. I also liked how dialogue listening payed off because conversations gets you clues about how to solve puzzles. And really clever humor was in there - I found myself laughing many times. Story is good so far - what starts as simple museum murder slowly becomes mystery which later turns into dangerous religious conspiracy and I bet you will enjoy the ride.. which ends in half indeed but with proper and rather satisfying closure - and you shouldn't be disappointed.
Technically, there are still some bugs that needs to get patch soon, like occasional missing lipsync or 1080p assets but while some little polish is still needed this is really nothing game breaking. Graphics are top notch, mainly some hand-drawn backgrounds and cell-shaded characters are done pretty well at least. First I was afraid that it ruins the atmosphere but I got used to it rather quickly. You can also switch to old-fashioned subtitles instead of comics bubbles and turn off hint-system (which is something I really recommend as the game isn't too hard and every puzzle can be solved rather logically).
In the end I have to say the folks at RevSoft managed to bring Broken Sword back to its glory and now I really can't wait for their next game.

All in all a great adventure game and a must have for adventure fans. Can't wait for the second part.

Gigachess was developed and published by Gigatross Games. The game itself is interesting because it takes the rules of chess and makes it into a game of it's own, which it being both challenging and fun to play.
This game is rather clever, with the way that it takes the game of chess and twists it in a way that makes it both fun yet challenging to play. The basics of the game are that your chess pieces can be either a Bishop, Rook or a knight. Your enemies are a number of pawns which you must take out before they reach the end of the chess board and take a life from you. That's basically the whole game.
Although it doesn't seem that much, this game only has to two different types of gameplay. This doesn't mean to  say that the game is limited to it's gameplay value, that would be an understatement to say the least. These two modes that are in the game are Endless and Puzzle mode, puzzle mode creates a scenario and you have to try to take out the pawns before they get to the end. Endless mode, you are able to choose 4 pieces and try to defeat as many pawns as you can before you run out of lives.
In endless mode you can choose 4 pieces and your objective is to take out as many pawns as you can before they reach the end and take all of your lives away. The game makes you think about where you would move and how that would affect the gameplay altogether, much like a game of chess. You will be presented wave after wave with a number of pawns that you must take out in order to succeed. The pawns are laid out differently each time, usually only on the first two rows in order to try to take some of your pieces.
With endless mode, you are given the choice of four different types of difficulties depending on how advanced you are with the game, Novice, Medium, Expert and Master. Novice runs at a slow rate, you are able to take out the pawns easily and have a move or two to get your pieces set up. Medium is a bit more of a faster pace, making you have to think more and spawning the next wave more quickly. Expert seems to be the same pace as Medium, but they add a new type of pawn that flashes and jumps two spaces forward each turn, as for Master, every turn a new wave spawns. A bit of overkill on the difficulty if you ask me.
The game also includes power ups that you can use by collecting enough SP by killing the amount of pawns with the amount of pieces you have in a single turn. These power ups give you the ability to block the pawns for a few turns, makes one of your chess pieces move in the sense that it was a queen for a turn and a mine that you get to place down and blow up a pawn. So overall there is a nice variety of powerups that you can use to help you play through endless mode.
Puzzle mode is what you would expect it to be. You are given a set of pieces and have to try to take out the pawns before they get to the other side. This time you are only given a single life, so each move is crucial in order to succeed. There are around 48 puzzles for you to complete. But they only unlock 8 at a time after you have completed the previous 8 puzzles. For me this can sometimes limit the way that I play the puzzle mode, as I get discouraged by playing a single level over and over and fail too many times.
There is always a best way of being able to complete the puzzles in a certain number of moves. So you might get a puzzle and it reads par 6, meaning that this puzzle can be done in 6 moves at the best. But you can do the puzzle in more moves than that, you just won't obtain a star on that level to say that you have completed it in the shortest amount of moves.
The music to this game is really fitting to the sort of game that it is. You may find that the song gets repetitive, in which case there are 2 others that you can choose from or you can just turn it off completely if you so wish to. For me these 3 music tracks were decent enough for me to keep switching between them to keep me in the mood for this game.
The graphics of the game seem to fit the chess sort of feel to the game, being sort of older looking to the game. This makes the game look more appealing to me because of the consideration of the chess board and pieces looking less like you would expect modern ones to look like.
+ Challenging yet fun gameplay
+ 2 different modes
+ 4 different difficulties on Endless Mode
+ Nice power ups
+ Lots of puzzle levels
+ Nice music
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards
- Master difficulty on Endless is overkill
- Sometimes puzzle levels can be a bit of a drag
Gigachess is a fun yet challenging game, it balances these two elements well for the player to enjoy the game and not too challenging either. The two game modes seem to limit the game, but really there is a lot of replay value for the game, the music and graphics are both great and really suit the game.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

- features of the game didn't appear to work (couldn't establish trade routes, for example, despite following exactly what i was instructed to do).
- found it really easy to delete hours of progress with a couple of clicks trying to understand what to do next. I found no way to undo something whilst experimenting/exploring how the game worked.
More detailed comments
1.0 Reminded me of the game alchemy, where you have to combine two elements to try and make something new. However here, you're given the answers of what to combine (instead of having to figure that part out yourself), and each time you created something new, you're forced to sit and wait for five minutes before you can continue. A lot of the game play is repetative.. you need to produce some resource for you colony, to produce this resource you need "this building" to collect some raw materials, and then "this building" to turn the raw material into the resource.. and repeat.
2.0 Lack of tutorials/proper guidance.
To start with, upgrading buildings. This is possible in the game, but not straight from the start, and i dont think i was ever told when upgrades became possible. So, in my first game, I had a real problem with space, and there simply weren't enough special oceon and mountain slots to produce nearly enough of what i needed. Being able to upgrade obviously fixes this, which i stumbled upon, but it would have been nice to have been told when this became an option. Obviously I was expecting this to be a feature, but when I first looked at all the buildings, doing upgrades didn't appear to be an option.
3.0 On many occassion I managed to reach points where i was completely stuck due to a poor credit production
I feel this was through no real fault of my own, just lack of understanding and screwing my economy over by experimenting. The game warns you abut this problem, and there were times where i thought i understood how this worked so that I wouldnt end up massively in the red. One memory of my experience, which I can't ever forgive the game designers for, was when I reached a point (after hours of painfully slow progress recovering my economy in the arctic). I'd definitely maxed out all my avliable oceon construction site. There were no more avliable, and i needed many more to progress. I thought that maybe the game wanted me to delete some i was no longer reliant on. and replace them to mine new resources. So i deleted all my fisheries. I then deleted any buildings that needed fish, and then deleted some work force that wanted to eat fish that was no longer being produced. I then had 1 avliable oceon site to generate some resources for the greedy scientists. Within about 20 seconds my economy plumeted, my work force had been deleted, and i was unable to undo this. Estimated it would have probably taken me an hour to get back to a state i was in before. In my eyes, this is unforgivable and a bit dumb. A game should not result in an experience like this, especially when the player is experimenting themselves how the game works.
I guess i'll never underastand if i should have been able to explore different islands on each world and to be able to build more mining, or ocean sites, as i wont be playing this again.
4.0 My thoughts on side missions
There appeared to be many side missions, which should let you kill time if you ever need to wait for credits to build up and gives you some nice achievements on the side. The ones i did were very samey, and pretty uninteresting. There were also ones I couldn't do because I simply had no idea what i was expected to do. There was some guy who asked you to do something, but all theyd ever do was give you the same witty quip when I clicked on him. I assume this was meant to act as a hint, but it was a pretty useless to help understand, especially as the initial mission explanation was only a sentence.
examples of missions that came with no guidence and were therefore not possible at the point in which they were introduced:
"use some iridium to upgrade a building instead of the normal resorce." < dont even know how you would even do this.
"help me break through this ice by exploring it" < what are you on about you crazy admiral, are you drunk, what are you talking about.
5.0 Expansions
I assume i've not been playing any of the content from them.

Two things ahead: This ain't Anno, and it requires UPlay. Apart from that it's actually really neat.
This game plays more like a SciFi version of Ceasar. You get a sector and build your city without much interference from other people on the map. The game does however include many functions of the later Anno games, like expandable production and chains, albeit them being simpler than in earlier games. Or not, since as the games goes on you get additional sectors with their own intermediate and end product, which you need to ship around, turning the game into a mix of city building and the old school german economy from the early 90s.
Storywise the game is a bit more expansive than the previous games by framing your expansion into a program to settle the moon. Again. Because the first wave of settlers ♥♥♥♥ed up, and some of them even want to you dead.
That's also where all the military conflict in the game comes from. But unlike the previous games where you could build a bigish, freeform fleet, here you've only got a fixed number of ships and you're limited to special fighting sectors. One of the DLCs added invasions into your settled sectors, but you should really switch this off (you can do this at the start of the game, with advanced difficulty settings), since while the invaders don't destroy anything, they hinder your trade routes in and out from the sector, and they happen so often that they're quite a nuissance.
Additionally to the framing device, each sector has a sector project, which gives you number of tasks to create some deco or some kind of special material generator. The text blurbs for this tasks is also where the games tries to connect to previous game (Anno 2070), building a resemblance of continuity.
As for the replay value, there is probably none. No multiplayer, no random maps. But I needed at least three tries to actually get to a point where I could perceivable reach the end of content, so it might entertain you just as long (yes, the game takes forever for some stuff, just like the predecessor).
TL;DR: It's a nice game, if you're willing to forego any kind of Anno purism, or if you like german style eco sims with avoidable conflict.

Definitely, a game worth buying.
So what is this game about? It's a crazy mixture of RPG, Thirst Person Shooter and Tower Defence. Normally I dislike videogames like TF2 because they have kind of grotesque cartoonish graphics, yet This game managed to make graphics somewhat eye-appealing despite said cartoonish style.
So yes, back on a track: In this game your task is to kill orcs, who are swarming dwarven mines. You should prevent them from reaching certain place. There are various things that can help you in your task. For instance, you can install different traps, purchase and upgrade your character's armor and weapons (although, the amount and variety of weapons and wearable items isn't too wide, I must admit).
What I really love about this game is that it has pretty decent tactical aspect and if trap A is great at narrow tunnels, then it'll be entirely useless on wide plain places. You can purchase and upgrade traps, making them do more damage and reload quicker. Each trap has two bonuses, bringing even further tactical aspect (what's better? make orc die of bleeding, or stun him and let other traps finish him off? The choice is always yours).
You can also hire AI guardians who will help you at clearing places from orkish threat. Guardians can also be upgraded, just as any item and trap in game. Although, I can't say I play with AI a lot.
One last thing I would like to speak about is level design and layout: long story short - it's awesome. Orcs can attack from various directions, switch lanes, and leave through several exits, which sometimes makes you sweat. Quite often levels are equipped with some extra stuff which can help you in battle. For instance railroads with trolleys can run over orcs. You can even switch the lanes and trolleys would go different direction hitting different orcs.
So yeah, I'd definitely recommend this game to people who enjoy tactical games!

Love this game.  I've been playing Creeper World since the original, and have been hooked all along.  Definitely worth the buy.

Creeper World combines strategy, resource management, and meditation.
Ok, technically you can just crank up the speed to remove some of the meditative aspects, but usually on those levels I'm too busy micromanaging my energy flow moment by moment to do that.
If you've played the other Creeper World titles you'll already be familiar with the franchise approach - the enemy is simply evil water, and you're equipped with a variety of anti-water weaponry that costs energy to use, while you seek to reach and destroy the faucets that spawn your dire nemesis.
With a reasonable single player campaign and a huge quantity of additional levels, there's plenty to keep you busy.  Level quality can vary a great deal, with some really clever ones, and some that are truly just boring, with little to warn you which will be which.
Even so, if you enjoy this sort of challenge, you'll find you have a lot of quiet moments of personal accomplishment where you puzzle out some elaborate resource management or timing issue.  The game has a lot of depth, and even once you've polished off the campaign, there is loads more playtime to be had.
Overall, good stuff.  If you enjoy strategic puzzles and resource management then this is an easy buy.

So I just finished playing as Rogue. I bought on sale because I love old adventure games like Quest for Glory, King's Quest etc. I generally think this is a poor substitute, I would only recommend buying on a significant discount. I liked the 'infamy' aspect of the game.
1) The combat sucks. It is easy, sluggish and boring. Unlike in so many adventures games that require clever solutions, most of the story in this is advanced by beating a boss, but I killed them all on my first try with little effort.
2) The map is overly large and annoying to walk through, especially the dwarven mines.
3) Despite the fact it is years from original release, the game is still super buggy. The triggers for interacting with objects are not properly set to the image, and you end up just randomly clicking around a thing to get the right interaction triggered. Same issue entering/exiting scenes in the game. A few puzzles can be bypassed (e.g. jello cube thing).
4) The voice acting sucks, it is too loud and echoes, I played the whole game with it off.
5) You tend to accumulate a large number of items that you have no use for and clutter up your inventory. It would be nice to have a chest in your room. Even QFG had the sense to include that....
So buy it for cheap and play through if you like adventure games, but it isn't worth full price.

If you've ever played a city building game like Banished, you'll probably know what you're doing as soon as you get in. If not, that's okay too. It's pretty easy to learn what everything does.
Despite the graphics simplicity, the population actually does start to take a toll on your FPS. I started to get some issues with my FPS sometime after 300+ villagers. Hopefully, this gets a fix in the future because I would love to continue my game and expand out as much as possible. One temporary fix I found was saving, exitting, and reloading the game.
There is no actual "end game" to this really. You can keep building as much as your land and your machine lets you. It's more so whatever you make it to be. Personally, I decided that I've done enough in one save when I built all the structures, was capable of defending against 4 ogres and 8-10 Viking parties, and could no longer stand the 1-5 FPS.
If there's anything I'd like to see improved on or added, I guess I'd say difficulty scaling since there's really only 3 difficulty levels (i.e. No Threats, Easy, and Hard). There are also some mechanics I noticed were non-existant that could be beneficial in key structures like healing heroes, auto tax management, priority building, etc. Could also maybe use some extra variety in things like structures. Heck, even better if they added "theme packs." Would love to play as a different culture.
Overall, This game is more of a casual experience and as such, I'll recommend it because I did get my money's worth in playtime. It was pleasant to just sit back and watch my little city strive and grow during peacetime.

Based on  the german version with 5 hours played and around 30% completed.
UI:
Well, let's be honest the UI (Main Menu) isn't beautiful and looks like some alpha/beta version. The ingame UI is the standard backpack inventory which should be well known to every gamer that likes point and click adventure. Sadly there seems to be no option to open the menu with a mouse click/wheel action. So you have to move your mouse to the icon on the bottom left side of the screen.
When hovering over a usable object the UI will present you with the right (=only) action you can perform. In addition to that you can inspect every useable item to get a response from your active character.
Voiceover:
The german voice actors are really superb. George got his old voice actor and Nico got someone who almost sounds exactly the same as her usual voice actor. If I hadn't known beforehand that Nico got a new voice, I wouldn't have noticed it. The other characters got pretty good voice actors as well and those that made an appearance in a previous installment of the Broken Sword series seem to have their original voice actors as well.
Graphics:
The backgrounds are beautifully hand drawn and look amazing. Seeing those backgrounds with George and Nico really took me back to the old days. Sadly the animations aren't on par with the backgrounds. Don't get me wrong they aren't bad but compared to those backgrounds they just lose.
Currently the supported resolution of the game is only 1280x720. But they promised to deliver a 1080HD patch.
Puzzles:
The puzzles so far have been good (=fun) and till now I havn't encountered an illogical one. The puzzles range from dialogue puzzles to item combination puzzles to the likes of reconstructing a destroyed message. If you're an experienced adventure gamer you'll probably have no difficulties solving those. But I still had fun and enjoyed them.
Story:
A painting is stolen from a gallery and during that a man is killed. Nico and George happen to be there and are trying to solve the robbery/murder. While doing so they discover that the painting has a special history and that it wasn't just a regular robbery.  During that they meet some old friends and visit different countries.
Bugs:
Well I havn't ecountered a real bug till now but there are some things like e.g. really hard to spot items or a big item where the mouse courser has to be at a specific spot to make it useable (like a whole blank page)  which could frustrate you. Other than that I havn't encountered anything.
Conclusion:
I'm loving the game but I'll be honest here and tell you that I'm a fan of the "Broden Sword" series. So I might be a little biased here. Revolution Software delivers a good (definetly better than 3 (ugh) and 4 but not as good as 1 and 2) sequel to the Broken Sword series and every fan should get it asap if he hasn't already. Every other adventure game fan should ask himself if graphics (UI/Animation) is really (!!!!) important to him and if so he should maybe stay away from the game. All those that value gameplay and story more shouldn't wait and get this game. With that you'll support one of those developers who still make adventure games.
Warning: The second part will be released at a later date (January). If you buy the game now you'll get the second episode as soon as it becomes available. So you'll probably have to wait till then to experience the full story. On the bright side the game will be complete with the second episode and the wait isn't a long one.

For a mod of Half-Life, it isn't really that good. Which begs the question: why did this mod get greenlighted on Steam instead of better Half-Life mods? We will probably never know. Since this game is so terribly short, I'm going to some up the story on this one review. I'll try to figure out and explain it as best as I can.
You magically get teleported onto a boat by a lightning bolt (no, I am not kidding). After appearing on said boat, you find out that most of the crew of the boat are dead or tuned into Zombies, with other different creatures blocking your way. After killing them and getting through some weird and confusing level design, you find a man on top of the boat that's "guarded" by some sort of soldiers, who instantly attack you (why? I still don't know. As for the man, we'll just call him Bob). After "rescuing" Bob, he tells you that they (whoever "they" is) have made a "very smart genetic modified creature". He gives you a medkit and activates the cargo lift at the front of the boat that has the creature inside. You leave him and go back to destroy it. But you also have to get through one of the more stronger enemies from Half-Life, which is still pretty easy since it gives you almost all of the weapons from that game. After plowing through them, you jump into the cargo lift which triggers an unskippable cutscene (which is gonna be very repetitive since everytime you die from the boss, you have to sit through this cutscene over and over again). The cutscene shows the "very smart genetic modified creature" eating some sort of yellow crystal. The yellow crystal might have been the artifact that Bob was talking about while you were talking to him. But why does the creature eat the artifact? I STILL DON'T ♥♥♥♥ING KNOW! After the cutscene, you are greeted with both the first and final boss of this game, the creature. The boss is... interesting. It's the same final boss of the original Half-Life only smaller, has an instakill attack, and spawns Snarks. I found a glitch where the boss kept going through the walls and didn't attack me at all. Anyway, he is kinda easy to take down aside from the instakill attack. After killing him, you are greeted with the credits. And that's it.
I got this game because I was curious, and it was for free. If you wanna try it out, then go ahead. However, if you don't wanna waste your time, then just don't bother.

Ok so this game isn't finished, and to be considered finished it needs a lot of work.
game play is like final fantasy tactics
only 3 classes,
Cabberjack (melee)
hunter(ranged)
alchemist (hybrid, glass cannons)
At first glance I feel like there should be more classes, like maybe 2 more, a healer and a assassin.
However if you play long enough you find that in place of a generic "healer class" any one can be a healer, but it's a little hard to figure out.
It's little things like this that make the game interesting, but it runs into problems. For instance to be a healer you have to research this health potion, that you can equip on anyone. (you only get 1 health potion per character if they have it equipped, and it heals for 10 hp). But you are limited to only one item per character, this wouldn't be a problem if your characters could hit anything for their lives.
So you have to get the item that makes their accuracy higher (by 15%) even with this I found my guys still missing point blank shots, or missing against inanimate objects. More often than not I had scenarios where my guys didn't hit a single thing, and everyone just died. I mean come on! their warriors, dedicating their lives to protect a kingdom and they couldn't hit the broad side of a barn.
Also the mechanics of their hit rates seemed all over the place, Sometimes I found  at the furthest distance you can be from an enemy you get a better hit percentage, but sometimes that idea went right out the window. Also there is no indicator of how far a move can go before you move your character. leaving me with guys one space shy of being able to hit something a lot of the time. (attack ranges of at least your characters needs to be displayed) many games like final fantasy tactics, or Disgea execute this much better.
Some voice acting issues
some of the banter between your 2 chalice deities or w/e seems like it was cut short, and some cut scenes show a glowing light when ever they talk, but they stop talking and the light keeps flickering, and it feels like you missed the end of a conversation half the time.
illusion of freedom
you are given a lot of choices to upgrade your kingdom, but I found myself not making it past the 4th or 5th battles If I didn't stick to a precise set of upgrades. Enemies get a lot harder each time you have a battle.
There is a nice pull and push in fighting back oncoming enemies. You are attacked by 2 groups, one you can kill, the other takes 1/3 of the tile. So you have an important decision on what you need to defend. However some tiles ie. the most outer ones (going to be attacked 1st every time) have perks to them. like makes research faster, or lvls up your guys faster. having them only on the outer edge of the map seems stupid. there should be a perk per tile. You're going to loose tiles no matter what and it feels like a whole one step forward 2 steps back process.
Leveling up your heroes:
This is a hard mechanic to get your 1st play through, and you won't rly know how to do it efficiently until like your 2nd-4th play through.
You heroes die of old age pretty fast, so instead of lvling them up you really need to pass down (items/relics) that get better with every generation. Also parents pass down traits, some good some bad. So don't get attached to anyone, get attached to bloodlines. This is a cool mechanic too, buuuuuuuuuut to do this you need higher lvl heroes to become rulers of their keeps (bloodline homes) and it's rly hard to start a bloodline when all you ever have are clumsy dorks who usually have crappy stats to begin with because they are lvl 1, and you can't really get anyone better because they have to die off, and by that time you may or may not have already lost the game.
level design:
some levels have really cool mechanics, like moving obstetrical that can be pushed or destroyed by enemies and this lets you block off areas, obstruct enemy vision ,and is a pretty cool mechanic, buuuuuuuuuuuuuut( sigh) it's only in 2 levels. The one with the egg shaped blocks that can move around, and the other level with geysers.
visuals:
AWESOME! Doublefine is great at making games with their own character, and this game is no exception. I just wish the game was not so frustratingly, and sometimes, impossibly difficult.
This game has a long way to go if it's going to be good, and I want it to be good, that's why I got it.To support them, there was a kick starter and stuff, but they still need a help.     :(

Note: This is my first game from this developer. I've become aware of a small scandal brewing about this developer's past games, but this review is written with ONLY THIS PARTICULAR GAME in mind. I have no idea what happened with the developer's previous games, and thus that is not the concern of this review.
In the time I've spent with this, I've really enjoyed it. It has all the features it claims to in about the way you'd expect them, so if the description looks interesting, you'll probably enjoy it. The game has a fairly simple core mechanic: survive until x year. However, the facets that go into maximizing your chances for survival are many and are quite novel. I really enjoy pairing my strongest fighters and securing even stronger future generations.
The music in the game is lovely, and the voice acting is far better than I had anticipated (actually I hadn't anticipated ANY, but the voice acting is really very good). The visual style is a little... art over realism, as it were. But it serves the game well enough that I, as a huge fan of realistic graphics, found myself not caring at all that I wasn't looking at lush forests and TressFX hair. The controls might seem slightly limited at first, but I quickly found they did their job effectively.
All in all, this game is great fun and I encourage you to grab it if you're on the fence about it.

I can't say that the game is bad, rather that I expected more.  My greatest dissapointment comes from my expectations of the game being more akin to an Ogre Battle title with long term bloodlines.  What was delivered was a very blatant X-COM  clone changing the setting, and switching the time scale to years.  Becase of the small squad size, you would think you would get invested in the development of individual heroes. I found I tried to, but by the time I did, I had moved on to the next generation.  Fights only seem to happen every 4-8 years roughly,  heroes are viable from say ages 15-60, An active hero that you don't send to do another job might last 8 fights before dying of old age.
I only saw 3 types of heroes, if there are more they were either difficult or unclear on how to unlock them.  Caberjacks, Alchemists, and Hunters.
The game did not seem very well balanced between the classes.  Caberjacks are strong all around in offence and defense.
Hunters hit a bit weaker, and can't take a hit, but at least have ranged attacks.  they seemed a bit weaker than the cabers, but on facing the exploding enemies, I saw a clear reason for using them.
Alchemists have bombs, but they bombs tend to be embarrasingly inaccurate, short ranged, and mediocre in damage, not to mention limited in supply.  When they run out the have a mediocre melee attack, but no durablity to speak of.
Game dynamics seemed like a stripped down Xcom engine.  They have similar controls, but with less classes, and lack of cover mechanics (best I could tell anyway) I found myself thinking If I get in the mood for this kind of game, I'll just fire up X-Com again, and play the better game.
So in short, not a bad game, but an inferior X-Com clone.

I just finished my first run-through of the game, and I can honsetly say I enjoyed it immensely. A lot of people are jittery about DF having another early access game, but the situation has been made perfectly clear: MASSIVE CHALICE is COMPLETELY FUNDED for the next six months, which is the perfect amount of time to tweak this game to perfection. You may notice a few rough edges and for some people an intimidating learning curve, but the mechanics of this game are solid and have a surprising amount of depth. Like many tactical games, you might build yourself into a corner or find yourself on the wrong end of RNG, but when this game is humming, it's an amazing experience. I can't wait for DF to put the finishing touches on this game and I hope you guys enjoy!
Other Misc Facts:
-3 base classes currently, hybrid classes planned for future update (which ups the number of options significantly)
-Get your highest level characters to be regents: XP is passed on to children of the house. The higher the XP, the higher level your trainee heroes become.
-Relics spawn occaisionally when a hero dies. Usually happens when a hero kills a lot of cadence throughout their life. Get these early and keep them in the hands of the fighting members of the family. They level up and turn wimpy heroes into super men/women.
-Be smart about movement and sight. Scout ahead with Hunters (using their sneaking ability). Sometimes your sight range is greater than theirs and often it is greater than their movement/attack range. Find the enemy first and utilize crowd control abilities to slow down the enemy (Flarrow blinds enemies for a turn, Knockback can shove enemies into other enemies and can stun each one affected, Prime Target can draw strong opponents away from weak or stranded heroes)
Have Fun guys!

You're thrown into the game almost immediately, as you work towards the main level/teleporter hub. Hidden throughout the levels are keys that unlock other levels, which is your main progression. There is minor backtracking, but finding secrets feels very good.
Levels are actually fairly linear (eg, there's one core path, but several dead ends or branchbacks with powerups), but it's presented in such a way that you wouldn't ever notice this. There's lots of different weapons to use, and a sense of progression from weak ones to strong ones (assault rifle is basically a replacement for the pistol, automatic shotgun replaces the shotgun, etc.) and lots of fun endgame weapons to use, such as the Alien Weapon, Fusion Gun, and Chronoscepter. Levels also have really good pacing; you'll spend a good amount of ammo exploring and killing guys, then find a room that replenishes some/most of it. You never really feel starved for life and ammo, but you don't feel like its in abundance either.
Overall, probably 7.50/10. Not sure how much replay value it has, but it was fun for the time it took to 100% it.

This review contains minor spoilers and self opinions.
As one of the first FPS of its generation, Turok surprised us with big enemies, big guns, big levels, lots of secrets to find and nice graphics back in early 1997. Turok has shown that the FPS genre is not limited to the Quake formula, expanding its genre with big open levels, keys, lives and a HUB, for exemple.
Turok is a great shooter even for today's standards. The variety of weapons, levels and challenges sums up to make Turok a nice and intense experience. The graphics are simple and not much something to notice to, but Night Dive Studios remaster brings new graphics features which can make Turok an entirely new experience from before without lag, HD resolution and fluid animations. The controls are simple and work exactly the way you expect them to with gamepad support. If you don't like them you can change it anytime in the pause/input menu. The game is about 7-10 hours long with every secret found. The price is just about right too. If you liked the old 1997 Turok, buy and enjoy this great remastered version.
: Great remaster of the 1997 classic. If you enjoy fast-paced action, lots of guns and challenging levels, buy this.

Lifeless Planet, while it is a very short game, is a game that exemplifies the idea of the adventure being more about the journey than the destination. WHile I wouldn't necessarily recomend it at its current price, it is still a very good story for those fond of very outlandish oldschool sci-fi.
The only real complaint is the fact that it was blatantly not designed for Keyboard and Mouse primarily, in the fact that the camera will move based on the direction your character moves, always trying to face where they're moving. This isn't a massive issue, but it stands out nonetheless.
To avoid spoilers, there are segments in the game that require the usage of geysers to lift yourself upwards. They are very finnicky in how they want to work, and if they want to work. This can lead to about five to ten minutes woth of frustration, but I do not feel this ruins the overall experience.
Overall I would give the game an honest 7/10. Reasoning being that the game was very short, though I do understand that this was a kickstarter project, along with other small issues. Otherwise, this game is excellent for those wanting to be immersed in an interesting sci-fi world that gets more and more interesting as you progress, giving a very classic sci-fi vibe in the meantime.

If i'm honest, this game felt and played a lot like Portal 2. Between the mysticism of the woman and the wrecked terrain with a beautiful past, combined with the small collections of puzzles ( -which I *really* grew fond of) I really enjoyed just admiring the story that was presented to me.
The only thing I could nick at is that the wallpaper shown on a loading screen (the screen with the writing and mathematical equations) didnt really fit the story. "Three or Four crew?" really became redundant as after we'd met two of them and progressed far into the storyline.
Generally speaking, this is one of the best story-driven game i've played since Portal 2. I'm really happy with how it plays and functions as more of an experience than a game (which, contrary to some peoples opinion is OK!) and would love to see more games like this in the future.

A surprisingly satisfying experience, Creeper World 3 combines a compelling mystery-story about an enigmatic and impossibly powerful enemy with the satisfaction of a tower defense game that allows you to precisely nail that moment of satisfaction that comes when you just barely gain the upper hand, and turn the tables on an opponent that has had you against the ropes for most of the battle.......or at least that's what I experienced with my turtle-style gameplay; blocking off key points and slowly amassing an economic juggernaut that allows me to employ brute-force tactics and give the enemy a taste of his own medicine, so to speak. The story I found to be equally enjoyable, so much so that I found myself making sure to play through every planet of a given sector in a single session just so I could move on to the next and hear more of the narrative. It also included a worthwhile (if a bit predictable) twist at the end.

Yesterday I was taking a walk in the park, I sat down near a lake and pulled out a sandwich I had bought at a nearby deli. I was stricken by an overwhelming sense of serenity and appreciation. Over out at the lake there sat an island with a giant tree, who's branches had been made home to a number of birds nests. From the lake, I could catch sight of elderly men fishing, children playing with bread crumbs and ducks, a couple holding hands and taking a walk, a shirtless man on a jog, two women passing by on a bike. Every one of them wrapped up in their own world, but all the same, part of an ecological system that brought upon a feeling of peace, safety, and a certain pure beauty that made me aware of just how nice the cool breeze felt running across my skin from the hot summer heat, the underlying frailness of some waterside flowers that reflected beautifully on the lake's surface, and the pleasures of smell the fauna brought simply from its own life and death cycle.
None of that resonated in this lifeless game, it has absolutely no artistic merit, and the song sucked.
10/10, would put my wrinkly old woman butt on a bench again.

What draws me to these games is their originality (native americans fighting dinosaurs, aliens, cosmic horrors.) and the colourful and epic weapons. The levels are pretty big and fairly linear, so you won't find yourself getting too lost, the enemies have decent AI (they roll to the side to dodge bullets etc etc) and if you shoot them in the right way they clasp at their neck gasping for air before dying.
The platform sections can be a bit irritating, but, they had those back in the halcyon days of FPS games, so I can't grumble too much about it.
All in all, a must buy if you loved the originals. and for those who haven't played a Turok game, give it a whirl if you're sick of the same cookie cutter 'realistic' modern military shooters.

The main thing is that it's hard to grow attached to individual characters as they get rotated out pretty quickly; however the bloodlines seem to often breed a couple of traits 'true' for many generations, giving them a bit of a personality of their own.
Combat is fairly simple, but this isn't necessarily a bad thing; I found that I didn't really want to spend hours on a tactical map at a time, since so much of the activity happens strategically. The tactical combat is just enough to be interesting without being too time-consuming, maintaining a quicker pace than e.g. Medieval.

Massive Chalice (beta) is an interesting new spin on turn-based strategies. There are several levels of strategy you need to think about when playing.
You only control a small squad of 5 heroes when in combat, which means you need to use terrain and other tactics in order to survive. The death of a single hero in combat affects other areas of the game.
Everything surrounds a single goal: protect the massive talking (multi-personality I might add) chalice at the center of the map. The chalice is surrounded by regions which in turn are surrounded, from all directions, by the enemy which creeps ever closer. The big talky chalice promises it has a way to defeat the enemy but says "It takes time. A lot of time", so we have to defend it until then.
Placing keeps and guilds in each region takes time - I'm talking years. Fortunately the years move quite quickly. Unfortunately, the lives of your heroes span those years in real time, which means they get old and they eventually die of old age (unless killed in battle).
In order to maintain a line of heroes you have the option to make them regents (or regent partners). This stops the heroes from entering the battlefield and instead focus of making the next generation of heroes. You now need to find the right combination of heroes to produce offspring with attributes that can defeat the enemy more efficiently.
Overall I found the game to be semi-light hearted, enjoyable, and also a challenge. You're often attacked on multiple fronts which means you have to pick your battles. The character models could do with a little bit of 'prettifyling' I suppose, but hey, you're not pairing them together for their looks now are you? :)
If you're looking for a new turn-based challenge, have a look!

Already incredible.  I think it'd be easy to write this off as an interesting tech-demo, something cool, but ultimately too flakey and hilarious to be taken seriously.
- Think again - you'll start out looking like a drunken fool stumbling around, but put in a day or two learning and practicing, and it starts to click.  What you'll find is a game that is mechanically incredibly deep, where you can and will learn to shift your weight, anticipate and avoid attacks, follow through on a swing to clip someone in the back of the leg, lunge into someone to push them over a chair before smashing them with an overhead blow.  It quickly starts to feel very natural, and incredibly well balanced.
I know a little of dynamics simulation, and I'm truly astounded by what Bare Mettle have achieved here.  To make it functional would be impressive, to have made it feel natural is beyond my comprehension!
My only wish would be to have it a little more traditional RPG - with dialogue and varied locations, rather than what it appears to be at the moment - a pure labyrinth dungeon-crawl.  A stunningly beautiful one - the lighting and attention to detail is sublime, but exploring does start to get a touch repetitive.
(Edit: I just realised that Exanima is a "prelude" to Sui Generis, and that it looks like pretty outdoors locations shall be arriving eventually - whoop whoop!)
I'm not sure the combat could ever get repetitive though - so far I've battled nothing more than countless generic zombies, and yet each and every fight feels intense, unique, and absorbing.
Even at this stage, where there's very clearly only half a game here, I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone willing to put the time in to learn it.  Once it clicks, you won't be disappointed!
I very much look forward to seeing how the completed game ends up.

Ahh Exanima. This is an updated version of my previous review for this game. I'm going to try to be as objective as possible in this one.
Exanima is the ambitious project being developed by Bare Mettle Entertainment. It serves as a prelude and fully-functioning tech demo for Sui Generis - more on the tech demo part later. It was developed to give those who had backed the original project, Sui Generis, a chance to experience the combat first hand and then flourished to include what it has today. Everything that you see in Exanima is going to be pasted over to Sui Generis, and Sui Generis is going to have the full package. Think of Exanima as a very thorough demo that showcases everything that you can expect from Sui Generis.
Exanima has the most unique combat engine that I've encounted yet. Think Mount & Blade meets Physics class. You control your character's torso with your mouse cursor, and you attack with your left mouse button. The game uses a 360 degree isometric camera (top down, at an angle). The way your character moves is based on your cursor, not your camera. For example, no matter which way your camera is facing, 'A' - which is right - will always move your character to the right. This might be tricky at first, but actually allows for more advanced maneuvers such as circling your opponent. Again, it's a very tricky system, but after a while you get used to it and it fits like a glove.
Combat can become the major turn off in the game. At first, I was skeptical of this game's success. The combat seemed wonky and sluggish, and the AI seemed too good at making hits. But as I got better, and the developers improved animations and gameplay mechanics, the game became easier. I still die, but I can handle myself in combat better because I learned from my mistakes.
Quite honestly, this game is not for everyone. You have to accept dying, and have to think of your character's suffering as fun. It requires distancing from your character, and the only comparable experience is Dwarf Fortress. In other words: "losing is fun."
If story is your bag, look no further. Exanima has a "you're just walking into it" type story. You find scrolls and books laying around detailing the world that you stumbled into. A world of confusion, of labor, and of death. As the game is finished, more story content will be added. As of writing, Exanima has recieved a massive update including a new level, fixes, and armor.
The atmosphere in this game is top notch. The books, scrolls, objects, and locations make it feel alive, but now long abandoned. The many rooms feel as if they had a purpose. You'll find a cobbler workshop, blacksmith, sleeping quarters, bar, etc.
The graphics are amazing. The game in its current state is very well optimized; however, you have to worry about the processor. If it's not good enough, you will have issues such as slow-motion/fast-motion, causing a very unpleasant experience. If your processor isn't top notch, or you're experiencing problems, try running the game in high priority mode.
I have the game on the lowest setting and it looks really great and runs at a smooth 60fps on my not-so-good Laptop. If you want a game that not only looks good, but performs well, Exanima is your choice.
With many Early Access games, the devs seem distant. With Bare Mettle, they seem like they are personally involved in the game. Some may not agree with their "it's our game" approach, but I find that respectable, especially in today's market where many games get dumbed down for the average gamers due to the complaints of the majority. It shows that they are faithful enough to handle developing the game themselves, and don't really care what people think. Answer this: Did Pink Floyd ask their fans for help when writing their songs? Did Quentin Tarantino care if Pulp Fiction was too violent?
- Combat is extremely unforgiving. This is a massive turn off for those who want an easy experience.
- It's unfinished. The game is really short once you figure out the combat, and new areas will take time. There is a lack of unique loot and the skill system is mostly unfinished.
- Slow updates. As the game gets more complex, natually so will the updates. Luckily the devs keep in contact with their fans to a degree.
- REALLY HARD! If you plan to purchace this game, educate yourself before you buy it. It's a tough game and it really one of the draw backs.
- A complete gamble. Like most Early Access games, this game shows huge potential; despite my faith in the company, the game could flop on release.
- The controls are still wonky. The devs are putting their efforts into making it smoother, and they are better than they were. However, they are still wonky and that needs to be addressed.
- Story. Even though I said that there is a good story, it might not be the story most gamers are into. It's vague, much like Dark Souls, and it doesn't really relate to the character at all.
- Bugs. There are bugs in the game. Mainly they are visual and very rarely affect the gameplay.
- Reworking. There is a lot of stuff being reworked. Namely the blocking system. Nothing is really set in stone.
Overall this game gets a 9/10. Its orginal presentation and massive potential warrents award alone.
- Fixed minor gramatical errors and improved flow.
- Added bit about computer processors.

I didn't already review this game? o_O Well I'm gonna fix that now.  Gonna try to make this as comprehensive a review of AA as possible.
What it does: Gives you a virtual "holodeck-like" environment in which to build a 3D "desktop" to suit your whims. Using the HL2 engine, it allows you to upload or create any kind of map you desire, then populate it with "cabinets" which are really virtual links back to your PC to begin running--whatever you wish. Steam, Firefox, a game of choice, Internet Radio (Netflix no longer works though :( ), you name it! With VR, there are certainly other, "flashier" options for things such as a virtual movie theater or a virtual home. But for those of us that can't casually shell out $800 for a Rift or a Vive, this, IMO, is the much better option.
Personally, I haven't found anything that "needs work" in the app, other than my own personal dislike of having Netflix not work, though the developer has explained why this is so and I understand.
As a F2P game, you lose absolutely nothing bu downloading it, trying it out, and seeing for yourself whether you'd be interested in it or not. It's a niche game, to be sure, but for those of us that are in the niche, I'd say this is the killer app to have. The community's great--very helpful and has helped me out with the problems I've had, too!

9/10 [SPOILERS]
Despite the painfully slow start (in which i would've suggested adding more curious observations by our character about his crew or the 'alien planet' or possibly about his wife to engage the user), I was engaged into the campaign from the second we heard about the Green Fire and how it affected the soviets, then when we first saw the woman (whos name slips me) I was undoubtably hooked on following her and to find out who she is, or was.
The second I picked up this game, I played the campaign straight until I was finished. The story just became so addictive that I really couldnt put it down without finding out *all* the answers. If i'm honest, this game felt and played a lot like Portal 2. Between the mysticism of the woman and the wrecked terrain with a beautiful past, combined with the small collections of puzzles ( -which I *really* grew fond of) I really enjoyed just admiring the story that was presented to me.
The only thing I could nick at is that the wallpaper shown on a loading screen (the screen with the writing and mathematical equations) didnt really fit the story. "Three or Four crew?" really became redundant as after we'd met two of them and progressed far into the storyline.
Generally speaking, this is one of the best story-driven game i've played since Portal 2. I'm really happy with how it plays and functions as more of an experience than a game (which, contrary to some peoples opinion is OK!) and would love to see more games like this in the future.
(Thanks for bringing my attention to this game, KurtJMac and YogscastSips!!)
