Oh boy...
Really wanted this to be really good, and in some cases it still maintains the anno series. However its nowhere near as good as 2070 and in some cases its taken a step back, almost feels like a mobile game in some parts of the game (ill touch up on this later).
For the core game as a city builder in the anno series. It's there, you can still build massive cities and have to manage your resources, and for this. It's done well. One thing I saw and didn't like at first is the game tells you how much your production buildings made and updated depending on what resources we're being used and created. I didn't like that at first, however I grew to like it because I could see what was holding back 100% production and instead of guessing what I needed I could see what resources we're limited and increase production for them resources. I also liked having limited resources in different regions as it would make sense since the world resources are almost gone.
Now you’re wondering why I feel at parts it was like a mobile game, and that was from the parts of the game where you had to do missions where you have to do combat, oh fun. 2070 combat felt limiting as you can only fight certain parts of the island and cant bombard the owner into submission forcing them to give up the island (unless you make nuclear weapons) however. This was just select your ships, collect abilities, use abilities and defeat enemies. Do side quests in combat, and that’s it. It almost plays itself. It felt boring to me. I just wanted to go back to building my city but then the story will be like, someone needs help at this region and you have to help them to progress through the story and I’m sat here thinking "but I just wanna build a city." I haven't been much of a fan of the combat of these types of games, but please don't make them so boring where it could literally play by itself if it had auto targeting or an auto play button.
The story, without spoiling it was meh. Understandable if you leave humans on the moon they will not be too happy and eventually turn hostile if given a influential person. It was kind of boring and didn’t have much to do with the main game, you progress up and eventually get to settle on the moon (Love the visuals).
However it didn't have much tie in with 2070 which I was really looking forward to, other than one of the region missions having you uncover an arc, and a few mentions here and there. Nothing, no mention of F.A.T.H.E.R and his Crazed A.I Rampage and all that, nothing to do with S.A.A.T Advancements.
I feel this was a missed opportunity.
The multiplayer isn’t there, well... Kind of. It’s a market where you can sell goods to increase or decrease the demand and price of items to make things cheaper or more expensive and players can trade for these goods on this market, but other than that. That’s all there is for multiplayer. No one can join your game and look or interact with your region, you can’t fight over these regions because every time you play, it’s the same three regions you get to choose from. It’s almost non-existent.
I could recommend this game if you didn’t have to be forced into the combat, like make it optional and some of them are optional, (once you reach towards the end of the "story,") and the city building part is okay, however if you just want to do the city building part of the anno series just stick to one of the older ones like 2070 or 1404. I still recommend it however if you can get past some of the problems.

The game thrusts you into the Lost Land, a place I can only describe as the garbage dump of time and space. Pretty much anything can get sucked into this land, and you were no different. As Turok, your duty is to assemble together the pieces of the Chronoscepter and put an end to the Campaigner's tyrannical reign.
The problem? None of this is explained to you in-game. You're left with an opening cutscene that tells you to locate keys to open up level portals in the Hub. The lack of any proper introduction makes you think there would at least be 'something' that builds the plot up as you go along your journey; however, without spoiling anything, the game's ending has a similar feeling of short-sightedness to it that will still leave you completely dumbfounded the same way the introduction did.
It was jarring in 1997, and it still is now.
Night Dive Studios has put such an untold amount of work into fixing the original game's flaws while still keeping true to the source content, even with its minor changes made to level design.
One example of this is that you can now choose between four difficulty modes in this game: Easy, Normal, Hard, and Hardcore. Veteran players will find an added emphasis on survival with conserving weapon ammo and dodging enemy fire on later difficulties that was not present in the original game.
Unfortunately, the pathing for enemies seems to be messed up in this remaster. Simply put, enemies nowhere near your vicinity will detect you and start running towards a wall. While it didn't affect me too much on Normal, it becomes far worse on later difficulties when mixed with the relentless respawn timer and increased enemy speed.
has never looked better, but that's not saying much. While this version of the game boasts the smoothest Turok experience to date, running at 60 FPS in 1080p, it still looks like a prototype of
.
The textures are muddied and lack variety, especially in the game’s early stages, but if you're used to games from the Nintendo 64 era, it shouldn't get in the way of your enjoyment of the game. Much appreciated changes were made to saturation, the addition of bloom, god rays, anti-aliasing, and water reflections, as well as an extended draw distance. All of these changes help make the environments in this game pop and stand-out from each other, though I wish shadows and other dynamic lighting effects were added into the game.
While the Nintendo 64 soundtrack still does this game justice, the sound effects need a lot of work for creatures like Raptors and Leapers, traps, and enemy footsteps. These inconsistent sound effects, which I don't remember being nearly as present in the original game, are so bad at times that they can cause audible pops in feedback for your speakers or headset, no matter the volume settings of the game.
Luckily, the addition of ambient environmental sounds adds a new level of atmosphere and does so without feeling out-of-place.
Fortunately, Turok fans will feel right at home playing the game on Steam as the remastered version of
achieves a great balance between platforming action, puzzle-solving elements, and shooter-based mechanics to make an experience that feels unlike anything else on the market even today. While it still has its fair share of issues that can be ironed out by Night Dive Studios, this is by far the most definitive version of
out there.

Figured I should probably update this review now, since some major things have been addressed and I no longer need a wall of text.
Put simply... now the game is great. Especially for an early-access title. It's the most unique sword themed fighter you will ever come across, and I'm tempted to say one of the most realistic as well. The physics driven animations and combat makes everything fluid and tense in a way no other game has done.
And the physics are really, really solid. A sword smacking into a solid steel breastplate doesn't feel like you're hitting something with higher stats, it actually feels like a shard blade clanging into solid metal. Likewise, you can feel the jar of a weapon smacking into a helmet, and you'll wince when something sharp connects with flesh.
And when you land that finishing blow... so satisfying.
Of course that doesn't come without a learning curve. And it has one, believe me. Much of the learning comes from the fact you play it so differently from other games. Both in controls, but also in concepts. In many games, it comes down to "is this character attacking" and "is this character defending", or "is the character blocking right" etc. There are no definite states which makes combat in this game so dynamic and tense.
Your character's fighting style will reflect your learning. You'll start off appearing drunk and flinging wildly, and as you improve your character will reflect that in a deadly dance of blades.
My biggest issue with the game previously was the campaign, and the relative lack of ways to play the game beyond that. That's no longer an issue, since a full arena campaign style mode has been added which adds limitless replayability for those of us, like me, that want to enjoy the game's combat. The combat is certainly the real highlight, for me at least. The campaign is interesting but is largely a puzzle dungeon crawler, which isn't quite my thing.
With the constant updates adding some heavy layers of polish to the game, it feels better than ever and if you're into anything that involves swords, dungeons and fighting, then this game will blow your mind.

That's a very original and entertaining game, like if X-COM met Game of Thrones for a crossover.
People tend to focus on combat, but what's really great about Massive Chalice is the strategy of breeding heroes and trying to have a minimally acceptable team to defend your lands when the Cadence attacks. It can be challenging as you have to plan ahead to have a balance of classes and also take care of the special buildings that give bonus to hero development and research of new 'technologies'.
What should you do? Have your best hero available to do battle or marry him with a fertile hero of another family so his offspring have a better chance of being as good (or better!) than himself? Should you appoint your most experienced hero as the standard to be followed by young heroes and risk having only inexperienced youngsters to fight the next invasion? Will they be able to survive without more powerful items and armor? Who will research it?
Combat itself is not that original or satisfying at this point, mostly because of balance issues. There are some enemies, especially later in the game, able to single handedly criple or even destroy an average party. Also, there are only 3 classes available. This greatly limits the number of tactics you can use to overcome the battles, and can lead to some repetition during the 300 year timespan of the game.
Of course, this is an unfinished product, so we can hope for the combat to get a little better and the planning phase to get more polishment and shine even more.
That said, if you like original and challenging games, Massive Chalice's world is surely a good palce for you to play only one more turn.

I was pleasantly surprised by Creeper World 3. I've always been a fan of tower defense style games, and creeper world mixes up the formula a bit, adds a few elements that are almost puzzle-like, and ties the whole package up with a story that I found novel and refreshing. There are no "lanes" or marching mindless enemies, but there is a network of towers that will desperately fire a nonstop barrage to hold back the enemy long enough for a careful strike against their resource nodes. You hope. For a faceless enemy, you truly feel like you are facing down an infinite and eternal threat. There was never any hope for survivival in this unforgiving universe, but you will carve out a section of peace in your small quadrant for as long as you are able. For what alternative can there be.
AI War is similar, and a little bit better, but I am glad I stubmled upon this all the same.

This game captures a much larger amount of strategy than most tower defenses.  You can play defensively and hold off the creeper until you build a large enough power supply to overwhelm it, or you can go on the offensive and try to lock the creeper in a choke point.  With all the different kinds of units you can build, there are lots of ways to go about either one, and each map calls for a different approach.

Lifeless Planet Review
Hello I'm Cosmic and welcome to Lifeless Planet, an Indie action adventure game brought to you by Stage 2 Studios or more specifically Stage 2 studios sole employee David Board. Yep, thats right this game was entirely created by one man in Alaska, an impressive feat to say the least.
Lifeless planet tells the story of a lone astronaut who crash lands on his destination planet. Alone and running out of air, its time to go into survival mode, find air and see if any of your crew mates survived. You embark out into the wilderness of the Mars like planet with its red canyons and sand filled landscapes.
The sceptical astronaut soon discovers not only scientific wonders on the planet's surface but begins to see and experience things that cannot be explained. You soon come across signs of life, not alien signs of life mind you but instead the remnants of humanity from earth, specifically remnants of a soviet union outpost. This leads the astronaut to question not only if he is indeed on another planet but also if any of this is even real.

I bought this during Early Access.
The game you'll play today is VERY different than the game I first played. The core mechanics are still there, but this version has a lot more heart.
I miss the old UI, but I have gotten used to the new one. The old UI was reminiscent of Terraria or Minecraft in the way that you had ten action/item buttons and now you have six dual slotted buttons.
I miss being able to stack food, now food takes up one slot per item without stacking. I do like that we now have four inventory tabs for more room, but your inventory can still fill up freakishly fast.
Don't listen to people who call this Minecraft/Terraria in space. Minecraft and Terraria are excellent games in their own right, but they are not favored for their limited number of similarities, but for their extensive number of differences. Starbound is independant of the others. This game has always been a favorite of mine because while it does have similarities to other games, this one is defined by space exploration, a semi-linear story option not present in some other sandbox games, and a level of quality that is often missed in the Early Access genre.
This game has been fully released, and constantly updated with an active community. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes space exploration, sandbox games, survival elements, and no microtransactions/pay-for-DLC/etc.

First things first, I like the game. Would I recommend it to someone else short answer no.
The combat is interesting and different and the Arena mode is good fun, the AI is also very good and does a fine job of being challenging but not unfair.
The problems start in the single player campaign game. The lack of save points is a real issue, I have had a look around and I understand the arguments against them, however adding in different difficulty modes would change nothing for hard core players and would lower the barrier for entry for other people with less time.
The loot system is random so some times I get nice armour others nothing of much use, this can be irritating in a game where you are expected to replay levels over and over. I feel like the loot should be fixed. This is how every other element of the game work so why chests are random makes no sense.
Due the the amount you will have to replay sections of the game while learning much of the immersion and atmosphere are lost, while permanent death dose make the game tense a lot of that tension is lost when you know the exact layout of the levels and the enemies in them. In many ways this seems a strange choice as the initial play troughs are great fun but quickly turn frustrating or just boring.
At the moment this is only a game for the hard core player, I don’t think its a bad game but I do think it has an extremely limited audience in its current form. I would say to anyone think very carefully about how much time you have lean to play. Also think about how much repetition in a game you are comfortable with. You will have to replay the first levels a lot even with the save points at the end of each level.
So in short:
- Interesting Combat
- Nice concept
- Lots of repetition (Destroys the sense of immersion)
- Will take a large time investment to get good.

This game has a combat system like nothing I've ever seen before. At first it's really difficult, I recommend for new players to play through the arena (novice and preferably expert too, or at least until the first 4-6 fights on expert level) before attempting the main game. Otherwise there's a great risk you'll find the controls confusing and frustrating and more or less give up on the game.
That's what I did anyway, at first. I bought the game because I saw a playthrough of the first level and it seemed really fun, then when I tried it myself I failed miserably.
But now I've gone through the arena fights and just finished lvl 2 (I think there's only 3 currently, but the levels are pretty big, hard and unforgiving). I love it. No saves and permadeath means you have to constantly be on your toes (I've heard you automatically save when exiting though, I really hope that's true or else I'll have to go through levels 1-2 again..)
There are numerous game mechanics tutorials on youtube, I had some help from one of them, can't remember which and when I look now there's quite a few to choose from. I'm really glad I gave the game a second chance, once you get reasonably good at it it's very rewarding. And that's just how it is in its current state, there's lots of stuff not yet implemented, this might become a very nice (and cheap for what it is) game indeed.

You know those virtual desktop thingies we used to see touted in the 1990s as "the future"? This is one of them, and while it's kind of neat, it's more of a rich gamer's toy than anything of actual convenience.
It's rather complex for new users to get into - probably to its detriment - but the basic gist is that there's two modes: one for constructing 'virtual desktops' for your media, and one for a persistent multiplayer world where everyone can add things to the various levels.
You can load any Source engine BSP/level, import libraries of your Steam games, place shortcuts for emulators/non-Steam games/media on your computer...and play interior designer with them. This means you can put
in picture frames and spam them all over a modest apartment, or ctf_2fort, or wherever.
More importantly, if you place and use an item that points to a game, Steam or otherwise, you can actually launch that game from Anarchy Arcade. Unfortunately this means you have the game AND Anarchy Arcade running on your system at the same time, which on slower computers could mean worse in-game performance. Really, the program in general is too janky for anyone with a computer that costs less than $900 and a monitor smaller than 1600x1200.
The persistent multiplayer 'metaverse' is interesting, but it seems to have displaced custom server capability from the previous versions in favor of something more akin to an MMO. Fortunately, Anarchy Arcade doesn't seem quite popular enough to attract griefers bent on destroying you and your friends' attempts at building the most ridiculous gamer mancave ever.
As of right now the developer is still working on optimizing and smoothing the game out, with a promising update currently in the pipeline, so we'll see where this goes.

So my daughter gave me this as a mother's day present, because of the title so she says, but I still suspect that it had more to do with the fact that the premise of the game is that mom gets distracted, faceplants a planetary system and ends up in pieces talking gibberish. Obviously I never get distracted and flal over my own feet or talk gibberish *cough*
Anyway it has a lovely atmosphere, some interesting skills and if you fancy really chilled out exploration this may be for you (with lots of strange little things hidden away in various corners). You can scan all the flora on the planet it and reproduce it at will - from purely decorative plants, through to useful stuff like bouncy mushrooms or catapult plants. Whether you're just interested in them for their function or you fancy some landscape gardening you're ok. There are challenges and crystals to collect that offer you various upgrades, some awkward enough to keep you going for a considerable amount of time.
It has a weird control scheme that I really didn't get along well with, that's not to say it was bad, just not my cup of tea and you may enjoy it far more.
So the downside is that if you hunt around for stuff like crystals you quickly find yourself picking up upgrades which make many of the other features utterly trivial. The map is weirdly pinioned in such a way that despite it being a globe you can't actually rotate all the way around in any direction and you can only have one marker on it making keeping track of things difficult. This is then compunded because the teleport map just flips you between points which can be very hard to identify when you can't easily see the surrounding area. The star plants are initally cool but after a while when you're aiming to get something to reach a specific point and nothing seems to want to grow in that direction (and you have no control over that) it can get a little more tiresome and the payoff seems less worth it. Lastly of course POD, your ever present companion has a memory like a sieve and continue to bug you about collecting certain things and fixing mom even after you have done these things.
Overall though it has some nice moments and if you can get to grips with the controls and enjoy poking your nose into every little crevice to find strange and random things, you may enjoy it.

Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal is a under-the-radar tower-defense game that is both fun and challenging. It's basic yet complex appearance may overwhelm those new to the genre, but Knuckle Cracker did a good job on slowly pacing the user into the concepts around Creeper World 3.
The graphics of Creeper World 3 aren't anything extraordinary but they are pretty solid. The terrain is in a variety of colors and the illusion of layers is clearly there. The various tools and weapons stand out from the terrain and are simple to realize through the variation in shape and color. While everything looks basic throughout the game, the graphics are crisp and clear - and that's good enough for a tower defense game.
The core gameplay of Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal is one that is new to me. While I have played other games in the same sort of genre, Creeper World 3 is unique in the sense that it's attempting to fuse both Tower Defense and Strategy-Simulation. While the majority of tower defense's have you place your weapons on a certain path as enemies start to come at you on a predictable path - Creeper World 3 is adds a refreshing twist. Your enemy is the creeper. The creeper spreads outward in all directions, covering the terrain and destroying everything in it's path. It is your job to use the weapons at your disposal to take out the source of the creeper - being the emmiters. While it may not sound that hard, which it really isn't at first; the difficulty begins to ramp up. It will be very challenging for newcomers - including me at times, but I never really felt that the game was cheating. I also realized what mistakes I made if I were to fail. Throughout the game, you will play a variety of maps with the inclusion of the story. The story arc is the weakest point about this game, it's very forgettable and did nothing to increase the immersion or gameplay. It's a good effort nonetheless. The mouse controls are also great - with the ability to pause the game, plan you moves and move your units around where you please. Overall, the core mechanics of Creeper World 3 is great and will be something for all games in the similar genre to beat.
The audio is good for a game like this. In all honestly, what can you expect. The music is fine with the occasion of it being repetitive. I found myself turning off the music at various times. The sound effects are pretty simple. Nothing special here.
Creeper World 3's greatest strength is it's value. Like Skyrim, Portal 2 and Torchlight 2 before them, the sheer amount of user content is mind-blowing. At a cheap price of $15, it's pretty hard to not pick this one up if you are a fan of the genre. There are an abundance of maps, both pre-made and user-made all varying in difficulty. It's also good to note that some maps have been known as unbeatable. A random map generator is also here as well as an in-game editor to create your own maps for others to try. Creeper World 3 also has over 130 achievements for those who are into them.
In conclusion, Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal was one of the more surprising buys for me. I didn't think I would enjoy the game this much. It is something I will continue to play for years to come.

This game definitely scores high in the city building sphere but does leave something to be desired. The developers improved the production chain management issues from the previous version, where it became impossible to determine whether you're over-producing or under. But in doing so it has dumbed down the whole game quite a bit. Now in the later game, it seems, you're just playing around with numbers and not really doing playing a game.
The combat is a disappointment, there is no planning/preparing an army and attacking anymore, there are just standalone missions that you go and finish. These become repetitive very fast because there are only 3-4 of them, but you have to keep playing them to get some much needed resources.
Not sure why the maual save game was removed. Now you can't take risks and see how that would turn out to be. Instead you have to play very conservatively, the entire time, so you don't go bankrupt.
Late game pretty much becomes a drag because you're left with nothing to do. There aren't any factions ether. So you don't feel like playing as another faction, which was a major plus in earlier games. I guess the different zones (arctic, temperate, lunar) are their replacement but they still take some replayability away. If each sector had some unique achievement/reward then there'd be an incentive to finish them all, but right now there isn't at all.
Overall I will still recommend it because of city planning and building. The graphics are pretty impressive, zooming in on a production facilities and watching what is going on is quite cool.

OMD!2 is the kind of sequel Hollywood produces - repeat the screenplay but add in new locations and a new star name. In the OMD! universe, this is achieved by adding co-op with the adversary from the first game, a lot of new maps and the twist of being able to completely re-spec your spellbook before every level. There are also more enemy mobs, a new set of nicely designed maps (the DLCs add more mobs and more maps, including some 'Classics' from the original), more traps and weapons and the introduction of trinkets (giving passive and active effects). All this means you can really craft your own style of play, notwithstanding the unique demands of each map.
All the things that made OMD! such great fun are here - smooth gameplay, plenty of humour, a variety of options (Nightmare mode, endless, etc.) and basically such levels of orc-destructing carnage that you might begin to start feeling a tiny bit sorry for them. If there's a better TPS/TD game, I would love to know about it.
In terms of value, I would call this an obligatory purchase if it's on sale. If not, the DLC is a bit steep (particularly for a game of this vintage) but if you play through twice you'll get your money's worth; if you have a friend to co-op with, playing Endless opens of a LOT more replayability. The advantage of its age is there are plenty of gameplay guides available if you get stuck...

Lifeless Planet is certainly a novel idea, and although this review is a "recommended" one, this game does have its issues, and to be honest I can't really say I RECOMMEND it right now. I just feel that anyone who sees the red thumbs down on a review for a game that they like will just instantly hate on it without seeing what it has to say. Overall, I have mixed feelings about it. This is a spoiler-free review, so please read on.
I'm not going to say anything about the story, except that the ending felt really unsatisfying for me. Other than that, I enjoyed it, and it certainly is a memorable experience... but it's just one of those things that I feel would work better as a movie than a game, at least in its current form. There is SO much walking without much happening, so many jumping puzzles which are made extra annoying by the walking mechanics--which make you move FORWARDS a little upon pressing S, before turning around. This has made me fall off of the edges of things countless times. There are very few puzzles and gameplay elements in between the walking, which aren't paticularly challenging... just dull.
As for the graphics, they generally look a bit dated, but the skies and distant landscapes do look
. The lighting isn't that bad either. However, I do seem to run into very random and inexplicable frame drops. (I have an i5-2500k and an AMD 7950.) Although this doesn't occur very often, one minute I can be getting 120FPS, the next it drops down to 15-30 in similar environments. Yes, I'm running on the highest settings, but my setup SHOULD be able to handle this game on the highest settings. The performance in this game is kind of unacceptable right now. Maybe it's something specific to AMD cards, who knows. I'm very disappointed with the performance in any case.
Now, I love games about exploring desolate and abandoned things, such as in Portal 2 when you went though old aperture. That was honestly my favorite part of the game. Despite my frustration over the excessive walking and lackluster gameplay in Lifeless Planet, it managed to capture the same sort of atmosphere that made me enjoy the old aperture part of Portal 2.
Really, whether I would recommend this game to you or not depends on your attitude towards "walking simulators." If you're one of the people who can tolerate Dear Esther, happy to just sit back and take in the pretty environments, then I'll hazard a guess to say that you will probably enjoy this game. If you dislike games where there is more walking than gameplay--in the case of Lifeless Planet, FAR more walking--then I would advise you to steer clear.
To clarify, I am someone who dislikes Dear Esther, but loves The Stanley Parable--in fact it's one of my favorite games of all time. So I don't necessarily mind games where there isn't much "gameplay", just ones where there is too much walking without anything particularly interesting happening. Which is sadly, at least in my view, the case for Lifeless Planet.
I'd like to state that I enjoyed the preorder demo, the sense of discovery when you come across that
is wonderful.  But unfortunately that's where it peaks. From there on out it's mostly pretty dull. I've been looking forward to the full release for a while now and I wanted so desperately to enjoy it. If the rest of the game was as interesting as the first few levels I could forgive all of its little faults, but unfortunately I found the rest of the game not necessarily BAD, but mostly disappointing.
I bought this game for £8 from the humble store and I've gotten about 4 and a half hours out of it, excluding the time I spent on the pre-order demo. It had its good parts, and for that I don't regret purchasing it.
Maybe you'll absolutely love it, I don't know, I'm not you. I'm not saying you shouldn't buy this, I just feel that someone needs to point out this game's issues so that they can be taken into consideration before you purchase it.
TL;DR Lifeless Planet is a nice, pretty, atmospheric exploration game with an intriguing and original story--let down by excessive walking, lackluster gameplay and, at least on my hardware, unforgivable frame drops. If you have a tolerance for "walking simulators" then you may enjoy it. If not, steer clear.
Not worth the current $20, but shows promise when there is more story added. :)

Edit: I have a much longer list of issues here:
I have played a lot of early access games, and I've never thought poorly of them because I knew what I was getting into when I bought them. However, this game is not marked as early access, and it should be.
This game needs a lot of polishing with gameplay mechanics, visuals, and performance:
- Micromanagement & Functionality:
Each building needs workers to function: The player has no control over what buildings are worked, or how many workers. There are time when you
to be able to micromanage this.
Just having a +/- button next to the worker count in buildings would make a world of difference.
There are also times when new constructions will have 0/7 workers despite having many idle civs with no indication as to why.
Some tasks become very tedious due to lacking functionality. Clearing a forest should be doable with 2 clicks: Highlight and queue chopping. Unfortunately every single tree requires 2 clicks.
Building around an area with a forester is very difficult. Coming from Civ V I’d like it if my workers cleared forests automatically when I tell them to build something, but I have to clear it
before I can even queue the building. Because you have to wait quite a while for a worker to come chop the trees you may go do something else, only to come back and see the forester replanted the tree.
Building a road through a foresters forest is harder than defending against invasion.
- Visuals & Interface.
When winter comes the game visualizes this by making the screen very bright. Not only is this very hard on the eyes, it also hinders gameplay making some things impossible to see. The different colors of soil and rocks all become too faded to tell apart because of the blinding light.
Fortunatly the couds that cover the screen and compleatly blind you are disabable, however the winter time filter is not.
Ingame menus do not function properly with scrolling. Scrolling in menus will scroll the ingame camera in/out while only moving the scroll menu a pixel up/down. The camera should really be locked while in menu
As your town becomes cluttered it becomes hard to click on buildings. You often end up clicking random civilians or the building behind even if your mouse is on a building. This sentence is short but it's a very very big issue in game, and it makes me wish I could disable clicking on civs.
Some buildings have no useful description. The grand hall says something about having big meals every day, but no information on what is actually does. Even after building it I was not sure.
When a civ dies of starvation I don’t know what house he was in, and If I find the house I have no way of knowing why the house can’t get food. In one playthrough I had plenty food and homes were all nearby, buy all homes would report they could not get food.
Every few minutes 1 would die of starvation and there was no ingame information for how to fix this. This is a very big issue in the game and the advisors are the biggest offenders:

When I get a message that some food was wasted I don’t know what to do. I have 3 granaries a mixed my farms yet food can’t reach them? The advisor tells me to improve paths to a granarie every season yet they are on top of eachother.
Somewhere in my town 1 building does not have access to a library. The advisor reminds me of this and many other things every 30 seconds. There is no way to click this message and see which house does not have access.
Edit: The latest update seems to help with people not getting food and food not getting stored before winter.
Which brings us to the next issue:
All these building effect range indicators also appear under buildings, making them hard to see in the first place.
It seems fps returned to normal after relaunching, But the game does run into fps issues if run for a long period.
- Conclusion:
This game was fun, but It plays like a very early access game. This becomes an issue because the game is not marked as early access. There is no guarantee that any issue I have with this game will be fixed, because the game is unfinished marked finished.
I don’t usually write reviews, but I want to play this game again when it’s stable and finished.
I hope that this highlights the things that are missing and that I can come back and have my review no longer be true.

A drunk man stumbles round a dungeon.
Who is this man, what is he doing there... who knows.
This game basically steals the tagline "Live. Die. Repeat." from the movie Edge of Tomorrow but without the exposition at the start letting you know why or any sort of character development (ok, you do get to name your totally generic person).
The physics are touted as a great leap forward but I think there's a very good reason no other game tries to go down this route: what you end up with is a very slow paced hack and slash. It's like all the fun has been surgically removed.
A good RPG has characters you care about and storylines moving the game along. It doesn't need non-stop action.
A good Hack and Slash has lots of action but can survive a weak plot and poor characters.
This game has no character, no story and little action: it's a game engine without a facade.

Stream of consciousness starting... now
I've been gaming for thirty plus years and never felt compelled to advocate a game before now.
The combat in this game is phenomenal.  Perhaps even revolutionary.
While I rejoice in this game's creation, I despair that the control scheme will be too intimidating for some, and that they will not be able to appreciate the depth of the mechanics therein.  If you enjoy Skyrim, but find the combat sorely lacking and unbalanced... if you think Dark Souls is great because of the relatively challenging combat... I strongly recommend Exanima.  Not only for the experience itself but for the support you'll be giving the dev team as they work on Sui Generis, for which Exanima is a prelude.
I can't remember looking forward to a game as much as I am Sui Generis.
I can't muster enough praise for what Madoc and the Bare Mettle team have done here.
While additions and enhancements are still being made, the Exanima campaign in and of itself is nothing to write home about.  I personally found a lot of the exploration to be tedious.  Some will disagree with me but the game desperately needs some automapping.  There's a bunch of crap lying around, and if you don't use a guide you'll wonder how much of it you have to sort and sift through to find everything.
However, all of these complaints pale when viewed in light of what should be the focus here... the great combat mechanics and dynamic environment in general.  I really hope this game succeeds and other developers use the game engine to make their own games, because there are so many possibilities.
The arena mode in this game is worth the price alone.  You'll struggle with the novice arena first, gradually getting a hang of the controls and gradually progressing through the ranks.  You'll come to the first shield bearer and get frustrated with how hard he is to hit. And if you're like me, you'll do it all over again and again because it's so cool and fun to try with different weapons and playstyles.

The CONTROL SYSTEM LEARNING CURVE here is a thing of painful beauty.  Over 24hrs i grew from a stumbling drunken bum tripping over his own weapon, to an aggressive clumsy berserker dashing about performing huge looping sword swings that sometimes connected with messy results, on the way i learned to barely survive by tangling my opponents weapon with my own and tripping them, or barging them into walls, combining sidesteps with horizontal cuts, and overhead swings with lunges forward or back, before finally reaching the pinnacle of defensively keeping my opponent right in my weapon arc and my neck out of thiers while slicing in accurate ripostes to counter their attacks and hamstring them while they flail madly at me.
Having said all that about skill, luck still plays a huge factor here, the AI is mean, well armoured, apparently drunk and holding some truly unpleasant weaponry which they have no compulsion about swinging madly at your head or sometimes even their own.

Classic beat em up mortal kombat tower climb game structure, with added looting, hyper-realistic physics/shadows/lights/everything, all rendered in very crispy 3D  with a truly awesome skill-based control system, slapped with a thick gout of blood and drizzled with moody baroque modern classical music.
Not even touched the story mode yet and already got more than my moneys worth outta this game.  Very nice workmanship.

Where to begin? First and foremost I'll say Exanima is unlike any game I've EVER played, and I've played hundreds of them. It's not a game that you can jump into and do well with, on the contrary, you will suck at first! I consider myself quite adept at any game I try but this one took me 4-5 hours just getting used to the control system and combat, but that's a good thing. I can't begin to describe the satisfaction I got from beating my first zombie in the dungeon and my first opponent in arena mode, but you must be willing to invest the time. And oh man what a sweet reward! You can almost FEEL the weight of the weapon you're wielding when you swing. The "thunk" you hear when you connect a blow to the head, the splash of blood when your weapon slices into your opponent, and the sound of armor and shield being struck, all these things and more immerse you into the game unlike anything out there.
At the moment there are only 3 ways to attack- swings from right to left, left to right, and overhead bashes. That being said, with just those 3 I have still gained immense pleasure trying to slice and dice enemies, but there are more to come soon. Once the new moves are implemented I'm sure the game will reach new heights of enjoyment and more hours learning them! This game will draw you in and not let go, you only have to be willing to invest yourself and open your mind to new things.
Which brings me to controls. I've read a lot of complaints and ideas for camera and charactor controls but I believe most of them stem from the need for instant gratification. You ain't getting that here, but again, that's a good thing! The camera is stationary unless you press the space bar, which will center it behind you, but if you're in combat that won't last long. The best 2 tips I can give at the moment are to leave the camera alone unless you need to see a certain part of the place you're at better, or if you simply have to have the camera behind you, hold down the space bar and the RMB simultaniously while exploring/moving, but not in combat. As for movement, the WSAD buttons stay the same no matter which way the camera is oriented. W will always move you forward, S backwards, A left and D right. It takes getting used to but once mastered it becomes second nature. If you have problems or would like to see examples other than the trailer look on youtube, there are plenty of helpful videos there.
All in all, Exanima delivers on all levels, and keep in mind what is here is far from complete. I think we are on the cusp of a revolutionary way we will see RPG games done in the future because once this hits the market and more people are exposed to it who the hell is going to want to play any other way? I won't! Buy the game, help support the devs, and you won't be sorry. It's the best 15 bucks I've spent in a long time.
PS. A lot of people suggest playing arena mode before the story mode to get the feel of combat. I suggest starting the story mode first but stay in the room you start in. Find a piece of wood and a barrel lid, equip those and enter combat mode, and get used to the mechanics of fighting that way. Take some swings, experiment with placing the cursor while you swing. Move about while swinging, slide the mouse around while swinging to add momentum. Step into overhead bashes, practice any kind of move you can think of, then log out of story mode and play the arena mode. If you just jump into the arena without doing what I've suggested, you may get frustrated and decide the game is too hard. DON'T DO IT! Take 5-10 minutes in story mode first, staying in the first room. You lose nothing by doing so, but will gain invaluable experience. While I will keep my first review below (it was negative) I've sunk enough hours in to admit I love this game. It wasn't easy to get into and I still think the tutorial and story missions need to be reworked.... ...but geez... this game is cool. It was worth my money for sure.
The thing I love most about this game is troubleshooting my design in the builder. Most of my hours have been spent pitting my designs against each other and the built in ships. It's the best feeling to see the more recent version of your favorite destroyer rip the older version to pieces. I have also enjoyed the campaign, although I haven't gotten into it as far as I would like to. Capturing and controlling resource regions (and defending them from marauders...) makes for some of the best strategic gameplay I've played in a while. Seeing your designs succeed against the enemy is so satisfying and great fun.

The voxelated building is a great. The variety of blocks lets you build in great detail. I decided to learn the keyboard style vs. mouse style, and while its not perfect it is worth giving a go.
The Advance Cannons are VERY cool. While I found them frustrating at first, the satisfaction of figuring out how to implement them was worth the learning curve. While CRAM cannons are simple (yet not ineffective), I really liked the customization of designing my own shells using Advance Cannons. Worth learning to use!
Although the AI is customizable I find myself turning off the movement function of the AI and commanding ships myself. The AI is very capable of using weapons but doesn't navigate well. There is an option to write programs to control how ships move (which is pretty sweet) but I'm not so technically inclined. The AI for enemy ships seems pretty well done so this is likely my short coming and not the game's.
This game isn't perfect yet I am confident it will improve like a fine wine. I found myself very frustrated at first but kept coming back every day to improve my ships, and to do battle in the campaign. The two hours steam gives you to try this game won't be enough to learn how to play, so check out some gameplay videos before you buy!

So what is Anno 2205? It is a supply chain management city builder sim. The vast majority of the game is managing supply chains for various resources while maintaining a positive income. Depending on how good you are at the game, you can end up waiting VERY long periods of game time to do anything because your income is only a hundred credits a minute or so and everything costs a lot more than 100 credits, or you can very rapidly expand.
How do you make credits? Your income is entirely based off of taxes. The game is balanced so that your temperate regions will generally have a positive income while the arctic and lunar regions will eat credits (but provide resources you can ship to your temperate regions to make more money by upgrading your population).
Pros:
Supply Chain Manager.
More forgiving than other games in the series.
Combat can be mostly ignored if you do not have the DLC that allows your regions to be invaded.
You get the feeling of success that comes with expanding your company from nothing to controlling a number of regions.
Game does not "end" as you can always improve on your optimization.
Signifiicantly variable difficulty.
Pretty graphics.
Campaign is not pressing but has a truly awesome reward.
Each region is slightly different in management because of regional projects, bonuses, and "negatives".
Addictive for people who like to optimize / perfect stuff.
Cons:
Limited combat that is repetitive.
Not a lot of variance in building appearance.
Gameplay can get repetitive quickly for those who do not like managing supply chains.
Stock Market DLC can be very annoying in spite of large benefits.
Space Station DLC will drive you insane if you like to have full supply everywhere.
Tundra DLC gives you a "benefit" that in most cases is actually a detriment.
Multiplayer gameplay does not exist.
This is personally my favorite Anno game because it allows for a larger degree of error in supply chain management than the other games so it is more forgiving for people who do not enjoy micromanaging but still like supply chain management. I also do not often play multiplayer in anything so the lack of multiplayer does not bother me in the least.

Building up the city too wasn’t very interesting either. You add some more homes and then add some more support buildings to match. That’s pretty much it and it’s as dull as it sounds.
The trading between the temperate, arctic and lunar zones just extended this mechanic by adding somewhere else you needed to build-up after you have increased the population in one of the other zones.
To be honest, I’m still not sure what the ship battle side missions are for. They are such a disjoint from the rest of the gameplay and are very samey. I think you can just ignore them if you wish and once you have done one then you probably will.
Though a pretty looking game, after looking at some animation once you will zoom out and not be interested again as it tells you nothing. Similarly with the little voice clips that play each time a home is selected, just an annoying distraction after hearing it the first time.
The mechanism of the stock market available later in the game is annoying and seemingly pointless and I’d recommend not turning it on when it becomes available in the game.
Halfway through, I found myself having to grit my teeth and get on with grinding towards a game end. Not a happy situation with an expensive game.
I came away with the impression that this was a game built by a team that didn't communicate much, with each feature bolted together loosely at the end of development.
Except for die-hard fans, I’d say this franchise has run its course.

Quest for Infamy is a point and click, open world adventure RPG; a spiritual
successor to Quest for Glory. This game easily has one of the best musical soundtracks
I have heard; it syncs perfectly step for step for the entire adventure, and varies
according to what you do and how you play. The voice acting is professional, and the
game offers the option to turning it on or off, and having subtitles with or without
the voice. There is a comic/ satirical undertone throughout the game, making it one
of the funniest point and click adventures I have played.
You have the option to play as a warrior, mage, or a rogue. The story incorporates
your choice throughout the game. The warrior is a solid character to play if you
are new to this style of game. The rogue unfortunately has limitations to what they
are capable of doing, such as not being able to pick all the locks even though you
have 100% lock picking, and the stealth element that prevents enemies from spawning in
any area you go to, instead of stealthing around enemies. The mage, who relies on
spells, is actually the strongest in the game. The spells add a level of depth
and make the mage feel well rounded.
The level design of the game is a true open world, where you have the option
to travel all over the map. There are also puzzles that are tied into the open world,
which adds a level of depth. Some things did take away a bit from the old school feeling of
games such as Quest for Glory in that they did present a map for certain more confusing
areas, instead of having the player write out and figure out how to get through those
areas. If anything, I found that the game opens up too soon, making it more difficult
to understand or follow the main story, as you can easily get bogged down by side
quests or errands. This is only in the first chapter however; it focuses and progresses
very well in the second and third chapters. The game also offers a day and night cycle,
which adds a huge level of depth by what creatures come out during what point of day,
and how you can complete certain objectives giving it a greater feel and personalty.
Although you do get tips and clues, the game does not hold your hand and lead
you to each step, which is nice to see. The usage of items in the game made sense and it was up to the player to figure out what was needed and where from the sea of items in the game. The story was entertaining, and unlike many of the current games out, I was really blown away by the ending. This game is highly recommended.

Quest for Infamy has the forest setting of Quest for Glory I: So You Want To Be A Hero.
Its got the varied class-specific sidequests of Quest for Glory 2: Trial By Fire.
It has the vast scope (over 200 hand-drawn areas!) of Quest for Glory 3: Wages of War.
Part of the plot concerns the fate of the cursed Killington family, an eldritch tale right out of Quest for Glory 4: Shadows of Darkness.
And the massive port city of Tyr feels a lot like Silmaria from Quest for Glory 5: Dragon Fire.
In short, if you liked Quest for Glory, you will REALLY like this game. Play it for the nostalgia alone.

Pros
-Great music
-Quest for Glory (RPG/Adventure) style of gameplay with some modern adjustments. You get a notifier when your skills level up, for instance.
-Gorgeous pixel art
-Some really funny lines
-Good homages to the classics
-Good sense of progression with stats/loot from enemies. That good RPG feel where you can tell you're getting stronger.
-Sensible puzzles. Make you think, but no absurd 'How could anyone guess *that*?' moments. Good clues built in to dialogue with people to help you think your way through.
-Balanced difficulty for combat
Cons
-Odd pacing, Act II/III don't have as much meat as Act I. Minor quibble. Still a meaty game.
-Voice acting could be hit or miss. Funny lines would sometimes be delivered in ways that made the joke less effective
-Fan service in female designs was overkill. I'm usually fine with it, and to a certain degree with your character it makes sense. But it was laid on a little too thick. Rohem needed a few more Larry Laffer style cases where his ego gets pricked a bit.
9/10, if I had to give it a number. Pick it up!

Two years ago I gave Quest for Infamy a 'Not Recommended' review. I thought the game was too cluttered with crushing bugs, unnecessary items and a clunky layout resulting in a game full of fluff and confusion. Throw on top of that a $20  price tag and i ultimately felt that there were better games out there that had a more fullfilling and polished 'Quest for Glory' experience.
After posting my review, i was surprised to hear back directly from the creators of the game. They thanked me for my honest opinion and then requested i replay the game with their first major update.
Well - I didn't replay it. I figured I gave Quest for Infamy plenty of hours to prove itself a contender, concluded it had not, and moved on.
Earlier this year I downloaded Infamous Quest's newest adventure game 'Order of the Thorne' (on GOG) I respected what the indie developer was trying to do for classic adventure games and figured I'd give them another shot. To my surprise, Order of the Thorne was quite charming. I felt like they nailed the old-school 'King's Quest' vibe and found myself eager to play it's next chapter.
So, renewed with confidence in Infamous Quest's products, I decided to give Quest for Infamy another go. Replaying the game, I instantly noticed a difference from the updates with how the game presented itself. Gone were the bugs that plagued my first runthrough, cluttered item menus were made more streamline and that clunky feeling that hovered over the game felt far less 'unfinished game' and much more 'Authentic retro adventure game style'. Like my reaction to Order of the Throne, I found myself surprised by the changes and eager to see what the future of Quest for Infamy held.
Quest for Infamy isn't perfect, but it's a commendable effort from a developer who cares about their product. Think Quest for Glory with a sprinkling of Liesure Suit Larry - It's a bit raunchy in a good way, and a lot of fun in a retro way. AAAND, for only 10 dollars now, it's definitely a contender.

The Graveyard is quite possibly the simplest game I have ever played. Interestingly enough, for a game that has absolutely no gameplay The Graveyard actually has a gamebreaking bug. If you remain seated during the song and die you will be forced to use ALT-F4 to end the game as the only real way to exit is to get up before the song ends.
Poetry, Art, Experience. I do like that there are game developers out there that are experimenting with new things but charging gullible consumers money to play, what is essentially a postcard where you have to press the forward key for a few seconds to see it all, is just dishonest and greedy.

I Kickstarted the game and I am writing this review not of the full game, but the current early access version.
And as it is now - I would not recommend anyone to get it. Yet.
The game clearly has huge potential, but overall lacks in content.
The turn based combat is rather fun. Not that many options, so sooner or later it will get repetetive, but unlockable skills help in that regard.
Outside of combat, you are managing a very small group of lands, on which you can build one building, to improve the building times, hero training or just add keeps for your existing heroes to breed. As you pass years, not turns, your heroes will drop like flies. I personally don't like how fast that happens, making one generation of heroes fight from 1 to 4 times usually.
When they die, they can leave a heirloom to improve other hero from thier house.
The game is about limited resource management (heroes) and combat proficiency (again, heroes).
Outside of that simple mechanic (to not die out...) there is nothing else to do. If you do that, your heroes will eventually level up and get stronger.
He story wouldn't exist if not for the two "voices" of the Massive Chalice, that bring some falvour to the, otherwise lifeless world.
Events (text + choices) happen, to help with that. So far, I've seen mostly negative outcomes though.
I would say the game would be quite awesome, if there was more lands available, more building types (3!?), more hero types, customization of houses and heroes... Maybe item crafting? The game is begging for those,
The game does provide a bit of fun, and while it certainly IS PLAYABLE and enjoyable (if for a short ammount of time), the potential for it is so, so much greater than what it currently is.
So, no. I do not recommend the game at this point.
Wait a little while, maybe they will improve the game in the places that it's lacking?
If the game was already finished and the price was half what it is now, I would recommend it. But there is still time to release date.

SUMMARY:
A unique and interesting RTS/tower defense sci-figame. You use nodes to create webs which energy then passes through to power your weapons/defenses and beat back the ever-encroaching purple creeper "mist". Its addictive and you will have the temptation to go "one more level" everyime you think you're going to quit. The graphics and sound are adequate, but not great, But who plays these games for the graphics? If you are an RTS/TD fan, this game is defintely one to pick up even at full price. It's tiny bit pricy at full price for those who arent die-hard fans of RTS/TD games, but if you see it on sale, get it!
MAIN:
This game is fascinating. Its a really unique RTS/tower defense, the style of which vaguely reminds me of the Zerg in the original Starcraft. But there are no barracks for units, no movable parts. No vespene gas.
You have awoken in space after a 5-billion(!?) year stasis sleep, to find that the Creeper has again rampaged around destroying humanity's galactic empire. Of course, you must stop them. Its kind of difficult to explain how this game works without seeing it, but I'll do my best:
The Creepers have emitters which slowly start filling the map with purple stuff. If this purple stuff touches one of your buildings it is destroyed. You need to destroy all the emitters to progress. Sometimes there are other objectives as well.
So you build a command center far away from the emitters. Then you start building nodes and weapons such as cannons. Each node creates lines to the nodes next to it, and power flows through these lines from the command center to your weapons/cannons as well as newly placed buildings to construct them. Cannons cant link to each other, but only to nodes and relay nodes. So you want to build as many nodes to create a web, then a front line of weapons to hold off the onslaught, slowly building more relay nodes and weapons as you manage to beat back the "purple mist".
The nodes also generate energy, which you need to power your cannons and build things quickly. Build too fast, and your energy goes out of balance, weakening the ammo resupply to your cannons and allowing the evil purple stuff to overrun them.
There are also specialty nodes, such as relays which speed up energy transmission to new nodes and weapons, reactors, which provide lots of energy, special weapons, and many others I havent seen yet.
Theres a lot of strategy, figuring out the best place to put your nodes to create fast transmission of power as well as beat back the purple mist, but not overbuilding so you end up overrun.
Missions are timed, although as of yet I havent seen any where you "must beat the mission in (x) amount of time", but I wouldnt be surprised if they were out there (I hate those types of missions...I'm naturally a careful player who tries to do/see everything in any game I play. I HATE being rushed.). The fun of being timed is a global leaderboard where you can see rankings of how fast people have beat the missions.
The graphics are nothing to write home about, just little representations of the terrain, units, your node web, claimed territories, ect. But who cares? The strategy is what matters here, and I'll take gameplay over graphics any day of the year.
Sound is the same as graphics. Its ok, but nothing spectacular. Lots of pew pew and booms.
Overall, this is a unique and interesting game. There appear to be many many levels to play as well as a storyline. Its really fun, and if you see it on sale is a must buy for any RTS/tower defense fan.

Turok: Dinosaur Hunter was a first-person shooter released in 1997 on the Nintendo 64 and later ported to the PC.  Now, we finally have a remastered version of it up on steam.  This game is still extremely fun even today, especially now that we can play using the good old WASD + Mouse setup.  The game is set in the Lost Lands, a place where time has no meaning.  You play as Tal'Set, a Native American warrior fighting many enemies, ranging from dinosaurs to robots to these weird alien beings.  There are eight levels in the game.  Each level has a certain number of keys to find and a chronosceptor piece.  The goal of the game is to find all the pieces of the chronosceptor and kill the Campaigner.  The leves in this game are huge and there are many hidden areas to find.  The gameplay is extremely fun and very fast-paced, similar to games like Doom.  Also, this game has some of the coolest guns, including a fusion cannon and pulse rifle.  This game is extremely creative and you should defnitely check it out if you like retro shooters or shooters in general.

OMD2 is a solid Tower Defense game. I'm a huge fan of Tower Defenses in general.
Difficulty
The first few levels are super easy (as an into should be). It ramps up and becomes more difficult as the game progresses (as you would expect). I found myself replaying certain levels to "grind" more skulls to unlock/experience other traps, but I could have gotten by just fine without doing that. The game has a refund option where you can get all your skulls back and rebuy your traps, which was a really good idea. When you bump it up to Nightmare mode, the game gets hard. I still find myself looking around each level trying to find spots to place "kill boxes", but that's only really necessary on the hard levels. You can still be creative and have fun on the normal mode.
Polish
This game is beautiful. I would like to experience a wider variety of level environments as the side/inside of a mountain/mine quickly grew stale. Even so, this game is pretty. It supports 4k and the music is pretty good too.
Bugs
My only complaint is that there is a definite bug where mobs will sometimes just start attacking barricades when there is a super obvious route that they can take ( that their comrades are currently taking ). I even gave it the benefit of the doubt and thought that maybe the other mobs were blocking the path. However, even after you kill those guys, the bugged out mob will continue hacking away at your barricades.
This is kinda a big deal because if your barricade drops, your entire strategy falls through. On easier maps it's possible to work around this, but on hard levels like "crunch", it'll cost you the game.
Replayability
I find myself wanting to replay certain levels. You can beat the game and still have tons of traps left to unlock. I also find myself replaying levels simply to try out new traps in a pleasant environment. I also find myself replaying levels to see what the most efficient setups are.
Pay to win
If you dish out some money and buy the rocket launcher (which is part of a DLC set), the game gets a lot easier. The flyers and Earth elementals die quickly to the rocket launcher. You don't need it though, but the DLC definitely makes the game more fun. You get new levels and new traps / weaponry. The prices for the DLC are cheap as well. I don't think it's a bad gig. Yes you can buy stuff, No you don't have to in order to win and have fun.

As it stands Kingdoms and Castles is not a bad game for the price it is being offered: it is cute, quaint and enjoyable. However it is unlikely to last you more than perhaps a week of occassional one-hour sessions. The game you buy is a full experience, but after a point quickly reached the experience becomes repetative. The building trees are not very complex and it doesn't take long to build some of the higher tier structures, some of which (at the time of writing) have little to no purpose - such as the Great Hall, aside from being aesthetically pleasing within your town.
Therein lies the core of this game: aesthetics. You are mainly here to build a pretty city. Though there are Vikings and Dragons that randomly show up, the game offers little challenge: it doesn't take long to rebuild if you fail to see off one or the other of those threats, and after a point seeing off dragons becomes very easy leaving only the innumerable viking hordes to challenge your dominion of your little island. If you are like myself and enjoy the idea of watching a village naturally expand into a town, then there is a lot of fun to be had here for a while, but the fact of the matter is that there is only so much fun to be gleamed from building cottages when those cottages are no longer building towards the next goal - say, a new bakery, and are simply being built because you've hit the population cap again and have nothing to do.
Kingdoms and Castles presents a good core around which a very appealing game could be built, and thus far the Devs have shown that they are interested in doing just that. As it stands however, this game is a bite sized one that is, nonetheless, worth the price if you've the cash to spare.

Sometimes in cases like thunderstorms, my FPS could drop to as low as 15 FPS.
But overall with that set aside, I could easily rate this game an 8.5/10!
Because of the base aspect of the game and the strategy involved as the player has to not only build a kingdom with defences, but they have to manage the amount of food the peasants are getting to make sure they do not starve to death and also keeping up with materials and making sure water is easily accessible in case of random fires which could potentially ruin an important building.
The vikings are a challenge, however once players get the hang of the game and how it works, they will be nothing more than fun to watch as they "attempt" an attack on your kingdom and fail hard, only being able to possibly damage a first wall, But careful because the further on in the game you get, the more vikings will come and also some other enemies.
If players do not want to stress the fact of fighting off vikings and simply want to relax and build a nice little kingdom, there is just the right option for that. Personally I do prefer to play peacefully as i am not too fond of being raided by the vikings, although they are not too hard to defend against, I am however a more relaxed gamer and would rather build without any threats and just peaceful gameplay.
As I said, I will rate this game a reasonable 8.5/10, simply because of the occasional FPS drops I experience.

Exanima is an interesting dungeon crawler. The combination of tight corridors and sparse lighting creates an eerie, claustrophobic atmosphere that'd appeal to anyone who wants something a bit darker than your typical dungeon experience. The game seems to change completely as you progress. It starts as a more survival-like experience, with you darting through the shadows, using planks of wood and metal pipes as weapons as you try to scrape together some decent equipment.
Once you're tooled up, the combat system really starts to shine as you get decent gear and become competent at using it. As most people reading this will already know, the game uses a sophisticated physics system to procedurally generate animations. With this combat system, the player uses the keyboard and mouse to generate and direct force to try to damage the opponet, as opposed to pressing a button to execute a pre-determined attack animation. This results in extremly dynamic fights, with no two moves looking the same and making predicting the outcomes of your actions more challenging than in most games. As a downside, characters do tend to look rather drunk if the player isn't practiced, which brings me to the issue most people have with this game: the controls.
This game handles unlike any game I've played so far, and with a lack of a tutorial beyond a text note from the developer, it can take a very long time to learn the controls. This has led to those less patient players to get frustrated. My advice to new players would be to take your time in the arena learning the controls before you go into the story, where perma death and scarce checkpoints will probably result in you getting frustrated. Give yourself a few hours to learn how to move, swing and control the camera in a way you find comfortable.
And finally, do remember this is early access. After about 20 hours or so you start to notice how barebones the combat system really is in its current form. Don't get me wrong, there are many more hours of fun I can have with the game in it's current state, but the lack of thrust attacks, ranged weapons, and the games magic system (Thaumaturgy) can leave you wanting. This being said, the devs are working tirelessly on the game and the next patch will breath new life into the combat system with more skills and some unarmed combat. For more info, go to
and search the forums there.
I'm giving this a positive review partly because of the innovation and quality that has already been shown, but also on the potential this game has.
TL;DR It's good. It'll take you hours to learn. Bit barebones, but the developers are working hard and I trust them enough to give this a positive review.

It can be great, special and original, like Mount & Blade. But right now it's not, because of just horrible steering solution, which made the game unplayable for me.
Why did I buy it? Because of the procedural-physics driven animation and combat system. Just look at the videos and you will instantly see why it's amazing. Swords actually hit each other and the environment. The damage depends on physical velocity, hit area etc. It's more of a simulation than a "pretended" fighting, like in practically all other games, except M&B.
So why is it unplayable for me?
1. Becasue of really wrong and unintuitive steering. The character always faces the mouse cursor, but the directional buttons don't adjust to the direction, where the character is facing. 90% of the time when you press "Up", the character will go down, or left etc. In combat, this is so confusing, that it just doesn't work at all. And sure, you can say "get used to it", but why get used to so ridiculous solution, when they could just do it normally, like every other game does (so when you press Up, the character should just go up (the screen).
2. Because the steering combined with ultra difficult enemies and combat make it hiper-difficult and therefore unplayable.
3. Because the progress doesn't save (or at least not for the first couple of hours?). Anyway, whenever I die, I start over (and create new character). Another hour of playing, dead - start over. 1,5 h of playing - dead - start over. Dungeon is always the same.
4. You train and get used to the steering in Arena Mode - spacious, rectangular arena. When you think you got a grasp on the combat, you start playing the real game - and surprise - super narrow corridors with piles of junk all over the place. You meet your first enemy, take a swing and... your weapon gets stuck. And you think - oh! cool! realistic. But after 3rd and 4th try, you realise, that it's not cool. Weapon ALWAYS stuck, because there's no room for fighting anywhere. I'ts just bad level design.
So in conclusion - if you want to play a game - skip it for now. Come back in 6 months to see if it became a game. But if you want to just check out how cool the physical-ragdoll-combat looks, then buy it. The price is ok for something that innovative.

If you're considering buying this, don't.
I get that this is supposed to be a small, artsy endeavor that shouldn't really even be classified as a game properly. I do. I've actually played other 'games' like that. The thing is, those were mostly very well done. This is crap.
It uses standard wasd controls, but a and d turn instead of strafe. This makes movement awkward unless you're going straight forward. Fortunately(?), the camera angle is fixed and you have literally nowhere else to go because invisible walls block you from leaving the path forward in any meaningful way. Technically, you can travel a brief distance down the side paths before encountering them, but that hardly makes any difference.
The worst part, really, is that it fails even at what should be its strength. The movements are poorly executed and frequently fail to match up properly with the environment. The birds, about the only moving things in the game apart from the protagonist, constantly clip through objects such as your character and the pavement. And the art assets themselves, even on highest settings, are mediocre at best in comparison with other 3D games of the last 5 years or more, and often considerably shabbier.
Your experience of the game will not even vary in any significant way as near as I can tell. You will walk her to the end of the path where she will sit on the bench. Then, a transparent profile of her will appear along the right side of the screen, and a song about death sung in German plays, with subtitles. At some point during this song, she will die.
The instructions are misleading, as they say you will walk her back out of the graveyard, ending the game, after it is done. I did three playthroughs, altering various things to try and see if she would survive so that I could, indeed, walk her back out and end the game properly, including going very slowly and letting her rest frequently and at length, in case it was linked to overexertion (perhaps as a way of punishing the player for not taking the time to appropriately appreciate this 'art'?). In the end, nothing worked. One of the only things I did not try was turning clockwise to sit down on the bench instead of counter-clockwise, and the idea that this could be the deciding factor is asinine, and I refuse to waste any more time experimenting with it because the game is so tedious and boring.
I honestly don't even know why this is for sale. I could see this being made as a hobby project or maybe some kind of tech demo, but charging money for it seems almost unconscionable. This is easily in the running for the worst game on Steam.
In short, if you still have any interest in this, just watch a youtube video of a playthrough instead. You'll get the exact same experience minus pressing the w key and then a or d to turn around and sit (which she does automatically). Don't waste your money on it.
