The Early Access build which I’m currently reviewing is now around 3 months old and the game has moved on significantly from what I’ve found. The full version of the game will be noticeably different and should be released on 6th June this year.
This game was developed by one man army – David Board, who was based in Alaska in time when I was getting preview code which apparently should make game experiance even more amazing .Game is platform adventure with puzzle elements to solve while levels are unfortunately mostly linear but thankfully to good level design you will have feeling that everything around you is completely open and full of secrets. Apparently game was originally planned to be a action platformer but in my opinion with good decision from David Board this game went to different road where story is in main focus. Game was inspired by LucasArt’s’s The dig and Another World, also by Cold War sci-fi movies posing questions about humankind’s desire for space travel.
You are taking roll of USA astronaut, waking up on far and unknown planet with ship wreck around. You are unable to find any of your crew while everything around is completely empty without any living soul except dust, wind and your needs for oxygen.
Although with that being said planet isnt completely in sand-brown colour pallet, in fact soon after begining game gives you not so lifeless mountain ranges and flats where you can clearly see designer skills. The interiors of levels are also surprisingly well rendered, which provides some of the creepiest moments through whole thing.
Eventually through your journey you will find out that this isnt really completely uninhabitable planet, while you are going to search for your crew you will stamble on abandon city full with old houses, a lot of russian logs where you are going to learn more about events which happened somewhere in time before our protagonist arrived on this planet. Seems like that Russians won space race after all ?
Experiments, green footsteps, mechanical arms and systems for activating devices which were suited for slim and much taller beings rather then for people are only one part of discovery which will take your mind on couple different thoughts about who or rather what made this wasteland as it is now.
How and when Russians found way to this planet ? How at first place they even brought that amount of people to build whole city or even more ? Hallucinations about empty beds perhaps even a russian girl who appears here and there, are complete mystery to everyone.
At current stage of the game you will not find any settings related to controls beside Invert Vertical Look and Auto Center Camera while ingame settings offers and Higher Quality Effects option. Another problem which can be quite frustrating for some people is not being able to strafe properly which kinda limits your observation while you are running in some direction but still it can be done after couple minutes of practicing.
Beta and currently available unfinished version is released on March 6th 2014 and includes only first six chapters from 20 expected overall which will provide you around 2 hours of gameplay if you are playing for first time and around 40 minutes of just rushing through the game.
Release date is only in couple days from now so be prepared for Lifeless Planet which might not be so Lifeless after all.

is speculative science-fiction in the form of an alien world across which you trek in search of answers.
- Gripping story.
- those who find classic science-fiction and speculation about other planets exciting.
Since experiencing the entire game I can say that all the promise of the Early Access demo was completely realised.  The story became even more engaging, the lifeless planet even more mysterious.  The resolution was satisfying.
It is difficult to classify this game without underselling it.  There is a great sense of exploration, like you are really trekking across an alien landscape, but the landscape itself - though it sometimes doesn't feel it - is very linear.  You have to learn to jet from ledge to ledge, but it's not really a platformer - even though there were two points in the game where I had to reattempt a jump repeatedly to get it right.
Although there are puzzles, don't approach Lifeless Planet as a puzzle game in the style of Myst et al, because the puzzles here are really there to emphasise the alien wonder of the place, not to challenge.  On that front the alien nature of this place is well thought out, cohesive and, looking back, with all the information, absolutely realistic, even though as you progress it is hard to see where all this is going.
No, what this is is an exploration of an idea of what life could be like on other planets, and all the rest is the vehicle necessary to take us on that journey.  From that perspective it is very well executed, both technically and as a story.  The game is beautiful and stark and alien, the plot is perfectly paced, and the experience is deep and engaging.  When you stumble across the journal of someone who was here before you, you spend the next part of your journey pondering the meaning of their words until the planet throws something new at you you distract you, perfectly bridging the human story and the story of planetary exploration.
You can complete the game in one sitting of about three to five hours depending on how long you marvel at the scenery and how much time you spend thinking on the things you find.  There's not a lot of replayability here, as with most narrative games, but it feels the perfect length, with no padding and nothing skimmed over in too little detail.
One word of caution: I would advise ignoring the achievements, as hunting them can break your immersion.  If they come organically, they come, although several won't unless you do things completely unnatural given the circumstances, like loitering for a long time at a location where there is no reason to loiter.
Beautiful and evocative and mysterious.  Just be aware that it cuts off rather abruptly at a certain point when things are just getting really interesting, as that's as far as this early access game has been developed at this point.  Still very much worth a quick play though, even in its trunctated form, as apparently more elements will be added to the game so far, as well as its continuation.

All in all get this masterpiece and enjoy a true classic.

At first glance, most people would be put off by the low quality textures and the dated geometry, and the updates such was reflective water or light casting would not be enough to consider this a remaster.
But underneath all that is a true masterpiece lost to the ages and remembered only fondly of a bygone era in console gaming. At it's core, Turok is a FPS from a time when you could carry around enough weapons and ammo to arm a small country facing down an actual army of soldiers, dinosaurs, aliens, or soldiers riding dinosaurs with rocket launchers.
You'll quickly start to realize that what the game lacks in beauty, it makes up for in fierce combat. There is no hand holding here. No hiding until the booboos go away. Just you and the savagery of The Lost Lands.

What a great way to revive a classic. The HD enhancements that NightDive did are spectacular and give new live to this already amazing game. If you like classic FPS, like Doom or Quake, you will love Turok.

I picked this game up one afternoon during the summer sale and started playing.

So it's rather successful by that measure. It's quite satisfying to take back ground from the creeper, and when one word is safe, jump right into the next. One more level. I don't think I've played the other Creeper World games, but it feels like after years of making them they've got a pretty good handle on what makes a Creeper World game work in that regard.
I've just finished the main
campaign, after 27 hours. (I play defensively and pause a lot. Your mileage may vary.) The campaign is pretty good at making each level just a little different, providing some new element of challenge and giving you a new ability to use. Some levels are more different than others.
The game's weakest moments, I think, are the maps that become simply an ocean of creeper. Any distinctive features of the terrain are all but lost under the sea, as you slowly entrench and advance. Maybe more aggressive tactics could prevent ending up in that situation, but since I wasn't actually
those battles, I didn't give up and try different techniques. Then came along a different map that makes things interesting again.
This isn't the sort of game you play for the story. Yet there is a story, told in bits of dialog at the beginning and ending of levels, which shows some significant thought has gone into the lore of the Creeper. I might have appreciated it more if I was familiar with the other games, but it provides some interesting atmosphere.
I can't comment on the other content outside the main campaign, but there seems to be a lot of it, with a strong focus on giving the community powerful tools to make more.
I played this on Linux (Ubuntu 14.04). Everything ran great there; the only hitch I found is that after switching out of the window with Alt-Tab, I had to hit Alt again after returning to the game to get the keyboard input recognized correctly.
To sum up: Surely not everyone likes this style of game. But if you're interested in this sort of thing (which you likely are, if you're looking into the reviews), I recommend it without reservation. It's an excellent implementation of the idea.
And also very good if you want to forget to eat or sleep.

I've been waiting to review this until I've thoroughly beaten the three levels there currently are. Not sure if more are in the works. I'm writing this as of version 0.5.3
Short version: Most unique combat in an RPG I've played in many years. The most tense RPG experience as well. Interesting physics that works very well with the style of the game.
So, the first thing to note is that combat in Exanima is unlike any other RPG I've ever played. The closest I could describe it would be to take Mount and Blade's combat, throw it into an isometric RPG like Diablo, and then add a heavy dose of physics. It takes a little getting used to, but that's not too surprising since it's so different. Some people can get frustrated, but give it a few hours of honest trying. Try different weapons. They all handle differently and have their perks. I found it to be a very satisfying system that generated new thrills in each encounter both in the arena and in the dungeon.
Speaking of which, I enjoyed both game modes thoroughly. Arena mode should definitely be played first, unless you like to die due to unfamiliar controls. Being in the arena gives you a great sense of progression as you down each opponent and loot their gear. Opponents get more and more aggressive and are generally smart.
The dungeon mode is very atmospheric and is quite tense. More tense than any isometric RPG I've ever played. In fact, extend that to RPGs in general. Once you get decent gear, learn how to survive, and take out a few zombies, the tension eases a bit. However, death still comes easily in this game. The tension also comes from the copious amounts of shadow in this game. You'll be stuck carrying a light source for most of the adventure mode.
There's not a whole lot actual game content in this at least just yet. However, I'm not at all disappointed in my purchase. I can't wait for either more content or for the release of Sui Generis, the game for which this is a prelude to.

A refreshing twist on the franchise.
If you've every played the Anno series of games before, you'll be familiar with the crid-craft system of perfect placement combined with 3rd party calculators to aid your gameplay. Typically it ended up with long grinds of scrolling through various calculations and tweaking your supplies in order to hit the sweet spot for supply vs. profit... It was fun for a while, but usually ended in utter boredom.
This new approach has decided to aid you with a more user friendly interface for keeping track of your numbers. Making supply vs. profit much easier to follow. Which in turn leave you more time to enjoy yourself building and refining your city and manufacturing zones.
With the addition of space and a whole new transportation system, the game feels more polished and refined. Sure it's a bit easier but, when you look under the hood, there's actually more to it. And it's still possible to get overwhelmed as new unlocks come along and your people demand more things. Especially as you have to jump from country to country (and space) in order to manufacture certain items.
Combat is better, with the dull and annoying system from the previous games replaced with more entertaining, almost arcade style, engagements that take place on their own special sectors. This gives you more focus on the task, as there's no city planning to do while dealing with enemy fleets. There's also the usual side quests sytem to entertain the player when they need a break from building. It's simplistic, but not bad.
All in all, a really fun and refreshing direction for Anno, with some extremely beautiful graphics thrown in for good measure. Ignore the hate and check it out for yourself. you might just be surprised!
Recommended!

In the 8 hours that I've played this game, I've only owned it for ~15 hours and I absolutely cannot get enough of this game. I was looking for a simplistic, but fun game to play late at night last night. (Not an easy thing to find on Steam as of late..) I stumbled upon Kingdoms and Castles and immediately fell in love with it. The simplistic but charming art style, the engaging yet afk-able gameplay was just a perfect fit for what I was looking for.
So allow me to list some Pros and Cons of the game..
Pros:
-Super charming art style
-A lot already in the game, so a lot to work towards
-Sounds in game are pretty good
-A great time killer
-Feels good to expand your town and get more peasants
-Game keeps it's difficulty throughout the game
-Replayability is extaordinary (as long as you don't mind starting over, which I don't)
There's a million things I could list off but those are a lot of the main things I love about this game.
Cons:
-Random events happen too often (Dragons and Vikings timing is pretty good, but the random fires happen WAY too often. I'm always rebuilding from fires and it's like a 50/50 chance you put them out, even with Wells)
-The game isn't always clear on what it wants (No tutorial) (You can have a surplus of food in your Granaries, but if you don't have a good enough "pathway" to them, your peasants will starve to death anyway, even with your surplus of food. I had all of my Granaries on the paths (roads) but it still told me that peasants were dying, and to make better paths to the Granaries. So I don't know what the game is asking from me)
-Late game you should change your city name to "Lag City" (I got about 4 hours into my city and built on the majority of this big island that I started on. Before I knew it my fps went from 120+ to ~40. It was really hard to continue playing with the consitant jitters and lost frames. I have a pretty beefy computer so seeing that was a little disappointing. It's still playable but it could definitely use a bit of optimization for the late game)
-Your advisers are really annoying (So you get these 3 advisers in the game; Argicultual, City, and Military Advisers. The Military Adviser doesn't say much until a dragon or some vikings come along, but the other two....They say the same four things over and over and over again. The reason this is so annoying is becuase there will be a giant "!" over your castle until you click on it. And they say the same four things so often that you spend most of the game clicking on your castle. Not anything majorly wrong with the game, but fixing that up would be a great quality of life update)
It may seem like theres a lot more Cons than there are Pros, but that's because I went into detail on the Cons so that hopefully a developer sees this review and acts on some of (if not all <3) of the Cons that I've listed.
This game is fantastic and I recommend it to anyone who needs a laid back, micro management games with a dash of charm added into the mix. The $10 price tag might not be worth it to a lot of people, but once this game gets some updates, it will be more than worth the price. I only have high hopes for this game.

It's a great-looking, cheap and easygoing city building sim. Definitely worth the maegre cost, but it has some very glaring flaws that prevent it from going from good to great:
- Map size quickly becomes restrictive once you get past mid-game
- Pirate raids are OP in the early game and irrelevant in the late game due to invasion mechanic loopholes
- There isn't a huge amount of building variation, and it feels like there are a few building cost balance issues
- Starts to get incredibly formulaic after multiple playthroughs,needs more elements of randomness (terrain types, natural disasters... multiplayer???) to remain interesting
- Generally speaking, once your city begins to cover more than half the map it feels like you've already won and there's no end-game goals or point of continuing, much like when it's you verses that one last AI in a Civ Domination victory
I'll summarise by saying that this game feels like a more relaxed, less punishing version of Banished, but as it is crowdfunded and seems to have regular updates, in a few months/years time this might become a staple of the city building genre. For now, it works well as just a quaint little game.

As an old fan of Quest for Glory and the point and click adventure series in general, I very much loved this game.
Quest for Infamy follows the adventures of Roehm.  Certainly no hero, Roehm is a roguish fellow, although he's not a complete villain either.
The game is quite huge in terms of places to visit and things to do.  The artwork for the game is well-drawn and it has an entertaining story with an interesting cast of characters.  It also offers a lot of replayability in that one can pick from a Thief, Brigand or Sorcerer.  While Thieves can sneak into houses the Brigands can engage in caravan attack missions and Mages can collect spell components and learn new spells.  More than just changes to the combat system, each class has its own unique storylines and its own way of dealing with problems.  For instance, while a thief may sneak past 3 unruly hunters using the thief tunnels the Brigand can simply fight them off while the Mage can cast a fear spell that sends them running in terror.  Each class has unique missions to accomplish and can befriend different casts of characters to learn more about the world around them and those who populate it.
The game's story itself is quite good and has a very dark, gothic style to it as well as mischievous and perverted sense of humor.  The game functions well as a loving tribute/parody to Quest for glory and the adventure/fantasy genre in general.  Longtime Sierra fans of olde will appreciate many of the Easter Eggs hidden throughout the game thought it's completely unnecessary to be an oldschool Sieera fan to enjoy the game in general.  The game also features very good voice-acting and narration to accompany the story.
There are some complex puzzles to the game that can be quite tricky and confusing though, but it's well worth the effort to make your way past them and find out what happens next.  The focus of the game is much more on adventuring and solving puzzles and soaking in the fun than on combat, so pure-adrenaline junkies should probably stick to Skyrim.  If you're easily offended and want something more PG you should probably stick with Quest for Glory instead.
Overall I'd give it a 9/10 and I do hope it has a sequel someday. :)

Let me open with a quick summation: Quest for Infamy is a great game!
Now, for those of you who like a bit more detail, there's certainly more information to share. To begin with the game is very reminiscent of the classic adventure games of the past. The fact that QFI draws inspiration from the Quest for Glory series is made obvious, not only by the name, but by the graphics, music, sound effects, and even characters. It is the finest example of this type of game I've played since QFG IV was released.
As not all of you may be familiar with these type of adventure games, I'll give you some details on game play. The core game is centered around exploring a fantasy world filled with memorable (and humorous) characters, finding out what their problems are, and helping them solve them. In Quest for Infamy you take on the role of a character who is, in essence, a self-centered jerk. However, as the player you have a fair amount of control over just how much of a jerk and just how self-motivated you actually are. In my case, for instance, Roehm was merely a smart mouth with a heart of gold deep down. Of course, that's all down to personal preference. It's just as easy (or easier) to be a genuine scum bag that goes around stealing or destroying everything he can.
Whatever Roehm's background motivations may be, creative problem solving is a major part of the game. A great deal of moving the game forward is about finding the right item to use in the right place at the right time. In similar games of yesteryears this could often lead to frustration. Quest for Infamy, however, manages to remove this frustration almost completely by leaving plenty of clues around for the player to follow up. If you're ever stuck, there's no need to bang your head against the same brick wall for hours at a time. You can simply pull on another thread until you have a breakthrough.
Another aspect of the game is combat. Although it's true that the system is fairly simple, it's also very enjoyable. Being able to bash bad-guys and loot their corpses adds a real element. The fact that it's simple (and even easy) doesn't take anything away from the game. Combat isn't the focus of Quest for Infamy, it's merely one of it's many enjoyable facets.
I feel I should also mention the voice acting. In most cases it was very good and all of it added to the experience. In all honesty, some of the microphone work could have been better. However, considering the production budget of the game, the job was very well done. I feel certain that the success of this first game (in what I sincerely hope will be a series) will lead to even higher production quality in future.
The music fits the game perfectly and the composer deserves hearty congratulations. I actually found myself humming some of the tunes absentmindedly. In my book that's a sign of a quality musical score.
My one complaint is about the language in the game. Although it's certainly not as bad as most modern television shows there are a number of curse words throughout. In my opinion there was no need for that. The writing is excellent and the humor often brilliant. I personally see curse words as a comedic crutch. It's one I feel QFI didn't need.
All in all, I feel that Quest for Infamy is an excellent buy. I'm hoping to soon hear news of a sequel in the works. I missed the Kickstarter campaign for the first game. I certainly don't want to miss a second one.

Many commonalities fondly recall the adventure era of PC gaming, back when purchasing a game didn’t mean beating it and there were no walkthroughs to guide you into solving the cryptic puzzles. At that time PC adventure games, unlike their console counterparts, didn’t require skill or reflexes, but rather patience, wit and persistence. They presented the player with gripping stories or humorous situations and each problem in the game was solvable only by the sharpest of thinkers. Long has since that age been forgotten by most, but die hard fans refuse to move on from the fascinating genre. Luckily enough, some developers are just as reminiscent of the time and are more than ready to bring the nostalgia back, and with crowd-funding options like Kickstarter, these games are now becoming a reality. One such game is Quest for Infamy, a point-and-click adventure which raised over $60,000 and gave hope to adventuresome fanatics everywhere. Does the game manage to bring you back to that golden age of the 90′s, or does it fall flat?
Quest for Infamy‘s gameplay stays largely the same but refines the already familiar points and introduces new modern mechanics to make an even more enticing experience. After escaping an angry baron, the cynical protagonist, Roehm, lands in an alien world where choosing whose side he’s on and what he’ll do falls upon the player. The game largely bases its likability on the humorous dialogues and situations Roehm gets himself in, with the lack of point and direction in the start only making the situation even more ridiculous. While the game soon does get a goal and a fantastically well written plot as mysteries arise all around you, the world moves and progresses unrelated to what the player does, making it seem alive and moving. However this isn’t only a point-and-click adventure game as it tries to combine certain RPG elements in the already established core. Some of these work to immerse you further in the plot while some of them feel tedious and tacked on. Having to eat, sleep and manage your money as time moves on, for instance, make it fairly challenging to go out at night, but they do well in making you feel like you are a part of the game world, something not a lot of games excel in. Sadly the combat is simply abysmal, lacking any kind of depth or ingenuity.
The world itself is beautifully made, every background flawlessly representing the diverse atmospheres and locations. The nostalgic art-style coupled with the small resolution and mandatory windowed mode do well in capturing that classical adventure climate, and are sure to bring any avid player back to that special age of gaming. From the lush forests to the medieval towns, this fairy-tale like world never ceases to amaze, and the events that periodically occur throughout the game make it feel alive.
This is also coupled with an excellent soundtrack that fits just as well as the visuals and manages to pull off every atmosphere impeccably well. And since there’s an insurmountably large amount of them, at no point will they get old so you will oft have a hard time leaving the screen you’re on simply because of the terrific tune playing in the background. The sound design further proves to be well made with the voice acting, speeding up the classical process of having to read every dialogue line. While the voice acting is cheesy for the most part, this is intentional and when the game gets serious the cast does a good job in doing so as well. Not to mention each character has their own personal actor behind them making the world even more immersing than it already is. Special props need to be given to the sarcastic narrator who delivers each line as humorously and condescendingly as possible, giving the entire game more personality.
Technicalities aside, this is still largely a point-and-click adventure game, and since the world is foreign to both you and Roehm, exploring it and learning about it can be satisfying. In fact the story and setting are one and the same, building atop one another as you progress – it’s very open-ended structure. There’s also a lack of hand holding as you can do as little or as much as you want in this stunningly realistic world, and this allows you to organically learn about the environment as opposed to just giving you info, making every conclusion gratifying. You will have to write down notes as you study the magnificent structures and learn about the intriguing and cheerful places you visit, whether it’s by finding items or conversing with the characters. The inclusion of a journal could have made this game a lot easier though, as some of the information you gain is easily forgotten. Since the game is far from linear, you can choose which characters to side with and how to go about playing the many sub-plots and quests that litter the game, which blend perfectly with both the world and setting. Not one person will have the same experience as every choice impacts the plot and tailors the rest of what will happen.
Since the game does feature such a vast and open world with varied locations and atmospheres, it becomes harder and harder to actually solve the presented problems. The usual puzzle structure is just as difficult to figure out as any of the games of yore, meaning you won’t be able to simply solve a puzzle by going from point A to point B, but will mostly likely have to run across points A, B, C and D just to get a piece of the puzzle solved, made even harder by the enclave of distractions and side quests which all offer more opportunities for new adventures and loot. And since there’s always only a slight hint and/or lead as to what you might have to do, actually drawing conclusions and managing to solve the puzzles is acutely enjoyable. The puzzles are focused more on exploration, dialogue and most importantly experimentation and then drawing conclusion from the information that you have rather than the usual mini games, even though these aren’t lacking either. And since you’ll usually prematurely get the items you require, seeing how the seemingly random trinkets fit into the story never fails to amuse.
Exploration sadly isn’t all rainbows and flowers, as your clicks have to be extraordinarily accurate to move on to the next screen and Roehm may sometimes glitch out while you’re trying to get him to do something.
Quest for Infamy isn’t lacking in problems, and it sometimes doesn’t even attempt to fix a lot of the ones the games of yore held, but it also manages to wholly bring you back into the nostalgic world of adventure games with captivating plots and witty dialogue. The large and diverse world feels alive as the player can decide how much or how little he wants to get involved with the unique characters and intriguing sub plots. The setting and story build on top of one another to create an unforgettable and believable experience and they both immerse you in the overall silliness of the quirky story. And while there are some design flaws, namely the awful combat system, pointless grinding and awkward controls, some of the layered puzzles, beautiful locations and enticing events will surely draw you in and lead to satisfying conclusions. Whether you’re experimenting with items or organically learning about the world, the game is sure to draw you in. Just don’t be fooled, this isn’t a game made for people with short attention spans and a desire to let off steam, this is a sophisticated game that makes you think and perhaps makes you laugh here and there. Quest for Infamy‘s wittiness is undeniable and it’s unique and organic flow of gameplay and story will leave even the veterans of this genre scratching their heads, trying to figure out some of the complex puzzles and mysteries in the hours of fun challenge this game provides.

I'm not good at writing reviews, so I'm gonna write a list because it's easier.
Good:
- Voice acting. Characters like Roehm, Kit and Rayford sound great.
- Puzzle design. Sometimes I did some clever things.
- 320x240. It's a pretty neat resolution. A lot of the artwork looks great, especially the backgrounds.
- Roehm. I like that he's got more personality and attitude. Similar games tend to have a main character with the personality of an apple. I'm not that fond of apples.
- That one guy wearing the clothing of the hero from Hero's Quest. He made me giggle.
- A lot of the writing is great.
Bad:
- Voice acting. Sometimes there's reverb, sometimes it's muffled, sometimes the accents makes no sense, and sometimes the voice actor honestly isn't good at acting at all. Overall, I like the voice acting, but it's all over the place.
- Puzzle design. Most of the puzzles are fine, but it's easy to do puzzles in the opposite order, and it's especially frustrating when you're denied to do the solution because you haven't triggered an event elsewhere which is an arbitrary requirement. There's also a few puzzles where logical actions not only fail, but give you a generic "Can't do that."
- 320x240. I like the graphics, but with the exception of the character sprites a lot of it looks like it was scaled way down. It would have been interesting to see it go for a higher res look.
- The premise of being a bad guy is neat, but you're not really much of a bad guy. You fight bandits, help out people, and well, have a bit of a potty mouth. There's a ton of wasted potential.
- Bugs, oh so many bugs. Background objects rendering in front of character. Clicking on edge of screen to move to next screen can be a surprisingly large challenge, especially in windowed mode. Some scripts can get very confused if you do things in an unexpected order. And I was able to find a way to skip a sizable portion of the game because I like exploring too much.
- The combat is kinda dreadfully boring. But I'm willing to excuse the game for it as the combat is dreadfully boring in every game of this subgenre.
If Steam supported horizontal thumbs up, I would probably lean more towards that. People who eat up adventure games for breakfast will enjoy this, but others might just get frustrated. I am definitely thinking a sequel has great potential though.

I'd absolutely recommend this game for puzzlephiles, but at it's current price point, many will object to such a short game for 15 bucks.

Grow Up is basically a side-grade to Grow Home. It discards the direct "upwards" linearity and sense of "height progress" and replaces it with a wide open environment to explore. You still work your way upwards using a wide varierty of tools, but the game "gets going" faster than the original - the movement abilities are more easily accessible, and decent jetpack/glider upgrades are available relatively early. Regular traversal never posed much of a challenge, and the game is more than happy to shower you in more powerful abilities than you know what to do with.
My least favorite aspect of the game are probably the checkpoint race challenges. They feel out of place and more tedious than rewarding. I'd suggest skipping most of them (besides the first one that gives the incredible BUG costume).
The world is as beautiful as the original was - with plenty of cave systems and gorgeous vistas to explore - but you'll generally be moving quicker through it than in the previous game, so despite being way larger it feels about the same. As the game's open nature gates progression less you can both "finish" the main objective quicker than Grow Home while also spending 10x as much time just aimlessly taking in the sights.
Grow Up - if only for the inevitable lack of surprising novelty - doesn't quite "feel" the same as Grow Home, yet my few hours of fun were easily as enjoyable and relaxing as my time with the original.

Do you like the old NES classics? If so, you'll love ASSimilation.
Taking inspiration from several titles belonging to the old 8-bit console ASSimilation comes with several different levels that remind of the old-school titles.
Movement is fluid and responsive, making the challenges in this game really fun to take.
The music perfectly complements the action and gameplay.
The difficulty of the game is vastly reduced compared to the first one, this due to the reduced amount of instant death-blocks all over the place. However the game still presents a fun challenge to beat and master. (Make sure to play on Old-school difficulty if you're used to old classics like Megaman on the NES)
The sequel vastly improves over the first tittle, for the most part.
The level design really shines this time around having different level mechanics across the 5 different areas of the game. Water levels, gravity shifting, portals, helicopters, something like the mine carts from the Donkey Kong Country series. The levels are more fun to play this time.
Collectibles on each level, upgrades that make the game more enjoyable and bosses that are not the same enemy with a different sprite!
No additional playable characters this time, though. Something that could definitely be a good addition to the game. And I'll admit the collectibles are not that hard to get, don't add that much replay value and the upgrades even when useful, could have been better implemented into the levels. (it took 5 hours to finish the game with all the N.E.R.D collectibles, upgrades and no deaths on each level)
The game obviously shines on its self-referencing humor, little nudges at several of the AVGN episodes and the staple humor of the Nerd.  But even if you're not a fan of the AVNG, you'll find the game enjoyable on its own right.
One of the biggest complains about the first game was definitely its over-reliance in death-blocks to create cheap deaths and artificial difficulty, this time the game claims to include less of them, which is true for the most part. However, as you keep playing you'll notice that these blocks are still present on great part of the game and sometimes they're all over the place with just a different sprite, sometimes even recurring to old tricks, like those “appearing” blocks on the haunted level from the first game.
The problem with the blocks becomes more apparent once you decide to go through the problem of completing levels without dying, a “Perfect” clear as the game calls it. You'll start noticing the placement, hitbox and recurrence actually starts to hinder the challenge making it more of a chore.
Well, you'll be glad to know that this time you can actually change the control configuration if you're playing it with a keyboard and it's pretty responsive too! You can also use a generic USB gamepad or an Xbox controller. Sadly still no resolution or video quality options.
While previously lacking an identity and just being nothing more than a weak parody, the games come back and becomes a solid platformer with lots of action and nostalgic value for those who love the challenges from the old 8-bit era. A great improvement over the first title and definitely worth getting, even if you're not an AVGN fan.

AVGN II: ASSimilation made me think about the quality of the first game. The first game, created by Clickteam Fusion 2.5,  is still a love-letter to the games of the NES era, specificially with the likes of Mega Man. However, the first game never seemed to have it's own identity due to the bland textures and unfairly difficult level designs. This sequel, though, improves on every level, and I am glad I pre-ordered it. The new game mechanics including the obtainable upgrades add more versitality to the Nerd, and thus, allows the stages to feature new- and more interesting- obstacles and designs that challenge your timing and coordination. By switching to the Unity Engine, Freakzone Games created a more visually-striking game. The color pallete makes the game stand out, and the retro-style lighting makes the game look beautifully retro. The story is just as lacking as in the first one, and the final boss,
. The sound track is just as great as the original, yet there's more variation to the tunes this time around. Overall, AVGN II: ASSimilation does a great job at fine-tuning out the problems of the original and creating a great, replayable, and overall fun experience. If AVGN 3 exists, I will buy it.

Much, much better this time around. The AVGN game series pays homage to classic games, particularly run-and-guns like Mega Man. It also is packed with watered down versions of some of the worst and nonsensical video game tropes, albeit without making the game a chore to play, as well as AVGN's own non-blocking commentary throughout the game.
The first game was good, but suffered from overly simplistic controls and its short length. In this one, in lieu of multiple characters, you get direction locking for firing and permanent upgrades based on NES accessories the Nerd donned during various cinematic sequences. (particularly the Nerd vs. Rob the Robot) This really streamlines the overall experience as you don't have to fiddle with awkward character switches and sudden control changes as a result.
As for its length, it's probably about 1.5x to 2x longer than the original, about equivalent to Mega Man X1-X3. There are 16 full-length levels (individual levels are shorter than in the original), the tutorial level (which is hilariously replayable), 8 miniboss fights in those levels including the tutorial one, and 6 boss-only levels for a total of 23. Your first run will probably last 2-3 hours but speedrunners could cut it to maybe 30-40 minutes or so, menus and cutscenes included.
The soundtrack is a mix of old and new tracks, but its scope reflects the longer length of this title.
Difficulty...it's almost
easier than the original. Hard (Old School) is the new Normal, since that difficulty still gives you kegs. (a secondary that recovers your health) The next difficulty (Hard as Balls) gives you only 2 beers and no kegs, (and nothing that replaces them either) shooting the difficulty of boss fights into the stratosphere.
: It seems they've added support for non-DirectInput gamepads, like the various SNES controller clones. AVGN 1 did not have this. Good for them for adding this support...it's a lot of fun playing an old-school game with a rigid dpad like NES/SNES had.
Last but not least, the humor and meta-references are surprisingly strong considering how they blew through so much A-material in the first game. The AVGN movie, the "feud" with the Nostalgia Critic, and Board James are the three major untapped wells they drew from and it all came together pretty well. Nostalgia Critic plays a role similar to Break Man/Proto Man in Mega Man 3 (plus his pattern is very similar), though it ultimately goes in a very different direction.
: One downside worth mentioning is it seems that boss patterns are way more RNG than in the first game. Minibosses and the Area 51 boss are especially RNG. This is somewhat compensated by "easier" high difficulty modes which give you more than 1 health and infinite continues, but it can become very frustrating nonetheless. This is still a minor issue.
Needless to say, AVGN fans who like run-and-gun platformers should find this one enjoyable.

Ever felt like being a humanoid Bird with a shortsword in one hand and a machine pistol in the other, driving a giant Aztec pyramid with rocket boosters strapped to it through space, looking for moons to strip-mine in a mech suit while literally haunted by a ghost, just so you can expand your galaxy-spanning agricultural empire?
If yes, then this game might just be what you were looking for!
It is definitely not just "Terraria in Space". Although it does, of course, have some similarities (the combat, thus far, feels quite similar), it does have a TON of other features which greatly distinguish it, not the least of which is space-travel.
The greater variaty of planets (and with it, biomes), many diffrent dungeons, the boatload of new NPCs gives this game a really different feel. And, mainly because of the NPCs and the central hub, the entire galaxy feels a lot more alive and consistent than the sandbox of Terraria.
It does kinda feel like an expansion of Terraria. Like that may have been just one of the many, many worlds you have access to now.
Unfortunately, I can't say much about the bosses, yet. After 45h of playtime, I only encountered four bosses and three of them boiled down to "dodge attacks until weakspot is presented, attack weakspot, rinse and repeat until done". So far, they were different enough to keep them seperate, but if this trend continues, this maybe letting down people who liked the bossfights of Terraria.
TLDR:  I certainly reccomend this game, especially for the combination of (very satisfying) exploration and "the sandboy-ness of modeling an entire planet to your vision"

It's very hard to give this game a pass/fail rating, but here's my take on it.
It's, in essence, very similar if vastly inferior to Game Dev Tycoon, a game also on Steam.  It's also less than half the price of Game Dev Tycoon, so I guess this could be your fix if you can't fork over the $10 for that game.
The graphics are positively hideous, as the characters look as though they were hastily designed in MS Paint or Photoshop.  The gameplay is functional, but is more complicated than Game Dev Tycoon which gave you simple mechanics that worked seemlessly to offer an experience more addictive than heroin.  Game Corp doesn't have that quality.  The tutorial is a complex induction course that, disappointingly, doesn't even offer much interactivity in the development of games like Game Dev Tycoon did.
Personally I wasn't able to make the game full screen as it crashed when I tried.  This meant I had to make due with the low resolution window making it near impossible to see the itty bitty graphics and text going on in the game.
Another problem was the music, in that it clashed cataclysmically with the tone of the game and was by default way too loud.  If you're wondering what music would fit for this type of experience, I'd point again to Game Dev Tycoon, which was backed with pleasant, relaxing, ambient elevator-like music that set the mood very well.  This game seems to switch rapidly between types of music that sound very over-produced for music that's just supposed to be a background soundtrack.
For $3 I suppose it's okay.  It's certainly functional, but it pales in comparison to Game Dev Tycoon, which is actually being very generous.
TL;DR: Alright for the price I guess but get Game Dev Tycoon instead.

So, Starbound.
Starbound is a 2D survival sandbox set in space.  Many comparisons can be drawn to Terraria, and yes, they are similar in many ways.  However, I will judge Starbound by it's own merits and not by those of another game.
-A vast, wide open universe to be explored.
-Appealing pixel graphics.
-Simple, yet satisfactory character customization.
-Much lore to be found about the world for those who want that extra depth.
-Simple, yet satisfying gameplay, particularly combat.  Movement is fluid and easy to control.
-Weapons and clothing are everywhere, you'll always be finding new things.
-Farming and colony building aspects.
-Highly moddable, the best part of the game by far.
-Active community, as far as I can tell.
-The story, while there, is average at best, lackluster at worst.
-Some people may not like fetch quests, and this game has plenty of them.
-The game can slow down in places where there are more creatures/people/NPCs.  Might just be me, but do consider it.
-To my knowledge, cutscenes are unskippable without a mod.  That's some nonsense right there.
-Some bugs and glitches here and there, but nothing gamebreaking so far.
Starbound is a very well made game with a thriving community and modding scene, but some core aspects may deterr you from it.  However, I believe the good far outweighs the bad in this case, so at least give it a shot.  You might just like it!

The story is, frankly, really bad, and lost my interest with the scanning missions. The exploration is the strongest point, but lacks variety from planet to planet. The combat is quite fun, especially since guns can destroy blocks, but it is missing depth and variety.
One of the big draw-ins of Starbound is its modability, something that I took part in. This is both a good and bad thing though. It is good because there are hundreds of community made mods that can fix certain parts of the game and make each individual experience unique. This falls apart when you realize how much mods are needed to make the game last longer. FU is a massive mod and overhaul that completely changes the game. It adds many things that I believe should have been in the base game, but now most likely never will be because a mod adds it. Whenever the game updates, there are sure to be many broken mods that need to be updated.
Multiplayer can become a hassle with mod conflicts, though for the most part it is functional. Definitely better than Terraria through Steam or Hamachi. Just prepare for teleporting teammates and enemies not taking damage.
Another strange thing is how poorly optimized this game is. I can run Metro 2033, Skyrim, F:NV, DXHR, Terraria, Minecraft, GTA:SA, and many other games with little to no framerate dips. This game tanks almost every time there is a massive shootout or a large number of destroyed blocks.
Overall, I would say give it a shot. I know I missed a lot of points in this review, but other people have probably said them.

It promises to have everything I want in a game. A well told story, a immersive world, a strong player skill based combat system. It feels real and even in Beta, has much of the polish of a complete game. The Developers love their product and the small team has really poured their hearts and souls into the game. It has a steep learning curve and rewards you with really feeling like you the player have gained experience. Not just another game of combat rolls. You have to earn victory with real risk assessment and taking care of your character.

Exanima is like an isometric Dark Souls with a unique physics-based combat system. If you're a fan of the Soul series' atmosphere and high learning curve, you'll probably be a fan of Exanima. Its combat is visceral and despite the rather unintuitive controls, actually very realistic. In all likelihood, you'll probably spend your first few hours in Arena mode learning how to manage distance and timing as well as how to utilize your weapon's weight and momentum. Admittedly though, the camera will probably be your biggest enemy. I don't know why the devs felt like the camera shouldn't snap to your character's back during combat, because most of your fights will be between you, your foes, and the camera. You will be tapping that spacebar. A lot.
While I can't fully recommend Exanima in its current state since it seems to be missing a lot of ease-of-life features, it seems like the final product has a lot of potential. Exanima is definitely a game to keep your eye on.

I found this game to be a complete joke.  How do you brag about your game's physics when your attack options are swing from right to left, swing from left to right, and do an overhead chop?  You guys know the pointy end of a sword is to thrust with, right?  Swords were primarily thrusting weapons?  Bueller?  A knife would be completely overpowered in this game because the attack range "right next to the guy" is the easiest one to maintain, and the attacks are so slow that there would literally be nothing stopping you from getting into his grill and shiving him to death. It's also amazing how nobody in this world really needs to use their leg muscles to swing with either, giving every weapon the virtual weight and heft of a nerf sword.

It's a difficult game. Very difficult. It takes a long time to learn to get used to the controls, to figure out good tactics on how to fight, and then more time making those tactics into a habit. And then each time your character dies, you need to relearn those tactics again. It's a deathly hard system, and it's very similar to Dark Souls in that way. Your character is no inhuman hero. Your character is only as good as you can make it, and that means you need to practice a lot.
This game does not hold your hand.
I've sunken almost two hours into the game and I've still only managed to beat the first 4 levels of the arena on novice difficulty.
A lot of people will be scared away by this. It seems a game made for hardcore gamers, and it is. It was made for the likes of those whom play Dark Souls, and admittedly, I'm not one of those.
But I still managed to get into this game. The story is told to you in fragments, you don't really know what's going on, but it catches hold of you.
The combat system does so even more.
It's tough because some of the controls are clunky. The fact that you must move your mouse a certain way to strike with more power, or in a certain direction is not something even hardcore gamers are used to. It's very much a system I would think would work better with a Wii or other motion controller.
Furthermore, movement is clumsy. It's impossibly hard to go where you want to go, and because these movement controls apply relative to your character, you have to pay constant attention to which way your character is facing, rather than trusting a camera angle.
But all of this, while they should be cons, feel... Right.
It's intriguing. It's innovative. And it's an incredibly captivating game in every aspect, from atmosphere to functionality and utility.
Even the level design was made with great care, and the graphics, though beautiful and almost photorealistic, run beautifully even on my mid-end computer.
I didn't expect to like this game.
It has, in two hours, become my favourite.
Buy it. Give it a try, because even if you're a casual gamer, this game is worth it, and you will fall in love with it.
And, thanks to Steam, if you don't like it, your money back guaranteed!
All in all, I rate this 10/10.

If world exploration and a story of secrets is your thing, get this game.
It is genuinely an experience that cannot be described properly. The environment and atmosphere are just stunning, and paired with a story full of secrets and mystery makes the player crave to keep going. I love it when a game makes you question things, try to figure out what's actually going on, rather than just handing you all the answers. The game reminds me a lot of Dear Esther as there are no monsters that need to be fought (thus far) and you are alone in this world (kind of...), but I feel that the story being told by Lifeless Planet is more compelling. I bought Dear Esther and plyed it a few times, and while the story was enjoyable, I have no real appetite to play it repeatedly. Lifeless Planet, on the other hand, I just cannot get enough of. I can't wait for the full release, or even to just get the next couple of chapters.
I will say that the controls can bug on you, but they're very rare and easy enough to fix. The graphics may not be the most advanced in the gaming industry, but are still very high quality and really shouldn't take away from your experience at all. The sound design is fantastic and I highly recommend playing with a good set of headphones.
All in all, I cannot recommend this game more, and I wish there were more games of this style.

For me, gameplay-wise, a uniquely frustrating experience. A lot of the original Anno experience has been gutted, the trading system is gone. The appeal for many is building on the moon. The devs knew that coming in so they hide it. First, the game says "Just build your town like you always do in Anno and to the Moon we go!" Alright I thought, so I build my little town noticing how weirdly fragile the economy in this version is compared to the past Annos (strange and inexplicable changes in production values) But wait! Some pirates are attacking and we can't just quite go to the Moon just yet. Damnit I thought, so I go through the dumbed down RTS-style little mission and beat up those nasty pirates. Now I'm thinking "Hey we're going to the Moon now right?" "NOPE! We're going somewhere better!" Me: "... Mars?" "No! The Arctic!" Me: -_- "Seriously?" So I go to the Arctic to build a new town, except it's not like the original town, it's waaay more difficult to manage in addition to being economically draining to run. You'll likely go bankrupt or run out of space to build before you even get to the Moon. I'm sure if I had actually finished the Arctic section the game probably would've tried to sell me a ♥♥♥♥ing time share before it would let go to the Moon.

Only drawback is the price (especially when you include all the DLC's, which you should since they add a lot of nice content and features), but other than that I highly recommend this game if you're into City-building.

I was looking for a casual city builder to take away stress and relax. This game hits the sweet spot for me, as it is easy to learn and fun play. It has an elegant design, accessible UI, and it is beautiful to look.
It is definitely not particularly involved simulator like Anno series or Banished, but has depth enough to keep you playing for several hours or more.
If there is a point to improve or critisize, I would say that it is the complexity. Adding a bit more depth with more buildings, or quests (but please no timers in a casual game!) would make the game even more fun to play and endure over time.

A love-letter to Quest for Glory that delivers in every aspect.
The guys at Infamous Quests got it right with this game. It is reminiscent of the good old games without feeling the need to recite them word for word. Beautiful hand-drawn backgrounds and character portraits, an interesting, funny story with memorable characters and true old-school mechanics. I am especially impressed by the feeling of epic scale and freedom in the vast lands of Quest for Infamy. I would however love if the developers could make the RPG elements more relevant to the game play. I also think it would be a great addition to include a female character option for the main protagonist in the next game.
Overall the feeling of interaction in such a grand world that lets me choose what to do next combined with a tounge-in-cheek story that never feels ridiculous sent me on an unforgettable adventure that fills my heart with joy! Thank you Infamous Quests.

The game is very much a homage to the old Quest for Glory series, but how does it compare?
The soundtrack is alright, none of the pieces are bad, and some are pretty good even. Still, nothing as memorable as most of the pieces in QFG.
The voice acting ranges from atrocious to great. Sadly, the narrator is one of the worst voices in the game and you'll be gritting your teeth at how aggravating it is. This coming from a person who loved Sadwick's voice from the Whispered World. Overall the voices are passable, with only a handful of bad voices and only a handful of great ones.
The writing is passable for the most part, except for the jokes and "generic" messages of the game(when you try to use an item at something that doesn't do anything), which are often painfully bad. It's possible it's just because of the narrator's grating voice, but I couldn't stand the game whenever it tried to be funny or witty in describing things or actions. The visual humor in the game was, after all, alright and even good at times, and I didn't try to play it with the voices off.
The graphics are as you would expect from a game of the middle Sierra era, although the character portraits are sometimes(minor characters only) extremely bad. Overall the visual side of the game is quite good.
I've only passed the game with one class, so I can't compare the alternative ways to solve problems, but mostly the solutions are logical and easy to come up with. A bit too easy most of the time. On the other hand, I faced two laughably poorly designed problems in my Brigand playthrough. Sadly, the other one is the very first quest of the Brigand story, which will leave you with a very bad taste in your mouth.
The overall story is alright, but some parts are extremely rushed and other parts aren't explained at all. It's possible I somehow managed to miss or forget some explanations or content, given that the game isn't too linear as far as point&click games go(for instance, I saw one of the main bad guys only twice in the game, in the beginning for a short monologue, and the final screen of the game for 5 seconds). You can do most of the things in the game in any order you want, which creates a dissonance between action and purpose, as you'll often be holding a handful of items you picked along your way just because you could, only to find out they're something very important that you're later on explicitly told to get. For instance, one character told me to get 4 pieces of a macguffin and explained it'd be a hard task and all that, and I already had 3 pieces in my backpack, creating a very awkward situation from the story perspective. There are also plenty of locations that I couldn't find a meaning to, although I suspect that's because they are meaningful only to the thief and wizard classes. Or perhaps I was merely too foolish to understand them or find out what they were about. Some were clearly alternative paths to take if you so chose, as you could in the old QFG games.
The combat mechanics of the game are lackluster and boring, although you can just skip almost all of them by just running past the enemies. So, pretty much the same as in QFG.
A badly missing aspect of the game, that was crucial to QFG, are skills. There are only a few skills in the game, that have barely any function. The fighting skills are meaningless since you can drink super-cheap healing potions when you need to(they cost 10 per, and you get 5000 coins within the first few hours of the game). Aside from them, there's sneaking, climbing and thievery. All of them are more or less only necessary for the optional content of robbing houses, which is pretty meaningless since you swim in money anyway. And since you can train the skills by just clicking repeatedly on a place, with no time passing, it is a meaningless excercise. The reason why it worked in the QFG games was that the games had a fairly strict time limit, so you had to choose what to do, when and why. Here, as far as I could tell, you have infinite time so the skill checks might as well not exist since you can grind them up if you choose to.
There is a sort of point tallying system in the game, where you gain infamy points for doing things. Unlike the QFG games, where you always saw the maximum amount of points, and could gauge your progress in the game and how well you were doing, here it seems meaningless as there's no comparison point. I got 300 points. I have no idea if that's good or bad. Also, the reasons for gaining points are seemingly random. Suppose you have 5 choices on what to say to a character, they all give different amounts of infamy points in increments of 5. That's the only difference, as far as I could tell. Obviously I'll need to play the game through choosing completely different options to see if there's a meaning to all of it. Sort of related to the points system, you can do small things that seem to have absolutely no point in the game, like giving an expensive gift to a character or the like. Sure, you get an achievement and a line of dialogue or two, but that's pretty lackluster for the cunning needed to purposely purchase an item, deduce whom would want it and give it to them. The deeds themselves aren't really reward enough, since there is little reactivity to it. Again, perhaps I missed something and didn't succeed in doing these "quests" properly, but as I have no way of knowing, it's frustrating.
Overall the game is pretty much as you'd expect from a serious fan homage to the QFG series. Some bugs remain(mostly voice clips mismathed with the text, some graphical bugs) but they didn't really affect enjoyment of the game. Nowhere near the quality of any of the QFG games, but enjoyable none the less, if you're a fan of the QFG series. If you have never played a Quest for Glory game, you're likely better served by playing one(all) of them rather than this game. But given that the main audience for the game IS the QFG-crowd, I have to recommend it. It's decent enough and will make you remember fondly the classics of yore.

Being an avid adult gamer, and actually KNOWING the creators of the Quest For Glory series of games, and speaking as a game developer myself (Pixel Piracy), I can honestly say that this game is akin to booting up my old pentium I and playing Quest for Glory again.
It hits all the notes, and then some, it goes so far out of it's way to provide an undistilled feeling of nostalgia, while being completely fresh and true to itself as it's own game that I can only give my most sincere thanks to the development team behind it.
I have spent years waiting for an adventure game as unique as Quest For Glory to crop up again, and the wait is now over. This game, to me, is Quest for Glory V (the 3d weird one they came out with at the end of the nineties DOES NOT count.), and yes I know it's a different studio, but this spiritual successor is THAT empowering, without lacking originality, that it deserves it.

Quest for Infamy is a wonderful homage to the glory days of Sierra On-Line, particularly the Quest for Glory series. The people at Infamous Quests don't disappoint in giving us a humorous look into the seedy underbelly of the world of Lonaria. After escaping from the clutches of a baron to the east, Roehm hitches a ride to the Valley of Krasna as he flees toward the north. Volksville, Tyr, and the surrounding countryside is filled with unique and interesting people that will either help or hinder your progress to save your hide. Let me summarise what I've seen so far and maybe that will help you decide whether to buy this game for 20 dollars or not.
First of all, if you are a fan of Quest for Glory series, you WILL enjoy this game - it has that same feeling to it. The art style does a great job at attempting to stay true to the classics and the music (at least for me) fits in the game perfectly. Regarding animations, this game succeeds with them and even the gory parts of the game have turned out good. As for the voice-acting, in general they've done a decent job with it and there are very minor flaws which probably won't even bother you. I've only encountered one monster but the fighting system is very simple and easy to learn (basically it's like in QfG, you hack, slash, stab or something of the sort). And last but not least, the game has a good amount of humour which you will witness here and there.
So in conclusion, aside from very small details regarding voice-acting, I would call this a perfect game. I understand 20 dollars is expensive for some people, but think of it this way - it's thrice or more times cheaper than your usual triple-A title on launch, so I would take it as a bargain if I were in your shoes, deciding. :)
EDIT: Alright, I've completed the game and I have to say that this game is TOTALLY worth the 20 dollars. It is very catchy, the world is just HUGE and the overall story is great. It's nice that, as others have also said, in the end you get to be a hero too as a perk. In any case, if you are a fan of good old Sierra games, you won't regret buying this game.

Grow Up is a 6.5-hour game (100% in-game completion) with a number of good ideas that I enjoy, but the change to open world brings both positive and negative changes. It’s still a mostly relaxing experience, but some aspects of the game frustrate me which the first one didn’t do. I still think that it’s a good sequel overall that failed to evoke the same feelings of joy and wonder that Grow Home managed to do for me.
Once again, you’re the clumsy, lovable B.U.D. and while riding inside of M.O.M., you both encounter a meteor storm and crash-land on a new and foreign planet. Your mission, collect the scattered parts of MOM and restore her to 100% functionality on the moon.
The gameplay should be immediately familiar for those that played the first. You have more Starplants to grow and different biomes to explore, including a place where mushrooms reign supreme. One of the other major differences is the rate you acquire different movement abilities since you have to cover more ground in this open world. You’ll be jumping, climbing, floating, utilizing different plant properties, jet packing, and gliding around a small planet. You’ll probably die several times too when hitting something at high speeds or drowning in water. Growing buds and riding those vines into energy rocks still feels great. It was as if I were riding great beasts and slamming their faces into floating rocks.
Some of the major differences between this title and the last is the inclusion of P.O.D., the POD challenges, being able to turn into a ball with a spin charge move, and the ability to drop seeds of scanned plants to help you along. POD allows you to view the globe and zoom in and out which makes finding collectables and abilities much easier; however, the quantity of them can still make the process take a big chunk of time. You can expect to collect 150 crystals, look for and scan 24 plants, and complete 40 POD challenges.
The challenges are a very weird inclusion in a series I heavily associate with relaxing or chilling out. They are all timed and some of them have plenty of leeway with 25-50 extra seconds available to complete the challenge. Others require multiple retries due to the very tight timing requiring fairly precise movements in a game with a klutzy robot protagonist. These challenges are the complete opposite of what the main game represents and I wasn’t very fond of them. I still completed them all as the skins were neat, but I was feeling very annoyed. I’d recommended attempting them after collecting a significant amount of crystals for upgrades and ability tubs.
So BUD can turn into a ball. Becoming a ball can turn a bad fall into a sweet bounce. Falling from space as a ball and then bouncing around the planet is somewhat entertaining since you don’t lose that much energy between bounces. You can also hold down the button to charge up a spin and then release it for a fast dash. Yes, you can roll around too. It didn’t see that much use for navigating the environment, especially once I had the glider upgraded to use the jetpack. Turning into a ball doesn’t seem like a useful addition to BUD’s kit and nothing seem crafted to take advantage of it, yet everyone should probably do orbit sized bounces at least once when playing.
Lastly, before you effectively turn BUD into a jet plane late in the game, plant seed tossing is a great way to reach higher places. I often used the bouncy plants before settling on the type that shoots you straight up. I definitely made great use of the giant lily pads to make water safe for robots. It’s a game mechanic I engaged with often, unlike the ball thing. Grow up is a beautiful and cute little game where your ship (M.O.M) crash lands and breaks into bits on a planet and you are tasked with collecting all the pieces.  The main twists of the game are:
1. In a sorta gang-beats way, triggers control the grip on your hands and your character walks...well oddly because the player model is run on procedural animation depending on what you are doing. Its not a clunky controlling game, really.
2. You basically need to reach higher and higher areas. You do this by growing plant life, climbing, gliding, rolling, and sling-shotting yourself towards your goal.
That much will take you around 4 hours but there are a lot of collectables and such if that is your thing.
- 4 Starseeds to grow to completion
- 150 crystals (which give you more energy)
- Plants to research (as you can plant new ones anywhere after doing so)
- 40 challenges to complete. These tend to be (as I could tell) timed races.
It is a short game for just the main game, but there is a lot more there if you want to 100% it. A very fun game that is beautiful with some really breathtaking moments, given the style of the world and the art in the game. Worth a playthrough. :)

Games like this make me wonder why Greenlight even exists.
Set in "another world" of the Half Life universe (which seems to be just an average ship), you play as scientist Andrew Winner, who must go to this new world to find an "artifact," as the title screen says. The story feels like some terrible fanfic, complete with a nonexistent plot and terrible grammar.
The actual control/feel of the game is good, mainly because it's Half Life (aside from a few areas where you can get stuck and must reload a saved game). But don't expect anything new or exciting. The store page of this game says that there are a ton of new features, such as new levels, soundtrack, and "high definition models." After playing through this game twice, I can safely say that the store page is a gigantic lie. While it does have a new soundtrack (which is decent at best), the other new additions are barely noticeable. The "new levels" consist of going to the back of a small ship, talking to a guy with broken English, going
to the front of the ship, and having to fight the final boss from the original Half Life. The "fight" if you can call it that is just you shooting in the air while running in circles for about a minute. By the time you realize it, you'll have beaten the entire game in about 10 minutes. As for the "high definition models," they are no better than Blue-Shift's updated visuals.
Of course some may argue that it's a mod, and that it isn't going to be high quality. But if you do some searching, you'll find some amazing Half Life mods that were made years before this. The fact that this even got greenlit still baffles me to this day. On the bright side, it's free, so you can at least play it just to see how bad it is.
It's only good if you use the select game mode to play other and better mods.

Turok is one of my favorite games of all time. And I couldnt be happier with its arrival on Steam! This is a pretty faith 1:1 coversion of the original game on the N64/PC to modern PC systems. So this is not your typical "Remaster" game that changes the whole graphics and gameplay, while ruining or forgetting some stuff in the process. And let me tell you something, Turok: Dinosaur Hunter is STILL GOOD AS IT IS! So I'm glad how they decided to aproach this. Instead you get the same classic game with slight but welcomed graphic improvements and the obvious advantages that mouse and keyboard inputs provide.
To those that dont know anything about this game, Turok is a classic FPS that wasnt like anything back in 1997 or even today. This game introduced something that FPS didnt have back then, platforming and verticality, in fact I think it was the first game that did. Basically this game plays like DOOM with Super Mario Bros. levels of jumping all in a 3D environment. The first thing you'll notice is the incredible speed your character has when you move around. And jumping is not just a secondary occasional action, its the key aspect of the gameplay and without decent control of it you will get nowhere as your shooting abilities wont be enough if you want to progress. But dont worry things can only get more fun and feel natural as you make your first jumps. The game teaches you the basic and advanced actions in a tutorial that WILL help further in the game, such as "long jumps" and "diagonal jumping".
The level design is very clever and complex, they are like laberinths, so forget about just corridors and buildings, you are out in the wild with dinosaurs and other hunters that want to cut your head off. The weapons as with all Turok games can be as simple as a pistol or crazy and inventive like the Quad Rocket launcher or the Chronoscepter which you must find all the parts to assemble it if you want a better chance with the final boss.
The improved PC controls and a simple increase in color saturation and lighting has made wonders to this old game. Dont let the blocky models and old looking textures fool you, this game still has a lot to offer today, specially in an era dominated by online multiplayer modes and the lack of fun and replayable campaigns in FPS games. Also, the gamepad support is still excelent, probably because the original game was meant for a console so if you are looking for an FPS game to play while sitting comfortably in your couch, look no further, this game plays great with BOTH mouse/keyboard combo or Gamepad. And trust me there arent many fps games that play this good with a gamepad (at least not without autofire, LOL), hehe you can thank me later.
I think this game still has the potential to entertain us for years to come, and hopefully it will be here to remember us and future generations what a fun FPS campaign is made of and what we should demand in FPS games and what not. Give it a chance I promise it wont let you down.
One last thing: a Real Dinosaur Hunter plays withouth crosshairs! Happy Hunting! ;-)

Lifeless Planet is simple. Very simple. But a return to simple game mechanics and letting intrigue take the wheel is something we definitely need to see more of. LP, while still in Beta state and definitely not finished yet, is regardless one of the most enjoyable games I've played.
Ever.

You feel nervous at times, but never get the sense that you're in danger. There is only moving about, some light world interaction, mostly just running and jumping about. No combat. Thankfully.

I cannot wait until this game is finished, and I have the feeling that once it is, it will be quite the adventure.
If you want an experience, buy this game.

This is the first review I've ever written, and I felt compelled, because I'm afraid this game might get overlooked by those surfing the store.

The physics engine is so refreshing. While unlikely if you're walking, if you're moving too fast you can easily trip over objects laying on the floor, or just trip, and take an enemy down with you, both stumbling up to try to bash the other's brains out. If you're iffy on this game, I would suggest going ahead and putting your money in to it. The learning curve is quite steep, taking quite a bit of time to master, but the basics only take a few minutes to learn.
