The most promising early access game available to date and with a forseable completion date given by the developer there is no reason not to buy this game.
A real old school dungeon crawler with a twist. Exanima forces and rewards you for being perceptive and aware of your surroundings, with an emphasis on searching every room chest and corpse to either progress with a key or find beter gear. Without any sort of HUD (aside from a health and mana? bar) Exanima very much makes the player look around the room and with no hints to pick anything up it is very much up to the player to interact with their surroundings and pick up what they see.
Aside from being this old school game Exanima is very focussed on being a game with an emphasis on physics whether this be to determine how much damage you deal to an enemy as you bash their head in with a blunt object or to hold a lever down with a rock (or to fall over a twig) you must be constanntly thinking physics.While this may seem obscene as you stumble around falling into your enemy once gotten used to clearly adds a huge level of depth to the game.
As mentioned the physics play a big part in this games combat this also allows the combat to be very strategic and indepth as every strike you make could be made more effective with how you strike an enemy and with what weapon. On this note Exanima can be considered a very unforgiving game with at current no check points or save points this game will leave you contstanly on your toes with the determination to not sent back to the beginning. Some people may say this is bad but if you enjoy a hardcore game like Dark Souls then this game is for you.

I discovered this game purely by accident. As a sci-fi fan I long for a game that can take me to unknown worlds and let me explore them and Lifeless Planet seemed to be that game.
I immediately acquired the early access and was very satisfied to it's initial promise. Plus, doing a bit of research I discovered that one of the main influences for this game would be my favourite game of all time - Another World - that not only is an excellent sci-fi work but, most importantly and in my personal opinion, it holds until today the top spot on how game mechanics can help you deliver a superb narrative.
And in did, on the early stages, the game delivers. The mystery starts to unravel at a good pace, the environments do a great job on setting a mood by first offering the familiarity, and at the same time the duality, of a world that can be either Earth like or Mars like, and then throwing you with a very interesting twist that finally launches the adventure.
Here the problems start, as the game is unable to hold the standards of its good beginning. With landscapes becoming tiresome and the wonders of exploration diluted on unimaginative mechanics and intrusive narrative.
Sadly the game never overcomes completely the said narrative and mechanics problems, but the world does gets better, with some excellent stages that made me connect again with my initial appeal for this game - I just wanted to feel like I was on another planet. Also, as you get to the latter stages, it manages to bring the narrative back to life and makes you realize that this could in fact be a much better game, but maybe due to inexperience it kind of get lost in it self.
Still, despite the wasted potential, I say it's worth to buy. Specially to sci-fi fans like me that feel like videogames lack offer when it comes to sci-fi adventures. Also, on the science part, the attention to (exo)geology is really cool.

I would not buy this game, wait for Sui Generis.
Ex Anima is essentially a smaller-scoped standalone game that gives you a taste of what the eventual full size release (Sui Generis) will play like. Basically this is Ground Zeroes, and Sui Generis will be Phantom Pain.
What you get with Exanima at present (and I have a feeling this is unlikely to change very much at all) is a single static dungeon with 3 or so rather large floors to explore, and an arena mode.
The dungeon is really pretty boring as far as a dungeon crawl goes, I can't think of anything that jumped out at me as something I hadn't seen in a dozen fantasy sewers before. The only unique thing about the exanima dungeon crawl is that it's more "hardcore" than your standard action-rpg due to the deadliness of the enemies (when you don't exploit their intentionally basic AI) and permadeath. It's as if someone took all the concepts of a hardcore, old school dnd style dungeon crawl, and then carefully removed any flavor or personality.
In addition, there is an arena mode, in which you will likely spend most of your time with this game. It's a no frills succession of fights that get increasingly difficult, and serves as a way to showcase how the various weapons in the game work, as well as show off the armor.
$15 does not buy you a tutorial for the combat, which is a head-scratcher considering that this is by far the most unique action-rpg combat I've encountered so far. The best explanation of the game's combat system that I can give you is that your character is a physics-based marionette, and you are attempting to control them from the rafters. If there was any reason to buy this game, it would be to see the physics.
Overall, I can't reccomend buying Exanima. Once the novelty of the combat mechanics wears off, you're left with very little game. This is a $15 demo for a much larger action-rpg, and I imagine that once Sui Generis comes out this game will come bundled with it or go on sale for pennies for anyone interested.

Two men facing each other in an arena. One dressed head-to-toe in full plate, the other in chainmail. Dramatic music trumpets through the room. The one in plate wields a two-handed hammer, the other a claymore. A clash of titans. They edge toward one another, keeping steady on their feet.
Claymore takes a swing, hammer steps back, then lunges forward in full swing, claymore blocks with an almightly clang of metal. Hammer swings again, risky, as claymore dodges to the side gracefully, slashing along hammer's back. He yells in agont, but this does not deter him. He gathers himself and sets himself on the defensive. The dance around one another, carefully assessing each other.
Claymore lunges, hammer counter-swings, but claymore was feigning, and immediately slashes in reverse. Its over for hammer...almost. Sheer luck dictates the blow struck his hammer's shaft, and grants him precious time to counter. A sharp swing doubles back along claymore's jaw. No cry of pain, no scream. Only blood. The blow landed, and was deadly. Claymore staggers around, clearly dazed. Hammer steps forward, claymore lunges. Hammer dodges back, the sword gliding off his chainmail pauldrons. Claymore swings back, becoming desperate now. Hammer crouches, dashes to the side and brings the mighty weapon directly into the ribs of his opponent.
This time he screams. His sword falls to his side, his body limp and lifeless. Hammer is the victor. What a fight.
"How hard could it be?" I asked myself after closing the above youtube video. I promptly bought the game, played the game and discovered just HOW difficult a truly physics based combat system can be.
Every swing of the sword, every dodge, or dash, feels weighty and dangerous. Even running down a corridor I felt as if my character might stumble and crack their face open on a stray rock. This isn't a bad thing. In the context of Exanima, physics is everything, and when you master it, and use it to your advantage, you can be unstoppable.
But it takes time, training, and quite a bit of frustration.
After watching the video, I tried a fight. Swung my sword too fast, twirled around three times, and fell over. My opponent walked up to me and brought pain down on me until I was dead. No remorse. No mercy. No chance to get up.
Now, 8 or so hours later, I'm dancing around my foes, slicing jugular's, breaking ribs, and crushing skulls, and it feels fantastic.
In a nutshell, if you're in the mood for some heavy, brutal medieval combat + a pretty nifty dungeon crawler thrown in around it too, then give this one a go. As far as early access titles go, I've gotten my money's worth out of the arena alone. But be warned, the controls take some getting used to, and if you can persevere, you will be a total badass.

In my opinion, this game is not recommended at full price compared to what its predecessors have. This game is also a tough sell. The only version that is recommended is the Ultimate edition.
I am starting with combat because in my opinion with the changes it should not be in. Anno’s 2205 combat is weaker compared to its past installments. Since there was a lot of changes made to trade routes, what ships you interact with, and now it’s a multisession singeplayer experience with different factions of your corporation on different maps. It has defeated why any combat should be in the game in the first place. It’s true the Anno franchise focus is not on combat but it’s past titles had purpose for it being in. With the new formula combat is just tack on feature. On the bright side you don't have to worry about pirates in the very begining of the game. You do have to worry about attacks with the frontier dlc but you don't have defensive structures or cool toys. Just a navy you have to call in to your sector. The game could have benefited if the feature was cut completely and resources + time could have been spent elsewhere. Also, the combat is force upon you for getting special resources.
Trade Routes are set up in the menu as always with some changes of course. You do not need a shipyard to build different ships to haul items for your citizens. You also don’t need to purchase the ship with currency and resources. It just goes onto your money budget expense.  Also, you can only transfer one item per ship per island where in past games you can do multiple items and set it up for multiple islands.
The level design decent at best. I like the cool sector affects and special missions that get you special bonuses. Other than that, compared to its predecessors the game could use a map editor with community driven content to help the game replay value. Since they took out random map generation even though it did not make significant variety changes in the maps. It was enough to help the replay value of the game.
Note: Cities Skylines is a different city game but it offers tons of replay value with community driven content. Blue bytes should have taken note of this before making it a complete singeplayer experience. Not having community driven content when Cities Skylines does makes it hard to compete in the market. Ubisoft should have at least let them implement steam workshop support.
The NPCs interaction is weak sauce compared it predecessors. In Anno 2205 NPC interaction is mostly through quests, stock market, and trade with certain ones of course. Very limited where as in past games you compete not just in stock market but resources, military power, trade, and land. You also had diplomacy. This adds to another reason to remove combat.
The Orbital building is underwhelming. Instead of taking advantage that in space you can build in whatever direction you want you are limited to a 2D building plane. I had a lot more fun being amazed at building things on the moon. Building the Artic, Temperate, and tundra regions is also a lot of fun. This dies out with the limited map variety.
The different factions in your corporation require different regions. Scientists in tundra + Artic regions, employees in Temperate region, Engineers on the moon. All contribute to research on the Orbital station you built if you did not get too bored building it.  This contributes to a problem the new anno game has compared to past games. Building variety in your main city. Past games you had three factions with different looking buildings in your main city. This is no longer the case.
This brings me to another main problem I have with this game, the multisession. You must load into every map to make a supply chain to satisfy and advance your faction in another region. You did not have this in other games. While I like making big cities. The tradeoffs they made to make big cities in this game was not worth it my opinion. I also notice they recycled assets from Anno 2070. While recycled is not unheard of. Some of the ways they do it looks bad.
Overall Anno 2205 is not a bad game. I like it but it has its faults. Something I would like to recommend at full price even to help the developers but compared to what you get in past games. You get your moneys worth with replay value in past installments. This could have been easily countered by mod support since they made this a singleplayer only experience.

This review will hopefully not be long, will touch on the highlights of this game.
--The story plot line is meh. You can get into it but the grind for materials makes it less impactful.
--This is a sandbox game. You can build anything you can think of like apartments on the moon that double as torture chambers. (My friends are a bit sadistic. :)   )
--The model designs of the main characters are unique and interesting but I love the random NPCs that teleport in at the 2- Stop tele-shop.
--This game is full of choices. You can choose to rebuild a planet full of ruins. You can also choose to level a planet to ruins or to nothing. The choice is yours, just don't go crazy like I did. Those poor agarans.... (I am also a bit sadistic.)
--The bosses in this game are reasonable to fight. Just be smart and run into end game level bosses wearing a loin cloth and wielding a bone spear. I did that once.
--The crafting system is decent but has some flaws. Some restrictions on items are a bit irritating like certain species can only build that armor. That same armor can be bought from a random merchant and worn by a different species. The crafting of food is decent. I love mushroom soup.   :)
--The multiplayer support/ connections for this game is hit and miss. There have been days my friends and I have no lag or dcing and there have been days where my friends appear to be floating and have blank character models with demonic symbols on them. Fun times and lag is evil.
--The updates to this game are wonderful. The mech and space station update has now made it even harder to leave some of my solar systems. As well as the tenants I have on the moon.
--Lastly, the modding...    My god the stuff I have done to this game. I have mods for my character, mods for the planets, mods for the solar systems, mods for the species, mods that change the entire game and mods that I would not write on here. (NSFW)
Overall: I highly recommend this game especially if you have a few friends to play it with. If you prefer solo games, this game is still fun to play by yourself especially with the new updates of tenants and your own personal mech in space. It just adds more insanity when you have friends. Also beware of random switches in tombs underground. I know this from experiance and death. Lots of death.

Story: Doesn't apply as the game lacks any story whatsoever.

Kingdoms and Castles is a streamlined city building game, combined with a tower defence element; the game's cast of antagonists consists of  grumpy vikings, ogres and dragons who regularly pop by to ruin your stuff.
Your defences from the various invading forces are your walls, towers and armies.
Walls  can be stacked to stupid heights, and one of two artillery pieces can be installed on the top with a higher tower providing more range.
Army management consists of hiring champions who are able to recruit soldiers from barracks- this process requiring a fairly established economy.
Principalities and Hamlets is perhaps better thought of as the most complicated turret defence game you will ever play.
The town management system revolves around creating  efficient and simple production chains to keep everyone fed and happy enough to collect  coin needed for town services and defence.
The game features 3 different modes with varying degreees of difficulty- I mostly played the hardcore mode as I found the normal a little bit too easy but I'm sure both of the easier modes serve as a means of practicing or just enjoying a more casual experience.
The game had a number of bugs while I played but also a fairly frequent slew of patches.
They  seem like a company interested in supporting their product, which for a 7 quid game Is good to see.
I spent about 40 hours with the game and look forward to checking it out in the future if they release any more content or difficulty tweaks.
Unfortunately in the late game,  once you have fortified the entire island, the vikings sorta give up which leaves  you building for its own sake in the hope the vikings would pluk up the courage to mount a worthwhile  assualt which may never come; some patch or rebalance is required to keep this game interesting past this point.
I definitely got my money's worth with the game and would suggest Nations and Motte and Bailey to any fans of city builders looking for an experience requiring zero learning or for folks intimidated by denser games but who want to try running their own town.
Empire and Towers Is like a big colourful Fisher Price city sim, its got its shortcomings and its bugs, but as of now is a fun timesink where you get to effectively build a medieval megacity. For me, this game could only be more awesome if someone actually made a magacity or 40k style hive city reskin. I'm not a fan of overtly cartoony graphics but this game gets a pass, would recommend.

This game is a lot of relaxing fun for the right price, and I totally endorse it.  That said, there's just one weird drawback: you can't force orders.  This is really only frustrating if you want to react to threats (vikings / dragons) with any agency.  Maybe that's part of the challenge and it's just lost on me, but you can order a structure to "close" thus saying "don't work here".  Makes a lot of sense to not have your archer towers fully staffed all the time with no threats... but then if you want to pause time as soon as a threat shows up and "reopen" your military structures... nothing forces your townfolk to staff them or do it.
Not being able to force that order throws that fun bit of gameplay out the window.  And it's weird for it to be that way if they're going to have that mechanic at all.  Same for hospitals and plagues, same for having queued "chop wood" orders, and being out of wood.
Sounds like a big drawback but I still really enjoyed the game.

The house looks pretty good overall, not AAA quality, but I've definitely seen much, much worse. The puzzles are good, ranging from easy and predictable to clever and original. The atmospere is appropriately creepy with some well timed jump scares. And there's a creepy story that is told through cutscenes (so no endless reading of notes, scraps of paper and diary entries) with decent voice overs.
But there are also a bunch of problems with this game.
First of all it's unclear where and when the game is set. Most clues seem to point at turn of the century England (around 1900), with the investigation taking place about 20 years later, so around 1920. But there are many items in the game from later time periods. There are cardboard boxes in the hallway and kitchen with the date 15-5-2007 stamped on them. On a chalk board displaying a calender the word "yoga" is mentioned. Yoga was invented in America in the 1960's and didn't exist before that, certainly not around 1900. In the living room a 1960's style television is seen (and used for a puzzle that is inspired by the lcd styled numbers like the ones you see on an electronic calculator). A 1950's style telephone is also found in the living room and I could go on. I could have lived with one or two minor mistakes, but the more attention I started paying, the more anachronistic elements I discovered.
While the puzzles work well and some are rather clever, they aren't well integrated into the story. There is no (contextual) explanation given why there are so many puzzles strewn about this house. Some of the more traditional point-and-click style puzzles work well, but the others break any immersion of being in an actual haunted house.
The story is creepy and I like the fact that it is told through flash backs rather than through a series of diary entries. But the mental state of one of the characters makes no sense. First she is presented as being psychotic, but later she mentiones that she no longer has short term memory (like the main character in Memento). Which is a completely different kind of mental illness, often caused by the brain being damaged after an accident and not something that is the logical conclusion of being psychotic. At the end of the game the developer mentions that he/she was trying to convey some ancient bhudist wisdom. Without going into detail I can only say that what is seen in the story doesn't match at all with what the developer was trying to convey. Which is a pity because I admire that he/she was trying to do more than just tell a creepy story.
As many reviewers have pointed out the English seen in the game is badly translated, which seems to be a returning problem for a lot of non-western based indie developers.
You're given journal early on. This is usualy used to give subtle hints on what to do next and to summarize the story so far. Not is this game. Three entries is all you'll get and they're kind of pointless.
My last annoyance is the fact that the main character is called a telepath, psychic and exorcist. He never shows any signs of being telepathic (being able to read minds or project thoughts in other minds) or of being an exorcist. Calling him a psychic detective would fit the bill with what we see him do. But telepath and exorcist?
In conclusion I'd like to give this advice to the developer:
- Do some research about the geographic location and period of time you set your games in. Find pictures, paintings, examples of news papers and magazines of the appropriate period and location and use this to determine how the game should look
- Try and blend the puzzles into the environment or give a good reason for the obviously gamey puzzles to be in the game (like in the 7th Guest)
- Find someone to proofread and correct all texts, preferably someone who speaks the language natively and if possible uses it professionally (f.i. someone who writes, translates or teaches a language for a living)
- If you use a mental illness as a central part of the plot, again do some research, find out how it would effect someone and use this to advance the story
- Similarly if you have a message that you want to convey that is based around some key ideas, look up the defintion of these words and make sure that the characters representing these ideas behave appropriately and that their motivations are clearly convoyed to the player

Grow Up—like its predecessor, Grow Home—is all about exploring a vast, open environment in search of crystals, plant life, wild animals, and nurturing massive plant stalks to reach higher areas. Just like in the past game, you play as everyone's favorite red robot, B.U.D., but now you have all new gadgets to play with. There's a new mission to boot: rebuild M.O.M., your space ship, after crash landing on a massive, foreign planet.
Grow Up improves upon the fun gameplay first introduced in Grow Home by giving the player several massive biomes to expore (compared to Grow Home's single biome), new means of speedy tansportation (such as a rocket-powered glider), and all new challenges to face.
In short, Grow Up is a fantastic sequel to what was already a very fun game. The visuals, albeit rather simplistic, can be quite beautiful at times; the soundtrack is as great as ever; the new missions are challenging and a blast to play; and the witty humor is at an all-time high.
I highly recommend picking up a copy of Grow Up.

Downsides of this port are the steep price of it and there's several fun bugs missing, such as the grenade launcher shot against dead enemies. In the N64 version, even though they were dead, they were still screaming when you shot them while they flew in the air. As for the grenade launcher, thats a very deadly weapon, against yourself. Even if you think you are outside of the grenade explosion radius, you are still inside it. I do not remember grenade doing this much damage on yourself.

I beat the game on normal difficulty in about an hour and a half.
The nerd now gets upgrades instead of character switching, he can slide down walls like in Megaman X, and the stages are broken out into bite size levels that are comfortably finished in 3-4 minutes if you get a solid run. There's some laughs to be had and the levels and enemies are all tributes to the AVGN series. It's not nearly as good as the first game but it's still worth playing. I would definitely pick this up if you liked the first game but you thought it was too hard.
With that in mind, my biggest complaint is that they weren't kidding when they said they made it easier than the first game. The level design is still a bit tricky but I managed to beat the game on normal without seeing the game over screen. They have higher difficulty options but that doesn't change the level design, it just gives you less health and the enemies noticeably more health. Spamming fire isn't fun. I started out on "Hard as Balls" before dropping down to "Old School" because I was blowing out my arm/elbow trying to spam faster... then I dropped it down to normal for the same reason after starting over and beating 2 bosses. Levels based around spamming fire as fast as you can have taken the spotlight over the first game's brilliant platforming. I'm honestly not convinced that you can beat the damn
level on Hard As Balls without an auto fire controller. It's really that bad.
They also removed the death screen that had a randomly generated nerd phrase which was quite possibly my favorite part of the first game. No more quotes about how he would rather have a hobo spit up his butt than play this♥♥♥♥♥♥infested game are waiting for you when you die. As trivial as it may seem, having the nerd also raging at the game along side you for a good laugh really was an amazing counterweight for the rage inducing levels. It was a perfect combination of diabolical level design and a hilarious death screen that would frequently make me swing between screaming at my TV and crying laughing.
Just as much fun as when I was a kid. Ran smoothly and had no problems of any kind. A classic game that is a must have for fps fans.

Oh where to begin. I would almost recommend this one. They've at least learned a bit from Infinity 1.0.
The premise is the same: Playsets (campaigns) and free play + challenges and some new extra challenge levels. This time, however, your characters can level up and use special skills, which is quite neat. The main gameplay is also smoother for the most part. However, there are some game-breaking bugs in the game, for example, getting stuck in walls (which can at least be remedied by loading a save, but still), or the game simply crashing after a certain cutscene. Every time. I guess, if you wanna fool around a bit it's ok and kids will probably have quite a bit of fun with it, especially when compared to the first one. I will, again, focus on the playsets and rate them from best to worst. So, there are only 3 this time: Avengers, Guardians and Spiderman...quality over quantity? Well, yes, and no.
Guardians:
- This one is hands down the best one. It's got interesting and fun characters, a moderately good story and really nice presentation. It's also the only one that makes following the main story a piece of cake, instead of being distracted by side quests and not knowing which quests advance the story. You play as Starlord (or any of the Guardians or villains) to repel Ronan the Accuser, who is after the Infinity Stone you've stolen. The only real bad thing about this one is that it's damn short and some story missions are really just time-fillers and annoying. Also, if you have enough points, you can instantly upgrade Starlord to be a rapid fire instagib cannon. The things Disney Infinity still have not mastered is actually crafting a good story with a smooth progression path...so these campaigns are just short "adventures". Thiis one is barely 1-2 hours at most if you ignore the various, boring side quests. It finishes with an interesting boss fight at the end...well, interesting for this game at least.
Avengers:
Loki has unleashed the Frost Giants on Earth. Actually not such a bad campaign, but marred by pointless side quests. Also, as Iron Man, you can simply hover over the enemy hordes and let your impulsor blasts clear the way. Most enemies can't hit you, but will occasionally throw something at you, which you can easily dodge. There are a few boss fights in here as well and with Iron Man you can quickly traverse the terrain at least. Just be careful not to get stuck in buildings during flight.
Spiderman:
Green Goblin has teamed up with Mysterio. Once again, this one is not terrible. It has some different mechanics and with Spiderman you can webswing your way through the city, only your ranged attacks are weak, but you pack quite a punch in melee. Of course you can simply play as another hero or villain. The story and especially the ending, however, are a letdown in the end, but I didn't even get that far, because my game refused to continue after a certain cutscene. The game would always close to desktop after that...annoying and ultimately the reason for not recommending it. Not for 28 bucks...at.
Also, if you're gonna let people play as various heroes in the story-mode, please don't lock every hero behind his own skill tree...it makes no sense to change from Spiderman to Venom if the latter has no skill upgrades...

Disney Infinity 2.0: Gold Edition is an improvement on both the first Disney Infinity and on the first game's port. The combat is more enjoyable, the characters now have skill trees and generally have more options for exploring the world, and the addition of Toy Box Games adds something to do for characters without playsets.
There's only three playsets in this version, though, based on The Avengers, Spider-Man, and Guardians of the Galaxy, and they all play more or less the same, with Spider-Man being the best for having the best character and gameplay variety.
As for the port job, I encountered an odd bug a couple times during my Spider-Man playthrough, and the cutscenes are low-res, but it's a technical improvement. It still lacks the online features and multiplayer like the first game, though.
Suffice it to say, if you liked the first one and want more of the same but with Marvel characters as well, you'll probably enjoy this as well.

A 2D platforming open-world game that relies on the same hook as Minecraft or Terraria (world building and terraforming), but with a broader narrative than both.
Starbound however has a lack of direction that leaves a bit more to do without reward than Terraria, and the hours can drift when you don't have goals in mind. And the worlds feel less tangible than Minecraft, but there is so much content to explore that these directionless moments can be overcome by searching out new things to see and do.
And it is this exploration of content rather than worlds that keeps you going, particularly once friends are involved.
Up there with Terraria, not quite as fantastic as Minecraft once was, but a long way ahead of anyone else in the genre.

I can't I say I could possibly recommend this game when it still has game bricking bugs since initial release. (I would have skipped this title had I known this, and became invested in it)
Albeit my time played stating 31+ hours (cause I leave games running in the background), I've played about 8-10 straight hours. The game is really fun regarding its focus on city building. I'd probably still be playing it had my save file not essentially "corrupted".
To claim new areas on a map you require a vessel which commonly will glitch completely out of your game rendering it unplayable. I just lost those 8-10 hours of gameplay. Why would I ever wish to invest my time in a new save file, when there is potential of this bug recurring?
Now not only is there this game breaking bug, but there are also other bugs which are irritating. Such as when you click a building, it will often click the wrong one. Or sometimes the game will become really bogged down for whatever reasons, and will take up 40 mins to unload, and load into a new sector (map). Now factor that into my 8-10 hours of gameplay, and most of my time was sitting at a loading screen.
Of course I don't have that issue any longer now I can't play but regardless of that I purchased this and 22 other games during the Steam Sale. And out of those 22 games this was the one I was actually actively invested in. The other games I played for 10 mins or so and didn't enjoy it. But anyways ...
I didn't mind the fact when you are adding modules it locks you to a single building. Or the fact when you highlight buildings you couldn't see a general performance insight into them, or even having a data screen of each buildings performance in a centralized place. Or when reconfiguring factories, and other buildings there was no temporary configuration function. You were forced to delete part of the factory just to move another piece, there wasn't a dialogue box simply to confirm or cancel a set configuration. Obviously this is a tad annoying. Or even the fact you can place multiple buildings, and even move factories with multiple components, yet you can't move multiple individual buildings. And part of the drawback here as well was that you had to often delete buildings just to place the same building again. Having an inventory, or even temporary plane of existence that populates on screen would rectify this. Move them into there and do what you need. And again confirm or not the configuration. Most of these games don't have inventories if we're being honest, but with such confined spaces such as what you experience with a game like this the ability to confirm configurations for both moving individual buildings, or factory components would have really made the whole gameplay experience a lot smoother.
EDIT: also the ability to fund buildings isn't there so sometimes building an extra place for logistics is way more then you need.
So it's a gamble to buy this game, you might get lucky not have an issue, but imo as I opened up with, I would not have taken the risk had I know such a bug existed.

Exanima is a game with a lot of promise. From a distance, it looks like the first game in a new generation of roguelikes, with actual graphics and an exciting physics-based combat system that makes beating someone to death with a hammer feel like beating someone to death with a hammer rather than clicking on a 3D model until its health bar disappears. However, it has a fatal flaw: the combat system is broken.
Trying to control your character in combat is like trying to use keyboard to drive an actual dump truck. To swing your weapon, your choices are a slow right-to-left swing, a slow backhand left-to-right swing that doesn't register 70% of the time, and a very slow overhand haymaker that is impossible to aim and is useless if you want to stay alive for long. I suspect that there's no option to thrust your weapon because, like real life, that would be by far the most effective choice. Characters move with an unrealistic lack of urgency, making it impossible to quickly step out of an attack or into a blow. Worst of all, there's no player input for defending, which is the most important part of real fighting. Your character simply does it passively whenever you're not attacking. Often you will be perfectly positioned to stop a slow overhead strike, and still end up watching your oppenent's hammer slide off your shield and right into your head, killing you instantly. All of this clumsy design muddles fighting into something more like a roulette wheel you can tilt in your favor rather than a system you can master.
As it currently exists, Exanima is less like a game and more like a toy. You will die many frustrating deaths, sometimes because of a mistake you made that you can learn from, but mostly for reasons outside of your control. This is bad design. If you buy Exanima, buy it because you want to hit a zombie in the face with a machete and are OK with dying a lot for arbitrary reasons. If you don't think you'd like that, I can't recommend it.

Publisher/developer EastFog Studios has made their Steam debut with the horror, murder mystery title Root of Evil: The Tailor. In the game, you play as a telepath named James, who has set out to unravel the enigma behind what happened in the house that a tailor shared with her husband and daughter, before she ultimately committed suicide. The house itself is said to now be haunted, and James uses his telepathy skills in order to find out the truth of what actually happened, in a surprise, twist-ending that is not all that guessable.
The game is centered around solving puzzles, and many of them are rather convoluted; mostly due to pixel-hunting to find out where you need to click in order to interact with some objects. In other cases, the solutions are difficult to find since they are not exactly straight forward, for instance finding certain number combinations. The puzzles themselves are often unique, and haven't been seen countless times in other titles. Needless to say, Root of Evil: The Tailor is definitely geared toward gamers who enjoy piecing together complex solutions.
As far as horror and atmosphere are concerned, the developer does need to work on those aspects a little further. There is very little in the way of ambiance, and rarely is there any actual background track within the game. The only real horror here is learning the spine-chilling story as it unfolds, save for a few scattered jumpscares. Surprisingly for a Unity Personal Edition game, Root of Evil: The Tailor performs at a steady 60 FPS on an i7 6700k/GTX 1080 combo rig, though the game does still feel stuttery every now and then. Aside from the pixel-hunting, one minor complaint that one can bring up is the fact that James walks entirely too slow, and there is no option to run.
The house is rather small, and as such gamers will be revisiting the same rooms over and over again in order to solve different puzzles once their solutions have been revealed. That being said, the house does seem uniquely built, and nothing here comes across as an asset-flip. The story within Root of Evil: The Tailor is a good one, made all the better by the surprising turn of events that are revealed at the end; making it worthwhile to actually finish the game in its entirety, which takes roughly two hours if you're good at puzzles. If you enjoy a good story and a bit of complex problem solving, then you will definitely benefit from giving this one a purchase.

Note: This game isn't made by a big name studio or backed by a budget...instead, it was made by one person. It's far from perfect, but decent nonetheless.
Pros:
+Great Puzzles (they are challenging, but not too complex. You're only able to carry one item at a time, which helps push you towards certain puzzles. It's very hard to wander, unless your objective is to wander.)
+Great Atmosphere (Though some of the jumpscares are predictable, the build-up to them is well-done)
+Great Comedy ("The Glass Is Breaked", everything written in your journal, the voice acting, the passive/clueless generic facial expressions, etc.)
Cons:
-Screen Tearing (there's no option to fix it either. Used "-vsync" on launch options/forced vsync via graphics card with no luck. After about 30 minutes of it, you get used to it...sometimes.)
-Animations (though they were "good enough", they're was definitely room for improvement. Of all the animations, the tree outside the window was best.)
-Graphics (some parts of the game could've used polish, but it doesn't take much away from the game)
In summary:
If your into RE1 style puzzles and bad/funny translations, this may be worth your time. If your looking for deep atmosphere/story, you may want to try RE7, Soma, etc.

. This review also assumes you already own and have completed Half-Life, my review of which can be read
.
Mod: Half-Life: Before
For the game: Half-Life
Developer and publisher: Andrii Vintsevych
Released: 4 December, 2013
Genre: First-Person Shooter
Canon status: Non-canon
Setting: 2003, Black Rock, the middle of the ocean, Earth
Spoiler-free plot summary: Sometime before the events of Half-Life, you, Andrew Winner, are teleported onto a research vessel of Black Mesa's called the Black Rock. You are tasked with eliminating the alien hostiles and their military handlers, and to retrieve an alien crystal.
Full review: Half-Life: Before is a half-hour-long prequel to Half-Life about how Black Mesa retrieved the Xen crystal. Other than that, there is no story. This mod is also incredibly easy.
You've got your basic Half-Life gameplay with only a few new things:
* Custom HD animations, models, skins, and soundtrack have been added.
* NPCs (or the one and only non-hostile NPC in this mod) have subtitles, whereas Valve didn't give any to the NPCs in Half-Life.
However, this mod is filled with more negatives than positives:
* The AI of the hostile humans is incredibly dumb, not reacting when being shot or when their allies run past them or die, and only react when you're in their field-of-view.
* What few "puzzles" that exist require very little brainwork.
* The soundtrack, though good, plays at random, inappropriate times.
* The boss is an unanimated copy of the Nihilanth from Half-Life with a Barnacle tongue that chases you around a square room.
Do I recommend Half-Life: Before? No; it has very little to give to your valuable time, and there are far better mods out there on the Internet that are far more enjoyable and of higher quality.

After a few hours of Jurassic adrenaline, I have to give my review of this classic.
Nostalgic Fanboy incoming.
This...f***ing....GAME!!
What more is there to say? Dinosaurs and you are already hooked, but I shall get into detail.
You play as Turok, a Native American warrior, and the story simply revolves around you going through 8 levels of action to defeat the Campaigner from taking over the world with a legendary weapon.
In those 8 levels is nothing but pure and non stop with a whole assortment of gun after gun after♥♥♥♥♥pounding gun.
Included with this levels you also get a variety of enemies that range from tribal warriors, aliens, and my favorite...dinosaurs..and dinosaurs with machine guns strapped to their backs and laser cannons for arms!
Enough to make a kid from the 90's wet themselves.
As said the weapons arrange from the usual knives, shotguns, to rocket launchers and weapons that still to this day I have no earthly balls of a clue, all these weapons you are death incarnate.
While you travel through the levels, your main goal is to collect the levels keys to advance and you also collect doritos to get a extra life once you hit 100.
The levels are really diverse as it will take time to get use to finding all the secret areas, keys, and collectables.
Luckily you have a map to guide you through.
Controls are fast and smoothe, and sorry COD kiddies but this is an old school gem so do not expect to aim down your sights and get kills so easily, this game comes with no crosshair so you will have to settle with nothing but skill and destruction through the later levels as enemies will be harder to strike.
Graphics for it's time are great and still hold up in my opinion, nothing to most people today...but still better than Duke Nukem Forever!
Music and sound effects are of course as awesome as ever, yeah..no complaints.
Overall the game is a great throwback and addition to Steam, thank you Iguana Entertainment for this badass memory.

Got this game as a gift this holiday and after spending 6 hour speed run the game i grew up on. i can honestly say that Nightdive did an amazing job bringing this game to steam. I can not recommend this any more for those people that enjoyed the original N64 version. I will have to mention i did notice a few new things that changed... they are minor things but they help out the game i feel for the better.
First thing... some level layouts have been changed just slightly to give a better chance of finding the things you need... no more obscure "must climb this almost hidden wall to get the 2nd key in level 1" they changed that area a bit to have the key in a much more obvious and harder to miss spot... and honestly it confused me a bit when i came around the corner to see the new area... things like this happen maybe once every level or two... its very subtle but helps with the flow of the game alot more.
Second thing i noticed.. and i could be wrong... but in the original N64 version of the game when you hit 9 lives and 99 life force... and tried to pick up another.. it would roll the lifeforce over to 0 without giving an aditional life. This version rectifies it by preventing you from ever picking up a life force if you are at maximum... you will never waste those Triangles anymore!
I find these two subtle but very useful fixes made the game even better for me... and seeing the game running at 60 fps on even my potatoe of a system is a possitive. even with all the settings on i got little frame drops when looking at the sun but that is because of the new optional bloom and sunray effects they added to try and make it feel a bit better.
in my oppinion.. this game is perfect... and hearing this company is going to be releasing turok 2 as well.. ooooo i am excited for this... definately pick this up when you can... the price is a bit steep especially compared to the console version used ... but its better than buying it new... this game goes for $400 on online auctions for the console... and this version is far far supieriour to the half baked port we got when it originally came out in 1997. If you really want the authetic feel.... grab a USB N64 controller online and hook it up... from the looks of it its compatible with gamepad rebindings so you can get an authetic feel of the game.
Edit: This game i nominated for the test of time award. This game other than Turok 2 (which is not out yet) are the games that i will always go back to enjoy. no matter how old i get. for that reason i can not think of a better game then this one to get this award!

Starbound you're constantly going from world to world, you never get the feeling of really knowing your world inside and out and getting to build a big, cool base (you can do it, but you have to do it on one planet and come back to that planet). Starbound is more of an adventure RPG, going from planet to planet doing quests, and very minimally mining resources or exploring underground as in the other two games. If you want hands-on game industry experience as a QA Tester or junior designer, this is a unique sandbox to learn in and hone transferable skills.
The core gameplay loop consists of identifying a bug or thinking of a way to improve a feature, using the in-app Report box to send it to the developers and then waiting patiently to see how they interpret your command. Sometimes you'll get surprising emergent behaviour and Crest will change dramatically, almost always for the better. If you want to be more verbose and involved, there's an ARG-style second experience that takes place on Discord.
I'll be a little sad when this hits 1.0 (estimate mid-2018) and the metagame tails off. This is a really interesting experiment to be a part of and as well as teaching me a lot there's some sense of ownership and pride in the "product" as it grows and develops.
A psychedelic experience for the patient and curious, recommended especially to people who have already worked on a game or want to and for anyone who enjoyed The Magic Circle.

Despite the title, this game has nothing to do with Minecraft! This is the first game I've bought in a long time at full price,  and it's worth every penny.
Creeper World 3 is a pausable RTS-type game with aspects of tower defense at its core, combined with a physics/fluid dynamics twist. The game is very well done, challenging and packed with a number of game modes, along with a powerful integrated editor. It's not ridiculously complicated with dozens of units or a mad clickfest where you need millisecond reaction times to survive -- those games are not really my style, but Creeper World 3 is very satisfying. It can get hectic, but there's always time to pause and breathe.
Terrain (including terraforming), energy networks and advancing your weaponry all play huge roles, and you will definitely be pondering strategies on every map. This is not a puzzler, there's not a single "right way" to win each map; given enough time, often times even poor strategies can grind out wins. That translates to a lot of flexibility and support for different playstyles and setups.
As the title suggests, this is the third entry in the series, so there's a level of polish and streamlining over the previous titles. There are a huge number of community-created maps, variable-driven procedurally generated maps, and advanced scripting options available in the editor to create a large variety of scenarios beyond just basic maps. You could basically play this game for the rest of your life and always see new content. Steam cloud, achievements and online leaderboards round it all out.

Bought the game for €10 because I thought it looked pretty and the trailers looked nice.
After playing for a while, I must say I do not regret the purchasee and was pleasantly suprised by its contents.
Kingdoms and Castles presents itself as a medieval city builder annex survival game, in which you become the ruler of a baby kingdom, which you must nuture to a blossoming empire. Your advisaries include vikings, (yay!) dragons, (whoow) and..rain (huh?). The game will make you very inclined to quote a certain sean bean line from a certain popular TV series over and over again, as your harvest will be consumed by the hard temperatures of winter. Your main challange will be to keep your citizens fed and happy; doing so will attract more peasant to do your bidding, leading to an increase in the size of your kingdom
Although the game lacks a tutrial, I found the controles to be very intuitive and, after playing for a while in a peacefull/sandbox mode, I had the feeling I did quite master the game (together with the help of my advisors). The mechanics of the game are also quite simple; farms and ochard give food, which needs to be stored in a granery and transported to a marketplace to be avalaible to the peasants. Other resources are coal, which is made by burning wood at a coalmaker, Stone, which  is carved out of white stone via a quarry, and iron, which is mined from a 'Iron stone' . All resources are infinite, but require peasants to work on them. This can be challenging in the beging, as you don't have that many peasant to commant and have to micromanage quite a bit to be effective. On the other hand; there is no problem with resource manangement, which leads both to tranquillity and monotony.
Futher more, the crafting three is again quite short. food and coal can be made into bread whose benefits are a bit mysterious at the moment, and iron kan be made into weapons for soliers or tools which increase the effectiveness of resources gathering for a bit.
On a positive note, the peasants themselves are fully automated, and do their jobs quite well. I say quite, because I did run into some bugs in which my peasants happely ignored the tons of food next to them as they prefered to wither and die a cold and gruesome death by their own hand. On the other hand, the AI is quite ingenious at other moments; effectivly transporting goods and resources from one place to another, and responding quite rapidly to your build orders.
The vikings and dragons mentioned earlier can be fended of by placing walls, ballistas en arrow towers. It is also possible to train a general and some soldiers. To be honest, I was quite let down by this facet of the game. From a game which says to be inspired by stronghold, the defensive options sure are limited. furthermore, with only 4 types of enemies in game, combat isn't the strongest nor the most challenging part of the game. In fact, the whole game as of now isn't that challenging; its simple mechanics are both its strength and its downfall.
The game itself strongly reminds me of caesar III (from 1998) in which you were a roman ruler who's job it was to build a city from the ground up. The main difference between these two games, is that Caesar III featured a campaign, individual scenarios and vastly more gameplay. In kingdoms & castles homes need 3 things to be happy; food, coal (for warmth) and acces to a library or church. you can add maybe 3 building more for kicks but that's about it. In caesar, you needed bout 3 elements to just keep the citizens in the city; to get any proper city going you needed atleast 5 types of food (some which needed 2 processors), temples to please the gods, a fire watch, a guard to quell uprisings, etc. the game had more dept then Kingdoms and Castle has and, regretfully, will ever have.
The game features a low-resolution polygon style which works quite well with the overall theme of the game. the soundtrack is short (maybe 20 min or so?) but isn't annoying at any moment and, again, fits well with the overal theme.
Kingdoms and Castles is a fun little city builder which burrows elements from various other games and blends it into a smooth running game which will definetly keep you busy for 20-40hours. After that, you've pretty much seen everything the game has to offer and there is nothing left but to wait for what the next update brings. There is a lot of potential in this game and with a dedicated team (duo?) behind it, I have confidence that its shortage of content will be resolved eventualy.

I can safely say that KnC is definitely worth the price. It's an inexpensive medieval city builder that doesn't ask for much, but provides a decent number of hours' worth of play if you enjoy building cities with some light army management stuff ala Black n White. It's more simplistic than most city titles but again, for the asking price, I'd say it's on the mark. There's a decent amount of buildings, information, customization, again...for the price. It's hard to say "it needs more" of these things, things that take time to make and code, without taking a price hike into consideration.
That being said, there's a few issues that become apparent that I hope they fix at the moment: granaries and markets, regarding food distribution, are a problem in huge cities right now. The map size could use an increase for those who want it, I say, particularly when going for the population achievements. I don't know when stockpiles or working places are full unless I click on them and try to visually assess their "open/closed" status. Similarly, opening/closing all of the military structures every before/after a battle is a big hassle/annoying, especially since I feel I need to in order to ramp up construction in between events. There's not enough information on some structures, or their sphere of influences not being visible at certain points, and the constant, random fires that villagers fail to put out when there's a well right across the street, are little annoyances.
I really do recommend this though, for anyone who likes medieval city/castle sims and doesn't ask for too much depth, but is fun to sink time into.

For the $10 price tag, I can recommend this game. However, any future increase in price must be accompanied by new content, in my opinion.
What I like about the game is that it is very relaxing. In-game music is soothing, and it's interesting sitting back and watching your townspeople complete their everyday tasks. It's a simple game, making it very easy for you to get the hang of very quick.
What I don't like about the game is that it lacks depth. While this might be a plus for someone who's just looking to blow off some steam in a casual/relaxing video game, there's just not enough here to keep me interested. Every building can be built within the first hour of gameplay. Aside from watching your town grow, there's no incentive such as advanced buildings to keep on playing. The game strikes me as Tropico lite in block form. Since I own Tropico 4 and 5, two games that I really enjoyed, I can say that this game is nowhere near their caliber, especially Tropico 5.
In conclusion, this game is a quintessential example of "you get what you pay for". It's a simple game for a simple price.

This is my third most played game at the time of this review.
From the Depths is my favorite game, conceptually. However, until this most recent update I did not feel I could recommend it in good faith because it was...not well optimized. The game lagged a lot, and had some stability issues. However, with this new update, the game runs very well, and only the largest of battles, often twice the size of the maximum battlesize before the update, cause lag. I have yet to have a crash in this update as well.
As far as the game itself:
While rather easy to learn the basics, it is incredibly difficult to master. This can be a source of frustration for some, I am sure. However, when it comes to a real time strategy that you can also control individual units which you designed and built, it is without equal (possibly because it is the only game that fits into that category, but it is still impressive). The game is amazing, and the graphics are far better than those you see in the now outdated images and videos they have on the page, so don't let that scare you off.
I could not recommend this game more.

Quick Summary: Orcs Must Die 2 is the co-op follow-up to the original game and while there are changes in maps and some of the traps, the core gameplay is the same. This is a good thing because the first Orcs Must Die is awesome, and only lacked the ability to play with your friends.
Spoilers Ahead
If you’ve played the first Orcs Must Die recently you will remember that at the end, the war mage (you) closed the rifts into the orc world and trapped the evil sorceress on the other side with her minions. Closing the rifts had the side effect of making magic unusable, so the power she had over the orcs is gone, and now they want her dead. In this sequel, one last rift is opened by an old wise wizard (presumed dead in the first game) and the sorceress has escaped being chased by her former orcs. It’s team up time, and the war mage must work with the sorceress to stop the hordes of orcs from breaking through the rift into the human world.
This time around you can choose which character to play the game as: war mage or sorceress. Mostly they’re the same but each has a couple of traps unique to them.  For example the war mage has the tar trap (one of the best floor traps) and the sorceress has the acid spray wall trap (decent against heavy enemies). Consensus seems to be that war mage is better overall. I played the sorceress and had fun with the polymorph ring against the super heavy enemies.
Just like the first Orcs Must Die, the game is broken up into a series of independent map levels, and every level you start from scratch setting up traps and barricades to kill all the orcs before they reach the rift (or rifts). It’s a hybrid tower defense/third person shooter, so you’re in the thick of the action, blasting enemies along with your traps, or mopping up the ones who manage to break past. Every level you beat gives you “skulls” which are currency to buy upgrades for traps or unlock new spells/traps. Unlike the first game, you can replay levels over and over to farm skulls and eventually buy every upgrade.
Pros:
+Co-op campaign! You can play every level with a friend. This along with the skull farming adds a lot of replayability to the campaign.
+Pretty much everything good in the first game is still there, including maps for the first game. You can play the “classic levels” with the new traps and sorceress character.
Cons:
-The “endless mode” gets buggy as you get to higher levels. Maybe it’s my computer but it really started to lag around wave 35. It actually crashed for me a couple times.
Overall, if you liked Orcs Must Die 1, you should like part 2. They’re basically the same game with added improvements, options, and levels for the sequel.

-Trading has been the main feature of all the anno games, I have no idea why they removed the MAIN feature of the game. Trading in Anno 2205 is no longer simulated in the game. All the complex mechanics such as ship speed, number of ships, multi pick up drop off locations, complex routes, carry capicity, distance, pirtates are gone.
-The combat levels are fairly boring and your are forced to play a LOT of them to get resources crucial to building upgrades. Combat used to be a side effect of trading since there were pirates and you would protect them.
PROS:
-It's still a fun game if you enjoy city simulation games. Even though this game lacks many of the best parts of the old Anno games it's still more complex than the vast majority of other city simulation games.
-Man you can build some REALLY pretty cities. Since some mechanics are simplified, you can get away with making more aesthetic cities rather than functional. The idea of colonizing the moon and orbit is also extremely fun and exiting.

I wanted to wait til beating the game to write this, in order to play through the whole thing and compare it to my well-loved N64 cartridge. Now, after having firmly lodged the Chronoscepter  in the Campaigner's robotic ♥♥♥♥♥♥, I can safely say this is THE definitive version of Dinosaur Hunter. Night Dive has put a lot of love and affection into this remaster, combining the best aspects of the N64 and PC versions, and adding some improvements of their own thanks to a custom engine. It looks better, plays better, sounds better.
If you've never played Turok: Dinosaur Hunter before, I wholeheartedly recommend it, it's pretty unique among shooters. Half Quake-style fragfest, half Tomb Raider-style adventure hunt; exploring the environment is just as important as shooting the baddies, if not downright essential to progressing. The price may be a bit steep, but be sure to grab this whenever it goes on sale, especially if you love dinosaur games.

First of all, I'd like to say that I very rarely write reviews. The only other game I have written one for was How To Survive, I believe. So that alone should show how much I feel for this game, but let's get right into it.
Pros:
1. The combat system is incredible. While hard to master at first, you eventually get used to and come to love it. the fact moving your whole character and swinging your weapon both make a difference together is marvelous and the way your weapons can sometimes clash and get stuck for a moment, just like they would in reality, is fantastic.
2. The character customization, yes, you can create your own character from scratch. Whether you're fat, thin, muscular or not. Your sex, height, age (physical), and hair style/colour is all interchangeable.
3. The variety in weapons and armour, and even clothing is quite fantastic. (this coming from a person who, out of his two hours of play-time, has only played through the arena mode and just started the story.) From simple linen clothing to light leather armour and finishing with things like full-plate suits of classic medieval armour. And with the armour, come individual weapons and shields to come with them. From greatswords to axes and sickles to spears.
Cons:
1. Perma-death. Let me start by telling you all that this game is -hard-, and I really mean that. The combat style, as I said, is difficult to master and sometimes a battle is won or loss by a matter of a single lucky swing makes it genuinely brain-numbing. The undeniable main appeal of Exanima is its novel physics-based combat system. What I like about the game—for all its well earned reputation for exceptional difficulty—is that once you get the hang of combat, it starts to feel very statifying, physical, and remains always dangerous. It is not at all about how quickly you can mash buttons and swing the mouse around, but rather a highly tactical system where you have to think about the most effective use of the weapon in your avatar's hands and the weaknesses the enemy reveals that you can exploit physically. Even hits from weak enemies can be lethal, if you are careless in exposing an opportunity. And, of course, the same goes for your enemies. In short, combat in Exanima feels more "real" than any game not based around firearms I've personally ever played: real in a satisfying and very fun way, once you get the hang of it. Getting the hang of it does requires patience and a willingness to try something new.
It's definitely important to try the arena for several hours before venturing into the dungeon. You have to think before you act, if you want to have to a chance at getting anywhere. There are VERY few health potions—none at all in the arena—and some injuries are permanent without them. But it is worth sticking it out, no question, if for no other reason than the satisfaction of physically and tactically defeating your enemies one by one in Exanima's very interesting combat system, and gradually improving your gear in a realistic way.
I admit the dungeon crawl itself is not among the more interesting out there in the gaming world, nor is the story particularly compelling at this time. For me, the interest in the game is all about the physics of the world and combat, as well as the terrific atmosphere. It is very difficult, certainly, but the sense of accomplishment is palpable.
A couple more hints: 1) Combat in Exanima is far more about your avatar's positioning and exploiting opportunities than frenetically thrashing your weapon around, or using brute force. You simply can't muscle or button-mash your way to success. 2) Counter-attacks are often more successful than atttacks. 3) If you can avoid a combat encounter, you probably should. (Remember that bit about the very few health potions and permanent injuries?) 4) Mind your surroundings. Your avatar can trip up and fall flat on his face; but, hilariously, so can your enemies.
The game is still in early access (0.5.3) as I write this review, but I believe it is fully worth the support of the gaming community.
I think the only thing I really wish the game had is a PvP arena mode, or dungeon co-op mode. That would be fun!

Creeper World 3 is a pausable RTS-type game with aspects of tower defense at its core, combined with a physics/fluid dynamics twist. The game is very well done, challenging and packed with a number of game modes, along with a powerful integrated editor. It's not ridiculously complicated with dozens of units or a mad clickfest where you need millisecond reaction times to survive -- those games are not really my style, but Creeper World 3 is very satisfying. It can get hectic, but there's always time to pause and breathe.
Terrain (including terraforming), energy networks and advancing your weaponry all play huge roles, and you will definitely be pondering strategies on every map. This is not a puzzler, there's not a single "right way" to win each map; given enough time, often times even poor strategies can grind out wins. That translates to a lot of flexibility and support for different playstyles and setups.
As the title suggests, this is the third entry in the series, so there's a level of polish and streamlining over the previous titles. There are a huge number of community-created maps, variable-driven procedurally generated maps, and advanced scripting options available in the editor to create a large variety of scenarios beyond just basic maps. You could basically play this game for the rest of your life and always see new content. Steam cloud, achievements and online leaderboards round it all out.

You would start off in an area with a high wall that has holes in it, and the creeper is advancing from all around you, you can only seal off a few of the holes. As for the levels, I have yet to put even a small dent into the other sectors, as they contain probably hundreds of more challenging, and maybe even impossible levels. And on top of the other sectors, there is also the DMD, which is basically loaded with user created maps. So if you somehow manage to top every single level with the game, there's plenty more where that came from.
If you've played Creeper World before, you will definitely love this game. It's all of the original gameplay loaded with levels, some new tools, a map creator, and, in my opinion, a story that will leave you wanting to continue and find out what happens next.

Crest is, at it's core, a God-game where "you . . . interact with [humans] by issuing commandments written in a pictographic language."  While the concept itself is novel, I can’t recommend Crest at full price.  The content is lacking: there are no formal objectives; no way to advance civilization; no rival tribes; no aggressive wild animals; no unforgiving environments; no way to interact with or smite individual followers.
The main draw to – and the only real gameplay mechanic of – Crest is the ability to compose commandments for followers from a Mad Libs-style, pregenerated list.  This is a great concept I would love to see explored more deeply in the future.  Unfortunately, standing alone, this mechanic is not enough to hold my interest.  Insert a subject, a verb, and an object into a blank, and
you’ve written a commandment; you’ve explored most everything Crest has to offer.
That’s not to say I didn’t enjoy Crest.  The game is aesthetically pleasing, the music is relaxing, and, yes, some of the commandments I issued were amusing (“The young shall consume the elderly” and “Thou shalt share thy blessings with the lion” were among my favorites).  I’m glad I experienced Crest, but it’s an experience I could have had watching Markiplier or MatPat's play through on YouTube.  And, unless more content is released, I doubt I’ll ever pick up Crest again.

Really interesting and unique concept behind this game, and there are some things that it does really well, like how you can review all the things that have happened in your game so far by interacting with a recordkeeping demigod.  Unfortunately, for me at least, there's just not enough here yet to make gameplay enjoyable.
Interacting with followers solely via issuing commandments is a really cool idea, but given that this is the central (and essentially only) gameplay mechanic there's just not nearly enough variety in the kinda of commandments you can issue.  They all consist of three basic parts, essentially a subject, a verb, and an object.  Without going into too much of a tangent about how this works, I'll just say that in practice there's really not much control you have, and not much you can do.  For example, two of my cities went to war, and I wanted to help my initial city triumph; however since they were located on the same types of terrain and surrounded by the same animals etc, I wasn't able to issue any commandments that would only apply to one of them or the other, so any action I could take would equally help or hinder both cities.
Even when I was able to assemble a useful commandment, issuing it to the followers feels almost pointless: some cities simply ignore them, and those that are receptive will usually corrupt the commandment into something else before too long. The nature of the corruption was often arbitrarily different from the initial commandment: for example, a commandment like "those that are have metal, hunt lions" could be turned into "those that are near lions, make babies".  If you have enough influence it's possible to approve or reject these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥izations, but that seems to have little effect on whether or not they actually go away.  Finally, all commandments seem to have a time limit after which they simply expire, so even the most successful commandment will be relatively short-lived.
The final straw for me at least was the lack of any real goals to strive for, in either the short term or the long term.  There are no foreign civilizations to war with, and the wild animals don't seem to attack your people, so the only conflict comes from "civil war" among your followers.  In these battles it's not particularly important who wins, and indeed I'm not sure whether any of my wars ever ended: the UI does not make obvious the standing between cities.    It's supposedly possible to lose the game by having all of your followers die (of starvation, presumably), but even when I just let the game run by itself on max speed without bothering to issue any commandments, things ticked along just fine, with no danger of a species-wide extinction.
That is the fundamental flaw with this game as it stands right now: the player's role feels entirely superfluous, as he/she is able to offer at best only minor assistance to his/her followers, with little impact on the game world, and even less incentive to care one way or another.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is a tower defense game in which you must construct traps to defeat an ever-increasing wave of orcs and their minions. The game can be played in single player or two person co-op. For those familiar with the formula, the game follows the standard idea of building defenses, weaving the path that the enemy must follow and defeat them before they reach the exit. The game itself is set in a 3rd person view, allowing the player to control one of two characters that you may use to fight along-side your traps. During setup, the player may choose from a variety of traps: spike traps, arrow traps, teleporters, acid traps, barricades, guardians (AI), character weapons and trinkets for passive and active buffs. There is a healthy amount of customization what you can bring, making level design easily tailored to your play style and choice.
During the matches, the goal is simple: Do not let the orcs, or their minions, past the rift (exit). Each level has a set amount of waves, enemy types and number of rift points (essentially lives) that can be expended before you lose the round. Depending on your success, the player(s) can earn bonus points in the form of skulls. These skulls can be used to upgrade your weapons, trinkets and most importantly, your traps, adding active and passive abilities and increased damage.
The game has several different game modes, including story mode, several smaller DLC levels, a weekly custom mode and an Endless Mode, which, as you'd have guessed, goes until you lose or quit the level. Aside from different game modes, Orcs Must Die! 2 has three difficulties: Apprentice (Easy), War Mage (Normal) and Nightmare (Hard). As someone who has played very few tower defense games, War Mage is a nice middle ground for those just learning the game or the genre.
The game will probably provide anywhere from 20-30 hours of continuous gameplay, more so if you explore the different modes and difficulties that it has to offer. Orcs Must Die! 2 is enjoyable, yet challenging. It blends old features with new content very well. if you're a fan of tower defense games, then I think you'll enjoy Orcs Must Die! 2.


Overall, Orcs Must Die! 2 is downright fun. It's a challenge without being irritating and a ton of fun if you're able to play co-op. It's a great installment to the series and feels improved in every fashion. Check it out. I completely recommend it!

Game Corp DX is quite similar to Game Dev Tycoon, in that you get to create your own video-game industry. You start out small, and hire more developers as you progress. Developers all have individual needs and traits such as how productive they are, and need to be trained in various software to contribute to a project. There's also an aspect of the classic game The Movies by Lionhead Studios, with competitor studios and an awards ceremy that gives trophies to the best companies.
- A very fun casual game that teaches you about the game development industry.
- The gameplay is very easy to learn, though still incredibly enjoyable.
- You unlock more skilled employees and new equipment as you progress. You also get larger studio space at each city you unlock.
- The artwork is quaint and definitely adds to the appeal of the game.
- You're really pressed for space in your studio as you progress, as you must hire all 'local' potential employees before moving locaiton to expand your studio. This is exaccerabted by the fact that most objects take up multiple spaces, and you cannot move an object over any existing 'invalid' squares, even if doing so would be a valid move. For example, an object occupies two squares. You move it over one square, which the object itself is already occupying. The game won't let you do this, as you must move the object to a completely different location, *then* to the target location.
- Adventure games seem to take a random hit. I can only assume this is to make the achievement related to earning more than $20m from an advetnure title harder. At the end of the game, no-one has basically *any* interest in adventure games, making this task very difficult.
- The informtion boxes are ridicuously small. You can increase their size, but this blurs the text. Also, in many cases some text will float off the screen, making it unreadable. I set the text size to the highest setting, so this may not be as bad for smaller texts.
Game Corp DX is a really fun game and a great way to kill a few hours. It's an enjoyable game that does a good job at what it is trying to do. For the price, you get many hours of enjoyable gameplay, so I can definitely recommend this as a game to pick up!
