Released
EastFog Studios
EastFog Studios
3D “Horror”/ Puzzle
9th of December 2016
Singleplayer
I must’ve played at least a dozen indie horror titles on Steam, created with Unity Engine assets. Most were entirely decent and the obvious work of talented & dedicated individuals. And then there’s Root Of Evil: The Tailor, sadly. A game that should have either spent a few more months in development or at least be released under the “Early Access” label. The moment you start it, the loading screen lets players know that this is the work of a single individual and “the game will inevitably some small errors affecting the gaming experience”. Yes, you read that correctly as I quoted. Not even the disclaimer is spelled properly. And it is somehow still an understatement which never prepared me for the actual gameplay.
Where to begin? The Main Menu has no options other than audio settings. No control scheme (nevermind the fact that you can’t rebind anything) or graphical tweaks. Consequently, no resolution changes can be made (at least it’s running by monitor’s native res). Vertical synchronization was implemented only after some players complained on the game’s Steam Discussions tab. I’ve never seen a 3D PC game with the “rich options” of a console title. Starting on the wrong foot indeed. You might have forgiven the technical mishaps if the story would be mind-blowing. I’ll let you guess if it is, or not.
Actually no. I need to discuss at some length about that too. Not so much in terms of spoilers since the plot is so generic that even if you last watched a series or movie a decade ago, you’d still feel a déjà vu. Silent protagonist Dr. James is a private eye/psychic medium out of work (who would have guessed?) that agrees to investigate an abandoned house, merely after receiving a cryptic letter from “Kate”, along with a key to the location. Once inside the lobby, the mixed attention to details shall become quite obvious. Some objects have top notch textures while others seem even more abandoned by the dev than the house itself. Among the few strong points I did find to Root of Evil, has to be the nice 3D render of an antique Singer Sewing Machine which even features wheel and needle animation. I own such a model in near-mint condition and in all my subjectivity, I couldn’t pass such a detailed video game render of a seemingly random object. At least The Tailor in this tale, is a self-respecting man which knew quality when he saw it.
Too bad the gameplay is held back by technical and level design choices. Invisible walls, or more precisely unclimbable stairs and far too many locked doors. Apart from some puzzle sections, you don’t really get to explore the house except for a limited number of rooms. Even those mysteries feature zero explanation or hints. I honestly don’t know how many updates would be necessary to get this game in a decent playable state and with the many examples of Engrish (broken English), I dare not try the other languages included in Root Of Evil: The Tailor. As far as I’m concerned the game is more of a highschool project than actual entertainment and it is truly sad that the developer missed even the opportunity to properly sell it at an appropriate sum. The inclusion of Achievements and Cards never represent a decisive factor for me. If that Singer wasn’t present in the game, I would have rated it even lower. So just wait for the inevitable bundle or heavy discount if you’re looking for some unintentional humor. Horror, this is not!

An amazingly well done port of one of the best console original FPS games of the 90s. Now with improved draw distance, smooth and remappable controls and even increased difficulty options.
And while I may call this a port, saying that doesn't exactly do it justice. The engine it runs on is entirely new and doesn't actually have too heavy a relationship with either the N64 original or the somewhat shoddy PC port. And on top of that the engine also supports moddability, something the originals never had.
If you can handle the dated visuals this is totally worth what they're asking for, the game itself can be on the short side if you know what you're doing, but the exploration required to find level keys plus the chronosceptre peices if you want to build that too are fun in a way most key hunts really aren't. The levels are packed with secrets which helps with replayability too.
So TL:DR. it's good. And at that you should thank Kaiser for his great work on the engine. Keep an eye on him and Night Dive Studios for powerslave-ex (Possibly) and the upcoming release of Turok2.

I remember looking up the cheat codes for the game on Game FAQS and hand typing all of the best codes onto a notepad file because I didn't know how to copy/paste yet. The cheat codes made me feel giddy back then. Little did I know they would ruin the game for me.
So for Christmas 1997 I asked my Mom for this game. Playing this game back then felt so good at first. The guns felt really good and the enemy death animations were amazing. I was able to make it past the first level, but going into the second level I started to lose interest. I printed out all of my cheats and went HAM on the game, teleporting to every level and killing every boss with the extremely overpowered weapons and invincibility. I was bored with the game after that, because the cheats kinda took the game aspect away.
I later realized why I initially got so bored with the game. The control was terrible. Turning was slow but would quickly accelerate leading to overcompensation which led to very imprecise aiming. You just felt like you were in a vat of sticky goo. The N64 controller really sucked for FPS games. Turok 2 was better but suffered from similar problems.
Fast forward to 2001 I downloaded a Turok PC Demo and it was total crap with no mouse aiming.
Fast Forward to December 2015, Steam. I bought this game on the hopes that it would be playable and to experience nostalgia from 1997. I knew the game was good as it was highly praised in its day, I just wanted to really experience its goodness this time. So how does the game hold up?
That first level was not only a nostalgia overload, the control with the mouse, playing this game like a real and true FPS made me want to cry it was so amazing. The game was now fast and fluid, better view distance, no frame drops, a crosshair! It felt good. It felt like a really good classic FPS like Quake. I was having a lot of fun.
After those first two levels the nostalgia wore off. It went from childhood memories to totally new memories. Because the combat was now fun and engaging, I was able to just play the game and progress. The levels for the most part are pretty well designed. Platforming sections were no longer nigh impossible for me. Jumping was quick, precise and easy. Although the platforming sections were the weakest part of this game by far, they were pretty intense because you really didn't want to die and lose the Backpack that you have had for almost 2 hours.
The best part of this game are the guns. I feel like almost every gun has a situational use (except for the pump shotgun after you get the auto shotgun). The guns stand above all else in terms of memoribility. The coolest gun in the game being the Chronoscepter, which has 8 pieces that you have to collect through out the game. It has only 3 shots and you finish putting together before the last boss. This gun made me cream myself when I saw it as a kid. Now its just a bad♥♥♥♥♥gun with effects that still look cool to me to this day.
Definitely get this game if you played and loved Turok back in the day and want the real Turok experience.
Don't get this game if all you have played is Call of Duty/Halo
At 20$ It is definitely overpriced though, which is why I can't recommend this game to everyone. Now I'm crossing my fingers for Turok 2 on Steam!

Starbound is one game that has stuck with their fans throughout development. I've played this from time to time over the years and it's still something that I can come to, polished, and with a healthy modding following.
Pro's:
- Exploration feels worthwhile (going to another planet, or even just the entire surface is beneficial).
- Healthy modding community add a very rich aspect to the game.
- Collections allow for complitionist tracking in game.
- Expanding ship and new robot mech suit gives sufficient "space" setting instead of just a means to get to another planet.
Con's:
- Progression is a bit flat (armor/weapon tiers are just numerical stat increases rather than actual variances in mechanism).
- Unskippable cutscenes make re-play slow at times.
If you like 2D side scrollers with pixel graphics and a spice of building, this is the game for you. It won't break the bank and it has lots of development under its belt to provide content for almost everone.

UPDATE 0.5.3 REVIEW
Words cannot express how I feel about this game, and I have the deepest desire to play through it again and again.
This is the game ive wanted for years, this is the game I wanted so badly, and Dark Souls was the closest thing to this game and now this game is here and I have no more desire to play Dark Souls, a game I binged on for days at a time.
The combat in this game was frustrating and hard to learn, luckily they have the arena mode which really does help get over the major struggles of learning the combat in a permadeath situation.
Pros
-Very hard, yet learnable combat.
The core combat of this game is fairly simple, left click on the side of your character to swing from that side, WASD controls your character while in combat mode, W being forward of your character at all times and not the top of the screen, double left click to do an overhead, hold left click to continue swinging after you have already swung. Your character will automatically block or parry so long as you arent swinging and the attack is blockable from where youre facing and where the attack is coming from. The autoblock in this game allows you to focus on offense, instead of thinking about "press mouse2 to block right before he swings". Its second nature to your character to block, so you dont have to think about it. A good way to learn the combat is to play arena for a while. (I gasped so loud when I saw that guy have metal armor, and I beat him and got to take it).
-Indepth hitbox system.
You have to really think about hitting the enemy and I dont think any weapon can hit if youre too close, however its a good way to avoid someones attack, get TOO close to them, then back off.
-Rather smart and unique AI.
While playing in arena, the AI was very diverse. Some were aggressive, some were defensive, some were aggressive but very defensive as if trying to counter you but trying to make you do something that can be countered, some AI isnt smart but I think thats part of the point.
-Varied loot.
In adventure mode, the enemies and world items spawn with the same loot, but the chests and boxes spawn with different loot each time and the boxes and chests are usually where the good loot is.
-Smooth 60fps and beautiful visuals.
I dont really care about this stuff, but the visuals in this game are very impressive I have to say.
-Beautiful ambience and sounds.
All the sounds feel like they should, none really feel too weak.
Cons:
-Blah blah blah early access
Basically early access complaints that will be easily fixed later, such as:
Steam ingame overlay not working when the game is paused.
Characters become naked apon startup when starting new games, this is only a problem in arena mode as you lose your weapons and armor that you had before, so if the game crashes which it sometimes does, you lose your progress in that regard. However, if you were able to get that far, you should be able to do it again.
-Red health
I really love this mechanic, but earlygame is very very frustrating with the stronger enemies. Especially the ones with big axes. One hit can doom you to get destroyed later, and for early game this is a real problem, considering how much armor you DONT get earlygame. But to be fair, I engage in combat more than I should. The only time id argue its a real problem is when combat is forced. For example, the first level has a dark hallway with two guys in it, a guy with some blunt weapon and a guy with a big axe. The guy with the big axe must be killed as he has the key to progress. As much as I like him having the key, I do think maybe he sould have the SMALLER axe? I did manage to get past him but I didnt come out unscathed. I lost about 40% of my total health in one hit.
Basically I think earlier game enemies should have less lethal damaging weapons, not take them out, just less.
-Map
You dont have to, but id really appreciate it. I just dont wana look at a map on the community guide because im afraid itll label enemies and items for me and I just need to figure out some basic direction of where I am. That being said, after running through the same cooridors 10 times while learning the game, I did memorize most of the area, but im good at memorizing areas and someone else might not.
I love this game, I want multiplayer just like everyone else, preferably online. Im going to keep playing, this is one of the best 15 dollars ive ever spent on steam, and I really really really want it to come out of early access.
Please dont let this one sit on early access for years (like starbound *cough cough*), you have something special here and I really want it to be made full. Youve easily made one of my favorite games so far.

So, first things first, this game is not the best written and graphically designed, and that probably turns some people off. I am very pleased that I fall outside of that group because it is a terrific game. The basic mechanics are all easy to understand, shooting the creeper makes it decrease in level, creeper moves like a fluid (though I've heard it's simulated more like heat. But for all gameplay purposes you can think of it like a viscous fuid) to fill in gaps, you need to send out packets made from energy to supply turrets, construction and other things.
Then as these gameplay elements start to overlap the interactions between them get more complex. I won't go into too much detail but there is a special type of terrain that promotes the creeper to flow along it. This may completely throw what you were doing previously because suddenly you have to be cautious with the fact that it is much harder to clear the creeper.
The main draw of the game to me was the resource management system though, which forces you to manage between the space needed to get energy, how much you can afford to defend with that energy, and how you can expand from there. It is very easy to find you've just spent half an hour gradually shifting around units to allow you to push forwards, but all of that time feels engaging.
Overall it's a very engaging game and at £12 it's decently priced for the amount of gameplay contained within.

A great concept and honestly can't wait to see the finished product. As for the gameplay it's rather early into its dev so I'm going to give it some slack as I can see room for improvement. The game plays out similarly to sims but with a little less control. Actually, a whole lot less control. simply put you input a command every so often and the AI tries to acomplish the task as best as it can. It's rather reminiscent to when Bender accidently becomes God in Futurama since no matter what input you give they somehow all starve to death or get eaten. So the challenge in this game really is more along the lines of how long can your civ flourish for?
Overall an enjoyable experience but one that can bore you if you're not into Civ type games.
I do have a few suggestions, for instance:
There was a nice little narrative in the opening, that would have been cool to see get expanded a little.
The UI is more than a little tideous, could be streamlined in my opinion
While I enjoy the chance factor of the AI becoming independant of my orders but it get rather annoying when it happens often while I'm supposed to have 100% faith in my following.
Objectives for bonus faith seems to be an opportunity for engangement otherwise it starts to feel like watching an antfarm after 30 mins.

A civilization tree would be kinda cool, not sure how it could be implemented but again I realize that this game is still in development.
Having some other kind of omnipotent antagonist or parallel diety also competing for survival would make the game a bit more challenging and can serve to engange the player.

Crest is a lot of things, and bloody hilarious is just one of them. You are a god, but you can only interact with your followers by proclaiming commandments to them. You have no more control over them than that.
But, much as with real religions, your followers are prone to changing your commandments around to suit their desires, adding "associations" to the altered commandment which you can either bless or condemn. Unfortunately, proclaiming commandments and judging associations costs influence, which generates
, meaning you can often end up unable to do anything for quite a while, but when you can, it's quite fun.
First off, there's no real rules as to what can go in a commandment. You pick two words from your currently unlocked lexicon (which change based on whether they're at the beginning or end of a commandment) and an order to go between them from a list of orders consisting of "do" and "do not" versions of eight actions. I'd go further, but knowing the nature of Steam reviews someone's already done a better job of explaining the gameplay than me. So I'll describe some of the comedy.
Your followers have
weird preferences at times, and will twist your commandments accordingly. My first run ended because some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ decided to twist a commandment for people with food to give to the people in a desert city which had none into "God said eat people who live in the desert", and I was able to do nothing about it due to low influence. That commandment basically ended my game because my followers ate everyone living in the desert and proceeded to die of starvation afterwards. Morons. Not to mention that someone

Kingdoms and Castles: A light-hearted medieval city sim that is quaint and refreshingly simple.
So far, I've been playin on normal, and have accrued my current time of 11 hours within 3 days of owning the game. I've seen many negative reviews of this game, and I truly don't think it's deserved. At a modest 10 shmekles, this game is a smile city builder, with some basic key elements towards city planning and resource managing. I like this game most because it's honestly exactly what I didn't know I wanted, yet am so satisfied and engaged I have to stop myself from playing into the wee hours. I of course find at times the cycle of food, people, happiness, and defense a bit repetitive so I take a break. This is a game best enjoyed a leisure, with no huge benefit from forcing yourself to grind out hours of gameplay. The learning curve is not steep, and for me a lot of the fun has been from imprinting my own emotions and goals towards achieving the type of city I'd want to live in, and striving to reach all of the achievements. I think this game, in it's beautifully simple nature, will wear on me in maybe 10 more hours, and that's perfectly fine with me. It's been a grat journey so far, and I look forward to completing my city to the best of my heart's content. Currently, I'm striving to make a solid, high wall surrounding my city.
Overall, it is up to you what you make of this game. I think it's perfect for casuals like myself, and others may lose interest with it's lack of micromanagement. That's okay. I am so glad I picked up this game (at full price) and would do so again knowing what I do of the game. I loathe the idea of it when I'm not playing it sometimes, but once I get the craving it fills the spot.
DEFINITELY worth picking up on a sale, no doubt!

An RTS were you design everything out of blocks, even the weapons systems come in verious blocks and your design has massive impacts on its performance, from small AA guns, to cannons that lob huge shells (which you decide on its payload, frag HE EMP SolidAP) to a railgun that will punch a hole clear through enemy ships, then theres custom missiles, laser cannons particle accelerators torpedos... this may sound like alot to do while at war... but you can also test and save designs in sandbox mode and "print them" automaticly and watch as your ships are created for you plus steamwork shop is crammed with other peoples creations plus a load of premade stuff built in if you dont want to hand craft your every ship/submarine/plane/airships/hovercraft/space craft/tanks (yes you can goto low orbit and rain hell down upon the lowly peasants) you could even make a submarine fly or a plane submersable, you can even make a chicken fly... armed with laser cannon eyes!
Although theres no real limit to what you can create in terms of size, there is a limit somewhere between your PC spec and what the game engine can handle, i find my pc gives up before the game does as its not a brilliant spec
What this means in game play terms, if a huge ship made out of 100000 blocks shows up and tries to fight something, your FPS will drop untill either game or pc gives up. that is alot of blocks though and totaly unnesasary the CPU players wont do this to you they use sensible designs, this still leaves you aloooot of blocks to play with so your designs dont need to be entirely practical.
for an EA game this is pretty complete, i rarely crash and if i do its 4 hours+ into a game and a restart sorts this out, pretty well optimized compared to alot of EA games.
The game is real time stratergy to a point. when 2 forces area of infulence meet (a large circle centred on each fleet) the central point of each others circle, a countdown begins untill combat is started, or you can simply accept the comabt. once done all other forces on the map are pulled from play and you get some paused time to set your formations. once this stage is over real time continues but only the combatants are put back into play the rest of maps forces are kept in a frozen unrendered state for the duration of combat.
early game this is a little anoying, late game this is essential, it reduces the worlds "block count" which in turn keeps performance high and combat is smooth, so dont be put off by this early on as both sides use small craft, youll see the gains from it in mid to late game with your FPS staying in a playable range.
For sandbox mode you can disregard this section as the game will not pause or really alert u to combat it will just happen when enemys come in range, if you spawn enemies at all that is.

This game is not bad, as some of the reviews would have you believe. On the other hand, it's not really that good either.
I wasn't expecting a rehash of Anno 2070 when I bought this, nor did I want a rehash of an older game (although I truly do love Anno 2070). I wanted--and received--a fresh game with fresh mechanics. This is that game.
For example, there are no longer island-specific fertilities; instead, you occupy regions and produce region-specific goods. Therefore, you don't need the complex inter-island trade routes; instead, your trade routes are from region to region. To me, that's fine, and I don't know why people complain about it so much.
Instead of building modules or finding modules for your islands, you can add modules to your production plants and get bonuses from the Orbital Station (with DLC) and through industry bonuses in the stock market. The Tundra DLC will let you crank out the equivalent of crack for your factories.
Combat invasions (with the Frontiers DLC) can bankrupt your company if you get invaded just after an expensive build or purchase. Usually it's just annoying, though. Actually, the invasions are pretty much always annoying.
Those parts, for me, are fine (except annoying invasions). The parts that detract from the experience are having to enter special combat zones over and over again for rare materials, and the play balance in Veteran Mode makes for a lot of waiting around while your credits or materials slowly accumulate. If you can get past those few irritations, then you'll probably find yourself spending alot of time in Anno 2205.

Alright, I'm still having problems understanding why this game gets panned.  I played through it at release and enjoyed it, and then today I decided I'd check it out again as I had a craving, and had bought the Season Pass.
Being a fan of the previous installations in the series, this game is very similar in a lot of ways, and I think has really built on the franchise in a positive way.
Most notably, combat has been (for the most part) separated from the main game, which I like.  I always felt the combat in Dawn of Discovery to be lackluster at best and detracted from the true nature of the game.  2070 did okay with it, but I like that combat in 2205 is segregated into separate missions which are effectively optional for the most part.
The game instead really capitalizes on the city building, resource management, and trading.  The DLC has proven fun so far, having played around with the orbital station and the tundra zone.
Frankly if you liked the main premise of the original games in the series, and didn't really care about the combat aspect so much, I really think it would behoove you to give this most recent sequel a try.
I think Ubi actually deserves some credit for this one.  Its gorgeous, runs great, has all the polish you'd expect from a AAA game, and truthfully is really fun.
My $0.02, YMMV.

A fun tug of war game where you pick weaponry and amount of segments desired for your battlepillars and send them across the screen to engage the enemy who is doing the same. Various weapons are better in some situations that others, so you have to pick with care and react to what the enemy is doing, as well as determine if you want to armour up or hope to blast the enemy before you take too many casualties.
There is certain a lot to experiment with, as the various weapons systems are very distinct with different damage levels, ranges, side effects, as well as some other segments to add armour, slow the enemy, or apply a damage over time effect, etc. You also have to factor in length - the longer battlepillars have more health and survivability as well as firepower (normally), but move slower across the screen - so if you want to use heavy armored battlepillars with lots of segments to defend "glass cannon" units that do the damage you will need to plan ahead to ensure they get there before the previous one dies.
The single player campaign is pretty good, there is a reasonable amount of variation even apart from the boss fights which mix things up further, and of course you unlock new weapons and upgrades as you go along. Multiplayer is presumably pretty dead unless you have some friends to play with that probably isn't going to be a reason to get it at this point. Overall though, it is an easy recommend even for just the single player portion.

I love this game and have sunk many, many hours into it back in the early-mid 2000s and again in 2010.
If you have ever been looking for the best Diablo 2 clone, this game is it (yes, I love Path of Exile too, but I'd like to think of PoE being what Diablo 3 should've been...), period. If you haven't played it, but have enjoyed the Torchlight series, Fate, Path of Exile, Titan's Quest, Grim Dawn, and/or Divine Divinity (and Beyond Divinity), this title should feel right at home for you.
A few caveats:
1) The official multiplayer servers were shut down years ago and will require a third paty service (like Hamatchi) or a good old school LAN partay.
2) The game's resolution, from all of the documentation I've found, is fixed. So it won't look so pretty on widecreen monitors or 4K.
3) Keep in mind that this game came out in 2004. Most of the negative reviews I've read on here should've kept this in mind when they complained about the graphics
4) Unique and set items scale to character level, so that Sigon's set item you found at level 7 in Diablo 2 will have level 7 stats here, whereas that same set piece found at level 70 will have corresponding stats.

The road to disappointing mods is paved with good intentions, and good intentions is what
is made of. As a mod, it works rather well; it's short, well-paced, and doesn't feel too weighted down by the trappings of the previous - or should that be future? - games in the
series.
As a release on Steam, however - even as a freebie - you would rather expect a bit more to it than what is eventually delivered. There's no difficulty to speak of; there's three levels of difficulty, all of which seem exactly the same. The character animations also leave a lot to be desired; the one non-hostile character you meet walks like a robot, doesn't move his mouth when he speaks, doesn't talk when prompted, and meets an unsatisfyingly messy end at the hands of - actually, that's another thing, what the hell killed him? It's a closed environment, the only way out is through the vent and why would the creature go back in after Andrew left?
But
isn't big on logical, coherent plot. It just drops you straight into the action and expects you to sink or swim. There's little explanation as to why you're suddenly teleported to a boat to retrieve a crystal, and even less about what happens to you after you get it. Everything inbetween, however, is quite clear - clear as crystal, you might say. And that's the game's biggest shortcoming: it's far too short for Steam. It took me about half an hour on the first attempt - 20 minutes on my second. People expect Steam games, especially
games, to have a roughly a few hours of gameplay, but this is all over far too quickly. The explanation of the plot doesn't fit in with
lore (although it probably fits most people's expectations of how Headcrabs came about) and it plays fast and loose with the main boss, casually discarding the big boss of the next game as little more than a minor nuisance to be swept aside with two rounds rapid.
The biggest mystery of all in the game is why they decided to send one man into a parallel universe to retrieve the crystal? If the marines couldn't handle the breach (and which universe are these marines from? There's holes in more than just the universe), why should one guy (in a HEV suit, which really doesn't do that much) be able to?
The fact that all this takes place in a parallel universe has no bearing whatsoever on the plot. You might as well just set it off the West Coast during bad weather, that's what it looks like. And the water is abominable! The effect looks weird and you can see where the water ends and the skybox begins (which isn't very far).
had lots of promise, but in the end it didn't deliver. It's a shame really, as there's obviously been a lot of work put into this. I hope at some point this gets improved on because I think with some more voice actors and animators (not to mention a bigger boat), this game could really kick♥♥♥♥♥

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to play god? Even of just of a small area? Well Crest, the religion simulator may help you with that curiosity.
In Crest, you are the god of a small village. In order to keep your villages alive and thriving, you give each area a command. Yet, they can choose to not listen to you. At first youcan tell them to produce food or to produce children. The things is, is not only do you have to make sure that they are well fed, but happy too. The thing is, is that some may be producing lots of food, however they become pretty unhappy if they don’t have kids. Also, when they have kids, they’re happy but could starve to death.
On top of that, everything expands and you have to take care of multiple areas. Yet, there are some followers who will get disgruntled and leave. Thus they disobey your commands. In the end, the point of Crest is to make sure that you still have worshipers. When all your worshipers die, or no longer believe in you, it’s the end of the game.
Crest is totally a different game than what I am used to. It’s a nice change of pace. As a god, you can send suggestions but you can’t force your followers to listen to you. Naturally, when you’re trying to be a good god, people are not always going to listen to you even when you know what’s best. Those ones ended up dying for me though.
Either way, it’s totally an interesting game. So far, I have three different areas flourishing. Sure, there’s several dumb followers running around in the wilderness, thinking they know what’s best for themselves, but the rest of my followers are doing pretty well.
Now I can play this game without trying to re-rent it from blockbuster. I hope they make Seeds Of Evil now

Serious review:
I remember playing Turok on the N64 years and years ago and always enjoyed it, though playing it through now I don't think I ever got very far on the N64 version, because there are a lot of levels I don't remember.
If you enjoyed it before, or if you like that sort of old-school N64 shooter, like Quake for example, then I'm pretty sure you'll like this.
It's a remake, rather than a remaster, so the graphics are all basically the same as the N64 version. So if you're expecting an up-to-date look and feel, you won't find it here. The gameplay is simplistic - basically just run, jump and shoot, none of the features you might expect from the current generation of games, but it's still a lot of fun.

Okay guys, it's been years since I've played this but I've played it again and I've got my 2 cents to lay down here. Coming from the N64 to PC, it's freaking Turok. Turok man. So I gotta do this review right for y'all. If you want to know why you ABSOLUTELY should get this game, keep reading.
This was the first game I played on N64, and that it exists on Steam today brings back so much memories. From the opening sequence to the iconic "I AM TUROK", the nostalgic feels hit so hard. I have a PC N64 controller, but I decided to forego that flavor of input in favor of experiencing this game in the only acceptable controls: the mouse and keyboard.
If you're still with me, I'm going to tell you now, why you have absolutely got to get this game without any hesitation. It was a lengthy process, and I even rage-quit a few times. Despite the circumstances leading up to this, I have determined this is the kind of game you must buy. Even on a whim. Why?

OK!!!, this is hard because I do like the concepts of this game. However, give players the choice whether to go hardcore or not. I do like the idea of realistic game play; but, to die again and again without any type of reward or enjoyment is so infuriating. I can see keeping the arena the same. But, in game mode, either make the combat easier to control or put a save mode for those who don't want to go hardcore. I play video games to relax and unwind; not to get stressed out and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. I'm to the point now I kind of want my money back. I would really like this game to succeed; I don't see this happening if more options for the combat system and type of game play are allowed. Maybe even a multiplayer co-op where players can help one another get through the game.

For those who are wondering if its worth the buy.
Long story short, Yes. Definately worth a go for $15.
But, should consider what your getting into.
(Especially the combat which can be a double edged sword.)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Long Stroy:
Never seen anything quite like this. I'd say a breath of fresh air for otherwise a stale genre.
Unique combat+atmospheric visuals provide for a very immersive experience, and can be very rewarding at times.
However, it has it's fair share of drawbacks and flaws. To the point that it can be suffocating than fresh at some points.
Pro.
-Very unique combat system that adds to realism and challenge.(Easy to understand, VERY hard to master, but fun)
-Game mode for practicing combat.
-Realistic prop physics-including the player ragdoll-addding to realism and immersion.
-Enjoyable looting.
-Beautiful graphics fit for a modern dungeon crawler.(The shadows are especially well exectued)
-Very detailed and nice extra touches here and there.
-Nicely optimized.
-Realistic sounds that are affected by player interactions.(You can slam doors, if you swing your mouse hard enough)
Con.
-Very clunky combat and movement system.(Which I feel the devs will not tend to..WILL ELABORATE FURTHER BELOW)
-Very punishing despite the difficulty.(Perma death. Lack of checkpoints and No difficulty settings what so ever.)
-Environments can be sometimes bland. Easy to lose track of where you are if not careful.
-Difficult to read if npc's are hostile or not.(Your pretty much screwed if your trying to fight it out early game.)
*****MORE ELABORATION of COMBAT & MOVEMENT*****
Too be honest, I pretty much have no issues about this game.
EXCEPT Combat & Movement.
Which is fun and excruciatingly painful at the same time.
As of now it is very unpolsihed. Even in alpha game standards.
At current level this game feels more like a ragdoll physics sim than a dungeon crawler.
I like the devs intention realistic physics but, they could of executed it much better.
Button input-> Action is somewhat delayed.
Some attack inputs are unintuitive and downright awkward.
Matters get even worse with the camera and aiming.
You can reset the camera angle to face the point where your aiming. Aiming direction is done by the mouse.
But, why?... Why? would you make it so that it takes reference of where the ragdoll is looking! (ㅡ_ㅡ);;
Now I said something about delayed input. It apparently counts for aiming too.
I understand. Realism, right? its all good but, when you reset your camera angle while the ragdoll is turning...
well your up for some awkward camera angles that doesn't help in surviving at all..
More on the aiming. Some crucial attack options require you to press the left shoulder side of the player ragdoll.
However when you move your mouse to the left so does your character.
And when I mean by left I mean it.
If you press the left shoulder side when the character has already turned...
It will not use the intended attack, since where you pressed is no longer the characters left shoulder side.
(Meaning you not only made the wrong attack choice but, also facing the wrong direction. Your Screwd :) )
These type of aiming and camera angle problems bring about awkward situations often deciding life or death situations.
(i.e characters doing a 360 in combat, tripping over own leg... etc)
Devs. If your aiming for realism.
You shouldn't make it feel like your controling a ragdoll from Gmod with multiple physguns...
Kind of a bit too much when your trying to survive in a dungeon as a puppeteer.
Trust me if I wanted to play octodad I'd play octodad.

Nonetheless, I believe it is well deserved.
Especially for devs who seem to be thinking that "NEW" & "REALISTIC" is supposed to be an excuse for bad design.
(Read what they wrote in the description of the game and there in game guide. You'll get the feel.)
Sorry about the long bashing...got a bit frustrated I guess.
Despite that, I've spent only 6 hours in the game, I have completed both the novice and expert arena modes
and hopefully can say that I have grasped a bit of the game enough to make an evaluation.

This game does not deserve anywhere near the hate it is getting in the Steam reviews. The sheer ambition of this game is palpable, the developers are not very subtle in their goal of making a 3D desktop replacement and my lord do they almost deliver. Whoever on the team decided to use the Source engine is a genius. Its just as flexable and well optimized as ever which allows you to jump in and out of game without taxing your CPU or bugging up the whole works. Adding arcade cabinets is a breeze as well, if the community doesnt already have a cabinet made up for your game you can make one yourself with just a couple pictures and maybe a hotlink to a trailer if you want to get fancy. Not to mention the inexaustible amount of assets and resources that have built up in the decade that the Source engine has been around, all of which can be ported in with minimal effort, the customization options are endless. Yeah its got some problems for example the web browser coded into the game is in bad need of some updating. Also the interface for changing cabinets is not very intuitive, also positioning is a bit of a pain could really use some kind of grid just to make it easier to keep things level. But its free so who friggen cares. Why would you hate on something thats free what are you not getting your moneys worth? This game has so much promise especilly as we move into an age of VR. We need people out there thinking of ways to make our computer interfaces more than flat 2D menus. On that reason alone this game deserves your support, the fact that its so damn cool and fun to mess with is just a bonus and a sign that there is something truely special happening here. For god sakes recommend it to your friends, spam people about it on Facebook, name your kids Anarchy and Arcade, keep these guys working on this game. Because they probably could be doing something much more important with their talents, and if you keep hating on them they might figure that out.

If you're looking for a game where you build whole cities and then crush them in your iron grip... then that's exactly what you do in this game!  Only.. not at all.
You're a game developer with a small bit of money and have to build a team up from nothing basically.  It's a time management and adventure type game.
You have to increase the skill of your workers in various specialties like Sound, Coding, Writing, etc.
Your workers can get good enough at a specific skill to actually specialize in it and start learning new skills by learning new programs on training kiosks (that you build)  As their skills increase, so does the viability of your product.
Picking genres that directly support your team's skill is definitely a cool part of the game.  Especially when you are in the midst if training to new skills and/or have new folks on your team.
I really liked being given access to new training techniques and even the ability to "enhance" members of your team to get rid of bad habits like overeating or arriving late.  Later in the game you can also ADD enhancements to them to help them work harder and be more efficient with their time.
All in all, this game was a pleasant surprise and definitely worth your time.

Creeper World. (This is a review for the trilogy which you can get through links on the developers website for about $25 and includes a Steam key for the third game, which is the only game currently on Steam)
The Creeper World trilogy are RTS games, with a twist. The enemy is not (most of the time,) a specific unit, but instead a wave of blue goo that must be held/pushed back in order to achieve your goals. There are enemy units later on in the second and third games, but every level will be about beating the goo to some extent.
The feel of the game is somewhat similar to a tower defense game at times, but not so constrained. Most of your 'units' are emplacements/turrets, albeit ones that can usually be moved when you need them somewhere else.
The complexity of the game increases throughout the series, (so I would recommend starting weith the first game and playing through the trilogy,) but never felt stale even in the first game. The second game changed the style of the game somewhat, and whilst interesting and fun, it wasnt as engaging as the first game, and fortunately the third game returns to the style of the first. Dont get me wrong though, all three games are good.
There is a story, but its a minimal affair, a paragraph or two at the start of each mission, sufficient to add a bit of colour, but ultimately nothing to get excited about.
There are also downloadable demos for each game available on the developers website if you want to have a go and see for yourself.
including a web based version of the first game.
So, any drawbacks? The graphics are simplistic but functional, the same is probably true of the sound effects/music. but I tend to turn it off and listen to a cd anyway. The interface is a bit basic, could do with a bit of love and a bit more control, ie text sizes etc, but other than that, its an RTS and its a good one, with map editors, a lot of missions built in and literally thousands of player generated maps too.
As such, it is absolutely recommended.

I just finished the main campaign of Creeper World 3 today, a unique tower defense/RTS game that uses a thermodynamic simulation to control the "Creeper", a fluid–like substance that must be combatted to conquer the game's levels. A return to the top–down perspective of the original Creeper World, this game also incorporated many elements of the previous sequel, Creeper World 2 (which had a different perspective and significantly different mechanics).
While I enjoyed this game very much, my biggest complaint is that the performance suffers when you have too many units built, which hampers my preferred turtle/juggernaut strategy. On some of the large maps, even playing at 4x speed the gameplay would slow to an interminable pace. Aside from that reservation, I'd certainly recommend this game, particularly to RTS and tower defense enthusiasts. The story is bat♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy, but who plays this kind of game for the story?

I got sucked into a couple hundred hours of 2070 after eyeing this game and seeing some negative reviews.  200 hours in I couldn't take it anymore and my impulse got the better of me.  I'm glad I bought it.
One of the negative things I read was that it was a watered down Anno because you don't set up actual ships on trade routes anymore.  While that's true you still have to set up trade routes and balance them, sometimes fairly intricately.
The aesthetic of this game is just awesome.  Its just so cool as a city builder to organically watch all the details progress over time.  Seeing the shipping lanes form on your islands as skyscrapers build up around city centers or on the moon as your radiation shields absorb asteroids.
If you're a fan of the supply chain aspect of Anno, this game is better in every way than 2070.
A couple negative things I felt.  The naval combat, while still better than 2070's system, still feels pretty detached and after a while repetative.  Also the side missions from various other corps are just as boring as before but this time they're worthless in terms of rewards as well, unless you're in a pinch.  Also I miss the whole ecological balancing aspect, although there are other new things to balance.
Overall, I couldn't say I'd ever go back to 2070 after playing this.  It's great.

I read through the negative reviews, I thought I could stomach the weaknesses of the game compared to the earlier Anno games because of the interesting parts Anno 2205 had to offer. I was wrong.
More than anything else, I really miss setting up the elaborate transport routes that I used for the previous Anno titles. Now it's just a very bland pulling a few sliders and resources are automatically transferred from one zone to another for a small fee. Not a single ounce of creativity in it. Your people in one zone demand a good that can only be made in another zone. You create a supply of that good in that other zone, and then pull the transport slider, then you're done.
I will say that significant improvements to the naval combat game were made, but it plays more like its own distinct mini-game rather than as a cohesive piece of the larger game as a whole.
The only challenge of an Anno game that is really left in here is being able to do the best you can in effectively tiling your islands with various to maximize your space utilization and minimize any wasted space. This is a well implemented mechanic, and it was done at least as well as it was in the previous Anno games.
Do yourself a favor and pick up Anno 2070 instead if you're interested in this.
And if you choose to ignore my advice and buy this game anyway (hey, I did it too, I won't judge), you should also know that the DLC kinda does help to make Anno 2205 a more complete game, but it also does inflate the pricetag that much more.

If you're going into this wanting a well-presented time-killer of a flash game, you may like this. For someone hoping for a complicated base defense or tactics-heavy game- or even something as complex as a basic tower defense game- you're likely going to be very disappointed [as I was].
Pros
*Didn't seem to have any bugs
*Polished presentation
Neutral
*Putting together parts is as cool an idea as you'd expect, but you never really feel a good impact from adding a single part, and the aesthetics feel like they could have been made more interesting.
*Upgrading system is straightforward and uncomplex
Cons
*Available Parts have preferential- rather than tactical- relation to one another. This is emphasized by the small number of parts you can bring to a map.
*The map interactions are bland and repetitive, with the same tactics working each go, and the enemies feeling far too identical
*Combat is overly simplistic- hands-off combat can be fun, but only if team building/tactics is emphasized, which in this game, it is not.
*The game is far too easy- likely because making it harder'd require a more complicated combat system.
*The interface is lacking
In summary, the game is just overall lacking in depth.
It- as the store description states- is a tug-of-war game, not a strategy game.
Of course, if you want a tug-of-war simulator represented by sacrificial swarms of caterpillars with special woodland summons to affect the outcome, then by all means, this is your game!
This would have done a lot better as a free flash game- even for fans of the casual strategy genre, I can't recommend paying full for the game, not with better games cheap or even freely available.

9min of this game
It's a fairly a simple game.
On the left you will have a leaf counter that goes up slowly, this is used to pay for pillar parts or make the gain faster.
Your pillar parts are under the battle field and what the little guy will look like is above it.
Each segment of the pillar is added to the head and then you send the little tyke off to kill.
Each part you add gives them some hp + whatever bonus the segment gives like say armor, speed, hp, defense, but most are weapons.
When you send them out they will start at your tree (left side unless your in co-op) and move out until they come to an enemy or the opponents tree.
At that point they will attack with what ever weapon they have or bite if they have none.
Push them back and take out their tree without them doing it to you first.
If the level was at the base of a tree on the level map you'll fight a boss.
After fights you can upgrade your pillars segments, the tree's leaf gain, tree hp, the trees gun or change your pillars skin.
There are also 3 animal helpers that you can buy to call in during a fight, a squirrel (gives you leaves), a turtle mage (slows enemies), & a bird (craps on all opponents and they will lose health).

Bottom line: I don't think the beta has changed much and I don't feel anything for my followers, making this and unfulling god game for me.
A dev requested that I take another look at the game, saying much had changed. However, I find that it plays much the same (identical from my perspective) as it did a year ago. I do not see any main mechanics have changed and the game seems to run slower (I'm running on a newer computer than I was before even). As a god game lover, I'm not exactly sure why this doesn't resonate for me but I guess I still just don't find it fun. Honestly, beyond than some bug fixes, maybe some new words, and a cooler map, I'm not sure what has changed. The advisors are still unimportant, it seems like the icons in all the menus have gotten smaller, your commandments are still largely inconsequential (and maybe that's the point of the game, I guess I just don't find it fun) unless someone converts your comandment into some form of canibalism and then everything falls apart.
Maybe I missed in the tutorial if there was a way to name your followers something other than "Follower 3" ect. However, hearing that "Follower 6 migrated from Jackel Fields to Lizard Marsh" doesn't make me feel anything. I hardly understand if there are even any in-game reprocussions of that. I think a crucial part of any god game on this scale is that you feel something for indivuals and you have some stake in how they fare (i.e. Sims, Niche). The only reason I could to care here is that if they die the game is over. Although I guess this game is more on the scale of Reus or Godus, in which case, I can hardy experience anything on the city level (i.e. watching them catch food) because there is so much going on with lions and bright colors (and the choppiness of it running slow).
The best part: Your commandments can actually change the world your followers live in. They could hunt all the antelopes or turn savanna into jungle. Thats cool.
Fixes: Make menu's larger. Return game to a reasonable frame rate. Make me feel that each indivudal life matters (at least give them randomly generated names, maybe they need to life longer, maybe faith travels through family lines (it matters who has a baby with who) or even have event screens i.e. Stellaris or Crusader Kings II where I learn something of substance has happened to one of these things that I care for): I should care when one of them is killed by a lion. Or go the other route: make me feel achievement by growing larger cities or advancing trade or technology and unlocking new things (as is, unlocking by exploration does not make me feel like I've achieved anything: they may have just explored on their own and I unlock the easiest words first).

I was looking forward to this game when it was first released back in 2015 and I am now disgusted at how it turned out. A top down light fantasy world with 'realistic' combat and movement is almost impossible to ruin, except they did.
It's physics system is the biggest turn off in my eyes, which they gloat about being amazing and realistic i.e "Exanima's exceptional attention to detail and realistic simulation of all things aim to provide a deeply immersive and dynamic gameplay experience", is the most unrealistic combat system I've seen to date and I play a lot of crappy medieval action games. Very well polished for an EA game, with a few saving hiccups when it comes to arena mode.  The world looks amazing, when it comes to texture and lighting.  When you accidentally kick your torch across the room, you're in for a bad time.
While this game has great physics, graphics and a highly polished world, the controls are utterly garbage and inconsistent.  With movement being camera based, it's very easy to accidentally turn yourself around and give your back to the enemy.  And seeing as how unforgiving the game is when it comes to death, it can get very frustrating to lose a well geared character to clunky controls.  On top of the bad camera angles and control scheme, the most frustrating part of the game is when you try to perform a back handed swing.  It feels impossible to perform it consistenly, especially when it's the best way to beat shielded opponents.  Maybe let us bind back handed swings to RMB?
Overall, well polished EA game.  For $15, not sure but seeing as how I got this for backing them on Sui Generis I don't mind the issues it has.  I just hope the gameplay is more intuitive and less clunkly when Sui Generis is released.  And give us a 1-click backhanded swing.

Hey guys!
Check this game out if you're a fan of dungeon crawlers, a fan of simulation games using 'realistic' physics, and a fan of gritting your teeth in rage, Exanima is a really good game for all of the above!
When I first saw clips of this game, I was thinking "This looks funny as hell, I want to try it out"
An hour later, after I bought the game, I was running through the beginning door after figuring out how to open it with a topless fat chick with big old floppy pancake tiddies named "Patty" useing a bucket as a helmet (ala skyrim's cauldron) a torch as a weapon, and a barrel's lid as a shield.
What awaited me somewhat down the hallways were some Hollow like guys (and girls?) that fudgsicled me up real good with what looked like, and I soon out found out to be candlestick holders.
After recreating Patty (it saved my last Character Creation person, which I'm really happy about, since you only have 1 life on that person! Sadly only one save per game, though.) I set out a little more carefully this time. (still torch and shield, because what better way to go? Protect yourself, AND see the danger!)
Unbeknownst to me, this game would actually give me "NOPE.jpg" moments which I actually love! One example was when I was walking down a dark corridor, I opened a door on the side into a dark room just to see my torch shine onto one of the Hollows standing there in the dark, no shirt on, holding an axe. I closed that door and continued on my way, not to look back.
So yeah, it's funny, sometimes spooky, all around a good experience buuuut...
(Note: This game is still only early access, so no throwing blame around for what follows!)
It's controls are frustrating sometimes. Due to the physics engine, I find myself getting caught on invisible objects, or objects with hitboxes that don't seem to fit what it looks like sometimes. A great example that I couldn't stop laughing at is, Patty got her hand stuck in a closed door at one point, resulting in some funny moments that reminded me of stretching bubblegum.
The combat is a little hard to get a grasp on when you're just starting, but after playing for a couple hours, and getting a hold of it altogether, it's not as bad as initially thought!
At some points, mainly the earlier areas, the FPS dropped really low, and when they raised back up? It acted in a slingshot manner almost like the game was trying to catch up. I was zipping, and tripping all over the place while the Hollows were able to attack me at breakneck speeds, which caused a few Deaths for Patty.
Overall though, I've only just broke the surface of this Early Access game, and I expect to put many more hours into it.
I do not regret buying Exanima whatsoever, and recommend you try it out too!

Lot's of potential here, but the combat needs some serious tweaks. Rather than a fluid and deadly dance, what we have here is a drunken shuffle with swords. Characters lurch around like your uncle after too many beers, holding onto only the tiniest semblance of finesse and balance. The first thing that must be improved is the combat movement. Rather than big lurching steps, it should be smaller, more responsive and much more fluid. This would make dashing more important as well, helping you score a telling blow after your enemy leave themselves exposed. A lot of the time I would find myself ramming my opponent instead, due to not being able to control the size of my movement. If I didn't get closer, I would be out of reach, If I did move closer, we would start cuddling. Another option I'd like to see is an easy movement or key combination for a straight stab, which would be useful in aforementioned cuddling situation. Another implementation I'd like to see is a guard break or sword beat, meaning you would knock their weapon aside for a moment if you hit it hard enough, breaking their parry and allowing you to land a strike. I'd also like to talk about the tracking system in combat. I find myself spinning a full 360, no matter how much I keep my cursor in position in front of me and on the enemy. Perhaps slightly more tracking would help keep your bearings and get that sissy ballet stuff where it belongs. (France)

My absolute favorite shooter series. I've been a fan of Turok since I was very little. Turok 2 might be still my all time favorite game (and it'll be in my library immediately after the release next year). It's a fast paced exploration platforming shooter with a native american going berserk on everything in his path. That's the short version. Pro's:
+ Fast paced action
+ Very large explorable maps with loads of secrets
+ Cool weapons
+ Old school nostalgia
+ Great music
+ Bosses
+ Remastered --> 60 fps, 4k, widescreen... it's so fluent and awesome
+ I... AM TUROK!
Cons:
- Learning curve (differs per person)
- Newcomers could be disappointed by either graphics, old gameplay mechanics and difficulty
Fanboying aside, it's worth a try. I recommend this game for arcade like shooter fans, retro gamers, Turok and dinosaur hunters.

There's a link to my review in the Steam description above, but I figured I'd post some content here as well.
"When it comes down to it, “Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal” keeps the addictive quality of the original alive and then some.  The extra content is just icing on the cake and almost assures return visits. In terms of whether or not it is suitable for kids, I’d have to go on record and simply say, “yes”.  There is no blood/gore and as an added bonus, it promotes critical thinking in that you’re forced to tackle maps in a systematic way.  Coming at the creeper from one side may not work, for example, but establishing a foothold elsewhere might be what you need to advance.  In a sense, this game is not only a real-time strategy/tower defense hybrid, but it’s also part-puzzle and will certainly make you think.  This combination is great for kids and adults alike, in my opinion.  All in all, “Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal” is a brilliant addition to an already fantastic series.  While this game is without a doubt a keeper, there’s a free demo on the official website (link below) should you wish to try before you buy."
Full Review:

It's World of Goo vs. The Blob!
The Creeper is a simple, slow moving liquid and you have a literal army of sophisticated gadgets to fight it. However, you need to gather resources, build defenses, and figure out how to actually fight back while The Creeper ever slowly creeps closer and closer. At least, that's how things start out. Soon, you begin to find out why multiple human space empires could have fallen to this deceptively simple-looking enemy...
Each level provides a different challenge, and after you play a few levels it becomes obvious why this game has three installments already. It doesn't look like much, but then, neither does The Creeper. The game itself, like The Creeper, is deceptively easy to underestimate, but if you like strategy games, building games, or puzzle games, you should give this a try. There's nothing quite like it.

Okay, I am loving the hell out of this. This game is an improvement in ALMOST every way.
First off, the fact that the game is split up into five three-level-one-boss worlds is a lot better than the nine single levels of the original. The benefits are many here - Better artistic cohesion, better music with motifs that can go from level to level, and the ability to space the gags and gimmics out better rather than trying to cram them all into a single themed level. Area 52 is a prime example of this. Different-but-similar music in each, and the levels each working with a different gimmick.
Also, while it may seem a bit strange that we're down to only the Nerd as opposed to the switchable characters of before, I ended up liking this better, because in the original, some parts of levels could be utterly broken by some characters, so the levels had to accomodate for all of them. Not so with here - With one single character and one single line of upgrades - Yes, there's megaman-style upgrades this time around - the levels can be tuned far better. And they are.
Also, the soundtrack is fantastic, even compared to the original. While there is a bit less variety this time due to the aformentioned themed worlds, they instead re-tweak the music to be different in each world's levels. For instance, Browntown's music gets faster and and harsher in each level. I love it.
However, I have three minor complaints about the game.
First off...The difficulty. No, not because it's difficult, that's what most people buy into this for...It's the exact oppsite. Normal is as brutal as it was before, but...Easy is an utterly staggering difficulty downstep. Enemies are weaker, you have more lives, and you only take half-bottles (hearts) of damage. So not only does this give you double your normal hp, this makes it so that each bottle of health-restoring beer gives you two hearts back. I found myself able to utterly facetank most of the bosses.
And honestly? Part of me kinda thinks that's okay. Yeah, sure, this game is aimed at hardcore people, but being able to include less skilled people is totally fine. And trust me, no amount of health will help you in the final level. Good god.
...Though note that I said final level, not final boss. Thats my second complaint. Even accounting for me reaching that part on easy (Browntown's boss is too hard for me currently on normal), the final boss is utterly underwhelming, especially compared to the living nightmare that was Fred Fuchs in the original. The preceding level is insane though, so let that be your final challenge.
And finally...The music. The music is mostly amazing...But one thing I kinda want... Browntown's music without the fart noises.
Yeah. They incorporate fart noises as parts of the music in two tracks. While it DOES work, I kinda wanna hear it without that. Because those two tracks are wonderful.
At any rate, TLDR: Great game, better than the original, STRONGLY reccomend you don't go down to Easy unless you utterly have to.

Let me be quite clear. I strongly disliked the first AVGN game. I felt it betrayed its retro-themed spirit in favor of emulating a bad game as some sort of "joke", was highly flawed as a masocore experience, and relied far too much on referential AVGN canon humor rather than come up with original humor of its own. Now a sequel's come out, and I must admit that it improves upon many tiny aspects of the game that upset me before, making it far more playable overall. It still, however, falls into several of the same pitfalls that the previous game did.
As the Angry Video Game Nerd, you run and jump and shoot through 22 short levels, each with their own themes and gimmicks. This is a step up from the last game's Mega Man style approach of 8 longer levels; the brevity means that you're only playing a stage for 5 minutes or so before moving on, and moves things along at a solid clip. This also means that levels can be built around a certain new element; there are autoscrollers, swimming levels, stages with gravity flipping mechanics, and timed platform navigation, to name a few. The myriad and multiple placement of the first game's infamous "death blocks" has been toned down... mostly. Though the levels don't spam their instant death hazards too much, the game just couldn't resist the lure of the death blocks in the end, and there are sections where they get a bit overused.
The big new mechanics involve making the game more like Mega Man X; almost immediately you get a wall jump upgrade, and five more upgrades can be found hidden in the levels. They're welcome, but honestly don't add much to the game other than minor help on the stages. Beating the game with and without them is virtually identical, and the powers don't help navigation through the stage in any major way. Limited use items found in the game fare a bit better; the keg, which refills your health, is a welcome addition. It makes bosses a bit easier, as most of them give you a keg so you can damage race them. This is espeically apparant with minibosses.
The gameplay itself is fine, and the presentation is well done, audibly and visually. Some annoying filters are present in certain levels, especially the final one. AVGN references are still here in full force, unfortunately. The game does take strides to add its own humor, but more often than not the gags fell flat for me. The things that are references didn't amuse me terribly, either; though I understood the references, I was not particularly impressed by them. The two most prevalent in the game are the constant re-appearances of another Internet review type, Doug Walker's Nostalgia Critic, and a world themed around 2014's AVGN movie. Mileage may vary on this, so if you loved it in the last game, here's more of it.
It IS an improvement over the first game in a lot of ways, but in the end thanks to Steam's binary I gave it the thumbs down because I think you can do better with your money. At $15 USD, you're getting about two hours of play time. If you want a superior retro-themed experience, for that cash you can get Shovel Knight, one of the finest retro-esque games to come out in a long time. If you want an old-timey game that pokes fun at/references old video games, Castle In The Darkness is a third of that price, and longer to boot. If you want to see and hear AVGN gags, rent or buy the AVGN movie, or watch the videos on Youtube for free. If you see this on sale for 5 bucks in a year's time and kind of like the AVGN, you may find it worth your time. Otherwise, I'd steer clear and go for something else to get a better bang for your buck.

Don't let the deceptively austere environment fool you - there is a high amount of detail and the atmosphere helps build the mysteriousness of the story. As for audio, music is sparse - in a good way. The tracks build slowly and help illuminate the progress you've made. I really enjoy exploring open-world environments to find hidden secrets, and this game rewards you with bits and pieces of information relevant to the story. You can die, as I did during a variety of the platforming style puzzles, but thankfully a checkpoint system is in place that doesn't put you too far back from your current position. It's unusual for a game to have no interface on-screen, but it really helps heighten the enjoyment of the overall ambience the game is trying to exude.

Orcs Must Die is a tower defense like game where you set traps in a dungeon-themed level and then survive the onslaught of waves of enemies. There are a couple twists to this formula:
1. You play a character who can actually run around the level and take active part in the game (offensively).
2. As with any tower defense game, you are have (traps in this case) to lay down. The trick is there are more traps than you are allowed to have so you must choose what you want to use.
3. Of the selectable "slots" you have to equip traps in, you can also equip weapons and passives if you choose.

-Play the game on easy the first time through. Seriously. You need the drops to level up your stuff so that you can go back through and cruise through each map later.
There are also additional modes like:
- Endless mode
- Weekly challenges
- Classic mode - 10 remastered levels from OMD1

Have you ever wanted to play as an "Elf God" in a game?  Me too, so I asked the developers if it was possible with this game.  Here's what I was wonderfully told...
"Well, Vosoros. That's actually already possible, in a way. :)
Let me explain, if you tell your followers not to kill all the animals or farm too much, or mine too much they will leave their environment in a balanced state. However, since the ecology system is a little bit wonky still it's not very easy to get a balanced state. We're addressing this in our upcoming module called the Exploration module, which we will start working on during the autumn.
It's impossible to have a blanket statement that will tell them to live in balance, since that balance is relative to your island or your goals. We want to give you varied tools to make a balance you feel fits with the story you want to have.
Also, in the upcoming module called Faith (that comes out this month) there will exist a doctrine where people will be inclined to preserve nature, they're simply called "The Preservers". You can try to educate your followers to follow this line of thought."
Enough said, I'm in love with this game now...

I had one settlement in the middle of an island. Half the island was just desert, but the main settlement was in a savannah near two rivers and jungle. This settlement was very successful, constantly having children yet never running out of food. It was completely surrounded by farms. Soon new settlements started popping up, but they always appeared in the desert. These new settlements were good at only one thing.
Starving to death
I've gone through probably five other settlements in fifteen minutes, while the main one still thrives.
4/5 Still needs work, but it isn't too bad as an earlym access.

Crest is a game where you are a god and you are trying to guide your followers through the hardships of their world and have them survive as long as possible.  you can save and quit but there is no manual saving and loading (again the goal is to make your guys survive as long as possible).
The main twist of the game is you do not give direct orders to them but you give them commandments and depending on what they need they may or not follow them. They also may add their own addendums to your commandments or may completely disregard them.
The game is in early access so there is not a ton of content right now. You have your basic need (food, procreate, materials) you can migrate and build more cities and interact with the fauna (lions and antelopes). There are other things coming like economy or ideology. Game seems stable enough (i did crash but only once and that may have been on my end).
I could see people spending a few hours even at this state and be satisfied with the game especially at its price (which is kinda cheap).

Crest is an interesting game that feels more realistic than many other god games. The way the people are able to interpret your will differently than what you want is quite amusing to watch and frustrating at time. However I still say that it is a great experience overall.
