For those of you who don't know it, Exanima is sort of a prelude, demo and experiment all baked into one for another game called Sui Generis, so this review will probably apply to both of those games.
For starters, let me just say that this game is awesome, there's just no other way to put it. Having that said, let's get down to what this game is all about.
It is a 3D top-down RPG set in a medieval-ish universe. Exanima places a lot of focus on physics (character movement, combat, interaction etc) and it's being performed very well. Im not really sure how they've done it, but movement in the game is not fixed animations from what I can see. If you run through a hallway and your foot get's caught under a fallen chair, your character will fall flat on his/hers face.
Not because of some trigger on the chair, but because your foot was caught and was not in the place your character expected when he/she lifted his/hers other foot up.
Same thing applies to combat: If you smack a warhammer right across someones face, it will send them twirling to the ground, again, not because of some script telling it that it was a special move, but because that character is simply not able to maintain balance and resist the sheer force.
This would apply both ways however, if your character swings that warhammer and misses, then your character will most likely be forced to follow the warhammer with his/hers entire body in an attempt to slow it down and bring it back into position for another attack. That's time that your opponent is likely to take advantage of, provided he/she is equipped with a lighter, more manageable weapon.
There will also be a kind of magic called "thaumaturgy". However it is not in the game yet and can only be seen and read about in lore and videos from devs.
Right now there are two game-modes, Arena and a gamemode that has not been named yet, but it strongly resembles a campaign-mode, so that's what I'll call it.
In the arena the player is pitted one on one against NPCs with various equipment. When the player has beaten the NPC he has the ability to loot the NPC and use his/hers equipment. When the player so chooses he/she can then move on to the next stage of the arena, with a more well-equipped (and possibly slightly more tactical?) NPC waiting for him. After each victory the player is also rewarded with a slight healing boost (not much though).
In the campaign-mode, the player wakes up in a dark room without anything else but the shabby clothes on his/hers back and a part of a note (I won't spoil too much). He/she is then left to explore the area, uncovering the story as he/she progresses further.
Ow right, forgot to mention one thing... Damage is permanent, as is death, and healing is rare, bordering on non-existent. So be careful when you fight.
Remember, heroes die fighting, cowards live to backstab another day...

May be the most fun I've had with hand-to-hand game combat.
Hope great things happen throughout the rest of the development process.

It has been a long time since I have found a rougelike and dungeon crawler that excells above and beyond the expected standards that seem to have been set for the genre. Exanima not only has a fun and engaging physics based combat system that take your momentum into account but also isn't a text based adventure. The maps extremely atmospheric and almost everything that isn't nailed down to the ground can be inactivated with; from the boxes on the ground to the tiny coins resting atop counters.
The Combat System - As I said before Exanima uses physics based combat. If you hit an enemy with your weapon they will be pushed back slightly. Your body will also move with the attack rather that standing in one stationary place. Everything is based on momentum. If you move with the swing it has the ability to deal more damage to your target.
Damage dealt to your character can come in two forms, the first being yellow damage. Yellow damage dealt to your health bar will slowly heal over time. This is know as temporary damage. The second type of damage is red damage or permament damage that lowers your maxed HP and can only be healed by health items.
Your attacks and direction your character is facing is dependant on where your mouse cursor is located on the screen. You have the abilty to swing use your weapon from either right or left and an overhead strike. As long as your character is facing where the attack is coming from they will automaticlly block; if you aren't already attacking. The combat may seem rather easy and simplistic but there is an extreme learning curve. Your characters can use multiple weapons with different stats, such as a one handed sword or a two handed maul.
Skills - In the current build of the game there is only one skill tree avaiable for players to use; the close combat skill. Within the skill tree there are currently four different subskills that you can choice to learn in whatever order you want. Each skill works well with different fighting styles they player may choose to use.
Effects and Soundtrack  - From the sound of a man running in chainmail armour and a sword scraping along the floor to doors being opened close every sound in the game feels and sounds very 'real'. The ingame effects have the ability to truly help immerse you into the game.
The soundtrack has a very atmospheric feeling to it, while also playing heart pumping music during fights. All in all I feel it fits.
The Core Game - The game is currently divided into three maps with many enterable rooms, loot to find, and enemy to fight and die to. The game, being a rougelike, is extremely unforgiving with permadeath and very few health potions(three in fact). There are many ways that game can be played, either fighting through everything or using hidden passways to bypass dangerous areas. There are puzzles and traps within the dungeon that can be avoided or beaten.  It is all up to the way you want to play the game.
There is also a Arena mode that you can play to learn and practice your skills in melee combat. It has two difficulties, Novice and Expert, each with their own enemies and challenges.
Things that could be viewed as failures -
1. Not having a save feature for Arena
2.Somewhat buggy physics and combat system
3.Errors and bugs(the game is only in beta)
4.Limited content: The campagin only has three levels that you can progress through and depending on your experince with rougelikes this might take a couple of days to only a few hours.
5.While the development team plans to add multiplayer(PVP) and Co-op to the game there isn't anyway to share your experinces with your friends currently.
6.Other than lore and backstory there doesn't seem to be any strong narrtive to the game, which in my opinion is fine. You make your own story.
Overall I feel that even in its current limited state, Exanima is a great game. I feel that it is better than the majority of recent dungeon crawlers and rougelikes. I found the game extremely enjoyable and I definitely recommend it for players seeking a wild adventure.
PLEASE NOTE THAT EXANIMA IS ONLY A PLAYABLE TEASER FOR BARE METTLE ENTERTAINMENT'S UPCOMING GAME, SUI GENERIS. Here is a link to their website:

Written Review (Video series can be found at the bottom):
Overview:
Exanima is a game that i have been looking for for a long time. It is a mixture of frustration and excitement, mingled with the joy that i find myself feeling whenever i choose to delve into its dark and mysterious world. The fact that the story is not laid out in front of you is a challenge that almost anyone who has ever played an RPG would be more than happy to take. Every time you find a parchment, a book, or even a signficant room - it's like lighting a candle in a dark room: the more candles you light, the more you can see and understand. It can be interpreted any way you want. Some people may see it as a story of death and destruction, and others may see it as a story of heroics in a time when heroes were few and far between. You will run through the campaign (what's implemented so far) multiple times, and always find something new to either play with, or discover. Unraveling the story of this world is the objective (IMO) - but you will find yourself fighting tooth and nail for every page of it.
Once you step over the threshold of the first room, there is no going back. You will be sucked into the cruel world known as Exanima - where around every corner there is a different evil, and every sound leaves you clinging to your torch, and praying that you might soon find the light.
Will you survive long enough to tell the tales of the underbelly of the world?
Combat:
Exanima features a very unique combat system. Understand that you will not be able to master it within the time frame of your first session of play!
I have been told multiple times by one of my friends (who is new to Exanima) that the characters look like drunken hobo's fighting: but i do not see that. I am not going to sit here and say that i have mastered the combat, but i certainly understand it more now. To me, the characters seem very controlled and professional. They no longer flail around wildly swinging swords and -maybe- hitting each other. Having said that, the combat can be seen in multiple different lights - and mastered in a variety of ways.
The two sides of this spectrum are "realistic/historical" and "Gamey/competitive".
Those on the realistic/historical side tend to incorporate real life experiences that they've picked up from studying historical manuscripts, or from learning other styles of combat (boxing,wrestling,ect.).
Those on the gamey/competitive side tend to see the AI as what it is. They know how to shake up the AI so that it is defensless, and easily take them down with minimal harm done to yourself.
Regardless of how you personally manipulate the combat of the game, each side has their up/down sides.
(The spectrum i have explained above is formed from my own opinion!)
World:
One of the most interesting dungeon/underbelly worlds I've ever seen! The world is not only made up of torture chambers and prisons: this world truly feels like it was lived in. There are hospitals, housing complexes, training areas, storage rooms, manufacturing areas: everything! If i had to compare it to anything, i would compare it to the world of Metro. There is more to the world than just the metro and stations. Does that make sense?
The environment in the beginning is very true to the dungeon crawling genre: dark hallways, cold stone walls and floors, prisons and gritty areas. I find that this is good to have in the beginning because it quietly tells you that the game won't be a walk in the park. The details are amazing. You will find everything in this world that contributes to the fact that people lived, worked, and died there. I absolutely love the detail of this game.
You will find, though, that the world is not as bleak as it seems at the beginning of the game. I won't spoil anything, but the world becomes really beautiful - but even more deadly!
One of the biggest and best things that caught my attention as soon as i entered the world was the fact that nothing was bolted down. You can ransack a room if you want, barricade a door from enemies with the items at hand, build bridges across endless pits. Hell, you can even put a bucket on an enemy's head and watch him flail around a bit! The fact that you can truly do whatever you want with the world is a big plus.
AI:
The AI is something special to this game. Each one is different. They all have different personalities that contribute to the way they behave (obviously).
Some enemies you will find run straight at you even if you are not a threat to it. Others will stay stand-off-ish until you get to close. However if you keep your distance and don't look directly at it, it will leave you alone. Some enemies will watch you fight another enemy, and some will join in. You will find that some run away and hide, and others will run to bait you into an ambush.
Understanding the AI, and figuring out what to do in almost any situation involving it, is a huge part of this game - and is quite exciting!
Difficulty:
Understand that there is no difficulty slider in this game. The game is simply hard - and it continues to get harder as you move further into the world. Nothing is handed to you. You must fight, desperately sometimes, for everything you have.
Some AI (like the ones at the beginning of the game) are easier to take down - but are still a threat because you have nothing.
As you progress further you will find the fights more tense - but still relatively easy.
Three quarters of the way through the current content you will be fighting for your life. it will not be easy. You will encounter enemies you never expected to encounter, and you may die because of the shock.
It doesn't matter how far into the game you've gone. It will always be a challenge. The payoff is survivng these challenges, and moving on to the next one!
Conclusion:
Exanima is a magnificent game that can only get better as it is developed further. Everything from the world around you, to the secrets it holds - to the monsters that you fight, and the dangers you are confronted with. It makes a reputation as being difficult, but rewarding. Anyone who is interested in hardcore roleplaying games should definitely pick this up. Those of you who are not into perma-death can still play because they have early checkpoints: but understand that there will not always be checkpoints to fall back on!

Let me just start off by saying that the physics in this game are absolutely jaw-dropping, and easily (in my opinion) puts Grand Theft Auto V's physics to shame. Don't be fooled, the physics are no gimmick! The game heavily revolves around the realisticness of you, the other NPC's movement and the environment around you. If you were to run into a piece of rock on the ground then you are very likely to trip up and smash your face in.
The combat, again, relies heavily on the physics. It will require your complete attention, a good deal of practise, and a tiny bit of patience. It is not easy, but it is not badly made. How you perform in combat depends on the individual that is playing. Great fun.
The game is incredibly good looking, and can be run on its highest settings on most machines. The environment and its inhabitants are extremely detailed for a game of its size.  Also, the lighting is perfect, this game can be very dark, and with a nice warm flickering torch in your hand you can truly appreciate the shadows that this game offers.
One of my favourite features of this game would probably be the sound, if you were to hit a certain material (primarily metal and wood) against another object it will create its appropriate noise. If your sword accidentally gets dragged against a wall as you're walking by then it will create a fantastic scraping sound to accompany it. If you bang a bit of wood against somebodies helmet then you'll get a nice thud to go along with it. The music is haunting and can set a sense of isolation, though you will probably hear that same music during your whole playthrough.
So we know that the physics affect your movement and combat, but it also affects your interaction with the environment. You will need to use your cursor to open doors, lift items such as crates to look underneath them for anything of use and physically pick up and drop things into your inventory, straight off of the floor. It is very identical to the Amnesia series in this sense, and it works very well. But you are not limited to just opening doors and searching for items, eventually you will be given a series of puzzles which will require you to use whatever objects around you to advance to the next room, objects including chairs, planks and small rocks.
Imagine this, you awake in a large room lying on your face, you get up to find a flaming torch in the centre, equip it and venture off into the pitch black corridors, probably unarmed. In this dungeon-like setting you will encounter other neutral but wary humanoids like yourself. "Are they hostile?" You'll be thinking to yourself, get too close and they will be, give them some room, maneuver around them and you should both get away unscathed.
You are given one life in this game. Yes, you read that correctly. You get one life. If you so happen to die (which you most likely will) then your character will be gone, erased, bye bye. Go and make another one and start from the beginning. Think Project Zomboid.
And now I'm going to explain how your health works, You will begin with a full bar of health displayed in a nice bright yellow colour, this is good. If you get hit then your yellow bar will deplete a little and will be replaced by either an orange or a red colour, this is bad. Orange is a non-critical injury and will eventually fill all the way back up to the nice yellow colour we were talking about. If it's red then you have taken a nasty hit and this is considered a critical, this will not fill back up to yellow and you are stuck with this injury for life, critical hits are usually caused by sharp objects and you will notice a nice blood squirt to signify this. If you are in need of refilling your health then you will have to progress through the game to find one of the very scarce health drinks available.
And just so that I don't forget, yes, you can create your own character in this game, sex, skin colour, body mass, voice, hair, whatever. You can create your own character.
And along with creating a character you can personalise your individual by choosing what weapons/clothes/armour you're going to equip. And there are PLENTY of items to equip (if you ever get to find them that is, keep your eyes open).
This game is fantastic, it is fairly new at the time of writing and very much unique. It is packed with content already and is apparently quite close to becoming a fully released title (we're talking months!).
For its price you are practically stealing this game.
And if you do buy this game, then you are signing a virtual contract to say that you're ready to try something new, something unforgiving, and something unnerving and fun.
Enjoy.

isn't enough, there is a "Dial Map" service, which is a seed-based random map generator. So many potential battlefields..
So, yeah. Great game. Keep on fightin' that flood!

The updated PC release (not really a "remaster") of Turok: Dinosaur Hunter is a nostaglia-fueled adventure for those who grew up with a Nintendo 64 or fans of classic first-person shooters. The outdated graphics may be a turnoff for some players, but Night Dive Studios' optimization of the game for modern PCs has enough options to keep you satisfied.
+ Wide variety of weapons, powerups, and secondary ammo types awarded from exploration.
+ Classic FPS gameplay (Health pickups, strafe-jumping, fast movement, etc.)
+ Large maps with variety in themes and non-linear paths for exploration.
+ Updated visuals such as godrays, water reflections, better draw distance, and support for modern screen resolutions.
+ Controls are responsive and accuracy is better with a mouse than an N64 controller.
+ Blowing a guy up with tek arrows or the grenade launcher feels awesome, and seeing blood squirt from someones throat always feels satisfying.
+ Repetitive but otherwise catchy soundtrack with an electronic-tribal theme.
+ No autosaves, relies on checkpoints and saves like the good ol' days. Dying results in loss of backpack and sets you back a couple minutes of gameplay.
- FPS veterans may finish the game quickly, took me roughly six hours to finish the campaign. Not a huge issue for most players.
- The platforming takes getting used too and precise jumping is required to reach certain areas and make progress.
- The later levels do get confusing to navigate sometimes, and you may have to backtrack to find a level key if you weren't paying attention.
- Minor clipping issues, such as seeing through certain models or going partially into the ground. These are rare instances and never interfere with the gameplay.
- Outdated textures may be off-putting to modern gamers.
Simply put, Turok is worth it for the nostalgia factor and also worth it for newcomers looking for a challenging old-school FPS. Updated controls make it easier to play, and the updated visuals are a nice touch despite the lack of better quality textures.
You also get to be a shirtless native and fight dinosaurs using alien weaponry. The 90's had the best FPS protagonists.

(Mild spoilers may follow - if concerned, simply read the TLDR.)
I did not like the wispy, trailing sensation I got from playing through the story. For a game with such an onerous main plot, where you play a central role in the fate of your entire people under the volition of the gods, you meander far too much and far too distractedly on your journey to the plot's destination.
An example: On your way to the game's pilgrimage site, which involves the traversement of a tedious marshland (this is not to be confused with the journey which came before, involving the traversement of a tedious highland), you can be captured by slavers. who bring you to a random city utterly unrelated to your quest, an event which the gods bewilderingly allow to happen despite their propensity for intervening in more trivial pursuits. You spend far too great a portion of the game in an arena where slaves are made to fight each other to the death, isolated from your oblivious tribespeople.
Imagine the angst of playing through the storyline of an RPG, say, Skyrim, where one is to defeat a terrible dragon. And on your journey to its mountainous lair, you were abducted by slavers and hauled off to the bloodied sands of a coliseum halfway across the ocean - what a bewildering tangent! I am all for encumberments to the resolution of a quest, but only insofar as the villains are related to the quest itself, such that the fatal viccisitude would have been a trial to overcome, rather than a lengthy detour of misfortune devoid of your antagonist's malice, and empty of pertinence.
And thus I was away from my tribe for a drastically long period of time, separated by oblivious enemies from oblivious allies and when the time came to return to them - I was forced to leave behind the slaves who were yet in the arena, their fates unresolved and unintervened. This riles against me because what the game has done was introduce an entirely new playing field of story and morality, separate from the main questline, and then with a panoramic flick of the wrist dismissed the entire saga as though it didn't matter! A few sentences of guilt, and the entire tale vanished, never again remembered as we resumed our marshland hegira.
A tangent, and an empty one at that!
The problem with all of this is the lack of a sense of interconnectivity, which is exarcebated by the lack of a way to establish emotional attachment. A plot where you are chosen by the gods, and are leading your people on a diaspora to a hallowed ground, should be one which encourages you to actually care about the people and the gods. Apart from your advisor or two (you are limited in your interactions, being forced to choose from a rigid rubric of socialisation) you do not interact personally with individual members of the tribe. They are not a tribe of individuals for whom you care deeply, they don't even have names! None of them are family or friends, none of them are capable of dialogue or recurring interaction, they are all simply colourless pieces of resource meeples for you to collect and gather, and perhaps inspire on occasion with flaccid speeches.
I recall with amusement one of the scenes where you were forced, before a terrorist, to choose between two innocents who would be executed upon selection. You had to pick one over the other, and yet neither the damned nor the survivor in the aftermath of the damned would make any comment about your choice. I wanted to shake the survivor: "don't give me generic comments about our prison setting or how you in your infinite triteness want to be rid of it, I just murdered a person for you! Her decapitated head is right outside our cages staring! Talk to me, damn it, talk to me!"
Without a core of humanisation, there is no basal site for the player to establish emotional connections, no skeletal structure of plot to support small branching side-quests, let alone the meandering and convoluted monstrosities which had led me off the map several times to engage in unrelated storylines which were fleeting in significance and yet felt like an eternity to play through due to their abysmal and narcotic tedium.
The flaws of the game may be summarised thusly: You may collect and acquire members for your tribe, but will never speak to any of them. You may recruit members after a quest in which there is interaction, but once they're in your tribe, forget about ever seeing them again. They are now no more than a number on your screen as you trail from one scene into another, like an old-timey movie presenting a flickering series of images - between which the only connection is that you remain inexplicably the viewer.
The game was a terribly lonely playthrough for me. None of the tribe struck me as alive, and even those few clip art people capable of dialogue had cardboard personalities, being incapable of memory and utterly imperceptive of the dramatic events which unfolded around them. Saga of the North Wind was a long meandering adventure, which
have been a good thing, but unfortunately, there was no one there to talk about it.

I hate city builder games because of the micro-management aspect most of them have. (Tropico 3 was like filling out  tax form)
This game has only the bare minumum as far as management goes. You are left free to city plan, and watch your cool little town grow.

I usually see "minimalistic" graphics as a lame cop-out for developers who have no art skills. This game uses the minimalisem to its advantage. The game is not ugly. It has NO programer art. This art staff knew what they where doing. They took a look and ran with it. They kept the scale perfect, while still leaving room for small details that give the artwork its personality.
The characters are cute as hell even though they are only make out of 3 cubes. Animations are simple, but are REALLY good.
If you want another excellent city builder give Banished a try, but be warned, there is a CRAPLOAD of micro-management. I highly reccomend getting this game first, then later gving Banished a go. I play Banished for my long campaigns, and I play this game for my afternoon casual time killer. I think I actually have more fun with this game. I definately have much more playtime, and I look forward to playing it even more :)

I loved Grow Home, and this game is the most spectacular sequel i have ever played. They took the concept of growing a plant up into space and expanded upon it in the most beautiful way, with more collectables, a very interactive and friendly map and menu system, and a spherical map with a moon and asteroid belt. This has got to be one of my favorite games of 2016.

Grow Up is the first game but placed into Microsoft Paint and expanded to about 400%. It's a lot bigger but - taking both games as wholes - that doesn't necessarily make it better.
For one thing, the "oh look, there's this cool place that I can't reach yet" feel of the first game has been almost completely removed: you can pretty much get anywhere you want after just a couple of jetpack and glider upgrades. Sure it's fun to fly around wherever you like, but it changes the game into more of an open world experience in which you glaze over all the environments on your quest, as opposed to getting up close and exploring the interesting, meticulously crafted islands of Grow Home.
There's still crystals to find (as well as challenges to beat) so completionists like myself will be quite happy running around collecting everything, but as the dopamine wears off, hunting down the last few remaining challenges and crystals becomes a downright chore even with the crystal radar; as there's an entire planet and hundreds of floating rocks to scour.
It might seem like I'm not recommending this game, which isn't true. If you liked the first one, then play this one, you won't regret it. But if you haven't played either, play the first one first.
Like its predecessor,  Grow Up is fun and relaxing while still offering a challenge, and that's definitely a victory in my book.

A great sequel to the great platformer Grow Home. In Grow Up your spaceship M.O.M. crashes into a planet and it is up to you and another droid, B.U.D., and P.O.D, to find the original pieces of M.O.M. and repair her!
Compared to the first game this game plays on an entire planet instead of a map. This time there are different biomes all filled with different kinds of plants that you can use for your climbing. When you discover a new plant you 'analyze' the seed allowing you to plant these seeds wherever you like giving you much freedom for reaching the higher platforms.
I found this game a bit less surprising/fun than the original game since the much larger map also results in much more empty terrain, so I would have liked to see some more variation or use of terrain. However, if they added more challenges or pickups the game might start feeling like a grind to complete, so this is just a very small negative point.
As for the performance, the game ran at 100+ fps most of the time. However, I did have some minor hiccups every now and then but this did not distract me from playing the game.
I do recommend a controller to play this game though since it makes the game even more relaxing due to you leaning back in your chair instead of sitting actively using your mouse and keyboard. I played this game with the Steam Controller which control scheme works very well for me.
Conclusion:
If you liked the original game, you will definitely like this game. If you haven't, then If you are searching for a calm, cute, happy platforming game this is a perfect game for you.
If you played Grow Home and it left you hungry for more this is a must buy.

I don't like knocking a game which is the work of just a couple of people. It does have some upsides - an interesting art style, some nice music, decent strategic elements at times.
Unfortunately, it is all rather unbalanced. The main problem is the control scheme, which is designed for touchscreens. That does not translate well to PC at all. Worse still, it translates poorly in particular respects - melee movements are quite easy, but ranged and special moves are very hard. This renders the difficulty quite inconsistent.
Given that the combat is built around this system, it drags down the whole game.
Some of the effects are also a bit too strong - a lifesteal weapon feels like a cheat, while blindness desperately needs to have an expiry after a few turns rather than requiring a special move (rendered too difficult by the control scheme) to correct.
These unbalanced aspects unfortunately make it hard to recommend the game on PC. However, it may be more enjoyable in its natural home of a tablet.

Fearless Fantasy is a very very strange "tablet" game made for a touch screen.  It does have some very good humour in it that made me laugh.  The main evil king sounds like Mark Hamill's Joker.  Overall the voice acting adds well to the humourous tone throughout the game.
The actual game play is quite simple and based on timing your pokes and swipes just right to launch successful attacks and abilities.

This is a strange but fun title.
Fearless Fantasy's gameplay heavily features gesture-based combat which is something I haven't seen before in a game of this kind, so it's gameplay is new & refreshing. That said, gameplay is heavily reminiscent of traditional Final Fantasy titles with turns, status effects, equipment, et cetera. This doesn't detract from Fearless Fantasy as a whole, however - it's still a respectable, enjoyable experience.
As stated above, the game utilizes gesture-based combat. For example, the majority of melee attacks requiring properly timing & tracing "arrow tracks" with your cursor, while the majority of ranged attacks require clicking circles that shrink over time. The only real flaw I can mention on this title as a whole is the discrepency between Easy & Medium modes - maybe I couldn't grasp the game mechanics, but I had perfect "Flawless" strikes on Easy & had significant difficulty even getting the minimum of "Success" on Medium. There seemed to be some inconsistency here.
The characters, though not very fleshed-out, are distinct & serve separate roles well. Though the story isn't really here, it's worth mentioning that their unique & various callouts, responses & other verbal cues add some personality & emotion into what would be a much duller experience without them. That said, the story does not have much depth. In short,
. To be fair, a lack of story doesn't detract from the title's other merits.
The general look of the game is fun & often offbeat style, which fits the humor that frequently features in this title. I wouldn't normally go out & say "I like this art," or "this is a masterpiece," but the whimsical, cartoon-y art just "fits." When the game isn't making a joke of itself, the equipment of characters & creatures encountered are often fittingly sinister looking & the style of the gesture-based combat leaving an afterglow of the player's cursor is a nice touch.
The sound of the game is one of its strongest points. As briefly mentioned with the characters, their vocal cues & responses are a strong addition. While the voice acting in cinematics server their purpose, they're nothing to write home about - but their comments throughout battles, whether announcing their turn, or taking/giving hits add a lot to give Fearless Fantasy some life. General gunfire, melee strikes & other combat sounds are better than most titles of this kind that I've played. I must also praise the soundtrack of Fearless Fantasy - it's one of my favorite parts of the game. The music changes to fit new enemies as they enter the battle & throughout the title, it ranges from quaint classical to upbeat, faster-paced styles.
Overall, maybe the title isn't for everyone as you might be more critical than I am, it isn't flashy enough, or it isn't "new" enough to bring much to the table. Personally, I enjoyed the title & can recommend it to casual players, people looking for something new in their turn-based fighters &/or those intrigued by the gesture-based mechanics.

Examina is a unique game. Instead of using a bunch of pre-set animations, it treats everything as a physics object. Your character is essentially a ragdoll that you puppet around with the mouse. The result is a strange mixture of Dark Souls and Amnesia: The Dark Descent.  Attention to historical accuracy when it comes to Medieval armor, weapons, and techniques means that this game gives a great visual example of what two professional warriors would really look like fighting in the Middle Ages...if they were completely hammered.
Pros:
> Very original concept.
> Not very glitchy, considering it's Early Access.
> Creepy, morbid atmosphere--reminds me of Dark Souls and Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
> Nearly everything can be interacted with, much like with Amnesia.
> Physics are pretty realistic.
> AI is pretty smart.
> Very historically accurate. It looks like the devs really did their research.
> Showcases some types of Medieval weapons and armors you don't often see in video games. Again, clearly a lot of research went into the making of this game.
> Very challenging. Even once you get the hang of the combat, more than one "weak" enemy can easily overwhelm you. Again, reminds me of Dark Souls, one of my favorite game franchises. Very rewarding when you finally figure out how to outsmart your opponent and crush his skull with a mace after a long fight.
> Has a few elements that are similar to Rogue-likes. You start out the Adventure mode with no equipment and have to collect gear bit by bit as you go. Some of the items are always in the same places, but other items are randomized. You might find a battleaxe in this room one playthrough, and then there might be a padded vest or a mace in that room in the next playthrough.
> Armor really, really matters, especially if you don't have a shield.
Cons:
> Sometimes crashes during loading screens.
> Took me about five hours before I undertood the combat system well enough to actually kill an enemy. It's pretty awkward and unintuative, but that's sort of to be expected with a completely new type of game. Takes a long time to get used to.
> Characters look a bit 'drunk', especially while fighting. This doesn't bother me, because I don't see how you could avoid that in a game where you puppet ragdolls to swordfight, but it might be a bit off-putting to other players.
> Perma-death. Again, this doesn't bother me--in fact, I like it--but less hardcore players might find it annoying. You can enable checkpoints, but they're very hard to get to, so you'll still have characters perminately die many times before you reach one.
Unique and exciting game, although still in a quite early stage.

On a scale of 1 to 10 in terms of how complex the building is, I would give this a "Designing a f*cking rocketship". The game is very in-depth with building and mechanics, but this is not necessarily a bad thing. For the new player, this can be daunting, but the community is always willing to help. As a wise man once said, "It's not a learning curve, it's a learning brick wall." Fortunately, once you climb that wall, you start to have some real fun with building.

One thing to note, however, is that it is very rare to get large multi-ship battles, simply because there is a volume restriction to prevent setting computer's ablaze. I have a question that pertains to whether you can appreciate the game, and another pertaining to whether you will.
Can you hold large amounts of spatial information in focus simultaneously using your mind's eye?
Do you use this skill to build and manipulate complex objects in your head for fun?
The complexity ceiling is unreal.  So far I've learned how to build engines really well, as well as exactly one shell size of one caliber of one type of gun.  There is still so much left to learn, and an impossible amount left to master, and for this I am endlessly glad.  It is perhaps the best example of emergent gameplay I can think of: an intricate system built on a small number of simple rules.  Learn the rules, learn the implications, learn the interplay, and try not to get a migraine.
I'm very proud of my 3-barreled, recoiless, maximum guage, 180 rpm advanced cannon and its refined assortment of 3 shell types.  Now to mount it in an airship and rain down death from above.  Now I need to learn how to build airships.  Here's to another 60 hours!

Before you review any retro game I feel some background is neccessary. When Turok was a new title I only had access to a Playstation 1. As a result I'm confident that I hold no real nostalgia for the series. The only reason I bought this Steam release of Turok was from the suggestion of a friend and that I like Night Dive Studios who thankfully rescued System Shock 1 and 2 from being abandonware. For me the worst case scenario would be getting my money back through a refund.
I am happy to say that I've enjoyed my first hour and the first level of Turok and I'm certain I'll be coming back for more if not completing the full game. If you're like me and miss the days of FPS being "Doom-Clones" I am certain you will like Turok. The weapons are satifying to shoot, the enemies (ranging from Beasts to Humanoids who look like Scarecrows) all have lovely littlle death animations. The level design itself is one of the most interesting features. Whereas Doom and Quake had bitesized levels Turok has 8 levels. If each one is as big as Level 1 this is a fairly large game to explore. Much like Doom you're given a map and I personally find it enjoyable to see a blank map become filled out as you run around and kill everything that moves. I don't think you have to rely on a map much in this version but I'm sure it was a godsend for the console release with incredibly small draw distances the N64 version featured. To break up what could be a very repetitive game you have bits of platforming that I find enjoyable, only once or twice did I fall to my death so far.
There's some story about your lead character being a Time Traveller who has to stop some weapon from falling into the wrong hands but make no mistake you're just a Doomguy with a Indian Headress on. You're just going to be killing every monster in sight.
Like most action games with simple controls this game has aged very well, the primitive graphics are colorful and the game feels silky smooth in 1080p. The only thing I'm not digging is the music as at least in Level 1 it's just a repetitive jungle beat MIDI playing constantly. Sadly not every game can have a soundtrack composed by Trent Reznor.
The price is a tad bit steep, I'm used to paying only $10 for rereleases of 5th Gen games but when you consider Night Dive Studios made a brand new engine the extra $5 doesn't seem so bad for the work put into it. I say if you like an old school shooter get it and party like it's 1997.

Don't be fooled by its rather plain appearance. This is one of the most addictive and stellar strategy/defense games on Steam.
Struggling to build a small base and inching forward against an overwhelming and powerful enemy only to eventually gain the upper hand and wipe it of the board with massive power is satisfying again and again and again and again.
There is a lengthy campaign, hundreds of bonus maps, an active hub with constantly updated and often stellar community maps and basically infinite, auto-generated maps.

This game is awesome. The enemy feels really unique with the liquid-ness (is that even a word?) of it. There is a ton of content (virtually infinite) and you could play this game for a very long time before getting bored.
It plays like a Tower Defense game, but with a twist. Your enemy is the liquid creeper and you must stop the "valves" of creeper. Your towers can move and you must learn how to hold your own while also moving forward towards the creeper while also managing resources. If you want a sort of demo, look for the free flash versions on sites like Kongregate. I would strongly recommend this game.

Fighting against evil "water" instead of units in this tower defens / strategy game hybrid is interesting. The campaign functions as a sort of tutorial and is very well done. New tech on each planet keeps things interesting and the opponent gains more tricks over time as well - it's not the usual increasing numbers, but actual new abilities.

A great continuation of the earlier games, Creeper World 3 is a top down tower defense game where you build defensive units to contain and push back "creep", which is a type of ooze that slowly covers the map.  This game has tons of replayability.  I find myself coming back to this game again and again.  Highly recommended if you are a fan of tower defense games.

What a game.
I wasn't familiar with the previous titles in the series, but this is absolutely great.
Admittedly the game isn't really pretty and might put some people off, but gameplay-wise this is a gem.
I mean... how many games do you know where the main mechanics are attrition, network building and logistics?
At the start of the game I completely disregarded the story, but I quickly found myself wanting to know more... and the story is actually well-written and interesting! Which, I have to say, was a surprise (the game would have been as good without any story whatsoever).
Also, the pacing is great... every level holds a new mechanic, a new unit or a new obstacle to overcome.
The content is also monstrously gigantic, with custom maps, challenges, etc.
Now, not everything is perfect... the instructions on how to play are way too vague and the lack of tooltips coupled with odd terminology makes it a bit hard to get into. The UI is functional but could have been better.
Also, people who might panic when there's too much much stuff going on might not like it...
Despite all of this, it's still a fantastic experience and real surprise... especially considering that nowadays games tend to fail to hold my interest for more than a couple of hours.
I'll be keeping an eye on knucklecracker's future endeavours.

Note: Just like pretty much every other reviewer I have rated the game based on three different parts of it, Gameplay, Graphics and Music
Gameplay:
The gameplay of AVGN 2 is different from the first game, in AVGNA (The first game) you were able to unlock 3 different characters, all with their own attacks and special abilities e.g Double Jumping while in AVGN 2 you only get the Nerd but you can find different powerups to help you during the game such as: Wall Jumping, Gliding and Breaking Blocks. Apart from that the gameplay is like the first game (Lots of dying).
Graphics:
AVGN 2, like the first game uses a classic retro art style but unlike the first game AVGN 2 gets a sort of filter over the game, I can't think of a way to describe it but in my opinion it works well and makes the game look even better. In the end, don't expect AAA graphics, it's a retro styled game.
Music:
The music in AVGNA was fantastic, the soundtrack was easily one of the best parts of the game and in my opinion AVGN 2's soundtrack is even better and a remix of one of the songs from the first game is even used is AVGN 2's soundtrack.
Final Score:
9.5/10, It's a fun game with challenge and an amazing soundtrack, if you are a fan of the Nerd I recommend this.

I'm recommending this game not because I think you should buy it, but because I think you wishlist it and check back in a year. This isn't a game in its current state, its a simulation and not a very entertaining one at that.
First, I think this is supposed to be a critique of religion? I couldn't find any way to have positive interaction with my followers. If you leave your people to their own devices, they will flourish - farming, hunting, mining, and making new babies and founding new cities. If you do try to send out a commandment (the only way to "play"), one of three things will happen: The most likely outcome will be that your followers completely ignore you. This is the most frustrating, but its not as if the entire Bible isn't filled with similar stories. Of course in the Bible, God would punish the people in some way, while here there is nothing you can do except repeat the commandment. The second most likely outcome is that the command will be "reinterpreted". So if I said, "The hungry should eat", the people will somehow come to the conclusion that I meant "The hungry should mine.", which is annoying, but is kind of the crux of game. But the very worst outcome, in my opinion, is when the people actually listen to what you say... because they will suddenly forget all their needs and focus 110% on whatever the command was. So if you say "the young must mine", they will start mining...and will only stop once they have starved to death.
My greatest frustration, however, isn't with the fickle nature of my people, but with their lack of true culture or religion. Your proclamations aren't entered into some holy book or impressed upon a leader - they are either immediately implemented or immediately ignored, and no matter what, are erased from your "list of commandments" (and your followers memories), after a minute or two. The next generation will not be influenced by the orders you gave the previous one, except in how much food and metal your commands ultimately generated for them. The developers have promised futher development for a city/culture system, as well as an ancestral link system, so hopefully that will work out.

I really wanted to like this game! The cinematics and reviews held the game in high esteem but I was faced with a quite disappointing product. Nonetheless, I shall break down the review into both positives and negatives:
First and foremost, the game does hold up to the amazing graphics seen in the cinematics. Even on low quality settings, one can still appreciate the attention to detail and just generally the amazing scenery of past and present timelines.
In regards to the choice and consequence aspect of the game, I think Red Thread have done well in providing multiple story lines. HOWEVER, the characters and story line felt somewhat undeveloped and personally, I felt quite confused throughout both chapter one and two. Mind you, I had not delved into the lore of the story which perhaps would've helped immensley. UPDATE: many of the objective hints are very vague and you can find yourself pointlessly running throughout the town trying to find one person, or a clue or somesort. To complete almost all of the objectives, google will become your friend. Which, spoils the playing enjoyment of the game. My tip to the devs would be to provide more guidance for the player.
Following the holes in the characters, I found that there was a lot of unnecessary dialogue that dragged out the interactions with others. Despite the preface of the game being choice and consequence heavy, a lot of the dialogue can't be avoided, nor is there much you can do to guide the conversation. As a contrast, Square Enix's game series "Life Is Strange", and many of the Tell Tale Game's creations allow the player to opt out of conversations and much more avoid relationships entirely with specific characters.
SIDENOTE TO THE DIALOGUE: There are a lot of conversations with unnecessary and sometimes quite excessive swearing which I found quite spoilt the atmosphere of the whole situation. There are so many other ways that the feelings of specific character could have been portrayed eg. the character of Mira and the scenes in which she is displaying her anger towards "Shitbox" and her "Autistic servant", Wit.
However, in fairness to Red Thread Games, The Dreamfall series has a cult following and amazingly positve reviews. Perhaps I should have played the previously released games in the series and/or read the lore before starting the game, however I feel that in another sense that shouldn't be entirely necessary. Overall, I am relatively disappointed with the game, but will still finish it. Personally, I wouldn't recommend it to anyone for the sheer factor of its time-wasting factors.

The issues with this game are well captured on other reviews, I won't reiterate (I just wish I read them before).
* No difficulty setting, game expects you to grind lower levels until you get what you need.
* No buying guide. Game allows you to buy whatever you want, and the the AI assumes you have what you need to deal with rushes, not cool.
* Minimal to no strategy. It seems like you conduct the battle, the the problem is that a specific set of tools will work on a specific level. Get in, get beaten, try again with a different combo, again, again, until you realize you don't HAVE what you need, so GOTO 10; (grind)
* People put the gold challenges as a plus, but it isn't, because to get gold you need tools and tools cost apples and you get extra apples by getting gold, so you either have what you need and breeze the gold or you don't. Helps with the grinding, EXCEPT gold makes levels harder so it's not even grinding, it's hard grinding.
Would I recommend this game? No. If I do, someone will pick it up, get stuck at the 10th level or so, flip it off and go to sleep, never to play it again. Why would I do that, when so many great games are on sale for less? And for what? I'm not condemning the graphics, or the gameplay, or the music (fix that loop, BTW, at some point it just ENDS), I'm condemning the laziness of the developers to put in difficulty, which is mandatory for casual gaming, and a mild hind on what should use for a particular map. I don't have infinite time to waste on trial and error. Some people do. They play on Normal/Hard. I don't. I play on easy with hints. In good games.

This is a port from android game, a mix of oldschool Final Fantasy-esque battle engines and some mobile game where you slide your finger as part of some mechanics.
This sliding mechanics is the main issue here. Finger movement on a tablet is quicker than moving your mouse over some appearing arrows and clicking into circles. That wouldn't be so bad if those were not so strongly tied to the combat itself - e.g. some enemies can only be hit by EPIC attacks and those require quite good sliding over those arrows that appear during ANY attack. The only actions that don't require some crazy sliding minigame are taunting, using items and resting.
Beyond those actions EVERY attack or special move initiates this tedious mini game.
Pros:
- grotesquely fun monster design, it's really something
- music is ok, it's mostly playing some chilling tunes in the background
Cons:
- this game is grindy at heart, you'll need to replay some battles over and over to gain gold and level up your heroes
- every attack initiates this stupid mini game, I just don't get it
- plot is mostly pointless, the only meaningful and interesting character is king Xola (really cool design)
- the overall atmosphere is silly, it's like watching an adventure of a band of bickering Claptraps (from Borderlands) with their stupid gimmicks and punch lines (with the classic ”It's hammer time!” by a hammer wielding team member)
- graphics are ugly at hi-res, really really ugly, characters are looking as if they were cut from cardboard and painted over by some drunken artist. In game cutscenes are even worse
This game is not tragic, it's actually a good product from technical point of view - it didn't crash, there were no bugs that would affect gameplay. Still, it's short, the story is just not interesting enough, it's a grindfest, there isn't really any character customization here, etc.
If you want to see some of those cool monster designs just search them on googles or watch this game on some streaming site.

When I started playing this game I was sure I had somehow started the wrong game. I was not a scientist looking to find some crystal in Xen, I was some soldier on a ship overrun with aliens.
There the game's issues start to mount. The sea abruptly ends shortly from the ship and the opening cutscene only serves to point this out to you. The ship itself doesn't make sense. Why and where is Black Mesa shipping dangerous, live, ARMED aliens? Why is the military on board? Why are they shooting at YOU?
The combat is mostly an exercise in conserving ammunition (doubly important as the game fails to give you a melee weapon) since there is so little ammo in these first areas. It stops for a bit at a puzzle section that is not obviously a puzzle section; given the low quality of the game up to this point it's more likely you'll conclude that the mod is broken and quit right there.
If you manage to forage on (after moving a box somehow triggers an enemy to burst out of a nearly railcar... realism!), you reach an explosive box that easily kills you even if you're standing a reasonable distance away. So that's fun.
Oh, and you can find a hive hand weapon, so you go from having no ammo to having infinite ammo for that terrible gun (which is the point of it I guess).Solves the ammo problem at the cost of making combat annoying.
Next are some very unfun turrets which is great since the design of the map here is optimized for the turrets to take you down while making it frustrating for you to take them down. You get some grenades which is a step in the right direction.
Get past THAT and you find poorly lit spOOOky areas that just repeat the box puzzle (complete with bursting open door with an enemy behind it).
Then after a climb the game tries to kill you with half a dozen marines at once, and a bunch of snarks that will glitch and get you stuck inside them and suck most of your health. Are the snarks working with the marines now, or what?
Remember that crossbow? It's here, and you already killed most of the enemies so you won't really need it. Some guy will open a hatch for you to a thing you're looking for, which was news to me because I have no idea why I'm on this ship. The game certainly never told me.
Time to get back to the hatch as that requires backtracking through the whole level. Monsters have inexplicitly spawned along the way (in mostly predictable locations) even though you cleared things out before. This time the only item pickups are the ones you didn't use last time. Good luck.
Finally, drop down the hatch (there seems to be no "safe" way down, and it looks like it will kill you, but if you guessed this mod fumbled again you're right; it doesn't kill you).
And a new map loads! And all your guns are gone! Wait, what? Where'd they go? I guess I dropped them in fear after the Nihilith reference pose look-alike popped out of the wall and stole the crystal I was after. Gee, what a coincidence, how does it know I want the crystal?
It tries to suck you up with this barnacle thing for a one hit kill, and it will probably succeed the first time since you have no idea what's going on and it lunges for you right after a cutscene ends. Hell, I LET it eat me even though I was dodging it, because shooting it looks like it is ineffective and its movement was so terrible I assumed, given the poor quality of the mod so far, I wasn't supposed to dodge it and it was supposed to catch me and I just glitched it out. Nope.
Okay, second try, let's duck into the obvious cover where it can't get you and where there's all this ammo, finally! Nope, it was a instadeath trap. The metallic-looking cover is made of cardboard and the barnacle can cut right through it.
Third try. Now if you try to fire everything you have at the guy, which isn't much, while constantly running in circles to avoid his barnacle, he eventually dies. And you can get that ammo now, which you don't need because the level ends.
Not bad for just a scientist! Wait, why was I sent to this place anyway? And why was the military trying to kill me again?
After a cutscene at Black Mesa showing the crystal there, I assume I am now about to embark on the premise of the mod: to get a SECOND crystal just like this one from Xen, because reasons. What? Really? Just share the one we already have, you guys!
So we're about to... oh, the game crashed trying to load the next level. Well, that saves me some time I guess.
Anyway, there's a Wilson Chronicles mod that everyone says is bad. This is much worse, just to give you a frame of reference.

Creeper World 3 is a game that will catch you off guard. Unless you played the flash versions- then It's just more of the same, in an extremely good way. Beyond Creeper World's flash-era graphics, midi-era music, and long dialogues of exposition that seem to go on for ages, is a complex fun game that is more than your average tower defense.
I feel like it would almost be putting Creeper World to shame by simply just calling it a tower defense. It's more like it's own unique style of RTS, pitting you against the mysterious force simply called "The Creeper" (aka water) that is constantly spreading at an alarming rate. Your goal varies from mission to mission, either a simple one such as "Get from point A to point B, destroying everything in your way" to "activate these 6 thingies, go over here and kill this, and then do a loop formation with your towers and then go...." etc etc. The game varies it's missions very well, making every planet seem like a distinct new world with it's own gimmick rather than just something thrown in a level generator. The towers are extremely situational, and I actually like this more- there's no "Jack of all trades" tower, forcing you to vary your strategy depending on what is happening in front of you.
This all sounds very complex, and possibly at the later levels it is. But as of writing, I have not completed the first sector as I am taking my time enjoying each level, and it is quite managable. I have not tried the extra features that seem very interesting such as DMD, Colonial Space, and Tormented Space, simply because I do not want to spoil the towers for myself- but these seem all like extremely cool features to add replayability to the already large campaign. DMD Allows you to name a randomly generated map after beating it, allowing other players to play and rate the map and name for themselves. Colonial Space is a sector of space only containing user generated maps, and Tormented Space is full of hard bonus missions.
Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal is a beautiful game so far. It's mediocre graphics might not seem like it's worth 15 dollars at first glance, but this is much, much bigger than one might expect. If you like the base game, there is infinite replayability here with much more towers and many more planets to explore.

Unique and addicting, this tower defense game ranks up there with the very best in its genre.  Instead of fighting off enemies one at a time while they march on a base, this game has players holding back seas of purple slime.  Depth, density, and volume are all significant factors when planning your strategy against the slime emanating from various points on each map.  Where players are usually expected to only defend their base in traditional tower defense games, Creeper World has the added final, and extremely satisfying, goal of pushing through the slime and destroying the source.
If that was all there was to this game it could still easily be considered great; its community support through the map editor and its features however, makes it fantastic.  Players can create generated maps according to specified criteria, design maps from scratch themselves, and then upload all of these in-game to be played by the community.  It's one of the most simple and easy to use map editors I've used - I just jumped right in and never even looked at the tutorial.
If you like tower defense games, this is one you want for your collection.  And if you don't like tower defense games and you're still reading this review it's probably because your noticing how uniquely awesome this game is and you haven't even played it yet.

Second, it has some weird difficulty spikes. The game ain't really too difficult (and if you go with Bronze difficulty you'll rarelly even die), but there are a few parts that seem weird, mainly dragons. You're fighting the damn thing and suddenly it uses a fire-breathing attack and your hp, no matter how tanky you are, will explode. And almost without warning! There aren't much more enemies that are difficult on the game besides them, however then come things that are too easy, the final boss being the biggest example. It's quite the anticlimax when he barely does damage and you whoop his♥♥♥♥♥without effort. There's also enemies that deal poison as their main source of damage: poison is crap. Barely hurts, it's main effect seems to be slowing you down. That's quite dissapointing, however it also seems that using antidotes doesn't always even fix poison, which seems like a bug to me.
Lastly, the graphics, while neat (specially for it's time), they have issues. The world is mainly a 2D gigantic landscape with semi-2D buildings and lots of 3D characters. The problem comes when buildings and the landscape get in between everything: buildings not letting you see enemies, hills hiding the way you're supposed to be going, objects that seem to be blocking a tight road but it's actually the way you should be going and it ain't blocked at all, it gets confusing a lot of times.
Lastly, and mainly a minor problem, the English voices. They're a mix bag. The main characters actually do have a good voicecast, specially the Dwarf who's my favorite of them all. Then come enemies like goblins and orcs, which talk on their own language AS THEY SHOULD, instead of sh#ttified English, a really nice touch. Then, at the bottom of the barrel come enemies like the Sakkara Priests. The male ones sound okay but a bit forced, yelling each line at the top of their lungs, then come the female ones which SCREAM every line in the most stupidly hilarious accents possible and even keep screaming the most dumb death screams you'll hear in your life as they are decapitated with a damn hammer. I'd say 10% of the voices in the game are bad, only a 10%, but that 10% might even be a nice case of so bad it's actually good.
That being said, what does the game do for itself? Have you played Diablo 1 or 2? It's similar, but in a MMO-sized world. Just think of World of Warcraft in 2D and singleplayer and you'll get the idea.
The gameplay is enjoyable. There are 8 characters to choose (6 from the base game and 2 from the expansion included in the Steam edition) and they all feel quite different, with their own good and bad parts (although I've always felt the Dwarf was way more powerful and had a dumb negative part, not being able to ride horses). There's an insane amount of loot out there to get (and there are items which are only usable by certain characters) and each character has a good selection of skills you can use. It's fun, as you can just play whoever you feel like, and if you don't like it, just change your playstyle.
The map itself should also get a mention as it's actually quite f#cking big for it's time and coming from a not-so-well-known developer team. There's plenty of different areas to explore, all of them with their own kind of enemies and obstacles, towns and different crap. And something that you don't see often is actually getting to visit the towns of the monsters you keep killing, which I like and it's a good touch. Specially since the Devs took the time to add places to the map that you don't have to visit through the storyline, but have quests and other good stuff on them, making you want to deviate from the main quests and just see what you can find.
The game also offers a New Game+ option; you can export your character and then start a new game with it, which is great! It adds more difficulty and replayability to an already long game.
The main characters are also fully voice acted and will usually give their own opinion to whatever is happening, which is fun, specially when they decide to break the forth wall and talk to you directly. The game also has a few references to other games and media, something I do enjoy a lot.
Lastly, the game does have multiplayer... Although good luck finding anybody to play it with. After 12 years the servers are predictably dead and although you can play using third party software with some friends, it might be too much effort when you could just play something else instead.
Do I recommend Sacred? If you like Roleplaying games with big open worlds, yes. Totally. It's a fun game that lasts, with the expansion pack included, around 16 to 20 hours, depending on how well you do. There's tons of stuff to discover and fun to be had, and in a sale it's probably a safe purchase... Just expect some technical problems to stay in the way at first.
I will also say in advance that Sacred 2 is a decent follow up to this game (although more oriented to consoles than PC) and that Sacred 3 is a horrible follow up. You see, Sacred went the same way Dungeon Siege did: the first one is usually taken as the best, although it played it safe. The second one is a decent sequel with good aditions and other stuff that shouldn't be there. The third game however barely even looks like the rest and it's hated for it. If you ever look into this franchise, please stay with the first one, maybe just peek into the second one for curiosity. Ignore the third one, you'll be grateful.
TL;DR Edition: Good open world RPG that's quite long but does have both technical difficulties and some difficulty issues. However it's quite enjoyable to people who can overlook it's age and how bad it works with a modern computer. On a sale, it's a safe purchase, although ignore it's sequels completely.
Still better than Diablo 3.

From the Depths is the ultimate vehicle-building sandbox game. You can build guns, boats, turrets, configure AI, write AI(in LUA), automate everything, make custom shells, custom lasers, custom cannons(of two kinds), custom jets, prop planes, tanks, land cruisers, it's ridiculous how this game takes customization to a whole other level.
That said, initially it can be difficult to wrap your head around the complexity of this game and the dozens of mechanics and systems and how to put things together.
Once you do figure out how to play, however, there is endless content. Any kind of ship, or airship you can think of, from missile destroyers and cargo freighters to laser airships and 500mm autocannon battleships and nuclear submarines. There are also land vehicles, which I have played with a lot. While there are no tank treads and the wheels system is (currently) very rudimentary and has bugs, you don't have to worry about sinking or falling out of the sky.
For $20 this game is absolutely worth it. I could see myself racking up into the thousands of hours of playtime with this game just building every possible kind of vehicle fulfilling every purpose and then watching them shoot at each other.

A city building game with a possible future for the real world.
So what is ANNO series to begin with? Originally called "DAWN OF DISCOVERY" in North America, this series has been around for a long time. According to Wuppo, another steam user, it is even older than that in North America, and i have confirmed it is. Even one of the earlier games can be found on steam. Anyways, at it's heart, ANNO series is basically a city building simulator with missions and quests to complete stuff.
This version of the game, 2205, unlike it's last predecessor, 2070, has a few changes. At the time of this writing, it has no multiplayer in the game, nor does it include a sandbox  mode, even though if you finish the main storyline, it becomes sorta a sandbox game. The only multiplayer online features for this game at this moment is voting and world trade market prices. Both these things take info from all players on the game, and either increases prices on goods or loweres them. Also, it takes census of votes from everyone, similiar to the voting system found on 2070.
The game can be addictive if your into city builder games. Be aware this game uses UPLAY by Ubisoft, since they made the game. UPLAY requires a account to use the game on it. If you do not have one, when you 1st try the game, it will ask you to make an account, forcing you into making one for playing this game, but this is not uncommon for other UPLAY games, as 2070 also requires the same thing. Uplay, honestly, has improved than it previously was. As for me personally, i have used uplay in the past, and it has been worst than it is now, including outages and even not recognizing your game keys or even purchased games. Now, it seems these problems has been fixed on uplay and is much more stable.
One other thing is that there is a app that requires a smartphone. Since i don't own a smartphone, i cannot say how this app or how it works in the game, but i imagine it does what it says, gives additional rare building stuff to use.
I recommend this game if you like city builders.If not a fan of city builders, please avoid getting or buying this game. Also, if you can, buy on sale with all dlc's..as they add alot of more content to the game than what the base game contains and give you more options in the game.
Thanks to Wuppo for pointing out the information on how old the series actually is.

Love this game. Played 36hrs in 3 days. Realtime econ and managing settlements in various environments from temperate, to tundra to the moon and the trade routes between them that keep them growing is quite challenging. The game is really only a game on advanced difficulty, with unlimitted bailouts the other difficulties are little more than extended tutorials (no consequences for mismanagement is pretty boring). Overall a great real time, sci-fi, econ sim. The combat missions though are a net distractor. The only econ impact is that it gives you some rare material on the missions that you would otherwise purchase for a a heafty price. The blockaidng of settlements is an interesting but poorly executed touch. Critical trade routes go down while you wait for your fleet of static ships to arrive and repel the invaders. The fact that you cannot build any sort of colony defenses, actually build and leave ships to patrol an area, or have any sort of control of your defense fleet is broke AF. I would have much rather prefered that, like irl, security is an economic risk balancing act. Ex: you can build as many ships and static defenses as you want, and place them anywhere, but they have a net cost in energy, manpower and upkeep. It would be more fitting with the game if defense was more an econ balancing mechanic than a basic rts combat mini game.

(Review written for 2205 + season pass, if that matters)
I rather liked Anno 2070, so I really wanted to like this game when it came out...and then it came out, and I had other things to do, and there were enough negative reviews I didn't want to get it.  When it went on sale, I noticed it, again, and finally picked it up despite the mixed reviews - perhaps hoping that it would be a good game despite the stated flaws...
...and so far, I haven't actually noticed any major flaws.
- "The game doesn't have multiplayer."  True.  Don't care; I don't play multiplayer.
- "Supply chains aren't real time."  There's shades of truth to this, but not as a meaningul problem.  In 2070, if Factory B needed Factory A to produce Good A as an input so it could start production of Good B, you had to wait 20 seconds for Factory A's production cycle to complete, then for the good to be shipped, and
Factory B would kick off...and then you had to wait another 20 seconds for Factory B to finish.  Which...didn't add much; once that initial cycle had completed, goods would be delivered in time for everything to work smoothly.  In 2205, production also works on prospective output; so long as there's enough factory power, everything moves along - and you know whether you have enough production
.  Storage is still a thing: surpluses accumulate and will cover shortfalls, though the stocks aren't listed so far as I can find.  Overall, I
this change; I
like being able to see production balance changes immediately rather than having to wait a few minutes to see just how badly the new production chain is balanced.
- "Combat minigame!"  Well.  Not in the standard usage: combat spawns off to a separate map with a barely-configurable fleet, and the map can take a while to complete, if you're going after all objectives.  A new game can be configured to have enemies attack randomly at various levels - presumably forcing you to call your fleet in and defend your territory.  Mostly ambivalent on this one, as RTS combat isn't why I snagged Anno.
Production within a single 'sector' is essentially shared, without need for setting up transit routes within that map.  In trade for that, it is now possible to create multiple 'sectors' for the same corporation at the same time, and to trade goods between those sectors.  This adds an interesting mechanic, allowing and requiring multiple very-differently-designed city-sets to work together to get the most out of your cities and factories.  Putting time into research on the orbital level (DLC) can lead to useful production balance changes, or outright change the recipes of some of your goods.
There are some minor glitchy bits, admittedly.  Ship movement allows for parts of the ships to pass through each other - and it's not a hard thing to see - but that's purely a minor graphical wart.  Switching between busy sectors can take a little while for my now-aging last-generation gaming maching, but...well, that's partially on me.
Overall is a good production-chain game, with plenty to do.

I feel like this game has a worse reputation than it deserves. While the cons are large, the game itself is not objectively bad. The various sectors that you can go into, while not random, provided significantly more play time than a single play through in 2070. I'm at 25 hours as of this review and I haven't even finished one game yet.
Lacking multiplayer and random maps is the biggest problem with the game. It strips a lot of what made 2070 what it was and why people liked it so much. The combat in 2205 is kind of boring, but I never found it all that great in 2070 either. You longer make weapons or make ships and you don't do them in your sectors (most of the time). You are awarded ships and gain military experience to upgrade ships and that's really it. It's shallow and kind of boring, but it can be avoided for most of the game.
However, the same annoying production lines still exist, the perfect layouts still exist, and most of the core gameplay from 2070 is still in 2205. As a city building/economic game, Anno 2205 is wonderful. As a direct successor to 2070, it's lackluster. The graphics and UI are absolutely stellar, the different types of sectors are cool, and the sector missions are fairly interesting mini-stories in themselves. I wish they'd fleshed out the rival corporations a little bit more, but the game presents its own challenges without it.
So I'd say if you really didn't care about combat in 2070 and you want a good single player game, 2205 is a great addition to your library. I was skeptical going in, but I'm very glad I picked this game up!

Battlepillars is an absolute masterpiece of a game. Ground breaking graphics which put the Frostbite engine to shame, extremely good performance on computers which have less than desirable specs, and an encapsulating and emotionally deep story which will drive you along a rollercoaster of emotions.
Enter an engrossing world where the player assumes the role of a colony of caterpillars which rise against their fascist, oppressive brethern in an epic conflict which will try your resolve, morale and ability to lead others to victory.
With a limited ammount of resources and an unrelenting foe, you must lead your citizens in a revolutionary conflict the likes of which have never been seen before. The conflict of Battlepillars will make the Russian Revolutions of 1917 look like a picnic day.
Once you realise that the war against your extremist allies is fruitless with troops, you must call upon your allies in arms to lift the siege against your territories, including a large, blue feathered bird, which will decimate your foes in an unholy storm of hellfire.
After beating your enemies back, you must then press the attack deep into enemy territory, eliminating high ranking officials of the enemies war-machine, and steamrolling any resistance in your way until total and utter victory is yours.
Battlepillars Gold Edition was a gift from a dear friend, and I thank them from the bottom of my heart for blessing me with this masterpiece of a game. Anyone with polarised opinions of this game should definitely invest their money in this work of art. Some claim that The Last of Us should receive a Game of The Year nomination, some would also argue that it is Grand Theft Auto V which has reached the zenith of what is quality and an excellence in design for the gaming industry. These critics have clearly never experienced the ferocity that is Battlepillars.
Words cannot explain the utmost respect I hold for the creators of this game, who have blessed gaming community worldwide with a masterpiece which will not be forgotten anytime soon.
