18 years later Red Thread closes the loop with their seminal The Longest Journey completing the cycle that won so many plaudits back in 1999.  First things first: while you might enjoy this game without having played (or at least read/watched)
the first two games recently you really should go back and refresh yourself.  Alright, all done?  Then get ready to play.
Now for those of you who aren't already all-in from the previous games, or haven't played them at all, what are you getting into?  Dreamfall Chapters was produced piece-meal (in.. Chapters!) based on incremental funding, Kickstarter dollars, and a relatively small but dedicated team.  The result is more similar to Telltale games than older adventure games but generally to the advantage of this game rather than Telltale.  I particularly liked the inner monologue provided with dialogue choices.  No "why on Earth is my character being a jerk when I clicked the nice button" from Telltale or Mass-Effect style choice wheels.
The world-building that was relatively novel in 1999 can come across as a bit derivative in 2017, in no small part due to the influence this game's predessors had on many other writers and designers.  There are some nice twists and a few well placed emotional tugs thrown in.  Most of the puzzles are relatively simple one or two-step affairs with only a handful of clunkers (I'm thinking of you sleepy goats!)  You won't feel like a genius solving most of them but you also won't put your head through a wall too many times.  Graphics are pretty good given the resources brought to bear and set the tone well.
To sum up: you don't need to play the older games to enjoy this one.  But if you like adventure games, imaginative fantasy narrative, euro-personality tropes from the late nineties, or names like Ragnar Tornquist give it a go and better yet dig up the older games too (The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: The Longest Journey).  If you can't stand how episodic adventure games chop things up or disliked the previous games in this series you won't find much to change your mind here.
Postscript: God, there must be a better way to create "hub-zones" in 3D adventure games.  Aren't we all too old to spend 5 minutes slowly jogging from one end of town to the other?  If you're going to put map shortcuts and hints into your game, do it all the way and provide quick-travel.

"The Longest Journey" is one of the best 2D point-and-click adventures I've played. Its sequel, "Dreamfall", was a disappointment not only because it was in 3D or introduced combat and stealth or because the first game's protagonist, April Ryan, had more of a supporting role, being one of three playable characters; but, most of all, because it was an unfinished story, ending in very unsatisfying cliffhangers. Finally, after more than a decade, the third game in the series arrived.
It plays similarly to "Dreamfall", but without combat and with only a few stealth sequences. It's like Telltale had recovered its knack for puzzles... only here the puzzles are not very good. Most of them are frustrating because you need to resort to pixel hunts. There are choices and consequences that branch the story a little (making it impossible to get all achievements on a single playthrough), but not different endings.
The reason to play this is for the story. It's not a masterpiece like the first game at its time (I wonder if it still holds up today) nor a letdown like its sequel. Again, you have three playable characters: Zoë and Kian, from "Dreamfall", and a girl called Saga (who in fact is
; she made a
at the
making a lot of people think
in this third installment). Several other characters reappear and new ones are introduced. Writing and acting are OK, and the game gains some points for its sense of humor.
Despite not being perfect, it gives you a bang for your buck, because it costs the same as a Telltale title, but lasts about 3.5 times over. I finished my first game after almost 40 hours, with 81% of the achievements. I recommend it for fans of the series, even at full price; newcomers should really play the predecessors first. Although a lot of questions are answered, there's still a lot to explore in this universe (multiverse?), so I hope the developers will come back to it someday (preferably before another ten years).

When you purchase this game you are essentially purchasing a demo (first 6 out of 20 levels) in which you can easily complete in an hour and a half. This review ONLY covers the first six levels! With that being said, this is the best EAG I've purchased on Steam. This is one of those games where gameplay kind of takes a back seat for the story. It really does have the spirit of classic action-adventure games. There is no life bar, no weapons, and no HUD whatsoever. All you have is a flashlight, a one-time rechargeable boost jetpack (with an exception...), and a robot arm to grab things. From what I have seen so far the game is fairly linear, with some small diverting paths to grab some 'collectables.'
What has won me over to this game is the atmosphere and the mystery of the story (No spoilers, I will be as vague as possible). You start off with one simple mystery: "Where are my buddies?" Then it grows to: "Who is that lady?" Then it snowballs into: "What is that thing!?!" Then the demo abruptly ends… My curiosity has never been so enticed for a game's story in a long long time! Needless to say I really want to play the next levels.
This game is different and I have trouble thinking of a genre to place it in. It's a Sci fi mystery, it has some elements of horror, some elements of plat-forming, and some elements of puzzle-solving. If you are looking for a horror, shoot 'em up, space horror, this is not your game. If you are looking for a story driven, creepy, atmospheric, sci-fi mystery, this is your game. I would definitely recommend this to anyone who needs a break from typical AAA gaming and who doesn’t want to play anymore 8-bit style indie games (sorry my 8-bit buddies, I need a break from you as well).

The Witches' Tea Party is an amazing prequel hell you could say it’s even better than the first game. But let’s start of this the story.
You play as a young witch named Charlotte going to her first witches Tea Party with her grandmom Marilyn. When they get there all seams okay, but soon it goes awry among the other witches at the party. So it’s up to Charlotte to find out why and to make friends with the other witches.
Now in every way this is a great prequel, we find out more world, about Charlotte. About her grandmom Marilyn. We get more endings and some fun mine games like cooking, or doing side quests.
And we get a bit of sad and heartwarming moments too. Now what I liked most about the game is the characters. I find them interesting, like Andrea and Renee, I won’t tell you why because of spoilers but I hope to see a game about these two.
The music was good and I liked the art you get after you die or get a bad ending or a cutscenes. And I loved that this game is longer than the first game.
Now this game does have one or two bugs like a slowdown/lag and it kind of crashed one and two times for me but that all the problems I had.
So all in all The Witches' Tea Party is an amazing prequel to the first game that was already vary good too. This game gives us more about the world and its characters, why’ll this game is not that scary it still is party spooky.
So I say get this game and its ost and art book, and I look forward to the next game by Rabbiton and StarAura.

If you've played Trick & Treat, this isn't as much like it as you might think. But if you liked it, this is better. Lost are the Mad Father influences-- the horror elements, by and large, and the approach to the puzzles-- which would be a bad game if this wasn't generally strong in its own right. The focus is more on the story this time, so puzzles are much simpler, there's more side elements and a little more player agency, and although the game is referenced as having "disturbing rooms," they're not actually disturbing and only happen once or twice in very minor parts anyway. If you look at this and want a cute game with no bait and switch, that's almost exactly what you're getting.
The story's not anything incredible, but it's compelling enough to carry the game. It's only a few hours long, but at the dollar something price point in the last sale, you're definitely getting your money's worth. If you think of it compared to an actual RPG Maker RPG with combat, you're essentially getting something like that but with all the combat cut out, so there's no real bloat added to the time.
Do you want a fun, satisfying little game? Get this. If you're looking for horror or anything like it, look elsewhere.

Exanima is a physics and simulation-based dungeon-crawling Action-RPG and precursor to upcoming open-world ARPG/simulation Sui Generis. You must use your mouse to swing your weapons, and to interact and move objects around in the world. Just about everything has collision. Enemies can hurt each other; AI is engaging, and unique to each one you find, reactive to your behaviours.
The game involves a lot of survival/scrounging in the beginning and is more about steady exploration/discovery than pure dungeon running and looting.
Exanima has a dark and minimalist low-fantasy setting. with a magic system in development. The dynamic lighting, animation, and graphics in general are really nice, and create an immersive atmosphere.
Even though  there are still things to be implemented, once you get a taste of the combat and concept, and if you are a fan of action RPGs and adventure games, you will know supporting this is really without question.
If you like: Ultima, Dark Souls, Diablo, Elder Scrolls, Baldur's Gate, Divinity, Planescape, etc. you'll probably find something you like here with many more features, weapons, and mechanics to look forward to!
Highly recommended.

An oldie but a goodie.
As a long time FPS fan that hadn't played this game prior to this release, I can attest: the fun to be had here is on par with Doom 2 or Quake 1.
The action doesn't truly start for a few levels, but when it does, it doesn't stop and it's intense non-stop fighting all the way through until the very end. Your movement speed is rather fast, so is some enemies' speed, a lot of them shoot projectiles that are still a challenge to dodge, and most enemies respawn constantly! It's not so quick that clearing areas out loses its purpose, but its quick enough to constantly keep you on your toes.
There is also a satisfying exploration aspect. There are a lot of secrets which yield useful goodies as well as pieces of the Ultimate Weapon. In every level you don't just have to run to the exit: you need to grab three keys to unlock the next levels (with some minor exceptions). The exploration sometimes verges on overwhelming but as soon as you gather the willpower and start mapping a level out passage by passage, it usually becomes very simple. Heck, the only truly exploratory level is level 5, although there's room to wander around in the other levels too.
The graphics are really outdated, but you can judge them from the screenshots. I can just say that unless you are really sensitive about amazing graphics (in which case why are you even reading this?) you won't mind because it is perfectly functional and depicts the game's environments adequately.
The music is nothing special, but it excels at making you feel pumped and ready for action, as well as creating the atmosphere of the Lost Land.
Now, lastly, the port's quaity. The controls are pretty much flawless. There's all sorts of options like head bob, FOV, extended draw distance, crosshair, bindable keys, etc. Apart from a few minor things that might as well end up added after this review is written, I don't know if I can think of anything I would've expected out of this as a port that it doesn't have. It'll also get extensive modding support and level editor, so there's that. If the community engages in making levels, this game's humble length won't matter at all! And someone might make, say, HD textures and models and whatnot. But that's all hypotheticals.
Summing up, if you are at all interested in a good action FPS and aren't afraid of levels that are more open than a narrow corridor, you'd be doing yourself a huge disservise by not getting this game. Recommended as much as I can possibly recommend a game!

A satisfying game, where the enemy is totally predictable (it is literally as dumb as thick goo), yet no less challenging for that.
The eponymous "Creeper" is a thick sludge that spews out of emitters in the game world, and you must force it back. The creeper isn't smart, it doesn't think, and it doesn't even have anything in the way of AI. What it has instead, is a pleasingly viscous fluid simulation. It flows downhill, it pools in low areas, and it can't cross high terrain without building up behind it and overflowing it like a dam. This is the key to the game. Work out where the creeper will flow, and divert or destroy it to survive and achieve your objectives.
The game is one of thoughtful management. Rarely is there urgency, except during scripted missions, or if you seriously mess up and end up watching a purple tidal wave swamp your low-lying energy collectors. That's okay! The challenge is one of incremental advancement and the satisfying conquest of areas that were drowned under a layer of creeper 8 stacks high.
I'm a little concerned with balance issues (there is one early-acquired unit which seems overpowered, especially in groups) but I'm content to tend my garden of creeper without abusing it, which is an unusual state of affairs.

I got this game in a bundle, and it was easily the best one in the batch.
I've played many line defense+attack games on websites like Kongregate and newgrounds, and Battlepillars is remniscent of those childhood memories.
If you like line defense/attack games where you have to create units to destroy your enemy, you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are nice, and the music is pretty decent. The weapon effects are not too flashy, but it still works well.
The controls are simple quite, with visible hotkeys if you don't want to click on your caterpillar parts. The learning curve is minimal, and the tutorial is fast and helpful, allowing you to get a feel for the game very quickly. The feedback for both the enemy and your units are provided as small health bars and a minimap helps you keep track of the action. You can zoom out to view the entire battlefield.
Unlike most games of this style, you do not have separate unit types to send out. Instead, you have caterpillar parts that you can add to the base (the head). Each piece has a different function, and the cost increases with each added component. Your "mana" to send out units comes in the form of leaves, and you can upgrade the maximum leaf pool (which also increases the generation rate). Periodically, leaves will drop on the ground, and you can click these to add quick points to your pool.
There are quite a few pieces to choose from (ex: long range cannon, armor, speed legs, slow gun), and you have the option of upgrading each to a maximum level of 3. At each level, the aesthetics for the piece changes, something I particularly like to see in games.
A few levels into the game you will unlock base defenses (a fixed turret) and the ability to upgrade your base components. You also get special weapons (like a bird bomb, a turtle slow, etc) that are one-time use (and very expensive). To buy upgrades, you use apples that are rewarded at the end of every level. As you attack the enemy base (a tree), apples will randomly fall - picking these up are optional but highly recommended.
The grinding is actually very reasonable and can be quick. You can even afford many of the upgrades if you just progress through the levels.
There is an option for getting a gold (flower/medal) for each level if you complete a specific challenge. For example, some might ask you to beat the level under a time limit, or to use x max number of leaves, or x max number of caterpillar parts.
The game plays very well and can be a lot of fun if you enjoy this type of playstyle.
Definitely recommend!

Ok, I can understand why this is getting mixed reviews, and mine is going to be no different. As has been said before, I wish there was a 'Meh' option in the reviews.
There ARE good aspects to this game, visually it is pleasing, as far as scope is concerned it's the biggest one of the series  and yet it somehow feels smaller than its previous incarnations. It managed to put each aspect of gameplay into a little 'box' that the player enters when they want to do it, so battles are one box, each city is another box, with these tendrils of trade-routes connecting them, there's little evidence that they even co-exist other than those routes, and they exist purely as numbers.
In some ways, this is no longer an Anno game, they've actually taken a step backwards in technology because production and supply is no longer real-time, so the game kinda becomes a spreadsheet that you have to balance up.
That said, the game itself IS one you can spend a bit of time on, the growth available is the largest scale in an Anno game, and the production system is probably one of the most difficult to balance, and Anno IS a game for people who love to set up systems and balance the books, so the right idea WAS got, just not implemented very well. All in all, whilst the game is fun, it feels kind of 'soul-less' compared to the previous incarnations.
I'm not going to recommend this game, even though I do find it quite playable, because I'm assuming that people reading this are new to the Anno series, and if someone asked me, I'd tell them to buy 1404 or even 2070 for a game with a bit more flavour and a feel like your cities are more than simply 'money generation centres', rather than go straight to this one.

Anno 2205 replaces much of the micromanaging with more of an emphasis on City Building. Not so much that it's now a Cities Skylines game, it's somewhere in-between. You still handle macro-level trading between regions, but not between islands. Goods are represented by amount consumed per minute minus amount generated. There are still static amounts, but it's used for buying and selling or when building. Being the biggest change for the series, it's going to created some mixed opinions. The changes fit my tastes completely, making it my favorite of the series.

Crest is a coll little variation on a God game, where you pass down slightly fuzzy commandements, which people sporadically ignore, follow even after it stops being relevant, and take way too seriously, even it leads to their deaths, possibly making this game the most subtle and clever critique of religious fundamentalism in any game.
It's a fun idea, and the graphics are cute (especially the awesome triangle-mane lions), but the game is possibly-intentionally a bit frustrating, as you can't directly control or instruct your followers. When you get your commandments right, it's cool to watch a community grow and prosper, but things can be wrong and it can hard to recover.
The islands are currently a bit small and lacking in variety too, quickly ending up either exclusively lions or exclusively gazelle depending on your religious view on lions.
In its current Early Access form, I'd give it a modest recommendation, and I'm interested enough to give it another look when the commandments get more complex in the coming iterations.

It is an Early Access game which is sitll in very heavy development. This game along with all other Early Access games in such an early stage such as Crest are not to be destroyed since they are going to be fully fleshed out in the future. Now to the review.
You are a god who commands a small group of people to do actions, for themselves to evolve and populate the island they roam. If you ever played godlike games like Black and White or Black and White 2, heck, even Godus, this is a brand new addition to the god genre. Instead of you, lets say, slaying animals or chopping down trees, you command your people to do all of that work for you. This is a very innovative method of just simply making rules using icons. There are only 3 icons in a sentence if you want to call them that. "If ___ are ___ then ___", the blanks are filled in by those pictures which then translate into telling your followers what to do. A great command to have is "If I am unhappy, then I should gather food" or you could swap out food with metal. You can even bring some awesome commands such as "If I am a young follower, I should gather metal" or "if I am an old follower, I should go to the lions". It's not guaranteed to work, but it's quite funny in my opinion over the range of things possible.
Crest has a Polycraft like artstyle that make it look so pleasing to the eye, as if everything was carved out of a material, such perfect cuts to demonstrate that games can be good while looking beautiful all at once. I'm in love with this genre in terms of gaming and art, so it has an easy 7.5 on my rating so far. The graphics are very smooth and look interesting from different angles to give a unique playstyle. If that didn't make sense at all, I mean it can look 2D or 3D depending on the angle, or make a mountain look different from what it actually is, such as from a mountain to a house,  if you were to look at it from top down view.
Crest is actually pretty realistic for an Early Access game in terms of features. You give out commands, if those commands are not useful to your followers then they shall just carry on with their lives according to their needs so they will not die due to some stupid commandments such as "If I am a young follower, I should not prioritize food/metals". Also every single person has their own stats such as if you gave a commandment of finding food, ever person will have their own seperate stockpile of that item, same with ore, happiness, ect. That is what happened many times in different tribes long times ago and even now, you work for yourself,  if you fail, well, you fail for good. Realism is 9/10 already. I can only imagine how it will be like in the future.

Nothing so far that's a con
Buy this game is you loved Black and White or even Godus! There is much to come.

It’s a game that presents you with a tools to overcome the challenges that come with raising a bunch of humans. And rather than commanding troops you take the role of spiritual advisor. Dreamfall Chapters
by Red Thread Games
Genre: Graphic adventure
Release: (Final Cut) July 21, 2017
-----
Zoe Castillo’s in a lot of trouble! This young woman who can walk between the worlds of waking life and dreaming is caught in a beautiful, yet horrible place called the Storytime, where all the souls of people who use Watilla’s Dreamachine go, and her job is to set them straight, and encourage them to never use the soul-sucking devices again…
And so is Kian Alvane! This stalwart religious warrior discovered something horrific about his religion, how corrupt it was and how his superiors were using misinterpreted beliefs to stamp out all magic users within his home realm of Arcadia. He refused to kill a major resistance leader: April Ryan, the protagonist of The Longest Journey, and has suffered and been sentenced to death for it…
If my descriptions seemed to suffer a bit of continuity lockout, fear not! This amazing episodic adventure game, for now the final entry in The Longest Journey’s saga by Ragnar Tornquist, comes complete with a “Story so far” video (more fleshed out with July’s Final Cut update!) that fills you in on all the salient points as they were introduced in the previous game, Dreamfall.
And for those of you worried that the game totally abandons the lore of The Longest Journey even more than Dreamfall seemed to, don’t worry; threads will emerge that bind the very beginning of that absolute classic to both the intermezzos (the side-story shown between chapters) and the very end of this one. I wish to be intentionally vague as to not spoil anything; but, keep with the story! You will love it and how it resolves, I’m sure.
There are a few brilliant new open-world areas which you can explore and take in all the details, and your choices during dialogues will matter in the long run, as to how your story plays out!
Most definitely recommend this amazing adventure game!

Okay. Where to begin?
I suppose I'll kick this review off with a recap of my latest escapade in Crest.
My game started as any other. My village situated under a mountain, in the midst of a river delta, and in the thick of the only forest on the entire isle. The numbers of lions and antelope were astonishing, a true gift from the gods. My people rejoiced and consumed grains from the earth and the flesh of the wild beasts that trekked across their hunting grounds. The wise guidance of their god revealed to them how to survive and thrive in this harsh environment.
That was when the dancing began. With their huts full-to-bursting with the finest meats and plants, the Tribe became restless to procreate. Coital dance ceremonines followed, and a springtime baby-boom resulted. To fuel this extravaganza of conception, our tribesmen began to hunt the wildlife at an ever-growing pace. This greatly alarmed me; I hailed to them from the mountaintop, commanding them to steer clear of the antelope, and to only hunt lions (In order so that the lion population would still have food in the form of antelope).
They didn't listen, much to my astonishment. They completely wrecked [shrekt] the antelope, with much help from the ravenous appetite of lions. After the depletion of that food source, they stuck to farming.
Prides of lions encroached ever closer to the villages, stalking the youngest of the Tribe. this could not stand. I Divinely mandated my followers to be through with their feline agressors. That issue was resolved quick;y.
By this time, my pious subjects had extended their reach across the island they called home. At one point the settlemetsn even numbered eight. The end, when it came, was swift and infuriating.
The lag did us in. I, of course, had to piece together some role-play reason for this ignominious demise, and so I concoted this tale of 'lion-spirits' and evil 'antelope daimons'.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I'll spare you the unnecessary boredom of a long list of pros and cons; I'll just make a short list of things I'd like implemented.
-Buildings that you can indirectly cause your followers to construct; and example commandment might be [All in desert-I command you to-god], and that might cause them to, say, build a sacrificial altar to you.
-More diversity in villages; they are quite generic.
-More components for the commandments.
-Balancing the non-follower ecosystem (I.E. making itso the lions don't eat ALL of the antelope by themselves).
-More animals.
-More actions that the villagers partake in, such as: fishing, swimming, worshipping, etc.

Overview and talking about the experience of the game so far: What can I say about a 12 year old game? I mean i'm 13 myself. Being a 12 year old game the game is unfortunately not the prettiest to look at aswell as having many bugs in the game with some quests. If you can overcome that you have an amazing game especially if you like exploring. Just by exploring random places instead of doing the story missions I'm still on the first act and I'm way overleveled for the normal areas. Even if you are overleveled there are still challenging enemies if you explore enough , they are dragons , the first time I encountered one in the desert as part of a quest I just went up to it and died....... then I walked back trying to use a bow as a meele character and died again. After leveling up a bit I came back to that dragon using my vampiress and I still foolishly ran into the dragon but this time I beat it by using her teleport ability. It was awesome and certainly a step up of difficulty even with some legendary items.
The bad parts: Some parts of the game are badly optimised if you explore in the wrong places , you walk through a path that's lower than you by 5 levels for like 2 minutes then walk past a bridge and you find enemies 3 levels higher than you which really is annoying finding useless areas that you haven't explored. Another annoying thing is that some quests are buggy and won't finish ( I had problems with 'The Painter' and that quest about the blacksmith early game.). The controls of the game will annoy people when they start the game as it is mostly controlled with the mouse as well as some keys like space to use a healing potion which can't be changed in the options.
The great parts: Loot in the game is amazing. I've had 4 different legendaries equipt in 4 slots that were for 4 different things with some focused on damage and some focused on defence. The loot is very complex and you can't just look at the damage or defence stat to just determine if it's better you need to check all parts resistances , magic damage , amount of slots. From the vampiress alone you can see a huge variety of skills from summoning the undead bats and wolfs to turning corpses into your own vampire slaves to mind controlling people and teleporting away.
Conclusion: Basically it's just a complex game , it may be considered boring and slow to people who just look for action but for those willing to explore and be patient you will become this power house which is just the most fun thing ever. Dragons become just mini bosses you slay for some of the best loot causing you to get even more powerful. 9/10 from me but it is certainly not for those action seekers.

At the time of the writing of this review, I've currently played a mere two hours of this game. I am hooked. Although the videos of the game make it look complicated and mask its true nature, I can assure the reader that it feels like a proper tower defence game. I am a big fan of the StarCraft "turret defence" games of old, and I'm particularly enamoured with TD games which allow you to maze. This game may not involve mazing, but you can freely place buildings and "towers" anywhere you deem fit. Do not feel dismayed by the lack of monsters and lack of paths. The "creeper" (which is the enemy) is a creative way of presenting said enemy. It is much too easy to think of it as StarCraft zerg creep to be honest, and needless to say it is not nice stuff. I feel that this game has been lovingly crafted, and I'm looking forward to the replayability that other reviewers have mentioned.
Your objective is to defeat the creeper on each world. You do this by building up an energy grid and using that energy to build and maintain various weapons (akin to the traditional TD tower). These weapons can move to a new location as you push the creeper further back, and they can be upgraded at the forge.
You use the keyboard and the mouse. All of the buildings, and many actions are linked to hotkeys, and those hotkeys can be rebound. Unfortunately the build menu does not tell you the hotkey when you hover, so you must go into the key bindings menu to discover what the hotkeys are in the first place. However, once you've learned them they are easy to get along with.
There is a plot in the Arc Eternal galaxy. It is fairly basic, and mostly explains the existence of the creeper. I didn't know what precisely was going to happen, but I certainly had a general idea of what direction the plot was going in. But this isn't the sort of game you play for the plot after all.
The music is fun, it's energetic. However it is very repetitive. If I play this in the evening, I go to bed with the music stuck in my head.
The graphics are pleasant and functional. Things seem a tad fuzzy if you zoom in really close, but I personally like to have an overall view of the map and so I don't zoom in close. Otherwise, despite all the layers upon layers of creeper, the game runs quite well for me and is not laggy.
non-traditional tower defence
free placement and movement of "towers"
can rebind hotkeys
default hotkeys make sense once learned
make your own maps and play others' maps (great replayability)
wide range of difficulty level (depending on map)
first levels of campaign form a tutorial on how to play
music is repetitive
hotkeys are not immediately obvious

Yes.  Yes, yes, yes.  I bought this game because its cross-genre TD/RTS looked nice, and because of the overwhelming horde of good reviews.  I'm happy to add my own to the mix.  There's not a lot I can say that the video doesn't cover, except that it controls real well and the challenge is an appropriate level.  Currently my favorite single player game in my library.  I'm about fifteen hours in, and there's at least another ten left for me.  Apparently it's kind of like Populous, with hordes of randomly generated worlds to play on.  Looking forwards to it.
This game reminds me somewhat of Immortal Defense.  While the gameplay is entirely different (it bends "Tower Defense" in the opposite direction), if you're the kind of person who gave that a try, you should probably try this as well and vice versa.
There's one keyboard-throwingly hard mission late in the story, but it doesn't end as soon as you might think.  Trying to keep this spoiler free, but I did almost unjustly ragequit, so don't give in.

It's like a Tower Defense game and a real-time strategy had a baby.
Do you like the combat puzzle of TGDs? Do you appreciate the magnificent sprawl of your towers? Does the average TGD leave you feeling like all you do is sit back and wait for the enemies to make their move? Then have I got a game for you!
Creeper World 3 is the TGD that forces you to be aggressive. This game changes the Tower Defense rules so much that it is debatable if the term "Tower Defense" should even apply.
This is definitely one of the most addictive games I've played in a while. I highly recommend it.
On the downside, the graphics are rather poor (but about as good as can be for the simple top-down view). The music is good, though a little too upbeat, and the songs are short, making them repetitive.
If you're still not quite sure what to expect, give the demo a try.

Well, after putting in hours of gameplay, and dying a grand total of 457 times, I beat the game, and I can tell you if this game is worth picking up.
The game is fun, much like the first, but now there's no infinite lives.  When you're on easy, you get only 50 to beat the stage in, and trust me, you're gonna need them.  The platforming is old school punishing, requiring perfect timing to get out alive.  Shame the same can be said of the bosses, which can be beaten quite easly (on easy mode, I was able to beat most of them without dying).  The humor is also spot on with the AVGN series, and the conflict with Nostalga Critic is also amusing.
But there is one BIG flaw in this game.  The game's graphics have a much higher setup than the last game, which will cause lag and low frame rates on anything other than top of the line machines, making many stages more frustrating that challenging due to controls not regestering correctly due to lag.  I think this is probably due to the graphical effect many stages have (water effects, film grain, etc...), meaning that most run of the mill computers cannot handle many stages, and it will be more luck than skill to get you by (which is not how this should be, because when running at the proper frame rate, the controls are solid).  This lag can be much worse if you plan to record gameplay for Let's Play videos.
So if you have a really good computer made to play high end games, pick it up.  If you have a standard computer system, wait for a patch to fix the lag, and/or some kind of graphics option.

One good thing about the game is the upgrades.  As the game progresses, new tools and upgrades become available.  Some of them use unit that will help your team or hurt the other directly.  The unique thing about some upgrades is that some of them do not work until later.  For example, one upgrade acts as a revenge bomb.  Once the unit dies, it will unleash several smaller units that will start attacking the enemy.  Another upgrade is calling in allies that will aide your side through effects like attacking the other side or bring in extra supplies.  These ally units come at a steep price, but they can turn the tide of battle if ever in a tight situation.
Unfortunately, the weakest part of the game is the battle itself.  Like most strategy games, you need to send your units towards the enemy base.  However, these games usually have a detailed map where terrain is part of the strategy.  With
, it is always a straight line with no option of changing direction or even sidestepping.  Without a way of changing things along the way, it becomes merely a battle of unit selection.  Even with that area, there is not much strategy to use there, either.  As mentioned earlier, you can buy new units in order to use deeper strategies, but that really is not necessary.  By using a few powerful units with a little speed and/or armor, it becomes too easy to overwhelm the enemy with only a few units.  This is especially true with multiplayer.  In multiplayer, the first player that can send three strong units will usually win the battle.  Without the need to think, the battles are merely a series of crashing units.
The battle’s one redeeming quality is the gold challenges.  Along with simply defeating the enemy army, a gold challenge asks you to complete the battle under special circumstances.  Some of them are simple enough like using a certain size unit.  However, others require things like limiting how much you can use.  When working under these conditions, it forces you go use some strategy.  It is not enough to save the game, but they help it from being a total lost.
Maybe I'm a sucker for 2D RTS, but for $1 this is a really enjoyable game.

I'd say, initially, it's like trying to control a combatant that decided it'd be a great idea to flail his greatsword around while blindingly drunk. In the beginning, it was quite amusing attempting to control this character that seemed to be fighting with me at every moment, but, as I kept playing, I started to realize there was a finesse to controlling the combatant’s movements and swings.
Exanima's development background is an interesting one. Published by Bare Mettle, it is a precursor to their Kickstarter success; Sui Generis, which will be an open-world RPG. Exanima is designed to give people a taste of what their larger game will be like, and allows their fans to experience the unique combat system.
Exanima's combat relies solely on realistic physics. The direction you swing and the weight of your weapon determines your character's movement. While you use the mouse to direct your swings, you use the keyboard to direct how your character moves their feet. The initial effect feels like you're controlling the local town drunk, but, once mastered, you will be using that momentum to make your swings even more devastating. You can even knock down your opponent if you have enough momentum or hit them just right.
While this system has a steep learning curve and requires a certain amount of mental dexterity, the payoff is worth the initial frustration. When you manage to use your forward momentum to crash your greatsword into the enemy, and the physical force drives him into the ground, you can't help but exclaim in excitement! It takes some patience, but if you stay the course, you will be rewarded with a highly satisfying combat mechanic.
The combat isn't the only thing that follows the physics engine, though. The way you interact with the environment is also governed by realistic physics. For example, if you're fleeing from a nasty group of enemies and find yourself running in a dark hallway, and you run over a chair, there's a good chance your character is going to face-plant into the floor. I've encountered this scenario on many occasions, and it always makes me laugh (until my assailants catch up with me). In addition to chair-tripping and face-planting, the way you open and close doors is physics-based, as well. You click and drag the doors to open them. You can open a door slowly, or, my favorite, swing the mouse really fast so the door bangs open loudly-- that will scare those pesky undead, right?!
Exanima has two game modes--arena mode and story mode. Arena mode places you against one enemy at a time in a square room, and as you defeat each opponent, you are matched against harder (and better-equipped) opponents in subsequent battles. When you are vanquished, though, you begin again from the first combatant. However, there's a twist-- as you progress through, you get to keep any equipment you pilfered from your previously-defeated opponents, thus giving you a feeling of progression (albeit a small one). The arena is a good way to practice game mechanics before jumping into story mode
Story mode drops you in the middle of a dungeon, unarmed, except for your trusty torch. It’s a dark dungeon with no real direction, and it's up to you to piece together what's really going on by finding various hidden notes containing information, and by battling multitudes of armed undead, looting them for better equipment along the way.
The atmosphere of the story's dungeon is foreboding and moody. Most corridors are impenetrably dark without a torch. The dungeon is not without it's well-lit rooms, but those tend to be occupied by individuals that aren’t exactly concerned about your well-being. The music and sound effects add to the tension provided by the visual atmosphere. The mystery of the story, and the lack of information given, only adds to the enigma cake. “Why are there so many wood logs in here?” “Was this an underground saw mill?” “What diabolical goal existed to where something so logistically backwards was necessary!?” I must know!
It is important to keep in mind that Exanima is a 'rogue-like' game. That is to say, that when you die, you start over entirely. The developers recently added checkpoints for when you reach other floors, but each floor is a huge labyrinth, and I have yet to see the second floor. So, if that is not your cup of tea, then Exanima may not be for you. However, you can always have fun with the combat in the arena, which has a pseudo-progression system.

Attention to detail:
1: The maps are designed in such a way that all objects and rooms have purpose. I can tell the purpose of each room by the arrangement of objects in it that room. Rooms seem practical. The dungeon really feels like a credible and livable environment.
2: The fantasy elements are used sparingly, which makes them more important when they appear. This is why I enjoy low fantasy settings. High fantasy has the tendency to overdo the fantastic and throw out logic, which forces the developers to continually ramp up the scale until things get ridiculous and unbelievable. Fantasy based on spectacle is superficial and boring, whereas low fantasy builds and builds in an exciting progression, where all of the times feel important, even the simple ones.
3: Weapons and armor are clearly created using real world influences, but with a healthy touch of artistic license where it's needed. Never once did I think that something looks too overdesigned to be appealing, or too impractical to ever be used.  Even the expert boss' armor, despite clearly being fantasy, doesn't appear too implausible to break my suspension of disbelief. In Sui Generis, my bet is that it'll take some serious treasure hunting to ever find something like that.
4: Item randomization is really cool. I love how you can find all sorts of clothes with different colors, fabric, stitching patterns, etc. Even when two objects are of precisely the same kind, they'll still have slight variations to make them appear different. I've always found it bothersome in RPGs where two objects are precisely the same, and this game does away with that. Item randomization also adds another layer of replayability.
5: Looting is actual looting. I despise when you can find the "+10 polearm of irascibility" somehow inside the entrails of a rabbit, or how stealing someone's clothing creates an exact duplicate on you instead of taking it off them. This game does away with that, by actually taking the clothes off of corpses, and putting important "loot" like weapons and armor in personal chests or in actual armories.
6: Important objects are reasonably hard to find, but still fair. Seriously, I found the magical helmet in the third level before I found the sword in the bucket in the first level. It's very impressive where some of these items are hidden, yet I never thought anything was too hard to find or placed unfairly. Keys were never placed in the middle of nowhere and were often found in places they'd logically be. The armorer had a key to the armory, the jailer had a key to the jail, etc.
Combat
1: AI is impressive. I never expected to play a game where the AI would be challenging to a human ever again. This game was a nice refresher. Although the AI do have certain mildly exploitable patterns, they're still challenging and require focus. Even seemingly pathetic zombies can kick your butt if you play your cards wrong or underestimate them.
2: Physics based combat, using the cursor for turning, a difference between dashes and steps, and character direction based WASD controls made this game have a VERY difficult initial learning curve. Nothing in this game made sense and I thought it was a pile of rubbish. However, I stuck through that learning curve and discovered the true beauty of the physics and movement. At first I felt like a disconnected puppet master jerking about an unresponsive marionette, but now I feel like I know the character I'm playing and can feel them move. It's really something that can't be put into words.
3: Physiques are extremely interesting and have wildly different impacts on playstyles. Muscular characters have more control over movement, better balance, and can knock other people around better, but are a bit slower and less explosive. Skinnier characters can perform fast and extreme maneuvers, but have slower swings when not aided by movement and can be knocked down more easily. Fat characters can swing faster and be pretty aggressive, but they have poor balance and are easier to hit. This is only for male characters. I haven't even explored female characters in nearly as much depth, but from what I can tell they're generally faster but easier to be thrown around. Effectively, physiques replace the need for "strength, agility, etc" stats in the best way.
Personally, the only negatives I can think are this game's incredibly difficult initial learning curve and current lack of content. The former is a non-problem for dedicated people who are mature enough to learn a game before calling it crap, and the latter will be solved over time. Exanima feels like a complete game (even though it's still under development!), albeit a short one. If this is a taste of what Sui Generis will be, then I have full confidence in Bare Mettle. It's been so long since I've seen enough good from one developer to trust them.

I'm writing this as I go.
+ First look, it's impressive, the graphics are surprisingly good.
- Lack of tutorial, but there is a lengthy quick guide. It just wasn't helpful in helping me learn the mechanics of combat or how to interact with objects. That came mostly from trial and error, mostly error and death.
- NO ADJUSTABLE DIFFICULTY: This is a huge negative right now. I suppose they can always add it later because I'm not one to enjoy learning a quirky combat system the hard way, just to play an indy game with quirky combat no one really understands except for the dev team, and maybe people who've been following the game development.
I'm not gonna lie, my patience went from full to zero fast. Instead of destroying my keyboard I downloaded a trainer from a trusted source and proceeded to explore. :/ I wish there was an easier difficulty for n00bs. So take note of that before buying. This game is hard and combat isn't easily mastered. Think of Dark Souls, but with you constantly tripping over crap in the environment and falling on your face while a zombie rapes your butt with a handsaw, true story.
+ Very immersive and dark environment. I want the lead level designer to be my interior decorator, it's like being inside one of my nightmares, confusing, dank, dark, and all around creepy.
+ Surprisingly large amount of layerable armor. Right now I have on Leather boots, leather pants, shirt, leather jerkin, leather cap, leather gloves, and leather vambraces. Bassically I'm ready to go to a BDSM convention. I'm just walking around carrying a barrel lid as a makeshift shield and a bloody wood axe as my weapon of choice. Considering I started with pants, shoes, and a shirt, this feels like a huge improvement.
- Despite supposedly being a way to make friends and gain trust among the shambling corpse like beings I've encountered, I haven't seemed to manage it. Perhaps I'm just too tasty looking? I don't know, everything seems to walk up to me, stare, then take a swing at me. A tutorial would seriously help.
- While the concept for the combat is great, I'm really struggling with the controls. They just aren't very intuitive. It's like trying to learn to ride a bike with the steering reversed. Yeah, it's pretty bad, and they don't seem to be contextually sensitive so the response isn't always what you'd expect, but rather in relation to either the pointer, or which way the character is facing. The controls get a 1 out 10 from me. Seriously, cool idea, terrible experience. Another reason why it is not n00b friendly, aside from lacking in adjustable difficulty.
- No save file system. Why? I don't know, probably some lame tripe about it being more "hardcore" or some crap. If that's seriously the dev team idea of fun, then they need a reality check. If you want iron man mode you can add it as an option. The rest of us have crap to do. Like feed our 9 foot python our neighbor’s annoying yuppie chihuahua. Then wait behind the bushes on Monday morning to chase the mailman with a machete, because he didn't leave you a note about that package that was waiting for your at the post office for over a month before being shipped back to the dealer, well... and he could use the exercise. Point is, the game needs a damn save system.
*While you can smack things, and trip over them, there is one thing you can’t seem to do. Destroy things, yup, you can’t smash stuff. Which for a game that’s supposed to be all about realistic physics and stuff it kinda breaks the immersion. I was really expecting that locked door to splinter apart. 50 axe hits later it sunk in that I was expecting too much. I had the same result with barrels and crates, and pretty much everything else.
- No map!!! Aside from the cool atmosphere it’s pretty much a maze of very similar rooms. Writing a review has me lost. A compass would be nice too. Maybe I can find these things? I’ve yet to find some wine and cheese though so I’m not too optimistic about my prospects.
+ A compass can be found! :D Except I’m still lost without a map. Maybe I can find a crayon set and some paper?
- Items like keys aren’t marked, and easily blend into where ever they are located. I ran in circles for 20 minutes and eventually had to look up a guide to find the first two keys. Luckily they seem to be in static locations, unless on enemies. Can we get a highlight interactive items key? FFS That’s 20 minutes of my life I could have spent washing my crotch, trimming my nose hair, or cleaning my bathroom floor tile crevices with a toothbrush like a strung out tweaker!
- Took me a minute to figure out how to use the keys. I thought I could just insert them into the doors, seemed reasonable as I was able to rotate them as I dragged the keys around. NOPE. Click key, get weird reticle, click door. *facepalm* Ever hear of tooltips? Because the dev team clearly hasn’t. -_- What are we in 1986?
TO  CONCLUDE
I wanted to like this game. It’s beautiful, very nice graphics and level design. However, that’s simply not enough to excuse the terrible experience it delivers. The entire control system needs an overhaul, so does the GUI, especially whatever passes for a HUD. There’s also the need for adjustable difficulty and save file management. I would say it needs more polish, but it’s one glossy turd at the moment. That being said, it’s still a turd. It was funny at first how I could trip over the corner of the wall(how? did my character decide to parkour?) or how my arm would get stuck behind a doorway or corner… but after the 100th time I was far from amused. As nice as it looks, it’s far from anything that could remotely be considered a finished product. I’m giving it a thumbs down, as I don’t recommend it at this point. I’m hoping the finished product will be as fun to play as it is to look at. At the moment it feels like having a hot bossy girlfriend, looks great, but how long can you put up with that?

This is by far the best oldschool Hack&Slash RPG of all time. In my honest opnion, gameplay wise, it beats the old diablo 1 and 2 by a long shot. The world is huge, the enemies are many, the leveling and difficulity setting is epic and the classes are way more defined.
The story is... Just okay... But that is pretty much it. Do not even get me startet on the expantions storyline, because that is just wierd...

I have spend countless hours in this game, and it is a beastly fun game for LAN parties, if you can get it to work tho. It requires some research and guide reading to make it work properly and you should disable your firewall entirely. You also need to create a LAN server, and there is a file that lets you do that in the game folder. Oh, and you need to switch some internet/LAN setting in the options menu as well!
Now for the bad stuff! Some people need to play this in windowed mode, and i would highly reccomend it for everyone, since the resolution is not realy fit for the big screen. The worst thing about the game, is that internet play is not something you can do anymore. Damned shame!
All in all, i would reccomend this game to all who likes a good Hack&Slash game!

Crest dares to experiment and explore the God game genre. Breaking traditional conventions of you smiting or leading your people by divine acts or wrathful fire. Instead your intentions and words are spoken through commandments. Your followers interpret what these commandments say and can end up doing many different actions. From basic farming/mining to cannibalism. However Crest still has a long way to go. The AI of your followers can sometimes be rather wonky. Fetching resources on the other side of the island. While there are a variety of commands and suggestion for you to give. Only a couple of them truly seem to matter.  While experimentation is key, the game moves at a rapid pace. Each session is only supposed to last anywhere from 15 to 30 minutes. I found that with the wrong commandment, it can last 5 minutes. While rapid replayability and changing environments are a great idea. The game doesn't leave you much time to go off the beaten path.
Over all the gameplay works, but you end up feeling like your watching an ant hill that is suicidal. While the hands off approach is the point of the game. It leads to some frustrating moments and lack of excitement. Mind you, balance will be implemented during development.
Graphically the game is stylized and I enjoyed it. The way the land evolves as it rains, droughts, and is farmed. Adds a feeling of evolution to the area. The followers shift gear for different tasks and perform a strange mating dance. The music and tone of the game is done well. The game also has very little bugs.
I enjoy the idea of Crest and the game has potential. It speaks of building a legacy and seeing it live through your people. I want to see more of this in the game. I hope by the time It's fully released, we will.

This game is an interesting take on the God Game genre where instead of having direct control of your followers, you instead issue commandments that influence how your worshippers choose to live their lives. Sometimes they will thrive and flourish... other times they will starve to death because you told them food should not be touched. It's actually far more interesting to watch than to play but trust me, that's not a bad thing! It's actually really awesome to watch clouds pass over your island creating new forests with rains brought from the oceans and an overabundance of ran on an oasis can cause severe flooding that wipes your entire civilization out. It all feels... alive... despite being on a small scale with limited visual representation.
The main negative thing I notice about the game is once you've figured out what does what, the game can sort of drag down then again this is still very early access and the devs are pushing out updates at least once a week. All in all, I definitely recommend this game, not just for the small price tag, but because it's a God Game where you actually feel like a God who follows the "laissez-faire" approach to divinity!

In it's current state, Crest is all about experimentation. You give your followers commandments, and hope. I love the concept here, but I do hope the developers add a feature that lets you see just how your followers read specific commandments. The tutorial has something like that, but I would love to see it later in the game as well.

Crest is a light-hearted take on a god simulation game currently being developed by Eat Create Sleep and is in the last stages of Early Access here on Steam.
In the game, you are a god and you are given a small island civilisation to rule over... you in a way, play an omnipotent parent who watches your children grow and live their lives. You can guide them and instruct them by issuing them three symbol commandments (condition, the action you want them to do, and the target the action is for) which they can interpret and follow. For instance, you can instruct unhappy people to move out and form a new city or build a new hut or you can urge well fed followers to gather metals or lumber.
+ Simplistic minecraft like graphics that both my laptop and desktop could run with highest settings on
+ No stuttering during my gameplay.
+ Nice concept and take on the genre
+ Terrain can change by the amount of rainfall the island gets and by how you prioritize
+ The game is very relaxing to play after a stressful day
+ Music is relaxing and fits well with the game, isn't overbearing.
+ Easy learning curve
- No saves at the moment, though devs say the save cloud is coming soon
- No Achievements or trading cards
- No way to see what the results of your commandments are, and no way to tell if your followers interpretted the commandment the way you wanted
- Cannot terraform the land or build things
- Cannot currently explore and inhabit other islands
- Cannot advance tecnology
- Repetitive after a few games
- Games last maybe 15-20 minutes due to early access. Dev's say gameplay when out of early access will be 1-2 hours each playthrough.
There are seventeen unique symbols that represent everything from metals to food and young people to old people, but I wish there were more symbols to represent actions/wishes because I feel the game is still too restrictive at times, since I'm supposed to be this omnipotent being. Adding 5-6 more would be a great bonus.
Crest definately has a lot of potential as a god simulation game, and it seems that the developers really care about the game as they've taken suggestions from players and update the progress page quite frequently. While the game is short as it is right now, the developers are on the right path to make this a great game in terms of balancing strategy with simplicity and adding more features. As it sets, this game is not complete, but given the small price of $5 in USD, it's definately not going to be a waste of money if you enjoy games like this. The game in its current state, I give a 7/10 and when it's out of early release I will probably update the review again to give my thoughts of the completed game. **As this game is still in early access and has been since I wrote the original review, I have decided not to update this review as I feel it will never leave EA**

This walking simulator is in early beta stage and not even close to be functional. It seems to have lots of potential, but sadly, the only thing I've been able to see of it so far is a golden occasion for game makers to spam players with commercials.

What to expect of Anarchy Arcade: A walking simulator with movable 3D items where you can watch the pictures, game and web content set up on the game cloud. You are supposed to be able to watch video files too, by (aiming, click, aiming, clicking, aim and clicking again) starting a cmd, that will start local files, that you have previously set yourself on an in-game 3D model.

I love weird games in any kind of sense and Fearless Fantasy is such. The creatures are not typical, the battle system is not entirly typical. At first glance, it seems like another mobile port and to some degree it is, but make no mistake – it's defenently worth your time and money.
The main character here is Leon, the best bounty hunter in the world. He's tricked by princess Alice to save her from arrange marriage and they start a quest to stop an evil king. Along their journey, the company is joined by Vonn, friend and fellow bounty hunter of Leon, to help them with their quest. Together they have to stop the bad guy and kill a terrifying monster. The story is cheesy, simple and there in nothing to remember, except the character interaction. The writing is surprisingly fun. Cheesy, but fun. Dialogs between everyone is good. It won't win any awards, but I didn't want to skip any of the cutscene.
The option are bare-bones. Sound sliders, fullscreen, dynamic camera and visual effects. There are non rebindle key, because it's entirly mouse driven game.
The developer put a little twist on the traditional JRPG's battle system for the player to be more involved. You choose a regular attack or special. Then arrows and/or circles appear on screen and with the mouse you have to slide and/or click on them at precise moment. Better you do, more damage you make. Different skill have different patterns. Some even takes quite a few seconds to do and this keeps you on edge. This is the case with the enemies. When they make a move, you will do the same thing. Better you do, less damage you take and later in the game, this may be the difference between life or death. All skill require energy. Sometimes character can be blinded, but you can still make a flawless move. I really like this battle system. It's not just click to choose, it involves you and it's awesome! But it can also make you rage-quit, if you mess up.
All enemies have description and from here comes the strategy part. Some enemies while they are alive, his allies receive less damage from range attack, but when they are left alone, they die and so on. So you have to decide to kill the other creatures first or the single one that provide this buff. And this is kinda cool.
The skill are acquired by leveling up. When this happens, you have one point to put in stats and one in skills. All skills can be level up 5 times. Their sound and especially visual design is great.
After a battle you will get gold. With him you can buy weapons, items and gadgets. All are pretty standard. You have to be at certain level to get better weapons, items and gadgets. I wish there were more things to buy.
Beside the battle system, the graphics and charatcer design is what caught my eye at first. Both are amazing!!! All creatures are non standard and I can't even describe them. A mushroom with a some sort of shotgun and an evil flower. This is the best I can do. They are really weird in a good way. A lot of thought is put in them. The backgrounds are great too. They have this oil painting style and I like it. It's different than the characters. The bosses are really fun to fight. All have some sort of support, like tentacles or other characters, that have some buffs and you have to decide from who to start. They require some strategy.
As for the level design, there isn't much to say. You have a static map and there appear the next level. You click on it, choose the difficulty, represented as stars, fight 3-5 wave of enemies and that's it.
The suprise for me is the soundtrack. It's great!!! I want to listen it every day. It's that good. All tracks are fast-paced techno and really fits the combat on screen. Sadly, you can't buy it or find it anywhere.
Sound effects are great. All have enough punch to feel satisfying and when you combine  it with visual effects, they get even better.

I have few problems with the game. The first and most important is the lack of any information about the debuffs you get. Some you can recognize, like poisoning, but others you can't, at least in the beginning. All have icons beside of characters name and with time you will know them, but I think it would be better if I hover the mouse over them to show me some information. The second is grinding. It isn't much, but had to repeat few level to get some money for new gear. Next is minor. When enemy is about to attack on screen you see “Tap when ready”. Come on, it's a PC game remove tap and put click. Next is audio in cutscenes. It feels really compressed. Other conversations have much better quality. And lastly the combat. I can't comment the mobile version, but the games feels kinda clunky when you have to use the mouse to execute the moves. Further into the game they become longer and complicated. It feels more natural to swipe with fingers. Despite that it's really fun. Oh, and tutorial for the combat is nowhere to be found.
Overall I had fun with the game. It's defenently worth the asking price. If it was more, I would say wait for a sale. The game is not super long. It will take you 3-5 hours to beat it. There is three star rating system and from here come some replayability. I didn't maximise all my skill and I still beat the game, so for me it's not worth on the hardest difficulty, because the fighting become faster and this can make me break my mouse. The battle system, creature design and soundtrack are really great and because of them you can overlook the shortcomings. I recommend it.

Firstly, I would like to say that this game is primarily aimed towards systems that enable touch screen technology - or at least from what I can see based on the reviews as well as my own experience playing this game. However, I have a wireless mouse that I use with my laptop.
So what I'm getting to is: if you don't have neither a touch screen, nor a [wireless] mouse for your gaming experience - this game would be highly difficult to even try to play. For instance, if you were to try and use the laptop's built in mouse system, it would become increasingly hard to actually manage to complete a single level given that there are patterns that you need to trail with your mouse, and with the built-in mouse, moving quickly enough for that would just be impossible.
TL;DR: TOUCH SCREEN, OR MOUSE IS HIGHLY RECOMMENDED FOR GAMEPLAY.
I always like the function of upgrading weapons and leveling up, it's so addicting in that sense.
Whenever you upgrade your weapon, an extra mouse/touch pattern will be added whenever you use your skills. When you upgrade your skills, eventually this will add extra requirements when clicking and trailing the little symbols that appear.
As many people have mentioned before, this game mechanic is very similar to the game many of us know as Osu! Like Osu, it would be much more practical if it were to be played using a touch screen, but given that I do not have one, it is a bit challenging. HOWEVER, this game can be played with a mouse, and you will still be good to go.
I've been playing the game now for an hour or so, and I'm quite addicted. I had to step away in order to prevent playing too much to the point where my family will be screaming at me to get out of my room!
Some of the levels were quite challenging, and I had to die a few times in order to finally beat certain challenging levels, but hey - what fun would a super easy breezy game be?
Bottom line: I think you should invest in this game given that the following conditions are met as mentioned above.

You also need to manage your peasants, and sometimes have to sacrifice the happiness of the people, for the good of the people. Honestly, sometimes it feels like the peasants can be total cry babies... but it adds more things for you to do. So far, with my sort of early Kingdom, I find that I never really have enough people or enough of anything to really do what I want, which is a problem I had in other building games. I felt like things were just handed to me to build, and I didn't have to worry too much about one structure, in this game, you need to make sure every single building will have a positive effect on the town/city/village whatever. Maybe I'll eventually get bored of it down the road once I've done everything, but for now I can say that it's quite enjoyable.
As for negatives of the game, I only really have small complaints. Sometimes, the peasants are complete idiots, they'll take really complicated paths to somewhere they need to be which they dont have to, usually it involves the peasants having food wasted because they took such a stupid route. Also, maybe this is a feature already, but I'm not sure if it's possible for you to set your own customizable limit to who is working at each structure... so far I've had to completely close down an entire structure in order to get them off their butts to go build the thing I want them to build for me elsewhere. Controlling your heroes to fight off invaders can be really annoying too, because sometimes when I send a hero to a group of invaders, he attacks one of them then stands there are the others advance in to my City.
TL;DR, The game so far for me has been pretty enjoyable, with some issues that do bother me but nothing I can't really look past and enjoy it. Overall, really fun time!

Making video games is not an easy task. Many games these days can take years to make, cost millions of pounds and require a lot of people to work on them. It’s a big industry, but, for all the times you have played video games, have you ever considered giving it a go?
Game Corp DX is based on the online flash game of the same name (minus the DX) and challenges players with the task of building a video games company from the bottom up. Players start out with a small building and need to hire and train staff members and create game projects for them to work on. When the game is complete, they will then need to publish it, check out the reviews and get right on to the next project; providing they still have enough money to make them. As the game moves on, players can hire more staff members, upgrade and relocate their base of operations to places around the world, work on bigger projects, while also keeping the books balanced and win big at the annual awards.
“The game really does grab the attention of the player. It may be rather simple to look at and play, but there is an added level of depth in that you begin to panic when your money value is in the red”
Game Corp DX is a pretty simple game to play as it mostly involves moving the camera around with your mouse, and clicking on objects and the interactive menu to do stuff. The graphics are presented in a nice 2D style with no real shading or angles, making it easy on the eye. The soundtrack is rather nice and pleasant and kind of reminds me of the soundtrack from Theme Hospital.
The game really does grab the attention of the player. It may be rather simple to look at and play, but there is an added level of depth in that you begin to panic when your money value is in the red. Creating the video games your company produces takes the form of a simple little selection of menus. Basically you just name the game, choose the genre, choose staff members with the best appropriate skills to produce the game and select from programs and resources to make the game. Then your workers will design and create it, followed by you publishing it, checking out the reviews, then hope it makes money. It’s a rather nice easy way of doing things, but you begin to care how well it does at the reviews stage, how much money it makes and if it wins big at the awards ceremonies.
While it is a nice simple game, I feel that some bits of it are rather random. Games work depending on whether or not you have the right people with the right skills working on a game, but when it comes to making money, it just feels random as to how much money it takes and how well it does at the review stage. One moment you could produce a game that would put Halo to shame, but then you could release something worse than E.T. As soon as you hit your stride and are able to know how to make good games, it gets rather easy. There are some in-game trophies and challenges to complete, but once you know what to do, it just feels like the challenge is gone.
At best, Game Corp DX is a nice filler game. While it is rather addictive and you are able to get fully engrossed in the game, it does not offer much for long periods of gaming. It’s a game that is best played when you have some time to kill. It has some replay value but suffers from getting too easy once you get the knack of making games. It’s a nice little game but still has some issues in its current state; some of these are more technical such as not being in full screen mode when you first load it (something which you’ll need to change in the options menu). Despite the niggles though, it’s a pleasant way to pass a bit of time, and it’ll be worth seeing what updates are implemented before it’s out of Early Access.

I'll start this off by saying this game probably isn't for everyone.  To me, that is a good thing, because appealing to as wide a base as possible can strip a game of what makes it unique.  That's just my own personal bias, though.
This is a game that rewards you for thinking and practicing  and offers little in the way of hand-holding.  You won't jump in and be great from the get-go, but every inch of progress feels like a worthy accomplishment.  You will die, A LOT.  At first you might blame the game (go read some of the more frustrated discussion posts on the forums) but with enough time in the Arena or crawling through the dungeon, you'll find how much each-and-every keystroke and mouse-click affects your character.  I've probably spent half of my playtime so far in each game mode, and only now am I getting decent at surviving...the first floor.  Hell, that's probably my own fault, too, because I try my darndest to kill each and every undead SOB that I come across.
Currently there are two game modes: Story and Arena.  The story takes place amidst three floors or sections of an underworld (so far).  The arena comes in two flavors: Novice and Expert, and serves as a good 'tutorial' for learning the game mechanics.  All things considered, you can easily get the $15 worth out of the arena alone and never reach the Expert level.
There's more to be said in the forums about individual mechanics, but the long and short of it is a love/hate relationship.  Every step matters.  When you click your mouse and how you move it matter.  The direction you are facing when attacking or dodging matters.  This is the first game where I've been able to trip someone over a sawhorse and smash their head in with a mace, and that's a plus in my book.
If you're looking for a challenge, want to support a dedicated development team, are tired of reskinned and repackaged Call of Assasin's Whatever, I fully recommend this game.  Whatever the reason.  There are few games in my library that I feel as happy about buying as I do with this game (I can probably count them all on one hand).

A pleasant diversion with little interaction from the player.
You give commandments to tell your people what to prioritize, and they mostly do so. They mine, harvest food, make babies, get flooded-out, then die. If you speed it up, a civilization takes about 5 minutes before everyone dies. The devs are completely up-front about a playthrough lasting 15-30 minutes, and that seems accurate. I assume that meant on the slowest setting, with the fastest being triple-speed. It's fun to watch, but there isn't a lot going on, at the moment. There also isn't much for you to do as a player.
If you sometimes find yourself playing a two-minute hand of solitaire while doing other things on your computer, this is a perfect game to mix up your card-matching routine. There is very little strategy and not much of a late-stage to be reached, though, so be wary if you're looking for something complex.
All in all, it's exactly as-advertised in the Early Access information, and is solidly play-able in its current state.

AVGN 2 is an amazing platformer/shooter, but what makes it really unique is all of the sick and twisted humor within it.  My personal favorite is when you have to ride a Tanooki that crushes enemies with its testicles and defeat another giant tanooki named Scrotoro.  What sets it apart from the original game are a few new mechanics.  FIrst off, you can wall-slide like in Mega Man X, which is a great feature that's easy to pick up and use.  There is also reverse gravity like in Gravity Man's stage from Mega Man 5.  There is also a lot more replay value, since the letters N,E,R, and D are scattered throughout each level, which are basically the same as KONG letters in Donkey Kong Country.  The Nerd's powerups from the ROB episode can also be picked up, such as the power glove.  The game is very difficult, even on Normal Mode, but it's overall very rewarding to beat, and I'll definitely replay it for all of the hidden stuff.  I've had the game crash a few times and there is some really cheap enemy placement in a few spots, but it's overall a great game.  9/10
