(Note: This is a VERY gimped version of the review I wrote for ticgn . com. To see the full review, look up Valcarta there.)
While I often stay away from RPG games (with exceptions such as the Mario ones and the GBA Pokemon games), I felt I could still set foot in the independent portion of the genre since there’s no telling what exactly they could offer. However, there are polar opposites among the indie spectrum. Players could revel in the uniquely charming world and innovative play of Undertale, or they could accidentally look up one of many failed attempts to make loads of money via Kickstarter from an amateur-ish game cobbled together in RPG Maker.
Mind you, I’m not one to condone people for using a certain kind of game engine to create stuff. If anything, I’m just going to say I personally prefer Game Maker if you want to make anything you would want to safely call your own work. I am open to playing games made in RPG Maker that are at least fun and enjoyable, though. If I can be engaged with the story told and world on display, I’m good. That said, Valcarta really wants to be such a thing, but ends up being a very, very middling experience.
Graphics
Easily one of the weaker categories around here; the graphics in Valcarta are mostly, if not completely, made up of stock graphics developers can use for RPG Maker projects. I wouldn’t have too much of a problem with this if it weren’t for the fact that they are simply the most overused graphics I’ve seen in any game engine! That, and the settings in particular are as generic as any fantasy RPG, notably other ones made in RPG Maker. You have your grass tiles, town areas, caves, castle tiles, and whatever else gamers have seen before. I’m not saying there should be grasslands or caves at all; I’m saying that they should at least look fresh rather than bland and arguably dull.
Audio
The sound effects are the ones pre-made for RPG Maker, but the music selections are composed of royalty free songs elsewhere. That said, the choices used in the game are actually stellar stuff. The music is diverse, fun to listen to, and has every right to be used in an RPG. In fact, the music (and even the sound effects) are memorable, which is more than I can say for the story.
Story
Now I know why there are critics on the Internet that take notes while playing games they review.
Valcarta‘s story is complex on a massive level, to the point where it feels unnecessary to have it at such a scale! And considering the atmosphere is still that typical fantasy setting RPGs are most often associated with, it, along with the graphics, neuter most sorts of actual personality from the environments the protagonists find themselves in. It’s basically a blur a lot of the time.
The basic sum-up is that there’s this dude named Valek, and he assists a mayor in a simple town named Olm. But then destiny is calling him to go to some shack and choose between a letter and an orb. This is where the game splits into light and dark paths.
The dark path sees Valek work for a Lady Astrid, who is seemingly nothing but a mystical creature wearing a black cloak. It is revealed that the mayors of Olm and Malvern are working with the Empire, and Valek responds by instantly killing them. Hang on – even in the dark path, Valek seems as good-natured as any protagonist in a game of this genre. Why would he suddenly have the (lack of) heart to kill the mayors? There was even a scene where a guy was trying to sell Valek the boat needed to travel to other islands and places, but he gets killed simply for charging too high.
Anyway, after meeting up with Astrid, Valek is tasked to rally up allies, and then he and his team set off to perform some Cleansing Rituals in sacred locations containing special crystals, as well as stop the Empire. And Astrid apparently isn’t a spirit, but a woman Valek is somehow sexually compatible with.
There are so many details and tidbits that it makes my head spin. I didn’t even mention that robots also become important plot points, and that one of the team members eventually abandons Valek for personal reasons that I have in no way recalling because these characters just aren’t that memorable. I’ve never gotten to understand Valek’s relationships with the world around him, let alone the people he talks to.
Ah, well. I’ll give credit where credit’s due. Even though there’s a lot to bicker about with the characterization, I can at least applaud that the story tries to be an epic that divides itself into two for the potential of replayability.
Gameplay
First off, I would certainly thank the game for letting me run around without holding down any buttons. That’s something more games of its kind should do. Otherwise, the game does more-or-less follow the typical conventions of an old school RPG title, albeit with some subtle things thrown in to make it its own. There are towns and similar locations with NPCs, places to buy things, and important plot points occurring. There’s an overworld map the player travels through to go from one major location to another, and random enemy encounters happen at appropriately…random timings.
One thing that’s interesting about the battle mechanics is that while it is mostly the same as one may expect for the genre, there is a stamina bar for each character in battle. The bar automatically fills up, and when it does, the character gets to attack. Or so that’s the case if you set the ATB settings to “Full” instead of “Wait” before beginning the game. If the player chooses the latter, the enemies’ bars won’t increase when it’s his or her turn, effectively turning the majority of battles into “take your time to select Defend when the enemy bar is nearly full”.
Battles with regular baddies can be over in less than a quarter of a minute if the player can button mash attacks and specials whilst still keeping an eye on the enemy’s stamina meter to make sure when to defend, but I do like the quick pacing of it all. The more interesting battles are with bosses; some of them could be genuinely fun and show a sign of brilliance for the combat design, but there are also bosses that feel like a chore since they take so much damage (making them waiting games).
The same thing can be said for roaming territory. There are some puzzles that are enjoyable to solve, while others (especially ones in the form of mazes) feel like they’re only there to pad out the game length. This feeling gets driven home when enemy encounters pop up in places one would prefer not seeing them appear in. Areas like the spider web forest complement the enemy encounters since the player is challenged to race against a time limit, but there are other areas that feature more direct puzzles; yet they include enemy encounters.
Verdict
This is a meaty package, but only a fraction of it is what I believe is good enough to eat. I may not play RPGs super often, but when I do, I expect to appreciate the characters, their personalities, the worlds they travel to, and the story being told. There’s a reason I constantly give the original Paper Mario series my praises; if writers can have Mario join a wrestling federation, spoof train mysteries, fight an anime-loving chameleon, and still be able to balance the crazier antics out with genuinely moving and emotional moments such as Princess Peach’s interactions with a computer trying to understand the concept of love, then they are darn good at their jobs to say the least.
I’m sure loads of people find writing to be difficult, but if you’re going to do it, you have to make sure you could really pull off such a feat. With Valcarta, I don’t feel it does that well, especially with its generic fantasy setting the graphics plague. Similarly, the gameplay as a whole isn’t really that fun, with moments here and there demonstrating a sense of something more yet lacking enough fulfillment in the long road.

Let me preface this by saying that I have played my fair share of RPG's over the years. At first look Valcarta would appear to be another sword & shield RPG churned out with RPG Maker's stock art & sound clips. Look deeper and you will find a compelling storyline & some custom sound effects.
I found that the Boss fights in Valcarta were challenging and forced me to think each encounter through and did not allow me to take the same plan into each fight.  Each boss was unique, requiring me to formulate new strategies to achieve victory as opposed to using the same battle plan and button mashing until they were dead. This reminded me of battles from Final Fantasy in the past.
Another element of Valcarta's gameplay I quite enjoyed was the puzzles that were encountered along the way.  Brought me back to the Zelda days of puzzle gameplay.
I found the story to be compelling and elaborate, comparable to that of some other RPG franchises. It kept me wondering whether motives presented by key characters are actually true or simply ruses to enlist henchmen to assist the key characters to achieve their true motivations.  On occasion the dialogue can be juvenile, but that can be attributed to the nature of certain feline characters. Felines will be felines. Information was consistently provided and I was not left wondering where I was headed next to progress the story.   The story also provides the opportunity to discover some hidden gems and entertain you with comic relief.

On the day Anno 2205 was announced, it's fair to say I was utterly ecstatic.  By that time, I had logged more than 2,000 hours playing Anno 2070.  It was and continues to be one of my all-time favorite games.  I felt very confident that I would love the next iteration of the series, so I pre-ordered it, complete with season pass, the day it was announced.  I even registered the official Wikia address for the game so I could contribute to what I expected to be a comprehensive resource for a stellar product.
Then we were told that those who pre-ordered the game would not get early access.
And much later the game finally launched.
My initial impression of Anno 2205 was complete and utter dismay at what I thought was a money-grabbing, subpar product, the likes of which never should have carried the Anno name.  I had never in my life felt more disappointment in a game launch as I did this one.  My complaints were similar to the many other reviews that were made here.  I hated it so much I refused to work on the Wikia and gave it to someone else to mange.
Over time, Ubisoft continued to make DLCs for the game, but I did not care.  I had no interest in this game and I did not bother to try any of them.  It was only in the past week that I decided to give it another look and to my surprise I've been enjoying it.  There's a lot to like about this game.  But there's also a lot to hate.
First, I want to focus on the negatives, because they are quite pertinent to the Anno series.  This one veers sharply from its predecessors in countless ways.  There are no random maps, which for me is the biggest and most severe disappointment I have.  There's no meaningful connection to the NPCs in the game; we do not share maps or interact hardly at all.  And that was really important to me in previous Anno games.  The developers brought combat back into the main maps, but I've found them more annoying than anything else.  You can't build ships like in previous games.  The upgrading is just silly.  There's no strategy involved.  It's just not fun.  There's no Ark, and no reason for one, since there's really nothing to be stored anywhere.  And there's no ferrying of goods or setting up sophisticated trade routes.  Switching maps is jarring.  It feels incomplete.
With all of this said, it's an enjoyable distraction.  The graphics are great.  The music is awesome.  There's quite a bit of complexity in building product chains.  There's a lot of "little things" that make the game as a platform better than its predecessors.  So I can't complain too much at this point; it has come quite a long way since it's initial launch.  I don't know if any more updates are planned; the game is pretty much a flop as far as I know.  But there's potential, and if they keep with it, this whole experiment into a new Anno just might work out for the developers.  And the one advice I'd want to give them in a future Anno is to try to go for hex grids -- that could be interesting.
They tried something new.  It didn't work out.  But it's not a complete waste.
However, it's NOT worth $40-$50.  Only buy this on sale.

Overall: a great game and an excellent successor to Anno 2070.
The world in which you can build is enormous as compared to 2070, and there are far more things to build and commodities to trade.  For trading, you focus on inter-region trade rather than inter-island trade now, and 2205's trade interface is much smoother than 2070's.  Combat is different, fleets are different, and combat quests are different, but I like the change.  Both trading and combat are simpler now but feel just as rewarding as they did in 2070.
Anno 2205's menu UI has some bugs, and I've had to restart the game two or three times after the menu widgets became completely unresponsive.  The English translation is pretty rough in places, too.  These are my only two complaints so I'm very pleased with the game so far.
I haven't played enough yet to comment on the end-game, but I'm encouraged.  I purchased Anno 2205 and all its DLC on sale for under $40 and would do it again happily.

I loved the first Angry Video Game Nerd game so I was super excited for the sequel, so i pounced on the pre-order and eagerly awaited release day... and here it is! Angry Video Game Nerd 2 Assimilation!
So what's different? Well like all good sequels they've taken everything that was good about the original and expanded upon it.
There are new power ups that permanantly upgrade the Nerd such as a power glove that lets you smash certain blocks, the ability to slide and a charged shot for your zapper.
There's a brand new overworld map that let's you choose which order to do stages in and N E R D cartridges to collect scattered throughout each level.
There's also a bunch of cameos and references to Nerd episodes and Nerd movie which are hilarious.
Each level has a different theme such as NES Ninja Turtles, old school horror games, sci-fi games, japanese games and a Board James themed level!
They toned down the death blocks from the first game and i can safely say things are a little easier in this game than the first, the bosses in particular are incredibly easy. Graphics look about as good as the first game and the music is ok, I don't think it quite matches up to the brilliant soundtrack of the first game but there's some catchy tunes in there.
So yeah, if you liked the original game you will love the sequel as it's more of the same but on a bigger scale.
Here's looking forward to Angry Video Game Nerd 3!

(Full review follows below)
With a cursory glance, it would be easy to dismiss
as another mediocre game, with mobile-game-era mechanics (oh my), that isn’t worth looking into.  I will tell you: that may be a mistake.
If video games were people in a Hollywood high school movie,
would probably be that odd, quiet girl who sits alone during lunch.  Most people know she exists, but don’t necessarily acknowledge her existence— best she just stay in the corner “where she belongs.”  Then when the jock has to talk to her (on a dare), we find out she is indeed a bit odd and won’t ever fit in with the popular crowd… but she is also surprisingly fun and suddenly attractive when you give her a chance to take off her glasses and let her hair down.
Many people will automatically dismiss this game because it uses ideas rooted in mobile-gaming.  That is their prerogative.  All I know is that I only play games on PC, and I play many different games— and I found
to be one of the more enjoyable games I have personally played.  It isn’t the best, but it is better than many.
What makes this game enjoyable is the combination of nostalgia-evoking, tried-and-true, core RPG mechanics (turn-based combat, level ups, skill points, and items) with some modern zest (using the mouse to make gestures to execute abilities), and a light, casual style and storyline.  While you play, it simultaneously feels comfortably familiar and interestingly novel.
Many games try to find ways to spice up the classic turn-based-RPG combat style; one of the best I have seen is the swipe-and-click gesturing used in
.  Instead of just clicking “attack” and watching your character attack, you have to use your mouse to perform various combinations of swiping and clicking, involving timing and precision.  I thought it was exceedingly fun trying to pull off the advanced moves on the high difficulty.
With the relative ease and short length of this game, it is a great candidate for a quick bite of a variety in your gaming diet.

It was the first game that introduced me into this kind of gameplay and I must say - I loved it! Turn based fights where you do not only click on enemy to attack, but the better you do in an mini-game during your/enemy's attack - the more/less damage you deal/recieve. I found it really rewarding and it kept me focused all of the time.
Do not buy it for complex story, because it doesn't offer one - it just fills the basic need for it. As for the RPG part - I also do not recommend it for hardcore fans of the genre who love to fiddle with their characters' stats, abilities and equipment. You can always reset and change everything between fights with no additional in-game cost, which in my opinion is
for this kind of game.
Game offers choice of difficulty for each battle, which makes it good for anyone to pick up and play. You can really feel the difference between each one and it's even more challenging with a mouse.
If you have a choice - get and play it on a touch device, especially if you are going to play on hardest difficulty.

I grew up on the N64 and this game got a regular rotation among my gaming habits back then. about a year or so ago a friend and I played through the entirety of this game on an N64 with no cheats and I was surprised at how well it held up to modern shooters. now that it's been ported to the PC and I've had a chance to blow through the first level, I figure I share some thoughts on the port and the game itself.
- looks and feels like the N64 game just with less blurry textures. (personally I love this. I am a huge nostalgia sucker)
- mouse and keyboard support! gamepad support as well but i'm yet to try it.
- everything is still where I remember it. i.e., so far it seems like a very faithful recreation of the maps, item/weapon loacations, and enemy locations.
- Turok plays surprisingly well with a keyboard and mouse. almost like Iguanna studios made the game that way first then stuck it in an N64 back in the 90's
- the old save/checkpoint system is still in effect. ahhh, the good ol' 90's era of "save when we tell you it's ok to save".
- music and sound are still great as ever.
- additional fancy lighting and V-sync added. no more crummy framerate. though if they do that for turok 2 as well it will be an instant purchase for me.
- late game becomes an excercise in ammunition management. "sure the quad launcher will wreck that group of cyber-raptors.....but then what will I use against the rocket launching triceratops?!"
basically if you remember turok for the N64, this should be a must play. $20 may be a bit steep however. so if you see it for no more than $15, I'd pick it up in a heart beat (which i did, and then I did.).
I VERY MUCH look forward to seeing this studio's work on Turok 2. until then, I'm going to battle my way through to the campaigner and chronocepter his face into next week.

I had no idea Turok was being remastered and released on Steam, so this came as a great surprise. This was something I had hoped for a long time but never thought would happen. The original Turok games are some of the most nostalgic games from my childhood and I really couldn’t have asked for a better re-release. I have never played the PC version of this game before, so any comparisons I make will be based on my time with the N64 version.
There are a multitude of options to choose from ranging from visual to simple convenience options including things you’d usually have to edit an .ini for in almost every other game.
The game runs smooth and controls amazingly well. I doubt I could go back to playing this game with an N64 controller again after playing the remastered PC version with mouse and keyboard. The platforming and aiming in particular are far improved.
Graphically there are some improvements, though the look of the game is still very much the same. The improved draw distance is definitely one of the better improvements. There is still distance fog but it is nowhere near what it was on the N64. Another one of the more noticeable additions to me was god rays, which were very surprising to see in an old N64 game. They look really nice though. A bloom effect has also been added and it looks nice, and is definitely noticeable. There are some added water effects like reflection and refraction, though the reflection effect looked pretty weird, so I disabled that one. The game comes ready for HD resolutions and automatically detects your display settings. The game immediately started for me in 1920x1080(144hz), though I did have to disable windowed mode.
Another addition to this release of the game is achievements. Definitely a welcome addition in my book, even if they are rather simple and there are only 8 of them. Hopefully trading cards will be implemented eventually also as a Turok background could be pretty cool.
There are some small glitches like blood sticking to invisible surfaces, or occasionally being able to see through a wall as you’re falling or moving in a weird way, but these are very minor and for me they don’t detract from the game at all.
The price tag seems pretty high for an old game like this especially if you’ve never played the game before and it holds no nostalgia value for you. For me this was definitely worth getting though since I have been hoping for this for so long and I’ve always loved the game.
Now I just wait for Turok 2, and when that releases my life will be complete.

Comat is great and has the feeling of weight behind it but in terms of content it can be found wanting.

You see a nifty side effect of being physics based is the care with which you have to plan almost two moves in advance- spacing and timing can be critical- so can your movement speed. you might connect what you have been a deadly blow but..oh no you tried to out manuver yourself and you tripped up over your two handed sword. Weeell..... I think it is good in its own way. I like the setting, but i don't like battle mechanincs so far, not in this way. I had to spend a lot of time and get killed like a hundred times to finally understand it. The idea is simple, you hold your sword by doing nothing and the player parries himself as long as you keep distance and you are in front of the enemy. Once you've parried you hit him back. One at a time, or he will hit most likely hit you on your second click. And you do this until the enemy is dead. If you come across 2 enemies or more - you run away and try to kill them one by one. This is game's batle mechanics. Sounds simple enough, but gets extremely complicated and frustrating once you try it. And the problem is that even though i understand it, i don't like it.
The game has nice picture, but level design is too complicated. You can wander around for 2 hours to come across closed door, and than look for a little key for another 2 hours. I couldn't make it beyond the second level because i couldn't find one of those keys. Loot is boring as well, at least for now. Comparing items is too complicated.
Pluses:
- Nice graphics
- Entourage Interaction
- Interesting world design
- Optimization
Minuses:
- Blank looking levels. I know that this is a setting, but orienting in these corridors is damn hard. If this was intentional, than good job.
- Very complicated level design. The reason for this is lookaliknes of all the rooms and corridors.
- Every fight looks like a fight of drunk people(yeah, yeah_

- Bad player control system. To explain in short - it is like controlling heavy mindless puppet on strings. Luckily your enemies are the same. You know it could have been made more comfortable, but devs decided to walk the road of experimenting and individuality.
- Camera position. I know it is meant to be like this, but it does not sum up with battle mechanics.
To sum up - this game is definately not for general gamer auditory. These mechanics will surely get their own fanbase, but do not rush into buying this game, if you're not interested in spending 5 hours mastering your controls over the player. I'm recomending to try this game out, since there are no analogues of it, and you will get an interesting (or frustrating) experience. Exanima...where to begin...
It's an experience. Not so much as a story (which is kind of half♥♥♥♥♥at this point in development) or as an atmosphere (nothing you can't experience elsewhere, though it is engaging), but more so as a game with interesting mechanics. The game takes some getting used to due to the fact that many conventional gaming mechanics are replaced with more challenging ones; Combat is difficult, not just because of the A.I., but because learning just to
the weapons is challenging; Useful objects have no different appeal from useless objects (until you learn what's useful or click on the item). It's these mechanics (and a few others) that make Exanima unique.
It's not perfect; the camera (ESPECIALLY in combat) is difficult at times. It's not due to poor controls (you have decent control over the camera), it's only problematic in certain senarios. For example, in combat, it's pretty easy to get backed into a wall. When this happens, you can't see your character, and thus can't block/attack effectively. With more than one opponent, it's a death sentence. The camera causes a few annoyances along those lines.
Another downfall (keep in mind, it's still in Alpha) is replayablility. The "Story" lacks actual plot; there's books, scrolls, letters and the like that somwhat explain the purpose of the structure your in, but that's about it. The character is given no incentive to do much of anything except stay alive and figure out this wackjob story that feels like a last minute pull together by a lazy Dungeon Master. The "Story" also is fairly short; depending on how long it takes you to get used to the game (took me a few hours of messing around in Arena mode), the story could take you only an hour or two to blaze through. Say you took 2 hours to get used to the game, blew through story in 2 hours, played again to find different stuff...6 hours? For $15.00? I'll let you decide if it's worth it, but after beating the "Story", it's basically over until the devs release an update.
Which brings up another point....it's been a while since there's been an update. Now, you read around and it seems like they're working on it. But you also read how this is the warm up for some other title their putting out later. Call me paranoid, but I worry about this being the unloved child that Day One: Garry's Incident turned out to be (not to say this game is anywhere near that horrid; it's not even remotely close to that ♥♥♥♥ing piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Final verdict:
Story: Sucks
Combat: Fun; unique
Atmosphere: Scary and immersive at first, but it quickly becomes kind of blah and repetitive.
Graphics: Seem good, but my low-level machine isn't apt to give you good opinoin.
Running on a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ machine: Close everything else and lower graphics settings. 5 year old HP Pavilion, 1.9 Ghz AMD GPU and it runs with minimal lag. Rather pleased.
Outta 10: 7/10 with expectations of a better score once the developers release a freaking update.
Edit: Oh, I have 17.5 hours? The game is good if you're bored as ♥♥♥♥ and want something to attempt to be good at. It's getting bland, though it is still fun

Some people bemoan the changes that this Anno brings, but for my money it is different from it's predecessors in some very positive ways.  I am not a fan of competitive RTS games, so I have always treated this game as a realtime economic simulator.  My favorite Anno mode is continuous mode, and I have only play the series multiplayer a handful of times.  With that in mind, here are some changes that I liked in this iteration of the franchise.
In the past the game was needlessly complicated by a lack of communication of the rules.  A big part of the game is creating production chains (e.g. 2 of one resource, makes 4 of another resource, which is used to make 1 of a third resource).  In all previous iterations, quantities were hidden and had to be either referenced by an outside source such as a wiki, or meticulously observed and recorded in your brain.  Now the values are visible from the UI and the game can be learned and mastered without an outside aide.  This is a huge improvement, and cannot be understated.  The reason for not making the production chains visible was baffling to me as they were obviously hard-coded and learnable--they just served to obfiscate the game and make it harder for new players to enjoy.
The main change in this iteration though, is the definite shift from economic RTS to city-builder campaign game.  No longer do you compete with AI (or players) over territory, and build up your base until you "win" the map.  Now, there is a single, over-arching campaign which drives your entire time with the game.  Instead of starting over from scratch with each new session you instead move to different maps and start a new colony there expanding your current company's foothold and resources. There is no longer an AI presence on the map to compete with for resources.  Now, there are invaders and catastrophies, but generally speaking the only limit on your expansion is your own efficiency.
Most of the mechanics of Anno remain in the campaign but are refined and expanded to great success.  There are quirks of each map that affect your production, goods that have to be transferred between civilization types, and there are one-off missions which provide an alternate method of obtaining resources and making progress.  This is the first game where I felt like missions were woven into the fabric of the game well.  In previous iterations, I often just ignored the missions that were given, and even if I tried to do them I often found them to be obtuse.  Now I feel the missions are both important and engaging and I do them all the time.
I also feel like the season pass really adds a lot of intrigue to the game.  Between the stock market, space colonies and the new sectors, the game has hundreds of hours of gameplay.  Unlike most games where DLC doesn't interest me, I'm glad to have purchased this season pass.
I have loved every version of Anno since the first one I played, 1701.  Each time they improve the mechanics and the presentation, and this version is no different.

Alright so after completing all of the chapters, I am prepared to issue a reccomendation on this game, but I would be remiss if I did not qualify it heavily.
There's definitely a lot of interesting story here, with a surprising amount of choices, with interesting characters and settings, unfortunately that does not quite extend to the gameplay, there are a lot of unfortunate design decisions that hold the game back in my estimation.
I ask you, the reader, what benefit is there to adding psuedo open worlds to an adventure game?  Doing this makes many puzzles boil down to a scavenger hunt for interactible objects.  It's all the lack of fun that pixel hunting was in the adventure games of old, but in three dee.  This led to many so called guide-damn-it moments, while nothing reached the memorable height of the inflatable duck puzzle from the original game.  This scavenger hunt gameplay can get very frustrating.
I would also like to issue something of a warning on the overall writing quality.  While the dialog wavers between ok and good most of the time, when you hit cringe, you hit cringe hard.
Anyway, final verdict, if you liked the other games in the series, this is a fine send off.  If you're looking for new adventure games, I would kind of advise picking up the wadjet eye published games first, but if the setting looks like something that interests you, it may very well still be worth a look.

Grow UP is the polished-up sequel of Grow Home. Similarily to the Portal franchise the first game was mostly just an experiment while the successor is a full-budget game. Has everything improved since our last journey with BUD the botanical research robot? Here's a short list of pros and cons:
+A Whimsical adventure game with lots of places to explore and things to experiment with. The  game is fueled by the player's curiousity.
+Don't need experience with the first game to be able to play this one. It's very easy to get into.
+The graphics are cute and bright but easy on the eyes, showing off quite a bit of beauty in it's own style. Which is perfect for this type of game, and will surely age well. Love the little critters and glowing flora.
+Different plants and tools which you can use to explore and shape the enviroment.
+The game is purely physics based that might need some getting used to in regard to controlling BUD, but you can learn at your own pace and take bigger challenges as you get more confident.
+Sound effects and music are all fitting and satisfying to the ears.
+Bigger in scope then the first game with increasingly improved means to get around the varying landscape.
+Messing up and accidentally falling to your death has no penalty aside from being respawned at the last teleporter you visited which are all neatly scattered across the world.
+Cheesey but endearing humour that replaces the more ordinary, point-of-fact tutorial and mission objective dialogue we're used to.
+Feels less clunky then the last game. The need for climbing everywhere and picking up singular leafs to use as gliders has been replaced with more satisfying rewards that help you get around.
+Guaranteed 9-12 hours of adventure which can vary based on your skill and ability to create your own goals. Example: "I wonder if I can fling myself into orbit... hmmm let's find out!" (spoiler alert: you can and it's absolutely amazing)
+Absolutely worth the 10 dollar price tag. Even if you're not sure if this game is for you, it really doesn't hurt to try it out.
-The physics-based controls might not be to your tastes. They're tough to get used to and you need patience and precision to get BUD to move properly in tight spaces or slanted platforms.
-No battle-type action or hidden horrors here. If you're looking for that, this isn't the game for you.
-If you don't care for finding secrets and just finish the primary missions of the game without stopping, it might only be a few hours long depending on your skill.
-Less focus then the last game. This can be good or bad depending on your taste. The game is completely open-world and you can choose where to go yourself, but does feel lacking in direction and progression. Star-plants are way easier to grow then in the last game, and aren't as much of a focus in this one.
-Though you can grow your own plants, the mechanic is rather bare bones and you will probably only use about 4 or 5 plants as actual tools. The rest are basically just decorations that only fit in their specific enviroments and look out of place almost anywhere else.
- Following up on that; If they wanted people to go all-out in exploring and using the fauna of the planet, they should've made ALL plants scanable and growable and make the planting less frustrating. BUD lazily throws seeds in a tough to predict arc which is hard to aim on any surface that isn't perfectly flat. And sometimes the way the plants are facing can be completely random making sure you have to correct and re-correct yourself a lot.
And those are my quick thoughts on the game, if the cons don't sound too bad to you then I suggest you go and buy it right now! I can safely say it's one of the best 10 dollar I've ever spend on one product.

The Creeperworld series is by far one of my favourite time wasters. Like others that I have read, I played the first 2, including the extra missions, all on Kongregate and eagerly awaited this third installment. I'm so glad to see it here on steam as the Dev can finally make a decent buck from his amazing efforts!
What makes Creeperworld games so unique amongst other tower defence games is the energy currency system. Unlike other games that require you to save your resources, research, etc etc until you can build what you want, you have the ability to build straight away and as many of each structure as you like. The danger lies that the energy required to build, is the same energy required to fire weapons. So if you exhaust too much energy into building, you will surely die! This is balanced by the fact that the more "collectors" you spread across the map, the more energy you have, so there is always an incentive to keep building!
Although not as graphically amazing as some TD such as Kingdom rush, Giants and Dwarves, etc or even the older Dune 3D, Starcraft, etc, etc it makes up for it in fantastic TD gameplay. The second installment of the series seemed to push for better graphics, though this actually seemed to tear away slightly from the charm of Creeperworld and I am personally glad to see an this version return a bit truer to its roots... With one great advantage... NULLIFIERS!! You can explode those nasty emitters. Something that you dreamed heavily about in the first game.
There are a bunch of new features in this third game all which so far (I know it's still early for me) are very welcome imrovements. One of the best improvements has to be the TERP that literraly allows you to redraw the level!! No space for that turret... No problem, I'll just terraform some extra land in there :) It's a low price for a game that will guarantee you hours and hours of addicting gaming.

NEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEERD! The Sequel.

Lots of replay value with collectable game cartridges that spell N.E.R.D. in every level, and perfect rankings for finishing a stage without dying
Classic Nerd humor returns from the first game, and is a lot funnier with more joke potential
Soundtrack is as fantastic as the first game's soundtrack, maybe even better in some areas
Graphics are greatly enhanced when comparing to the original's
Cons:
Not as hard as the original game, but still difficult
Can be finished on easy within about 2 hours, not including the different upgrades that can be collected
The final boss is a lot easier then the previous game's final boss
Lack of powerups from the first game, like Glitch Gremlin and Super Mecha Death Christ.
Final Thoughts:
Overall, I'd say this game surpasses the original in just about every way apart from difficulty. Apart from this, I'd definitely recommend it to any fan of the AVGN series, or retro games as a whole.

I can certainly recommend from the depths. I have sunk in a pletora of hours already, and I simply keep being drawn back in. In part due to the fact, that there are after these 850 hours of playing STILL many new things to learn and discover.
Don't let the flashy "early acces" sign put you of! the game is currently very playable and very stable. It also stars far more content than many supposedly finished indie games.
The main gropes the game currently struggles with are low FPS in big battles, but this issue is being adressed as we speak; and some balancing issues that are being steadily resolved by the devs while new content is being added. I've bought this game years ago, and currently it is a very different and far more feral beastie due to the continued dedication of the small dev team.
the community is sometimes branded as being slighty acidic; but as always, if you are respectful in the forums and formulate your responses and questions properly I've found they are a very comely bunch of chaps (and ladies, undoubtedly). Many forum members are quick to offer concise answers to newbie questions, and are more than willing to aid newcomers and veterans both in resolving harder matters. there are many debates about game balance and techniques and the community is quite active.
Of course, if you barge in shouting hell and damnation about your rediculously top heavy overgunned wooden ship capsizing all the time and taking it out on the game in cromagnon english, your reputation will be somewhat tarnished. But that is not unreasonable. Still, many forum members will be happy to point out gently that keels work wonders.
The game has the player building vehicles to beat AI designs on a large RTS map, with maneuvers and resource gathering and many different and distinctly flavoured factions. there is one such campaign dedicated to tank warfare, which is ruddy fun; And a larger campaign dedicated to Naval, air and space and sub combat. Yes; There is a vast amount of possibilities.
And those are only the official campaigns, as the community has free reign to design its own factions and maps at leisure!
The armament, armour, and weapons available are staggering. there are missiles, multiple cannon variants, Particle accelator cannons and lasers and more. Each of these has a great amount of customizability to tweak to your personal needs and satisfaction. A great pleasure of mine is busting enemy AI designs with EMP weaponry, leaving them dead in the water, hulls intact (more scrap for me!).
The game has difficulty customization options, quite a few graphical settings, and as many variable playstyles as you could dream up due to the above. Many layers of complexity can be switched of at player discretion, such as detection systems (think sonar, radar), and extended logistics and fleet upkeep.
there is an active multiplayer scene, with a selection of deathmatch modes in which the players pit their designs against each other. There are also AI wave survival modes, and several others. You can also play the campaigns in coop mode with friends. I am not personally into the multiplayer community, but it's out there.
There are often complaints from new players that the building mechanics and how everything works are not very transparent. there are tutorials, and many sources on the internet; but it remains a fact that it will take some time to get the ropes of this game. As it is, learning has been and still is a very rewarding process for me. Just do not expect to be able to tackle the campaign immediately, and take good care to make a few functioning designs in the sandbox vehicle constructor first! the youtube channel IreLan gaming has info on many systems, even if some of it is slightly out of date. A small amount of knowledge in the subjects of hydrodynamics and mechanics is advisable (archimedes' law, stability in the water, centers of mass and thrust). The game has a fairly accurate modeling ,so it pays to know how these things work in real life, even if at a "for dummies" level.
If you are still in doubt; I would suggest checking out fellow Chaos Lord Lathlands from the depths series on youtube. His latest campaign playthrough reflects the current game state, and he should give you a good idea of what the game is like.
Cheers from Belgium.

When you played with Lego as a kid, you either built for building's sake, or you enjoyed building crazy things only to smash them into each other. Well, this game is for you if you were the latter sort of kid.
This is one of the very few block builders I've seen where the gameplay has a clear purpose: You build terrifying war machines, and use them to fight other terrifying war machines in order to get the resources to build more terrifying war machines. There's a surprising amount of depth in the building mechanic, and the controls themselves are intuitive enough so that joining together a bunch of bricks ad nauseum doesn't become (too) tedious. Battleships, submarines, naval bombers, tanks, it's all in there, and more. One player made a vehicle for the land campaign that was basically an F1 car with lasers.
It's still officially an Early Access game, and it has some of the typical Early Access idiosyncracies, such as certain types of weapon being kind of OP, or the AI being dumb as bricks. But if you know block builders, you know that's par for the course. It's also a game that can't really be played without the community, as they provide a lot of interesting tutorials, designs, tips, and tricks that simply aren't included in the base game. The community is even responsible for the vast majority of designs used by the enemy factions, which means they have all been made with care and attention to detail. Though, after an update, it's not uncommon for designs to be in need of their own, individual update as well.
tl; dr: A block builder where you actually do stuff with your designs

FF is a fun mix of arcade 2d fighters and jrpg games. The game has 13 different battles, each with multiple waves of enemies and 3 different difficulty levels. You can replay previous levels to improve your rating [which is determined by the difficulty you completed it on].
The game's battle style is centred around "slicing" and clicking. If you're familiar with fruit ninja, although I hesistate to draw a comparison, you'll know what that means. Attack effectiveness is determined by you accuracy in these actions. While this might make it suited to being played on a tablet device, it in fact works very well just with a mouse. You may need to tweak you sensitivity in windows though, as there is no way to do this in-game. This doesn't get boring and remains challenging as each enemy has different attack patterns you need to match, and the sensitivity to sucess goes up as you change difficulty level.
The graphics in this game are very nice, colourful and detailed. Much like any jrpg, you will encounter lots of bizzarre enemies, which is always a plus with this type of game. The story of the game is told through speech bubbles an dcutscenes, but the quality of the cutscenes is pretty questionable. It's not a major detrement to the game though. The music in this game, matching the graphics, is top-quality.

Really cool RPG with a touch screen-like type hitting/dodging mechanic (using your mouse, however) that feels at home on a mobile device. Not really a deep story (small twist: you fight alongside the princess you're trying to save), but generally fun over all. Music is very good, often with a good beat that works well for combat. Voice acting is excellent- characters are all fun loving or light hearted, without being too over the top. Art is the real draw here- it reminds me of the style seen in "The Yellow Submarine", with maybe a hint of Alice in Wonderland. The Blue Meany would fit right in there! Worth noting that the hit detection is fairly good, although there's some occasional bugginess in some attacks (one boss monster had an attack where their dodge arrows disappear prematurely at a certain step).
Only downside that stuck out to me is how long the fights can go on for. There's a point where, while you won't really lose to the enemy, they take forever and a day to kill, dragging otherwise fun fights into monotony. There's also a significant difficult ramp up from Casual to Normal mode, but you don't really need to play the higher difficulties unless you're showing off. I will say you probably shouldn't be sleepy when playing this game- your reflexes define just about everything.
I feel there's a lot more good than serious detractions to Fearless Fantasy and I heartily recommend it.

If you loved the classic arcade game Asteroids, you will love Rock 'N Roll. In Rock 'N Roll, you take the role of a space pilot trying to save Earth from a horrible asteroid filled doom. This game adds it's own touch as well as maintaining that classic Asteroids feel. This game offers a fun challenge, as well as giving a rewarding experience.
My playthrough of this game has been very enjoyable.There are power-ups, enemies and a unique endgame system that make this game stand out. This game is very addicting, and offers so much more than the original Asteroids.
One major upside with Rock 'N Roll is how unique it is. Every game you start you will start with a little thing called "Spi-Rolls" It's a special system that gives your ship the ability to a crazy spin, destroying all rocks around you. Another unique system in this game is called "crumbling". With crumbling, there is a chance that every asteroid you destroy will crumble into minature pieces that are incredibly hard to shoot.
Another thing this game has done very well is it's endgame stage. At the end of every game, you will be given a chance to save Earth. You will collect GEOS every level depending on how many asteroids you destry. And once you've finally run out of lives, you will meet a screen containing 50 Earths, but only 1 of them is the real Earth. You will get an X amount of chances to save the real Earth depending on how many Geos you've collected throughout your lifetime.
Another downside with this game is it's difficulty. Yes this game is challenging, and yes it's fun to have a challenging game. But, this game can be downright brutal at times. Past certain levels based on the difficulty you've chosen, the game becomes nearly impossible to beat. Asteroids will be practically impossible to dodge, enemies will spawn at ridiculous rates.
However, with such unique systems, enemies and power-ups, I would
this game. Yes this game can get very difficult, but that's only if you've made it very far into the game.
My score...
VALUE: The amount of content is insane for such a small amount of money. This game will keep you entertained for hours, and will have you addicted. This game can be replayed over and over, making an enjoyable experience and giving you your money's worth. 40 out of 40
FUN: This game is crazy fun, and crazy addicting! However, this game can still be very difficult if your just starting out. But, with the new enemies, power-ups and endgame mechanics, just makes this game very fun overall. 25 out of 30
CONTROLS & BUGS: The controls for Rock 'N Roll can be very frustrating and awkward to use. It definitely takes some time to get familiar with the controls. From my experience, I have not encountered any bugs unless I was looking for them. 10 out of 20
GRAPHICS & SOUND:
The sound for this game is very nice. There is a sound effect for almost everything in this game. 10 out of 10
---------------------------------------
MY SCORE: 85% - Recommended! This game is sure to have you hooked.

The dragon's lifeless body fell right onto the exact spot where I laid the foundation of my town. As I watched the dragon's body clip through the Keep, a sense of relief washed over me. Not relief for my townsfolk, whom I had just saved from a fiery demise. No, not for them, but for me.
With the slaying of that dragon notched on my archers' scoreboards, I had done everything there was to do in Kingdoms and Castles....and I had just hit the six hour mark.
Technically, I hadn't done everything...there were some Steam achievements leftover for hitting certain population milestones, which would take a lot more downtime than I was willing to pump into Kingdoms and Castles. So, more accurately, I had done everything there was that was worth doing, in the game.
Kingdoms and Castles started out as straightforward, town-building, strategy game. With around two-dozen buildings to construct, everything had a clear purpose and their functions alongside the other buildings made sense. There were no obscure rules to learn, or elaborate game mechanics to keep track of. Wood, stone, food,  and population were the only major things that needed monitoring; adequate water coverage (either from coastlines or wells), citizen happiness level (boosted by the presence of churches or taverns), and smart guard tower placement (to defend against invaders) were the only other facets of the game that necessitated the most attention.
There are a handful of other resource systems that need monitoring, but those that I mentioned represent the core of the game. As far as strategy city-building games go, they don't come much simpler and easy-to-play than Kingdoms and Castles.
The game's graphic style mirrors that simplicity. Featuring peg-like peasants, the game's visual appeal comes from watching the dozens or hundreds of peasants scurrying around doing their duties. Once open housing is available, peasants will randomly "move in" to your town and they will automatically pick up on any available task that needs doing. It was fun to zoom out and watch the town in action. Watching the peasants all hopping around doing their own jobs reminded me a lot of watching tiny fish in a fish tank. For awhile anyway, it was quite a relaxing time.
Unfortunately, as pleasant as it was to watch...I could only watch so much before I found myself rapping my fingers on my keyboard, awaiting progressing. Once I had read all of the little tooltips for every building there was to build, and had a basic understanding of what a good city layout in Kingdoms and Castles should look like, I had very little else to do as I waited for more citizens to move in, or for more resources to be collected.
Occasionally a viking raid would arrive, and while they increase in strength over time, they're easy enough to repel that a few archer towers will do you just fine for the first hour of gameplay. They show up, slowly make their way into your town, steal resources and peasants, and make their way back to their boat. If you kill all the vikings you get to keep your resources, if not, you lose all they managed to snag on their way out.
Dragons would also show up, but their presence was a complete joke. The dragons would fly in at random times and mostly just float above my city. Perhaps the dragons in these lands had some sort of amnesia, because they acted more like butterflies than dragons. Only occasionally did they every drop a fire-blast or two down onto my town. Sometimes they never even flew near my town to begin with.
But I finally encountered a dragon that flew right through the heart of my city. After being pelted by arrows for a good half-minute, it was over. The dragon's body vanished as it fell into my Keep, I breathed a partially-annoyed sigh of relief, and my peasants scurried on, unaware that their lives were about to end forever.
Kingdoms and Castles wasn't a bad game in that it was broken, and it was even fun for a short time, but after I killed that dragon and I unlocked the achievement, I resigned as Lord of [Tom Already Forgot What He Named His Town] forever. I just can't recommend Kingdoms and Castles; the game was not fun enough for long enough, and gave me absolutely no reason to play it all over again.
[[Not recommended]] There just wasn't enough variety of things to do to keep my attention past an hour or two. Feels very much like a stable, early-access release, rather than a full retail game. I will monitor Kingdoms and Castles for major developments and update this review as necessary.

Going into this game, I didn't know what to expect. I finished it in about 4 hours. That's with leaving the game running while taking short breaks every once in a while.
The beginning of the game starts off very enticing and intriguing. You get to talk to all the characters and learn little unique aspects about them. However about halfway through, the plot seemed to take a turn I wasn't expecting. The missions began losing their sense of seriousness to me. This happened to the characters as well, particularly Turn. I understand his character goes through an internal conflict, but his conflict seemed pretty humorous to me.
I'm going to break this section up into two sections. There was the length of the game, sense of interaction in the levels and then the actual puzzles themselves.
Length - I finished this game in about four hours. I thought the plot was rushed; I really wanted time to relax and fall in love with the atmosphere of the game by being able to interact with more objects but it didn't have that. It was more : Objective, objective, and objective. By chapter six, the final chapter, I stopped for a moment and said, "How'd I get here? Wasn't I just applying for this job like 2 and a half hours ago?"
However, in those four hours, I felt very attached to the, sometimes seemingly, goofy characters. I really want to know what's next for all of them. If a game can manage that, I feel it has done it's job.
Interaction - For the most part, you only get access to the parts of the levels that pretain to the puzzles. I feel like if there were more objects to interact with, reguardless if they pretained to the player's current objective, to make the world feel more real than I would have been more immersed.
Puzzles - The puzzles were amazing. Cudos to the development team for the puzzles. I legitimately was stuck for a while on a lot of them in the later chapters. I really wish there were more honestly because those were my favorite part of the game.
I really loved the graphics. I truly felt the Indie game vibe and thought it was very unique. The water was amazing looking!
If I could reach out to the devs, I would say to continue the amazing work they're doing. I was surprised it was a ten person team during the credits. I would ask for a longer game. I don't think this game is worth the price it is for the length of gameplay - I'm sorry :/. I think there is an amazing game here, but the pacing was too fast. At the end, I felt slightly confused. It ended on what I thought was a good midway climax to the story's plot; there could have been six more chapters.
Overall, The Low Road is a great game for what it is. I became invested in the characters and the world created. I feel like if you are to buy this game, try to do so during a sale (30%-50% off) due to it's short runtime. The puzzles were fantastic. I really hope there is a sequel to expand upon this game.
Really can't wait to see what this company puts out next!

So I really, really wanted to like this game because the graphics look amazing and the plot sounded very interesting for a point/click adventure game; however, a lot of small issues ultimately led to an underwhelming experience that lost my interest in the game within about 45min. It says I logged about twice that time, but that's only because I quit at one point without realizing there was no autosave so I ended up starting over (blaming myself for that assumption).
Pros:
1) Interesting plot (from what I experienced in terms of the overall direction)
2) Graphics look fantastic
3) Sound is pretty good and voice acted characters is always a plus
4) Despite my complaints below, I can tell a lot of time and effort went into creating this game since certain aspects were polished very well
Cons:
1) Character mouth/audio syncing: The character's mouths don't sync up with the audio which irks me (intentionally it seems). Typically after the character stops talking, his/her mouth is still moving for a second or two. However, this by itself wouldn't bother me if it was my only complaint.
2) Audio issue with some dialog: With one particular character, it sounded like the audio recording was done over a phone. It seemed off compared to the rest of the characters that I'd encountered so far.
3) No in-game settings/options: There's no menu option for any kind of settings like audio or key remapping. Can't recall the last time I saw a game without even a basic option menu.
4) Main character can't move during dialog: While someone is talking, whether it's your character talking to herself/you as she examines items or talking to another character, you aren't able to walk around at all. I can understand it for talking to characters, but it's annoying that I'm frozen while inspecting a random item.
5) Can't re-examine items in inventory: This one really annoyed me since I can't remember the last time I played a point/click game that didn't let you do this. I picked up a flyer with lots of info on it, but I accidentally clicked off so it went into my inventory before I could read it in full. I tried to right-click on the item from my inventory to re-read it, but the game wouldn't present me with the blown-up flyer again nor did my character even narrate what the item is. The only hint is a tooltip that appears when hovering the item which describes it in about two words (in a font that makes you squint). Luckily in this case the contents of the flyer turned out to not be too important in terms of how it needed to be used, but I had a feeling that this issue could easily get me stuck in the game later on (at least without relying on save points to re-examine items) which made me hesitant to continue playing.
6) Can't skip dialog using mouse: The only way to skip dialog, which I found by trial and error, is hitting spacebar. And of course since there's no option menu, this can't be re-assigned at all. Space bar for skipping is fairly common, but personally I like being able to play point/click games using only mouse when possible. Considering your character can't even move during dialog, allowing a mouse click to skip seems reasonable.
7) Examining documents should should be layered over the dialog text options: The first scene in the game has you making a phone call with documents for reference to help manipulate the caller into telling you what you need to hear. When examining a document up close (not the normal inventory items which can't be re-examined as mentioned above), the document is layered behind the dialog options even though you can't select dialog while examining the document. It was slightly annoying trying to read them since I had to keep re-adjusting each document to fit within the available real estate.
8) Poor feedback when you fail at something: When making that first phone call in the game, there's three pieces of info that you need to extract from the caller - but aside from being told by another character prior to making the call, you never see those objectives again so it was confusing as to which I did wrong/why. Another short scene has you pick-pocketing someone which I was positive that I did right, but it said I failed without any indication of why... felt like it was an impossible task but presented otherwise.
9) Unmemorable characters: I didn't really like any of the characters in the game that I encountered in my short time playing. Most of them I actually found a bit annoying, including my character who I think I liked the least. I didn't care for her voice acting or even her design (the weird clown make-up on her face, the way she awkwardly walks, and her pants that swallow half her body). In general, even though I'm not exactly sure why, but I found myself not caring about anything that the characters had to say.
10) Strong start with high expections but quickly dulled: After the first task/puzzle in the game where you had to make that phone call and apply some logic to manipulate the caller, I was really excited to play since it felt like a different experience than most point/click games generally offer. It set the first impression for what kinds of things I'd be doing/solving, but then five minutes later I'm simplistically talking to some old coworker coming up with childish rhymes and haikus so he'll help me with something (despite him previously telling me that he'd never risk his job for someone he just met, but apparently he can be convinced for a rhyme).
11. Autosave would be nice

For an in-depth review, tune into the video below:
Otherwise, here’s a summarized write up.
At random times, the game will disable interactions with all items in a given area and, it being a point and click, this causes severe issues. Sometimes you’re able to reset the bug by moving between locations but it’s equally possible that you’ll have to restart the game. Considering how The Low Road doesn’t autosave at all, you could potentially lose hours of playtime because of this issue.
The low road has you playing as Noomi Kovacs, a college graduate on her first day at the local spy agency. The game has 6 chapters and while the introduction has you trying weasel your way into some field work, the rest of the plot centers around your main mission and its associated repercussions.
Most characters here are have their odd quirk in the game’s attempt to be more comedic with the spy setting though only your main cast, that being Noomi and her boss Turner (Turn), has good writing. The rest frequently suffer from things like repeatedly using the same sentences back to back, overexplanation of simple concepts and dialogue that is out of their respective characters.
This usually happens when the game tries too hard to be funny and it happens quite frequently. But on the positives, TLR actually has some genuinely humorous moments in the natural and witty interactions between Noomi and Turn. The story also spends proper time to flush out Turn’s character, giving him more depth and a decent amount of payoff as he starts to respect Noomi as more of a colleague than an assistant.
The overarching story is also easy to follow but can be a little absurd at times. TLR’s attempt to be yet another title that doesn’t take itself seriously only works when it doesn’t run into writing issues and given how frequently that happens, it only gives a mildly entertaining and humorous experience.
The core gameplay loop can be broken down into the title’s 2 types of puzzles. The first plays like classic point and clicks where you’re gathering items to be used on objects so that you can get past a certain obstacle. Separating the items from the rest of the environment is easy since your cursor changes its shape when you hover over items you can collect.
While the game does allow you to hold more than one thing at a time, you CANNOT combine these resources in your inventory, so there isn’t any experimentation on that front. These puzzles are also ultimately pretty easy, since there are so few items to collect in each of them. Despite not having answers given explicitly, the significant lack of trial and error means you’ll likely have a simple time.
The second type of puzzles are called first person puzzle segments which are the more frequent and varied bunch of challenges. These include things like looking up information to determine the best conversation option to deceive characters, figuring out the correct sequence of disabling alarms, and even something as dead simple as hovering your mouse over obvious locations on a metal gate to open it.
Straight up, these aren’t difficult puzzles but I especially dislike the last example given since it’s a glorified scripted event that requires on skill so it’s good to see them only appear once or twice. Overall, the first type of puzzles are pretty bog standard while the second type add in a nice touch of diversity, though it’s unfortunate that both lack any real challenge.
1) Decent visuals – nice water color aesthetic
2) Witty interactions between Noomi and Turn
3) Good variety in puzzles
1) Game tries too hard to be funny at times and suffers for it in writing quality
2) Voice acting quality is all over the place
– Noomi and Turn are the best and most consistent in terms of delivery and overall quality but most of the rest of the supporting cast suffer on both accounts. Their performance is usually stilted and at worst, some of them even show a huge disparity in audio quality (likely due to the different mics used). It’s really jarring to hear Noomi’s clear voice followed by a character’s tinny one.
3) Puzzles lack any real challenge
The Low Road is an enjoyable game with plenty of complications. The writing is questionable at times, the gameplay isn’t very challenging and the audio can really take you out of the experience. I did like the product but having to go through numerous issues, including technical ones, the game never felt like it hit the desired level of quality. As such, I’m recommending you wait for a patch and a sale on this one. Only get it once it’s ironed out the bugs and even then, 15 dollars sounds like a more appropriate price.

As a fan of both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: The Longest Journey,  I was extremely intrigued to see how this story was going to be wrapped up.
I was not disappointed.
Does this game have its faults? Sure! There are some plot points that I felt still went unanswered, some characters who said, "I'll see you again at the end of your journey" (or something to that effect) yet never showed up again, (though I think this may have been referring to the actual "end" of someone's journey i.e. death), but this was still the game I had been waiting for for so many years.
Let's talk about some of the new things, shall we?
This game introduces the choice or "balance" system. Other games have had choices but none that really impacted the plot aside from some extra dialogue or, in the case of The Longest Journey, an extra cutscene or two. I'm happy to say that choices in this game DO have consequences. Characters can die, relationships can be affected, and new scenes unlocked depending on your choices. This, in my humble opinion, added an extra level of depth and tension that fully fit the story driven theme this series has thrived on.
3 playable characters! So, yes this isn't exactly a new thing as Dreamfall also had 3, but hey, we have one new playable character so therefore I'm adding this here.
Now let's get onto the juicy stuff. Did I enjoy this game and did it continue the story from the previous two games in a manner that was satisfactory?
In my opinion, yes. The story in this game, while convoluted at times, was heartfelt, well written, and deeply enjoyable. Characters are well voice acted and likeable and I genuinely cared about my allies and keeping them safe. The game also seemingly did the impossible by wrapping up 99% of the questions left unanswered at the end of Dreamfall: The Longest Journey and (no spoilers) had a bit at the end that I admit, made me almost cry at the nostalgia.
Kian and Zoe are both well rounded, well written, and enjoyable protagonists who both had their own journeys to traverse throughout the course of the game. It was so interesting to see them evolve and grow as characters, and I gained an appreciation for both of them by the time the credits were rolling.
As for Saga... well I can't say too much without spoiling the plot but she was a welcome addition and I have to say, I'd love to see a spinoff game focusing more on her journey in the near future!
Other things of note:
SOUNDTRACK. Absolutely gorgeous and fitting, perfectly suited for making those emotional moments just a little bit more special.
VISUALS: Yes, the graphics aren't necessarily the most advanced, but the game is still beautiful and colorful and I found myself anxious to traverse different locations just to interact with NPC's and take in some of the sights.
Some tips for players: INTERACT WITH EVERYTHING!
Protagonists will comment on various objects, sights, etc. in the world. Make sure to click everything to hear extra dialogue and fill in some of the gaps in the story. Players are rewarded with such activities by extra dialogues, some funny moments, and achievements.
With that said, that's all I got folks! A wonderful game with its flaws, but those flaws are ultimately outweighed by a wonderful story with great characters, varied settings, and the conclusion all The Longest Journey fans have been waiting for.

Slamming down a review like Pogs right now.. And I've only (shamefully) played less than 3 hours, BUT I'M QUALIFIED. This game is great :P I wanted my review to be my original thought about the game from looking at the screenshots, which was:
"What are tho.. Ah, so.. The lines mo.. uh.. Wait, then those bubb, er.. And they.. ? What is tha.." :P
In short, this game is about the primal fear of water ruining your cool stuff. Imagine your kitchen. Its awesome. Except now you've decided to catalog your prize comic book collection, THE WHOLE THING. Its going to take a while. The table is
piled so full that you've had to start making piles on the floor here and there. Suddenly, your child drops a full glass jug of apparently antique milk and it shatters!! *suspenseful music* Now, the antique milk hasn't splashed on your comic
books.. YET!
But its spreading!! And, lucky you, besides collecting comic books you also design small functional mortars and cannons that fire small liquid-absorbing sponges, all supplied by intricate wiring relays that transport power from a central battery. For the sake of cohesion we'll say you developed the sponge cannons because of your mortifing phobia of dish cloths, also, so you can't just mop the liquid up.. *cough* If you're quick enough, you can set up an intricate web of relays linked to your tiny armada of sponge-launching war-machines aaaall along the kitchen floor in a milk-encircling radius and potentially combat the comic-ruining liquid menace before your precious copy of Jurrasic Park #1 is ruined.
That's what the game is about. Yep.
In all seriousness I think its pushing it to call this game a tower defense game.. I tend to reserve that title for games with MUCH less features and elements involved than this, particularly concerning tightly placed pathways. As stated elsewhere, if you have any doubts about purchasing, the first two games are on Kongregate free to play, and there is also a demo of this game on the devs website. But you don't need a demo. Did you need a demo when you decided air was good to breathe? Did you!? ;)
Also I wanted to mention that til this game showed up on Steam I had no idea it existed, so there is that :> I'm fresh as a daisy to this and can already smell the deep possibilities here and have barely touched the main campaign just yet, but I still hope the dev isn't fully done adding to the main game, especially since its life on Steam has just begun.. Now if I can just muster a little focus and make time for myself to play..

This is a surprisingly compelling little game.
The gist is that you are fighting back against goo of the sort you'd expect to find in a dystopian science fiction novel. To do so, you maintain an array of collectors interconnected by an energy grid that conveys construction and ammunition resources throughout its network. You plunk down turrets, which can later be moved, that feed off the grid. The goo itself has a few tricks that complicate matters, but I'll leave that to you to discover.
What sounds simple ends up making for a fairly compelling asynchronous RTS. Wrapped in an intriguing story, and garnished with pleasing graphics, it ends up being a fun ride.

I loved the story and the worldbuilding - and these should be the main points why anyone would want to play this game. If you're looking for high-octane gameplay, then go look somewhere else.
That being said, I found the political and xenophobia innuendos rather unnecessary and forced. I get that devs really wanted to focus player attention on these IRL issues, but found these the most boring parts of the story. The first book is rather off-putting in that regard - main protagonist working for an election camping? Come on - I couldn't care less! - I came for the story that spans multiverses not some stupid election camping. Fortunately, the said story was there as well.
The choice system was nice. Though, at later points it started to get a bit annoying and forced - you'd be constantly reminded of the choices you made - like the game cannot just move on - no, it has to remind you that there is this choice system and that your choices really, really matter. Some characters seem to hold a grudge, because of something you did or didn't do 4 chapters ago. But hey that made some other choices easier. For example - this Likho guy simply couldn't shut up about the fact that I did not kill some enemy soldier, but instead chose to let him go. So then, at a later point, when the same Likho guy asked me to take him with me on some important mission, I didn't have to think long to refuse his company.
8/10
Pros:
+ Story
+ Worldbuilding
+ Music
+ Visuals
+ Choice system is interesting
Cons:
- Election and xenophobia elements of the story feel forced and unnecessary
- Choice system is rather annoying at times

For all those who hesitate to buy this game, I would like you to read my review carefully. If you play this game, when you'll finish it, the only desire you'll have is a sequel. The story, the characters, the universe... Everything is excellent.
Since The Longest Journey, this game has created an entire universe with lots of elements you'll love to discover. Two worlds: Stark, our world in the future, the world of science, and Arcadia, a medieval world, the world of magic. I'd like to tell you about the story, but it's going to take way too long, and it's going to spoil you. Just know that the story is quite complex, because there are a lot of elements to remember, but it's one of the reasons that makes the story strong, and the characters... Oh man, you'll become attached to the characters... The characters are all charismatic and they all have their own personalities, believe me you'll never forget them, there are countless of cult replicas, and the humor of the game will make you laugh a lot, it's at good dose and there are never too much. That game give you feelings! Happiness, laughter, anger, sadness... it's just incredible. On the graphics side, after playing Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, I didn't expect the game to be so pretty. I mean, for an episodic game, it's really impressive. I even think it's themost beautiful episodig game I've ever played, there are details everywhere and the light effects are amazing. And finally, on the gameplay side, it's certainly simple and basic, but why ask for a complicated gameplay when what matters most in this game is the story. In this game you can interact with almost anything, objects or characters, and it's really cool. Then, important thing: The choices. That's another thing I really appreciated, the choices you can make have consequences. I mean, real consequences. If you finally want a game with choices that have real consequences, Dreamfall is for you. I don't usually talk about soundtracks but even on this point, this game did a good job! The only thing I can advise you before playing this game is to play The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: The Longest Journey since these are the previous Dreamfall Chapters games and they are important enough to understand the history and universe of the game. Otherwise, go ahead. This game is a real piece of art, a real jewel. And I really mean it. I've played so many games, seen so many different stories, universes and characters, and I assure you that this game is a rare pearl that stands out from the other games, this game is unique, and please, really, believe me, you won't regret your purchase.
If you decide to buy it, please add me. I'd love to talk about this game with you.
