AVGN II: ASSimilation is an unforgiving platformer with colourful swearing.
Although AVGN fans are the ones that will get the most out of this game's humour, the inside jokes from the show are funny enough that anyone can get a laugh out of it.
The gameplay feels almost identical to the first game, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. The movement feels very responsive, and you never feel like the game cheated you out of a life. If you die, it's your fault.
The game brings back a lot of mechanics, but does a good job at adding new features and giving you new weapons to keep things fresh.
Although the game might follow a few typical game tropes, it is fully aware, and makes fun of it to keep it from being annoying. For example, the slightly hand-holding tutorial has the nerd swearing and annoyed at the fact that it just keeps explaining stuff.
A lot of the jokes are slightly more subtle callbacks to AVGN episodes. Sometimes it can be simpler things like using an "F-bomb" as a weapon, which literally just is a bomb with the letter "F" on it.
You select the level you want to play using an map screen. You can freely choose which level to try next, and can come back to a level later on if you rage quit it. Each chapter is meant to parody a game or is themed towards some sort of joke from the show. They all look colourful and diverse, so you don't get tired of the levels you're playing.
Overall, I think the game is a lot of fun. If you enjoyed the first game, this is just more of the same, but with a few new and cool features. If you haven't played the first game but are into platformers or difficult games from older consoles like the NES, then you will also enjoy this. It's got potty humor, and is quite immature, but it's just silly fun.
Again, fans of the Angry Video Game Nerd are the ones who will enjoy the jokes the most, but they can cater to anyone with a similar sense of humour.

A worthy sequel to Grow Home.
Grow Up takes the themes and mechanics of Grow Up and applies them to a whole free-roaming planet instead of just one tiny island in an endless sea.
All the things that made Grow Home great are here again in Grow Up, but with even greater abundance.
More crystals and plants to collect, more starplants to grow, and improved aerial traveral mechanics to make getting around up in the air that much more fun.
Along with the improved flying mechanics, you get checkpoint race challenges that allow you to test and show off your flying skills.
I completed (100% in-game completion, but not all achievements) Grow Home in 6 hours or less.
Grow Up kept me playing for 11 hours to get 100% completion including all the achievements. (I have to admit that I did use a guide to find the letter P block to get the final achievement, but everything else was all my own effort.)
Over all I'd say again it's a very worthy sequel. Twice as long and twice as fun.
Well worth the full retail price, and a must buy if it's on special.

TL;DR: You liked the first one? Good. Here's a second one with more stuff over a much more vast world.
Yesterday, after playing the first game of the "Grow" series (Grow Home), I decided to pick up "Grow Up" from the Steam Store. I was very impressed with Grow Home, and how it was a simple masterpiece of a casual game. Grow Up, however, failed to capture the same wonderful feelings.
I was able to complete this game within a few hours. Seeing how this game was about 10-20 times the size of the first game, you'd figure that this would be more of an epic adventure, right? Well, I'm sorry to disappoint you when I say that the game pretty much hands you all the tools you need to beat the game within the first hour. All you have to do to get to the end is
.
In this episode you've got a satellite-type friend that helps you navigate the planet. While I loved the additional feature to zoom all of the way out, the controls were a bit too jumpy, while the labeling system that identified discovered and undiscovered items/territories, was inefficient and sometimes outright ineffective.
You've also been given the ability to absorb plant identification and store its "seed" in your backpack. It's an interesting mechanic to say the least. You can store "bouncy" plants, or plants that shoot you out of a fountain, just like in Grow Home. You have a portable botanical lab in your backpack. It's a great idea. However, the types of plants were either boring and/or didn't work most of the time. This, combined with B.O.B.'s inconsistent movement, made for some frustrating moments trying to jump atop a plant's leaf, only to be thrown off the side of a platform to my death. Put simply: Once I found a plat that I knew was consistent, I stopped caring about gathering other more complex plant life. Also, I had a jetpack and glider early in the game. Why would I care about getting anything else at this point?
The map design felt unintuitive. While I liked the simple design, I felt lost a lot of the time, constantly going in and out of the "satellite" mode in order to find a beacon I placed on the planet.
Rating
"Game/game". Eh, I felt just a bit underwhelmed with this one. It was still a nice game. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoyed it (which is why I'm recommending it). But after playing Grow Home, I felt that Grow Up was more like an expansion pack once I realized that this game was more-or-less a "let's take the first game and make it bigger and add a few things" type of deal. And there's nothing inherently wrong with this type of a sequel. People want more "Grow"? I'm fine with selling more of a great product. However, this felt mostly just "good" and not "great".
And that's O.K. too.

While the price is debatable and could safely be brought to $15 or perhaps even $10, Nightdive's Re-Release of the N64 Juggernaut classic still feels like it could be an excellent value.
Its a cult classic brought back with 60+ FPS support, 120+ FOV, high view distance, 4K support, bug fixes, enhanced level design, tons of optional eyecandy, and  proper WASD Mouse control that makes Turok feel like Quake's cousin.
Did I forget the game is easily moddable and they are planning on mod support? The developers have excellent communication on the forums and the game even just had a patch today to fix a few issues. Beyond reliving a forgotten legend in a land before time I also feel good knowing this game is being taken care of by people with a geniune love for classics such as this. Even if the price feels a bit steep, I am going to be having a lot of fun modding the game and making new levels and enjoying the new ones made by other people.
A classic piece of gaming history, one of the most influential console shooters that had its release date become known as "Turok Tuesday". Featuring over a dozen of high tech awesome weaponry across 8 huge and varied levels battling foes ranging from disposable mercenaries to killer cyborgs it can easily be said that Turok has lost none of its attitude in the decades gone by.

Kingdoms and Castles is a very casual society builder with enemy attacks thrown in. I spent about 30 hours on my first Kingdom crafting it to perfection. By that I mean solving starvation, resource build-up, food distribution, defenses, and so forth.
Enemies - Enemies will attack in the form of a small dragon, a large dragon, and vikings. Dragons are fairly easy to handle if you have an evenly placed defense throughout your kingdom. As long as you have wells covering your buildings, dragons won't be much of a problem. Vikings are a different story. As your kingdom grows, Viking attacks will grow in size. The only way to stop Vikings from attacking is to build castle walls around the entire island which takes quite a bit of resources and manpower. A few times the Vikings destroyed a lot of my Kingdom, but once you get your defenses and manpower issues straightened out, you should be fine.
Overall, it is a very satisfying game when all of your citizens are fed and you have a Kingdom of over 1000+ population with 100 overall happiness.
I thoroughly enjoyed the first 30 hours of gameplay on my Kingdom and will return to this game once more updates roll out. I am looking forward to the fishing update!
TL;DR: For $10 you can get about 20-40 hours from start to finish with your first kingdom. It is definitely worth the price!

Fearless Fantasy is a uniquely designed Turn-based RPG game. The player starts with the protagonist saving a damsel in distress and from that point on, their adventure begins. Though the voice-acting and cinematics aren't that good, the game art is actually great but the main selling point of the game is its battle system. Unlike the traditional turn-based RPGs where you just click attack and then your character performs it, Fearless Fantasy brings the excitement in every turn because for each attack command you execute, you have to successfully complete a certain minigame (like you have to click some circles at the right time or follow an arrow path at the right time) in order for your attack to successfully land on your enemies. The same also applies for dodging enemy attacks. The game design is also more like that of the minigame Cut the Rope where each stage is rated by stars but in Fearless Fantasy, the stars corresponds to the game difficulty on each stage.
I recommend this game to those out there who wants to try a different kind of Turn-based RPG game. The game's rate of replayability would rely more on how you can adapt to the game's battle system. Get it when it goes on sale. The game has a lot of potential but I hope the devs would reconsider a sequel to it.

From what I've played which is, admittedly, fairly limited (I was sent a press preview demo, which only features the first 2 chapters of the game) I am both pleasantly intrigued and a little disappointed. A great looking point and click adventure with some neat little puzzles and some pretty decent writing & performances is let down in a big way by some definite quality of life issues.
For a PC title there are no options or settings available except for the standard Unity graphics launcher outside of the game and a choice of one of two languages on the main menu (English or French). There are no graphics options within the game or keyboard prompts. And there are definitely no audio settings, which leads me on to my next point.
Though the voice performances for the most part are pretty good some of the audio editing and sound design is a little questionable. One of the first puzzles you face features a phone conversation in which you must extract information, unfortunately the person on the other end of the line is a lot quieter than everyone else you speak to. And one of the other agents in the office, it sounds like their entire audio has been recorded through a tin can. This may sound like I'm nit-picking but when a significant portion of the game is based on having conversations with people this can be a little distracting.
Also from a user interface point of view, I really like the look and style the developers have gone for unfortunately the difference between the standard cursor and the "oh look I can click on this" mouse pointer is very subtle. In other words you may well walk past an interactable object several times without ever spotting it.
Also I can't speak to length of the full game but I can say the first couple of chapters will only take you an hour or so to complete, and feature 6 of the "15+ first person puzzle sequences" mentioned in the game’s description. This definitely feels like a reasonably short game that could well be completed in a single sitting. (Although, as I said, this is just based on press preview version I was sent.)
From what I've played it's not a bad game and is certainly worth checking out if you are an adventure game fan. But it's definitely not for everyone, some of the writing is a little annoying (namely the poetry) and it is definitely let down by a few of its limitations and technical issues. As such I'm giving it a hesitant thumbs up as Steam doesn’t allow for “completely average” scores and it’s style & presentation probably outweighs its flaws as a game. But I would say this is one to maybe wait and pick up during a sale.

Battlepillars was originally a phone game, and it certainly shows. But does that mean that this isn't any fun? Certainly not.
Here's a Quick Look video of what you should expect when heading into this. Take a look if you're interested or just read my summary of the game below. Just a warning though, it has birds carpet bombing with their crap.
I'll start by saying the basic premiss of this game is a tug-of-war between two sides, something you've probably seen before in other games. But does this do anything different? No, not really. However, it's still pretty fun to play.
You construct your units with a regenerating resource that can be upgraded to regen faster for the same resource, the cost gaining in price every time. The units  themselves are mashed together by a decent number of parts you can select before going into the match, and each one does different things, such as make your guy charge faster, shoot enemies at a distance, knock the enemy backwards, set up mines, poison an enemy, heal the soldier over time, and so on. The charm to it is constructing the unit you want to make and seeing it charge into battle and (hopefully) crush your foes. You just have to keep in mind that even though you're creating a stronger unit, it costs more to make it while the enemy might be swarming in on you.
The other fun part to this game is customizing your soldiers with skins and upgrades, and you can choose which upgrades/skins you want without having to go through others first, which is always appreciated. I also like how open ended this game is about beating certain levels/challenges. There isn't always a correct way to go about something to achieve victory. You can either spam out fodder to overwhelm your enemy, have a mix of certain parts that benefit off each other, or have titans with every expensive part you can throw on it that stomp mostly anything in their path. There's just a good number of things you can do.
But lets talk about some of the negatives now. Because this is a phone port, there isn't much interaction with you and what's happening on the field. You're kind of farting around and waiting to send out your next unit. While it is fun to to watch your units do the work, I wish there was more you could do than just summon an animal friend.
I'm also not a fan of buying straight upgrades for parts you already own. That doesn't encourage swapping parts from ones that you made better than others. I much rather play with a different weapon to give my units than use the same ones for every mission simply because the game is that much easier with them. The fact that the game limits how many parts you can take into battle also irks me. There could've been a lot more depth to the game if you could always choose a counter unit to what your enemy was sending at you instead of being stuck with what you chose and hoping it works out.
But to sum this game up, even with the lack of interactivity, this is still a solid title for under 3 bucks currently, and possibly still worth it for 5 if you enjoy a decent time waster. The multiplayer options also open this game up for more fun if the campaign and endless modes aren't your thing.

How personally crushing must it be to be a person in Anno 2205? With your hopes and dreams either to live in a sterile, homogenous, prefabricated building based on your social class, OR to live and work in some of the most hostile places imaginable-- in the arctic regions or on the otherwise dead, lifeless moon?
I can imagine a teenager, tired of the daily humdrum, seeking to live on a colony on the moon. Only to arrive and realize that every action is dictated by pages and pages of safety rules and procedures the government-company imposes. Not one loss of life is acceptable, every action for your safety. No local decision making, just feed up raw numbers to "The Player." If you have a better idea to increase local output or lower labor costs just keep it to yourself, you're just here to work, leave it to the experts in charge.
With this moon laborer having arisen to the ubermensch (overman), what is the point anyway to seek war and conflict? Rarely spoken about, it seems like everyone knows the weekly wars in the "conflict zones" back on earth are scripted and fake. The super-villain of course vaguely evil with a thin revenge backstory (no doubt to to push the safety at all costs bent), and the winning team a little too goody-goody, complete with the gruff but wears heart on sleeve mechanic John Rafferty in a starring role as commentator.
A recent update to "the program" has seen war come to the nearby shores. But can anyone believe their eyes anymore? Almost everyone has neuro implants (fake eyes), and of course like most big pharma inventions they don't last particularly long as the body breaks them down. But who would want to go back to the crappy 60x60 pixel central vision that nature has given us? All that mental energy spent constantly darting your eyes around in a futile attempt to see the big picture, those savages.
So work for the sake of work, hopefully feel some emotion, and increase "the numbers". Hope for the day one receives a promotion into a higher class, and just be happy to enable the highest investor class on earth to have kinky zero-G sex with androids in a holodeck projection powered by quantum computers.

A top down dungeon crawler which seems like it will someday feature rpg mechanics (but as of right now you are apparently limited to visual customization only).  The main draw is the physics-based combat, which turns out to actually be enough to carry the game in its current form.
It definitely takes some dedicated practice in the arena mode to even begin to understand how it works, and there is a definite knack to it, which may frustrate some.   My first couple tries at the game itself were near instant death, as without an understanding of the combat you will die to the very first enemy you see.  In fact, the first time I was able to kill an enemy at all I felt an enormous sense of accomplishment.  Every engagement is unique and interesting, and you'll be trying to carefully analyze enemy weaknesses, landing hits in exactly the right place at exactly the right time.  I particularly enjoy that the physics engine allows friendly fire, meaning that several times I've been able to funnel clumsy zombies in tight spaces where they actually deal more damage to each other with their wild swings than they do to me.
These moments make up for the fact that the game seems pretty light on content--to the point that it almost seems more like an excuse to feature the combat system.  It also requires that you like your games with a little frustration and required practice.
A Tip:  Once you've got the hang of swinging your weapon, try swinging with carefully timed couches.  By crouching at the right part of a swing you can get a diagonal up or down swing, depending on whether you're starting forehand or backhand.  This is particularly helpful against well-armored enemies who seem to be deflecting every attack, as a downward forehand swing can easily chop at their exposed legs even when they are in a full defensive stance.

I'd like to be kind to this game, it has fantastic art and atmoshere, but an awful combat system.
I'm really not sure what I'm supposed to be doing -- my character's obviously numb arms and drunken feet flail about even when I'm carefully moving the mouse. I thought I was supposed to guide the tip of the sword or something, but the character drunkenly swings at his foe when simply clicking the mouse. The game has no tutorial level, or anything of that sort, so good luck figuring out key commands, no end goal, and no back story (though I suppose that's good for RP purposes).
Now for the good part. This game really embodies that clauster-phobic, "what's behind the door", "I can't run fast enough" feel that I love about dungeon crawlers. : No April, crappy characters, crappy everyone’s motivation, shortly: bad story. Nice graphics and music though.
The first game was so marvelous that I can’t really describe what I felt after playing it. Warmth in my chest, comfort in my head, joy in my smile. Cozy feeling of strong confidence in the future of this story, feeling of upcoming adventure, of big things that are yet to be done by April.
The second game was so tasteless… I don’t even remember it much except for one and main event, the event that game was created for (April’s death). I don’t think it deserves a review, it’s just a colorless near-RPG with stupid inappropriate songs and absolute zero of humor. You changed April, you literally ruined her life, but well, I could deal with it. Character development and stuff, makes it even deeper and more exciting to explore the story. I hoped that April would somehow be resurrected in the next games. But there was one moment that rang a bell of this series death: a pair of new protagonists. I’ll comment on it later.
As for this game… It’s beautiful. And empty. Just like most of art nowadays. Pretty wrapper and nauseous candy.
Yes, it is gorgeous. The music is freaking magical, the scenes in the first chapter were head-spinning, they made me hold my breath and look at the screen with eyes wide open. It was touching. But nothing more.
The gameplay was okay. It would have been better if it was a point-and-click, though, because a lot of meaningless 3-seconds actions by a player that could be easily added to a cut-scene were weird. But okay. I also didn’t care about an episodic structure.
And now about a story. I tasted a bitterness here right from the beginning, but I couldn’t find an explanation for it. With every joke, with every twist I understood more and more. I finally realized it by the third book, I think. That you ♥♥♥♥♥ING WATCH TOO MUCH OF GAME OF THRONES! I know I’m in a minority for hating that crappy book and show, but you have responsibility. You made the first game as it is now with your own hands, you yourself started it all as a fantasy, as a bright story about a young sarcastic girl who becomes lost, as a story about adventures in a world full of magic, as
. You made it kind and warm, you made it full of hopes, full of humor. Some can say that you can do whatever you want to your story, well of course, no one can physically stop you, but are you an honest person after that? Are you satisfied with your work, with your breaking all the hopes your fans had?
You know, you killed this game in so many ways when you killed its protagonist. April Ryan is the only reason your first game had a success. April Ryan is a heart of this plot, she is the symbol of this game, just like she was a symbol of rebels. It was a
good written character with a
unique life story and development.
Instead of her we got pitiful dull characters without a good story or whatsoever. The main heroine in the second game was an abomination: faceless woman who tries to find her ex-boyfriend during all the game, WHAT THE HECK?!  I didn’t want it! The game was not about it! No emotions, no logical questions in her head, no opinion, just endless “Ah, Reza, oh, Reza, wow Damien! Eh, Reza…”
I consider us lucky that we got some emotions from her in the third game, and all thanks to the diary (what a surprise). Still, she is not in the slightest a replacement for April. She has no motivation except for ♥♥♥♥ing, she has no development, and I think, if she was voiceless, the game would not have lost anything. I didn’t give a ♥♥♥♥ about her relationship, I didn’t give a ♥♥♥♥ about her destiny, why didn’t you kill her?
Kian… Kian is better of a protagonist, but still not a match for April. Despite many plot holes Kian is fine. He is honest, he has purpose in his life, some history, he has no humour, but that’s quite nicely fits his personality. I bet he was easy to write. Still, no detailed history, not enough emotions for us to feel him, no actual time to develop him.
So…
I say you should, well, for a game to be okay and not to be crappy, in general you shouldn’t, of course. And  you didn’t do it. You didn’t write a good replacement for her. However, you still wanted to play a super genius author of Game of Thrones and you killed April, that’s what a good author should do for an unexpected plot twist, yeah! Well, I’ll try to enlighten you. You obviously understand that this is a giant IMHO and that I’m crazily possessed with April. Okay, I finally finished off the series with this third installment in the longest journey saga. This game is by far the most polished of the three. It made me tear up at times, and it made me scratch my head in confusion at other times. It was both full of life and sometimes devoid of purpose. In the end, it is the 2nd best of the 3. The first game, the longest journey, takes the cake for being a masterpiece, terrible graphics aside, but this game does take a broken and haphazard 2nd game and right the ship. Honestly, this game should probably have gotten more hype. It is up there with modern RPGs in terms of depth and character choice. The development team spared no detail (although some of those details got lost in translation). And the design and characterization are beautiful. Ultimately, some of the choices were quite hollow, while others made a big difference.
That basically sums up the game tho. It does most things extremely well. And its hard to pinpoint why I feel so negative about the game now that I'm done with it. Maybe its the way they treated April Ryan. Maybe its the inability to truly delve into the lives of the new protagonists. Maybe its simply the little things that add up to detract from the overall experience.
In the end, however, I definitely 100% recommend the whole series. I put many hours into the series and it was worth it. Zoe and Kian will still drive your emotions, just not as well as April did in the first game. I got to experience a whole new world (or two (or more!) in this case). And the depth of the story was enriched and inspiring. I will remember this experience for the rest of my life. I just wish they did a few things differently.

I've been a fan of the series since the original.
In a nutshell the game is hard to put in a nutshell. It's vaguely reminicesent of tower defense titles, but with an absolutely monstrous, game-defining twist. The enemy is not units, but rather Creeper-goop that covers the map and damages or destroys your structures on contact. The game is to fight back, and then destroy the goop spigots-"emitters"- or complete other objectives. The structures and enemies are all very simple and direct in their purpose and utility. The game itself however is extremely various in difficulty based on the map itself-size, features, and the strength of the emitters. There are additional enemies in addition to the emitters but they are not in all maps.  The challenge of the game is all about defending yourself while you build your energy resources up before you push to destroy the emitters. Later, you can redo the maps to attempt to do so faster.
The game has a great custom map communtiy and a custom map generator after you finish the decently long and challenging campaign. Replayability is top notch.
I've gotten more fun and more hours out of this than a shameful number of AAA titles. All things considered, absolutely amazing for an indie.
I've had no issues with bugs, and the developer has been pretty good with support for those that do find them.
The only downside is there is no direct multiplayer of any sort. However, it really doesn't detract from all that you're already getting in this well-fleshed out title.
Newbie Tips:
-There is no such thing as too much energy
-Stick to high ground when you can
-Don't land near emitters
-Don't build too many structures at once
-Don't botch your startup
-If you don't push, you can't win

Not quite as fascinating as Grow Home, but still worth playing.
Grow Home was quite a surprise for me. Despite its linearity there was this odd sense of freedom. The controls were a bit wonky, but once you've mastered them you feel like you've developed some skill. Seeing the ground disappear in the distance while you slowly made your way up was satisfying - and sometimes terrifying! I felt some vertigo when climbing over an edge, carefully planning each grip while dangling from the ceiling. That's because there was something on the line - I didn't want to fall to my death and lose some of the progress I had made. Only late in the game did I finally level up my jetpack enough to not really be afraid of heights anymore, which was good since I had to zoom around the map a lot to find the missing crystals.
Why am I talking so much about the previous game? Because unfortunately the developers had a different view of what made the game fun in the first place, replaced it with more "open-worldness" in Grow Up and failed to make the updated concept work as well as the first one did.
Before you had a real sense of progress - you went *up*, and the higher you got, the further along you were in the game. Now you go wherever you want. Instead of one huge whale-sound-making plant being your massive companion on your quest, you half-heartedly grow a couple of them to nowhere in particular. For that last leg of the journey to the moon you don't really have to do anything at all! Instead of wondering what you'll find next on your journey, you almost immediately get to see everything you'll ever see in the game. There's no real element of "discovery" there. Basically you see what you need to do and then you go to work collecting items and breezing through checkpoint-races.
The vertigo and sweaty palms are gone. You hardly have to climb anywhere, and falling off the freakin' moon is about as scary as slightly losing your balance while walking. You can jump, glide and jetpack almost anywhere. Even the huge catalogue of plants with odd kinetic abilities I hardly used at all. Once you've got the powered glider you don't even need those star plants anymore - you can basically fly into space on your own.
The "challenges", which don't really matter except for getting 100%, seem to be carefully designed for certain player abilities and cease to be challenging once the player upgrades past that. I focused on picking up crystals and space ship parts first, which meant that once I really started doing challenges, I was way overpowered for them.
To finish up my criticisms, the framerate is a bit wonky for a game that has zero textured surfaces. And there should really be an option to turn off those "video transmission error" effects because they get old pretty fast.
I am ranting a bit, not because I hate the game, but because had it actually improved upon the first one, it could have been close to "Nintendo quality" - you know, fun and tight gameplay from beginning to end that's not very common on the PC. It's still fun to play while listening to podcasts because flying and climbing is still fun. The aesthetics are nice, the cutesy story is kinda charming in a way, and the moment I started playing I knew I'd have at least two afternoons of solid fun ahead of me.

I originally played Turok on the N64. Being a "remastered" version, I was expecting to see a little sharper textures and some better particle effects. It seems that the game itself has just been brought over to another engine or something that supports better shader fx.
Maybe my mind is foggy, but I don't remember there being such horrendous camera tilt in the N64 version. Pair that off with the insane speed Turok accelerates to and I feel like i'm riding a motorcycle. The respawn rate seems to be a little bit high as well, especially since ammo and health are limited and targets (unless firing physical projectiles like pulse rifles) can't miss you.
All of this stuff is easily dismisable, though -- it's all part of the learning curve of the game.
What gripes me the most is the amount of visual bugs in the game. Insane clipping, massive frame rate drops when underwater/ in the clouds, uncapped meshes, Z-fighting, and that's only what I found in Level 2! There is literally no excuse for some of these things!
If you're looking to shell out 20$ for a quick nostalgic trip, go for it.  You'll get it. But if you're kind of on the fence about revisiting it, I'd hold off for now.

Oh hello! Didn't see you there.
I'm here today to talk to you about this game called Final F... I mean, Fearless Fantasy.
It's a neat little Indie RPG game with some hilarious and over-the-top dialogue, phenomenal soundtrack and great voice acting.
The game has no free roam option or anything like that, you go from mission to mission, level up and buy new stuff.. The usual. The combat style is really similar "as you can imagine" to Final Fantasy games, turn based combat.
But the combat itself is something pretty different and unusual for these kinds of RPG games, Have you ever heard of or played "Osu!" because that's how the combat plays out. You pick what you wanna do when it's your turn and then you move your cursor around according to your attacks like you were playing Osu!.
As mentioned before, the voice acting, overall writing for the dialogue and soundtrack are all freaking amazing.
In addition i'd like to say that the character designs for especially the enemies are absolutely gorgeous, well maybe not gorgeous but unique and likeable.. I'll still go with gorgeous, gorgeous in their hideous and ugly way. I also love how the camera works during battles, it's very cinematic and makes everything look so darn epic.
There's not much actual story being shown discarding the cutscenes that look like some childs' doodles on Paint.
But i do love how the characters have their little discussions with each other after a battle, teaching us more about the lore and the story and doing some character development which is always a plus in a RPG game.
I have to admit though, the game felt bit too difficult at the beginning.. Or maybe it's just that the game is so fast paced i just didn't have time to really practise anything.
The game also looks like a Mobile port but i'm pretty sure Fearless Fantasy actually never was a Mobile Game to begin with. So that's cool.
Overall it's a pretty solid game with very few issues and a cheap price tag.
Buy it if you enjoy playing either Final Fantasy or Osu!.. Or both!

Fearless Fantasy is a RPG that seemingly tripped, fell down the rabbit hole and landed somewhere in an anime universe. There are strange creatures, over the top dialogue, and some interesting reactive based combat. One thing I will say about Fearless Fantasy is it doesn't really hold back, it wears what it is on its sleeve. This is very obviously meant for a mobile device but nonetheless finds itself on Steam. To be frank, Fearless Fantasy is like a funny tasting alcohol, it is unique but definitely an acquired taste. One that certain people may like, others not so much.
The reason for that is Fearless Fantasy goes against the grain in most regards of traditional RPGs. The art style is what caught me off guard the most. The monsters in Fearless Fantasy are not your typical, orcs, goblins, and oozes that we have all grown up with. These nightmarish creatures seemingly stepped out of a Dr. Seuss book. With strange vibrant colors and wicked smiling faces coming out of other wicked smiling faces. This sets the tone for the game and lets you know that this isn't your standard RPG. On top of the onslaught of twisted creatures, Fearless Fantasy has a bit of an anime edge in the character design.
The story of Fearless Fantasy is very simplistic and very light on plot. There is a Princess, Hero/Mercenary, evil fiance, giant monster that can eat everybody. It's story, in my opinion, is not really the main focus but it is present and quirky. In between missions you are occasionally gifted with slight animations that give some personality to the characters. The characters have a light-hearted tone that is reminiscent of anime, this makes the characters seem somewhat vapid in nature. This will throw some people off but I didn't mind it all too much. The scenes are voiced acted well but sadly they lack any color, which takes a bit away from the scenes and also some footage is reused in certain situations.
To shake things up even more is Fearless Fantasy's combat. Again this is where this game holds its heart on its sleeve. The combat is completely meant for a mobile platform, you poke, swipe, and swish for all your abilities and attacks. On the Steam version, your mouse replaces your finger and this is quite jarring at first. I love the idea of the combat system as it keeps the player involved in a way that traditional turn based RPG's don't. If you miss an attack there is no one else to blame but yourself, if you critical hit, you did well. Where the problems begin is that there is no time given for you to practice your skills. You essentially learn the combination of swipes and taps as you play. This leads to wasted attacks and some grinding just so you can figure out what you're doing. On higher difficulties? Forget it!
While I cannot comment on the mobile version of the game, I can say that on PC the mouse feels somewhat clunky in combat. Lacking the swishing grace that a finger has as the attacks get more complicated and faster as you progress through the game. There is other minor issues with combat, while the tutorial does explain the basics. Things like enemy status ailments are never explained, it was only until my fifth mission I realized I could click on my party and see what the negative buff was. Despite the issues though the combat can be fun and highly reactive. I should mention there is also a shop with items and upgrades. The shop fills in the required RPG aspects and gives that grinding a point, and lets you spend gold.
Other areas of the game do what they can for being a mobile heavy game. The options menu is somewhat bare. The map which contains your levels is drawn well but static.  On the other hand, the audios of Fearless Fantasy are fantastic. The music never got dull for me and was exciting and fun when it needed to be. The sound effects having the necessary oomph when a critical hit landed or swish of a dodged blow. The attack animations themselves while eventually repeated, looked fantastic the first time I used them. Dazzling the screen with effects I wasn't expecting.
Replay value and length are up to the player. The game includes the standard 3 star achievement hunt. This is divided by difficulty per area/scene of the game. Increasing the difficulty of the reactive combat. This feels a little grindy but still adds welcomed replay value. The story mode can probably be beaten in about two to three hours. The higher difficulties will take much longer.
To sum up, Fearless Fantasy is not everyone's cup o' tea, but I was surprised and interested to see how different the game was. I think some bold moves and design decisions were made here and I think the good far outweighs the bad. Even if you're not a fan of the art decisions and story. The combat is unique. I would love to see what this kind of combat could be like in a dedicated PC title and made a little bit more friendly for the mouse.
As always I encourage you to do a bit more research, but the game isn't overwhelmingly priced at $6.99. You could always catch it on sale but I think the game offers more then enough even at its base price. Especially if you are looking for something that dares to try something a little new and a little weird.

I didn't honestly expect this game to be that good, having picked a key up for free. While lacking in higher strategy, this game has managed to turn a simple concept into a decent experience, my main issue being resource management and economy. The simple concept of 'build minion, send at enemy' could have been done quite poorly, however with Battlepillars there is a decent amount of customisation that makes the game fairly enjoyable to play. The current price level is reasonable (as far as steam goes when there isn't a sale on) so you may want to pick it up if you have younger children who are better suitable for a simple mechanic.
Note: Please bear in mind that the stuff you unlock in single player is what you often get in multiplayer (there are options to limit the opponent to mutually aquired items, and to grant opponents the items you have if they don't.) This allows for some  seriously unfair matches (+150% resource gain for example) that will often sweep you quickly.
In conclusion, it's not perfect and it may be a bit too simple for some, but it's still reasonably enjoyable to play.
Overall, 5.5 - 6.5/10
EDIT: Accounts from other people have highlighted problems I have not yet experienced myself. Please take into account these other accounts before considering purchasing this game. Thank you!

For many years I listed the original Longest Journey as my favourite computer game of any category.  Whether this ending to the trilogy does justice to the original, as the positive reviewers insist, or lets it down (as the negs feel) I don't know. But my reaction to the game was mixed. I found the first couple of hours boring and nearly stopped playing. In fact I only continued because I was persuaded by some of the favourable reviews. It did get better. The gameplay is relaxing and the visuals are beautiful. But I still can't give it a wholehearted recommendation.
If it had been released 10 years ago it would have been excellent. But there is now so much sophisticated fiction based on AI, mind control and mind storing, the concept of the dream machine feels feeble. Event the dual worlds and the "balance" is uninspiring and corny. And despite the beautiful scenery it is not as atmospheric or immersive as good modern games. I am thinking of Witcher, Dragon Age, Guild Wars 2 but depending on taste most people will have played deeply atmospheric games that makes this seem old before its time.

I wish they had worked towards creating new stories instead of attempting to extend this one.  I waited years for this closure, and it wasn't worth it.  Play The Longest Journey, and just stop there.  Dreamfall and Chapters aren't bad games, but they do not live up to the legacy, and they do not provide the closure Longest Journey fans are looking for.  In fact it retroactively ruins some aspects of The Longest Journey's plot.
(on a technical level, I dragged through half of chapters pre-final cut; if you are going to play it, make sure you have final cut, because the visuals are the only reason to play).

One of the best stories I've ever had the pleasure to experience. For me, it was not predictable at all - there were so many twists and I honestly had no idea how it was going to turn out. The setting is unlike anything else, the characters are so well done, and there's no cheesy love story that gets in the way of it all (as is usually the case with promising stories).
When it was all over I sat there for around 15 minutes just staring at my computer screen because I was so astounded (and confused). There are still so many questions, though less so than the end of DF: TLJ, though it all manages to wrap up beautifully in the final book.
I can't recommend this enough, although I'd say it's essential to play DF: TLJ first to fully understand it and make it 10x more enjoyable.

This is my first review here. I have to start with the statement that The Longest Journey is my all time favorite game. The sequel, Dreamfall was pretty good but rather strange.
As Dreamfall Chapters appeared on Kickstarter I was among the first backers. I wanted to get a conclusion on the story, I wanted to relieve the magic of the original game.
After 3 years I just finished the game a few moments ago. 3 years. First we had to wait because they decided to make it episodic, then I had to wait to upgrade my PC because the game is poorly optimized. I mean it is really bad, just to understand it runs at like 40 fps on a machine that runs Crysis 3 on 70-80 fps.
But now I have finished it and I just feel like instead of gaining new experiences I have just lost something. The story is confuse, filled with boring characters, shady dialogues. The game is empty, two medium-large maps with just a few interactive NPC-s, lots of long and boring conversations.
What happened to The Longest Journey. Where is my adorable April or at least the half-interesting Zoe from the second game? Why all the politics and shady Dreamtime, Storytime plot? Why can't we just have some funny, lovable characters with a simple story? Where are the Dragons, exotic Arcadia places from the original game?
I may sound a bit strange, I just simply can't explain how disappointed I am. I can't believe that this game was made by the same people who made the original. That game had heart, had a warm atmosphere and a lovely story. Dreamfall Chapters is full with forced conspiracies, politics and other embarrassing plot twists.
I can't understand the very positive rating. I know, nobody forced me to play it, but it still made me really sad.
The last scene also made me cry, because of the nostalgia in it, and because of the missed opportunities, and the fact that this is really the end it got.
Please, If you loved The Longest Journey and found Dreamfall's story too much of a change, please don't play this. I wish I could forget it.

TL;DR : A great sequel to Grow Home, Grow Up improves on nearly all aspects of the previous game, and is definitely worth the $10 CAD.
Grow Home was one of my favourite games of last year, and while it was only really a concept at the time, it has evolved into a truely great game. All previous gameplay mechanics have been improved upon, such as the ability to boost while gliding, essentially becoming a plane, while also adding more abilities, such as the ball mode. The map featured in Grow Up is an entire planet, which can be completely explored, as opposed to Grow Home which was only a small area, however it does not extend upwards to the degree that Grow Home did. There are more costumes that BUD can wear, each with their own abilities, obtained by completing up to 40 challenges, as well as 150 crystals to find. Grow Up is all about exploration, and it does it very well. Clocking in at 12 hours of playtime, I 100% completed the game, including completing all of the acheivements, which are interesting and quite fun and sometimes challenging to complete. At only $10 CAD, anyone who enjoyed Grow Home, or anyone who likes a casual, exploration game about climing, flying, and falling, I cannot reccommend this game enough.

No Mans Sky - 18 Quatillion planets = boring, repetitive, same crap different planet.
Grow Up - One Planet with a moon and a ton of plants, flowers, animals, and a ton of different abilities and ways to move around this planet = a smaller sandbox, but with tons of beautiful variety.
10 outta 10!

I feel like a 10 year old kid getting addicted to Turok all over again.
-Much easier and more precise controls compared to the N64 version.
-The game still looks old, but the graphics updates are still very welcome, especially the resolution/widescreen settings and the increased draw distance.
-There are some mostly minor changes to enemy spawn placement, and level layouts. I don't want to spoil anything because you should find out for yourself, but this is refreshing, especially since I played the original Turok for more hours than I can even count.
-Get those Beetle Bugs and other enemies in the same room, and hilarity ensues. Don't mess with the bugs (Hilariously comedic punch noise included).
-Lots and lots of secrets. Keep your eyes peeled and look EVERYWHERE.
-The only con in my opinion is the price, which I think is a bit high. If you're interested, get it while it's on the launch discount or wait for a bigger sale.
Overall, I would recommend this, especially to anyone who played the original. If you haven't played old school 90's FPS's, this might look primitive at first glance. The key is in the gameplay, and this game plays great for an old title.

First off: Ubisoft's decision to make the Frontiers DLC free to season pass owners restored a bit of my faith in a gaming industry that seems to be out to screw over customers recently.
Anno 2205's ratings took a major (and deserved) knock after they decided to charge for Frontiers. I don't know whether or not the original season pass description said that all future DLC would be free or not (it is claimed that it did) but charging for more DLC stretched the meaning of a seasons pass a lot. Ubisoft needs to be commended for reversing this decision (Take note Hello Games, you solve problems by communicating, admiting you messed up and try to fix it. Not by going underground).
Now onto the game. I did not spend more than 20 minutes on Frontiers content so I will not cover that. I will also concentrate on only 2 points because these are mostly raised in negative reviews (barring the DLC policy comments): the new way of managing resources and combat.
I will kick off by saying that this version of Anno will not appeal to all fans of the series. I have been playing the series since Anno 1503 (roughly 2003 / 2004) and I really enjoyed the the micro-management of resources and production chains, the careful placement of resource production, consumption and storage. For me this style of play culminated in Anno 1404 and more so 2070 because available building space became a scarce resource.
This Anno does not play like that. In a sense it has been simplified a lot which may be good or bad, depending on what you want out of the experience.
The management has now moved to a grander scale and keeping track of all your resources over multiple sectors with unique play styles and resources can be almost as challenging as getting a perfect production chain going on the older games. Individual sectors however have become a game of watching resource production digits and fixing the negatives.
If you want something that plays like the older versions, then this is not for you. That said, I enjoy the new play style but only because I see it as a different game altogether. I still have the older versions to go back to if I want to scratch that particular itch.
The only area where the experience doesn't work for me personally is the combat and the new crisis sectors. I get the idea behind them but the exceution lacks depth. In Anno 2070 for example you had to work to get to bullet and advanced weapon manufacturing to build a decent sized military. It had the feeling of a small scale military industrial complex behind it and I would have loved to see the developers expand on that idea instead of taking away from it.
Overall as a city builder with RTS elements I would give it a 7/10, but as an Anno game only 4/10.
I would also recommend it to anyone that enjoys city building and resource management that doesn't get too complicated.
-------------------------------------------------
TL;DR: kudos Ubisoft for changing your minds and not charging season pass owners for Frontiers DLC, good city builder game, not very good at the military aspect and overall not a perfect Anno successor. Would still recommend it, especially if you can find it on sale for 75% or less.

I really do like this game but I wanted to bring up a few of the flaws it has so that those who check the negative reviews know what might be disappointing (spoilers for the game):
1) Once you get 60 crystals, the main objective (rescue MOM) becomes trivial to complete. If you take collecting the crystals seriously like I did, then you'll accomplish this in somewhere in the second area. This allows you to apply boost to your glider, which means you can fly literally to whatever height you want because of how quickly the boost comes back. You no longer need to bother growing or collecting anything because you can simply check the map for MOM parts and go get them. I firmly believe you could complete this game without growing a single starplant, which kind of defeats the purpose (MOM literally remarks on how you've been growing starplants when you rescue her, what if you didn't?).
2) I've found no practical reason to use the ball form. It seems like it serves the purpose of faster ground travel, but honestly you spend so little time on the ground it seems pretty pointless; and you can get up to pretty good speed just by running and jumping off a champoline.
3) Useless and far too useful fauna. One of the cool things introduced in this game is growing plants. However, a lot of the plants you collect seem either useless or redundant. Why grow a tall mushroom to climb when you can achieve greater height faster with a champoline? Why would I need to grow a cactus? Why do many fauna serve the exact same function? I wouldn't mind it as much if they didn't stay in the cycle. If I'm cycling through the fauna I might start to speed up to rush through the useless ones for the one I'm looking for, but accidentally pass it. There are also several fauna that can be a bit game-breaking (especially if you've unlocked the gardening suit, which is very easy to do): lily-pads could probably just remove water from your life (though I haven't tested that), and there's one that throws you a ridiculous height which, again, with the rocket glider adds to the pointlessness of trying to grow starplants. It's also very awkward to use a lot of the plants (catapult plants come to mind), though I think this was partly intended. And I couldn't figure out how to uproot plants on the PC, which I've seen people do in videos. I don't know if POD said it and I just missed it or what, but that was kind of bothersome to me that it doesn't tell me in the controls page.
I think this game is great for people who want to 100% it. However, if your goal is to complete the main objective, then this might not be the game for you. I accomplished it in a few short hours thanks to how broken rocket glider is. You can very easily complete the main objective without growing all the starplants (which is supposed to be the whole point of the game), and I really think that is kind of disappointing.
Fortunately, I am a 100%er, so I will probably return to this game pretty soon to finish my adventure.
-----
Also, for me personally the game ran fine. The controls are very wonky but you get used to them, I never had a crash or lag.

To me, Dreamfall: Chapters is probably the best thing to have come out of Funcom since The Longest Journey (the original 1999 TLJ, not to be mistaken with Dreamfall TLJ).
The story is really well written and, although not perfect, the game mechanics are excellent. Chapters has one of the best story affecting decision making systems that I've seen in a modern game. I'm not talking about that fake Bioware/Bethesda dialog/decision system that gives you the same outcome no matter what you choose, I'm talking about decisions that could end up with people getting killed 8 chapters down the road. Moral decisions that will make you question your values sometimes.
I own a copy of the older games and replayed them both before embarking on Chapters. The original Longest Journey was tough to get into because of the graphics and the sometimes asinine puzzles but it had an excellent story and intensely memorable and lovable cast of characters. Dreamfall The Longest Journey on the other hand was very disappointing: (a) the story was rushed, the original plot threads of the previous game were completely trampled on for a new Dreamer plot thread that came out of left field and at the time it wasn't all interesting: very little happened through out the game and the story ended on a very unsatisfying plot hanger; (b) TLJ's April Ryan was a pure joy to get to know and play with, she was lovable and goofy, resourceful and strong. They sucked all the life out of her for the sequel and replaced here with Zoe Castillo who (in Dreamfall TLJ) was really boring and one dimensional. Where I care for and related to April Ryan in the first TLJ, I just couldn't be bothered to care what happened to Dreamfall TLJ's Zoe.
Dreamfall Chapters in my eyes is Dreamfall TLJ's redemption: Zoe Castillo was completely overhauled for this game and was far more interesting and engaging, additionally a ton of really amazing characters have been introduced; the Dreamer's storyline introduced in Dreamfall TLJ is much much more fleshed out and interesting, the game mechanics are far better, the really broken fighting system introduced in Dreamfall TLJ is gone and they introduced a really wonderful alternate storyline and decision making system that for the first time in my life makes me want to replay a game right after finishing it; the 2014 graphics look absolutely amazing and although it's not quite an open world game, the maps were beautiful enough to make me want to explore them and expansive enough to make feel like I'm in a city rather than just going from mission to mission or room to room.
In these dark days of loot box gambling and AAA studios f-ing over their clients at every turning, this game is a gem and a treasure, do yourself a favor and grab it. I would also recommend playing the previous two games just to give yourself some context.

Examina has an extremely unique combat system, and in some ways, Examina's system is better than all other existing ones.
As I understand it, there's a few popular existing ways to model medieval combat:
-Directional Blocking: Mount & Blade Warband, Kingdom Come Deliverance (not released). You can attack and block in a number of directions. Fights between skilled players can look quite ridiculous as players spin, feint, and jump. Mount & Blade: Warband is my favorite game ever, but its combat system is not exactly realistic.
-Chivalry Medieval Warfare's system: Regardless of direction, blocking is dependent upon timing. Skilled players do unrealistic things like jumping and angle their swings in ludicrous ways that drastically affect the time that their blow lands. It's a good system, but experienced players use extremely gimmicky tactics like the aforementioned angling of swings.
-The Assassin Creed/Witcher/Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor's system: This system of combat is set up for a really strong protagonist that can take on legions of enemies. While it requires a degree of skill in the timing, it's not realistic (leaving an enemy to your back is a fatal mistake, even if you're a brilliant fighter). Nonetheless, it's a functional system for the types of game the use it; just don't make a game using this system if you want it to have good multiplayer combat or realism.
-Mindless hack and slash, Skyrim's system: Awful! Skyrim's combat does not entail any real skill. It is the least rewarding of any of the above mentioned system in my humble opinion.
Exanima, on the other hand, is extremely unique and one of the more realistic systems. Examina:
+ Takes into account forward and lateral movement into weapon damage better than any system
+ Takes into account weapon alignment/"accuracy" better than any other system. To elaborate, if you hit someone with the shaft of your polehammer they'll shrug it off, if you nail their helmet with the head of your polehammer they'll be hurt badly. This means that if you are right in front of your enemy and they have a pole weapon they can't really hit you- which is a good thing, because it wasn't possible in reality. This advantage of Examina is perhaps entirely unique; unlike Chivalry, Assassin's Creed, or Warband, if you aren't the correct distance from your enemy in Exanima and you hit them with the shaft of your poleaxe you won't do any damage.
+ Semi-Realistic treatment of plate armor; slashing weapons do not cut, but only impart the damage done by the  impact of the weapon (plate armor will treat an enemy's sword as blunt)
+ Doesn't have bull♥♥♥♥♥♥gimmicks in combat. Every tactic you can employ in Examina could also be employed in real life (probably). Beating your opponent in Examina relies upon timing your attacks when your opponent can't parry (because they're starting to attack), feinting, or otherwise disadvantaging your opponent (by knocking them over, backing them into a corner). This lies in stark contrast to the spinning of Warband, the jumping and angling of Chivalry, or the ridiculous "mob combat" of games like Assassin's Creed.
+ Customizability: You can make your character very tall or short, fat or muscular, although you can't change their facial aesthetics (which doesn't matter from your perspective when you play). The layering of the armor/inventory I especially liked, you can wear a gambeson (layered cloth), a tunic, mail, and plate all at once (just like in real life), most games don't allow you to pick and choose.
- Exanima's movement animations, while not bad, could be better. Running looks a little odd, and at times combat will look a little off. The animations look good in my opinion, but they're not as good as what some people might expect.
- Currently, Examina has no thrusting; while Sui Generis will have that feature, it remains to be seen in Examina
- Blocking is passive. While Examina's system certainly requires skill to defeat an opponent, to merely parry the vast majority of an enemy's blows only requires that you face your opponent and don't begin an attack as they are landing theirs. To be fair, combat in Exanima already requires the vast majority of your attention, and asking people to time their parries on top of that might make combat too complex for a human who is already paying attention to footwork, timing their attacks, and making sure their opponent's attack isn't really just a feint, etc.
- Hitting an opponent while they're down is unrealistically hard. The AI is very good at hitting you while you're down (which doesn't happen often), but hitting them if they fall over is really difficult. In fact, overhead attacks (which are used to hit downed opponents) are difficult to land in general. I hope that thrusting isn't as difficult, but due to the perspective of the camera, I expect it will be as difficult if not moreso.
- Grappling isn't an option- not that I'd expect it to be! In the medieval period, it was not at all unheard of for knights to wrestle each other on the ground and try to stab each other in the visors/armpits/groin with a rondell dagger, but this is not a feature in the game. It's not a feature in any medieval game, in fact, because it would be so difficult to model this kind of combat.
-The "campaign" is pretty short. It's not story-driven, has no character development, and has limited replayability.
Get this game if you want to try out a unique combat system with lots of detail. Don't get it if you want an engaigng storyline, or a lengthy campaign. I can't say it has no storyline, it has some scrolls that I am willing to bet set up plot points will be evident in Sui Generis; after all, Exanima is a prelude to Sui Generis.
The combat will take a few hours to get a hang of, and probably several hours more to gain the skill to defeat the final boss in the expert arena. Personally, I'd recommend that you defeat every opponent in the Novice Arena before starting the campaign (as the opponents there are just as unforgiving as the Arena's). Finally, once you're actually crawling in the dungeon, beware that you do not have to fight every opponent and running away is your best option 70% of the time.

Engaging TD game with very bad UI, explanations and diversity.
I don't remember when and why I bought this game. I suppose it's connected with the awesome preview and good rating (Very Positive 85%)
First of all, the preview of the game is a lie. "Stunning Detail of levels" - there is nothing stunning. "in-depth gameplay", actually, the TD elements at this game are bare to bones; "finely tuned balance of all levels and turrets" - "The balance is bad. See below for more info".
I don't like when people lie.
Let's talk about gameplay. There is only 8 towers. Each tower has 4 levels. When you upgrade a tower it gets x2 damage and small attack radius boost. Each tower gets Hellfire ability (which is the same for all towers except Tornado), which increased attack fire by 200% for 5 seconds. That's all. There is no buyable abilities, there is no tech tree for towers. There is nothing else except these 8 towers.
The balance of towers is bad. There is 1 overpowered tower, the Mortar, which has long range, high attack damage and splash. So, the tactic for all levels are simple. Place cheap tower, save money for Mortar, place mortar, upgrade mortar, when save money for the next mortar. Repeat until 30 wave is done. Add some lasers for air waves and some ice towers for better mortars' performance. All other towers has much lower DPS than mortar. I tried to pass 4th map on hard 10+ times to realise that.
This is the second huge flow of Defense Zone 2. There is a lack of information. You can see the damage and attack range of tower. You can't see attack speed, attack type, dps, splash, bounce count and etc. An it's really bad. There are tip in the game loading screen which says "Build your defense depending on enemy units". Ok I go to tower info and see, that this tower does extra damage to Light units. But what are light units at this game? I can't select enemies, I can't check their HP or type.... tt
As I said each tower has Hellfire ability. It should be interesting. But you need to manually use for each tower ( you need to select tower, and click at the button). At the end of the game you have 20+ tower and you are forced to click on towers and activate abilities. I played on Mac with touch pad and I was really tired to do these repetitive actions. TD is supposed to be about strategy and not about ability activation

Defense Zone 2 is a very interesting tower defense game. There are eight type of towers, that of course can be upgraded. Speed can be accelerated to 2x and 4x. The game allows you to pause, while still being able to manage your towers, which is very helpful and necessary because Defense Zone 2 is a very difficult game.
The game has 31 levels and each level can be played in easy, normal and hard difficulty. You start each level with 20 lives, which means 20 enemies may exit the map before it's game over. If you manage to survive without losing a life, you collect an achievement. So the main goal of the game is to collect 93 achievements, one for each level and difficultly.
This however is easier said than done. Hard difficulty is quite extreme on all levels and the final levels can hardly be won in easy mode. So the game offers quite a challenge.
Nevertheless it's a lot of fun to test your skills. As many other tower defense games, the game is very addictive. Whenever you lose a life you immediately want to start over to try again.
In order to win you need to analyse each map, perfectly place your towers, and use the correct timing for hellfire, a special attack mode each tower offers for a short period of time. Towers can be placed freely and sometimes a few millimetres can mean the difference between victory and defeat.
Pros:
- nice graphics
- very good music
- great sound effects
- pause mode that allows you to command towers
- 1x, 2x and 4x speed
- keyboard shortcuts
- upgrading towers increases their strength significantly
- towers can be adjusted to fire at nearest, weakest or strongest enemy
- enemy ground and air troops
- several lanes
- several exits
- several entry points
- enemies in different directions on same lane
- option to save your progress for each level and each difficulty in the game (very helpful!)
- air strikes
- cheap
Cons:
- no story
- some players might find the game too difficult
- enemies often escape because your towers don't fire at them, aiming at other enemies instead. This can be very frustrating.
- winning all levels on all difficulties seems almost impossible
lots of fun

PC; Win 8.1/10 64-bit; Sacred Gold v2.28
completed; playing time: 147 hrs
Pros:
+ Several characters to choose from, each with his/her distinctive advantages and drawbacks
+ Replayability: characters start in different locations, have different backgrounds, and some different quests
+ Numerous weapons, armour types, spells, items, and whatnot...
+ Countless ways of developing your character during gameplay (by developing favourite skills, attributes, and combat arts, as well as modifying properties of your armour and weapons...)
+ You can create combos
+ In addition to the traditional swords and bows, there are firearms, muskets, and mines...
+ There is a huge area to explore
+ There are a great number of quests
+ There are portals to facilitate travel between distant areas
Cons:
- You only play as one character and can't create a permanent team. Sometimes an NPC may join you, but only temporarily, and you can neither control him/her nor have access to his/her inventory
- Monster respawning can sometimes be a real pain in the neck... There's too many of them, too often...
- The manual doesn't explain some aspects of the game well. Before you commit yourself to playing the game seriously, it's a good idea to read some extra information on how things work and how to develop your character on the Sacred wiki or find some good forums
- Although the expansions - e.g. Sacred Underworld - introduce some interesting areas and quests, my overal impression was that they were worse thought out than the base game, with fewer good-quality quests or areas
- A few quests broke becasue I accidentally started them "from the end," e.g. I found an item at the beginning before a quest was officially initialised; then, when the quest officially started and I was supposed to find the item, the game acted as if I had not found it, even though I already had it. The result was I couldn't finish the quest. However, I experienced very few quests like that (2 or perhaps 3...)
- Remember that it's a 2005 game, so graphics are a little dated
To conclude, despite a few problems, it's a solid RPG worth getting and spending hours of your life playing it.

This game is a rather old one, but if you haven't tried it and like Diablo-esque games, it's a good pick-up on a sale.
Even though it's very clunky, you can easily waste half your day just playing this game and discovering new stuff. The major feature that differentiates this game from it's cousins is the skill-system, or rather the level up system. As you level up, you get to branch out into all kinds of passive skills, from Horseback Combat to Dual Wielding, allowing you to really customize your character in addition to the usual Strength, Agility and Intelligence attributes. To level up skills, you need to find "skill-items" or whatever they are called. These items are class-specific and these are the sources of your skills. You can obtain them en-masse from quests. You can right click these items if they belong to your class and consume them, gaining a point in that skill. If you find the skills of other classes, you can trade them in various amounts to the Gandalf wizard and he will give you a skill of your own class.
You can also string your abilities together to create some basic combos (skills don't really synergize with eachother). Only negative things I can say is that it's clunky as mentioned above, is extremely hard in the early stages and items are rather scarce. You will be lucky to find an unique in one playthrough, and even luckier if it belongs to your class since a lot of items are class-specific. Angels can't wear pants for instance.

I really do like this game but I wanted to bring up a few of the flaws it has so that those who check the negative reviews know what might be disappointing (spoilers for the game):
1) Once you get 60 crystals, the main objective (rescue MOM) becomes trivial to complete. If you take collecting the crystals seriously like I did, then you'll accomplish this in somewhere in the second area. This allows you to apply boost to your glider, which means you can fly literally to whatever height you want because of how quickly the boost comes back. You no longer need to bother growing or collecting anything because you can simply check the map for MOM parts and go get them. I firmly believe you could complete this game without growing a single starplant, which kind of defeats the purpose (MOM literally remarks on how you've been growing starplants when you rescue her, what if you didn't?).
2) I've found no practical reason to use the ball form. It seems like it serves the purpose of faster ground travel, but honestly you spend so little time on the ground it seems pretty pointless; and you can get up to pretty good speed just by running and jumping off a champoline.
3) Useless and far too useful fauna. One of the cool things introduced in this game is growing plants. However, a lot of the plants you collect seem either useless or redundant. Why grow a tall mushroom to climb when you can achieve greater height faster with a champoline? Why would I need to grow a cactus? Why do many fauna serve the exact same function? I wouldn't mind it as much if they didn't stay in the cycle. If I'm cycling through the fauna I might start to speed up to rush through the useless ones for the one I'm looking for, but accidentally pass it. There are also several fauna that can be a bit game-breaking (especially if you've unlocked the gardening suit, which is very easy to do): lily-pads could probably just remove water from your life (though I haven't tested that), and there's one that throws you a ridiculous height which, again, with the rocket glider adds to the pointlessness of trying to grow starplants. It's also very awkward to use a lot of the plants (catapult plants come to mind), though I think this was partly intended. And I couldn't figure out how to uproot plants on the PC, which I've seen people do in videos. I don't know if POD said it and I just missed it or what, but that was kind of bothersome to me that it doesn't tell me in the controls page.
I think this game is great for people who want to 100% it. However, if your goal is to complete the main objective, then this might not be the game for you. I accomplished it in a few short hours thanks to how broken rocket glider is. You can very easily complete the main objective without growing all the starplants (which is supposed to be the whole point of the game), and I really think that is kind of disappointing.
Fortunately, I am a 100%er, so I will probably return to this game pretty soon to finish my adventure.
-----
Also, for me personally the game ran fine. The controls are very wonky but you get used to them, I never had a crash or lag.

Yes, it is good. Yes, it is flawed. If you liked Grow Home, you'll probably like Grow Up. If you haven't played Grow Home, I recommend playing that before starting this one.
I bought this right after it came out, since I enjoyed Grow Home so much.
I'm going to complain about a lot of issues I had with this game, but keep in mind that I like the game overall and I still recommend it.
I immediately had to turn the graphics down to minimum settings to make the game playable. Not sure if it's due to the sheer number of objects the game is trying to display all at once or the fact that the play area wraps all the way around the planet, but it was running very slowly. This doesn't help in a game where the player character is already difficult to control.
Like Grow Home, this is a "search, collect, upgrade, repeat" game. There are more starplants, more crystals, and more species of wildlife than in the first game.
Grow Up attempts to give more significance to BUD's purpose as a botany droid. The player is able to grab onto a plant and save a copy, unlocking the ability to grow more instances of that plant by tossing seeds (unlimited, with a cooldown). Most of the plants grown through this method have some sort of mobility function for BUD (bouncier jumps, water platforms, etc). You may find one or two types of plant that you like to use in a pinch, but as BUD's own powers increase, the plants are less useful. One particular annoyance is that the plant-selection menu keeps defaulting to the Youch plant, which is arguably the least useful plant you can grow. Most of the plants that can be used for launching yourself require you to jump and land fairly precisely onto a small area. You can't just step on, so hopefully you'll master BUD's ragdoll movements pretty quickly.
Despite this weird precision requirement for using plants, the checkpoints/spawn points still have a ridiculously strong pull. If you stand too close you'll get dragged in, and once you're in, you have to fight to get back out. There's no specimen analysis in this game, so I don't understand why they kept the tractor beam effect.
I'm not sure what real benefit there is to using the ball transformation. I guess it's fine for quickly traveling across the ground, but much of the game takes you near cliffs, water, or just very small platforms. It's a cute feature, but there doesn't seem to be a good use case for it.
The glider is fun to use, but it's frustrating that steering directions change based on whether BUD is facing toward/away from the camera.
The ring races are terrible (especially in the late-game), mostly due to the fact that the "rings" are more like floating two-dimensional brackets that are part of the HUD rather than the playing field. They rotate to face the camera at all times (kinda like sprites in an old Doom game). Because they have no form and no depth, it's difficult to judge their positions. You have to determine the position of a 2D object in 3D space, which is disastrous if you're doing a ring race that requires the glider. Many of the races cause slowdown, and there are a few races where the rings are placed in hard-to-see positions, but giving the rings a physical object would make the challenges CONSIDERABLY less annoying (and, by extension, more fun).
I felt like I got too powerful too quickly, but the game can be very frustrating before you start to amass upgrades (as was the case in Grow Home). BUD has 2 types of upgrades. There are crates that contain special parts, and there are power upgrades that come from reaching certain crystal-collection milestones. The desert starplant was the first one I grew to completion, and I used the non-upgraded glider to just maintain altitude & soar around to other biomes, collecting ship pieces without coming back down to the ground. It felt like cheating, but I guess that was the intended action, since there weren't as many total starplants as I had anticipated.
My assumption was that each ship part would be the culmination of a "chapter" so to speak. Like, there would be a starplant or a lengthy cave exploration or something unique assigned to each ship part, but they could still be collected in any order. The "unlimited flight" options wouldn't really be available until the main storyline was complete.
The camera can also be a pain the butt in this game. Toggling camera distance can be very slow, and sometimes the camera likes to rotate to a different side of BUD to... I don't know, try to help? -be more cinematic? Either way, it's unwelcome when you're trying to maintain a specific camera angle to gauge your flight/fall trajectory.
DESPITE all these gripes, it's still a fun, charming game. Whereas Grow Home was a very polished proof of concept, Grow Up is a more thoroughly expanded exploration of the same ideas. Hopefully Reflections will make a third entry with better pacing, because I still want more.
