Third game in the
franchise, this brings a conclusion to the cliffhanger ending of
and concludes the trilogy as a whole.  All in all, a satisfying ending to a fantastic trilogy of games.  The recent "Final Cut" update also brings the graphics up to 2017 standards, which makes the game look, sound and play amazing, top to bottom.
The story, as always, is my favourite part.  Also, all the flaws from the second game have been cleaned up and polished to make a truly magnificent final installment.  The control scheme is actually not that different from Dreamfall, but the few changes made make all the difference.  Unnecessary combat mechanics have been dropped in favour of QTE-style timed puzzles (which is how Adventure games are
to do combat, if they need to do so at all.)
The addition of a "choices matter" style of decision making, common to modern Adventure games, is also welcome and well done.  I particularly liked how they highlight which decisions will actually cause significant changes (without telling you what those changes are) at the end of each "book."
Also, I really like the "story recap" menu option.  Well done and not too long.  Not nearly enough to justify skipping the first two games, of course, but a good refresher if it's been a year or six since you played the older games.
The plot does get a little bit... convoluted... near the end.  Feels like they were rushing things a bit to wrap up all the loose ends from the first two games.  I'm still pleased with the ending, mind you, it just got a bit twisty, that's all.  Also, remember Lord of the Rings with all the "epilogues"?  Same sort of thing going on here.
If you enjoyed the previous games in the series, absolutely!
To finish off the trilogy in style.

Dreamfall Chapters is a mixed bag, a game that is 80% there, but those last 20% are sometimes glaringly obvious and drag down the overall experience a bit.
The story is mostly coherent, mostly well-written and has good voice acting for the most part. The story and atmosphere are the main selling points for the game actually. The amount of content is good, and there are many plot twists to keep things interesting. Often, the game has a nice cinematic feel to it.
However, the pacing can sometimes be very off, like how some cutscenes seem to kind of pop up out of the blue (after a 5-10 second load), last for 30 seconds, and then abruptly cut off again, often in the middle of a piece of music (and then another 5-10 second load screen). I feel that a little more attention to detail in the pacing and delivery of the story could have really done wonders here. There are also parts of the storyline that the game spends a lot of time on, but in end are completely irrelevant. This is a shame, because it would have been better to cut these parts away and develop others a bit more.
Some parts of the game are simply a drag to get through. It is not enjoyable to keep running chores (literally), even if the locations are often well designed. It gets old after a while. Some puzzles can feel a bit like chores as well, rather than enjoying challenges. This is not just a matter of difficulty. I don't mind easy puzzles. But a little too often, the challenges in Dreamfall come from simply not looking in the right place, and it can get a bit frustrating.
In the end, it almost seems like the game designers tried to do too much with the game, and ended up with something that is good, but not quite
. I'm giving it a thumbs up though, because I did enjoy the journey for the most part, and I think fans of story-driven adventures would enjoy it too.

I feel so salty about the presentation of this game that I want to give this game a thumbs down but honestly I would be lying to myself if I didn't admit that as a fan of the series they didn't tie up mostly all of the major story lines from the older games and answer most of my questions, although the way this game gave me those things to me felt like it plopped some goop on a plate and told me to enjoy.
I know people are saying we should be grateful for whatever we get but sorry no, I’m not that type of person. I can appreciate something while also noticing its faults. I can also find entertainment in something I overall didn't enjoy (example a party's music might be terrible but as long as the drinks are good, what would I care about the music lol or going to a terrible movie and walking out thinking at least the action was great). Man that actually brought a tear to my eye, and I was beginning to think this game couldn't possibly make me feel like that, but the feels definitely were strong.
Like I said I could right an essay on this game but since id rather not hit the character limit on this review I'll just simply end this with an analogy, This game is like a "Sloppy Joe Sandwich"-The other games was you buying the ingredients and cooking them. Now this game is you putting it all together. It looks great, Its Meaty, seasoned, and with a hearty filling bun holding it together. By the time you pick it up and bite in half the meat fell back on the plate and the ground...Cursing the sky, your left wondering why the gods of old hate you. After coming back from cleaning the food on the ground you discover the bun is soggy as hell now. Now you can finish your messy meal with a happy go-lucky smile on your face or wallow in self deprecation shoveling it down your gullet like some sewer rat (This was the route i took). You could also shove this slop in the trash and treat yourself to a premium 5 star deliciousness (an actual good game) for dealing with the stress of this game...If i could give this game a "Meh" i would but it doesn't deserve a thumbs down. If they ever create another game in this game universe I wont be picking it up. This game killed any interest i could have with the future plot line ideas they laid down.

I am no longer stumbling about.  I am moving about in a clear concise manner.  I am dodging attacks, blocking.  I even duck under a broad sweeping horizontal slash.  I rush the enemy and knock them onto the ground and finish them off with a powerful overhead slash.
Next round.  I die in a single blow.
I played for a few more hours.
I am excited about where this game is going and hope that the makers continue to fine tune the controls.  They are amazing when you get them to work.

I've spent well over 5 hours just trying to learn how to fight, and another 10 to learn how to fight effectively.
....
And I've loved every minute of it.
*Extra info*
Pros:
- Graphics are great and the designers have done excellently for optimization to where you can get 60 fps with a 4 yr old comp.
- The fighting is simply revolutionary, and the attention to detail in this game is extremely refreshing. YOU control your character, I don't mean A+up for a high attack, your mouse input, timing, and footwork determins where you will land.
- Funny things can happen with physics. I don't mean glitchs or anything, I mean fighting someone, you trip and fall, and he/she trips and fall over you, then you trip over him.
- Developers are transparent and seemingly make good progress.
- Sound is very atmospheric and realistic.
Cons
- There can be a problem with animation speeds suddenly slowing or speeding up depending on cpu/gpu usage ratios, but its avoidable and workable.
- Combat can take a long time to learn, but its very rewarding once you do get proficient.
- For better or worse this, this game does not hold your hand ( a pro for me)
- No thrust attacks yet (at least not without highly advanced footwork and timing to turn a slash small enough to be 'thrust' like)
- I really really really wish this game was open world like torchlite 2, something like that is rumoured but I can't confirm atm.

Exanima is tough. Exanima is hard. It's not for everyone. It's a very different kind of game. Different to what we've become used to.
That being said, what it is, is a lot of fun if you can get into it. Immerse yourself into a high risk dungeon crawler with purely physics based combat. The controls are clunky and take some getting used to but eventually something just clicks and things "just work". At times I'll find myself frustrated that I can't understand how they work, cannot replicate something impressive that I did previously, and yet there's a certain joy to watching things play out differently every time.
Fights in Exanima are quite dynamic. As you tread down a gritty dungeon corridor the shambling form of some zombie or ghoul lurks up ahead. Having played other games you'd expect it to lurch forwards to attack. Not in Exanima. While some of the foes are automatically hostile others stop to size you up, decide if you're a threat or if they think they can take you on. Many's the time a shambling bag of bones takes one look and thinks better of it. They shuffle off in another direction.
Do not try to kill everything. Attack everything and you die. Health will not generally replenish without healing items (which are few and far between). Attacks can cause lethal damage or nonlethal damage. One regenerates naturally. The other does not. Armour doesn't reduce damage so much as it transforms percentages of lethal damage into nonlethal (and then reduces the total a bit as well). Fights in Exanima are visceral, gritty and nasty. Fortunately most of them are avoidable. Patrolling ghouls can be lured into empty rooms and then the doors shut upon them, locking them in.
To begin with darkness will be your greatest enemy. Take the torch. The torch brings light. Unfortunately it also brings it's own problems. When one hand is occupied with the torch it cannot also be used to bear a shield or assist in the use of a two handed weapon. Enemies thrive in the dark. In the earlier portions of the game you'll really need the torch to see where you're going.
The game also currently features an Arena mode to hone your fighting skills. This is quite a popular feature with many players although I have yet to fully master it.
While this game is still in Early Access it's been quite a positive experience. The devs are supporting it with updates. More features are planned. Some of these have already been implemented. There should be a list on the game's store page. Overall I'd highly recommend this game if you like difficult challenges that feel very rewarding but are hard to master.

Game Corp DX is a business, 'Tycoon' style game in which you found and build a computer/video game company, expanding your team, technology and budget with each game you successfully publish.
The business model is fairly simple and the task of designing hit games comes down (primarily) to the team you assemble and their previous experience, rather than picking the suitability of the genre, or having to guess which aspects are more important, as with Game Dev Tycoon (sadly I can't yet compare with Mad Games Tycoon, as I've purchased the title, but have yet to play it).
When you release a game, you get a star rating for the various aspects of the game, and some basic responses from industry critics, The only downside with the model used in Game Corp DX, is that once you've established a fully experienced team, and maxed their training, you can't really fail to release a massive hit. There's much less 'chance' involved, as with Game Dev Tycoon.
The campaign is fun and took me around 6 hours to complete. Bear in mind that I took my time with this, and didn't rush the campaign, to see it through. I suspect that if someone was truly devoted, they could complete the game in a fraction of the time. The Steam achievements are also easily attainable, and provide a little more playability for the title. Within ten hours, I'd completed the campaign and got 100% of the achievements.
This game will never be a massive hit, on par with those huge releases by developers with deep pockets etc, but for the £1.49 I spent on it, it's provided me 10 hours of entertainment - and provided me a fix for my 'game cravings' whilst on holiday and using a very technologically limited laptop!

I just bought this and am running win10.
The game froze after the initial game company and nvidia intros.
Froze on loading the main title screen.
I immediately browsed to the Sacred Gold application launch icon in my steam library and tweaked it and got it running.
I don't really prefer this method as launching from steam library or the desktop icon still produces the bad result.
Then I saw the Config application icon which was the best answer to my issues.
Fix the game like this
-Right click Sacred Gold in your library
-Choose Properties
-Choose Local Content tab and select Browse Local Content
-Scroll down to the Config application Icon and select it
-Check the "32 Bit Color Depth" and "Video Compatibility Mode" boxes
-Exit with OK
You should be good to go now.

Risky's Revenge follows the exploits of the titular Half-Genie hero Shantae as she explores a very small map to collect the three Macguffins, and along her way she discovers MORE Macguffins to collect! The story begins with some boob named Risky (also titular) coming into town and dropping her massive canon balls all over Shantae, resulting in a cutscene defeat - and these opening unskippable cutscenes are indicative of the quality of writing for the rest of the game. Overall, the game's story barely keeps together the gameplay in any interesting way, occasionally delivering chuckles but mostly providing excuses. I think the biggest disappointment in this regard is Shantae herself; she is bossy and bratty with little redeeming quality to her. Since this is a sequel I feel like I've missed a lot in her character development by starting with this entry - maybe I'd like her more if I played the Gameboy Color game first. But judging the series by this game alone, its charms fell pretty flat with me.
And charm unfortunately is probably all this game could have had going for it, because the gameplay is pretty bog standard, with the stink of amateur game design permeating throughout. Levels generally consist of rows of enemies you need to take out one at a time in a painfully slow fashion. Your hair attack has no weight to it and its hitbox feels a little off at times, particularly when hitting small flying enemies. Platforming feels "sticky" and inaccurate, making the more interesting level design a little more frustrating than it needs to be (And for the wrong reasons.) And finally I don't feel like its "metroidvania" elements are very well utilized - it doesn't surprise me that the latest game in the series drops them. Everything is "functional" but it also feels slightly off from the kind of polish you'd find in other games.
With all that said, I want to emphasize that I don't think this is a "Bad" game. It's just really average. If the game looks like it appeals to you based on its aesthetic alone, and you happen to like Saturday Morning Cartoon humor, Shantae isn't a terrible pick. If you're looking for a charming game with hard but fair challenge and a good story - go play Shovel Knight or something else. I personally stopped having fun with this game pretty quick and I was grateful that it only took me about 4 hours to complete.
I think for many people this game would probably achieve what I consider a 3 out of 5, however, Risky's Revenge has to compete with so many better options within the Metroidvania Genre, and the Action Platformer genre in general. With that in mind, I can't in good conscious give this a hearty recommendation. If you are attracted to Shantae for... reasons, this game isn't terrible, and you may be willing to look past its flaws. If you're looking at a game specifically for the gameplay and are still interested in the Shantae franchise, I recommend skipping to Shantae and the Pirate's Curse and leave this one alone.  It improves on just about all of my complaints about this game.

shantae is a sidescrolling game for those whom aren't picky about what games they play.
on the one hand; it has a decent aesthetic and is by no means a 'bad game'
but on the other hand it doesn't really compare to the vast majority of other 'good' 2d sidescrolling games out there.
you see, the thing is that sidescrollers are one of the oldest genres of video games out there, and since the genre's inception, developers have learnt a lot about what works and what doesn't.
although shantae doesn't exactly fly in the face of all this industry knowledge, it certainly does ignore a lot of it, providing the player with nonsensical map design, weird level progression, unintuitive controls and a degree of backtracking that even most metroidvania games would sniff at.
now I haven't written this to spit in the faces of those who like this game; shantae has a rightly deserved fanbase whom are happy to enjoy its unusual design, and I am more than content to let them have at it, as I said earlier; this is certainly not a bad game.
but to those few of you still on the fence about it, I'd like to say this:
though this is a game that would have been competitive a decade or so ago, today, it is merely average.
regardless of whether you're talking about mass marketed sidescrollers or indies (including those from around the time of it's release) this game is rather mediocre by comparison

A fun little adventure with enough charm to make up for the few mistakes.
Shantae: Risky's Revenge isn't the most intuitive back tracking adventure ever and getting "stuck" seems to happen a handful of times. But, a keen eye, ears, and memory will lead you along when you're stumped and also to every secret. The one big thing they get wrong is the gamepad controls. 'Menu Confirm' and in-game 'Talk' are bound together in the code. So with A already being jump you're left with opposite menu controls than you've grown up with in the Western World. A is back and B is confirm. This can be mitigated with a hex editor but you're still left with Talk/Confirm being the same as Jump. It never gets overtly in the way, but hopping around town will get you yappin' with townsfolk when you didn't mean too. And it obviously goes without saying that it shouldn't take a hex editor to get buttons bound to your liking. Also, the game is kinda short in a way. Especially when you factor in the amount of back tracking for the sake of back tracking. I was thorough (but still missed one secret) and got lost plenty and I barely broke 5hrs on my playthrough. Not bad for the price at all though and there's a harder mode and a couple different endings. So some replayability.
All that hardly smudges the fun and charm though. Its a unique world and fun to explore. There's no rhyme or reason to why there's a Pumpkin Patch or Sunken Cavern zones or mummies that explode but it all somehow works together. Blobs, goblin things with wings, zombies, pirates, fat mayors. It just creates a unique world all with well done 2D sprites. The writing is very tongue-in-cheek and is light and funny. Controls are tight and power ups and abilities discoveries steadily expand the fun. Platforming gets a little challenging in parts but is mostly easy given the tight controls. Bosses are interesting, but, few and mostly button mashable punching bags. Maybe the music could've used a little more variety but it fit too.
Easy recommendation on sale if you're in the mood for a 2D adventure. And there is sequels to boot!

After collecting the final achievement of 'Grow Up' it's not easy to leave B.U.D., your little robot and P.O.D., your satellite orbiting device and M.O.M., your mother-ship behind. I will miss them. I will miss the sunsets and the magnificent colours and varied shades of light, that enlighten this peaceful and beautiful world. I will miss the freedom of floating through clear air, higher and higher until I reach the stars and move from dazzling light into silencing darkness. I will miss the song of the whales, echoing through this world and the beauty of it's plentiful exotic plants, covering every bit of this planet and it's floating islands high in the sky.
In this amazing sequel to 'Grow Home' this time B.U.D. is on a rescue mission. After crashing into an asteroid field, M.O.M. has disintegrated and her pieces are scattered all over an exotic planet. It is your task to pick up the pieces and put them back together. Besides, you will have to catalogue all plants, find upgrades, collect all crystals, find all telerouters, complete all challenges and reach the moon. Not a simple task, giving the fact that at the beginning of the game you're pretty helpless, stranded without devices. But this time you're not alone. P.O.D., a satellite, is there to help. It allows you to scan the planet making it easier to find your objectives.
In comparison to 'Grow Home', 'Grow Up' is bigger. B.U.D. has received enhanced abilities like converting into a ball and rolling around or storing plant seeds right in its own database, making it possible to anytime grow all kind of plants already found. You no longer need daisies to parachute or a leaf to glide. Glider and parachute are permanently available, once you found the upgrades and collected the necessary amount of crystals. Star plants don't grow as high as in 'Grow Home' and climbing has become less necessary. It's more about floating and flying this time. All in all it is a great evolution.

I also among so many others in the review section love this series, and I actually have played the past games again very recently (Literally one after another just to get to this game, and I have written reviews for them also – Shameless plug). I was hyped at the idea of learning more about Stark and Arcadia, I really do love this created world and its characters, but I would be lying if I said it was the best game in the trilogy; in fact to me it’s the worst.
Now, its not a broken game and it definitely looks amazing but that's just the shell underneath this game it lacks the same soul of the past games, and its 90% mainly the fault of the writing. Honestly I gave Dreamfall:TLJ a negative point for that because the story flowed so smooth and fast that right when everything (The story) is heavily stacked up and you're completely invested, it ends.
I feel so salty about the presentation of this game that I want to give this game a thumbs down but honestly I would be lying to myself if I didn't admit that as a fan of the series they didn't tie up mostly all of the major story lines from the older games and answer most of my questions, although the way this game gave me those things to me felt like it plopped some goop on a plate and told me to enjoy.
I know people are saying we should be grateful for whatever we get but sorry no, I’m not that type of person. I can appreciate something while also noticing its faults. I can also find entertainment in something I overall didn't enjoy (example a party's music might be terrible but as long as the drinks are good, what would I care about the music lol or going to a terrible movie and walking out thinking at least the action was great). This game is a product that I paid for no matter what way it came about to being and deserves a consumers glance and review.
Anyway this game has so many low moments for me in the early chapters that I could write a lengthy essay but I think it redeems its self for me in the later chapters primarily chapters 4-5 like the ending parts of the saga story line, or that scene where that you get the achievement “The Longest Journey Home”. Man that actually brought a tear to my eye, and I was beginning to think this game couldn't possibly make me feel like that, but the feels definitely were strong.
Like I said I could right an essay on this game but since id rather not hit the character limit on this review I'll just simply end this with an analogy, This game is like a "Sloppy Joe Sandwich"-The other games was you buying the ingredients and cooking them. Now this game is you putting it all together. It looks great, Its Meaty, seasoned, and with a hearty filling bun holding it together. By the time you pick it up and bite in half the meat fell back on the plate and the ground...Cursing the sky, your left wondering why the gods of old hate you. After coming back from cleaning the food on the ground you discover the bun is soggy as hell now. Now you can finish your messy meal with a happy go-lucky smile on your face or wallow in self deprecation shoveling it down your gullet like some sewer rat (This was the route i took). You could also shove this slop in the trash and treat yourself to a premium 5 star deliciousness (an actual good game) for dealing with the stress of this game...If i could give this game a "Meh" i would but it doesn't deserve a thumbs down. If they ever create another game in this game universe I wont be picking it up. This game killed any interest i could have with the future plot line ideas they laid down.

[SPOILER HEAVY RANT]
As most people that have played this game, i come here as an old fan of the TLJ saga.
While i don't own the other two entries on steam, i still own the original copies.
Despite sitting in my backlog for an uncomfortably long time, i was still very excited to revisit the world of Stark and Arcadia. It was a well crafted world most of us had enjoyed years ago and i went in expecting the same old game i was so fond of.
That was a mistake apparently.
It's hard to dislike the game as it starts out great and agreed, it does start out incredibly fast paced but personally i found that to be fine. Most of the characters were established in previous entries. Fine for returning fans wanting direct continuation, probably immensely confusing for new players. My issues started halfway nearing the end. It becomes very clear that their choice of adopting this "telltale-choice-related" gameplay put serious strain on the writers. The game starts biting off more than it can chew with very disappointing consequences as a result. There's a ton in this game that simply goes nowhere.
- "Be careful, Dad. That's not Reza."
I remembered that line and it made me distrust him for obvious reasons. Even going so far as thinking the only reason they were together was because she was stuck in a simulation and was programmed to be in a relationship with him. (oh.) However, instead of uncovering this and having a plot twist where he could potentially be a Stark antagonist or have the option to save him? Nah, the character disappears halfway in the game only to show up in the epilogue like literally nothing has happened. Yes, he was a brainwashed sleeper agent but this was a plot point.. why? A red herring i suppose?
- "Zoe found the stickiest of the icky in her last couple of chapters and i found myself more weirded out than she was."
Going back to my impression of the writers being overwhelmed and having to.. actually finish the story in this final chapter, i felt this was glossed over so quickly. I get that she already went through a lot of weirdness so not a lot would phase her but learning you're a test-tube baby and getting double the confirmation on how much of a double whammy♥♥♥♥♥♥your mom actually is to only go "oh, okay"..? The complete lack of emotion near the end (of a ton of characters, not just Zoe) just reaffirms they were rushing through things to get it over with.
- "Benrime"
Multiple mentions of her throughout the game, would've been a small nostalgia nod to returning players. Jakai's sacrifice/betrayal was met with zero payoff, not even a small nod if she's okay in the epilogue for it. I'm simply going to assume she's okay.
- "Kian & Alayna"
Ragnar says he always intended for Kian to be gay, i seriously find that hard to believe when he's made various comments about how hot the magical women look in Marcuria and the sexual tension between him and April in previous entries. Ultimately, even with Alayna shoehorned in as a physical gaydar, i don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about his sexual preference but i do have issues with how poorly it is delivered and how it contradicts established lore. I wonder what compelled them to even add this, i get that you get some brownie-points with the LGBT community for this but really, what did it even add to the narrative? Why didn't blind bob shout he was straight awkwardly? At least we get a boatride with what is probably the single worst delivery of the line "I AM GAY" ever. Couldn't we have skipped the boatride and seen some people getting rescued, Benrime perhaps?
His sexual preference wasn't the only odd design choice for him. Early on in the game when arriving at the pub, he mentions he doesn't drink at all. later? he remarks that the beer is okay. Even later? He's comparing wines to the ones he's had back home. Which is it?
- "Saga/Lady Alvane/Deus Ex Machina"
It was great to see the tie-in for this character, i could even argue her character as a standalone was actually pretty decent but her implementation into the story is horrendous. Little to no backstory. All we get is this shifter is "special" and her dad is extremely overprotective. Whatever plot point the game was trying to tie up or hurdle it was trying to overcome nearing the end, she was the answer. Why? "muh prophecy." I'll allude to it again, it came across like the writers needed to tie things up quick and what better way to do it than introducing a character that is (out of nowhere) near omniscient?
quoted verbatim "i feel like i'm playing life on cheat mode."
Another big shame regarding her character is how they gloss over what would've been vastly more interesting stories than the one they gave us regarding her. (Her learning about the prophecies. The war and her helping Kian become the bloodless king. All off-screen.)
"I became amazing off-screen. Now go pick up my drawings." I understand that in an ideal world, we would have gotten all of this in an extra game. My issue just lies purely with the poor implementation of it all. Beyond lazy and why i can not recommend this game.
There's plenty more characters that are extremely underdeveloped for a story heavy game given the lackluster epilogue.
Onor Hileriss (more like Hitleriss) getting nearly double the screentime as opposed to Hanna and Hope, Zoe's sisters and oncemore the lack of anything interesting regarding Saga and her offscreen action. At least we hear about Sully.
I am fully aware i should be thanking the stars for even have gotten this game and in a weird way i am. Despite my rant and frustration with it i am grateful. I did enjoy playing but my god, the last chapter sours the entire experience.
Such a shame because it frustrates me that i dislike the writing so much.

I mean: come on. It's like a child designed this: ooh scars and chains are so great: I'll put them at random places, and don't mind if it makes sense or not. And fysics also don't matter.
And I don't mind if some things don't make sense, after all it's a story, but on the other hand: if you trying to make a game that's almost a movie and it's not a comedy, you have to take care of the design and there has to be some logic to what happens.
Story: If you haven't  played the previous games, you end up asking yourselve what the story is about. You start with a women in a coma and the same woman in a dreamworld and next chapter you're in control of a guy in a medieval setting who's in prison and who used to be an Apostle. There's a lot of referring to the past, but you'll need the previous games to really understand what happened.
And you have to love these games. I don't. Too much talking. It goes like this: 5 minutes of cutscene with a lot of talking. Then you get to solve one puzzle. And again a cutscene with a lot of talking. Again one small puzzle and a decision to make (kill or not kill) and again some cutscenes.  I was more hitting the space-bar to skip the moviescenes then I was actually solving puzzles.
It's like a movie with minor interaction. So after one hour I quit playing. I was completely bored by the lack of puzzles and adventure. Even the movie scene didn't trigger any excitement.
If you like Syberia, you might like this one. For me there's too little on the adventure/puzzle side. I'm more into adventures like monkey island, broken sword and Deponia. Fun and brainteasing, not boring and cinematic. If I want to watch a movie, I'll watch some TV or use Netflix. But an adventure games needs clicking and solving puzzles, not hitting the space-bar to move on.
So, I can't recommend it, although I know there will be people who just love it.

This game is sadly a testament to the saying "Biting off more than one can chew". It is clear that the decision to turn it into a choice-related game bogged down the development process and challenged the writers beyond what they could handle. This means that the characters are mostly forgettable, the locations are few and the plot is filled with numerous holes. There are also several sequences when it is noticable that the game wants you to feel something, yet it has failed to sufficiently get you invested enough in the characters to really care. Maybe this is because of the chapter system, that chops the story up into pieces of different size and quality, which also disrupts the feeling of having a grand journey of sorts, which the previous games did so well.
Speaking of which, you'll be seeing two hub areas over and over again, whilst new locations are few and far between. In previous games you set out on a journey of discovery, showing off the interesting worlds of Marcuria and Arcadia. In this you'll mostly find yourself struggling to navigate two hub areas filled with heavily re-used assets, trying to locate the needle in the haystack of non interactive assets. Whilst the comments and banter of the main characters is well written, it quickly becomes repetetive.
I can live with the janky animations, the numerous graphical bugs during earlier releases and the lacklustre music, but when you jumble up the story of what is essentially an interactive book, I'm out. This all results in a very unsatisfying end to what has been my favourite adventure game series. I'm so disappointed that I don't want to consider this canon.

It is fun playing in the arena with a mate/s (IRL) switching player after each death. The difficulty is on the difficult side for a lot of players these days. It reminds one of videogames during the 80s only with incredible graphics.
I recommend starting in the arena to try combat before starting a new game. Winning your first fight is a rush. After each fight you can loot the NPC body and take clothing, armour and weapons. Some loot can vastly improve your survivability.
There are saves in the game (to a point). Finishing all opponents in the novice arena will permanently unlock access to the expert arena. In the dungeon however you must finish the entire game using one life unless you check the Early Checkpoints box in the options. Early checkpoints will save after completing each level, enabling restarting a level.
The physics engine effects can make for some very interesting, funny, unique and spectacular moments. Your character (and NPCs) can trip over objects in the world. Objects like tables, chairs and other debris all collide realistically. A fight in a room crowded with objects will usually result in objects being knocked over and flung around all over the place. Picking up objects and placing them carefully can be used to build traps or obstacles for the NPCs to trip over and make themselves vulnerable to attack.
The mouse cursor controls where your torso faces, WASD control your movement and left-click and hold to attack. Dragging the mouse over the opponent while using good footwork to put power into your attacks. Right click is used to move your character in the direction of the cursor outside of combat.
Defense is controlled automatically (to an extent). Place the cursor over the direction the attack is coming from to attempt to block it. Attacks that have enough force can still hurt whether you block it or not. A lot of the time avoiding an attack by stepping away is an all round better idea. The speed, angle, force and range of the weapon attacks will affect how much damage is inflicted during attacks.
Movement during fights is controlled with WASD and can be used to great effect to increase power during attacks. Be careful though, bad footwork will throw you off balance and possibly cause your character to stumble or fall over completely. The movement is also cursor relative. It can take some getting used to. With the cursor on the enemy, pressing W will move you toward the enemy, S will move you away, A and D will sidestep.
Finding items can require a keen eye at times. There is no help given for finding items. YOU have to see them and click on them to pick them up. Sometimes this will require moving objects to search underneath objects or move things to gain access to a door.
A lot of reviews have made some very harsh criticisms of the controls. While I do not have a problem with them overall, they could use some fine tuning. It is not an easy game to pick up and play. Lazy or bad use of the controls can make your character appear drunk if not done correctly.
This game uses OpenGl instead of DirectX, some users have had problems running the game. This issue should be reported and a crashlog posted to get the issue fixed.
The graphics are brilliant thanks to good use of textures, lighting and colour palette. It looks super realistic. Remarkably they have accomplished this all using very little VRAM resources. Minimum specs to run it are a 512MB GPU.

As of v0.5.2 Exanima is at best a tech demo for Sui Generis (SG). That isn't to say it's not fun, much in the same ways Gang Beasts and Surgeon Simulator are fun.  The novelty of the stumbling combat physics wears off pretty quickly, but you feel like a complete bad♥♥♥♥♥when you to get feel for it and start killing♥♥♥♥♥♥
Who knows if we'll ever see SG, or where SG will begin and Exanima will end.  This "game" currently has three levels and an arena mode. The game itself has nothing much in the way of quests or real objectives. The core of Exanima is the fighting system, and you'll probably spend most of your time running the arena over and over before making any real progress in the game.
The biggest pain in the♥♥♥♥♥is the fact that you can't save. Although there are checkpoints, you will probably want to scream if you hate the idea of rouge likes and starting over a lot.
That being said, Bare Mettle has made no false claims from what I can gather. They said it would be different, hard, incomplete, require patience, but it would be rewarding if you give it a chance.  So far all of these things are completely true. On that alone I have to recommend Exanima.
As long as you know what you're getting into (and paying for), you should enjoy Exanima for what it is, and hopefully what it will become.

I love the way the combat feels, it's so much more alive than any other game I've played. It may seem really hard at first (it will punish you for any mistake you make) but when you get used to it you will feel like a bad***, slaughtering everything in your path.
The atmosphere is also great, it is set in an expansive underground complex that is filled with undead warriors patrolling it's corridors. The feeling of suspense is tangible as you never know when you're going to run into another baddie; I have opened many doors to promptly slam it shut when I see the undead guy with a rather large axe on the other side.
Another great feature is the armour/clothing, it's not simply about stacking equipment into slots  to get a stat boost, it matters what you wear, and it can all combine creatively; no more head/chest/hands/feet. You can stack your clothing on top of each other to get the maximum benefit of everything. For example you can wear a shirt, put some chainmail over it, put a tunic over that, then wear a plate breastplate to top it all off.
The only criticism I have is the health, and it's not even a criticism, more like I see room for improvement. Considering how ambitious the developers are for the the sequel game Sui Generis, I thought health would be a little more advanced than a health bar. For example; the game Kenshi has health for all your individual limbs and body parts, you could lose the function of your left arm for a time, or if it is damaged enough you could lose it permanently. There is also a blood count which is lowered by being slashed and bleeding (duh) and will knock you unconscious but will regenerate over time and bleeding can be stopped with bandages applied to the damaged body part, which will also heal in time. Sorry for going on about that.
Overall this is a very good game that is definitely worth buying.

The game itself is simple in it's mechanic. The only real challenge is knowing when to push through and when to borrow as the tutorial leads you, more or less, by the hand.  It is possible to make bad decisions and lose out, but with the daily autosave (a more or less standard feature these days), it's possible to take a different approach and get through it. That, however, isn't a bad thing at all.
Graphically it's very nice with a simple UI and approach, yet tools are provided for the more hardcore players of this type of game. The music creates a nice ambience without being irritable, unlike some games. The price is low compared to some of the other "tycoon" style games out there and, although I feel it's worth a little more, it's not too short a sell.
I would like to see more in the way of features and options, particularly once you get to the end game and are making millions per "day". The ability to set up additional studios or buy out competitors and put them to work on supporting projects for your AAA titles or some other way to invest/spend your money end game.
However, the game plays very well without anything added to it and is good value for money. I look forward to seeing what these guys do in the future with the tycoon genre. This is a great foundation to build off of and definitely worth a play.

Anarchy arcade is one of the few games that can manage to take a good concept and actually roll with it. Anarchy Arcade is essentially a 3-d desktop giving you the abilty to load up any map, weather it be a default one or a custom one(You can use any map from source games like cs go ect.), and you can then place essentially well ANYTHING. Images, movies, games, youtube videos,websites, i tunes, netflix, old nes and arcade games, and even those videos you prefer not to watch on your regualar browser if you catch my drift. Each thing you place down acts as a shortcut like one would work on your desktop, you just simply click on it and launches the item at hand weather that be a game or video or whatever so long as you have it or its of the internet.
The game allows for you to be droped in an area and to create an arcade of what ever you can imagine, its a briliant idea but not only that it actually works suprisingly well. Your given the ability to place down again ANYTHING, place a picture from google on the wall, make a room full of snes and sega genesis games, fill a room with youtube videos or music, or even just make a room full of entirely props and manequins of charactrs from your favorite games. Props are essentially "acessory" items and can be placed anywhere to add more of a feel to the game such a couch, shelves, plants and ect.
Despite its earliy acess state, and the game being a one man development project, it still manages to get updated constantly with each one ading new things such as the metaverse mode. This is a mode that allows for nemourous people to be in the same map and create stuff at the same time and build an arcade together. The best part about is that if you have the game or item placed then YOU can launch it even if someone else placed it. The game is free and kind of hard to understand at first but its one of those things you have to try before actually judging it, also the game is described well in the description and in the videos.So despite some of the work it may or may not need it still stands out a unique and interesting so i would say to just try it and if you dont like it then so be it, but atleast give it a chance.

Turok: Dinosaur Hunter was originally released on the Nintendo 64 back in 1997 by Acclaim Studios (R.I.P) and was a staple of FPS & platform gaming. The recently released PC version of Turok has been developed by Night Dive Studios and is pretty much identical to the original version except with updated and better controls & less blocky but still classic 90's visuals.
What little story there is, Turok is a Cherokee Dinosaur Hunter that goes around and fights Dinosaurs, Mercinaries & Aliens in a somewhat modern era. Not only do you use Bows & Knifes but have access to firearms such as Handguns, Shotguns & even some very futuristic weaponry.
Along the way Turok has to stop the aliens from attacking and destroying human kind, Aliens have become a real problem, along with the Dinosaurs and it's up to you to save mankind from them.
The game operates mainly as a fast paced FPS with somewhat moderate platforming elements to frustrate and divert your attention.
The controls are fluent, (especially compaired to the original games) but feel very fast for a game that was designed to be played on about 20FPS, the extra 40 FPS certainly feel very fast for a game of this age and can be somewhat disorienting for lovers of the classic game.
The gunplay is fun but certainly feels very dated & could have used a bit more attention in the development process, however this certainly does not ruin the experience. (Especially if you're a fan of the originals, you will not be let down).
Turok has certainly stood the test of time, graphics wise this game is certainly nothing special & the developers didn't change any of the visuals except for the addition of standard PC settings such as, resolution, bloom effects and texture smoothing, other than that this is the same game from 1997.
Turok: Dinosaur Hunter is and always will be, (in my eyes) a classic title and a must own title for those from the Nintendo 64 era of gaming. If you had a Nintendo 64 then you already know exactly why you must own this game, for those who didn't own a Nintendo 64 now you can own Turok right here on Steam.
Turok is a fantastic game & it's certainly a game that if you're a lover of FPS games & platform gaming then this game will certainly tickle your fancy, on the flip side, if you're all about the graphics then this is not a game you're going to enjoy because the textures are very much classic 90's textures, flat and very little detail infact how they made Turok's face look is somewhat laughable, I certainly don't remember him looking like that on the Nintedo 64.
4/5 a pretty flawless game but needed more done to it, like proper graphical overhauls in certain area's and better frame matching on animations for the enemies and AI.
Yes I do recommend the game to fans of the classic 90's games or just fans of the Turok series in general.
The price may be slightly to steep but this is 2015 not 1997 pricing is always expensive. Could this game have been cheaper? Yeah it probably could've been a more acceptable price of $10 but I'm not complaining as I enjoy the game regardless.
I look forward to getting my hands on Turok 3: Shadows of Oblivion on the PC.... Hint, hint!

Grow Up is a satisfying sequel to Grow Home, but unfortunately suffers from rather counter-intuitive design progression.
By that, I mean that there are a lovely selection of new abilities for BUD to use, however they rarely come in handy. The ball form, for instance, I literally only ever used to break a fall which I didn't even need the ball form to do, because at that point I had plenty of jetpack fuel to slow my descent, or could have used my air breaks which are much more effective. Never used the ball charge seriously, only ever fiddled with it.
I also almost never used the plant seeding feature that allows BUD to drop down plants he has discovered and use their features at that exact spot. When you have a jetpack and a glider, you can essentially go as high as you want, and the more you play, the less valuable this seeding feature becomes.
The multitude of new plants with new ways to ascend is a good concept, but their functionality is extremely redundant. Do the devs really think we're going to use a plant that releases an extremely slow-to-ascend bubble or a rocket-pod plant when we have a jetpack and glider that are only ever constantly being upgraded with each crystal milestone you unlock? I certainly never did.
The game had a lot more content and places to explore though, with an increase of 50 extra crystals to find over Grow Home's original 100, there was plenty of reason to glide around and explore the planet, but far too many insignificant methods to do so.
The Pod Challenges were a nice touch though, however, while it was obvious they intended for you to use certain pre-placed plants to complete a certain challenge, all challenges I did were completed with jetpacking and gliding, with the occasional air-break stop to change my orientation mid-speed-flight.
There also weren't any challenges that emphasized the use of the ball BUD ability, which is a shame. At least, none that I ever noticed. No stretches of terrain that clearly resemble a make-shift racetrack with a very tight timer that would encourage ground-based speed travel.
The Pod Challenges needed to emphasize use of the new Grow Up abilities much more heavily, and should have had restrictions tied to them, such as certain challenges once started, lock your jetpack, or force you to only use your seeder with a certain plant, or disable your glider until the challenge ends. Something that really can't just be done with jetpack hopping on the first try. The only challenges I couldn't do on the first try were 2 or maybe 3, and they were all challenges that clearly emphasized glider thruster use, as the time was very tight.
Grow Up also fails miserably to fix some of the more irritating issues from Grow Home, such as the feature to
.
This is by far the most aggrevating aspect of the game, and it's disappointing even more so because it's the exact same issue Grow Home had.
If you are walking across a large Starplant branch, Bud will occasionally (but sharply) shift his movement to the left or right as the game attempts to keep you on center with the branch so that you don't fall.
This sounds nice, but the way it was programmed was sloppy, and can easily lead to you falling off more often than if the game had left it well enough alone, and just let the player grow accustomed to BUD's controls, and learn to balance their movement on wonky terrain shapes themselves.
This feature of the game forcing BUD to move to certain zones also applies for plants.
Certain plants, like the ones that launch you into the air when you sit in their center, BUD will bee-line for the center of that plant, which is useful enough, however, like I said, this is sloppily programmed. Other plants, like the small orange flower-catapult plant don't do this at all. In fact, it seems a bit broken, as BUD seems to ignore some of my movement input and actually attempt to step off the plant, or just straight up REFUSE to stop right on the plant no matter which keys I press as he walks over it.
This inconsistency with BUD movement in a game about exploring and traversing makes it just as much of a nightmare to explore on the ground or use the climbing feature as it was in Grow Home.
Fortunately, flying is so quick to unlock and effective (and a bit better programmed) that you will rarely find yourself frustrated by the movement scheme they clearly didn't put enough thought or care into. BUD's controls are looser and
more inconsistent than they actually need to be, simply because the programmers think it's smart to take partial control away from the player at random intervals for random tiny durations just so the game can auto-correct your movement/positioning for you, regardless of if that's what the palyer was actually trying to do or not.
For people like me that enjoyed Grow Home enough to do self-imposed challenges like crystal-less runs of the game, this embarrassingly brain dead position-correction system they stupidly didn't refine even slightly from Grow Home being left in the game for the sequel just makes there be no excuse.
Grow Up has so much extra content it really doesn't know what to do with a lot of it. The sequel seriously needs more achievements and/or special challenges that span the entire length of the game once the player has beaten it initially to utilize the new aspects rewardingly.
As a sidenote, the game also suffers from clearly not having a proofreader. Multiple plant data entries, and even dialogue from characters in the game is blatantly improper grammar. I'm not talking about "then" versus "than", I'm talking about the word "so" being used when the word "the" should have been used. Really middle-school-esque English mistakes.
Also, on launch day there were a few issues, which is normal and not something to crucify a title for or anything, however one was very serious.
I came across it myself in fact. A glitch where, after prolonged periods of playtime (3 hours, in my case) a horribly loud blaring noise plays at random over and over again. It's not part of the game, it sounds more like a soundeffect that is played 5000 times all at once, resulting in a genuinely ear-damaging sound that, if you like playing with loud volume to begin with, could very well lead to some sort of lawsuit against the devs for negilgently allowing such a serious issue to go into the final version.
It was patched 2 days later, but the note claims it's only "less likely" to occur, not fixed...
Overall, it's a solid sequel that has everything you would expect a sequel to have over its predecessor, Grow Home. 5 Starplants to grow, instead of 1, with each growing to different maximum heights and having their own themes and gimmicks. More adorable critters to play with. Extension of the satisfying music from the first game. More means of getting around (even if many are redundant) and it's overall a bigger more intricate Grow Home, but at the same time, bigger is not better in this case, it instead means messier in a way. I recommend the game, absolutely. However, it is not without its flaws.
If you want a relaxing, enjoyable experience you'll never return to after beating, absolutely give it a try, but there is obvious polishing the devs CHOSE not to focus on. Again, for a sequel, there is no excuse, but it is legitimately more of what made Grow Home enjoyable through and through, so there's that.
That "Seizure Warning" disclaimer right when you start the game up that fades away far too quickly to give anyone time to read the entire thing made me chuckle though. Clearly they didn't care about people who might actually receive some sort of seizure trigger from their game, they were just legally covering their own butts. Come on, guys. Make it a click-away screen so people can read the warning. Don't just
it there so you can't be sued.

Grow Up, sequel to the wonderful Grow Home that released 18 months prior, stars the goofy little robot BUD as he attempts to rescue his MOM after their spaceship collides with an asteroid. Where Grow Home featured a lone Star Plant on a mostly featureless space of water that you needed to grow to harvest its seeds, Grow Up features an entire planet that you get to explore from the get-go. Basic movement is still as much silly fun as it was last time thanks to BUD's unique animations and simple (but fun) climbing controls. In terms of the exploration, finding new abilities and secrets is now more engaging in spite of the much larger scale thanks to BUD's new companion, POD, who hovers up and above and can scan almost anywhere in little time. All these small things come together to make Grow Up one of the most entertaining platformers that I've ever played, and one of the best games of the year.
Short pros and cons:
+What looks cheery and happy is smile-inducing to PLAY
+Old school platforming with a vibrant, fun world you want to just live in at times
+Like Grow Home, another great Ubisoft game on Steam without a Uplay requirement...
~...but there are bonus outfits for BUD only in the Uplay version. (Not a negative necessarily, but it's worth mentioning.
-Some upgrades, if acquired too early
, do make the game lose some of its charm.
Grow Up is a worthy sequel to Grow Home, and will probably be seen as one of the best games of the year by those who play it (and for good reason). If something should be noted, playing Grow Home first does make you appreciate this game's scale more, but otherwise this game is a delight start to finish. Highly recommended.

Now I bet you're asking to yourself looking at this. "This is the cheapest Shantae game on the Steam market! Wohoah, I wanna get this!" Now hold on buckaroo. Before we do that, as a person who has beaten this game through several sittings,  let's go over a few things you'd want to hear for.
Shantae: Risky's Revenge is the sequel to the underrated Shantae game on the Gameboy Color.Shantae's Risky Revenge technically takes place right after the events of Shantae, and it pits you in another conflict against Risky, in which she steals a forbidden lamp and seeks out to steal the seals in order to restore the lamps power.
As the plot goes, don't really expect too much for it. What you should focus less is on the plot.
Now you may be wondering. Is this game actually worth it? Well, it certainly is currently the cheapest game, but it fails on a lot of aspects. The world sometimes does feel very barren and weak in comparison to the first title and it focuses less on showing you where to go, so the game decides to be very subtle and non-explanatory that it begins to get infuriating to navigate the areas of Sequin Land and all around it. Sometimes it can be very weird that many of the dialogue of the characters mainly talk in jokes and humorous phrases that it makes it hard to put everything together to solve problems and get to new areas. The game's navigation however, is very interesting, even though for it's metroidvania style, it is nothing astonishing, it settles on making discovering new areas compelling and fun, despite it's
shortcomings.
However, as the sequel to a groundbreaking Gameboy Color game, this game is also rather short, and could be beaten in about 6-7 hours depending on your skill on navigating and backtracking for collectables or necessary items to go deeper into the plot. Or certainly, you may sometimes need to bring up walkthroughs or google "what to do next", because I guarantee you, this will happen at least once or twice, which can be rather frustrating.
An interesting aspect I find that this game has is that it could certainly have a lot of upgrades for magical abilities and attacks, so stocking up on money is a good idea to make Shantae stronger and more affective. Looting off of enemies in areas for their money is essential, and it puts a lot of meaning into collecting money and spending it on the right things. They also have items and accessories like Potions of Health and Magic meter. Sometimes, I do feel that the Potions can be a little bit over the top with how much health they restore, that it makes fighting bosses a cakewalk at times, but
that's merely just my opinion.
As the game progresses, you will end up fighting many bosses with tons of humor and nice designs. Speaking of which, I do certainly find the textures and areas of the game very appealing, as well as it's upbeat soundtrack, reusing many of the classic tracks of the previous game, and extending them with more top notch beats. Certainly, I will feel that if you do enjoy many soundtracks from games like Kirby or Sonic, they may somehow reach up and get stuck in your head, but I am not
one to judge your preferences.
Certainly, Shantae is much more badass than the previous game, but somehow the transformations just weren't very vast to me, as it was a bit less transformations that you had than the first game. The environment doesn't really make use of the transformations abilities too often so they end up not have many uses.
Well, we're reaching the conclusion. Whether this game is up to be purchased by you is entirely your own opinion. While the game has many good features that make it an excellent platformer, it just doesn't quite live up to the others in terms of actual content and length. It remains humorous and upbeat and jolly, with many interesting areas and good to explore locations, but sometimes it just doesn't seem like it's enough and less work was poured into it. Navigation can be a pain and sometimes kills the fun value, but of course you can still teleport to marked locations once you gain access to several statues so it isn't as bad as you think.

Shantae is one of those fringe franchises that has been around for 15 years now but hardly anyone has actually played. The original released for the Game Boy Color back in 2002, well after the Game Boy Advance had already released and frankly, the game would have benefited from the increased resolution of the newer console. Turns out, playing metroidvania-style games with large sprites and very little screen space isn't that fun. Yeah, I'm looking at you, Metroid 2!
Still, despite the low sales, the game was well-received and a sequel was eventually greenlit for the DS to be made available for download on the new DSiWare service. This game was Shantae: Risky's Revenge. Another 4 years passed and we eventually got to play the Director's Cut version on Steam.
So, that's the backstory but what actually is it? Honestly, there is very little apart from the art style to set Shantae: Risky's Revenge apart from any of the numerous other metroidvanias out now. While most of those games are dark and mysterious, often taking place in caves or at night, Shantae is very bright and colorful, taking place on a tropical island. The music is also cheery throughout most of the game and it does a lot to break up the monotony of grimdark games, for sure.
Unfortunately, not only does the gameplay not stand apart, it actually doesn't even copy the formula very well. Shantae: RR's world is just small. When you first get the world map only a few minutes into the game, you may actually have the same reaction I did and think, "this must just be one section of the game". It's not.
Due to the small game world, the game could have gone with really tough, challenging gameplay OR tedious backtracking and aimless wandering. Guess which way they went? I have seen some people talk about how Shantae is known for its challenging gameplay but they must not be talking about Risky's Revenge. The only times I ever died were because I wasn't paying attention or I was so bored going through the same area for the 20th time that I charged through the enemies hoping I could just get past that screen.
While the game does require you to go back to the same areas several times and has an abysmal warp system to support you, the main cause for all of the backtracking is that the game never tells you where you need to go to do anything at all. One character may say, "next up, go find the Ammo Baron!" and that's all the instruction you will get. Go Google this game's world map. Do you see Ammo Baron listed there? Look really hard, maybe you missed it. No, still nothing? THAT'S BECAUSE IT ISN'T THERE!
At least those sections though, you know what you're looking for. There are several late game items that you need to get that the game never even tells you to find. You will just stumble upon some obstacles you can't get past and need to scour the entire world looking for the hidden artifacts you missed without even knowing what they are. It's not a challenging game and rarely will you even need to heal up but this type of tedium extends the game by hours.
The dungeons are even worse. Each dungeon in the game thrusts you into a confusing labyrinth that never provides you with a map or a quick exit back to the outside. One dungeon makes you flip switches to change where the nearby door will take you so if you get lost in that dungeon, good luck finding your way back outside! Fortunately, there are only two real dungeons in the whole game.
The one break from the tedious backtracking and small world are the bosses. Each boss you have to face provides a unique challenge and usually involves some puzzle mechanics that you'll have to figure out in order to succeed. The bosses take a TON of damage so don't expect to just muscle your way through. While this can be repetitive once you've gotten the boss strategy down, I appreciate that it at least forces you to find a pattern and truly master the boss.
Too bad there are only 4 unique bosses in the entire game. One boss you get to fight twice and they are also the easiest of the four. Even though none of the bosses posed a particularly great threat, they broke up the monotony and more would have been greatly appreciated.
Shantae has the bones of a good metroidvania. The setting and characters are interesting plus the plot is charming, if not particularly engrossing for anyone over the age of 10. The combat feels alright and the movement is likewise, not the best but not the worst either. Unfortunately, massive amounts of tedious backtracking and poor warp zones make even this 5-6 hour adventure feel like it has overstayed its welcome. If you really must play every Shantae game out there, you can find this on Steam for 10 bucks but if you just need a metroidvania fix, there are plenty of better games out there for the same price.

Shortly:
There's not much I can tell about this game, except its an 2D platformer. If I presume right, this game is a sequel to the original Shantae game made for Game Boy Color device back in 2002.
Shantae: Risky's Revenge is old-schooll styled 2D platformer. The game follows semi-linear path, meaning that you can explore the entire world once you've obtained the required items and skills from dungeons to do so.
The game is not very long, in fact you can finish it in 4 hours if you rush through it (there's even an achievement for that). But if you explore every nook and cranny, collect every collectible like I did, you can extend that 4 hours of gameplay into ~10 hours.
Pros:
+ Has this old-school 2D platformer feeling in it
+ Save system - if you don't save manually, you'll be punished for dying
+ Simple dungeons and bosses
+ Pixxelated graphics - who needs triple A quality graphics when the game itself is enjoyable?
Cons:
- Could have been a little longer
- Not much replayability (unless you're achievement hunter)
Do I recommend:
If you're into old-school 2D platformers, I do recommend you to try this one out.
Verdict: 7 / 10 - Good 2D platformer

BUY THIS GAME RIGHT NOW... and take 3 hours of time to get used to its awful controls.

But it is all worth it. This game was made with real love - the environments, which at first seem to be Baldur's Gate-era grey grit, actually have deep and distinct detail - the rooms are laid out smartly, the lighting well-planned and the objects feel real and weighty.
The combat starts off like jello ragdoll and ends up being a fluid, organically dangerous ballet of real swordsmanship. You will at the same time dread, panic and delight when you see the shadow of another person in the doorway.
Exanima deserves your attention.

First off, this is not a "total HD remake", as that's not what Night Dive Studios focuses on. The game has been "cleaned up" as I like to call it; upscaling everything to modern resolutions, increased draw distance, optimized for smooth 60fps, and modernized the controls to the familiar WASD scheme. Even the menu feels right at home, with the same look and feel, albeit a few new options for PC specific settings. All of the classic music and sounds return. The precision of the mouse is a godsend from what I remember as horrificly cumbersome N64 analog stick aiming.
Literally my only complaint would be that the audio side of things doesn't match up with the visual upkeep; everything is still low bitrate sound clips and music. A minor nitpick at what is otherwise another very well done gravedigging from Night Dive.

Then it starts to become intuitive, you learn to handle the character, to flow with momentum, feint, judge range, control your movement rather than letting your weapon control you.  This is where the game REALLY blossoms, the tactical importance of a step forward or a step back, judging your opponent, finding ways inside their guard and directing the cutting edge of your strike for the weakest armor (often enough it's the face).
It's still in early access, but based on what I've seen things can only get better.  I love coming home and dumping an hour or two into hacking away at the NPCs.  For anyone interested in this game, I'd highly suggest you also look at their website for their open world game Sui Generis (still in production as of this writing).

On The Eight Day God Created Turok
And what a creation it was, Turok was a landmark game for it's time and a classic on the N64. The game would later be ported to PC with some minor changes and a better sounding soundtrack but the game was locked to Voodoo graphics cards; didn't have one? You're screwed. I'm not sure if the game saw the amount of popularity that other shooters on PC saw at the time but the game faded away with time.
Until now the only way to really play it was on the N64, but Night Dive has revived it for the PC and they did a tremendous job. First off the game controls perfectly but you can change anything to your liking if need be. Visual options allow you to turn on some modern graphical effects (sun shafts, reflects on water) that were absent in the original PC release. You also get an option to increase the draw distance which helps a LOT, the game was damn near known for it's notoriously short draw distance due to "fog." You can even change the FOV if you care to, very nice touch. Overall the game runs perfectly and I haven't had any issues with it in my 5+ hours of playtime. Well done.
How does the game hold up? Really, really well. Save for the dated visuals the gameplay is really fast-paced and fun. Turok himself moves at a ridiculous speed but it's all for the better, enemies hit hard if you get careless and there's a lot of weapons to toy around with and find out what works best on which enemy. The levels are also nice and varied, starting off quite linear and short and slowly growing into large and complex sprawls with various ways to go. Secret areas are hidden all over and there's some backtracking to do if you didn't get all the keys in your first go. The game always keeps you engaged without feeling unfair or bored. You'll find things to shoot around every corner.
So what're the down sides? Well, the enemies are only programmed for the aforementioned short draw distance of the original release, so a lot of the times you can just see guys standing around waiting for you to get into sight. Since you can see them, you can free shoot them without any issues and sometimes they won't even become hostile if they're far enough. Night Dive also decided to redo SOME of the graphics, this is minor but things like the font, main title logo and ammo counters are done up nicely; the issue is only SOME of the UI art has been touched up which is a little jarring. Turok's head is the original art but the number next to it (signifying lives left) is nice, crisp and completely redone. Also having the giant stone "PAUSE" sign on top of the pause screen looks terrible as it's really low res and muddy.
If you loved this game as a kid, you'll love it still today, it's still a great title that's aged well. If you've never played Turok this is the best one to start with. Night Dive is working on Turok 2 and I can't wait.
Update: With the sequel released, I can say with confidence that Turok 1 is the better game. Start here for sure if you're interested in these games.

As a massive fan of city-builders, this game lodged itself solidly into my heart. The art style is simple but beautiful - you can play the game for hours without feeling like your eyes are being strained by some cloudy color scheme. Menus are exactly what menus need to be, no more and no less. I really like how the game doesn't have a tutorial level that is separate from the main game - the tutorial and main game are integrated very well.
The main game struggles from a lack of challenge - unless you're on the hardest difficulty, there is barely any punishment for failing to defend against dragons and viking raiders. I managed to build and maintain a city without keeping an army, which doesn't quite seem realistic, even on normal difficulty.
Once I had upgraded my village to a city, there were no longer any upgrades to make. This is probably my biggest problem with the game - you max out pretty quickly. However, I still love this game! If you're looking for a laid-back, endearing city-builder to play from time to time, this is the game for you. I know that I'll definitely be coming back every so often to build a dope-looking castle and unsuccessfully defend against viking raiders.

Kingdoms and castles is pretty decent but lacks depth and long term playability. It's fairly bright and pretty and at first there's enough to be getting on with, but after a few hours it becomes quite repetitive and gives no real payback for investing more time in it.
That said, it's early access and it has potential if the developers can add more layers to it. It's definitely a good start and already a reasonable example of the genre, although I feel  games like banished have more management to them.
For seasoned city building veterans - you'll get ~10 hours of enjoyment, and then you'll maybe come back every so often to see if the game has evolved.
For city building novices, it's a good entry game into the genre, leading to harder games with more depth and also more incline.
I count myself as a veteran and I enjoyed this and look forward to revisiting.

Pleasant to eye if you like futuristic aesthetics, and has rather similar edges and problems of anno game with few major points however; before I start let me remind you this game operates in FIXED sectors, basically each 'city' you build, in terms of resource flow and requirement is divided into said sectors; Big issue with them is the fixed part - no matter how many times you restart, game will ultimately compose of exactly the same set of sectors ready to grab; If you value order of conquest highly that may give some replayability, but has major limitations:
- Trade System - As mentioned above - game operates on sectors; It allows for transfer of goods between sectors [no, rly?]; however all transport system is limited to 'go to planet menu -> set trade route by choosing two sectors, goods to transport and amounts ('per minute' or more practically - 'the change in stock per minute], and you're set; Of course these trade routes are impossible to interdict [even with frontiers]; The second reason is:
- Combat - or practical lack of it; Your combat choices are limited to tactical control of few ships on combat maps; Composition? dependent on your level; Strenght? Dependent on your level + minor resource 'investment' for upgrade; Even frontiers push combat to... borderline activity. But that's not that big of an issue because:
- Enemies - in past game enemies did something in game; here - they are just arbitrary numbers that slowly increase; Their actions affect you in marginal level, mostly giving you access to temporary upgraes.
- Rare Materials - I'm not sure who got the 'genius' idea to make it available from combat sites alone [few predefined, at some point you could simply record a macro to blitz that, as of course - specific maps do not have variations in enemy locations, number strenght or any other that would make each combat unique], but that's not a problem; there are 2 more ways to get them: first is buil a special project [tough luck - the moment you build it chances are these resources are mostly worthless anyway], or via... mobile companion game.... yes, I'm not even kidding; To get resources in PC game if you're bored to hell with in-game combat system and methods, you're reccomended to play a mobile game; Is it at least fun? well if you like connect X games you may be not bored to hell; Of course - yu have chance to easen your burden... by paying to get diamonds; You can of course grind them, at extremely slow rate. I.E. what is limiting your progress in Anno 2205 is not your own skills in game, but wether or not you get bored to hell with either combat system in game, or simply - don't want to bother with mobile game.
Some previous games of this series had fun multiplayer option; this one cannot have it; it's mechanics are so single player centric, based on single meaningful playthrough [unless you count other starting sectors as 'meaningful playthroughs], with no ability to find anything new [maps are all the same after all], that multiplayer interaction would be impossible to implement. Too bad.
And there's a final nail to the coffiin. Ubisoft Policies; Truth be said - I despise false advertisers, and Ubisoft intended to pull just that at moment of Frontiers release. Initially Biggest edition was to include 'any future content INCLUDING Tundra and Orbit expansions' later with addition of Frontiers it was quickly corrected to remove words 'ANY' and 'INCLUDING', making collectors' edition basically incomplete. Only after massive uproar of community, followed by [according to Ubisoft own forums] even report to consumer rights representatives Ubisoft announced that 'now Frotier Expansion is included in collectors edition'. As such Ubisoft credibility, however lax it was plummeted down in my eyes to non-existent. I decided to pick this game up as part of the 2017 summer sale.  Although there are a fair amount of rough edges in this game, it was overall a very enjoyable, quirky, and funny experience, and had solid platforming / metroidvania mechanics to go along with it.  I would definitely recommend picking this game up, although this wouldn't be my first pick if you wanted to play a game in this series.
My main gripes were with regards to the teleporting... some of the locations for the teleports were awkwardly placed, to say the least.  Like, why wasn't there a teleport directly to town?  Also, some of the dungeon design was a little unnecessarily complex and I didn't have the patience to figure out a good portion of the puzzles on my own, although that was partly because I wanted to move through the rest of the games in the series.  Also, the controls felt unresponsive at times, especially when compared to the Pirate's Curse, the next game in the series.
Besides that, though, the game was very fun, the story was quirky and didn't take itself seriously, and it was a nice length.  Also, the music is fantastic, as is the art / animations.
