I've been playing Starbound for a couple of years through it's development.  Chucklefish has signifiantly improved this game since the initial beta release. I love being able to explore plants and discover different places. Yes, it looks and sounds like other games, but the gameplay is different and that is what makes it stand out.  I enjoy sandbox - strategy - RPG games!

Chucklefish did a decent job making Starbound. Of course, it has it's vices, but so does every game. If you don't mind interstellar "fetch quests" for the main story, then the main story will seem alright to you. However, at the end of these "fetch quests", there is a chance you'll encounter a boss fight that you'll enjoy. Each one has some unique kick to it, whether it be invincible through conventional means, has waves of minions to assault you, or otherwise. Couldn't care less for the main story? Then don't bother with it! The main story offers little to no bonus besides satisfaction and story telling. Lore fanatic or completionist? Codex entries are scattered throughout the universe to detail each of the seven playable races, and even more to describe to many more entities that occupy the same vastness. Story Missions have extra loot, such as weapons, cosmetics, codex entries, and more, and offer even more loot to those who come back later on.
I've have Starbound for a long time, an amount which I cannot recount when I first got, but I've recently re-completed the story. I've gone ahead to add in Workshop content (And maybe even a few mods from the internet) to spice up the post-game. Sure, it can be boring, but you can do plenty of things. Wanted to create that ultimate castle full of servants? Go ahead! Need a military base camp on that moon? Consider it done. Wanted to re-create Atlantis? Easy. Honestly, Starbound has more to offer than most people bother to look.
Pro Tip: The Hotbar at the top actually has a second layer to it. If you want a Combat Hotbar and a Building Hotbar, that makes it much more convenient, rather than opening your inventory and switching tabs every ten seconds.

They need to make better controls and a better way to handle the camera. Unless that's done you shouldn't bother with this game, especially because of random sh*t like not being able to bind the alt key to "toggle combat". (You can bind it to "interact", for example, but not to "toggle combat". JUST to give you an idea of the bs you're confronted with in this game.) Also, as you can see in the trailer it has a rather interesting way of handling interaction with the environment. In the trailer it seems as though you can support your character by handling all kinds of objects in your environment independently from what your character's doing or where he's located (as if the player character was getting help from something supernatural that is controlled by your cursor, while you're navigating your character with the W, A, S and D keys. Then, when toggling combat the mouse is used to swing at opponents and block and all that while interaction with the environment is disabled. That would have worked brilliantly I would imagine.) - But in reality, you can't really use the W, A, S and D keys to move, because as you will realize yourself when you take your first steps in-game, it's extremely impractical, as the reference to where your character will move when pressing W, for example, is actually where your character is facing, NOT toward the upper end of the screen. THAT they need to change. Being able to interact with the environment is, in fact, very limited to what your character is doing and where he is. You can still open a door from like 4 meters away, but not from 5 meters, you see what I mean? It's really impractical and unnecessary, especially because the controls are so clumsy; they'll have you walk all the way up to a door where you could finally open it, but oops: you can't, because your character is now blocking the door. The camera should not have to be adjusted by the player. Walls that are blocking your sight could be made transparent. Other than that I don't think there's much to complain about. Great idea, poor execution regarding controls so far. I'd love to play this game, but personally as it is now I can't.

This review is being edited now because when I first wrote it I was very frustrated by this game.  I say "very frustrated" because I'm lacking words to adequately describe how I was feeling.  I was frustrated because the game is so lovely to look at and to be in.  It was like opening presents at Christmas when you were a child.  I proper settled down to it and I was convinced I was going to enjoy this.  The setup was perfect and I couldn't believe my luck at finding this gem.  When my character woke up in the first room my expectations were met; I was set.  It is so obvious that the devs of this game have perfectly created their vision for the one thing that, just the very hope of, most immediately attracted me to their product:  Atmosphere.  This game oozes atmosphere.  And it isn't style over substance.  It's real atmosphere.  Measured, disciplined, detailed:  Atmosphere.   And it is gorgeous to behold.  The lighting engine, the minute attention to detail, the music, the props.  It is all fantastic.  You want to really immerse yourself in this.  Like a hot bath after being in the freezing cold all week.  But I couldn't.
The game is effectively impenetrable for myself.  A lot of people like this game, love it in fact.  The Devs have a very loyal fan base, and deservedly so.  Like I say:  The care and attention to detail in the very, very small part of this world that I've been able to see is very attractive.
I should have stayed in that first room and not opened the door.
The combat in this game is not intuitive.  I know they state that on the product page, but you think to yourself you'll give it a whirl, "how bad can it be?".  But I mean this is really unintuitive, you may not be able to enjoy it, you may not be able to do it at all, and then you effectively can do nothing in the game.  This is a negative review because you could buy this and basically not be able to use the product.  Like me.  This game was a waste of money for myself.  Other people obviously love it.  I can't get down the first corridor.
The combat is physics based.  And I hate it.  Momentum, inverse kinematics, collision detection.  It's all in there.  A technological marvel really.  There is some very clever mathematics going on here.  But you'd expect that. . .  It's in keeping with the beautiful attention to detail in the rest of the game. . . I would expect to see a Game Programming Gems article from one of the Devs at some point in the future.  And it's very polished.  It's slick in fact.  It should be everything you ever wanted.
What this physics manifests itself as though is a very unresponsive interface.  You want to swing your weapon, and time passes, and then you sort of swing half heartedly.  It's awkward.  You might swing your sword as your body turns into it and the blade sort of just doesn't swing.  It's unsatisfying to play as I know that in real life I can swing a bat.  When you walk there is no strafe, so you slide down the corridor walls then fall over something, or you correct this with A or D but turn too much and you walk like a drunk, over-correcting in an uncoordinated way, winding way.  Fighting exacerbates this.  Combat feels like you are exhausted and disorientated.  You can't just do what you want your avatar to do.
Never have I thought I'd do better if me, myself, replaced my computer game avatar.  I found myself literally screaming at my monitor for my character to do. . . just something. . . To walk in a straight line. . to swing a weapon without falling over.  To hit just something, anything.  To do something when I pressed the button for that action to be carried out.  It wouldn't be so bad if the delay was predictable.
It was this combat that was the worst part for myself.  I was almost 6 hours in and I’d never won a fight at the point I wrote the review.  I did win one fight after I wrote the first review.  I'd stopped playing the dungeon part of the game and was doing the arena part.  It didn't feel satisfying to win, I was just surprised, I got lucky.  Not really sure what I did differently.
It's got character movement and impact physics, in combat, a bit like Die By the Sword.  That game was played for laughs and didn't offer much.  You don't exactly quite control the sword swings in this game.  It's got a lot of Mount and Blade in it too.  But whereas Mount and Blade's combat felt connected and solid and immediate - this is just detached feeling - like I saw it's just not responsive.  Mount and Blade’s game play was difficult to learn.  This game's game play is obviously difficult to learn too.  But I feel Mount and Blade benefited from being in the third person.
As I stagger and fall over all the time playing this game it starts to feel more like Sumotori Dreams crossed with gang beasts.  I felt my character was pathetically weak, and almost an unconscious drunk just staggering around a dungeon.  I would slowly waggle your weapon in front of myself, staggering two steps at a time away from, towards, around, maybe a bit more away from, then trip and fall over.  My feet were always uncoordinated for my attack.  And although you auto parry, so does the enemy, and sooner or later you'll get hit as you misjudge when you can try a strike.
Because of the physics, momentum, there is no immediacy to your actions and I guess you need to play the game a few milliseconds into the future, because you need to overcome inertia before you can start to do the thing you wanted to do, (but isn't a good idea anymore), a few moments ago.
Also.  I didn't find continuing to bang my head against a wall to be worthwhile because:  There is no save.  There never will be either based upon the community feedback on this feature.  It’d be like starting Dragon Age Origins or Dark Souls, and having to complete the entire game in one sitting.  You can't come back to it as every time you die you have to start from the very beginning and retread the same content as before.  Over and over again.  It isn't procedurally generated.
At this stage I'd love someone to tell me the cheat code - so I could at least just enjoy walking around the beautiful world in god mode.  Please will a Dev give me the console command?  I want to see what's at the end of the corridor - I gave you my ten quid - I just can't care about the combat anymore. . .
The community were helpful when I asked for help.  It made no difference.  The game is just fundamentally impenetrable.  For me at least.
But the community and the Devs might want to think about this.  As much as this is your game.  And it's how you want it. . . . . .  And you are very protective of it. . . .  What proportion of gamers are going to be prepared to spend hours before they kill their first enemy, do you think?  When that first kill doesn't even feel like an achievement?  When it felt like luck?  What proportion? .  Dark Souls is hard.  But most people can get some satisfaction and progress in that. . Enough to keep them going.  PvP in EVE online is hard, but you at least know what happened when you die.  You at least can relate your actions to the result. . . .  Is your learning curve too high?  Can everyone actually enjoy your game?  Or is this product essentially useless to some people, like myself, bearing in mind Steam doesn't do refunds?   Are you going to address this in anyway?

INTRO:
Exanima (V0.5.2)
Developer:  Bare Mettle Entertainment
Publisher:  Bare Mettle Entertainment
£10.99 as of 21/05/15
Exanima is  Bare Mettle Entertainment's first steam release and is a new, early access RPG which features a unique physics engine. The engine gives the user a refreshing control system that is easy to learn but hard to master. You wake up in a medieval prison of some sort, with just a letter in your pocket and a torch on the ground next to you, the rest is up to you to find out. Alternatively, you can play in arena mode which puts you in a one on one combat situation with 2 difficulty settings.
In combat your character is subject to balance, physical limitations and momentum. For instance, swinging a huge sledgehammer will send your character off balance and running into the same direction and it is up to you to correct it to steady yourself. This isn't particularly recommended as you'll most probably end up staggering around like a guy who's had too many flagons of mead. If it's not the mead that makes you fall to the floor it'll be your opponents weapon colliding with your face. If you've ever swung a heavy object you'll know exactly how it feels and best of all, the movements in the game are believable. You really get a feel of how your character moves and how to adapt to the weapon you're using. The combat makes for a challenging yet rewarding experience that can lead to a very intense, addictive experience.
*Insert picture of title page*
GRAPHICS:
In short, the graphics are excellent. The gloomy visuals really put you in place of a medieval dungeon. The lighting effects are exceptional, the shadows provided by the torch and other scarce light sources are very good and realistic. If you stand next to a crate all the individual gaps inside it shine the light through the object and at a wall. I spent a considerable amount of time in the starting room just admiring the graphics, as well as chuckling at the potential of derpy legs and comical trips, which I will cover a bit later. Also, my girlfriend took a short look and compared the game to an “Indiana Jones Gladiator” aesthetic which actually isn't too bad of an analogy on a first look, which also gave me a giggle.
AUDIO:
Exanimas ambient audio really fits in well with the game setting, the music is gloomy and spooky, easily being reusable in a horror game. The footsteps echo nicely and the weapon noises are realistic and well created. Both the graphics and audio give the game an impressive first look.
GAMEPLAY:
So now to the gameplay, with most of this section will be dedicated to the games physics system.
If you don't want to go through all the technical aspects, the TL:DR section provides a nice, humorous story of one of the situations I caught myself in game.
Controls are quite minimal but complex in the way they can be used. Generally WASD can be used to move in an old style resident evil type of way out of combat, with A and D rotating your character whilst moving forward or back with W and S. You can alternatively hold the RMB which will make your character follow the cursor. I opens your inventory  where you drag and drop items from either the environment or from a dead body onto your character or into your inventory (which is seemly unlimited I might add … where in his underwear is he hiding all those axes?!). There is possibility for a situation I call “derpy legs syndrome”, where the character can easily trip over objects or gets his feet stuck into the environment. Whilst being a little annoying in the middle of combat it's actually quite amusing when it does happens.
TAB puts your character into his/her combat stance, when you do this, WASD changes to now react relative to the direction of the cursor. As of this, your body rotates to the direction of your cursor, which is actually a very important part of the controls and can help or hinder your character's balance. A and D will make your character strafe whereas W and S will move your character forward and backward.
Holding LMB will cause your character to swing his weapon, the direction and force depends completely on how you control the character. The damage you cause is dependant of:  the speed of the strike, where the strike hits the enemy, the area of your weapon that hits, your character's balance and the stats of the chosen weapon. When you're not attacking, your character attempts to defend automatically. It's helped by your character's posture and the direction you're facing, which adds another element into how you position and control your character. Or you can just run head on into your opponents body and hope for the best (which is actually a decent tactic against weapons with a sharp or blunt edge on a pole). In a matter of speaking, the game puts all the pressure on YOU. The game is very skill based and only you can mess it up for yourself.
There are an infinite amount of tactics you can apply as you play like for instance counter striking your opponent as he starts a huge swing towards you. Beware though, the only place swinging like a madman trying to dismember your opponent will get you is face down on the floor. The AI is in no way dumb, especially in the arena mode. Your opponent also tries to look for your mistakes and weak spots and will capitalise when you're off balance.
Weapons have 2 main stats, and a large amount of others which chow what type of damage they cause (slash, crush, pierce etc)
Weight: Self explanatory, the heavier the weapon the harder it is to swing. They also have the potential for the highest damage however they are harder to use.
Balance: Balance dictates how balanced the weight is. For instance, a small sword is well balanced and controlled easily whereas a top heavy sledgehammer can send you flying and staggering around like a lunatic if you don't stay in control.
Pro tip: As much as I have tried to figure out, the physique of your character doesn't effect your strength of ability to handle heavy weaponry, as of this creating a skinny character leaves less for your opponent to hit, making you a harder target.
TL:DR
So after getting used to the controls I hop into the arena. I get to a fight between a somewhat rotund guy with mace and shield. With my superior intellect I end up whittling his health down by taking advantage of his wild swings sending him off balance constantly. As the fight was folding to a conclusion, I wind up a huge swing with my trusty two-handed sword. My opponent barely blocks it with his shield, staggering him and spinning him around exposing his back to me. This was it, I prepare to end my domination with a huge finishing blow but just as I start my swing I see my opponent flailing back towards me. I release LMB to bring my sword back to defend but it was too late. What I inevitably ended up doing was helping my opponent pull off a 360 bludgeoning that was reminiscent of how kids spin around in circles as fast as they can pretending to be a tornado. Next thing I know my character's body fell to the floor like a sack of potatoes whilst sporting a large, mace shaped crater in his cranium.
The thing is though, I wasn't even frustrated! I winced, chuckled, shook my head and pounced right back into the action to exact my revenge. The unpredictability that the physics and AI can provide, leads to amazingly tense combat, potential for hilarious scenarios and challenging gameplay.
OVERALL THOUGHTS AND CONCLUSIONS:
The combat system is very well thought out and surprisingly realistic.
Exanima has a very refreshing take on the RPG genre, giving the player a unique and connective experience with the character and the combat system. It's enjoyable and addictive and the unique and unpredictable combat means I will be coming back for more for a long time to come.

Basically, this game is not as good as the original. While the game world is very big and detailed, the game itself just isn't very challenging: within an hour or so, I had all the equipment and enough power to simply travel anywhere I wanted to, so the whole world is almost immediately just a big, open plot that you maneuver very easily, no major obstacles, most important objects easily obtained with no major challenges, and no real risk of dying or losing anything, not even altitude - you can always just fire your jets if you lose footing...
The biggest problem with this game, is that there is no real meaningful progression - and therefore no real incentive to play, beyond gawking at cute animals and huge beautiful landscapes.
I played it to the point of collecting all the ship parts and making it to the moon. Completing all of the challenges and collecting all of the crystals? Meh. Why. I couldn't be bothered. And for comparison, I played through the entire first game twice, collecting every crystal and every animal - because it was actually challenging. This game, not so much.
All in all pretty disappointing - I guess, to me, the first game was such a novelty, such a new experience, that it set pretty high expectations for the sequel. Honestly, I don't know that there's any way to successfully follow up a game like this...
I will recommend this game, however, just for it's visuals, general feel, and humble price - but do play the first game (Grow Home) if you haven't, or this one will likely spoil a great experience, as many of the plants, animals and game mechanics are the same or very similar.

I'll try to explain a bit better.
You start on an island that you have previously chosen with a temperate climate, with 4 levels of difficulty.
Your goal is to build a maximum of habitations, and level them up according to population needs, which are different for each level.
To that end, you'll need a local production that will provide what the first levels needs.
Then, to provide for the next ones, you'll have to produce somewhere else. And this is where Anno 2205 Differs from the previous ones.
As a matter of fact, You'll have to choose and open an artic zone to produce some goods, and then a Lunar one , to produce the other goods, and services such as Energy, which will be your bread and butter during the whole experience.
To connect these maps, you have to upgrade each spaceport, and trade those goods and services through traderoutes, which will cost income depending on quantity, and location.
A main quest will guide you through these points helping you understand how it all works, but you should nt worry, as it is really really 5years old accessible.
Also, secondary quests will give you a bonus which nature will depend on the locations you choose, whether it is temperate, artic or lunar. That's actually the reason why you get to choose the zones....A bonus in energy, in special materials, or even ornamentals.
Then, if you have nt chosen the highest difficulty, tertiary quests which quality i won't comment, will pop up in your zone, helping you get more special materials in addition to those you get in the "conflict zones".
Special materials are essential to the game, as they give you the possibility to upgrade production buildings in order to save space. And that's anno 2205 in a nutshell. As space management will be your only challenge, and the engine powering everyone of your decisions in the game.
As i said before, and especially in the highest level of difficulty (as you don't have tertiary quests), these materials will be earned in repeating the same two conflict zones over and over... With "warships".
I'll behave and just give you a hint about the level of crappiness the conflict zones feature : Right-click is used both to move your units AND move the map (like mid mouse button in other games). You can't disable that. Gj ubi.
All of this, basically, the main quest, will take you maybe 10-15 hours depending on your familiarity with the soft.
Then your ultimate goal will be to reach the highest possbile population, by opening the other maps and doing the same stuff you did...again and again. This is actually the new version of Anno "sandbox".
So what's your goal in this so called (by them, definitely not me) sandbox ?
Is it the most money , to have an impact on other players in the infamously absent multiplayer they initially bragged about ?
Nop, as your money is capped, and your income will be useless 90% of the time, and 100% once you unlocked the few zones in the game.
Also, what they call "Multiplayer" is actually an AI led Market, which traderoutes are also capped at 10, featuring the most basic offer and demand system, without any human interactions whatsoever.
So your ultimate goal is actually...The most population. Your corporation level will raise itself depending on your population, and so will the money, and traderoutes cap. (altho the traderoutes with Marketplace wont go higher than 10).
To that end, you get now why the only challenge of this game, apart from 95% of clamhead accessible problems, is space management.
The zones are limited in space, and number, have fun with that.

This game is a compact simplified City Builder, however you will quickly realize just how much optimization in your build is important to maintain happiness in your kingdom and preventing your peasants from starving.
If I have learned anything from attempting to Min/Max my builds, location location location!
I've ran several "peaceful mode"(no enemies spawn, but buildings can still light on fire and you can have flooding among your crops) games just building up my kingdom learning the ropes, it was a very relaxing experience and you get the hang of it fairly quickly, I spend 10 hours just building and rebuilding alone across different maps.
Once I got the hang of where to build and in what order (I am a strategy game player so even with a basic game I look for the depth and what I can do better/quicker in my next game to achieve max efficiency) I gave an "easy mode" game a go, which throws enemies such as Vikings, Ogres and Dragons at you, but at a slower pace than the next step up in difficulty.
Since I already knew HOW to build and organize my buildings to keep my citizens happy and from starving, learning to manage defenses and walls was the next step, and even after a bad attack, recovering isn't difficult, so it's much less intense than other city builder games.

The game is still a bit light on content, with more supposedly on the way, but for my $10.00 I've already gotten 17 hours out of this title and look forward to returning to it, It's a simple game about optimization that you can learn as you go due to a soft learning curve with little punishment (some things may seem wonky but the Devs are working on tweeking and balancing some aspects like random buildings starting on fire) And I can watch something on my second monitor while playing this which is a nice change of pace from some other City builder styled games.

Overall I would recommend this title if you are into the City Builder genre, but are looking for something a bit easier to relax with and less punishing, also a good pick if you are new to the genre!

I think Fearless Fantasy is a great game, and I'm going to tell you why. But always remember: This is my point of view, and only my opinion.
On first glance, Fearless Fantasy looks realy strange. Some screenshots may even look poorly made, and unfinished. You aren't realy sure what type of game it will be. I was first sceptic, about how the game will be and if would have been worth the money. I started playing and soon played an hour.
The game starts with a nice little video sequence to get the story starting. Then you find yourself fighting against a few dudes. After this you learn your second Character and the Story gets started.
The game itself has a nice amount of levels. You get 39 Levels. That doesn't sound very much at first, but a level can be realy long. As you fight your first enemies, you will soon see the unique fighting style. Everything you do requires precision. I only played on Casual mode, to get to learn the game, but the game is realy challenging. The further you go, the harder the enemies become, and you need more tactics. It's basicaly a usual turn-based game with a interesting way of declaring attacks and casting speciall attacks. The better you get and the better you precision gets, the harder you hit. The Game is quite fun to play, and challenging for a casual gamer.
The story is realy okay, and it progresses quite fast, as the game goes on. The story is simple but still good, and the characters are realy funny. The dialogues are also pretty funny to listen to.
The Price of the game isn't high so it was totaly worth the buy.
This is my review of Fearless Fantasy. To make it short: Good Gameplay, Funny Characters and interesting Story. I would recommend a buy, for the little money it costs.

Though hardly revolutionary by any means, the original
rightfully earned a cult following through its technical proficiency, solid game design and sheer mystique -- a Game Boy Color exclusive two years after the Game Boy Advance makes for a rare find. But what of its first sequel in this director's edition?
Flawed, limited once again by budget and original platform choice.
The pixel art and animation are arguably the highlights here, ridiculously detailed and full of life, admittedly WayForward's staples. The music? Also on point, particularly in regards to the rearrangements.
The controls are tight -- fluid. Hit detection seems somewhat biased, however, but given how ultimately forgiving the game is (migraine-induced apathy leading to taking hits left and right is a testament to this), it doesn't matter too much in the end. Level design is solid, but the frequent back-and-forth grows thin somewhat fast. Is it a staple of
-esque game design? Sure, but the world presented in
lacks the variety to make it tolerable.
Thankfully the game is short; a blind playthrough averages about six hours. Multiple endings adds some objective replay value here, but given the amateur writing, I can't see myself attempting the other three I haven't seen no matter how adorable Shantae is as an unsung heroine.
Just not enough incentive to play this one more than once. Does that make
a bad game? Hardly, but it doesn't make it a great one, either. Above-average? Totally, and that's more than can be said for most of its contemporaries.

Between the *adjective* Fantasy name and bizarre aesthetic, first impressions of this game are sure to raise eyebrows and I know it certainly made me cautious if not curious. Thankfully this isn't yet more RPG Maker garbage endlessly♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the Greenlight colon(y) but a quirky game that plays on cliches in a predictable but enjoyable manner.
The combat is engaging with both basic attacks and techniques/spells requiring the player to draw through an arrangement of arrows at precise times: missing results in extremely lowered damage while hitting all/mostly perfects will grant further, sometimes esssential bonuses. It often straddles a line between fun and frustrating but overall it works well, Levelling up grants you both attribute and skill points which are pretty straight forward, adding more points onto a skill will typically unlock more hits or damage and often more arrows to complicate matters.
The story is a typical save the princess and then beat up the bad guy fare but the characters are a little more aware of their situation and are either hammed up or cynical/realistic. They never quite break the 4th wall and there's nothing revolutionary about them and their motives but it's refreshing.
Despite being a three hour game it does feel like it can wear away at your patience towards the end once the QTE sequences get quite long and enemy HP balloons along with them gaining a plethora of obnoxious passive abilities (e.g. 50% less ranged or melee damage, slapping your party with a status effect or damage on death etc.). All things considered it is a neat little game and worth picking up for a couple of bucks or in a bundle.

Super Treasure Arena:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Regardless of which class you are, the stakes are extremely high! Who of the four contestants will collect the most coins? 3..2..1… IT’S ON at the Super Treasure Arena!
Super Treasure Arena is a local/online co-op game where you fight against three other competitors in six small top-down maps. The game has two modes to choose from: Free for All and Treasure Run.
In Free for All, you have to collect as many coins as possible, and in the Treasure Run, you have to carry has many treasure chests to your home base as you can. In both game modes, you only have 180 seconds to amalgamate either coins or chests and finish first in the battle.
After selecting which mode to play, it will be time to choose your character class, with five classes in total to choose from: Warrior, Rogue, Mage, Ninja and Mystic. Apart from looking slightly different, it really comes down to special ability. For example, the Warrior can activate the shield ability for a short period of time, and during that time no-one can inflict any damage upon him. Each class has its own ability which makes the game really fun to play.
In each map, you will find weapons (shotguns, torch, bombs and others) on each corner and sometimes in the centre. As soon as you run over one, it will automatically become your main weapon, but don’t panic, you can revert to your favourite weapon with the LT button on your gamepad. Each map has its own enemies to deal with, too. At the Cove map, crabs and bandits might spot you and chase you for the kill - it’s madness!
Each time you hit a foe, he will drop chocolate, presenst and different goodies. They are actually the coins, so run over them to acquire them. If you get killed, you will drop your goodies. . . Fun, Fun Fun! Find the chest and destroy it to collect more coins!
Super Treasure Arena is not easy to master and it is part of the charm of this game. However, I think the controls should be better and you might find aiming with the projectile can be a bit of a struggle. I really like the pixel graphics and the soundtrack is good.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice pixel graphics
-	Good soundtrack
-	Fun and fast gameplay
-	Online and local co-op
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls need to be improved
-	No trading cards
Whether you play online, local or against the AI, the next 180 seconds in Super Treasure Arena will be manic fun!
7/10

I am a huge sucker for four player local/online co-op games, I love them. From Towerfall, Lovers in a Dangerous Spacetime, Duck Game, and most recently Overcooked, these are all games that I have enjoyed immensely for many different reasons. From the distribution of tasks in Overcooked and Lovers, to the utter chaos in Duck game and Towerfall. These games all manage to bring a unique flavor and idea to the four player setting while drastically being different from each other.
For the most part, Super Treasure Arena has all the right ideas. Collect gold, kill your friends/npcs using a variety of weapons/classes. Whoever at the end of the round with the most gold wins. Sounds simple enough but that is where I find fault with the game. It is rather too simplistic, what you see is what you get, there is nothing really that separates this from the rest and makes it shine on its own. It's a chaos = fun equation that you see in these types of game.
That being said what currently is in the game is made rather well. You have five adorable pixel classes, two game modes, six levels with varied designs. The graphics are rather smooth and animations, explosions, effects all seem fluid and colorful. The UI is super simplistic and the game does feature controller support, although I found aiming a tad bit easier with my keyboard/mouse. Additionally the game does feature online support and local support which is no small and easy feature to include. (Multiplayer is scary to program)
Sadly, I didn't get to play any online matches as the community is still growing. The game does have Bots that you can use in the place of players. So I got a basic idea of how chaotic things can get. Of course that is the linchpin with these types of games, if you can't find a match or have four reliable friends to play with your not getting maximum enjoyment out of the game. Your mileage may vary and that is true with all games in the genre.
At the end of the day, I just want more out of this game. More classes, more game modes(CTF, Team matches, co-op, horde mode, etc), perhaps customization of our sprites, more weapons, you get the idea. The Steam page does make mention of more content in the future. What that content is and when it is released is yet to be seen. The core of the game is in place now it just needs to pull ahead and define itself.

As you would imagine, in a game called Investigator you will be mostly trying to find answers to many questions. Like "What is happening?" or "What am I supposed to do?" or my favorite one: "Why do I even play this?".
Investigator follows a simple formula. Nothing needs to make sense if it's horror. And it's horror as long as it has jumpscares, weird noises and spiders right? I would like to write a few lines that would sum up the story but honestly, I don't have a slightest idea. The premise is that there's a guy and he's a detective (I know that because he said so). And he goes somewhere to investigate a murder. He's in this place now. Now I'm gonna make a courtesy spoiler alert and go ahead and tell you the rest of the story in few short sentences, but there's really no story to spoil, just a pile of nonsensical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
. There is basically no writing, just random things happening. Convoluted nonsensical mess that feels like a work of a person with a bipolar disorder.
The game is approximately 1,5h long. There are two types of environment you encounter. First is just a place you go through. Second is place where you need to click on some trigger item in order to open a door you then go trough. There is no real gameplay which would be okay for a walking sim game, but since there's no story either so there's really nothing that makes this a game or worth-while your attention. There are no real puzzles, no dialogues, no choices, no real story, nothing. Unskippable scripted sequences an absence of any pointers make this hour longer than it really is. So it's 30 minutes of unskippable sequences, 30 minutes of pressing W to go forward and 30 minutes of pressing W again because you have no idea where to go. Levels are not big so it's not hard to find what to do because sooner or later the "press LMB" prompt shows up but the walking is so damn slow that even that takes you some time. Since there are no gameplay elements and no story either, the only motivation to play can be achievements you get for progressing trough the mess.
The graphics are nice. The levels looks good and are nicely detailed and the sound desing is also decent. But that's everything there is to it really. It feels like a game that was developed by a whole team but right after the start of the development everybody, except graphical level designer and sound designer/composer, left the studio and these two guys made the rest of it.
Investigator has to be a worst game with positive Steam rating I've played. Frankly, it really doesn't feel like a game but more like a tech demo two people made in order to get a job but after they failed to do so, they patched some achievements on and sold it as game to get a few bucks. But since it's presented as a game, I reviewed is as such. The fact that this "game" has very positive reviews on Steam leads me to believe that either 1) russian dev was boosted into positive rating by russian fans/bots or 2) people gone mad.

I'm torn on how to recommend this game after this new (beta) update.  The story mode/dungeon is still abysmal, and many of the below complaints become magnfied by the narrow confines and questionable design choices of that mode.  However, the arena.... this is where this game shows  promise.  The mechanics of the game are far better suited for this type of game mode, however since most are buying for Story Mode, it's hard to recommend.
The new arena mode (in beta right now) is much better than the previous iterations.  Persistent character combined with progression (that needs tweaking) as well as a in-game shop, new arena matches (including a 6 man FFA), NPCs that you can recruit...all of this adds much needed depth and content to the most enjoyable part of the game.
Be warned : this game is difficult to learn.  The control/camera system is unlike anything you've played, some say unique, some say downright clunky/broken.  Death is permanent, a lot of progress can be lost.  There is NO mapping feature.  You will get lost.  You will get frustrated.  There are no saves, only checkpoints that are few and far between.  If you want very different combat system and an arena combat type game - I recommend this.   If you want an enjoyable dungeon crawl RPG ...I would do some more research.  You might be disappointed.  Also, the community is filled with hardcore cheerleaders/fanboys/kickstarter backers who will defend EVERY mechanic with religious fervor.  The Devs make no bones about it, your opinion, if its not in line with their 'creative vision', is not wanted, and is in fact, meaningless.
Summary of negatives
-You will die many, many times adjusting the camera during a fight because of the wonky system they have in place where your mouse cursor's location is what you use to turn and face your character.
-If you get too close to a wall, camera will go to a top-down view, rather than turn the wall transparent like other isometric games, which can really screw up your ability to attack/parry/dodge
-Swinging weapons feels wrong. You don't need to throw your entire body into swinging a sword. It's not realistic, I could handle a sword better IRL. Even after 10 beers. Your character displays no finesse or dexterity whatsoever, he swings all his weapons as if they're a 30 pound baseball bat, many times spinning around or ending up wildly out of position because the game engine requires you to use movement/footwork in order to enhance the strength of your blows.
-movement in combat (dash / walk) is sluggish and unresponsive. Your character behaves as if he is fighting in a swamp wearing 200 lbs of armour (regardless of whether you're actually wearing armour)
-Blocking is done automatically and really feels broken. Many times the AI will swing right over/under your parry, some times right through it.
-Overhand strikes are incredibly slow. These are also the only decent way to hit an opponent who has been knocked to the ground, but you will miss more often than not due to abysmal aiming system and terrible control of your character. Inputs are just so exaggerated and lagged to give any real feeling of precision in combat
-Dungeon mode is boring and dreary. Same map every time. Mobs roam, sure, but many spawn in the same spots and don't move until you open the door they're standing behind.
-Loot is limited to armour, weapons, clothing.  The game tries to follow a realistic medieval gear system.  Keep that in mind, this is not Diablo by any stretch of the imagination.  Armour is incredibly valuable for your survivability, and it is not easy to come by at first.
-no map, terrain all looks the same, so unless you are blessed with an incredible direction sense/memory, be prepared to continually retrace your steps until you cave and google the homemade maps people uploaded (yes, they had to make their own maps using graph paper)...or you straight up memorize the lay out of the 3 current levels. You are provided with a compass, and nothing else currently.  This is a major issue for me, I absolutely hate wandering aimlessly through the same areas over and over because I just can't tell where I've been and where I haven't.
-no voice acting, no cinematics. It consists of finding scrolls, books, letters. Story is told in bits and pieces as you explore.
-very little in the way of options and customization
-can't save your game, though every level does have a check point system now, which only came after a large vocal outcry when the game first released. Ironically, requests for a system for saves were met with derision and condescension ("Maybe this game isn't for you." / "Go play another game.") by the Insider Kickstarter Elitists.
-devs and staunch defenders of this game will constantly defend game flaws as "realism", "immesion", "physics", "hardcore", "challenging" when in reality they're just defending bad design choices and wonky mechanics because they've played the game for a year and have "grown used to it". Suggestions for different control schemes / camera options are met with "We tried it. Didn't work. End of discussion."
The best way to describe the current system, where the controls can get reversed on you based upon where your mouse cursor and character are is this: tell someone who is right handed to learn how to throw a ball with their left hand. Tell them to practice practice practice and eventually they will get better, and get the hang of it.... Ignoring the fact that though they may vastly improve from that first day they tried, it will still never really feel natural, and never feel as though their skill will reach the level of their dominant hand.
"Story" Mode :
Going from debris-filled room to debris-filled room, finding damn near nothing of interest, tripping over objects or getting stuck on the environment.... Having to back track and re-trace steps constantly because there's no mini-map of any type, searching for tiny, hard to see keys because they blend in with the drab colour palette.... No way to zoom in half as much as you should be able to...
Mouse cursor is not dynamic when hovering over objects... No rhyme or reason to why some objects are movable, and others are not.
The game is pitch black in a lot of areas which forces you to juggle a torch with your weapon/shield, constantly having to drag it to equip/drop it, but having to be super precise or you "miss" the torch or it won't drop because you dragged it too far away from your character...try doing this while being charged at by a hostile enemy.  The inventory management in this game is absolutely atrocious.  Can't easily drop an item or switch items/weapons, have to click and drag.  You will die because of this, multiple times, and lose hours of progress.  It's bad.
Can't recommend it for story mode,  however, if you have the time/patience/desire, there is definitely something to be said about the arena combat mode.  It seems as though the developers are putting more emphasis on this aspect, so for the price of the game, you're getting potentially a lot of game hours.  Whether or not you're actually enjoying those hours, well, that's the real thing with this game.  A lot of people are going to be way too frustrated after the first hour to even bother going on.  It takes significant time to get decent at the mechanics of this game, so if you don't have the patience, don't bother, you will be smashing that refund button before 2 hours up I guarantee it.
I suggest you look up Sui Generis, a concurrent project the same Developer is working on and has ripped Exanima from in an effort to garner more revenue to fund Sui Generis.  The Developers never planned on Exanima, it only exists because they ran out of money, so they took a few levels from SG, plopped in an arena mode, and voila.  All the original backers of SG received Exanima for free.  Purchasing Exanima does not get you SG, whenever it releases.

Now, let's try some random letters. I got me the inventory. Oh my, the torch can be dropped in the box or on my guy. MY GUY HAS A TORCH NOW. Yes. I like that.
Now we're walking, the halls are dark and I can only see what my torch illuminates. Things are getting real. Really real. Almost too real, ouch my eyes. Okay, a doorway, let's... oh click and drag. I love it. I LOVE IT. I mean seriously... clicking the word "Open" doesn't do it for me anymore. Let's continue, oh whats this? A ZOMBIE... and dead.
THIS time, we're going to try looking around a little more. OOOO, you can trip and fall on stuff. You can move stuff, you can blockade doors, make trip traps, find cool little things with the double click and look at the stats and stuff.

I've watched games I love stagnate, and many of them, but it's time for you to peel off those kiddie gloves and dive into a seriously hard, incredibly fun, dungeon of dungeons.
This isn't for the casual gamer. Or maybe it is. The masochist casual gamer would get a kick out of this. You will too. Seriously. Alright peace.

The UI is very polished, and i really think this game is the epitome of how point n click adventures should be like in 2017.
Bottomline, highly recommended. My gametime was 16 hours.

SHORT VERSION: This is a terrible way to read books. If you want free ebooks, head to
for the texts, and go to
for a library & reading app.
Unless you're an ebook fanatic who loves innovative ways to read books, don't bother with this. Reading Simulator is nothing like a *good* way to read books, just... different. I am an ebook fanatic; I wanted to like this, but, it falls short in so many ways.
The library setting is pleasant, but the books are scattered, unmarked, and poorly formatted: they don't include italics or bold from the originals; the line breaks from whatever source file was used are copied, resulting in orphan words all over the place; sometimes text overlaps other text.
There is no skip forward or skip back so it's flip through one page at a time; no bookmarking; no way to mark where a book is in the library. No edition notes - no note of which translation or version a book is. The book itself is shown in a small window in the middle of the screen; there is no enlarging it, nor the text within it, for easier reading.
No copyright info. These are all presumed to be in the public domain, and likely grabbed from Gutenberg (which doesn't explain the line breaks), but some Gutenberg books aren't in the public domain in other countries. It has Joyce's Ulysses; only some versions of that are in the public domain in the US.
It's cheap, so you won't need to feel cheated if you bought it out of curiousity. But it's not worth using to read, and there are better-structured walking sims if you just want to enjoy some quiet ambiance.

First impression review:
As an enthusiast of literature and literacy, I'm highly impressed by this. Upon first glance, I was about to think "Oh great, another silly 'simulator' made just for laughs". That is not at all what this is. The beautiful 3D library environment offers a great ambience. And the ability to read these classic texts all in one spot is a great idea. A great idea, in that it actually encourages reading, and prose literacy, while more or less emulating the page-turning experience of an actual book.
I'm going to give it a fair "4/5 stars", as I feel there are a few technical points that could use improvement, which I will suggest to the developer here:
- It is difficult to interact with some of the books throughout the library. It is also difficult to tell which books can actually be interacted with or not. And it is also difficult to tell precisely where to click in order to successfully interact. I would suggest providing some form of visual indicator on the interface to indicate which books can be interacted with, and also where to click (or simply telling if you're in range and/or clicking the right spot).
- A nice aesthetic would be the ability to interact with the chairs to emulate sitting down to read.
- Some variance in music would be a nice touch, as well. This could be remedied, however, by muting the game, and turning on your own music.
- I would like to see a "bookmarking" system, along with a gamesave system to remember the bookmarks. This would be nice for coming back to unfinished reads.
- I would also like to see maybe a map or other form of index to give players an idea of where certain books are found in the library.
- Personal request: I would like to see some works by H.P. Lovecraft, if possible in the future. :)
I also noticed a small bug, as well, where sometimes, text in books would initially render invisible upon initially opening a book. This was quickly remedied by either closing and reopening the book, and/or turning the pages back and forth a few times.
So far, I am greatly pleased with Reading Simulator. Looking forward to the future. Keep up the great work. :)

Turok in actual playable form!  No horrid mouse input here.  In addition, there are many new gameplay and input options, the UI has been redesigned slightly, there are new graphics features as the description says, and the levels have been redesigned in a few areas (for better or worse).  The more modern draw distance actually makes some parts much easier, but it's good to have acceptable draw distance.
Widescreen support is fine.  I run it at 2560 x 1440 144 Hz with no issues related to this.
For those who never played Turok, know that this game is known primarily for two things: setting and weapons.  The setting is distinct; The Lost Land, a place that looks ancient in some areas with its ancient ruins, overgrown jungles and dinosaurs.  Fast forward to levels 7 and 8 which are filled with aliens and massive Sci-Fi constructs.  Like other classic FPS games, Turok is filled with hidden areas so be sure to explore.
And the weapons... the Turok franchise has always had some of the coolest weapons you'll find in FPS gaming, although the sequels are better in this regard.
This remake has some bugs though.  Sound is glitchy like the original PC version and unlike the N64 version, and setting projectile collision to Precise just crashes my game.  It also has only preset FOV values but you can edit them yourself in config.cfg with any text editor.  Likewise an FPS cap is in place (60); you can try removing it but do so at your own risk.  I haven't tested it myself but the originals get insane when the frame rate is too high, since game logic was tied to frame rate.
Most of the original cheat codes still work, although the gallery cheat (THBST) seems to be gone.

When I first saw this, my reaction to the artstyle was basically "What the hell is this nonsense?" Having played it, the answer is that it's amazing nonsense in the best traditions of oldschool JRPGs, and full of hand-drawn cutscenes and fairly charming amateur voice acting for when you're not in combat.
Beyond the artstyle, Fearless Fantasy is more or less a standard JRPG with some clearly mobile-influenced elements, like the interface and being divided into short, selectable levels with three difficulty modes each. Despite its fairly short length (only about 3 hours for me, including 2 replays of every level except for the last two), it manages to fully develop all of its mechanics, the well-tuned battle system making it so every action and decision really counts by the end of the game.
The only real issue I have with Fearless Fantasy is that the gestures required for the attacks feel like they were designed for a touch interface, but the game hasn't been released on mobile or any platform that typically has a touchscreen yet. However, their website indicates they intend to release a mobile port sometime this year. As a result, while this game comes with my recommendation, I would suggest waiting for the mobile port if you have a smartphone with a decently large screen or a tablet.
(Of course, having beaten the game, I don't plan on playing another version of it. As a result, I won't be updating this if the mobile version doesn't come out or is terrible or something.)

Shantae: Risky's Revenge is an action/platform where you play as a shape shifting half genie and is overall a nice game but it suffers from numerous issues pertaining to porting, input, combat and level design.
+ The pixel graphics are really nice and seeing that it's a port of a DSi game, they've aged rather nicely.
+ The music is really pleasing from what little I heard.
- The game will crash if you decide to enter the Options menu once in game. You can open it from the main menu fine but once you;re in game it will promptly crash.
- Movement feels sluggish and not tight like I'd expect it to be.
- Combat is rather lacklustre and boring where your main combat mechanic is your hair whip attack where you can only attack directly in front of you.
- You have magic but its damage is rather laughable. Your starting spell takes so long to kill anything that you're better off only using your melee.
- Button presses are unresponsive at times or present some levels of input lag. This is a major detriment to any action/platform game. So much so that it haults my progress in completing a dungeon by not being able to beat a boss seeing that my jump commands aren't registering 100% of the time resulting in unwarranted damage. Same goes for transformations, sometimes I can transform instantly by tapping the dance button (Y) other times I have to hold it until kingdom come.
- Horrible boss battles as bosses are straight up sponges.
+/- The multi-layer approach to level design is quite nice initially but instantly becomes tedious if you're lost and don't know where to proceed. Seeing that you have to constantly locate jump pads in order to jump back and forth between layers rather than simply scrolling to the left or right.
+/- Buttons (A) and (B) seem to be swapped for whatever reason with (B) being the Action command and (A) being Cancel. I don't think they can be rebound.
+/- Black bars on the side of the screen seeing that it's a port of a 4:3 ratio game. That's not the weird thing though, the logo splash screen and title screen covers the entire window but you're greeted with the gutters once in-game. It's not jarring or anything but just inconsistent.
While the game does have a certain level of charm to it, the issues which it has hinders it from being enjoyable. Do note that I couldn't finish this game as a result of all issues noted but judging solely from what I played I simply can't recommend it which is a shame.

I had fun playing Risky's Revenge and will definitely play the following 2 games in the series. The platforming elements are exciting, Shantae as a protagonist is endearing, there are several cool powerups and extras to collect, and the art style and music are just what you'd expect from a game of this kind.

HOWEVER!!! As a "seasoned expert in platformers", I really cannot justify the Metroidvania elements - not in this game. Basically, Shantae "unlocks" 3 transformations (monkey, elephant and mermaid), and each of them can be upgraded once. They all let you progress in the game and reach previously unreachable locations in areas you've already visited. But there is so much backtracking, so much running through the same areas (some of which are very uninspired - SO MANY CAVES AND CAVERNS!!!), that you'll find yourself losing interest midgame.
Plus, the map is downright useless - its design is terrible and doesn't help you when backtracking in any way. Oh, and killing the same monsters over, and over, and over again (yes, they respawn in true Metroidvania fashion in ridiculously large numbers) becomes boring in the 2nd half of the game.

I'm perfectly aware of what "Metroidvania" stands for, but if you want to see it executed flawlessly, play Ori and the Blind Forest. As for this game - if you're willing to look past the terrible Metroidvania choices, you will like/love everything else about it. However, if the love for Metroidvania is what brings you here in the first place, you may find yourself annoyed more often than not; which is a real shame for an otherwise adorable platformer.

This game is absolutely wonderful and well done. It is a voxel based ship/vehicle combat simulator. However, the campaign is what takes up most of my time as the author of this game singlehandedly built over 400 individual ship designs that over 6 factions actively use to kill you. I myself am a humble builder preferring a couple smaller effective airships or boats, but the limits in this game are astounding and the author plans to continually update this game even though he is working on a successor to this with an actual game company so support for this game will not stop.
The community on reddit steam and elsewhere is very friendly and helpful and the game has a rudimentary multiplayer support for the campaign with no game breaking bugs. This game is hard to pick up at first I would 100% recommend turning the diffculty to easy and basicallly make yourself next to invincible while you pick apart enemy ship designs to learn their building designs and weaknesses.
Even with the incredibly friendly and in-depth tutorial you will still have some issues fighting the campaign ships on normal difficulty(they are really well done).
A con is a memory leak issue that happens if the game is open for hours at a time. Causes the game to stutter at 3 hours. He is working on a fix in the next update after his hiatus from this game( approximately 2 months away).
perhaps another would be that the ships the creator designed are really god damn good. You need to cater your ships to their weaknesses but in all fairness this is a positive to me.
The game has a somewhat realistic fuel efficiency and ballistic damage with different shell types, barrels, gun velocities. There is even a IAMS defense system as well as an offensive laser/railgun. All somewhat realistically modeled.  The biggest ship in the game is the Meteor and probably one of the hardest designs to fight one ship vs one ship. in game i belive it is 50000 m3. Its a flying saucer with an array of missiles and a giant laser that cut my flagship in half.) The ship is completely controlled with ingame modules however, you can use lua scripting to get a more precise control (I only use LUA for hover ships as it keeps them at a nice altitude while programming a couple purposeful kinks to dodge bullets. I can program LUA, but i found a design online that was much more well put together so i copied it.)
You can be as hardcore as you want but sometimes cruising through on easy trying to beat the game with only 1 ship is somewhat casual fun.

There is three difficulty mode ; Hard, Normal and Easy. Easy is really easy. You can learn the game basics as like as it's a tutorial. Then you can play normal or hard without getting bored easily.
The game mechanics are basic. You can build workplaces, training stuffs into your office/studio. You can recolate your studio from X to Y. You can hire new people with pros and cons. You can speciliaze your employees, remove their negative effects.
There is four specialities. Sound and Art Designer, Writer, Coder. You can specialize your employees with one of them.

There is four game sizes. Micro, Small, Medium, Large. Earning money is a bit hard after a time. When you get f.cked up, request loan from the bank. Making micro or small games always worth to get a shot. Well, the magazines like VGN and Kotokoo or whatever... are sonuva♥♥♥♥♥. Your employees have to work hard and train themselves to make a better game.
At last it feels more simulation and complicated than Game Dev Tycoon or any other else. You can earn awards in game festivals. Stats are (your own stats and global stats) verQy well designed. You can expand your capacity and studio. You can see that your studio is grow up with your very own eyes.
I give my thanks to special dev/devs behind this game.
The only one con is making game projects are easy and not very complicated. So it means you can beat the game without getting tired. There is a lot of special thing in build mode, employee hire and management but not game projects. They could be similar or upgraded version of Game Dev Tycoon.
Also there is some framerate drops in studio with a lot of workers.
Please don't ask me as like 'Why are you comparing Game Dev Tycoon and Game Corp Dx' cuz Game Dev Tycoon is another succesful game dev management game for a long time.
PS : There is dozens of funny easter eggs and achievements. You can hire Tim Schaffer, Sid Meier, Gabe Newell and you can make Half-Life 3 ! My dream come true!

I didn't like this, especially the 3D view: it zoom out so few (probably for performances limits of the engine) that you feel like you are seeing nothing of what is really going on in the city.
I'd say that if you feel like wanting to play a Caesar game, you should play Caesar III. It's still full of bugs and weird things, but at least it's enjoyable.

A fun game and better in most ways compared to Caesar III, thanks to mercifully improved pathfinding and areas of influence of your buildings.  However it is lacking a certain....something. Soul, maybe. Combat is bad, the map involves a bit too much finicky building placement (the squares are too small, organising a city layout was actually easier in C3). Some reviews have commented on difficult camera and annoying rocks blocking your placement etc and these comments have some justification, but can be worked around. I've encountered a couple of bugs regarding combat, which is wonky as all hell, and if you doubt me just try to send your men across a bridge while there's barbarians on the other side.
Once you know what you're doing you can blast through the game in no time at all - i finished both republic and empire campaigns in 15 hours (played on normal difficulty and max speed). You rarely have much wiggle room however and I often struggled to get my city running - kept running out of favour and was always going into bankruptcy scrambling to build an industry to supply whatever new thing Caesar wanted this time.
I return to C4 every couple of years so there is definitely something here, but I'd recommend picking up on a discount.  By the end the game feels very 'samey' as there is no gradual unlocking of resources + things like there were in C3. Perhaps it's because there are only 3 tiers of pleb and equite buildings and no real incentive to improve their quality of life with theatres etc.  A buy, but get it on discount.
It feels like a dumbed down version of Caesar III. Also, controls took some getting used to. Not a fan.

This one takes a slight bit of work to get going, but once you do, wow! This was one of my favorite games as a young adult, and if you enjoyed it when it was first released, you really owe it to yourself to give it another go on your modern PC. I was even able to run it in 4K DSR with no modifications! Between that, and setting everything else on max, the game looks strikingly good for being nearly 11 years old.
This is one of the best city builders of all time, especially among the classics! I always wished they had made a Caesar V game... but on a modern machine, and after not playing the game for so long, it almost feels as if they did!
The one thing to be aware of is that for me to get this game running on Windows 10, I had to go to the game directory, the C4 directory under that, and run RegisterDLL.bat as administrator before the game would even launch. Once I did that, it ran flawlessly! If you still have issues, you may beed to run the game in Windows XP compatibility mode, but I didn't have to.
So, now that you're equipped with the knowledge of how to play the game on a modern system, go build your empire!

Kingdoms and Castles is the simulation, city building game I've been looking for for a while now.  The overall, the game is pretty decent.  You need to balance your industry growing resources (wood, stone and later gold) while making sure that you have food and storage under control to keep everyone fed.  There is also a third balance to keep in mind, happiness.  This balance has less of an impact on the game but, still prevents new people from coming and can result in people leaving your kingdom.
While this game is enjoyable, it is not without some serious issues.  I'm currently playing through the game on easy mode, which makes me seriously question what the hell hard mode is going to be like.  There are four types of disasters you can face in this game:  Fire, Plague, Viking, and Dragon.  Fire randomly happens to buildings at any time, including wells, stone walls, and ballistas.  Plagues happen with less frequency and are addressed by only a single building, the hospital.  The vikings and dragons, once they come, they come with an ever increasing frequency that is unforgiving.  In my game year 44, which is barely enough time to have a decent defense going on, I was dealing with two natural fires, a plague, a viking raid, and a dragon attack all at the same time.
There also appears to be an issue with vikings able to walk across open water.  I had built a defensive wall to keep a penisula and command landing area for vikings walled off and push them into a choke.  Instead of trying to use the ogres to knock down the walls and get past my choke, the vikings walked on water around the wall and set buildings on fire beyond it instead.
Another level of irritancy in the game are the advisors.  In my wonderfully above mentioned Great Disaster of 44, my happiness was knocked down to -17 and I was having a food shortage due to everyone putting out fires and food not being gathered.  The advisors, who I switched to ignoring anyway, would not shut up about building more granaries I didn't need or how I was a terrible ruler because they were unhappy.

Pros.
1. Great time waster. I played this game for a solid 8 hours one day. Not many games these days can do that.
2. Amazingly simple graphics. I love the art style and the simplicity of this game. It really brings out my creative side when organizing my city.
3. Easy controls. Despite not having much of a tutorial, this game is super easy to figure out and throws you into the whole governing thing, haha.
4. Potential. This game has a lot of good ideas and concepts of a city builder. It's just missing content.
Cons.
1. Fire everywhere. You're biggest enemy is fire. All the time. I find this to be the most annoying thing about this game. Both of the base enemies use fire against you. I am constantly finding myself rebuilding the same buildings over and over again. I've even tried combating fire by placing wells in every nook of my city and the peasants still manage to let everything burn. Taverns, Defense Towers, Hospitals and The Chamber of War seem to be "hot spots". Anything that takes a bit of resources to build really.
2. Lack of content. The game is super fun up until the point where your Kingdom is at the level of "Busling City". That's where the lack of content shows. From then on it's really just a bunch of rebuilding things that get burnt down and expanding a little. Then getting set back by things burning down for the fourth time, then expanding a little and so on.
3. It needs some fixing. I don't know if I'm doing something wrong here but after the 250 population mark, people start dying of starvation despite having 1500 full storage of food and markets all over. They just starve themselves. It's quite the pain because it spams the notification bar at the top left. The combat controls with friendly soldiers is tedious and annoying. They do not automatically attack or follow vikings or ogres. You constantly have to click away and keep up with them to make sure your troops are actually doing damage. It needs work. I also am not a fan of how the maps are generated. I really wish there were larger land masses with less islands and water all over making it difficult to expand past a point.
This game has some great potential and is already really fun, up to that 250 mark at least. I do think it is worth ten dollars  but not a penny more than that. This game entertained me for about 36 hours of game time now and it'll probably be more in the next few days. Try this game out!

As a loyal fan to the genre, I've played many a City-Building game. This game doesn't bring anything particularly new to the table (this game is very "Banished-esque"), but what it does bring is a flair that you can't find in any similar game. It has a wonderful color palette, and doesn't give this boding Doomsday appearence when you're in trouble. It's fairly light in structured content and storyline, and more features need to (and are supposed to) be added to make this game unique, but overall it's a wonderful game!
You will like this game if:
You enjoy CityBuilding, Economy, or any game variant there of.
You've played Banished, Dwarf Fortress, Gnormoria, Stonehearth, SimCity, etc
You will hate this game if:
You need constant action
You feel like unless you are visibly making progress in the game, you're failing.
Hope that kind of gives the appropriate vibe and expectation. I personally love this game, and it's pretty light on the pocket. In that regard, it's punching above its weight. Cheers guys!

Turok: Dinosaur Hunter is a relic of a different era of game design. One that was more at home with Super Mario Bros and The Legend of Zelda than Doom and Quake.
Turok bares a lot more qualities reminiscient of Mario than Doom really. The game features an overly cartoony art style with exaggerated proportions, it takes place in a vague indeterminate setting called the "Lost Land" reminiscient of Mario's mushroom kingdom. It features player lives and pickups inorder to gain new ones. It has a hub level strictly for warping to new ones ala Super Mario 64. It has platforming sections. And the general objective of the game is to "gather something from every level in the game and kill the final boss". It's weird to me coming back to it since, swap the graphics and change the protagonist into a plumber and the enemies into goombas and you have "Super Mario the FPS". Just add dinosaurs.
Now this game originally released on the N64 and has been ported to a brand new engine with this release. You have things like a water reflection shader, higher framerate, FOV options and widescreen. The higher framerate causes the game to feel much faster and more akin to Serious Sam.
Now all this being said. Whether it's worth the 20$ asking price is entirely dependant on if you like older first person shooters and don't mind the rough edges. Since you can beat it in about 6 or so hours. Personally I do like the game as is, and with the promise of a level editor and Turok 2 down the road, I'm more excited for the future of the series than I ever was before.

Fearless Fantasy strangeness drew me to it like a moth to the flame. I purchased it purely for its intriguing art style and was greeted with humor, two characters that nearly sound like Steve Blum and Mark Hamill's Joker, and a turn-based combat system based on timing and tracing.
I really like the art, especially for the monsters. They were just enjoyable to look at before I slaughtered them. The monster designs range from humorous to creepy (pay attention to their names too). The stills that were in place for the cinematics were not very interesting visually, but the humor usually takes priority during those sections.
The voice acting seems decent enough and light-hearted. Joshua Tomar kept throwing me off with his Steve Blum impression. Adam Harrington's voice kept on giving me serious Joker vibes. Both made my experience with the game even weirder.
The combat system can be difficult to master. Tracing with the mouse did not work out well for me unless I played on Casual or Normal (you can set the difficulty manually for each level). There are three characters with different specialities (damage/debuff, buffing/taunting, healing/defensive) with five different skills available for leveling up. None of them are too amazing, but it's satisfying to trace a perfectly timed path and scoring an epic or flawless rating for very high damage or bonus effects. Look at the first trailer for the game to have a fairly accurate idea of how the tracing mechanic works (you path your mouse through arrows).
Fearless Fantasy is a strange, little game that might be enjoyable for you. Let the art style consume you.

This is Fearless Fantasy—a JRPG inspired indie game with a very unique twist on the standard turn based combat system. This game is an absolute delight! With a great soundtrack, peculiarly nice voice acting, and a fantastic slew of enemies, Fearless Fantasy should be in everyone’s Steam library.
Let me start by acknowledging the work these developers have put into this game. The duo, Enter Skies are still working on this game, as there is a mobile port on the way. And despite being released in May of this year, they still communicate with their community over on the Steam forums (much better than, say, Code Avarice have been doing for the entirety of Paranautical Activity’s existence on the platform).
The overworld is quite reminiscent of Record of Agarest War, if I’m remembering correctly. You’ve got your difficulty options going in, which will require you be precise with the aforementioned combat system. Bosses, however, have other little stipulations which may further cause you difficulty in Veteran battles. The world is absolutely psychedelic, with beautiful battlefields and some damn trippy enemies.
The combat incorporates the use of an Elite Beat Agents or Osu! Style of board which will determine whether you miss or critically harm your enemy, or fail to or critically defend against him. Epics and Flawlesses will provide you with powerful turns, while misses will result in failure. You can attempt to troll the enemy, or be trolled yourself—that’s all up to you ;). And consumables are actually useful. Well, I don’t mean to say they aren’t useless in other games, but I can’t tell you how many JRPGs I’ve played where I hoarded the hell out of potions thinking they’d be useful later on, only to end up beating the game with a sack full of vials.
With general gameplay out of the way, I’ve got to say I was absolutely charmed by this game. The cut scenes are what look to be flash animated, simple, and delightful to watch, with some decent writing and great voice acting. The voice acting is reminiscent of the Tales games to me, and the actors definitely put in a lot of effort despite this seemingly small project. Seriously, the voice acting is absolutely genuine and high quality, especially considering the quirky, humorous nature of the game!
The last thing I’ll cover is the music and sound. The opening theme was the hook which made me stop what I was watching on the other monitor, amp up the volume, and really give this game my full attention. I may be overly optimistic but everything that’s been done in this game is far from lazy, which includes the use of sound. Attacks seem powerful, and Flawlesses feel amazing when you pull them off!
This game is an absolute trip. It’s a wonderful, if short adventure. There is a very positive feel and flow to this psychedelic world, in which your progress actually means something. I had a really great time with it, and at the very cheap price point of 7.79 CAD, Fearless Fantasy is definitely a worthwhile purchase.

Starbound! It's a wonderfully made game. I've played it irregularly, but so far I've enjoyed the content of the game. So basically Starbound is, in a way, like Terraria but in space and has way more replayability in my opinion. It has workshop support which means you're able to increase the enjoyment of this game ten fold.
