I know if I sit down for a metroidvania, I'm going to be collecting stuff. It might be keys or souls or artisanal cheeses but I get that I'll have to scour the map to nab things to proceed. Some games do this really well, with clever shortcuts between areas or unique new ways to traverse the same rooms. And some games don't, leaving you to backtrack through the same places endlessly. Shantae honestly doesn't even try for the former, electing to stick you with the latter in a criminally small world brimming with junk that other people want you to get. It's a really nice world, too, which makes it all the worse that it's designed so poorly.
Risky's Revenge is the second game in the series from what I understand, but don't let that get you down because the story is simple enough. You play the bouncy Shantae, the half-genie protector of sunny seaside Scuttle Town. Her uncle unearths a magic lamp that gets snatched by Risky Boots, Shantae's pirate nemesis, and so the task before you is to battle back against Risky, her mechanical pirate ship, and her gravity-defying breasts. Actually you won't see much of her for most of the game, because the bulk of your time is spent collecting junk to keep away from Risky that she DEFINITELY won't trick you into handing over in the end.
It's a shame you don't see more of Risky, actually, because the characters are perhaps the best part of the game. Shantae's world is full of colorful, animated characters that love to quip about their lives and your life and their weird little habits. I'm impressed at how much personality they get between their unique appearances and their short but clever blurbs. Each of Shantae's allies is distinct in character, from her kindly uncle to her falconer ally to her peppy zombie BFF. The townsfolk and other incidental characters all have their moments as well, just enough to make me wish more emphasis was placed on meeting people than scouring the world for items.
The ugly truth, if you haven't cottoned to it yet, is that the game is one big item hunt, even moreso than most metroidvanias. Your very first task in the game is to find an item Shantae forgot about, and then from there it's hours spent chasing three magic doodads so Risky can't have them. You have to find more items to get to them, not just powerups and keys but lunches, tickets, lattes, and squids, too. They're all scattered across a shockingly small world, so be prepared to hit every screen in the game at least twice to find different gewgaws to proceed. Seriously, there are only four paths out of town, one leads to Shantae's house and the other three dead-end at the dungeons where the magical thingamabobs are.
Backtracking is what killed this game stone dead for me, because it is orders of magnitude worse than in just about any other game. Retreading old ground is a given in any metroidvania but a large map with intelligently-designed paths of progression will keep it to a minimum while making the most of the rooms that must be repeated. Risky's Revenge, perched precariously on the opposite end of this spectrum, starts with a tiny, boring map and then crams as much junk into it as possible that requires multiple trips through the same areas. And these aren't gentle fields or straight corridors to traverse, no, these are dozens of rail-thin platforms over a bottomless pit to tackle over and over, or a cave network that the useless map function leaves you to puzzle out for yourself when you have to return an hour later to find a new upgrade to proceed.
The dungeons are somehow even worse about this (yes I am not done talking about backtracking) and not just because they have literally no map. While one is simply a timed gauntlet of battles, the other two are a messy network of cris-crossing rooms and secret passages and keys to distant doors. The first is plenty confusing with its numerous side halls hiding essential keys and forced backtracking through cavernous rooms, but the last, oh my God the last. There are doors that lead to different places depending on switches you flip, and some can have four different destinations. One part requires you to find four keys before BACKTRACKING to a locked door, to find another two-part key that has you BACKTRACK almost all the way back to the entrance.
The only way I could get through Risky's Revenge was by playing 30 minutes or so a night. The constant busywork of finding a new item to get another item so I could go back and get another item just wore on me too much. It's a shame, too, because the rest of the game comes together with some cool animal powers, vibrant enemies, and a beautiful world to run around in. The presentation isn't the best, with the fine pixel art clashing with the clean vectors of menus and dialog, but for a handheld port that's hardly its worst sin. No, its worst sin is making you scramble over every inch of a tiny map again and again until boredom or apathy claim you. As lively as Shantae and her friends appear, they sure do waste a lot of their lives chasing junk and that's not my idea of a good time.

Though I am giving this game the thumbs up, this is going to sound like a negative review, because all I am going to do in this review is compare Grow Up to the first game, Grow Home. I do this for the people who played Grow Home so they can know what kinds of changes to expect. You may like them. Or if you're like me: you may
I was very excited to purchase this game on day one, since I was such a tremendous fan of the first game. I remember finally reaching M.O.M. and being frankly a little bit sad that the game was finally over. I was looking forward to experiencing much of what I loved about the first game, which included such great joys as:
--The simple joy of going up, up, up, and UP! MORE UP!
--Exploration! What will I find in this little cave?
--Dragging objects and organisms back to a teleporter to be scanned for research
--Picking plants and using them to traverse the environment in various ways
Little did I expect that Grow Up would fiddle with each of these wonderful gameplay elements, making each of them sadly a bit more boring in the process, resulting in a game that is not bad by any means, but doesn't have the same hook as the first. I'll explain each in turn:
In the first game, you start on a small island. It is the only real landmass. Everything else is just water for as far as the eye can see. The message is clear: this is not a game about traveling over land. There is only one direction you need concern yourself with and that is the UP direction. BEGIN YOUR ASCENT!
This was wonderful in its simplicity. Climbing up rock faces and growing the stems of the star plant higher and higher was very satisfying if anything for the simple reason that you could always look down at any moment and SEE your progress.
Now you have to concern yourself with scouring the surface of an entire planet, which is a lot of time spent NOT going up. There are also multiple starplants to grow now, which means even while you are growing one star plant, you know there are other ones that you still haven't even started. And get this: the starplants don't even grow all the way up! There is a hard limit on how high they grow! While still having things above them! This of course feels like blasphemy.
The rest of the game follows this pattern as well: a move away from simple physical progress toward a more "checklist" style of gameplay, which is precisely the thing that makes it feel more pedestrian (figuratively and literally) than the first game.
Exploration felt great in the first game. As you were ascending, you would come across islands of various sizes. Exploring them, you would find new things. New plants. New animals. New strange sights. You could drag these discoveries back to the teleporter for research, so each discovery was also progress.
Grow Up makes exploration more boring in a couple of ways. First, it does the AAA thing of putting an icon over every important thing, so you don't even have to look for it. You just have to go where you're told. See what I mean about the checklist?
No, you can't turn these icons off. And if you try to just ignore them, they have also added a companion named POD who is basically this game's version of Navi the nagging fairy. Yes, I'm serious and not exaggerating. You can't turn this off.
You are also given a satellite view that you can use to get an aerial view of the entire planet at any time. You can move the view around, zoom in, zoom out. All of the important item icons appear under this view as well. No need to explore or look around. Everything is clearly marked and easy to pinpoint. Sigh.
In the first game, whenever you discovered a new plant or animal, you could drag it back to a teleporter to scan it into your research. This added a sort of physics puzzle to the game. Which teleporter can I feasibly get this to? How do I get it out of this cave? How do I get it down/up to the teleporter from there?
Sadly, Grow Up completely removes this element of gameplay. Scanning objects into the teleporter for research is no longer a thing. At all.
There is still "research" in the game.... kind of. Animals are now completely irrelevant. The only thing you can research are plants, and you do this by... just touching them. That's it. Sigh.
Researching plants lets you use them. There are 40 plants to research. But you will never use them because there is really no need to. And even though there are 40, they all do the same 2 things. Which means touching all 40 plants is... just a checklist.
This works MUCH differently than the first game. Grow Up has you just touch a particular plant one time and it adds an infinite number of them to your inventory. You can use them anywhere, forever. There are 40 of them that do 2 things.
In the original Grow Home, there were 3 or 4 plants that all did something different. However, you could only carry one of them on you at a time. So if you needed a parachute, you would have to GO FIND A DAISY and add it to your backpack. If you needed to glide, you would have to GO FIND A LARGE LEAF. No more! You have an infinite number of 40 plants that can be placed anywhere.
But you won't need to. Jetpack, parachute, and glide are all built directly into BUD now. No plants required. And you don't really need any abilities outside those.
The game added "challenge markers". These are objects you touch that make you jump through hoops on a timer. This is literally one of my biggest video game pet peeves of all time. I refuse to say more about it.
I don't know why, but the camera seems a lot worse than in the first. It only has two settings: 1) Way too close, 2) Way too far away. I also constantly found myself battling with it for the angle I wanted while it tried desperately to give me a fine view of a wall. Don't remember that problem in the first game.
Also, this game runs pretty poorly compared to the first. Possibly due to new shadow/lighting effects. I had to make a lot more adjustments to get it to run smoothly compared to the first game, which is kinda lame considering it uses Nintendo 64 sized polygons.
BUD has a problem hanging onto the growing starplants compared to first game. He lags behind the tip he's holding and will fall off while riding it or right after it connects with a crystal, even though you are still squeezing the grip. Don't remember that being a problem in the first game.
For all of the above reasons, Grow Up proves a fun return to our little red robot friend, but as a game, it has a lot of new features that feel useless, unnecessary, or naggy; meanwhile, it abandons the simple joy of going up, up, up with the more tedious affair of checking useless collectibles off a list. It also asked me to jump through hoops before a timer ran out, which I am still grumpy about.
7) A classic, essential, and/or must-buy game that is worth full price.
6) A good game that is worth the full price.
4) A fairly good game, but I'd recommend buying it discounted.
3) Not great, but a few redeeming qualities. Only buy if heavily discounted.
2) Only worth checking out if you are dangerously curious.
1) Avoid at all costs.

As a long-term devotee of the Impressions and TIlted Mill city builder series (decades now), I've had a long time to ponder what makes these games special. And I've recently decided it's not the games themselves: it's the subjective experience of playing, or having played them.
CAESAR IV succeeds in a profound way that CAESAR III, ZEUS and its expansions did, and PHAROAH or EMPEROR never quite managed for me: it makes my time spent in-game feel consequential. Like I've been building something that had meaning, not just "wasting time on a video game."
I suspect this is the appeal of the best city-builders (although I never got the same feeling from SIMCITY or CITIES: SKYLINES), that I was engaged in a creative act while playing, and this meant the activity had value, in and of itself. That the skills I honed playing this game were skills that would benefit me in other ways, in life.
I'm delighted that CAESAR IV is now available on Steam. I've just started my second or third campaign playthrough, and am enjoying it thoroughly. I'm happy to recommend this less-than-perfect game to anyone looking for an engrossing, humane, challenging real-time resource management sim set in a fascinating era. Enjoy.

This game comes with one item of DLC bundled with it which is nice. However I accidentally played it before the main game. In the DLC you wander round with no explanation, get shot in the face, wander around some more, murder some guy, wander around a lot more collecting gnomes and then it just comes to an end still with no indication of what is going on. So my first recommendation is don’t play the DLC first.
Now onto the main game, it does give you more of an indication of what is going on but it still really didn’t work for me. When I see a game described as a walking simulator I am expecting a game focusing on story, atmosphere and aesthetics. This game definitely has the last one nailed, the levels really look excellent and capture the sense of the wilderness reclaiming civilisation. Unfortunately it did make me nauseous, I think it is the slight swaying of camera. I could only play for short periods at a time but the game is split into nice short chapters.
The story however was not great. It is difficult to say much without spoiling it but the progression seems disjointed and nonsensical. The only way I can rationalise the plot is that it was all a guilty delusion or hallucination.
The biggest problem for me was inclusion of horror, it didn’t work in combination with such a passive form of gameplay. Since all there is to the game is walking around there is no form of peril so the horror elements have no weight to them. I just started shrugging off the cheap jump scares.
So if you looking for an excellent graphical showcase this is the game for you but if you are looking for more of an engaging story I’d look else where.

Fearless Fantasy is an adventure game similar to a JRPG in its combat
element.  To start with, the music in this game is wonderful;  it does an
amazing job of propelling the atmosphere and the combat.  The art style is
distinctive, and may not appeal to everyone, but for what it is, it is well
done. The game does implement a star system to encourage replay-ability
to see how fast you can complete each level.
You have the choice of three characters with a variety of different
strengths and weaknesses.  You level up abilities as a team, and each team
member has abilities that can be used to regain energy or mitigate attacks
not only to that character, but across to other characters.
The story is what ties the game together;  it propels you forward, and
the cut scenes are not overdone.  You can choose your difficulty level for
each mission, and the combat is done on a turn-based basis.  You attack by
drawing a line, and the quality of how seamlessly you attack will affect
how much damage you do.  Each ability has a unique way on how you attack,
requiring that you learn exactly what your abilities do, and think out how
you will be attacking each turn.
The game accomplishes what it set out to do very well.  The story
is entertaining, and the art style is unique.  The game provies incentives
to play it again through its' star system and plenty of achievements.  I
enjoyed playing this game, and can easily recommend it.

Though I am giving this game the thumbs up, this is going to sound like a negative review, because all I am going to do in this review is compare Grow Up to the first game, Grow Home. I do this for the people who played Grow Home so they can know what kinds of changes to expect. You may like them. Or if you're like me: you may
I was very excited to purchase this game on day one, since I was such a tremendous fan of the first game. I remember finally reaching M.O.M. and being frankly a little bit sad that the game was finally over. I was looking forward to experiencing much of what I loved about the first game, which included such great joys as:
--The simple joy of going up, up, up, and UP! MORE UP!
--Exploration! What will I find in this little cave?
--Dragging objects and organisms back to a teleporter to be scanned for research
--Picking plants and using them to traverse the environment in various ways
Little did I expect that Grow Up would fiddle with each of these wonderful gameplay elements, making each of them sadly a bit more boring in the process, resulting in a game that is not bad by any means, but doesn't have the same hook as the first. I'll explain each in turn:
In the first game, you start on a small island. It is the only real landmass. Everything else is just water for as far as the eye can see. The message is clear: this is not a game about traveling over land. There is only one direction you need concern yourself with and that is the UP direction. BEGIN YOUR ASCENT!
This was wonderful in its simplicity. Climbing up rock faces and growing the stems of the star plant higher and higher was very satisfying if anything for the simple reason that you could always look down at any moment and SEE your progress.
Now you have to concern yourself with scouring the surface of an entire planet, which is a lot of time spent NOT going up. There are also multiple starplants to grow now, which means even while you are growing one star plant, you know there are other ones that you still haven't even started. And get this: the starplants don't even grow all the way up! There is a hard limit on how high they grow! While still having things above them! This of course feels like blasphemy.
The rest of the game follows this pattern as well: a move away from simple physical progress toward a more "checklist" style of gameplay, which is precisely the thing that makes it feel more pedestrian (figuratively and literally) than the first game.
Exploration felt great in the first game. As you were ascending, you would come across islands of various sizes. Exploring them, you would find new things. New plants. New animals. New strange sights. You could drag these discoveries back to the teleporter for research, so each discovery was also progress.
Grow Up makes exploration more boring in a couple of ways. First, it does the AAA thing of putting an icon over every important thing, so you don't even have to look for it. You just have to go where you're told. See what I mean about the checklist?
No, you can't turn these icons off. And if you try to just ignore them, they have also added a companion named POD who is basically this game's version of Navi the nagging fairy. Yes, I'm serious and not exaggerating. You can't turn this off.
You are also given a satellite view that you can use to get an aerial view of the entire planet at any time. You can move the view around, zoom in, zoom out. All of the important item icons appear under this view as well. No need to explore or look around. Everything is clearly marked and easy to pinpoint. Sigh.
In the first game, whenever you discovered a new plant or animal, you could drag it back to a teleporter to scan it into your research. This added a sort of physics puzzle to the game. Which teleporter can I feasibly get this to? How do I get it out of this cave? How do I get it down/up to the teleporter from there?
Sadly, Grow Up completely removes this element of gameplay. Scanning objects into the teleporter for research is no longer a thing. At all.
There is still "research" in the game.... kind of. Animals are now completely irrelevant. The only thing you can research are plants, and you do this by... just touching them. That's it. Sigh.
Researching plants lets you use them. There are 40 plants to research. But you will never use them because there is really no need to. And even though there are 40, they all do the same 2 things. Which means touching all 40 plants is... just a checklist.
This works MUCH differently than the first game. Grow Up has you just touch a particular plant one time and it adds an infinite number of them to your inventory. You can use them anywhere, forever. There are 40 of them that do 2 things.
In the original Grow Home, there were 3 or 4 plants that all did something different. However, you could only carry one of them on you at a time. So if you needed a parachute, you would have to GO FIND A DAISY and add it to your backpack. If you needed to glide, you would have to GO FIND A LARGE LEAF. No more! You have an infinite number of 40 plants that can be placed anywhere.
But you won't need to. Jetpack, parachute, and glide are all built directly into BUD now. No plants required. And you don't really need any abilities outside those.
The game added "challenge markers". These are objects you touch that make you jump through hoops on a timer. This is literally one of my biggest video game pet peeves of all time. I refuse to say more about it.
I don't know why, but the camera seems a lot worse than in the first. It only has two settings: 1) Way too close, 2) Way too far away. I also constantly found myself battling with it for the angle I wanted while it tried desperately to give me a fine view of a wall. Don't remember that problem in the first game.
Also, this game runs pretty poorly compared to the first. Possibly due to new shadow/lighting effects. I had to make a lot more adjustments to get it to run smoothly compared to the first game, which is kinda lame considering it uses Nintendo 64 sized polygons.
BUD has a problem hanging onto the growing starplants compared to first game. He lags behind the tip he's holding and will fall off while riding it or right after it connects with a crystal, even though you are still squeezing the grip. Don't remember that being a problem in the first game.
For all of the above reasons, Grow Up proves a fun return to our little red robot friend, but as a game, it has a lot of new features that feel useless, unnecessary, or naggy; meanwhile, it abandons the simple joy of going up, up, up with the more tedious affair of checking useless collectibles off a list. It also asked me to jump through hoops before a timer ran out, which I am still grumpy about.
7) A classic, essential, and/or must-buy game that is worth full price.
6) A good game that is worth the full price.
4) A fairly good game, but I'd recommend buying it discounted.
3) Not great, but a few redeeming qualities. Only buy if heavily discounted.
2) Only worth checking out if you are dangerously curious.
1) Avoid at all costs.

I have not played Risky's Revenge for too long, but so far, I don't enjoy the game a whole lot. My main gripe is that there are way, way too many tedious dialog boxes that you need to 'click through' in order to progress through the game. There should be an option to quickly skip through the entirety of these dialog boxes at their onset, especially since the dialog is so simple, boring, and downright uninspired.
If you saw the episode of the Angry Video Game Nerd in which he complains about how the Megaman X series was ruined by dialog boxes constantly interrupting the action, you should have a sense of how I feel dialog boxes in this game. I'm not opposed to games having plots or dialog, but in Risky's Revenge, the excessive dialog boxes get in the way of the action.
The platforming adventure gameplay I encountered is acceptable, but not immersive or challenging. The action feels much too easy. This game seems to take a bit after Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. Perhaps its no coincidence that like SOTN, its hard to feel a sense of accomplishment from playing Risky's Revenge because the challenges posed by your adversaries and environments are very, very mild. The lack of difficulty in SOTN was its major flaw, but it excelled at pretty much everything else. I can't say that for this game.
Playing Risky's Revenge with my hardware is a little inconvenient because this game 'only' features partial controller support. (I'm using an original Xbox controller with an aftermarket USB adapter.) Because my controller isn't natively supported, I need to manually map keystrokes to controller buttons in third party software to play. For this kind of a game, full controller support is something that I intuitively expected for the developer to include, especially at the price this game fetches. However, the game's store page does clearly say that controller support is partial, so I don't feel cheated with the developer over this matter.
The one thing that Shantae: Risky's Revenge has going for it are the gorgeous anime stills that you see a lot during the excessive dialog sequences. It doesn't hurt that Shantae is pretty sexy as far as animated characters go!
Risky's Revenge isn't a bad game, but it's not something that I feel like I want to continue playing anymore as of this time. I'd rather re-play Metroid or Castlevania: Symphony of the Night than spend more time exploring new areas in this game. I find Risky's Revenge too mediocre to recommend, so that's why I'm giving it a negative score. Aside from having way too many dialog boxes that can't be skipped quicky, there isn't anything flat-out BAD about the game, so although I don't recommend it, I also don't hate it.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge is a Metroidvania-style game with great music, awesome pixel art, fun characters and tight gameplay. It's not as good as Shantae and the Pirate's Curse, but it's still a lot of fun. Recommended.

This remake of Wayforward's DS game from 2010 is the second entry in the Shantae game series, and is a fantastic romp through the half-genie's vibrant, colorful world that's fun, challenging, and over before you know it though it's entertaining enough to pick up for multiple playthroughs.
The in-game graphics are pixel art that looks a bit rough blown up to desktop resolutions, but that's to be expected from a DS title with its roots in the Game Boy Color. Bosses range in size from normal humanoid size to Risky's gigantic walking boat and are well-animated, each with its own distinct personality from Squid Baron's shameful dine-and-dash to Risky Boots cackling while her boat's firing away at you.
The music is enjoyable and fits the theme of each area well, done by the talented Jacob Kaufman. The forest theme is particularly nice, as well as themes like Scuttle Town and boss music that are reused in later games. The music doesn't loop seamlessly though, which is particularly noticeable late in the game during an auto-scroller section that lasts about ten seconds longer than the music for it. The sound effects are serviceable with a few nice touches - each of Shantae's transformations having different sounds when she's struck by enemies, for example.
The controls are a mixed bag. The game is generally responsive but mashing the attack button without maxed-out attack speed can actually cause Shantae to attack slower. The controls themselves are mapped in a less than intuitive manner (particularly the confirm/cancel buttons) but those can be remapped. The game starts by throwing you into an ambush without any tutorial, so if you're playing with keyboard make sure you know which buttons are which! Shantae learns several transformations over the course of the game and each animal form controls in a different manner - the monkey is small and fast but can't attack, the elephant is extremely slow when not attacking, and the mermaid is useless on land but the only one who can dive underwater. Transformations are done by holding the Dance button for a certain length of time and stopping Shantae's dance during a particular move. I like the notion of it, and it works precisely because the game is short. Had this been a longer title, watching Shantae dance for a few seconds before each transformation would have worn out its welcome but as is, it's a fun extra element.
As mentioned, the experience is only a few hours long. Beating Risky will take 3-5 hours the first time, and there's an achievement for completing the entire game in under 2. Besides Steam achievements and extra character art, the replayability is also helped by Magic Mode which changes Shantae's stats (less defense, more magic) as well as her outfit. It breathes extra life into a game that would otherwise be over all too quickly.
In short, Shantae: Risky's Revenge is a fun Metroidvania with a sense of humor and entertaining characters that overcomes minor control issues and delivers a solid platforming experience that's a lot of fun to play even on the second or third run through. It's a few years old and a port of a DS game but don't let that fool you, it's still a worthy addition to any action gamer's library.

Okay, waifu jokes aside, purely judging this game on it's own merits, it is honestly a rather mediocre metroidvania. If you want a FUN game, go get Shantae and the Pirate's curse, like seriously, that game is WAAAAY more enjoyable as a game.
The movement is slow as hell, maps are not very helpful at all, there's only really 3 different areas, 5 if you count the hub world of scuttle town and the final dungeon which is super brief, and there's backtracking up the♥♥♥♥♥ which, coupled with the slow movement and confusing maps, makes the game quite a chore to play through, and this is not good if I find it a pain to play through something meant for your enjoyment. It feels like half the game is backtracking with very slow movement, and if this didn't have any backtracking, it would be a very short game indeed.
As far as the gameplay is concerned, it's fine, plays like your typical metroidvania with your hair-whip as your primary means of attack that you can buy upgrades for, animal transformations that you unlock to get through obstacles, as well as magic spells and potions you can purchase as well; BUT I do not like how many of the more advanced upgrades you can purchase requires magic jams, which requires you to go searching for these super, super hidden magic jams with usually a very annoying tricky maneuvering or puzzle gimmick to go with each one you find, really limiting you to what you can unlock unless you use a guide.
Speaking of guides, advancing through the game itself and figuring out where to go next can and will get confusing as hell very often, as only vague hints are given. So if you do play this game, do yourself a favor and  go look up a walkthrough on youtube or something.
Overall, the game is...alright but I would say pass if you're looking to spend your time on a game that's actually enjoyable through and through and not a slog to play through; like the sequel game, pirate's curse. However, if you want the full shantae experience, then yes, this game is a better introduction to shantae, as it still uses the ol' transform into animals dance system instead of the pirate equipment in pirate's curse to get through dungeons; and it'll be real hard to go back to this from a modern shantae game like pirate's curse or even half genie hero.

Since the game is so much about dialoge and listening to the characters you play as, it is really important that the voice acting is good. One thing i always look for in games over breathtaking graphics or never before heard game mechanics are interesting characters (someone you can feel connected to when playing, something to take you into a jorney and make you feel part of it not just slide through the events of the game unconnected, leaving you feel empty). Interesting characters make (me atleast) players just so much more interested in the story. And well the voice acting in this game is superb. This game makes you think about your decisions that you make and hard, because well... you do not want to end up dead in the next chapter, but always making the best decision for yourself, isn't the best one for the cause. So yes there are decisions. Loooots of em.
Now the characters. There were characters that i immideatly fell in love with, for their character, funny and well thought out voice lines. It all fit. And yes the game story. This is my second reason why i loved this game so much. Characters and story. Again. Not playing the first game might give me a half understanding or feeling of the events of this game, but honestly i do not care not right now. The story is great. If you are a fan of futuristic, modern world full of technology and then also love the world of magic, non magicals and the world in which they live in, this game is like 2 fists in both of your eyeballs.

There were parts where i was sitting on the edge of my seat, holding my breath in, waiting to see what would happen now or bite my fingernails off worrying over some of my decisions.... There was also parts that felt really dragging on and really not well thought through in my oppinion or even neccesary. The game delivers the story well and the end was truly breathtaking with an unexpected twist at the very end, but it is not perfect. Still it makes together for an awesome story... still.
So i'd say this game is very much worth for a anyone who enjoys point and click game with awesome story and stunning graphics.
So really short: Point and click game, awesome story, great and awesome characters, really cool enviorment in both Zoe and Kians worlds, puzzles, and well the decisions.... many many decisions in this game.
Feel like home with that, I think you would enjoy Dreamfall Chapters. Yeah...
If you still want advice. Well i would really reccomend this game. It was very interesting and really really enjoyable.

Rating: 7.5/10
Overview: Third Person Adventure
The Good:
+ Great graphics and presentation, I personally love the cyberpunk aesthetics and the contrast between the magical and cyberpunk worlds
+ Fantastic story that does a great job of wrapping all 3 games together.
+ A small but cool ‘feature’ is when you select dialogue or make choices, you hear the inner monologue of the character giving you an idea of how choices affect the story.
+ Puzzles are greatly improved over the previous game, at times it feels like playing a traditional point & click adventure game
+ terrible stealth and combat have been removed from the previous game, focusing more on puzzles and narrative
The Average:
+/- The game has many different choices that affect the story however only a handful of choices truly change the story in any significant way.
+/- It takes a while for things to really get going in the story
+/- To truly understand everything in the story, you must play Dreamfall: The Longest Journey and to a lesser extent The Longest Journey. Playing both games will give you a greater appreciation for this game. I would not recommend playing this game without playing the first 2 games first.
The Bad:
- The game still has a lot of running around, often you must run from one end of the map to the other end to complete certain puzzles.
Conclusion:
Thank god this game turned out to be good and I couldn’t be happier with how the story unfolds and how they tied everything together. I did not expect to complete the trilogy almost 20 years later from when I originally played The Longest Journey so this was a nice surprise.

I've loved this series since The Longest Journey, and I think it contains some of the best storytelling, most delightful characters, and most enjoyable setting I've experienced in any video game. Dreamfall Chapters does have a few flaws, but it's a worthwile final outing into the worlds of Stark and Arcadia.
Cons:
- If you're looking for an adventure game full of challenging puzzles, this isn't it. There are more puzzles here than in the first Dreamfall, but it's still pretty puzzle-light, especially as compared to the original The Longest Journey.
- The game includes a "your choice will affect the story" system which is new to the series, and appears inspired by Telltale's recent games. I'm not sure it works as well here. In The Walking Dead, the choices system was critical for providing immersion and a sense of personal horror. Here, the meaningful choices are sparse, and I didn't feel they provide much tension.
Pros:
- It's a bigger game than the first Dreamfall, and provides plenty of opportunity to walk around, explore, and really dig into the various environments. I spent a fair amount of time just wandering around Propast and sightseeing.
- Like the prior games in the series, the setting and characters are fantastic. There are cool things to see, interesting people to talk to, and worlds full of lore and legends to marvel at. When I finished this game, I felt like I'd said goodbye to a cast full of dear friends.
In summary, I wish there were more games like this: games where the developers provide a bright and beautiful world that you aren't seeing though the crosshairs of a gun, where you win the day with your words and your wits, and where saving your friendships and your identity can be just as hazardous and compelling as saving the universe. I adored this game, and if those doors to Stark and Arcadia ever open again, I'll jump through without hesitation.

Don't get me wrong: if you are ready to invest the time it will(*) pay back. And 20€ for a game were you can dump hundreds of hours in is a good deal. I'd payed more for less and was happy.
(*) very low play time compared to others so this is an assumption. But reading the other reviews I tend to believe that. I do not regret the deal and I will come back and try it again ... two or three times ... maybe four. Also, maybe the starting phase will be improved as the game improves. Do not skip this game just because of this review. Just be warned: you'll have to spend some time before it's fun.

After playing The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav and Memoria, plus the Blackguards games, I figured that was that when it came to The Dark Eye universe games. WRONG. I had never heard of Demonicon, so I was eager to play it. An action RPG. I was looking forward to the change of genre. Overall, I can't complain.
First of all the game looks decent. It isn't the greatest looking game on the market but it does portray the world of The Dark Eye that fans will instantly recognize. The music is fitting to the overall dark tone of the story. The themes and overall story are very dark. There is taboo subject matter that may make some gamers uncomfortable. This was a fantasy RPG that you may not want the kiddos in the room. The story is very complicated and of course there are multiple paths and ways to conclude each chapter. I feel that this game tries to copy The Witcher with the whole "no good or bad just consequences", but instead ended up being Mass Effect's paragon or renegade options. Nice try though. I enjoyed the characters and I did feel a connection between the main cast. Be prepared for tons and tons of dialogue. There were times when I read and skipped ahead because I didn't feel compelled to listen to the actors.  It is a strange thing to like the characters portrayed in the game, but no patience with so-so delivery. I feel that this was a great story told in a long winded way.
Where the game truly shines is the gameplay. I tried to get through the the narrative parts as quickly as possible (which is unlike me completely, I sit through the Syberia dialogue and that is as mundane and every day as you can get.) just so I could get to side questing and saving the world from the demonic forces that want to enter our realm via very troubling sacrifices. Small interjection here: By the end of the game, I felt like I was playing D and D/ Dark Eye meets DOOM. The combat is hack and slash, but you have different fighting styles, magic abilities, general stats, and side abilities like Medicine, Fast Talk, Haggle, Lore etc. By aquiring AP points through fighting and quests you turn your main character into whatever you want. I found all the sidequests and the main quests fun. There were times I was so deep I forgot to use up my AP points so that when I finally did remember, my main had a huge ability spurt!
I am really glad that I played this game. I know there will be a second playthrough so I can be an evil renegade and collect the other set of achievements.  A friend of mine called this a sleeper game, and I have got to agree. I had never heard of this game, and I'm so glad that I was gifted this. For the price tag, I would say it is well worth it. It's not The Witcher but it is a dark, fun RPG that will take you about 20-30 hours to beat, depending on difficulty and how many sidequests you want to do (do them all!). I don't have a lot of games in the fantasy RPG genre so this was a nice change.

In many ways, I want to recommend this game as an underrated gem. The problem is, for everything Demonicon does well, a major flaw always seems to rear its head.
The textures are okay, yet the character models are ugly; the story is intriguing, yet concludes unsatisfyingly in addition to being paced poorly; the dialogue trees expose an abundant amount of backstory, yet several of your decisions lack impact; the leveling system is unique, yet entirely unbalanced throughout the game's five chapters... and so on.
Overall, I was actually pleasantly surprised by Demonicon, though just barely. While it's a game that you can easily lose yourself in for roughly twenty hours, there are admittedly far better RPGs on the market. Check it out on sale.

The first thing I simply want to say, awesome. I have been following the game for a while now, and at some point I started to fear this would be a heavily instanced game. Where you would fight over territory, but in the very standard form, where you are forced to fight 1vs1, 2vs2 or 3vs3. You would all start without anything and build up from the start.
However this is absolutely not the case, while you do fight in instance based areas, you can leave and join at any moment, without any restrictions. If you jump into an area, the enemy has often already set up a complete base where you start from scratch. Once you have defeated the enemy, you can decide to leave the area again, or you can decide to leave your army there (by default you have 2 'armies', but you can get up to 6 or 8).
War:
Something that does bother me a little bit, is that when you leave an area, it simply becomes neutral again, this makes the taste of victory a bit less, after all you have just cleared out an enemy army and there is nothing to do in that sector anymore. You only have 2 armies available, so you can leave it behind once, but if you have captured two sectors, you have no choice but to pick up one of your armies again.
A suggestion would be, that if only 1 faction is active in a sector, and all other enemies have been defeated, a small AI base is deployed, maybe just an outpost + couple of tanks. This would be enough to keep it yours, however not enough to really put up any fight at all.
Economy:
The buildings work exactly as you expect them to do, you have three resources which come down to 'power, metal, gas'. Power generators can be build everywhere, as where you need a node for metal and gas. Gas being a bit more rare and needed for more special units. The amount of buildings is not very large, however since the game is very fast, this might be for the better.
Units:
The units are very simple and I would say that at the moment the variaty is a bit on the low side. The strategy that generally works best is to simply make a big pile of units and send them into combat. Furthermore I also think production is a bit too fast (perhaps too cheap). It is very easy to just set up 15-20 factories and basically go from 0 units to the unit limit in less than 5 minutes. While the battles are interesting because of that, I feel like it becomes a stand-still very soon. As it takes longer to move to an enemy base than it does to create an entire army. Meaning that in theory, two opposing players could get to a situation where no one will ever win.
Conclusion:
The game is a lot of fun, every battle feels meaningfull, though it does hurt a bit when you need to pull out a unit and allow a territory to go neutral again. The economy is not very complicated, but this feels correct for a fast pased stategy game. Units need some more variaty and it feels too easy to get to the unit cap, increased cost might not be a bad idea.
The one fear I still have, is that this game is P2P, while the game is relatively cheap (at least in early access), the game does not to have a very large following yet, unless a lot of marketing will be done, the sales will probably be low. Since this game heavily focusses on multiplayer, this game, more than others, needs players to attracs more players. I fear that at this moment, this might not happen.

While this game has crashing and freezes (to be expected from early access), it also has storming enemy bases with hundreds of laser tanks, fun base construction, neat progression trees and interesting squad options that allow a range of tactics. I really enjoy the art style although my only familiarity with retro sci-fi styling comes from Futurama and the odd episode of Star Trek: Voyager. The opportunities for co-operation extend far beyond the scope of regular RTS games as multiple players can be landing and contesting different territories all at once with bonus cash getting paid out at certain conquest landmarks making it both fun and lucrative to work together. The population limit is currently set at 250 per territory per player, so with 9 players contesting a region the battles can get huge and are very satisfying to watch. It is pretty cheap to setup extra squads letting you contest large chunks of a planet single-handedly.
So yeah, I'm very much enjoying this game, it certainly needs work in its current condition but I'm positive about the direction it is going in.

Animal Crush is, and I say this without any malice, a game that doesn't need to exist.
When I received a 90% off coupon on release day, I knew something was off.  The game is, in its entirety: one screen, one song, five animal shapes and a timer.  You click and drag on matching animal shapes ad infinitum while the timer counts down.  Clicking on combos increases the timer, but only the most insanely large combos -- or creating matches with the relexes of a squirrel with a crack habit -- will earn you more than a fraction of a second, ensuring that you never learn the game's darkest secret, that this is all there is.  There is no second level.  There is no victory state.  There isn't even a trading card.
To its credit, it does run releatively bug free.  There is a glitch where if you click the "menu" button while the game is paused, clicking "Play" will start the game with a screen full of octopi and the timer frozen.  From here you can click until you've had your fill, which should be about six minutes.  Just take it from me that playing to see what 10,000 points looks like is pretty anti-climactic.
I paid with a 90% ticket and 10 cents from trading card sales, so it essentially cost me nothing.  You, my dear Steam friends, should just skip this one altogether.

I played the original a LOT for hundreds of hours on the Nintendo 64 when I was a kid. It was one the hardest and most fun shooters in its time.  Now I'm 33 years old and it's back out in HD on Steam. I'm stoked! One thing you must know is putting the graphical improvements aside this version of the game IS NOT THE SAME GAME.
Pros:
-HD graphics.
-Same graphics, just HD. Same clunky models. Same textures.
-Easier controls. Mouse and keyboard make it way easier to fly through the game.
-Faster Saves.
-Fog distance increased, but not completely removed.
-Kept old-school mechanics: no-reloading, auto-aim, etc
-Sound effects and music are kept the same.
-Lots of cool weapons to find and master. Lots of secret areas to find ammo and health pickups.
-You'll have fun tracking down hidden keys.  This isn't a linear game.
-Enemy AI is about as retro as it gets.  You can just run past them or waste your ammo if you prefer.
Cons:
-MAP COMPLETELY CHANGED- This was the largest surprise for me. Want that secret automatic shotgun near the 2nd key on top of that hidden cliff? They removed it. You're stuck with the regular shotgun for a long time.  The 2nd key isn't even on a cliff. It's now in a completely different area in a stone building, surrounded by raptors and militants.
-Fog isn't completely removed.
-No enemy AI improvemnts.
It's still a fun game but it's not at all the same game.  Because it still holds up as a great retro shooter I'm going to recommend this game.

[TL;DR AT BOTTOM]
This game brings me back to the summers of 1998 to 2001. I would fly down with my family to Florida to spend a few weeks at our condo. I always remember looking forward to seeing my cousin every summer because of the endless nights of gaming on the N64 and PS1 with no bedtime with him. I forgot how many hours we ended up spending on classics like Shadows of the Empire, Goldeneye, Dino Crisis... You name it! The one game that sticks out most to me from this time period is none other than Turok.
18 years later this game is as much of a masterpiece now as it was then, but I would wager that it takes an older breed of gamer to truly appreciate the admittedly clunky mechanics of what made Turok so great in 1997.
This is a great re-release/remaster of the 1997 Acclaim title done by Night Dive Studios. They are more known for what they have done to the System Shock series, first porting them over to modern PC systems, and then announcing they will be working on a remake of the original. I would say that this is a proper re-release, but I have no doubt that others will clearly disagree with me.
Yes, this is a game that begs for nostalgia goggles to be worn-- but then again, this is the game as we imagined it in our young(er) heads after all, is it not? Coming back to play classic titles can sometimes be a depressing experience, as we notice flaws formerly looked over, or things that in general, just don't hold up. This is not the case here.
For starters, this game got a graphical overhaul. It runs on, reportedly, an entirely new engine. While most of the textures look primarily the same, it is a bit refreshed. Probably the biggest fix is the draw distance fog-- it hardly exists anymore and you can see heaps more of the game as it was intended to be seen. There are tons of graphical options to tinker with in-game, but this is hardly a taxing game by any standards. I am running the game at 1080P and it never dips below 60FPS. The "enhanced" graphics might not appeal to some, and may not impress others, but this was one thing the game sorely needed.
As far as I can recall this is about the same game we got in '97, I don't believe anything was added or removed story-wise. Gameplay however is much smoother. No more fiddling around with an N64 controller anymore, praize da lawd. Platforming is a breeze now.
I would like to say that this game and its playstyle will likely polarize modern gamers. This is probably not something the COD/Rocket League crowd would enjoy. It's a slow burn you have to grind your way through, similar to Dark Souls, but not as difficult, and more rewarding.
The sound design is notably improved, with a higher fidelity soundtrack, and better quality sound effects.
Native controller support is very comfortable and all the controls are totally mappable to whichever configuration you prefer.
If you want a great, classic single player FPS game to play, look no further, but just bear in mind this is probably not for everybody!
I would like to express my thanks to Night Dive Studios for not merely pushing out a product that was not touched in 18 years, but instead, putting hard work into bringing back the glory of the 1990s with Turok's remaster. Thank you!
TL;DR Section
Pros:
-Vastly improved graphics and gameplay mechanics

This is an update for the original PC port of Turok: The Dinosaur Hunter, which is in turn, a port of the original Nintendo 64 game. What you get is new visual effects like FXAA, water refraction and bloom though the actual base game itself hasn't been changed in the slightest.
At its core, Turok is a series of maze like levels with a short draw distance due to the hardware of the Nintendo 64, where you collect 2-3 keys per level to access 8 different stages before defeating the final boss. Along the way you collect a bunch of weapons, kill poachers, dinosaurs and aliens and search for the 8 hidden pieces of a weapon called The Chronoscepter.
Great game that is very much a product of its time, with limited lives, manual save points and a fixed health bar system. It's definitely not a timeless masterpiece but still an enjoyable game with a unique theme.

However, this game does have an issue with it the longer you play on a single save file. In the beginning of each game, when you have nothing to your name but a few peasants and very little wood, this game is fun as hell. You have to be smart about how you allocate your resources, making sure you have enough workers to make sure your kingdom has enough food to keep the peasants happy, as well as collecting enough wood and stone and iron to make new buildings.
BUT, at a certain point, all of the strategy and planning can be just tossed out the window and you can just arbitrarily place farms, orchards and homes wherever you feel like without the slightest bit of thought. And this happens with each game I play after my gametime exceeds a few hours.

The game plays out on randomly generated maps at several difficulty levels (which adjusts the length of the growing season and the frequency of enemy invasions), but lacks a tutorial. The interface could be better: while tool-tips are plentiful, it is hard to find specific buildings. Basic resources (wood, stone, iron) are gathered from the map, while food must be grown at farms and orchards. More advanced structures require manufactured goods like charcoal and tools. Eventually, defenses and various services must be constructed to keep the villagers happy and safe. It can be easy to outgrow production, so steady growth is key to prevent an economic collapse. Overall, Kingdoms and Castles is an acceptable simplified city builder.

First of all, let’s delve into the
of Fearless Fantasy and let me be frank with you here, this game looks rubbish. Two-dimensional artwork that has a varying degree of texture resolution ranging from low to incredibly low. The characters are disconnected from the world due to a lack of shadows. The spell effects trot along the same lines. Honestly, the only good thing I can say about the aesthetics of Fearless Fantasy is that at least the enemy design is creative and even wackier than Dark Scavenger.
The
of Fearless Fantasy also has a huge variance in terms of quality. While the sound effects and music are decent, though highly forgettable, the voice actors on the other hand, oh boy. It has to be said though, that these voice actors had to work with possibly the worst dialog I have ever had the pleasure to witness. Just have a listen for yourself.
And “Jimmery biscuits.” Is not even the worst thing you will hear while playing this game. There is such an obnoxious amount of “something something … NOT” jokes in Fearless Fantasy, that I probably should go see my dentist due to all the cringing that I was forced to conduct while playing. So while the art style evokes possible humoristic influences of Terry Pratchett or the hitchhiker’s guide to the galaxy, the game instead throws boring and repetitive low-blow jokes into your way. Disappointing.
Now, let’s get to the
and the core innovative idea of Fearless Fantasy. The combination of turn-based combat with timed mouse gestures. Honestly, the idea is actually really good. The first few combat scenarios are interesting, require some getting used to in terms of timing, and are genuinely refreshing to play. Sadly, the fun only lasts for so long, as a ton of problems surface very soon. First of all, every ability and every attack each has its same pattern, so that sooner or later you will know exactly what is coming up and start mindlessly gesturing across the screen. I would have highly preferred to have a randomised pattern to keep things constantly interesting. To make matters even worse, sometimes my mouse clearly went through one of the arrows, for example in a straight line, however for whatever reason, one of the arrows was not registered and therefore the attack had a significant lower damage amount. Which brings me to my next point in combat. Even though I really do like that hitting the timing perfectly empowers your ability and matching the timing of enemy’s attacks reduces their effectiveness, this while system is incredibly inconsistent. I did several tests, restarting the same level over and over again and found that even if I managed to get a flawless block, I sometimes ended up getting no damage or 20 damage, which is a huge difference. The same is true for attacking, rendering the whole reward of actually hitting the timing naught and destroys the satisfaction of playing. Speaking of the non-existence of satisfaction while playing Fearless Fantasy, the cherry on-top of all the previously mentioned frustration is the grinding. As you can see, there are set stages in Fearless Fantasy, with a set amount of waves of enemies that are meant to be defeated. Once a stage was completed, you can proceed to the next level. You will soon hit a point, where a level is unbeatable because your party has not reached a certain experience point yet, thus requiring you to go back and replay previous stages, with the exact same enemy setups, abilities, waves, everything just to grind your way to a higher level. I am aware that grinding is a vital part of a lot of RPG games, especially for the JRPGs Fearless Fantasy is inspired by. The difference to those being though, that in these traditional JRPGs, your party usually went from A to B to complete a certain task, while on the way you had to encounter random monsters, which you then defeated and gained rewards from. The important point here being that you had a target. You were meant to be going someplace and this encounter just stood in your way, however to proceed in your mission, you had to defeat it. In Fearless Fantasy, there is literally no incentive to go anywhere, as the world is split up in levels and thus going back to previous levels just for the mere sake of gaining experience is incredibly tedious and frankly dull.
Now, I did not even mention all the little gripes I have with Fearless Fantasy. For example, the skill system poorly explains what happens after you upgrade an ability, only for you to find out later that due to the latest upgrade and the attached increase in energy cost, you now can only cast a spell once instead of twice, thus ruining the whole plan you had laid out previously.

I'll start my review early since the developer is asking for feedback (I have not yet completed the game - I just reached Level 6).
First of all, this game reminds me of the Metro series despite the fact that it's not a shooter at all. The environments are detailed, the story is interesting, and you can tell a lot of work went into this game. I don't recall how much I paid for this game as it's been in my library for a little while now before I got around to playing it but I'm sure it wasn't a lot. I see it's $1.99 right now - it's totally worth that price.
One of my only dislikes so far are the character models and the lack of collectibles. The squirrels, spiders, and even the humans all seem like they are a generation older than the rest of the game graphics-wise. I think if the team concentrates on character models a little bit more in their next game they'll be good to go. Also, since there is no gunplay in this game I feel like it could do with some collectibles since you spend a good bit of time scanning the environment. It might be nice to collect food cans (ala Hektor) and food would also be useful in this setting so it's not an entirely worthless collectible either.
I've enjoyed what I've played of this game and frankly I'd love to see what this team could do if it made a Metro-like shooter as it's definitely giving off that vibe in my opinion. I love the horror vibes and the sort-of post-apocalypic setting they have come up with (flooding was a very nice touch).
I'll update my review again when I've completed the game but so far so good. Recommend.

- Enviroments looks well crafted
- Story starts good
- Good music and sound design
- Fun for achievement hunting
- Unfortunately, the story is lackluster after the first maps
- Character models are very low-res compared to the maps
- Weird and confusing transitions
- The horror element feels either out of place or cliché
Enviroments are often stunning to look at. Very well detailed and crafted. However, character models looks very low-res, and the spiders even seem textureless. There were also minor things, such as the radioactive spill and certain decals that looked somewhat silly (one example of this was a hole in a wall that turned out to not really be a hole, but a plane decal), but overall the level design and lightning looks very well done.
I was very interested in this game's story for a while. A survival horror game, that isn't based on a zombie apocalypse or war, but rather something less common, cool! I loved to explore the island I arrived at and expected something cool to happen later on. It did, during the first 3 or so levels. Right after that it went down.
I still don't fully understand the antagonist's motive, why the extreme weather cataclysms began in the first place, or really what the protaganist hopes to accomplish other than reaching a certain destination. The weird and confusing transitions is also something that drops the story quality a bit. Like, at one part of the game, a giant spider destroyed my walkway. I fell down to what looked like my death. I then find myself in a snowy map with the explaination that two days had passed.
I will say this: The story idea is great, but doesn't build on that idea a lot.
Sound design was in my opinion well done. Protaganist sounds realistic and breaths differently depening on weather conditions and situations he is in, when I went inside the greenhouse in the first level I could hear the rain dripping on the glass. Music is real good as well, if perhaps somewhat overhyped for a story like this.
Seems to work fine and runs smoothly. I found minor things though. I could for example, jump on a wooden crate and it would vibrate hysterically and then disappear through the floor.
Great ideas here and there, and pretty fun for achievement hunters. I would have liked to see more ideas when it comes to puzzles. Sure, a few puzzles are in the game, but very few and often the same. I do understand it's a walking simulator, but it didin't have to be if more effort was put into the gameplay part of the game.
A well done game on a level design point of view, but it suffers from a lackluster plot. Having made mods, I know coming up with a good story isn't exactly easy, and in my humble opinion, this story ain't bad. You just could have done more with it. Shantae always been a bit underrated platform/metroidvania series and i don't see lot of people talking about it really. The series has improved a lot on each game and there are lot of graphical / gameplay related things that were really improved in Risky's Revenge compared to original Shantae that came out in 2004.
This game was originally released on DSi on 2010 and the game is slightly different in terms of level design, also additional magic mode was added among totally different interface. I actually believe that the whole menu system in Shantae Risky's Revenge is bit annoying to use versus just having a gamepad buttons for selecting items would be more convenient.
The game offers ~9h of gameplay for main story and 10-12h in total if you try NG+ and collect all collectibles, its pretty good bang for the buck i would say. The graphics are still good compared to 2D standards today, the music on levels is neat and controls are smooth and controlling shantae and her different forms feel fluid.
If you are a new fan and don't care about chronological order that much, you might want to try Pirate's Curse first - i feel that game has overall better graphics, story, gameplay and its twice as longer too. But i do recommend checking the all games out in steam because the stories are connected to each other and provide important background context.

If you are a fan of many of the more popular Metroid-vania genre games, and you're seeking much more crisp and beautifully animated pixel art graphics, then Shantae: Risky's Revenge is a great game for you!
The game centers a Half-Genie, Half-Human girl named Shantae who alongside her Uncle Mimic, is tasked with protection of the small village of Scuttle Town. Knowing this, you might as well ignore the plot of the previous, original Shantae title as acquiring it will cost you upwards $300 USD, unless you wish to hunt a valid emulator.
The characters all presented to you are all lovable and memorable. The  antagonist is named Risky Boots. A terrorizing pirate after the 3 magic seals scattered around Sequin Land that activate a forgotten artifact. Unfortunately, there's been a serious lack of "Risky" in Risky's Revenge. Very serious lack.. In place of this, you get 3 other antagonists with more personality than the 2x4 board that is Risky Boots. Squid Baron, Ammo Baron and Hypno Baron.
In the end, the gameplay is polished and dialogue is silly, fun and even fourth wall breaking at times! If you're into cartoony humor similar to what is decribed, you'll connect with the story very well in Risky's Revenge.
Regardless of the lack of the antagonist Risky's presence throughout the game, she makes bold moves in the ending of Shantae: Risky's Revenge that, provided there are multiple endings, result in a dramatic twist that will last even through into the next game. This only hypes me and supposedly others to play right through Shantae: The Pirate's Curse as soon as possible.
Definitly worth a playthrough, will enough admiration, you may also attempt to 100% the game in collectables, speedruns and multiple endings!

Rating: 7.5/10
Overview: Third Person Adventure
The Good:
+ Great graphics and presentation, I personally love the cyberpunk aesthetics and the contrast between the magical and cyberpunk worlds
+ Fantastic story that does a great job of wrapping all 3 games together.
+ A small but cool ‘feature’ is when you select dialogue or make choices, you hear the inner monologue of the character giving you an idea of how choices affect the story.
+ Puzzles are greatly improved over the previous game, at times it feels like playing a traditional point & click adventure game
+ terrible stealth and combat have been removed from the previous game, focusing more on puzzles and narrative
The Average:
+/- The game has many different choices that affect the story however only a handful of choices truly change the story in any significant way.
+/- It takes a while for things to really get going in the story
+/- To truly understand everything in the story, you must play Dreamfall: The Longest Journey and to a lesser extent The Longest Journey. Playing both games will give you a greater appreciation for this game. I would not recommend playing this game without playing the first 2 games first.
The Bad:
- The game still has a lot of running around, often you must run from one end of the map to the other end to complete certain puzzles.
Conclusion:
Thank god this game turned out to be good and I couldn’t be happier with how the story unfolds and how they tied everything together. I did not expect to complete the trilogy almost 20 years later from when I originally played The Longest Journey so this was a nice surprise.

I've loved this series since The Longest Journey, and I think it contains some of the best storytelling, most delightful characters, and most enjoyable setting I've experienced in any video game. Dreamfall Chapters does have a few flaws, but it's a worthwile final outing into the worlds of Stark and Arcadia.
Cons:
- If you're looking for an adventure game full of challenging puzzles, this isn't it. There are more puzzles here than in the first Dreamfall, but it's still pretty puzzle-light, especially as compared to the original The Longest Journey.
- The game includes a "your choice will affect the story" system which is new to the series, and appears inspired by Telltale's recent games. I'm not sure it works as well here. In The Walking Dead, the choices system was critical for providing immersion and a sense of personal horror. Here, the meaningful choices are sparse, and I didn't feel they provide much tension.
Pros:
- It's a bigger game than the first Dreamfall, and provides plenty of opportunity to walk around, explore, and really dig into the various environments. I spent a fair amount of time just wandering around Propast and sightseeing.
- Like the prior games in the series, the setting and characters are fantastic. There are cool things to see, interesting people to talk to, and worlds full of lore and legends to marvel at. When I finished this game, I felt like I'd said goodbye to a cast full of dear friends.
In summary, I wish there were more games like this: games where the developers provide a bright and beautiful world that you aren't seeing though the crosshairs of a gun, where you win the day with your words and your wits, and where saving your friendships and your identity can be just as hazardous and compelling as saving the universe. I adored this game, and if those doors to Stark and Arcadia ever open again, I'll jump through without hesitation.

Playing through this story, because this is far more a story than a game, has been a journey.
There were ups, and downs, stops and hurry ups, and many emotions were felt both good and bad.
Let me tell you about the good.  The story, overall, is immense.  If you like story games this one has many threads and choices.  But unique to Dreamfall Chapters, you can really get immersed in the setting and view the environment and characters through interaction.  There are puzzles and goals.  The length of the story across the 5 chapters overall far surpasses any other story based games I've played.  The music, sounds, animation and beautiful scenary add to story.  And the characters and voice action range from very acceptable to fantastic which includes a massive variety.
We should turn the coin over before you think this is my favorite game of all time, because it is not.
The story is vastly threaded, and unfortunately in some places, messy.  There are things that do not wrap up in the end.
I'm sad to say and some of the twists were not mentally tantalizing - they left me feeling a bit betrayed by my story teller.  However, the final chapter is fantastic and the threads of the story that are sewn into place are wonderful.  And the length can be a curse, I often found myself wanting to just move forward as characters repeatedly dwelled on a topic that then later turned out to be absolutely non-relevant to the story.  The gameplay itself can feel pretty linear beyond the immersion into the envrionment.  There were a few minor glitches but none of them caused me to lose any playtime, they were merely annoyances such as getting stuck temporarily in an environment or the character model becoming slight misshapenned.
It's hard to recommend this because you will either like the story and characters enough to justify the purchase, or you won't.  There isn't much for me to compare this too, and giving the inconsistent quality of the story throughout the game it's really difficult to make a solid recommendation.
Overall, I was fairly entertained and felt that the length justified my purchase.  Having the backstory from the previous games in the series (The Longest Journey and Dreamfall) will greatly help in understanding who the characters are so if you haven't played those, you should do that first.
6/10 - opportunities were missed.  Only fans of the series should consider.
If you loved The Longest Journey and Dreamfall like me, then its worth it. The creators were fans too, and executed this game perfectly.

Lets be very clear: This is absolutely not a survival game. Do not expect those elements to come into play. You may end up building one fire.
The bottom line is that this game is not amazing, however when you consider that it was developed entirely by a few dudes in Russia with no financial backing, it's pretty freaking good.
On a personal note: As a Russian speaker I found this game to be very true to the Russian Spirit. It feels heavy, but in a way that makes you want to carry on through it. There are minor translation errors, but nothing that will leave you confused. Honestly, Russian is very hard to translate into English. On that note they did a very good job.
TL;DR: It's affordable. Worth the cost. Not super scary. Not completely dull.
It is recommended but remember this is not a horror survival game. Just a walking simulator.

It's a short but sweet action rpg set in the Dark Eye universe. I can describe it most accurately as a smooth but not perfect game. It honestly reminds me of the old ps2 rpgs and for me that's a good thing.
Environment
This is a linear, on-rails game with maps that exist solely for you to complete your objectives. The environments are pretty and varied enough to keep things interesting.
Skills
It's very on rails with a choice of skills that end up mostly being those that are worthless in battle but make the game more interesting, or those that are very nice in battle but lock you out of more interesting choices. Because of this, even if I did play through it again for the opposite side I'd probably end up with the same combat-centric build because of the fights the game throws at you every few minutes, fights that can get tiresome if they drag on.
Combat
Combat is fairly predictable hack and slash fare with some minor clipping issues. I found the physical skills like parry and counter to be too finicky to bother with and went full mage. Magic will make most fights easy.
Moral choices
It has moral issues where you have to pick sides, but it's more like a pick your own adventure type of choice. In the end it's all pretty superficial and doesn't change much, it's just there to make the story feel more your own.
Story
The story itself is interesting, if pretty obvious. I enjoyed the dialogue and mythos attached to it. There's a decent amount of extra lore that can be found, but as I didn't skill up in lore I can't say much about that.
Overall I found the game to be a simple, fun romp through an interesting setting that harkened back to an older age of games. If you want complex or free roaming though look elsewhere.

The only people who are giving this game positive reviews are fans of the "dark eye universe"...  as a fan of high fantasy I can understand their Devotion to a beloved intellectual property.
However...
This game is terrible.
The combat is Clumsy, the animations are crude, and the voice acting would be an insult to a B Movie.
I did not make it far in the game, because of the glaring quality issues. The game ran fine, but nothing about it made it seem like a worthwhile endeavor.  The lack of polish recalled  PlayStation 2 ports that were rushed to Market before 3D games were truly understood.
I am not adverse to low budget games, I have to make this clear.   I have played several games on Steam that I picked up for $5 or less, released by Indie Developers, on evidently limited budgets...  a couple of these titles were very cheesy endeavors, but still good games with decent stories.  (Blood Knights, Marlow Briggs, Hunted-The Demons Forge - specifically)
Truthfully, I'm not hard to please...  give me a good bro shooter, or a God of War clone, and I will be entertained, I do not need every game I play to be perfect.
But on this one the developers just seemed lazy, in early encounters four legged enemies rotated on an axis, independent of their animations, to face me in combat.  The environments were  crudely conceived, the character movement janky.  Graphics seemes buggy, even when not.
The reason I am writing this, is because of other reviews praising the story...  While some intruiging concept may be brought forth later in the game, what I witnessed was fumbling cheese.  (A brother and sister bored of their fathers admonitions "never to mix their blood", yet who by adulthood did not bother to find out why)  I just failed to see the strength of the story.  And that DOES matter to me.
Is it the worst thing ever?  No.  Digital homicide bad?  No. But...  Don't let the fan-boy reviews make you think this game is Skyrim or anything nearly worth the asking price.
If you buy it, deep, DEEP discount.  (This is one of 2 games I have ever bothered refunding.)

Boy am I glad to see a Turok game on Steam! The Turok series are some of the most creative and mystical first-person shooters out there. Night Dive Studios took the rough PC port of this game and truly made it shine by adding support for modern resolutions, removing the 30 FPS cap, and adding several subtle yet beutiful graphical enhancments such as god-rays and realistic water shaders.
It seems as though we'll never get a new Turok game that retains the creativity of the first 4 (the 2008 reboot was a disappointment). With that said, it's very pleasing to see the orignal Turok get a proper 2015 face-lift.
If Night Dive Studios did something similar with Turok 2: Seeds of Evil (my favorite game of all time), my life would be complete.

Initially released in 1996 on the N64 and eventually PC, Turok was a fantasitc game that showed real evolution in the FPS genre. Its levels were expansive, graphics great, the animation was fantastic, the weapons were badass, and it took place in the universe of the already awesome Turok comic series. The game was a system seller, and boosted the sales of the N64 console. Its PC release was a good port, but was not as well recieved as the console version, and unfortunately has not aged very well (the code it runs off of has a hard time with modern setups).
Skip foreward to late 2015, and Night Dive studios has brought this fantastic classic back from the grave, with tons of nice new graphics options, gamepad support, steam integration/achievements, and supposedly mod support is to come; something that the original would have from benefited greatly.
All in all, this is a great and solid rerelease, and I can not wait for them to do Turok 2: Seeds of Evil
