Nicely animated pixel sprites, silly dialogue, and a great soundtrack to boot.  Risky's Revenge - Directors Cut gives you a re-worked warp-squid system so that you can warp to any one unlocked (instead of only being able to warp to the linked one).  Which allows casual players to get the speedrun achievement more easily while allowing competitive speedrunners very quick game completion times.  Dancing is simplified compared to the Game Boy Color game and takes shantae seconds to swap from transformation to transformation.  The Director's Cut also introduces Magic Mode which halves your defense and doubles your magic for either a fun way to enjoy the game after you've completed the story or an added challenge for those who find the game too easy.  Albeit short the game is fairly priced by giving casuals an average game time of 5-6 hours and gives completionists even more hours of fun.  If you're looking to get into the series this is a good starting point, it gives you a small taste of what to expect from most Shantae games so you can decide if you might enjoy the other entries in the series (Shantae GBC, Shantae: Risky's Revenge, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse, and Shantae: Half-Genie Hero) in that order.  I hope you enjoy it, I sure did!

Combat:
The combat system is about as complex as trying to swat a fly, whilst you are made out of rubber, and made to stand on a greased lamminate floor.
Controls:
Your character moves with the grace of an inflatable car-dealership mascot and has the spatial-awareness of a disabled blind man. If you have ever wondered what it would be like to have a skeleton made out of bendy-straws - then this game is for you.
Gameplay:
The enemies you have to face have olympic athlete like stamina, and will relentlessly swing at you until you are forced to either stumble away in panic or stand on your own two roller-skate feet and flail a stick around in their face until one of you drops dead. The map is a maze of depression and all-too-familiar doorways.
Narrative:
The narrative of the game exists as a few pretentiously cryptic letters, as if to draw the player away from the fact that the game exists just as some sick sadomasochistic self-torture device. You are immediately condemned to a groundhog day-esque maze game as you run bow-legged through a set of increasingly familiar corridors.
Graphics:
Good. Lighting and textures are pretty impressive for such a small download.
Overall, it may sound like I hate the game - and I do, I hate it with every fibre of my being. But I also hate myself for continuing to play it, and I also hate myself for starting a sentence with 'But'. Maybe it's because I lead a completely unfulfilling life, and have resorted to subconsciously punishing myself by playing such a ball-ache of a game. The repression of my dissatisfaction with myself and the squandering of all of my potential worth has manifested itself into Exanima. Maybe I'm not even playing the game, maybe Exanima is a product of my mind, or maybe I'm dead and this game is my own personal hell.
Is Exanima my bad dream, or am I Exanima's?

PLEASE READ: Due to the PC version lacking uplay (which seemed like a godsend at first), you cannot get certain items within the game that you can get on console versions. Effectively, that means the PC version has less content.
If you're still interested in getting the game on PC or just want to know if it's worth it at all, read on.
Overall this is in every way an improvement over the last game. It feels like a proper sequel; it's bigger, better, and still maintains what the original game was all about.
There are a few minor things that I consider problematic - the major one is listed above. That is the game's biggest flaw, that its versions are not consistent across platforms. This is a big deal in 2016. It is, however, possible to get all the achievements in the game and the devs did at least say they'll look into not making the content unavailable on PC appear in the trading cards anymore which was originally what led to a lot of people's confusion about "missing content."
Other problems involve some stutter that just barely avoids qualifying as lag. It can screw you up on challenges but I did still manage to complete them all and I am not a very skilled gamer. I am running a fairly high-end PC though and I am unsure how it would perform on lower-end machines.
And finally, there is the problem that even if the challenges aren't...well, always challenging, I personally liked the old system of finding things in the world and tossing them into scanners for completionist's sake, it was usually less stressful. I suppose the main issue I have with the challenges though is, the whole goal is to jump through hoops, literally. It's pretty easy to lose track of the hoops you're supposed to jump through and can sometimes make you repeat a challenge. I think having either some kind of dotted line to guide you or having a counter for how many hoops remain on each challenge would be helpful in those cases since you are timed during them.
The good points of the game are, not only can you scan plants just by grabbing them and pressing X (or square if you're using a PS4 controller) but now they also actually do something. You can plant them anywhere you want on the map and have them grow a new plant. It's a pretty good way to cheese challenges or just goof around when you're bored.
The newly-added POD view is also a great new feature, especially since you can be easily disoriented in this large new world you have to explore. It also comes with a waypoint system which I used constantly to find my way around.
All the familiar things are back, you still use tele-routers to get around, you still unlock new suits for abilities, and you still collect crystals to become super OP. It's overall very rewarding now and the crystal radar has even been improved to extend its range when you only have a few crystals left so you aren't left stumped as often.
I absolutely recommend this on consoles and do recommend it on PC if you don't mind that you are missing out on a few things. There is likely a video online that'll show you all the differences if you're interested.

From the Depths is probably worth trying out. It is a sandbox game that allows you to build vehicles out of components in order to fight other vehicles. Each system is quite complex. Say you need some energy. First, you need to decide how you want to get it; there are three main types of energy production: RTGs, fuel engines and steam engines. RTGs consume no material, but are expensive and have a low power density. If you go for a steam engine, you can produce power with pistons and turbines. You build out of boiling chambers, pipes, pistons, crankshafts, etc. then decide it ramps up too slowly and lower the amount of boiling chambers, or add a backup engine. Finally you can go for a fuel engine which is even more complex. The main choice here is whether to use injectors or carburetors and, if you chose carburetors, if you want to supercharge it or turbocharge it or a mix. Often the best solution is a mixture of the different methods. Each vehicle has lots and lots of these choices- notably weapons which are far more complex than engines.  Once it is built you can either set up the AI in the game or use a custom Lua script; there are plenty on the forums, but you can also write your own. Weapon systems can also be controlled by Lua - which can be made slightly more accurate then the default aiming system - and this is most common on missiles, where Lua can be used to make missiles with custom behaviors, for example sea skimming missiles. 3000 hours in and still learning!

The original Longest Journey (2000) remains one of the most cherished and formative gaming experiences of my life. Even then, the gameplay itself was not particularly engaging or even enjoyable. That was never the series' strong point, and Chapters is no different.
Where TLJ Chapters shines is in its unique worldbuilding and engaging story telling. Its marriage of dystopian sci-fi and high fantasy serves as the perfect backdrop for each of its hero's/heroine's transformative journey. Along the way are plenty of fantastical-yet-somehow-believable locales, and colorful and (usually) endearing characters.
While there are some sequences that are marred by either buggy or frustrating gameplay, or lapses in narrative progression, by and large it's a deeply satisfying story to experience.
Imagine mixing Mount and Blade with Space engineers and adding a naval twist to it.

Simple categorized review:
Looks: The graphics haven't aged well (pixels), period. However, the art style is pretty nice and the spell animations are still quite beautiful. This game needs a remastered version! 5/10
Story: I don't expect much of a story from this kind of game and I don't receive it, this is definitely what you neither should want the game to give to you. There is a story and the characters are likeable, at least the devs tried and got you some funny dialogues, always a goal in mind and, admittedly, even twists. It's better than in Torchlight 2 for example. 5/10
Gameplay: Rather slow-paced hack'n'slay, compared to Diablo and Torchlight. The characters can be handled comfortably while sometimes the menus feel clumsy and outdated. Combat is fun, especially when you try out the many types of weapons and sorts of magic. The flow of the game is very good all in all, and with character progression and tons of loot you got to try out various play styles in a single play-through. 8/10
Character classes: Eight unique classes (two from the expansion) that feel and behave very distinctively. The war/combat-mage-hybrid is arguably the most fun character class in video game history when it comes to preset ones. Even then, there is a lot of customization to be done, skills to experiment with and tactics (especially in later new game plus). The balance has no flaws, in my experience, and you just wanna try out every character with every single play style. 10/10
Complexity: This game is deep, even deeper than your first play-throughs will make you think. New game plus holds a bunch of surprises later in the game and weapons and skill runes work together in a perfectly balanced and intriguing system, though the game is not hard to learn. You get into it and discover what it has to offer over time. Equip sets, customization, smart combining of equip and skills, varied enemies that need different approaches to be defeated, lots of secrets, skilling needs to be thought through thoroughly unless you wanna be smitten later in the game...
The game is as complex as one would expect from a good RPG with focus on looting and leveling. 10/10
World: The world is huge, diversified and has tons of secrets to show to an attentive adventurer. Monster types are far from being copy-paste and the art style is nice, as mentioned somewhere above. The problem is that it might become a repetitive experience in later play-throughs, without level-generation (- except from the highest difficulty mode that holds surprises, as I also said earlier on.) The settlements and castles deserve to be emphasised when I talk about the world, they are big, you can enter every building and they are full of stuff to do and see. Also, the world isn't vast at all. In Torchlight, for instance, I miss a huge map showing me the land that I shall care about and defend. 9/10
Quests: Several quests are humorous and most of them are nicely written. Unfortunately, there is much stuff to be fetched, quests just lead to new areas and actually earn you very juicy rewards. There's quite a lot of quests to do, you can just do them on the run and have a good grin here and there when you track down someone's rabbit or speak to the "more simple" folks. Sometimes you make decisions. 7/10 in a game of this genre.

This is a tough one.  There are several flaws in the game that makes it difficult for me to recommend; however, this game does enough to make it more than passable.
I would not recommend:
I wouldn’t recommend the game if consumers expect a shooter game or a game with challenging puzzles.  The games description and features seems to be updated which is good because it’s better to be accurate rather than misleading.  With that said, no one should purchase this game, or any game, expecting more than what’s on the description and features because you may be disappointed.
Also, if you are not into walking simulators and games with little to no challenge, maybe you should avoid this one.

Give it a try:
Instead of recommendation, I think the idea of ‘giving it a try’ is more reasonable.  This game is indeed worth a try for many reasons and these reasons are the ones that give it more than a pass.
-The level designs are good.  Even though you are working your way through tunnels or buildings, the scenery looks good enough to take a snap shot.   Even in a post apocalyptic setting, certain areas are beautiful to look at in my opinion.  The screenshot section shows many good photo shots from gamers.
-Gamers should also give it a try if you do like walking simulators.  If you wanted to try out a post apocalyptic game without the trouble of baddies and difficult puzzles, give this a shot.
-If you like the Metro or Fallout series like I do, or even love playing any post apocalyptic games, this game is still worth trying out.
-Despite what I said about little or no challenge, there are spots where you do have to think and figure out how to progress.  This can either frustrate you or give it a little challenge.
-Finally, the other small reasons to give this a try is that the asking price is still cheap and the length of gameplay is alright.  The average game length should be about 5 hours to finish.  Also, it comes with a free DLC.
Gameplay Problems:
There are some areas in the game which were problematic and should be addressed but in the overall make of the game, it’s not too bad.
-There are some platforming issues in the game, especially in level 2.  If you’re one to explore the area, like I do, you might end up getting stuck if you are walking near the cliffs.  I had to reset the game on two different locations.  No amount of running and jumping could get me out of that one.
-Subtitles tend to linger longer on screen even when you exit.  Subtitles also tend to fall outside of my screen.  Maybe it’s because of my settings but I’m not sure.
-I like the controller support and that is what I play on throughout this game but I realize sometimes you have to rely on the keyboard and mouse on the fuse box.  Not that big of a deal but it kind of got screwy one time and I had to reset the level.
All in all, the game is alright and I enjoyed it for all the other positive aspects of it.

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.

6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Having read many reviews here and on other places I was positively surprised by this title. It reminds me of Risen 2 and 3 very much in the term of steering, character build and upgrades etc. If you like those games you will like this one.
I have played both the previous Drakensang party-based adventures and this game has only the world in common with them. What I like about this game is the character build. There are many attributes, sub-attributes, combat- and mageskills to improve and you always have to prioritize. Every time you get experience (AP) you can increase a talent or attribute and they get gradually more expensive. What I like best is that you immediately see the effects of your invested experience points. Something which is not always felt in other games.
The difficulty is just perfect. I play on normal and have to use healing potions to survive and heavily invest in combat intensive skills and attributes in order to win the tougher fights. The story is ok but nothing special and is quite hard to follow since the journal in the game is very bad. You can upgrade weapons/armours and brew potions if you invest in skills like plant lore.
Many complain about the combat but I like the slow moving combat. That makes it easier to see what you are doing and plan for combat or mage manouvers. The combination of them both works well. You immediately get loot and Experience which you can use to build your character. The voice acting is ok but better than in Risen 3.
You are very limited in the way you could explore. You have contained areas and have no possibility at climbing or jumping. That is a pity but otherwise this games reminds me of the older titles like Two Worlds, Risen and Gothic IV Arcanum.

I have to thank Splattercat for falling onto this little gem. Bare Mettle really haven't done anything another developer has done before in RPG, except they have created a physics engine that is truly sublime; especially for an independent label. You truly feel your reactions are the cause of your demise or success, and as much as you curse the sod that killed you, you equally curse yourself for your presumption. I've held off on writing this review because I want to be careful about how I approached it, at this time the game isn't complete and all I've really done is played through the Arenas focusing on the combat system, and that really is the selling point of this game, its unique combat system.
If you're like me you have a special place in your heart for all things Medieval, there have been low-fantasy and high fantasy settings, a variety of gameplay structures based on certain degree of random rolls and a lot of rules which, while somewhat immersive, didn't always make sense and seemed to miss that certain un-nameable something. The combat system in Exanima fills that void and sets a new standard for low fantasy medieval combat, truthfully what excites me most about it is the notion that if this game is moddable all the wonderful that can be revisited using this wonderful system, I shall explain.
First off, there is a learning curve, like learning to swim you'll have to figure out the combat system through practice which the Arena is really good for. After a lot of trial and error you'll start to learn the new system and adapt to it's unique mechanics, what begins to form is and intuitive display of medieval combat that really plays out like real combat. There is no arbitrary "% chance to block" your character will always do their best to block an incoming attack, unless of course you're in the middle of an attack and have left yourself open, the same rule applies to your opponent. What you get is a contest of timing which rewards a strong grasp of the mechanics and punishes a weak one, basically you get a lot stronger the more you practice and if you neglect what you've learned you'll lose some of the skill you've gained, just like real swordsplay.
What plays out is often a careful ballet of thrusts, parries and counter thrusts but there's also pushing, stumbling, tripping, falling down, over-extending and general brawliness. Very often you'll recognize the fighting from the choregraphed duels in some famous movies. The duel from Ladyhawke springs to mind, as do some of the more notable sword fights in Game of Thrones, I've never seen a game with a fighting mechanic so detailed it could pass for a movie scene yet being completely unscripted. There are no canned animations, push-button combos, special moves or keyboard gymnastics. The fighting is very intuitive, simple, elegant yet extremely challenging and highly rewarding. A long duel can come to a sudden end when at the opportune moment your blade sings through your opponent's momentarily open defenses and cuts across their throat in a spray of blood with the full momentum of your body leaning into the swing. Of course the same thing can happen to you.
Beyond this awesome combat system, which I'm hoping sees use in vast number of user created mods, and becomes the standard for all medieval games to come, there is the single player campaign. This is the part I've only barely scratched, but from what I've played it's basically a survival version of Diablo, harsh and unforgiving, where you start with nothing and through great resourcefulness scavenge enough materials to fight the zombies instead of running from them. I don't know how long the single player campaign is or if there are save points, but the first time you attempt to play through you should expect to die and start over from the very beginning a lot. It's like hardcore mode is the only difficulty level which I have to give kudos to the design team for taking such a ballsy approach. It will likely discourage new and casual players, but personally I'm glad there's a game that's been designed from the ground up to be unforgiving without being arbitrarily impossible. In any case, the Arena mode alone is worth the price and the more you practice with it the better you'll do in the main campaign.

I'll just say this. It's quirky. Combat and controls are unintuitive, but comparing it to other games doesn't really make sense. It was never supposed to be like other games. Every item has weight and combat is all about momentum. Since every item has a different weight, shape, and length, they "feel" different. If you expect to run into battle swords swinging, you'll be dumpstered. You need to figure out how your character and weapon moves, as well as your enemy's body and weapon. The game is very unforgiving, and if you die you start over with no armor or weapons. I quit many times after dying before i felt like I knew what I was doing. I wouldn't say it's hard, but there's a steep learning curve.
It's a fun game that is a nice breath of new air.

I played Exanima before it came to Steam, and not just the half hour or so it says here.
With physics like the ones in Exanima, the character has to behave differently, and I believe that it is just a matter of practice before you learn how properly control it. Since I have not yet mastered or even familiarized myself with this new approach, it doesn't feel that good. Everything I'm used to does nothing but impair my control over this seemingly sleepwalking super heavy sloth. The character feels clumsy and slow; nothing like I've ever seen before in a game. I have never since early childhood felt this lost playing a game.
However, I love it. Exanima takes me back 20 years or so, to a time when gaming was magical, exciting and truly difficult. While I do admit that it has left me extremely frustrated at times, the rewards of progressing are so much greater than seemingly similar games offer. Note that I say SEEMINGLY similar, because there is nothing really like it, and what makes this game stand out may appear to be a minor detail, but I believe it is the butterfly whose flapping of the wings eventually causes hurricanes.
As for the story of the game, I really cannot yet comment. My struggles have thus far consisted in surviving the strange freaks of the dungeons, and I have not yet felt so safe that I have bothered to find out why I'm there.
Exanima is a wonderful game with a new take on physics based combat. It certainly isn't for everyone, and don't expect an easy ride.
You're in for a great trip  :^)

Starbound: It's not Terraria in space-- but it's seemingly a completely different game than from Terraria. It's pretty large, and a save that I've had for over a year reached 2.13 GB big, and even though I've start fresh more often, My saves always build up by 10 MB per 30 minutes. This is basically a time machine-- I'm not joking around. It's that good.
Of course, nowadays, I mod my game to death and still have at least 40 FPS on average, but for a good while, vanilla Starbound is fun to play.
If you're a mod developer, Starbound is a great game to mod, it's got the Steam workshop, but beyond that, Starbound modding is very friendly to both beginners and modders who've been modding for a long time. In fact, even though player vanilla Starbound is fun, mods such as the huge, monster and god of all mod, Frackin' Universe greatly expand the experience and add brand new things into the game. Terraria, on the other hand, is a pain to mod for, especially to put mods in.
But, back to all 1000+ hours I've put into this game: I actually got my hours via both versions of the game; stable and unstable. I got this game all the way back when it was in mid-early access. From the early access, I saw this game change a lot. And it's amazing to see how it went from no final boos or intro mission to a complete storyline. I've always supported this game from the day I bought it, and it's wonderful to receive a new content.
All in all, if you love sandbox games in space that you can easily mod, then Starbound is for you.
(PS: If you want better FPS, turn off VSync or look for FPS increasing mods.)

Menuda joyita el Sacred. Un RPG de vieja escuela con una cantidad de contenido para aburrir, y adictivo como el solo. Lamentablemente, es bastante probable que si no lo jugaste en su momento, te parezca algo tedioso y simple como jugador moderno. Sus secuelas, en mi opinión, tampoco le hacen justicia, para más inri.
El nacimiento de este juego fue algo tardío, teniendo en cuenta que es otro juego de rol con una faceta dungeon crawler, visión isométrica y en 2D que nos sitúa en unas tierras medievales pobladas por las típicas razas de este tipo de juegos (goblins, elfos...). Se publicó en el 2004. Doce años después, y a un precio bastante ajustado, ofrece una experiencia duradera y entretenida. O mejor dicho, lo intenta, porque este juego NO ESTÁ ADAPTADO correctamente a los sistemas operativos y gráficas de los últimos años. Los glitches y bugs visuales son una plaga, y tendrás problemas de resoluciones sí o sí.
Teniendo esto último en cuenta, NO puedo recomendar este juego, al menos si no estás seguro de que te funcionará aceptablemente.
Pasemos a analizar el producto objetivamente.
LO QUE ESTÁ BIEN:
+ La historia principal es resultona y duradera como ella sola.
+ Juega con el factor nostalgia a favor para muchos. Revivir muchos lugares es una experiencia muy agradable.
+ La exploración está bastante recomendada y es adictiva.
+ Ancaria es un lugar que, pese a que sea algo genérico, es extrañamente encantador.
+ Variedad de lugares.
LO QUE NO ESTÁ TAN BIEN:
- Técnicamente desfasado, da problemas a tutiplén.
- El sistema de combate es demasiado simple en su ejecución.
- Las misiones secundarias son bastante repetitivas.
- Poca variedad de hechizos verdaderamente útiles por clase.
- Fantasía algo genérica.
LO MEJOR: duración y precio.
LO PEOR: su faceta técnica es pésima. No ha envejecido bien.
VEREDICTO: recomendado si lo jugaste en su día o si eres fanático del género.
NOTA FINAL*: 7.8
- Jugabilidad: 8
- Sonido: 7.5
- Apartado visual: 7.5
- Acabado técnico: 4
- Innovación (sólo válido para sagas): -
- Relación calidad/ precio: 9.5
*La calificación final NO es la media aritmética de la de los apartados independientes.

It's not an easy task to review this game. The biggest reason is that It absolutely shines in one area, but then fails to deliver an on par experience in other. It's not a bad game by any stretch of the imagination, but it has some not-so-minor flaws.
First of all, it's a 3D point-and-click adventure game, which heavily depends on dialogues and choices. This is the 3rd and final entry in The Longest Journey/Dreamfall Saga. It's highly recommended to play the first two games before playing this one. Most of the questions are finally answered and the story nicely wraps up in the end. Dreamfall Chapters has quite a lot of fan service: many returning characters, dialogues that hint to events of previous games, familiar locations, few easter eggs, etc.
Unfortunately, the game suffers from the same problem most of other games with multiple playable characters suffer: consistency. Without telling too much, you'll be playing as two characters: Zoë and Kian. While Zoë's story is mostly well-thought and consistent, Kian's leaves much to be desired. Thankfully, the game brings out few surprises throughout the story and absolutely nails the ending. Despite the choice-and-consequence structure of the game, there is really only one ending, but slightly different paths to get there, so playing at least twice is necessary to get the full picture. In the very beginning of the game we are introduced to Zoë's powers, such as slowing down time, illuminating the environment and reading minds, but as soon as we're awake, all of those powers are gone. Such a missed opportunity, the game would've been twice as good if they left her powers intact and gave us space to toy with it. But we got what we got.
Dreamfall Chapters is commonly compared with "Life is Strange", and rightfully so. Both are point-and-click adventure games, are heavily based on dialogues, are episodic, have the choice-and-consequence structure, have female leads, etc. But the main difference, however, is the consistency and brilliant writing of "Life is Strange" that Dreamfall Chapters simply lacks, which is a shame, since the first game "The Longest Journey" had the same brilliant writing as well. Sometimes it's a 10/10 and you can't wait to watch the rest of the story unfold, but then things start to fall apart. Fortunately, the final chapters more than make up for that.
So should I recommend playing this game? Yes I should! Fans of the "The Longest Journey" would want to pick it up anyway, since this is where you'll get all your answers and a little bit on top of that as well. Environments, character design and voice acting are superb and some of the "smaller characters" absolutely bring the joy and the spirit of the first game. And the actual final scene of the game... well, you're in for a treat, I can tell you that much.
Edit: The review was written before "The Final Cut Edition" update. After playing the updated version, I can say that the game is mostly the same. A couple of new NPCs have been added, as well as some characters have gotten a visual upgrade, for better or for worse. Also, a stealth quest has been moved from the main game to the playable "deleted scenes" section, although in the game the events of the said quest are still mentioned. And an in-game map has been added for easier navigation. All in all it's still the same game. If you want to play the old version (or if the game keeps crashing during cutscenes) just untick the update in your game page, as it appears as a DLC and not as a regular update.

Disclaimer: This rewiev is full of spoilers.
Where do I start… Frankly, I was neither hyped nor biased towards the game, when I bought it. Sure, it was in development for over 8 years, and that’s never a good sign, but at the same time it was still The Longest Journey. Even the *bad* Dreamfall was still okay and it was quite a pleasant (though at times annoying) experience. So, Chapters at worst would be not bad, right?
Boy, was I wrong. This game is a mess. Almost every aspect of it is all over the place.
I'm not going to write about technical stuff - people covered it already. Game runs poorly, lags, animation is hideous, voice acting wooden. Gameplay is a joke, there are barely any puzzles, and when they appear, they are poorly designed and you have to do "pixel hunt" in a big, 3D world. But most of time you just pull the lever or something - it's an interactive movie, not a game. Also, like these cool powers you have in the prologue? Forget them, you only get them partially back two times.
The pacing is either too slow, or too rushed. The first part of the game is just sluggish. It goes on and on, without any goal or purpose. It’s mostly exposition over more exposition, delivered in rather boring way. Also, a lot of political talk. Mostly political talk. Shoved right in your face. During the last two books there is a plot twist over plot twist, the game turns into a cutscene fest, where you see more cutscenes than gameplay. And trust me, there was not much gameplay to begin with. Oh, and most of dialogue and cutscenes are UNSKIPPABLE.
Story is an overly complicated mess. Chapters loves plot twists so much that instead of developing a strong plot and then punching you in the face with one big, equally strong twist that changes everything, it tries to throw smaller ones at you at least once for a chapter. Making the story so twisted and full of holes, that at the end of the day you neither know nor really care what it all was about. A lot of plot elements lack any subtlety. Like making most villains ugly, arrogant, stupid and smelly, with "EVIL" written all over them.
Also, the whole story is resolved by deus ex machina named Saga – a girl who knows prophecies and travels to exact place in exact time. We know nothing about her powers, as most of the game she spends as a child. And YES, you have to play her awkward sequences, where you run around as a toddler with a toddler voice actor. Oh, the horror.
Dialogues have some really good lines, but most of time they are either stiff and full of exposition, or trying to be personal and get cringeworthy. Most characters tell you their whole backstory and political wievs the very moment you meet them, because getting to know them with time is boring, let's get over with it, so later they can talk more exposition and jokes!
Jokes… well, most of them are either vulgar or based on the typical toilet humor. There were some dialogue lines where I was genuinely amused (like the talk between Kian and the engineer or some of the Crow’s comments), but most of time when the game was trying to be funny it was either tasteless or just… awkward. And when it makes a joke, it holds to it, repeating it at least few times, so you *wink wink* REALLY get it. Like, you know, the tavern name which is now the Rooster and the Kitten, but it used to be the♥♥♥♥♥♥and the ♥♥♥♥♥, or the finger puppet show named… the Fingerlings! Women love them! Because, you know, hehe, fingering.
But to be honest, something that really made me hate this game and made it cross the border between ”just bad” to ”absolutely terrible” was how it took all the nostalgia, crumpled it and threw it into thrash. When you take something loved by players, you treat it with respect. You don’t take the Journeyman Inn, which feels almost like home, and close  it down, arresting the aunt-like owner, and then just mention few times that she’s in jail and she may not survive. You don’t just take fans’ favourite character and kill her, then forget about her and half-a$$ some explanation of her being now free and reborn at the same time. You don’t take good characters and suddenly make them evil and mean. It’s like taking a kid’s favourite toy, breaking it an then giving it another and saying ”okay, now you play with it, I was bored with the previous one”. And that’s what Dreamfall did, to some extend, and what Chapters did in full.
Also, The Longest Journey was quite a positive game. It had a message about hope, about helping others, about being kind and understanding the world, about balance and peace. Chapters is so… mean-spirited and negative. Plots, corruption, concentration camps, genocide, sexual assault, murder, torture… and some of them are even things your character can do - hell, at least three chracters get severly injured because of what you have to do, one is set ablaze and almost burnt to death! And it's made as a half-joke. Some characters even laugh about it, or just shrug it off, because whatever. Really, game? Really? Maybe it's just me, but I find nothing funny in a scene, where somebody is burning and screaming in pain. Not in this game series. That was sick and shocking.
At the end of the day alomst everything is resolved by violence. More than few characters face a gruesome death, there’s fighting and killing everywhere. It’s a far cry from a story about the girl, who brought balance back to the world with her wits, courage and faith in what she did. Who had so much empathy for others and strived to understand them, to work with them, not against them, and who never really hurt anybody. The Longest Journey was inspiring, full of hope and dreams. Chapters is just mean and depressing.
TL DR: That game is terrible, if you are a TLJ fan, just pretend Chapters never happened, if you are a new player - just pick something more enjoyable.

Fearless Fantasy is a fun RPG that is rather short but is entertaining nonetheless and is worth the download.
The story is rather simple but it gets the momentum going so you can smoosh monsters in no time.
Leon, a professional monster hunter gets a request from someone to rescue a girl for 500 gold. That girl happens to be the same person who requested the rescue. As Leon finds out the hard way, the girl happens to be a princess who is running from an arranged marriage with the mad King Xola. They are later accompanied by Vonn, a fellow monster hunter, to stop the mad King and his pet Deothas to save the kingdom!
Gameplay, of course, is where the game shines. The game has a map which shows progression throughout. The player is given the chance to buy items before battles or practice previous encounters the player has already beaten. You can also spend experience and skill points on techniques on the overworld map.
The battle system is classic turn based with an Active Time Battle system similar to
the mid Final Fantasy games (4-9). Character turns are determined as these fill up. The fun part about the gameplay is the combat. When you attack, defend, or perform special techniques, special arrows appear throughout the screen. Hovering your mouse through these arrows will determine if your attack is effective or not or how much damage you take. A grading system is there to rate how accurate you are. Get an EPIC bonus on special techniques by filling up a grading gauge and you get special bonuses and buffs. These buffs are an essential part of combat and can be the meaning of life or death in the harder levels. Getting a successful buff and seeing that EPIC flash is a rewarding part of the game.
The enemies are fair and the game makes all of their special attacks and properties known by hovering over them. This gives you complete control over the battle and gives you time to plan accordingly. This gives battles a unique and strategic vibe where you are given all the information you need to be successful and not get caught off guard. Deaths are fair in this regard as you can only really blame yourself for not planning ahead.  Skill points and attribute points can also be redistributed before battles so you can plan your party beforehand. Items are also relatively cheap and you can also train in previous stages so beating the game is not too difficult.
The game takes on average 4 or 5 hours trying to beat both Veteran and Normal. This is pretty short but the game regardless is loads of fun and recommended for those who enjoy a simple and fun diversion.

Having played many other city builder games, starting with Caesar 3.
While I do not hate this game, there are several rather basic features and design choices that make it very hard to like it. I understand how early access and indepentantly developed games need to grow and evolve, I believe there are several basic design choices that will make it very hard to significantly improve the overall game without those elements being redesigned from the ground up.
Roads seem to need to connect to every building, and the placement of roads can only be made to other roads. While this is not a huge issue, it forces to player to spend more time than they should stuffing around with roads than they should. It should also be noted that the games building/tile size is quite large compared to most city builders, making the wasted space on roads quite significant, as a road takes up the exact same space as a basic home does, or even a quarry.
While I can see my population and idle workers, I have no interface that seems to tell me anything about my workforce. I can manually close down the staffing of certain buildings, but I have no greater control over the workforce in a simple interface to make greater decisions. For anyone familiar with this, I would refer you to the workforce interface used in Banished, which achieves this very well.
You can build a castle addition called the treasure room. As expected it collects tax from residents. You cannot turn off the workforce on this building. So once it is built, you are consigned to demolish it, or keep the workers assigned to it.
The interface in general is quite cumbersome, with elements taking up more space than I would like, and displaying less than I would like.
I will try to update this as I play it, but at the moment, I would warn anyone against experienced genre city builder players from bothering.

An atmospheric horror game that increases the number of horror-themed walking sims out there. Moreover, the game has a decent walkthrough time with its 5 hours for completion.
The protagonist is a detective who is looking for shelter under extreme weather conditions. The initial cutscene - his ride from a station which is followed by an accident - is not thoroughly explained. I understand he is looking for a place to stay but there's not much emphasis on explaining the background. We are in the near future where global warming becomes an imminent danger as it greatly affects the population.
Thomas, our hero, is a detective who happens to bump into someone he seems to know from his past. Johnny - a guy in a white mask with a military shotgun - plays with Thomas by chasing him regularly and unleashing some nasty spiders on him. The game is an interesting walking sim in the sense that there's a lot of action sequences but they play out in the form of cutscenes. We mostly just walk and solve some easy puzzles.
The game was made with the use of CryEngine. Naturally, it looks stunning - I especially liked the outdoor areas with particular emphasis on the ones full of snow. They reminded me of Kholat several times. As mentioned above the game has a decent length and a free DLC also extends the playing time. This extra level includes some more details on the backstory and sees Thomas reach the end of his journey for good.
Overall, I was satisfied with Investigator. The story was incoherent at times (I wish they could have elaborated on it) and while the voice acting is great the DLC does not contain any. Also, the main menu is unnecessarily bilingual (a language selection option could have been great) and beside picking "low-end" and "high-end" selection nothing else goes under the name graphics.
If you like walking sims Investigator might just be a great purchase for you. If you are new to the genre perhaps picking Kholat is better - this, however, should also land in your cart later on.

Exanima is an unforgiving isometric RPG currently available through Steam Early Access. In Exanima you explore, fight and survive while grappling with the game's tricky combat system. Exanima is set in a dark 'low-fantasy' underworld and from what I understand from the Store page it's a prelude for a bigger, open world RPG, developed by the same studio.
Exanima's main selling point is its unique, physics-based, combat system which tries to be as realistic as possible with a focus on momentum, forces and collisions between characters as well as weapons. In making their combat system so realistic Bare Mettle have inadvertently created one of the most difficult combat systems I've ever come across, even after just over 5 hours of gameplay I'm still really struggling to make heads or tails of it and the explanation of it in the in-game literature isn't helpful either, this is something you have to learn by yourself. However the game's physics doesn't just impact the combat, it also impacts movement and interaction with in-game items so if you run into something on the floor, chances are you're gonna fall over rather than kick it out of the way.
Currently Exanima is split into two game-modes, Arena and Campaign. Most of the time I've spent with Exanima has been in the Arena trying to grasp the game's combat but I will briefly explain both modes.
In Arena mode you start out with basic clothes and a basic weapon and you begin in a small room facing off against one enemy who has a one handed weapon and basic clothes. After you kill your first enemy you progress to a new room where you fight a slightly more powerful enemy and that continues until you die. When you do die, which you will, you will have access to any weapons or armour you picked up from your foes during your time in the Arena but these are only saved for your current session, quit the game and you will no longer have access to them.
In Campaign mode you start with some clothes and a torch and you must make your way through the dungeon which you find yourself in, defending yourself against enemies and then taking what you can from them to make yourself stronger. I've never managed to get very far in Campaign, which is part of the reason why I've stuck to Arena, so I'm not sure if there's any sort of end-game to it or if you just continue exploring forever.
+Very good graphics
+As mentioned, very realistic physics
+Hitting/killing enemies is oh so satisfying thanks to the combat system
+Quite a lot of weapons, items, clothing and armour
+Excellent character creator which manages to give you a fair amount of power while remaining easy to use
+Brutally unforgiving
+Requires some skill to play, it's not just button mashing which is a nice change for isometric RPGs
+Not all enemies attack on sight which gives you some time to prepare
+Very unpredictible enemies
+Good sound effects
+/-Permadeath in Arena and Campaign
-As mentioned the combat is very difficult to wrap your head around and the explanation of how it works in-game isn't very helpful so you need to figure it out for yourself
-One handed weapons feel underpowered compared to polearms
-Movement is based entirely on your cursor, for example W makes you walk towards your cursor rather than walk up relative to the camera which I don't really like especially as you have to move the mouse around a lot in combat which leads to a lot of unwanted movement
-Walking and running animations are a bit odd
Here's a short gameplay video I recorded of the Arena mode:
Verdict:
8
Despite some flaws Exanima presents a unique idea in a good way with very good graphics, interesting combat mechanics and good item variety. Even if you don't want to buy it this is certainly one to watch.

From what I have seen so far, the story itself is hidden in notes and other things around the levels. I prefer this to the big flashy 20 minute cut scene, which shows you something you could of figured out on your own in only two.
Over all I would say the graphics are good. It has a dark atmosphere to it that really suits the game. The sound and music also go a long way to adding to the eerie atmosphere. The crunch of your weapons when you land a hit is just perfect and makes landing those hits all the more satisfying. For a early access game it runs beautifully, even on my outdated and pretty bad laptop.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge is a solid, fairly straightforward platformer, and overall great fun to play through.
With brightly-coloured, skilfully crafted and well-animated pixelart, the game makes a good impression from the outset (just bear in mind that, having portable roots, the game plays in a low resolution so will look a little 'blocky' on larger displays). The core platforming and combat gameplay controls well, especially with a controller, and never feels unfair. I'd note that you shouldn't come here expecting too much in the way of challenge if you're playing 'naturally', but if you're a completionist then the conditions for the various achievements (for example, no health upgrades, a speedrun and 100% completion) provide a more testing experience.
I see the term 'Metroidvania' applied to the game by some, and it does have elements of that. The game takes place in a single contiguous world, with a few areas initially inaccessible until certain skills are learned - but this isn't really to the same depth that I'd typically expect of a game taking the 'Metroidvania' handle.
There's a lightweight story framing the game and proving impetus for your various objectives - nothing especially meaningful, but it does the job well enough. Do bear in mind if you're planning on a child playing that the game depicts most of its female characters in somewhat revealing outfits - this though is never anything explicit, more just being faithful to the game's roots so I wouldn't suggest that it merits being overly concerned, just something to be aware of.
I'll close just with one tip for playing the game - don't miss that you can purchase a map from town merchant, as this is invaluable in helping you to navigate the world and find your next objective without too much frustration. I didn't spot this at first and found navigation harder than it needed to be as a result!
Shantae: Risky's Revenge overall gets a recommendation from me; if I had to score it, I'd say it's a solid 7/10.

The wobbling little robot is back with a much more impressive world and a whole new set of toys to play with. Just like its predecessor, this game features a minimalist art style that reminds you of early 3D console platformers like Mario 64.
The largest changes from the previous game I have noticed include, first and foremost, a significantly larger world. It is now a sphere with multiple ground biomes, with a veritable swarm of floating islands. Verticality is taken to an almost ludicrous extreme. However, it does seem that what has been gained in scope has lost in detail : most crystals are not hard to find but rather hard to get to.
The second notable change is a much more user friendly bag of tools. All of the special plants can be scanned and deployed at will. A new companion (POD, MOM is damaged and the quest this time around) provides not only commentary and tutorial, but also provides an overhead view and the ability to highlight a waypoint.
Also added is a challenge system where by demonstrating your mastery of BUD and his...er..."unique" physics, as well as your knowledge of how the plants help him, you can complete tests by passing through a set of targets within the allotted time. This extra minigame unlocks additional skins for BUD, such as a bee suit named BUG.
I'm already addicted. The charm of the original is not lost and the game can be somewhat correctly called "more of the same"...which to be honest, is a fantastic thing.

I'm going to be blunt, the game is incredibly tedious and not fun at all at times since its just a walking simulator without any direction, so if you're walking through propast and you are on the wrong side get ready for a 10 minute walk since your character walks at a bloody snails pace ! . Puzzles can either be extremely easy or the complete opposite and it tends to make the game have this really odd pacing, however I don't play the dreamfall series for the gamely (because there really isn't any) but I just found myself incredibly annoyed and bored at times.
Now for the real reason why I love this god damn game so much is because of the story... The choices you make have effect on every one around you including the world. While the pacing can be abit odd since you switch between characters and worlds it also some really poor character development and I found myself not caring for most of them especially saga,  it seems like they want you to have a connection with her but its so poorly done that I couldn't attach to her at all especially when she one of the main characters, you don't get any real answer to who and were she is from and you are left frustrated at the lack of lore towards her.
The ending will leave you with a huge smile on your face however as you get to see something pretty special from the first game (I called it at the beginning!) and the last 2 hours are some of the best I have ever had in a story driven game !!!!!!
You do get to meet some old pals like my personal favorite 'crow!'' and the mad scientists 'clax'', all of the main characters are well voice acted but the not so important ones are just pure silly at times.
Graphics wise its a basic unity game with some well done models but the biggest issue is its performance. You could get 100+ fps solid on ultra then get 20 in populated areas even on the lowest settings so bare that in mind !
All in all its a series ending (please make another one for the love of god) that sums up a brilliant story and worlds, however the gamely is something left desired but its worth it on the story and characters alone if you have played the first 2.
P.S Crow is the best companion any one could ever ask for !

This game's AI is completely broken, and the resource hierarchy is completely unbalanced. It does not respond to instructions, and you need to manually "turn off" buildings to do anything -- ie, you have to micro manage building construction. The problem is that you can't because there is never enough workers / resources to accomplish anything. Additionally, there is no build queue, so you have to build things one-by-one -- the issue here is that you have to manually clear forests (buildings do not automatically cause your workers to chop them down any trees on the underlying tiles), and you cannot manually instruct workers to clear trees. Similarly, you cannot mark a swathe of trees to "cut down". Because you are limited by the resources available, and have no manual way to instruct workers / prioritize their work, it makes the game completely unplayable.
Additionally, even in the "easy mode" that claims to be conflict free, you will get attacked *MORE* than if you are in the "normal" or "hard" modes. Horrible game, will request a refund.

Well, I'd been looking for a game to play with my controller for awhile. At $0.54 on a steam sale, I figured why not, this looks silly and dumb enough to be enjoyable for a little bit.
And it was.
I was rather surprised by the quality of the game overall though. The animations are actually not too bad at all, there's quite a lot of enemy types with reasonable attacks that can be learned quickly without having much in the way of trial and error, and if you make use of all the tools you're given, you can generally make your way through with hardly a scratch.
There are some things that can't be avoided - attack patterns of most bosses and minibosses tend to fire in a slight spread pattern based on where you're standing, but it's semi-random. Sometimes you'll get shots fired in such a way that there's literally no way to avoid them, but it's pretty rare and you get a healing spell on a long cooldown moderately early on in the game, so as long as you avoid eating unnecessary hits you'll be fine.
The balance is pretty good throughout. You get more attacks total and stronger attacks as you need them. You always have just about the right amount of firepower to deal with what attacks you. If you're relatively competent, you shouldn't have any major problems getting through to the end.
The platforming sections usually have pretty big platforms, and even though you slide a little bit like you're on ice, it never actually interfered with the platforming, even when making jumps across smaller platforms with enemies attacking and timed environmental hazards showed up.
The story's nothing amazing, the humour's not bad but kinda rare, but it's never really annoying. The writing's just kinda there sometimes, but unobtrusive. Occasionally it makes a joke that's not too bad, but mostly it's just white noise. Not great but nothing actually outright bad.
Overall... I actually probably would've paid more than I did. Which is weird. But it's not bad of a game. The only real downsides are that it has fairly low replay value and the multiplayer is local only. It's cheap enough to burn a few hours on it though easily. ...Less than I have played, though, since I was tabbed out AFK for a few hours in the middle, so don't expect a super lengthy game. I think it could've been slightly shorter if anything, it started to drag on a bit towards the end, but wasn't that bad or anything.
My biggest complaint... is that the main character is Maia, a female corgi. Warlocks are male, witches are female. It should be titled Corgi Witch. It just doesn't have quite the same ring to it though, I suppose. But it kinda bugs me. With that being my biggest complaint however, there's really just nothing bad about the game. It's not going to revolutionize platformers by any means, but it's fun, cheap, and worth getting even if it's not on sale. I was pleasantly surprised.
I think the most important lesson behind all of this, is that I'd been wrong for so many years. I'd made the claim that Queen Elizabeth II was the world's greatest corgimancer. I was wrong. Apparently it was Maia. Who knew?

I don't normally review games any more, but Exanima has a lot of potential and I'd like to see some of it realized. Let me start by saying that Exanima is NOT for everyone. Exanima requires patience, skills, strategy, coordination, and a bit of memorization.
I've read a lot of reviews saying that the controls are "clumsy", that mouse only combat and movement is too infuriating. And my responce is USE THE KEYBOARD. It took me 15 minutes to realize how much easier combined keyboard and mouse combat is, TAB to switch to combat mode, WASD to move your character and note that your character will keep his focus on the mouse cursor, and strafe around that point. Use space bar to center your view on whatever your cursor is hovering over. Evasion works best if you follow up with a clean hit with the appropriate part of your weapon. And then it's just timing, timing, timing...
Also walk, don't run away from enemies, the enemies slow slightly before they take a swing at you so if you keep moving, they tend not to hit you, running usually results in getting cornered by a group. Also they are persistent in following you so as you walk close doors behind you with your mouse (because you're using the keyboard to walk now right?)
back to the review, the atmosphere is amazing, sure the graphics are a little bit dated, but the shadows and the physics make up for it (except when stuff gets glitchy, but it IS an alpha after all) there are story elements, that keep the exploring the dungeon/castle thing interesting for those who like lore. The enemies are varied enough to not seem too repetitive, and the difficulty scales appropriately as your progress through, however finding armour peices play a big part in this scaling. So you do have to explore a little if you do intend to fight anything later on. My biggest grief with the atmosphere is it's too dark, so for 90% of this alpha you need to carry your torch (sorry shield bearers.)
Also the Early Access offers no (in game) way to save your progress, which I think frustrates a lot of people. From what I've read the developer does intend to put a save feature in. And there is a way to backup the autosaves, which I won't divulge because many feel this is a form of cheating.
I really do enjoy this game, and look forward to seeing whats in its future, hopefully we don't have to wait long. Overall I'd give it a well earned 3.5/5 because it does lack content, there are a few glitches, the learning curve and difficulty combine to make it more of a "Hardcore" game. But it has an excellent story, that I hope will be bolstered by NPCs once they're implemented. The combat system is pretty awesome, once you've adapted to it, and throwing a box on a Mob's head and getting in a free hit never gets old.
A truly special combat system that outshines anything else on the market today

What if Skyrim had been constructed as a Diablo clone? That's pretty much what you've got here - open world, tons of quests, and freeform character development (within a few archetypes). For all of its point-and-click simplicity, Sacred will entertain for hours.

Creeping slowly and stealthily under the shadows of many contemporary upcoming games, Sacred never really generated much media hype prior to its release. What we have on our hands here, folks, is an action RPG coming from European development team at Ascaron Entertainment. Sacred uses the all too familiar design pattern long-establish by Blizzard's original Diablo. Basically, you have your average heroic fantasy tale, an ultimate evil unleashed by a dim-witted wizard, tons of monsters to mow down, and plenty of quests. More than anything else, this game focuses on character development and classic hack'n'slash gameplay. Still, you will find a bit more than that, so I'd advise you to read on.
Coming up with a decent and innovative fantasy-style storytelling is definitely a difficult task these days. So, in all honesty, it would be deceitful to claim Sacred entails an exciting plot. Players are presented a rather basic and straightforward fantasy-themed storyline. The introduction sequence offers precious little to let you know exactly what the hell is going on. An evil wizard Shaddar summons an ancient evil and unleashes its devastating powers upon the Kingdom of Ancaria. Someone, naturally, has to put a stop to the chaos and disarray engulfing the unfortunate inhabitants of Ancaria. The first couple of quests won't reveal much of the story either, I'm afraid. In other words, it's actually pointless to seek some deeper meaning in the narrative since it remains somewhat scarce and incomplete throughout most of the game. But, believe it or not, the omission of a profound tale never appeared to bother me much during gameplay, given that all my attention was directed towards tearing monsters apart and leveling up my character. There were also some surprising moments of humor in the game. Opening graves and crypts, for instance, prompts amusing lines like, "In memory of all the monsters we have killed for experience points." The developers weren't too lazy to throw in a little something for Lord of the Rings fans. A certain stone ruin marked the following words: "Et Earello Endorenna utulien..." - for those of you who watched Return of the King, this is the beginning of the verse Aragorn sang at the end of the movie. This has nothing to do with the game, but it's still a nice and fun touch for all fantasy fans.
At the beginning all you have to do is select one of the six available characters: a robust sandal-wearing Gladiator, a mysterious Battle mage, a sharp-witted and sinister Dark Elf, a light-hearted and valiant Wood Elf, a charismatic Seraphim, the tempting Vampiress, and the dark yet sultry Daemon. Each class concentrates on a unique combat style, either through magic and ranged attacks, or via melee attacks. The Gladiator, Battlemage, Dark Elf, and Wood Elf, offer a pretty standard range of abilities and skills we've already experienced in games like Neverwinter Nights, Diablo, Dungeon Siege, and so on. The Seraphim, Vampiress, and Daemon however, involve a few pleasing novelties combined with classic RPG character advancement. Although I was pleased with the statistics and overall appearance of all races, I somehow felt drawn towards the incredibly alluring Vampiress (what can I say, I just cannot contain my bloodlust anymore). Also, I got a bit fed up with spells, bows, and throwing knives, so this was just right... for me anyways. I'm sure all of you will find what you're looking for in other character classes, since they're all quite suitable for various styles of play.
I think most RPG fans would be interested to know more about the regions of Sacred. The most commendable aspect of the game is the elimination of loading areas. Up to 70 % of the existing world map is accessible at the beginning of the campaign which comes as most appreciated gameplay element and allows players to choose multiple paths towards their primary destination. Another helpful addition is the world map which specifies exactly where your character can locate blacksmiths, merchants, etc. Additionally, each initiated quest is highlighted on the map, so there's no chance of getting lost even if you wanted to. There are many helpful additions to the gameplay. Each town, for example, features a chest in the center where low-level characters may lay down extra items which can be used later on during the game. If you find a ring, sword, or any other item you don't have enough experience to handle, just store it in one town and then pick it up in the next when you've leveled up the character. The journey between the towns should give you enough experience points so you can upgrade to the next level.
Using the interface and inventory system should be a piece of cake for any gamer. Everything ran smoothly - upgrading general skills and specific combat abilities can be done quite easily, which also goes for exchanging items, upgrading weapons and armor, etc. As for the controls, about 80% of the game boils down to mouse-clicking (well, as you'd expect it from any Diablo style RPG).
Apart from solving quests and slashing your way through swarms of goblins, orcs, gargoyles, thieves, assassins, and other baddies, the game will have you concentrating on using the most out of your character's capabilities. Beefing up armor and weapons is not the only thing you get to do. There's also an intuitively designed combat system at work, involving special moves, combos, and so on. Another appropriate moment in combat is the addition of horseback riding. Characters can purchase various breeds of horses which in turn helps them get around a lot quicker and gives them leverage during combat (provided they advanced the right skill).
Visually, Sacred boasts a pleasing mix of 2D landscapes and fully modeled 3D characters and creatures. Even though the backdrops appear slightly outdated, especially when you zoom in, there's a pleasing amount of nicely drawn out details, such as trees, flowerbeds, bushes, and so on. Water surfaces look cool as well, and there's a whole choice of impressive and colorful spells to see. The camera allows you to zoom in on the action at any given time... even then the models appeared to show a meticulous approach in design and animation.
The game's audio is quite good. Gamers will be immersed the whole time thanks to a jumble of realistic ambient noises and a range of sweet tunes. The voiceovers are okay, but there's really not much to involve you there I'm afraid. Everything else seems to be in place.
If you decide to purchase this game, you won't regret it. There are no breakthroughs in terms of general design involved, but the open-ended gameplay and an admirably lengthy single-player campaign is enough to the fancy of any gamer. If we disregard the relatively weak plotline, this is really an enjoyable RPG experience with enough content and replayability to keep you occupied for days. Plus, this is one of those rare games I feel the incentive to play again after I'm done with the review...

Initially I've had some misgivings about Dreamfall Chapters. I was disappointed by the new voice actress for Zoe and generally unhappy with the character models for the protagonists. Another frustration was the way some episodes were structured, often requiring a lot of backtracking through the same areas. This was particularly annoying for the labyrinthine Europolis: with many shortcuts blocked off, the entire map felt like a racing circuit.
In my review of Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, I wrote that the biggest problem with the game is that the sequel took a decade to materialise. Consequently, the player's enjoyment of Dreamfall Chapters is entirely contingent on how much of the story they remember. Despite Red Thread's best intentions, Chapters simply does not work as a standalone game and newcomers might be overwhelmed by the plot or miss the importance of the many revelations and references.
On the other hand, if you have played both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, if you've come to care about the characters, if you had many unanswered questions about the last game and were anxiously seeking validation for your own personal theories, this is your game. 10 years later, there is finally a conclusion to Zoe's adventure and what a conclusion it is!
Ultimately Dreamfall Chapters has its flaws (and the frenetic final episode managed to pose nearly as many questions as it answered) but Ragnar and Red Thread Games can be proud of what they have achieved. 'Epic' is an overused word but it definitely applies to the sheer scope and ambition of Chapters. Offering between 25 and 30 hours of gameplay, this is definitely the longest game in the trilogy, a franchise which definitely lives up to the name 'The Longest Journey'.
Dreamfall Chapters is a remarkable experience, offering an excellent script and an engrossing story. It is also noticeably darker than its predecessors, featuring some truly abhorrent characters and showing once more that the banality of evil is far more terrifying than any doomsday scenario hatched by a scheming madman. As Zoe and Kian face their biggest challenges yet, there are also moments of levity, amusing banter and clever jokes (see the quote at the beginning of the review). I stayed up until 4 AM to finish the game and I will definitely replay it at a later date in order to try some different choices.
Dreamfall Chapters gets better as the game goes on! The ending is rich in story and full of surprises. I like it very much and highly recommend it if you're into story rich games.

Even it wasn't THAT scary (I peed myself just a little), it's actually a nice game. Yes it's cheap (the price), but not crappy. The setting is interesting, graphic and physic-details are pretty good. The gameplay itself is smooth and standard (wasd, crouch, jump, use) and just right for a dark night (or a basement). Since there isn't a difficulty-setting (would be unnessecary anyway), I would call it a casual story-driven game with "horror-elements".
Even with the main game DLC, I finished it within 2.6h (short-story-driven 😉) and I enjoyed every minute of it (and will play it again to farm all achievements).
I don't know if it would have been the same if I bought it for the full price, but I can highly recommend it for the discount.

In many ways this is a two in one game, there's the vehicle design aspect and the RTS aspect.
Vehicle design aspect:
This part of the game is an engineers paradise with ability to customise and alter almost anything within a complex physics engine. That's right, if you place a backwards facing propeller at the rear of your ship, starboard of the centre of mass, the ship will not only go toward, but will also turn port. But don't worry if it seems too overwhelming at first, the game does a good job of allowing you to figure out one thing at a time with the assistance of a few tutorials.
The combination of these two features, the customisability with the complexity of the physics engine really forces you to think and plan, but at the end you can come up with some truly spectacular designs in both form and function.
But if you don't want to bother with that, don't worry there are plenty of brilliant design already available on the steam workshop.
RTS aspect:
The maps in FTD completely dwarf those of many other RTS's and game is essentially taking and defending resources zones while building, repairing and even resupplying your own military forces over land sea, air and even space.
Now how you do this is completely up to you, remember you can fully customise your units, so if you want to Zerg rush your enemies with swarms of small cheap units, go ahead!
Or perhaps you build to slowly build a giant mother-ship to destroy all in its way, then go do it!
In the end, the game maybe hard to master, but with anything you do, you can do it your way!

I've been a VERY LONG and dedicated fan to the Turok franchise since I was a child. Turok and Turok 2 were my first FPS games I have ever played, and I played them repeatedly as a child and into adulthood.
I have every N64 game, PC port, Gameboy game, Turok Evolution, and even the incredibly average Turok 2008 on PS3 and PC. I even dabbled in the comics, toys, and collectables.
You're, most likely, coming here from the N64 version of Turok, and that's fine. To be honest, there were few differences, even visually, from the original PC port and the N64 port of Turok: The Dinosaur Hunter. On modern systems, there were a few glitches with the PC port, such as the music randomly cutting off entirely, and some visual hiccups.
This PC version actually has some dramatic differences from the original game. First off, visually, it's certainly improved in most areas, and unnecessary in others.
The most important visual difference is the increased draw distance. HOLY CRAP was I surprised to see the game with increased view distance.
Don't misunderstand, there's still fog, but it's almost doubled in the amount you can see in front of you. There was so much environmental detail obscured by the N64 fog that has now been opened for everyone to see in this PC port.
As someone who has played Turok more times than I can even hope to remember, for possibly hundreds of hours total, I actually felt like I was playing a different game entirely for a moment. To new players, you won't be at all impressed. In fact, you will for a fact say that the game looks ugly and the level design is terrible. But for long-time fans of the game, this will rebreathe life into the game visually.
The next major change is the added on visual effects. This was mostly unnecessary, but I don't dislike any of it. There's now God Rays, Bloom, real-time reflections on water, and other visual effects. Sometimes they all clutter together in a bit of a mess, other times it looks rather appealing and colorful.
Luckily, love it or hate it, these options are toggleable. You can turn off what you want and leave on what you want. You can make the game look as close to the original PC/N64 port as you want, even as far as turning the screen resolution down to good old 1997 graphics.
The next major change is in gameplay. The original game, on N64 at least, made use of slightly clunky controls that resulted in making it impossible to do any precise aiming. To alleviate this, auto-aim was present, with no on-screen crosshair.
In this PC port, there's still auto-aim, but I believe you can turn it off, and even put an on-screen crosshair. Since you'll likely be using a KB+M setup, this means you can finally aim (mostly) accurately with a typical modern FPS WASD setup.
Also, thanks to the VASTLY improved framerate (as this is on PC), moving, jumping, and shooting all feels responsive, and those first person platforming sections feel more possible than ever!
There is this horribly exaggerated headbob/sway. I know the original game certainly had headbob, but with the increased control and FOV it makes the sway dizzying to a degree. Strafing left of right has Turok fling his body and perspective by almost 45 degrees. Luckily, NightDive Studios provided and made the ability to turn this option off! Barely a couple days later they released a patch and now the headbob is completely toggleable, making the game much more playable to those who get sick from dramatic perspective shifts.
Finally however, there is the game environment itself. In the first level alone so far, there have been pretty sizable changes to enemy placements, environment positions, and even entire new sections of the level. Seeing these new areas made my head spin. It's
what you might remember, but certainly changed. I can't say if I entirely like this or not. On one hand, it's a nice change of pace, almost like I'm playing the game for the first time again. On the other, it does seem to mean that a lot I thought I knew about Turok is mostly useless. It hasn't been too drastic yet, however, but we will see how that changes as I progress in the game.
The music is still fantastic, easily my favourite percussion based soundtrack in any game EVER, fitting each level perfectly. Textures and character models are sharper and cleaner, but are exactly the same from 1997. Sound effects are also the same, though the sound design as a whole has been tweaked for the better to be more crisp.
I do have a few nitpicks:
1. No walk toggle. This was crucial in some of the platforming sections, and it seem Turok's movement speed has been slightly increased otherwise.
2. The earlier mentioned headbob/sway.
3. Gamepad controls feel floaty and imprecise.
4. The map overlay shows in areas that in the previous port didn't. For examples, in the original port there were certain areas where the map did not draw, forcing you to explore, mostly in maze like areas. To 98% of players, this might be a great change, but for the 2% that have brain damage like myself, we might prefer the areas where we couldn't rely on the map.
Overall, this is still Turok, one of the greatest old-school first person shooters I've ever played, and can only be topped by it's sequel, Turok 2: Seeds of Evil (Please be swift Nightdive Studios!!!)

I was hoping for more of the same gameplay that had me rooting for the jointless, ever-ready little red B.U.D. I had spent the last game with.
I was not dissapointed.

The island and epic star-plant has been replaced with a planet, complete with biomes and three star-plants! (I don't count the last one because [spoiler ommited])
Prepare to spend hours jumping, climbing, jet-packing, gliding, falling, and floating like before, only now, you will also be planting, rolling, spinning, boosting and scanning!
I only have a few acheivements left to get after ten hours intensive gameplay, but I can tell one of them might add a few more hours to my gameplay on its own haha!
My only complaint is that this sequel feels a little easier than the original. (oh no, too easy you say?) I know that's not much of a complaint in a game that is easily ten times larger than the previous, but you can get around much easier.
Thankfully, the developers chose not to include the achievements that you have to grind for hours in order to get, but a few more 'tricky' things to acheive would have been nice.
I suggest this game to anyone who wants a simple concept and a relaxed game.
