The perfect sequel to Grow Home. Totally surprised me with some amazing new mechanics, done in such a way that you feel you have actually progressed onward after the last one.
The map starts off huge, but just like the last one as you progress the world gets steadily smaller with each upgrade or ability.
The main mission is a great way to get used to the world. But it doesn't take you everywhere, and leaves you with plenty to explore afterward.
Lots of people have complained about Bud's walk. Honestly, if you're walking you're doing something wrong. Between climbing, gliding, rolling, flying and falling you'll never be walking for any great length of time. One of my favourite movement systems in a game.
To sum up:
Pros:
One of the best sequels to a game ever. If you liked grow home you'll love this.
Vibrant art style with a whole lotta charm.
Funny yet enjoyable movement system.
Between the challenges, collectables and places to explore I feel that I'm going to get many hours out of this game.
Cons:
Early days bugs, including crashes. Issues with surround sound etc
Bit thin on the ground for menu options. No custom view distance, resulting in a bit of pop in.

God damn it I want to like this game, a lot. I really do. The physics engine, the realistic duels, the setting, graphics, tone. EVERYTHING! I want to like this game! The game reminds me of part Diablo, part Chivalry, and part Resident Evil. The fight engine, OMG I love the realistic physics based fight engine. It feels like a top down version of Chivalry realistic melee engine, constantly trying to block and parry to land a crippling blow BUT with the current controls and camera it is so hard to simply walk down a hallway without tripping much less have a coherent fight. It reminds me of controlling a string puppet the way it moves but the AI doesn't seem to have this handicap as it easily pursues you and counter attacks your character on every one of your uncoordinated swings. The controls are Resident Evil style Tank controls along with a rotating camera (If it was just a fixed camera or locked behind you it would be fine), W moves forward regardless the direction the camera is facing. As the camera rotates you feel as if you are fighting the camera as well as the enemy and it becomes so frustrating because when you die you feel like the game unjustly killed you, mixed with the lack of no saves or checkpoints it gets harder and harder to want to restart every time you die. I feel like they were trying to reinvent the wheel by replacing it with 4 concrete blocks.
In the end this is alpha, the controls flat suck and you only have two attacks swing and chop, no thrust yet even though its listed in stats. The game can still be great just not yet, maybe in the Beta.

I've never written a review, so it's already a testament to this game that I would write one.  This is categorized as positive because of its polish, but I personally feel negative about the game.
It's difficult to describe; honestly, I don't think this game is that good.  After seven hours, I think it has a brilliant concept that is flawed in execution.  It has an absolute AMAZING idea going with its combat.   That AMAZING idea is pretty crap in execution.
The combat is, and I think all posters will agree, ♥♥♥♥ing insane.  It's fun.  It really is.  But you will die . . . and die . . . and die.  You click and attempt to hit the enemy.  They block.  They swing.  You definitely can block, but you move slow.  Your movements have weight.  Has the weight of your swings and movements been balanced for maximum fun?  I don't think so, not yet.
I'll admit: seven hours in and I can't defeat the novice arena (a training area).  Anyone who tries to compare this to Mount and Blade is wrong--there you could at least go PvP and end out on top after seven hours.  That is not your situation here.
Here, you have been roofied and sent into an arena.  Your drunken arms flail about as they attempt to roll dice to keep you alive.  As you get better, your roll better dice.  Nonetheless, you roll dice.  It's HARD to come out on top of the AI.  (You don't roll actual dice.  It just feels random.)
Despite my negativity, I think I'll buy Sui Generis in the end (the game this is the prelude to).  I will especially if there is co-op multiplayer.  But I think it will all fail economically.  Why?  Because people play games to be heroes, not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who get beat down like an AI bot after five minutes.  Most of my friends can't stand this game, and I predict many people won't want to play this game.  It puts the developer in a difficult spot: do you stay true to vision, or do you try to make a living?
I predict the game in its current state--and Sui Generis--either can't stay as it is or will be a commercial flop.  That said, I think I'll be one of the people who tries to make it NOT be a commercial flop.
Yeah, I begrudgingly recommend this game.

Physics. You will want to play this game for it's physics, although your character seems to sometimes have issues with face planting. The lighting is also very pretty. The actual gameplay is unforgivingly hard. I mean like lost souls hard, but with perma-death tacked on top of that. If you die, you start over at the beginning. No save points, no check points, no quicksave. The devs seem firm on keeping it this way, and that's a shame, because the game has a lot got a lot going for it and 90% of the players will never take the time to experience it. I've been using the 'save game' hack from the community forums to create artificial save points, which, trust me, only gives me a fighting chance.
You will need to play in Arena mode for hours to get the combat down. How you swing matters as much as what you swing. I'd recommend reading a "how to combat" FAQ before playing, because the game doesn't really tell you anything going in, and there is a lot of tactical maneuvering required I have over 6 hours into the game, and most of my fights look like the last round of a boxing match where both fighters just circle, and fall into each other.
Overall I like this game, but you either need to have a lot of time on your hands, and a neurosis about perfection, or you will have to fight the devs, and copy save games, if you ever expect to see the end of level 1. I love the idea, but I think the devs need to think hard about reverting the default permadeath, if they want to make their work accessible to a wider audience.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge is a very competent and enjoyable platformer that makes up in charm and aesthetics what it lacks in difficulty.
GAMEPLAY: This is not what you'd call a hard game, it's fairly simple, the world is divided into different zone levels, none of which are very large, and while there is some back-tracking involved after acquiring new items and power-ups, it doesn't quite have the depth one might expect from a Metroidvania game. The actual gameplay however is solid and responsive and doesn't ever feel cheap or poorly implemented. With a controller this game is pretty easy to figure out how to play and quickly becomes second nature.
STORY: The story while not overly compelling is enough to keep you moving forward. It does definitely continue on from the original Shantae game, however playing that game is not required to follow the narrative as it's pretty straight-forward. Shantae's nemesis, Risky Boots is a pirate who has stolen a seemingly useless artifact from the town Shantae protects, which is quickly revealed to be possibly more dangerous than it seems. This turns into a "travel the world, collect the things" type of plot fairly quick, but is nonetheless still fun to experience first hand. The delightful and colorful characters certainly help to make even the more drab plot points interesting.
GRAPHICS: The graphics in this game are gorgeous, with one noticeable caveat: Due to the game being designed for handheld systems, the resolution is very low and there are no filter options to make it appear less pixellated. That being said, it's very easy to overlook the low res and appreciate the level of detail put into the art. The environments themselves while vibrant and colorful don't hold a candle to the incredible detail and fluid animation of the characters. Even the most minor of background NPCs is given a lovely fully animated sprite that carries with it a lot of personality. The main characters of the game also receive lovely portraits that span the entire height of the window giving them a lot of expressiveness and detail. The artwork is rather unique, with an obvious eastern flair to it, it still manages to keep itself apart from typical anime styles and evokes a more 90's cartoon style.
The main character Shantae is wonderful, and has a lot of detail in every little animation she does, and it's a joy watching her move through the levels and fight enemies.
FAN SERVICE: It'd be almost a crime to not mention this. Shantae's art style is just... well sexy! It manages to do this in a way few other games do however, being both cute and charming in a way that is appealling and even appropriate for most all ages, while being not-so-subtle with how it flaunts it's character's assets and moves. Most female characters are drawn in rather revealing outfits that show a lot of cleavage with their usually large bosoms, but fails to ever cross over into sleaze territory. The dancing moves by the characters, and even a few other animations such as Shantae crawling do feature quite a bit of bounciness and wiggling that draw attention to the character's curves but should manage to keep from offending all but the staunchest of moral guardians.
AUDIO: The game is a joy to listen to, the music is vibrant and upbeat in most locations, even the dungeons, and it never gets grating or annoying to the point you wish to turn it off. I won't say it's the best soundtrack ever for a game but it certainly fits the mood of the game, and a few tracks may even get stuck in your head.
Overall I would certainly reccomend trying this game if you have any love for fun platformers and aren't too worried about difficulty. It's bright, colorful, and charming. A joy to watch and play through.

I'm not entirely sure why I finished this game. At first it was to either leave a fully considered negative review or give the game a chance to pull me in. However, it just kept going and going, and I believe it became an exercise in stubbornness with a small dash of curiosity.
Short version: This game is a good idea brutally murdered by it's execution.
If you want to hear why I think that, here's the long version.
This game is more like a slightly interactive movie occasionally broken up with agonising treasure hunts attempting to masquerade as 'gameplay'. If ever you get stuck in this game, I would advise against grinding through the problem like I would any other game, and instead hit up a wiki. It's not worth the waste of time, chances are they didn't give you good directions or it's a case of crippling level design of the kind that places the object needed to complete a puzzle on the other side of the map near where you started from, once again causing you to go on a treasure hunt. The map of Europolis is nearly useless. The dialogue is painfully drawn out with excessive monologuing. Often, it will prevent you running or, worse still and maybe even more commonly, ground you in place, forcing you to listen to the lullaby of poorly conceived gameplay.
This game certainly adapts to your choices wonderfully. The key ones at least. All the other ones brought me pain. I'm still not sure if it was physical or mental. I am all for the illusion of choice. I believe it to be a necessary evil in this type of game, hell, it's a fact of real life. I am rather forgiving of it done poorly too. Many of these choices went beyond poor, into the realm of looping me at one at certain points because I didn't do what it wanted me to.
The animation was painful to watch. It was so jarringly horrid it actually made it as a major point in my list. The characters stand there, spouting this boring monologue, standing there motionless but for their mouths that move like gasping fish. There is no emotion displayed through either face or body language. No the minor movement of eyebrows that occurs once every few hours does not count. I came across a cat that zoomed past me on it's loop. It was moving fast, certainly, but nothing that would usually break immersion so harshly. The problem was that there was no bob in the cat's walk cycle. It was as if the cat hovered across the ground, legs working furiously to keep up with it's body. Although hilarious, it was another straw on a broken camel's back.
Endless dialogue, poor game design, and shoddy coding has me truly confused as to how this game is reviewed as "mostly positive".

The story does not captivate as much as its predecessors. Political commentary on homosexuality and the holocaust feels very forced into the story, and no space is left to answer many questions about supporting characters, but overall the game remains true to the spirit of the series.

Dreamfall chapters is the third and final(?) game in Dreamfall saga. The game blends fantasy and sci-fi and it works very well. You’ll be traveling through beautiful worlds in this adventure.
Game plays from third person view, same as Dreamfall the longest journey but has less annoying things.
Throughout the game you will have to make some choices which will change some things in future chapters. I think that worked pretty well, some decisions have really big impact. Gameplay is typical adventure style. You run around, talk to people, collect some items, combine and use them to solve the puzzles and move on to the next location but you will do a lot of running back and forth too. The puzzles are pretty good imo, some of them are hard to figure out. Other part of the game plays like story driven adventure game where you must choose what to say. You will play as three character. Zoe Castillo, Kyan Alvane and Saga.
This game shines in graphics department. At the beginning when you go out in the city for the first time it looks stunning. Characters could use some work, their faces are badly animated and look emotionless, but good voice acting makes up for it. Character design in general is truly stunning. But you need a powerful PC to play it on the highest settings. Just to compare it performs worse than Witcher 3 on ultra + hairworks.
Now I need to talk what I disliked. I don’t like being lost. Yeah yeah the maps are small but I still got lost, I wasted so much time on just finding the place I need to go. Why in the future when people have holographic phones and intelligent flying robots making jokes there is no GPS? I must rely on some stupid map in some spots in the city which is not very helpful. In magical world, well there’s magic so you could just mark the locations on your magical map, but instead again I must rely on stupid map posters around the city. After some time you get used to cities and in later chapters you already know where everything is located.
Another annoying thing is auto saving. Just give us the ability to manually save for ♥♥♥♥’s sake. Is it so hard to do? The game saves when it wants to. You can play for an hour, click save&quit and reload just to see the game didn’t save and you just wasted and hour. Sometimes game saves every few minutes. That was the most annoying thing for me.
Achievement hunters should be happy with this game. It will require you to play through the game couple of times to see all the choices and the consequences of your actions.
Other than that I loved this game and recommend it to everyone. Developers have done a great job so I encourage you to support the devs.

Pros:
- Pretty good story
- Choices matter
- Good graphics
- Mostly good voice acting
- No serious technical issues
- Unlike The Longest Journey, the story has a satisfying ending
- It fixes plot elements from The Longest Journey that were bad, incomplete, or full of holes
- You do not need to play the previous games to understand the story
Cons:
- You will need a walkthrough. You often have to search for tiny hidden objects to click on. Puzzle solutions are often contrived. It has that same frustrating feeling as point-and-click games from 25 years ago. Other modern adventure games fix it, but not this one.
- Very very slow pace
- First chapter isn't too exciting
- Gameplay inconsistancy: some dialog lines can be skipped, some cannot. Sometimes you can run during dialog, sometimes only walk, sometimes you cannot move. Usually without a good reason. Makes the pace of the game slower than it needs to be.
Mind blown / 10

Build an office space, hire a team, train them and work your way up the chain of rival games corporations vying to win over the critics and collect awards.
Game Corp DX is a fun little management sim where the goal is to take your new games studio from the bottom to the top. With a limited starting budget, you have to choose who to hire, which of the 4 skills to train them in and which types of games you at to release. Your office can be upgraded with new equipment and a couple of adornments.
Choices all-around are fairly limited, which prevents you getting bogged down with choices during the relatively short playtime. Extra tasks are always available to net you some bonus money to put towards your games development and marketing costs. You'll get a few opportunities to expand the size of your studio and teach your employees new skills, which will enable them to make better quality games. The in-game time can be sped up and paused which is a handy feature.
Presentation is simple and cute. The game doesn't take itself too seriously either: critic's names are parodies of their real life counterparts, some of the employees are dressed like they are ready to sell you a sack of wheat rather than code a game, and your first reviews will be comically punishing. You might be surprised just who shows up at your door asking for work by the way!
Some nice touches I enjoyed were seeing some employees avoid the door into the office and walk through the hole I left in the wall instead and receiving extremely mixed reviews (another parody of the real World?). If you enjoy management sims and like the idea of a tongue-in-cheek games development theme, you should definitely get your money's worth of fun from the slim asking price.

Kingdoms and Castles - A simple medieval city builder
Being a big fan of the medieval era, city building and simulation games this was right up my alley.
If you're into that kind of stuff as well I'm sure you will enjoy it too but please note that there are much work still required on this game, however I'm 10 hours in and don't see me stop playing this game anytime soon, especially not with the exciting updates coming.
An important thing to mention as well is that you manage it all yourself when it comes to city planning. You manually place down everything so it's not a game like SimCity or Citites: Skylines where buildings are random, however anything you place down has to be built by your citizens which is simulated.
I will now list my personal pros and cons for this game.
Pros:
+ Beautiful artstyle.
+ Very simple and easy to play, if you like games where you get the hang of the game in a matter of minutes this game is perfect, it's also very simple which is a turn off for players who really likes to customize every aspect of a city.
+ Enemies and other catastrophes makes for a fine challenge and can halt the success of your kingdom.
Cons:
- Very limited things to build and basically no variety of anything.
- Performance and bug issues.
- Many things could be better
I definitely recommend this game if you like this genre, however if you feel unsure whether to buy it or not I would recommend you to wait for a while as there's not that much to do at the moment. The developers are working hard right now when it comes to updates which is great because at the moment it really does feel like an early version and should not be classified as a full game.
I have made my own thread of wishes for the game which you can check out if you'd like.
My rating for the game would be 6.5/10 as of now.
I believe it has a potential of 8 or even 9/10 if they add and fix many things.

At first impression, the game looked really good graphically. The first few chapters were ok, but as I played more and more, things didn't hold up so well. The game is incredibly incoherent and confusing, not in terms of story but in the fact that all these seemingly random things happen and never get explained. Without spoiling it, there are so many things that happen, but just don't make sense simply because they are forgotten within a few seconds. The character you play as could bring them up or have inner thoughts, but they just sort of happen and are never explained further.
This lack of coherence unfortunately made the game frustrating at times, some of it was enjoyable like the atmosphere and the graphical aspects of the game, but for me personally the story was very basic and was surrounded by seemingly random events which made it not much of a logical or understandable game.
Also, after finishing the last chapter and the credits rolled I was prompted to hit escape. When I did, the menu popped up but nothing happened after that, and I couldn't click on any of the options or even the exit game button. Assuming this was an error, I ended the task and made my way playing through the last chapter again just to see what was supposed to happen. When I reached the end again, I hit escape and assumed I was supposed to click exit game, however this just crashed the game. After looking into it online, I realised there was a button in the menu that said 'DLC' and found out that this is what I had to click to actually play the end of the game.
The thing I don't get is that obviously there was an error when the menu came up and did nothing, which is understandable, but how was I supposed to know that I needed to click this DLC button just so I could play the end of the game? Since the end was obviously added after the games release, it should have just been worked into the last chapter or added straight after, as I can see plenty of other people getting to the last chapter, seeing the credits roll and assuming that the game ends on a cliff hanger, and never knowing that there was more to it simply because they overlooked this button in the menu.
Overall, the game isn’t terrible, but I would only play it if you are prepared for a not so smooth experience as the game has its flaws.

Gameplay wise, well, this is a linear walking simulator with simple interactions and easy puzzles. Personally I like this genre a lot and had fun with Investigator, just don't be fooled by the trailer and expect something challenging. Regarding technics, I've had several minor graphic, physic and sound bugs. Nothing to worry about however.
Verdict. Investigator is a small walking simulator with mostly underwhelming horror elements and a very engaging atmosphere. Play Investigator not for the horror, play it for the environments. If you don't expect too much, it is quite a good experience.

I would describe "Investigator" as a short walking simulator with horror elements.
It is a fun game with beautiful graphics and easy controls.
As a former detective you are roaming a post-apocalyptic landscape in search of food and shelter.  You encounter strange and unnatural things and meet other survivors.
The game is in Russian with English subtitles, however, the spoken parts are not that many and most of the time you will be alone.
It is not a shooter game, but in one of the later levels you will be carrying a weapon for a short while and a few shots will be fired.
"Investigator" is about exploration and getting out of horrible situations, with a few minor puzzles involved.  It is definitely a jump scare game.
This game was beautifully done.  You can finish the game in 3 or 4 hours, but if you are intent on exploring every nook and cranny (like me), it will take a few hours more.  I found the story gripping and simply kept going until I reached the end.  "Investigator" gets my vote.

Man, this is a fun platformer! You play as a half-genie on a MacGuffin quest against a buxom pirate queen. In addition to your normal platform mechanics of jumping and wailing on baddies (with your hair as a whip!) you slowly learn to transform into various animals, each with their own special powers. (Monkey can climb walls, elephant can smash through stone, mermaid can swim, and each shape has its own upgrade to make them even cooler). You can also buy items such as health potions, mana potions, and weapons from the store from gems that enemies drop. There is a fireball, a lightning cloud, and a ball that swivels around to protect you. Each of these weapons has two stronger forms. (Like increasing number of orbiting balls, shooting more fireballs, etc.) There are tons of collectibles and secrets to unlock, such as more health capacity and another type of currency that lets you buy the more powerful weapons. Since many of these are hidden in early areas but locked by future powers, there's a lot of going back to try to see what you can unlock after a new upgrade or power becomes available. It's got great music (think Sonic with an Arabian flair) and a lot of stuff to do, even though the game itself is relatively short. (Apparently there are different endings depending on how fast you can complete the game, and 2 hours is apparently doable. It took me about 9 hours, but there was a lot of looking for secrets and getting lost involved.
I think my only complaint is that there is a cool little feature that gives this 2D game a pseudo-3D feel. It's really great, but as a new player I didn't really understand the mechanic very well at first. There are these jump pads that let you jump forward or back into the screen to another 2D area. The pads have arrows on them (which I didn't notice AT ALL) that restrict directionality, which was a little annoying. So I didn't know that in the first area you can jump forward a couple of times to get out of the first town, so I was stuck wandering around between the two areas I knew about before I happened upon the correct pad by mistake. It's much more obvious when you go out to the first big area after it, where you're already on the screen that's the most forward, and you can see a preview of the levels behind you. MUCH more obvious. But then, there is also stuff off screen, which I didn't realize at first because I was spending so much time going back and forth. Frustrating. It's a really cool effect, but I just wish it was introduced better.
So overall, great game, good replayability because of all the hidden secrets to find and speedrun options. 9/10. Would belly dance again.

As someone who was introduced to The Longest Journey franchise through this game, I cannot recommend it enough.

Although certain easter eggs flew over my head because I had not played the previous two installments first, I was able to both understand and be enthralled by both the visuals and the overall plot In addition, Dreamfall Chapters has a very intriguing means of storytelling absent in many video games, in general.
When stories debate fate versus free will, most come to the conclusion that humans have free will and that we choose our own destinies. This game offers a look into the opposing philosophy and does so extraordinarily well. Though the idea that we are not in control over our destinies may seem dismal, the game expertly manages to avoid falling into this pitfall, giving it a hopeful spin. As the story moved forward, I came to terms with the fact that my choices only made small ripples and was still going on a set path. And you know what? I didn't care. The journey through both the game's worlds was so captivating that I was more than happy to let go of the wheel and trust the developer's judgement as to where the story is going. Upon reaching the conclusion of the game, I am hit with a wave of nostalgic feelings, despite having all of the game's events in my recent memory. I remember my experiences fondly, will gladly come back to the worlds the game establishes, and cannot recommend this game enough to both Longest Journey Fans, as well as to newcomers.

I've 68 hours logged in this psuedo game and I'm pretty obsessed with it still. The physics based combat is a real challenge, and honestly a fun challenge. The first thing I did was fight my way through the Novice Arena, then Expert. Expert took me a long time to beat. Each opponent has their own quirks besides the unique physical contraints of their chosen weapon. Once you can reliably beat the Expert Arena, you'll have a false sense of confidence going into the real game. A say false, because the arena is this lovely well lit open space with the same opponents attacking you the same way each time you face them. The real game has dozens of objects in each room that can trip you up, doors that can tie up your sword arm or foul your weapons strike, and randomly patrolling zombies that can double or triple team you when you least expect them to. Narrow corridors and other tight spaces make swinging two handed weapons a crap shoot. And yes, sometimes (rarely) the engine itself will let you down and you'll find yourself stuck to a wall for seemingly no reason during a fight. This is why, despite the devs intentions and some players' strong feelings on the matter, I do suggest using the savescum method on occasion so you don't have to start all over again when something really stupid happens.
With a simple escape-the-dungeon crawl being this fun, I can't wait until they patch the quirks and add in all the other features like theurmaturgy, ranged weapons, weapon thrusts and other techniques. Oh yeah, and release the real game. If you missed the kickstarter like me, this is a good way to support the devs and still get a fun playable game out of it immediately.

The gameplay does not translate to the narrow corridors of the story mode because your trying to avoid objects (cause your character will stick to them) and maintain visibility of your character (where the third joystick comes into play). You get past that and the combat is actually pretty simple, imagine boxing. There is auto parry so you only need keep your character in the direction of the enemy. I believe the developers need to not kid themselves that the controls cleary need to be worked on rather than saying they are "tactical" and "complicated." Good or bad? Well... both. It depends what you're looking for, though.
Sacred's an old game. Like reaaaaally old. This brings with it some issues, unfortunately. The game itself is good, but the problems may be off-putting, so let's cover the technical issues first as they can be a dealbreaker for many people given what they are.
First off, Sacred is hard-coded to be 1024x768 resolution; this means that, under normal circumstances, it will fill a 4:3 square on a widescreen monitor with large black boarders on the sides. There are a few workarounds, but the largely involve forcing it to stretch out the horizontal which makes everything look remarkably fat. This also means that the resolution can't normally be increased, and it won't get prettier or fit more stuff on the screen.
The second major issue is that multiplayer is not naturally supported by steam, steam does not give out CD-keys when you buy the game, and it's irrelevant anyway because the servers for the game are down regardless. Hamachi, Gameranger, and most other options will flat out not work. Evolve, found at
, is the only one known to be able to run it (though some have reported that Hamachi can run it by changing some setting, but I don't speak german so have no idea what they changed). Evolve, however, can link itself to your steam account which... is a little unsettling. I didn't want to play sacred with friends quite THAT badly, so for me, it's stuck being a single player game.
With that out of the way, if you're still interested in the game despite the technical difficulties and problems with it being ancient, let me state that the game itself is actually quite good with nice gameplay elements.
Yes, it's old, and no, it won't be better than Path of Exile (which is free), but it has a certain charm and feel to it that makes it quite enjoyable. If you pick it up for $5 or under, it's probably worth the cost.
A few major things:
- There are quite a few different classes in the game (races, acutally...) and each get their own unique set of spells and melee attacks. They each play fairly differently, and have enough customization that each playthrough can potentially feel quite different even if playing the same class.
- Skills are a bit odd in that you don't get access to all skills; each class begins with two skills and get a number of new skills unlocked at levels 1, 3, 6, 12, 20, 30 and 50. Interestingly enough, you just get to PICK a new skill at these levels (starting at 3) but have more options than you can choose from, so you customize your character each time you play. This means you can have a melee mage or a fire mage or a mage that specializes in a wide range of elements or one that spams out a small number of choice spells more often, one which autoattacks, or one which utilizes combo attacks as their primary method of damage, or even one which tanks (well, alright, not so much a tank mage =P ). The point is, you get some pretty good customization so two players can both pick to be the seraphim and play her entirely differently and not step on each other's toes. Assuming you get the multiplayer to work from the earlier issue. *Cough*
- Mounts exist in the game and you can ride a horse. In fact, you can even learn mounted combat, use your horse to charge over people, or teach it to run faster. It's kind of a neat system, but isn't really explored too much, yet moreso than probably any other game of the genre.
- Combat's pretty fluid, enemies have easy to see radial healthbars around their feet which indicate their relative difficulty, level and remaining health clearly. You can highlight items on the ground as well, which is handy. It's especially fun to bounce around the battlefield unleashing multihit combos and seeing your character do more than just overhand swing 5x in a row, but instead actually use a variety of strikes from different angles, and some will even perform acrobatic attacks, backflips, and so on.
- The storyline's not the best the world has ever seen, but it's certainly not awful, and by diablo-style dungeon crawlers, it's way above average. There's actual reasons for going through the various quests, the world opens up in a reasonable manner as you complete them, bosses tend to make you want to slap them good and hard before you even fight them... generally it does a pretty good job at what it sets out to do.
- The spells in the game are pretty varied, and the characters do distinctly feel different from one another, even if they have a similar role. Sure, the vampiress and daemon are both female melee characters, yet the vampiress gets to change between a knight form and vampire form, preferring physical or magical abilities in nature, can summon wolves and bats to help her, drain health and so on. The daemoness, in contrast, gets things like the ability to fly over terrain, attach elemental properties to her weapons, fling fireballs and enact creepy japanese hentai tentacle porn scenes with dead bodies. No, I am not making that up, and my nightmares would prefer that I were. Alright, they're not nightmares. >.>;;
- Individual classes have different item slots available to them. Most of them tend to share similar gear, though there are a few bits which are very specific to certain classes, such as say... the iconic seraphim's wings.
- Money MEANS something. Zoh. Mah. Gerd. Know how in Diablo 2 and such, you'd get huge stockpiles of gold that were worthless? Or most any other diablo-style game? Yeah, turns out that you can actually buy uniques and set items off of vendors. In fact, if you get the skill for it (sacrificing a combat skill...) some classes can even actually increase the quality of stuff that merchants will sell (along with reducing the cost of such, and increasing the sale price of vendor trash, yay!), making it actually reasonable to build a set to some degree and not feel like your gold is worthless.
- Big bosses. If you fight a dragon, you know bloody well you're fighting a dragon because it tends to not exactly fit on the screen. There's things like "don't stand in the fire" on bosses as well, stuff that needs to be dodged and so on. As in things that you didn't actually see until much later games for the most part. Sacred's not quite as great as a modern game, but compared to anything else from it's timeframe, it was quite a few years ahead of it's time in this regard.
Overall, it's dated. Sacred has low graphics, major technological problems, and some real massive flaws to it... but compared to other games of it's time, I'd honestly recommend it and say it's quite a lot better than it had any real right of being. It's enjoyable for awhile, and worth a good $5 or so. As of the moment of this review, it's on for $2.49, and for the single player game, I'd say it's well worth the cost. It probably won't be a regretable purchase, as it's really not that bad and does a lot of good things that even many of the modern diabloesque games fail to live up to.
If you ever want to go down a trip on nostalgia lane and play diablo 1 for some reason (I get that every few years myself =P ) I'd honestly recommend playing Sacred for your binge this time around. It's the better game of the two in large part, and has some really attractive features to it. It has some nuisances as well, but hey, it's old, give it a break. NO! NOT THE HIP! NOT THE HIP!

I simply can't compel myself to carry on with this game. It's boring. That's all there is to it. There's nothing interesting about the game.
No manual saving, poor optimisation, nonsensical mechanics, mind numbingly boring narrative, lifeless characters, and♥♥♥♥♥♥combat.
I'm not even sure if God knows what's going on in this game, or the motivation behind why certain mechanics and systems exist as they do. Want to pull a lever to deactivate a trap? Prepare to waste a tonne of experience in smithing, for some odd reason.
You can't do anything without investing ungodly amounts of experience into passive skill trees - the same experience which you also need to increase other attributes. It's not as if a single point of experience equals a single point in an attribute\skill, either. Nope! That would be too simple. You have to pour your experience into unintuitive gauges which, once filled up, increase your level in that skill. However, until you do fill up these gauges then you will see no change in those abilities.
The combat involves nothing more than spamming the attack button. It claims you can dodge, parry, etc, but you can't. Well, not effectively, anyway. Try to dodge? Your bumbling protagonist only does so after getting hit by every enemy near him, and only after a painfully slow animation plays out. Want to parry? Only if the RNG gods decide you're worthy. What's the point of a parrying button if parrying itself doesn't always work, or the command to make it happen doesn't always appear?
The characters and dialogue are probably the worst aspect of the game, though. It's like watching wooden mannequins in a soap opera. The dialogue feels unnatural and just plain tedious. For the first time in my life I was glad there was a way to skip through dialogue in an RPG. The terrible dialogue is made even worse by the poorly animated, badly designed, characters which spew out this crap. Unblinking eyes, stiff movement, and uninspired design simply add to the tediousness of the game. The main character neither looks, nor sounds, interesting. His face reminded me of those old Action Man figures.
I wont talk about the graphics, because in my opinion they were pretty good. I've certainly seen worse. The game was kinda laggy, though. It's strange. The actual game wasn't lagging (button input and what not was fine) it just looked laggy.
Some of the environments look quite nice, it's just a shame you're given no room to explore them. Everything exists along linear paths (and I do mean linear) with nothing of interest to break up the monotony. There were a few interactable points here and there, but it's just junk fluff which doesn't serve a purpose beyond simply existing. It rarely, if ever, plays a role in the events which happen in the game.
The game does have some minor choice and consequences, but I'm really not sure if said consequences have any real effect beyond a few new bits of dialogue here and there. To be honest, I didn't have the will to find out.
Now, I did enjoy the non-animated cutscenes in the game. Well, the few I've seen, anyway. It has that whole Dragon Age vibe, using nicely drawn images with a voice over.
Oh! Did I mention that you can't manually save, either? You have to wait for checkpoints. No idea why this system even exists in an RPG, but it does, and should you decide to pick this game up you'll have to screw around with it. Enjoy.
I don't recommend this game at all. It's nothing but a chore to play.

I was looking for a game with controller support and this happened to be on sale and had very positive reviews. First off, the controller support is a joke. I could play the game just as well without any controller support with standard steam controller features. It is in large part a FPS and there is no aim assist when playing with a controller.
The unique selling point is the FPS mixing with a tower defense, but I must say that it is painfully obvious why TDs are usually from a top down RTS perspective. Flying enemies for example are very easy to overlook, because they are above you. The perspective also makes its hard to tell where hordes are going to spawn and which way they are going to take. The game only shows you where the first wave is going to go and successive waves might do something entirely differently.
Overall the game is terrible at explaining itself. It is so overexcited to get started that it is doesn’t explain its mechanics at all. How much damage does a tower/weapon do? What's its range? What type of enemy can it attack? How much HP do enemies have? Which enemies attack structures? Which enemies have what attack modifiers? What are combos/killing sprees and when do they happen?
If the game contains this information, it hides it well. I had to discover everything through trial and error.
The gameplay is pleasant, but repetitive and gets old very fast. The FPS perspective has more downsides than upsides and does nothing to improve the genre. Has its charm, but is not a good TD game and after you take that away, what is left?

On the learning curve:
This game has one of the greatest learning curves I have ever had to overcome. Hell, I'm still overcoming it. It is difficult to learn, and harder to master. The reward for my sweat, blood, and tears? One of the most satisfying combat systems I have ever had the pleasure of playing with. The physics based movement and attacks will challenge you, but once you accept that the combat is closer to real life melee than any game you've played; it will get easier. People who have had training in any form of melee combat may find this game easier to grasp.
Advice for starting out:
I strongly recommend playing a few hours worth of Arena mode to get started. If you jump straight into the rogue-like and try to kill everything the way you can in Elder Scrolls, you will die. You will die often, and you will loathe this game. So, with that in mind, please practice in Arena before investing time into a character that will die in 5 minutes or less. Thank me later.
Later Content:
The game is paced pretty well, and by the time you've mastered killing one or even two enemies at once, there are bosses. So far, bosses are larger and stronger than most enemies. You'll have to use a little more strategy with them. The game also becomes a little less punishing as you get better gear. When you take damage, you can lose some of your max health, and the rest will come back out of combat. Wearing plate and chainmail significantly reduces the amount of max health you will lose.
A note on the physics based engine they created just to make this game (and the one after it).
In most game engines with melee combat you are playing an animation, and checking for a collision between the weapon and anything worth hitting. The fancy ones will even shift animations upon finding the Hit Event it was looking for. This game simulates everything, in real time. Your character is a walking set of those equations you dreaded in highschool (and probably college). Yes, physics are back. Jokes aside, this is an amazing feat in game technology. I feel the developers should be proud of what they have created. I think we will see other games simulating more aspects of gameplay, following in this game's example, and the ones that will come after it.

Firstly would be to increase the responsiveness to movement, it can be infuriatingly clumsy and slow to respond and move when you're trying to escape someone chasing after you with a sledgehammer.

The atmosphere is dark and it’s gritty. The tooth and nail combat is unforgiving. Never before have I experienced an RPG that has catapulted me so far into the zone of helplessness. There are times in the story mode when I will catch a look of my reflection in my monitor and my jaw is on the floor, filled with suspense at what might lurk in the dark beyond. Equally exciting are the times in the arena when I will take a hit to the back of the head with a sledgehammer, after which I vocalize my avatar’s pain. The controls only add to the suspense as I spend a lot of my brain-power calculating where I can shuffle back to if a particular hostile starts swinging. Having the room to fight is always nice. I have been in fights that reflect the drunken brawls that many report as blades clink and clang against the walls of narrow corridors. Sometimes the fights are messy as baddies take chunks out of each other in an attempt to reach me.
It is clear to me that there is a group of people who are going to play this game for under 10 hours and call it quits and I understand where they are coming from. I often find myself exiting the game out of frustration because there are so many variables at play. Even so, the 12 hours I have spent in Exanima has been the most rewarding time I have spent in a video game in my entire life as far as combat is concerned. I started out feeling hopeless, and after 12 hours of practice I have garnered hope. So far, the story is lacking, and that’s fine. In my opinion this is an amazingly sugarcoated tech-demo that is allowing me to check out a physics engine and combat system that was built from scratch. And as everyone knows, cookies made from scratch beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of that store-bought crap.

Recommended, and unlike many Alphas, not purely based on its potential. As it stands, it's a nice little game. Personally I prefer the more passive setting that's available, allowing me to build up my settlement at my own pace without being too concerned with speed and hostile forces.
That said, there is room for improvement. When you mouse over food, you get a very handy breakdown of stock change over the past year. That same system should really be applied to other stock types. Now in regards to longer term appeal - regardless of if you play the passive or more difficult settings, it would be nice to see some sort of "adventure" option. Generals or guards could double up as "Heroes". Unused spots of land could periodically have tombs or caves uncovered. A "scout" might assess the danger of each, allowing you to prepare small forces to combat their denizens for experience and small resource rewards. It's a simplistic idea but with varying degrees of threat (some being extreme) would give something to focus on in the longer haul - ie "levelling up" heroes and increasing forces to take on threats at your own pace.
Perhaps a trade system too would be nice ie set how many units of X you want to sell each year, and have fixed exchange rates initially.
Regardless, it's a good solid start on a game with little in the way of bugs, and as it is will provide some entertainment. Further enhancements may add to longer term appeal.

I got this game in a bundle that I bought a few months back. When I first bought the bundle, I kind of ignored this game, instead concentrating on the centerpieces of the bundles. I thought it nothing but a throw-in, and because of the ratings, threw it to the side.  However, once I had beaten/gotten bored of the rest of the games in the bundle, I finally "Eh, why the hell not" and installed this game. After a story that took me about 13 hours to complete, I found that the game pleasantly surprised me.
As you can probably see from the videos and screenshots of this game, it's not a AAA game. It's not gonna blow you away. But it's not meant to do that, but instead draw you into the story/roleplaying elements of the game.
The game takes place in the Dark Eye Universe, a spin-off of the D&D universe. It's akin to other games set in the same universe, such as the Blackguards Series, or the Drakensang series, and lore from those two, though unneeded, would possibly help you appreciate this game. But unlike those two this is an action-RPG, whereas those are turn-based. However, I can't say that's necessarily for the better. The combat in this game primarily consists of button-mashing, trying to get combos, which in turn you can use to activate powers/magic. It is very clunky, but you get used to it eventually.
The story is probably the best feature of this game. Although it is flawed, it does have a fairly unique plot, along with semi-interesting characters. The quests aren't bad either. One aspect I did like was that you have a choice in a lot of the major plot points in the game. Although the choices don't really affect the ending, they do affect the characters you interact with, turning them for or against you. As for side-quests, they're your run-of-the-mill type quests. "Go here, get this, come back" or "Kill this, come back", but you do get some solid rewards from them, so there is SOME incentive in doing them.
Lastly, don't expect this game to be open-world. Although you do have partial free reign to explore the mission areas, your choices are pretty limited to either trading with merchants or looking for ingredients/treasure chests. There is a skills portion to the game, but it isn't very fleshed out either. It includes the standard RPG skills: Herblore, Lockpicking, speech, etc. But don't expect there to be a flasy minigame associated with them like the Elderscrolls Series. Also as a sidenote, don't let the Blacksmith skill decieve you, it's purely used to disarm traps (odd I know) and apply upgrades to armor/weapons. There is no actual crafting.
Overall I would give this game a 7/10. I wouldn't buy it full price, but if it's ever on sale, I'd strongly recommend grabbing it.

A decent conclusion to the "The Longest Journey" saga, although I think the Dreamfall games made the whole series more complicated than was necessary. The game takes itself quite seriously and feels like it's trying to be Game of Thrones sometimes with overtly "edgy" themes, but it falls flat because the plot doesn't actually explore any of the issues it brings up. The Azadi are almost literally just the Nazis.
There's lots of dialogue which is nice sometimes but overall it's quite poorly paced so you'll probably end up getting sick of it and skipping through the voice acting. The characters feel mostly fake and are written more like quirky sitcom characters than real people.
There's not much to the gameplay or puzzles, which mostly revolve around running around a large open area to find the one object or character you're allowed to interact with. Although this helps prevent the game suffering from "adventure game logic syndrome" where solutions to puzzles don't make sense, it means there's actually not much gameplay at all and the game feels more like a visual novel than a puzzle adventure like the original The Longest Journey.
The game is obsessed with offering choice, going so far as to regularly remind you when a choice you made is having an impact on the story, and even recapping how important your choices were at the end of each episode. The choices do actually make a bit more of an impact on the story than say, Telltale products, but ultimately the story plays out in much the same way regardless, so the extreme focus on your choices feels hollow and ingratiating.
My advice is: play The Longest Journey, but skip Dreamfall: TLJ and Dreamfall: Chapters. Chapters is only worth it to see the conclusion to the numerous dangling plot threads that Dreamfall: TLJ left on its cliffhanger ending.

It took me five hours, just playing casually, to collect all 100 crystals and log all flora/fauna in the original. Oddly it took the same amount of time to find all 150 crystals, complete all 40 challenges, log all flora, and bloom all four Star Plants.
Short of a few achievements that require arbitrary actions to be performed, such as launching an animal more than 100 meters, the critera listed counts as 100% completion according to the respective games.
The price for such short games is quite fair for its length, of course. I've seen games that are much shorter but have much larger price tags, so I cannot argue.

BUD's Log: 7 hours into the expidition and i have nearly completed everything. All I am missing is a single crystal, a single teleporter, and a single challenge. Granted the trend I've seen thus far, all three are likely very near each other. I used POD to scan near the surface of the planet and most of the lower islands. I've flown to all the upper islands to find no response on my crystal locator. I therefore deduce that what i seek lies amid the astroids, but i see nothing from the astroid teleporter. I take off in a random direction with my rocked-powered glider and keep my robotic eyes peeled, unblinking, doing what I can to solidify my wavering determination. It is then that I spot it. In the distance! A red blinking light. Could it be?!
I bank left and move at full speed toward the lone island floating in the air above a trail of astroids. I get near the island to find the crystal locator spring to life! YES, and I see the light of a POD Challenge too! As I reach the island I decelerate and flop onto the teleporter. I rapidly pull down each latch and it springs to life, an achievement is unlocked. I leap for the cystal and in one bound I land on it, ripping it from its floating prison. Finally I take the challenge and with that I am free. Free falling while dodging astroids left and right. And upon hitting the last checkpoint, I am finally complete!
So yeah... it's a pretty good game. For ten bucks I totally reccomend it.

Some people say Exanima isn't for everyone. I couldn't disagree more.
At first I was a bit turned off because I simply wasn't getting the combat. I thought it was wonky, I thought it didn't function like it should, I didn't like the camera.. for the first couple of days I was beginning to think I had made a bad purchase and that I simply wouldn't learn how to play properly. But the combat is just so.... different. Impressive, engaging, and unforgiving. I absolutely had to learn how to play, I want to go from a stumbling idiot to an elegant killing machine. Other people have done it, why can't I? All I can say is, my patience was DEFINITELY worth it. Oh, and the 15 dollars was worth it too.
This is one of the few games out there that legitimately requires skill and focus. In PoE or Diablo, you can sort of go into autopilot as you mow through hordes of enemies, only having to pay attention when you're fighting a dangerous group. In Exanima, you're heart will be pounding while fighting a single opponent, and you'll♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants when you notice an enemy has noticed your battle from a distance and rushes to his allies aid. Exanima's combat is very very engaging, on Youtube, commentators often have trouble speaking while playing because it's impossible to do both at once. You need to notice what your opponent is doing, what he might do after, which direction he's moving, and when he's vulnerable to strike. All the while paying attention to yourself! Which direction you're moving, how much momentum you have, and whether or not you should immediately stop what's happening and brace for a defensive block. The AI in this game is very good, No 2 battles are the same, you'll sometimes lose to a guy you've beaten every time, and you'll sometimes get a 1 hit kill on a dude you've always been afraid of. This game is all about opportunity and when to take it, and not so much merely "killing" things.
I see many reviews bashing the game for the weird combat and the camera and what not. Those people simply lack the ability to adapt and learn, as well as patience. When you picked up your first FPS game I doubt you immediately ran around killing, let alone shooting things! This game is completely fresh and unlike any other, so it should be approached as such. It's not just fresh on the combat level, but on the character level as well. You have no advantage at all over the NPC enemies. In fact, they often have an advantage over YOU because they are better equipped, and it is well worth the long, difficult fight between you and the enemy because you'll get their gear when they die. The enemies don't get more powerful, they just become better equipped. Just as you do. Of course, there's always the option of hiding, running, or trapping enemies instead of fighting them. Because in Exanima, fighting is legitimately perilous and often a bad idea.
There's nothing more satisfying than beating an opponent with 3 good slashes to the head, or tripping your enemy and delivering a finishing smash to their face as they're attempting to stand up, or winning a very long, drawn out, epic fight when you at one point thought you were destined to lose. This is one of those games where you're gonna do better if you think of the character as YOU. Not just "the hero Asgad" or something. Try as hard as you can to keep YOU alive, and eventually you will surely triumph. Don't get lazy or overconfident, because if this were you crawling a dungeon and fighting NPCs with a broken chair leg, I doubt you'd be so ballsy.
I give the game 8/10, I eagerly await all updates that come to it. The only reason I don't give it an early 9 is because it doesn't, and probably never will, support online play.

I'm a big Anno fan, and I put off getting 2205 for quite a while after reading all the negative reviews. I finally picked it up and I'm glad I did. It is a major departure from the way other Anno games work, but I find that it's still quite fun and retains just enough Anno feel to be something familiar yet new. I would like to have a "sandbox" mode, but I don't miss it as much as I thought I would. Working towards building a colony on the moon has been quite enjoyable (many hours in and I'm still not on the moon!).
A lot of the micro-management of trade routes and so forth has been modified in such a way to make it easier which I appreciate. Often in other Anno games, I got annoyed trying to figure out the best logistics strategy. So far in 2205, the logistic strategy element is still there, but it hasn't been as micro-managy.
I even like the way they do combat now. It's sort of a separate "mini-game" that you can choose to participate in (or ignore). If you participate, it's mostly just moving around blowing stuff up and collecting resources for use in the main game. I enjoy a click-boom game from time to time, so it's a nice mental distraction and doesn't feel like a necessary interruption to the main strategy game.
Overall, I'm glad I'm playing it now.

I'm not entirely sure what the aim of creating this game was.
Let me explain;
Nothing is explained. Why do you magically zap on to a boat? Why is the crystal on the boat? Why do you need to retrieve it in the first place from the boat and not on Xen? Why were the Xen creatures already there before the resonance cascade?
Why?
WHY?
WHYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYYY?
All of this is completely unanswered, but this is just the start. [Spoilers]
Once you magically apear upon the boat, seemingly sent by Zeus, you pickup almost all of the weapons available in the game, instantly making it very easy. If that didn't make it easy enough for you, then you're in luck! Right in front of you is a conveniently placed helicopter, complete with a mounted machine gun, meaning all those Xen creatures are dead before you move 10 metres.
Once you finally reach the main cabin, you are greeted by 3 turrets, which are easily avoidable. In fact, there are 100s of better locations for them, which would have proved challenging, however, the creators were obviously not in a creative mood, so decided to place them right in the open, however, they did take the time to ensure even spacing, which was a nice touch.
Next, you are inside, where you'll reach the lift, clamber through the overhead opening, and up the tedious ladder, and eventually reach the control deck, where you're warmly greeted by 3 soldiers, seemingly oblivious to the Xen creatures which have engulfed their ship.
After this, and a few random Xen creatures which magically appear, you find a man. The soldiers also seemed oblivious to him, which is surprising as he was literally next to them. The man is the most socially awkward NPC I've ever encountered, and was a walk suitable for the Ministry of Silly Walks. He opens a security coded box for you, containing a med kit. This was much needed, as the previous 20 were not quite enough. He the proceeds to open the cargo doors, containing a dangerous creature, which is obviously the best idea. On top of this, he automatically knows why you're there. No questions asked.
You then need to BACKTRACK THE WHOLE MAP in order to reach the cargo hold. Of course, it should be a nice brisk walk, after all, you have just defeated all the creatures, right? Wrong. They've respawned, and in seemingly higher numbers. Once you battle your way through the Battle of Somme, you reach the cargo doors. At first, I wasn't sure what to do, as surely if I jump in I'd die? I discovered that jumping in to a gaping dark hole actually heals you, which was a nice surprise.
So, the boss fight. Before anything even begins, you get to endure a lovely cutscene where the boss sucks up the crystals, which once again begs the question, why?
You've spent the whole game (10 minutes) collecting all the weapons in the game, conserving your ammo, well guess what? They're all gone. You can pickup a few off the floor, but ammo is almost non-existent. The boss itself is, well... interesting. It is a down-sized and retextured version of Nihilanth, and completely lacks any form of animation. To me, it resembles a over-stuffed teddy bear, so stiff that it puts viagra to shame.
Once you've finally defeated him, (Cooked grenades seem to work well),  that's it. That's literally it. The boss shatters like if I picked up your vase and threw it on the ground. Oh and the crystals? Gone.
The final credits/cutscene shows the crystals in a different location, which I can only assume is suppose to represent Black Mesa. I don't think I can truly express how underwhelming this game is. The idea of Half-Life: Before is brilliant, but this game, is certainly not brilliant.

●It`s such an amazing game! It absorbs you right from the start and till the very end. These stories, which are tangled together, are extremely touching, adventurous and striking!
● Even if I haven`t played previous games, but I hope, I will do it someday, I really enjoyed it. I don’t think that this somehow influenced my understanding of the whole plot, but, in my opinion, it has right to be as an independed piece of art with connections to the previous stories (as for the people who played only this part).
● Choices & consequences – I adore such style so much. You never know where your action may lead and that is what also keeping you up to the end. There`s always a choice. And not always this choice is the right one, you can’t know for sure. Moreover, it`s one of these examples when you can act peacefully and not use your fists to solve one or another issue. And I love it. Also you need to be attentive to things. There are things that you can do and sometimes should do that are not on your goal list. So, again, if you won`t do them, there will be consequences… And that`s cool as well. And sad, sometimes.
●Puzzles were quite puzzles (and under puzzles I mean not only puzzles puzzles, I also mean different situation like “go there, and do it there, under the right tree, which is near the wrong tree, which is in front of the house with some roof, which is not a roof at all”), but sometime it was almost impossible for me to figure some things out, especially on the moment with the references to the previous games.
●This part has fantastic dialogues and characters, that were well-designed (appearances and personalities). Especially Enu and Crow (who, I guess, also participated in previous stories).
●  Again – the plot is fantastic. And I’d been experiencing waterfalls of tears starting from the 3rd interlude. BUT I would like to see what happened to some characters in the end. I know, that they`re alive (at least for my story), but what`s happening to them now? And the epilogue was a bit messed up for me, as (in my opinion) I don’t quite know what was in the previous parts.
●  And two more things to say:
-	Amazing and stunning soundtrack
-	For the first time I actually had a feeling then one achievement truly reflected my “understanding” of “what`s goin’ on”. (the beginning of the 5th book, if you know what I mean)
To sum up, I would truly recommend you to experience this fascinating journey!

The major annoying thing I felt with this game is that it doesn't allow the player to save the progress manually. If you don't like a choice you just made in the game and so you load a previously (and automatically) saved game record, then you will need to go through what you have done since the previous save point all over again. Sometimes this means redoing everything you did in the past a couple of hours, especially if the choice you don't like is made at the end of a chapter.
The in-game tutorial doesn't really teach you any useful tricks in a fight, and the enemy/monsters in the game do not progressively level up as your character. Therefore, in your first a few fights, you may feel it difficult to defeat the enemy/monsters without drinking a few potions. However, once you get a grasp of it, you may start to enjoy the fights.
The equipment you can buy from the merchants usually is no match to those you get after a major (boss) fight. As such, the merchants in the game basically are places where you can dump the garbage which you pick up during your journey. In fact, as I can recall, I only purchased maybe 5 or 6 items from the merchants before I finished the game. From my point of view, the trading system in this game is useless.
The combat skill and magic systems, on the other hand, are more interesting. The storyline is okay. The 3D engine runs smoothly on my computer. I have completed the game once already, but so far my computer has never hung up during playing.
If the game is on a 50% or 75% off discount, I would suggest RPG lovers to try it.

Your character cannot be personalised, the story is quite linear, the world clearly has its lore, but you never get really sucked into it.
All of this said, the story keeps you interested long enough, the style is challenging without being frustrating, and the Dark Eye's world has a lot of potential that has been scarcely exploited in games, so it feels like a breath of fresh air. If you can accept its limitations, it is a game you will enjoy.

Investigator is its developer’s first Steam project and they show potential. Few indie titles use CryEngine, even less so its 4th iteration which was until very recently, the latest. Obviously the graphics look stunning, being able to simulate anything from lighting to the weather effects fairly close to photorealism. Sadly, great details demand even greater performance and I was dismayed to see so many frame rate drops when playing at 4K resolution. I remembered that true constant 60 frames at 4K on a contemporary title, are still far from achievable, least of which on Crytek’s creation kit. And I shall not deny that beauty can be quite skin deep. Far too many modern games forswear a fleshed out story, in pursuit of eye candy alone that might draw in gamers, who don’t bother scratching but the surface. Well, Investigator has a creepy story to it, split into 10 levels and a bonus stage. Despite lacking a save file system, all the levels can be accessed from the main menu, as soon as you install the game. This might be something odd from a game design perspective, but at least it gives you the chance to hunt for the game’s interesting achievements.
Apart from frame rate issues and a few non-game-breaking bugs, I didn’t like the game’s relative slow pace and lack of a proper challenge. While it’s not as much of a narrative walking simulator as some indie titles that have preceded it, Investigator is off to a slow start and will demand plenty of pacience from you. The original language is Russian, but the English subtitiles were spared of any typos so far as I’ve played it. Its decently priced even outside of special sales and also gives you the option to form a badge from its cards. Investigator is a truly good example of an indie horror game that doesn’t fail to deliver, like so many of its competitors on Steam.
+ Beautiful graphics.
+ Eerie atmosphere.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.
- Almost no challenge.
- Several glitches and frame rate drops.

Investigator was a very pleasant surprise, on sale for just 59 cents but definitely worth even the full price. Although it has some minor issues, the great atmosphere and excellent graphics make up for them. The game has a surprising amount of action and scares for a walking simulator. There's some nice attention to detail, and the colors, lighting, reflections and such make the graphics quite realistic (I especially like the look of wet surfaces). Not 100% photorealistic of course, but stands out from many other games. I don't speak Russian so I can't say much about the voice acting, but it sounds good enough to me. The English subtitles are good for the most part.
There are some issues though; the subtitles are a bit glitchy (they reappear briefly after they fade out, also they don't seem to be always in sync with the dialogue), and the game doesn't remember your mouse settings (when you adjust the sensitivity, it resets the invert settings, and when you quit the game you have to set the sensitivity again the next time). There are no audio settings, and the music is rather loud (the soundtrack is good though). You also can't save, but you can load each level from the menu. And you never know when the game's going to put you in a new place, so you might miss some things to explore on the first playthrough. Sometimes you lose the ability to run, which is a bit annoying. Also your character's beard disappears at times.
So the game could do with some polishing, but overall it's impressive for the price and I recommend it.
+ Great atmosphere
+ Excellent graphics
+ Good music
+ Good cutscenes
+ Sufficiently scary
+ Plenty of achievements
+ Cheap
~ Can't save (but you can start each level from the menu)
~ No audio settings; music is a bit loud
~ Sometimes you lose the ability to run
~ Your character's beard disappears at times
- Doesn't remember mouse settings
- Subtitles are glitchy
4/5

So, when I got this game for the xbox 360 in like, 2012 I think? I got it only knowing anything about it by hearsay. More specifically, "its ♥♥♥♥ing hard". When I booted it up for the first time, I was a bit overwhelmed. Having never played a game more complex than like, Halo.
I know. I don't wanna hear it.
Either way, I was confused. Why was I rolling so slow(knight class)? Why was I dying INSTANTLY, to the lame anemic zombies? Where in God's name am I even going? And don't even get me started on parrying.
Well, in any case, I pressed on, got BEAT by the taurus demon plenty of times(before I knew about the plunging attack), got utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥on by the fragon at the bridge, and got poisoned plenty of time by those rats.
THOSE. RATS.
After stumbling around for a pretty embarrassing length of time, I made SOME semblance of progress and made it to Lower Undead Burg(with a +0 weapon, because, you know, new n' such). And then I forgot the capra demon.
So I put the game down for like 2 years after an uncountable amount of deaths, blaming the game for its clumsy controls and unintuitive systems. And I mean, could ya blame me? In an era where games are made or broken by how polished and appealing to the eye they are, Dark Souls stood out by not bothering with any of that. But, I digress.
In the time I had dropped the game, Dark Souls had become a sweeping sensation. It had garnered a tremendous fanbase for a series once considered a cult classic, lost to the elite and those who thought they were better than others because they pressed buttons More Better Than You. Regardless, I picked the game back up after DS2 came out, intending to finish it out of spite. So I threw myself at the Capra Demon. And I did it again.
And again.
And again.
Eventually, I gave up, yet again getting nowhere fast. I gave in, and looked up "capra demon easy kill", and what I found quite literally changed my perspective on the whole game. See, by throwing dung pies over the entrance to the boss, you could poison and kill the boss without ever even setting foot in the arena.
That method, that unbelievable strategy was like nothing else I had ever seen. I know it might sound like exaggerating, but how many games have told YOU, "What do you mean you didn't try the Throw♥♥♥♥♥♥At Him Technique? What are you, an idiot?". I'm willing to bet not many.
So I made it past the Capra Demon, and I went through to the depths, and I made it through Sen's fortress, and I beat Anor Londo(good luck, btw)  all the while beginning to pick up on the intricate systems the game offered, like weapon scaling, poise, individual armor and weapon effects, and the numerous upgrade paths you could take with your weapons.
I did what everybody told me to, I got gud. After 2 years of dicking around, I finally completed Dark Souls for the first time, I beat Gwyn for the first time, and I didn't back out, for the first time. I've  given up on a lot throughout my life, on hobbies, on classes, on friends. Dark Souls gave me EXACTLY what I needed- something to complete, to see through to the end. And so, I did. And I haven't even touched on the lore. but you don't need to here that from me.
I've played a LOT of Dark Souls since I first beat it. I've played through every game numerous times, and I love them all. They are without a doubt my most important games, and I hold them all EXTREMELY close to my heart. Are they perfect games? Absolutely not, they have several GLARING issues. But, much like people, its problems can be looked past to see something wonderful and exciting. Something unique and beautiful in a way all its own.
Something, dare I say, Praise-worthy.
Tl;dr: Play the game. don't give up. the dung pies ARE good for something.

Dark Souls is an absolutely stunning game. I guess it isn't a new thing to be saying that, and by now nobody is really reading that many reviews for it, but this is my two cents.
Dark Souls is not for everybody. It's difficult, it takes commitment, it has an obscure story at times. But it is still worth it for everybody to try it. I have spent over 100 hours on this game, and I still only have one character. It is easily one of my favourite games of all time, and one of the few that has been so grandiose and challenging that my attention has been held captive for longer than many many other games. Few, if any, mechanics make no sense, though sometimes it may take a while to get the hang of them, and how to time the parries or the dodges, but these are things that can be learned through practice and perseverance.
The controls for the Prepare To Die™ Edition, that is to say, the keyboard controls, are horrendous. I played half way through the tutorial before giving up and aggressively force-feeding my computer software that would allow me to use a playstation controller instead. However, with the aforementioned controller, the controls suddenly make much more sense, and the game is far, far better. I highly recommend that anyone without one gets themselves a controller, whether it is a Steam Controller, an XBox Controller (especially for Windows), or a DualShock controller (which, as mentioned, requires software to function properly on Windows - get it
). Once you have either a controller, or the lack of will to live and self-preservation necessary to get off your bum and not use the keyboard, the controls are clear, easy to use and obvious, a necessity for a game which requires quick reflexes and eyes glued to the screen.
In terms of graphics, the game is beautiful, especially considering how little (re: none) fps drops may occur in situations were one might expect it. Enemy design is detailed and thoughtful, especially when it comes to the bosses. Gotta love Nito's frail old man legs. Level design is nearly as good, with the map layout being highly interconnected and clever, giving the player a sense of amazement when they open up a shortcut from Darkroot Basin back to the Undead Burg, and suddenly their mind clicks the map into place like an elaborate three dimensional puzzle. While there may not be a huge number of NPCs, their voice actors have all done a top notch job. I still get shudders from the undead merchants' laughter.
There are a vast range of weapons and attacks, and armour and... defences? You can play the game with swords or axes or spells or miracles or pyromancies or, if you really count it as a different thing, 'hexes'. (I'm looking at you, DSII) You can play with a shield and solid stone armour, or an empty hand and nothing but your ragged underwear, or somewhere in the middle, with light armour, and each style has a vastly different effect on how you play the game. You can parry every time an opportunity comes up and beat most enemies in less than three hits, or you can dodge-dodge-dodge-backstab, or just block and then wallop them over the head with a giant chunk of metal.
Regardless of if you bothered to read my ramblings or not, tldr: I highly recommend Dark Souls to everybody with an interest in 'hardcore gaming', even if you just want to see if it's the type of game for you. Just make sure you use a controller, and you'll love it.
