This is a fun little side-scrolling blast-em-up with an endearing, well animated art style.
You play a corgi named Maia, who has been tasked with rescuing the kingdom from an undead bunny lord.  To do so, you will employ a variety of spells, each with different cool-down times, against a myriad of enemies.
The enemies come in waves as you scroll to the right.  As you progress, the waves become bigger and the enemies more threatening.  You'll also encounter many, many mini-bosses along the way with their own combat patterns that will test your reflexes.
The controls are simple and highly responsive.  Any timing errors were always my own fault, and the only time the game itself ever lagged was during the final stage, when the enemy swarms were ridiculously thick.
It's not a short game, which is good on one hand, but on the other, it does start to get a bit repetitive in the end, which is the ONLY gripe I have.  All in all, a great title!

Oftentimes you'll see games on the Steam Store, with reviews saying things like "I wish there was a 'Mixed' rating for steam reviews, but I'll just have to say (yes/no)"
Well, this is one of those reviews.
GameCorp DX is a rerelease of a flash game you can find on ArmorGames. If you don't want to fork up the money for this, then go play that - this isn't much different. The graphics are the EXACT same, several features have been locked until later, and the creators still have no idea how to spell "ceremony". There are only a few new genres, the employees now have "personalities" (i.e they need to eat more often, almost all of them are negative), and you can finally pause the game and speed up those agonizingly long award ceremonies.
I was confused at first by the lack of a proper UI. I saw the buttons on the bottom but I had to manually count all my employees, I later noticed there was a centimeter-tall transparent bar at the top of the screen that had the information.
Playing the game, I had a few issues. Mostly with the edge-scrolling - I'd alt+tab out of the game (because even in windowed mode, the game tries to keep its custom cursor outside of the game and prevents you from doing any OS things) and come back to find that the view was all the way in the corner. Apparently it edge-scrolls when the window isn't even maximized, so I just turned off edge scrolling. The music is a bit obnoxious and loops endlessly (just remembered the company's name is Endless Loop). Workshop integration sounds great until you realize that the only customizable parts of the game are the employee's faces and studio icons. Not that big of a deal but I was expecting custom genres or at least different items.
Overall, the game - just like its original Flash game, is repetitive and lacking content. Absolutely nothing has changed in the way of graphics, it's a bit buggy, and feels unfinished, even for a game that just came out of Early Access. I don't like giving bad reviews, especially when it comes to simulation games, but this just isn't worth the price. Most of the positive reviews are sarcastic, but I wanted to provide some detail as to what exactly the game has in the way of content.
Thank you.

-Runs and performs great on lower end systems.
-Weapons each have their own strengths, weaknesses, ranges and damage capabilities.
-Armor really affects combat
-Graphics and lighting are great
-Fun Arena where you can practice fighting opponents and learn the game.
CONS:
-Learning curve is HIGH for the game, combat and controls
-Clipping issues in the game, such as getting stuck on objects (still Alpha)
-Lacks Tutorials in game at this time, but probably will be in for release
-No save game feature, this is for the hardcore - However if you exit the game when alive, you can continue where you left off. Your save gets wiped when you die!

Pros
- Dynamic and challenging combat. No two engagements are the same and if you let your guard down an undead with a wooden plank will beat you to death.
- Realistic weapon behavior and physics, so swings with a weapon while stepping in will do more damage than a swing without any leg movement. If you can't block in time, you can also step into the opponent and knock him off-balance or get hit with the pole of the weapon instead of the bladed part (in the case of an axe/halberd) to significantly reduce damage.
- Detailed physics mean your character acts as he/she should with the world, and can trip over objects or knock someone over if sprinting at them. Adds an extra challenge of having to be very aware of your character's footing.
- Can interact with the world to create very interesting scenarios. You can put chairs or ladders over the heads of undead and watch them flail around off-balance or get stuck in doorways. You can also just pile planks of wood on the floor and lead an undead onto it, making him fight with unstable footing.
- Atmosphere. The interiors are poorly lit, meaning it's difficult to move around with a torch, meaning you have to use a hand which could have been used for a shield or two-handed weapon to be able to see. Undead patrol randomly, meaning you can go minutes without seeing one, only to run into two in front of you and another behind you when you turn around and run. Opening a door is always done cautiously because you never know what can be on the other side, though expect to be surprised every once in a while. Undead are generally easy to run from, but that makes you let your guard down and unintentionally become cornered. There are times where I trapped myself inside a dark bathroom stall or a jail cell when I panicked and fled from undead. The undead will wait outside your door for a while, making you worry and think, "Is it gone yet? Is it gone yet? Maybe I should wait another 10 seconds." The soundtrack is very good from what I've heard as well.
- The challenging combat and unforgiving nature of the game gave me the greatest feeling of accomplishment I've felt in a single-player game in years once I completed all available content. Although difficult, the enemies always feel like a fair challenge.
- Game stability. Experienced no crashes or graphical glitches as of yet. Game runs at a high framerate and smoothly for me. The only bug I've encountered (twice) is one where I see the shadow of a person who isn't there that will vanish once I turn away.
Cons
- Clumsy, imprecise movement. Although I really enjoy being able to trip, at times it can be frustrating when the character is unable to step on a platform roughly equivalent to the height of a street curb without falling on his face. In combat mode, your character makes large steps (then pauses for a second) when you move with the WASD keys, making precise movements impossible, which is vitally important in this game where it can be difficult to aim the blade of a pole weapon because your character stepped too far forward or back. Your character also turns too slow, making it more difficult than it should be to run away to gain some distance on the opponent or for you to turn around to face the said opponent when you and the enemy step in to attack and the same time and bump into each other, sending you to the floor behind him.
- Lack of content. There's not much to this game at the moment than 3 levels in story mode, which you can run through in 20 minutes once you know where to go (but can take you ~3 hours if you explore otherwise), and two arena difficulties, where you face 8 opponents one right after the other. However, the story mode is replayable because the levels are large, there are locked doors with hard to find keys hidden around (I've found 5), loot in chests and drawers are randomly generated, and because AI patrols are random. No two playthrough will be the same.
- Controls and a steep learning curve. WASD movement in combat mode moves your character in relation to where he is facing, not where the camera is. It is fine once you get used to it, but I believe there should at least be the option to change WASD movement to be done in relation to the camera direction.
- Too punishing. Difficult enemies, combined with clumsy movement where you can trip while passing through a door, combined with unconventional controls and a steep learning curve, combined with permadeath don't mix very well. I think adding a checkpoint at the start of every level would solve this problem.

As someone who just finished this game, I'm writing this review for you as much as I am for me:
TL;DR:
Most spectacular adventure game you will play. Don't start on Chapters. The Longest Journey => Dreamfall:TLJ => Dreamfall Chapters.
Pros:
Epic adventure story, sci fi AND fantasy setting, music, voice acting, and visuals
Cons:
Empty large environments (fixed in later chapters).
Choppy Animations
Some don't think the choices affect the game enough.
For some of us, this was the longest journey. As a boy, my first adventure game was The Longest Journey and although I didn't understand all of it, it left me mystified. In 2006, Dreamfall: The Longest Journey cast my world asunder my childhood memories of April Ryan's incredible adventures were left on the ultimate cliffhanger and then there was the longest wait. Dreamfall Chapters and 2016 concluded this long painstaking wait and what a build up...
Let me tell you, if you start from the beginning, you will be rewarded. This story does not disappoint in any form. It flawlessly combines science fiction and fantasy into a truly unique setting. Stark. Arcadia..
If you are picking up this game and expecting a TellTale Games Walking Dead choices, this game was written with an ending in mind. It's been building towards finally connecting all the peices. You can make choices and they are going to make you cringe or worry or your characters might have regrets later in the game, but you're not going to alter the entire game.
At times, the visuals are breath-taking. Although, when Red Thread Games started, I believed they were too beautiful. I would have prefered the point and click format of The Longest Journey with more things to interact with. Sometimes the areas are confusing the navigate and there are only a few things to interact with. You're supposed to only go one place but you can travel the whole length of the area with little to do. It is annoying and wastes your time. But this problem resolved in the later episodes.
The animations are also stiff and choppy at times. However they accomplish the job of telling the story which is really all this game is about. I didn't mind using my imagination though. Fortunately, the voice acting really makes up for anything lost in the animation.
The music is amazing and gives me shivers every time I load up the game.
Right next to Life is Strange, this is my favorite interactive movie I have ever watched. It breaks your heart and swaddles it next to a cozy fire, simultanously.  I will never forget you April, Zoe, Kian, Saga, and Crow. Crow, thank you Red Thread Games for the best side kick that ever existed. I don't know how you pulled off such a satisfying ending. The wait was worth it. Every second.

If I could I would relive the whole story of all three games. It was such a beautiful experience. I recommend the series to anyone and everyone of all ages. It's beautifully created, and beautifully scripted.

This was really a tough one.
I wanted to like this game, i really did, i just could not bring myself recommend this game to anyone.
The first major flaw which i found to be HUGE was the improper loading, crashing and glitching of the game. If i wanted to load the game sometimes i would have to start the launcher three seperate times, using task manager to close the unresponsive instances inbetween. MAJOR pain in the rear. To make matters worse, sometimes the game would just decide to crash, just randomly. The only saving grace there is that the saves are frequent................but..................
The save file is singular, and by that i mean that any progress you make will overwrite your current save. That means if you screw up and pick the wrong choice, go into an area that advances the plot before finishing a side quest etc, you are stuck. The game will have overwritten with the furthest progress and you will have to start the game over to fix it. Not exactly something you like to see in an RPG were supposedly your decisions could effect how the story unfolds................but about that one................
Your choices dont matter. You are given the illusion of control of the characters destiny. The only things that will chance are slightly different cut scenes and your fetch quests will be given by either faction A or faction B. It just felt weak.
In terms of gameplay, there is some fun to be had there. The ice spells and the demon aura were quite good for stunning opponents and speeding your attacks. I found the Fire and Poison spells to be worthless, fire spell is point blank so you will get stabbed 100% of the time before the spell goes off and the poison spell burns through your magic wayyyyyyyy too fast. The attacking was done by simple chaining of your attack button (X for me since i used a 360 controller), the higher your chain the more magic you get back to refreeze your enemies. It got bland after about 15 hours in, which is not bad considering the whole game took me 18 hours and i did almost everything there was to do in a single play through.
The money in the game quickly becomes absolutely pointless. The only thing you will use it for is to buy potions and enchantments for your armor. The enchantments also get pointless as you get the "Final" set of armor at the end of chapter 3 (There are 5 chapters). I put silver enchantments in the armor because they were the best enchantments i had at that point in the game. Then in the next two chapters you get gold enchantments..............but no armor...........whatsoever. Since enchantments are permanent.............ya i was kinda screwed at that point.
The story starts out with good potential in the prologue and builds well in chapter 1 and 2 (chapter 2 was very well done). After that............meh...........just meh. Chapter 3 went in a direction i just did not care about and chapter 4 and 5 were just absolute crap. It felt like some other games i played where they started out with plenty of money and good ideas and then got rushed and had to wrap it up quickly and on a budget.
The bottom line is, i just will not recommend this game to any individual period. Between the software problems, weak story and mediocre gameplay, i just dont see anyone getting very much enjoyment out of this game.

Demonicon is an interesting RPG and, before going into details about it, I would recommend it if on sales. However it has some serious flaws, particularly for a relatively recent RPG and one based on a rather rich tabletop system.
The Pros:
* great story and interesting characters as well as moral quandaries. The game design goes out of its way to make you think about every choice and decision. It doesn't hesitate to go into seriously unconfortable territory right from the start.
* decent visuals, if not the most moder ones. The monsters are quite elaborate and NPC's look good, if not fantastic.
* enemy AI (at least for bosses) is hard to beat on normal mode and you will reload. Often.
* the character stats and development make sense and you need to make careful choices, especially at early stages.
* As expected for the porting of such a venerable tabletop RPG, the background is rich and you get the feeling of being part of a much wider world, as it should.
The Cons:
* the UI is not great. Although you can remap keys, the game system forces you into using key combos which is a big no-no in my book. And of course completely unnecessary.
* Invisible walls and "fake doors". This is a level design flaw but also a game flaw as the characters may not jump or crouch. Unacceptable for a modern RPG. It is completely immersion breaking and really a shame for a game with such an interesting world.
* Terrible dialogue system. Like in Fallout4, it doesn't really matter what you say and in any case, you don't know what you'll say before your character blurts it out. Very annoying.
* The combat system is interesting but suffers greatly from the above mentioned UI issue.
All in all, it is still a nice little game. Not worth buying full price, but certainly a good sales buy. Also don't buy it if you don't like fixed point saves. Seriously. Not only the game has no other option to save it but some of this saves are extremely far apart so you'll have to replay entire levels or areas forever.

Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes strategy-based games or city-builders. However, there are quite a few things that make this game a little frustrating:
- You can get to a point in the game where you have a large and healthy city, and living very comfortably. But within just a few seconds, pretty much everything can be taken away as you're hit by a plague that kills a third of your population, random fires that spread through all your houses/buildings for no reasons whatsoever, with very little way of preventing them, and then about 8 viking ships will come to ruin your day. I've also had about 3 sets of 8 viking ships attack me within the space of about 6-7 minutes which is quite a lot to handle as each attack generally takes about 5 minutes to recover from - especially if they destroy a stockpile or granary, which destroys pretty much all of your resources in an instant, which causes everyone to starve and die, as well as ridding you of resources to rebuild, and inevitably ruins your city as you have no people left.
Other than that, good game. A lot of stuff to add in though (minor additions), such as a fire emergency building that covers an area and ultimately prevents fires, or prevents fires destroying buildings. Also, maybe a heat mapping tool to show which villagers are starving to death, as I placed food sources all over my island yet people were still starving to death. Also, I think that plagues and especially viking hoardes are a bit over-kill at times.

The Escapists 2 is pretty good, all things considered. It definitely improves upon a lot of the core concepts introduced in the first game: There are a lot of prisons to try and break out of in a wider variety of ways, and the addition of both time-limited, mobile “transport prisons” and a unique but optional way or two to get out of every prison (such as posing as a TV crew member) makes it feel better than the original, where I just tried to cut my way through fences or dig through walls time after time. The ability to play with up to 3 other people also can’t be discounted, even if it cheapens the experience a little with some rather easy-to-accomplish co-op escape routes.
In case you’re not familiar, in The Escapists, you’re a prisoner seeking to get out of their sentence a little earlier than anticipated. By managing stats, items, crafting, and following “the routine” until you see an opening to do otherwise, you slowly (at least, at first) plan your escape by doing things such as figuring out where to get the key-cards you need or how to turn off the power. Your goal is to get out as fast and clean as possible, with the ideal performance usually being within a few days without drawing any attention.
This game is not without its flaws, however. It feels like a lot of minor bugs overlap to diminish the experience bit by bit, the netcode for online play is less than stellar, and after you’ve slipped out of each prison a few times, there’s not much reason to go back to them. It’s been patched several times since release to fix a few of the more glaring issues, but trying to revisit it with some other people still felt like it was more of a chore than it should have been. I recommend it, but with the catch that your enjoyment may vary wildly based on your tastes, and somewhat on your hardware.

As far as "Walking Simulators" go (which this certainly is..) it creates a very atmospheric, immersive, and at times downright scary experience. For whatever reason I feel like I have more player choice in this game despite it being a walking simular (which I am typically not a fan of...) although you are being bottlenecked toward the next story beat / area, the pacing of the game fits where other walking simulators may feel plodding and stuffy with their narrative.

Without spoliers, as it is only a 1-2 hour experience, you play as a survivovr who used to be a private investigator but after a devastating event now is just roaming the country(russia) trying to survive. Whether you are crawling in a dark cave, to the outdoor snow and rain effects, to some of the best cloth physics(looks so real) ive ever seen the game looked awesome and ran smooth with no crashes. Im not into horror games, and i would not classify this as horror, but the use of sound, light and shadows made exploring very tense. There are some really good didnt see that coming moments early in the game but those seemed to become less effective later. A Dark room and headphones increase the experience.
Investigator is an odd name for the game as its not your occupation(anymore) as it more pertains to your investigation of the world and story. Its not perfect but for a very small entry fee its an easy recommendation.

This is an
game, with some extremely obnoxious game design flaws and inconsistencies. (Sorry for the obscene length of this review, a game as painstakingly designed as this is bound to have a great deal to cover, both positively and negatively.)
I'll start with the positives. The game's combat is excellent, weighty, highly challenging, and immensely satisfying. There's an array of different weapons to choose from, and learning each one is like a game in and of itself. The atmosphere is awesome, the lore is subtle but very engrossing, and the way that every area seems to connect with one another is legitimately mind blowing. The amount of times I've exclaimed, "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm
now?" during gameplay is something worthy of praise.
. . . This game has some
obnoxious flaws and inconsistencies. There is a lot of legitimate challenge involved with this game, but a frustrating amount of atrocious design choices result in more unfair gameplay moments than there ought to be. The "git gud" argument only takes you so far, as there are plenty of moments where the game blatantly spits in the face of the player.
The most obnoxious example I can think of is the Curse affliction, and the method required to remove it. The Curse ailment kills you instantly, which isn't an issue in my opinion, as that's something that 80% of enemies in the game do. Being killed in one hit by that point in the game should come as no surprise. However, the side effect of Curse is that upon reviving, your health is
, and this persists not until your next death, but until you are able to find a healer to cure it. It goes without saying that in a game as brutally difficult as Dark Souls, halving the player's health is a
crippling debuff. Even weaker enemies will absolutely rock your♥♥♥♥♥♥with this affliction. Curing the Curse requires you to descend into the New Londo Ruins, an area inhabited exclusively by
, who cannot be harmed by your weapons without the use of a consumable found within New Londo. The most frustrating part about these enemies is the inconsistency in their design. They can go through walls, attack through walls, cannot be touched, BUT ARE IMPOSSIBLE TO WALK THROUGH. That is not an example of brutal difficulty, that is an example of inconsistent design. This is an
annoying trait when you consider the fact that not only do the apparitions have a massive reach with their attacks, but they're often placed right in front of doors or hallways. Seriously, what the ♥♥♥♥ is the point of putting a selectively tangible enemy in front of a doorway when there's already 4 of them in a small room surrounding you, and they can reach beyond the edges of said room? It's already brutally challenging, having them block doorways is arbitrary and frustrating.

This is only one of a few cancerous design choices in the game, but I don't believe they ruin the experience. This game is amazing, and it's an experience I think everyone who considers themselves a gamer ought to try. I'll conclude this review with three points of advice that should make your Dark Souls journey more enjoyable and seamless, and things I only really tried on my second character.
1. Explore every new area you find. Comb every corner, and make use of the camera to look around walls. Odds are, you're missing some weapons, armor, or even an entirely new area that's hidden right under your nose. There's a ton of staircases hidden around corners and behind doorways you might initially overlook.
2. Grind for souls every once in a while, perhaps after finding a new bonfire nearby some new enemies. This game relies heavily on trial and error, and grinding will not only give you the opportunity to level up, but help you understand the animations and attack patterns of difficult enemies. Additionally, you can pick up new weapons and armor this way. Also, don't overlook the parry. After you ♥♥♥♥ up for a while, you'll start nailing every parry, and it's immensely satisfying and very helpful.
3. Don't get discouraged. You're gonna die in this game, a lot. Sometimes the lengths the game makes you travel before being instakilled by a lowly enemy is frustrating, but you're probably closer to the next bonfire than you think. Don't let the annoying design choices of this game discourage you completely. It's a game worth pushing through.

Patience and timing will get you far in Dark Souls. Frustration and anger will lead to deaths. If you’re ok with old school difficulty in a more modern package, DS is for you. Just beware of the sometime hopeless difficulty.
Dark Souls has some great gameplay. It’s a great feeling when you finally beat that boss. Making it through a dark corridor and killing everything, or even just that perfect, parry, Dark Souls does a great job of making you feel great by overcoming challenges.
The main problems I have with it is controls and animations. The controls can feel clunky at times, which can easily spell death in a game like this. It almost makes me think that From Software in some aspects made it arbitrarily difficult. Things like walking on a narrow tree while flies are attacking you really exuberates the clunkyness.
With the animations, there are so so so many times where I died because of getting hit when my hitbox was very clearly out of range. See arbitrary difficulty from above.
Another arbitrary difficulty is that DS seems to lack many features of convenience found in modern games. A simple map would be nice. Even a less cumbersome UI.
For its age, the graphics in DS are surprisingly good. I noticed some graphical errors as I progressed further, specifically shading issues, but overall I think the graphics hold up considering its age.
Solid audio, while there isn’t much music, when there is music, it is acceptable and not annoying. The sound of enemies’ footsteps and archers are pivotal for knowing where they are. Overall the sound is acceptable and adequate without being exceptional.
DS has good content by allowing the player to choose where to go. What’s unique about the game is it is very skill based. What this means is that a common challenge of the highest difficulty is beating the game at level 1. Also, to add into this, the level designs are some of the best I have seen.
As mentioned in Content, with DS, you can pretty much choose where you want to go due to the excellent map layout. Also, after beating the game (disclosure: I did not yet), the option of NG+ opens up. NG+ from what I hear offers a nice replaythrough by increasing difficulty through monster HP and attack.
I enjoyed Dark Souls. I feel as if when I’m not playing it, I am constantly in thought about what I can do it become better at the game. DS is an experience and one that will most likely make you frustrated. It’s important to remember that the key is perseverance. I find it best to take breaks when I start to get worn out from constantly being on alert. Sometimes the challenges can seem impossible, but theres such a great feeling when you finally overcome it.

I've spent several hours playing Corgi Warlock, and overall, I have to say that I'm impressed with the game. It's a side-scrolling action platformer with monsters to kill, loot to collect, and upgrades to attain.
The graphics and soundtrack are good, and the controller mechanics are both consistent and responsive. I enjoy gaming with a controller, and nothing disappoints me more than a game that advertises full controller support but doesn't deliver. Corgi Warlock delivers.
There are 10 levels to the game, and so far, I've made it to level 7. What I thought at first was a casual gaming experience is actually really quite challenging. The layout of the levels isn't where the challenge comes in, it's the progression of monsters with varying degrees of health coming across the screen at a steadily increasing pace.
The additon of obstacles such as platforms over water, jumping sharks, and fireballs flying across the screen add unpredictability and the need for quick response time to the mix. As the levels progress, response time gets shorter and shorter while the difficulty increases, meaning that even the most hardcore gamers will find a challenge during the latter portions of the game.
I did experience a few oddities that I want to point out. The first is that killing a coin-dropping monster with a tower in the background results in coins getting stuck in mid-air on the screen. This can be re-created most easily in level 6 or any level where there are step-like platforms leading up to a higher level. The bottom level ends at a gray tower, meaning that you can't advance any further to the right. However, the monsters are coming from the right side of the screen, as well as the left, so if you stand right at the end of the bottom level and shoot, or jump up on a right-side platform and shoot, coins will regularly drop and fly up into the tower, getting stuck on the screen where your character cannot go.
This brings me to the second oddity, which is that the Steam Overlay doesn't seem to work with this game, and neither does the F12 button for taking screenshots. I wanted to take a screenshot of these trapped coins to publish, but I couldn't figure out how to do this. Neither F12 or the Print Screen button worked for me, and I was unable to use Alt-Tab and snip tool to clip a JPG. Anyone determined to get a screenshot would likely have to clip a frame out of a video streaming session.
Other than those couple of things, which really didn't reduce my enjoyment of the game, overall, I didn't experience anything that would cause me not to recommend the game. It's appropriate for young and casual gamers as well as experienced gamers looking for a challenge.

My first time attending a performance of Mozart’s The Magic Flute was something of a defining experience, though the reasons have less to do with the play than they do this particular performance and my…anatomical development at the time. Around halfway through a large dance began (what the actual scene was I couldn’t say), during which roughly a dozen women stripped off their jackets as they performed a line-dance in only sports bras. My mother was appalled, but being myself a sheltered, hormonally overrun preteen, I began to pay significantly more attention to a play I had been nearly sleeping through moments before.
It certainly wouldn’t be the most scandalous encounter I’d have with my burgeoning feelings of sexual attraction, though it seems oddly fitting that one of my earliest experiences would involve The Magic Flute, a play which, in many ways, is itself about sex. Mozart may have wrapped that fact within a family-friendly fairytale coating, but ultimately nearly every key plot point can be linked to sex and attraction, and the implications Mozart chose to make about them therein.
Tamino’s love for Pamina is almost entirely based on physical attraction, and he himself is saved from the serpent of the first act on account of his good looks. Monostatos’ character is effectively a shell of unrestrained sexual urges, and his downfall is in some ways a bigger condemnation of premarital relations than his near assault of Pamina (The Magic Flute is nothing if not a sexist product of its time). Act 2 even features a scene in which Tamino and Papageno are sworn to silence, lest they be led astray by the women seeking to mislead them. It’s all a bit of a mess when viewed through modern eyes, but that has done little to curb The Magic Flute’s popularity.
How exactly does this wrap around to Magic Flute the game? Well, in most ways it doesn’t. Though it shares its name, characters, and music, LabLike’s block sliding puzzler shares little thematic ground with Mozart’s opera. Magic Flute is far less interested in exploring the romantic elements of its source material than it is in adapting its scenes (“adaption” being a very generous designation) into tile-based logic puzzles.
I hesitate to say that Magic Flute actually shares the same plot as its progenitor, as its narrative is so thinly told that even being familiar with The Magic Flute I struggled to follow it. Some of Magic Flute’s incoherent storytelling may stem from it being in large part an adaptation of an adaptation, influenced as much by Mozart’s The Magic Flute as Amon Miyamoto’s video game inspired retelling of it, from which Magic Flute takes its low-poly art design and Neo-Toyko setting. Magic Flute is easily among the most creative revisions of the play that I have witnessed to date, but it strays so far from the original that at some point it is hard to say if the elements it does borrow from The Magic Flute are warranted or justified.
Much of these concerns fall away while solving Magic Flute’s puzzles, being themselves so abstract as to create a suitable distance between their designs and the bizarre echo of a past work that exists in the game’s cutscenes and narration. LabLike hasn’t reinvented the sliding puzzle, but their reworking of it is suitably engaging, if clumsily implemented. Magic Flute’s style allows its puzzles to succeed without an abundance of complexity or variance. They leave little impression, but the act of successfully navigating through the mazes you construct by shifting various types of blocks around is entertaining in itself.
The fun is lessened when Magic Flute asks you to navigate multiple characters through a single level, though, as the single input interface allows for an astounding amount of error, as the same button used to move is also used to change characters depending on where you click. It isn’t a game-breaking issue, but it caused me to fumble around and flub solutions often enough that I began to truly detest the game’s minimal control scheme.
Accounting for only the first act of The Magic Flute, it seems safe to say that LabLike has more planned for their tiny offspring of a renowned work. And I’ll be happy to see it, even if what is currently here is more intriguing oddity than anything I would call a suitable first exposure to The Magic Flute proper. Magic Flute almost certainly will not stick with me the same way my experience watching the play did, but I enjoyed it enough to hope it stays in my memory well enough that I’ll remember to return when its second act arrives (which at this point is not seeming incredibly likely, but I am keeping my fingers crossed).

On the surface,
seems like a simple puzzle game, however, once you begin to play you’re met with beautiful music and striking imagery. The story is based on the opera of the same name by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. The visuals are inspired by director Amon Miyamoto’s production of the opera which was in turn inspired by video games, using multimedia projections to bring the story to life. All this being said, you do not have to be a fan of opera, Mozart or even know anything about the story itself to enjoy this game. It’s a good stand alone interpretation of the original piece.
A young prince named Tamino finds himself lost in an unknown land being chased by a giant snake. He is rescued by three witches then meets Papageno, a bird catcher. After this brief introduction, the story gets underway.  The pair meet the Queen of Night, who gives Tamino a magical flute and sends the prince and the bird catcher on a journey to rescue her daughter, Pamina. The game follows the story of the opera, it is filled with adventure, plot twists as well as romance. The story is skillfully told through narration and cut scenes as you play each level of the puzzle game.
The game has thirty two stages of puzzle fun to explore and three characters you can play as; Tamino, Papageno and Pamina. The basic game mechanic is moving blocks to help a character reach the exit in a level. The levels are 3D so sometimes it takes looking at the problem at different angles to figure out to succeed. As to be expected, the game becomes more challenging the higher the level, introducing different aspects like crumbling platforms, ladders and new enemies. The game can be a bit hard at times but not in a frustrating way.
You’re treated to splendid music as you play the game, as to be expected of a title based on an opera. If you enjoy classical music then you will find it easy to immerse yourself in this experience. There is nothing bad I can say about the audio in this game, it’s top notch. As mentioned before, the visual are based on Amon Miyamoto’s production of the opera, everything is larger than life while also being simplistic with clean lines. It gives the game a very modern aesthetic which works well for a video game.
This may not be a game for everyone,
is a unique puzzle game telling a classic story. It’s calming and good to play when you need a break between other games. I highly enjoyed the experience, especially the music and how nice it made me feel. Even at full price it is affordable and it also has Steam achievements.  I recommend picking up this title if you wish to try something different.

I'm a huge and long-standing fan of TLJ and Dreamfall and had been waiting a decade for the conclusion of this story! I was so excited for this game that, after it launched, I WAITED IN NAIL-BITING ANTICIPATION for all five chapters to be released. The moment that happened, I dropped everything and played this game. And I was so disappointed, I was depressed. Just so you know, I waited a year before writing this review to see if some of the bitterness would go away with perspective. It did not. Somewhere in the span of time that Ragnar took off to make The Secret World, he lost his vision for this series. Chapters became his soapbox. He half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥pretty much all the plots left-over from Dreamfall, ruined April's story, and butchered the ending with a random Deus Ex Machina. At the end of the game, you have five chapters of poorly assembled mish-mash, and I felt more betrayed with this game than I did after the ending of ME3.
I’ll detail my major issues below, which will include spoilers, so read at your own risk.
I never even considered Arcadia to be a place where homosexuality might be a problem! Don't remember that coming up in the first or second game...but for some reason, in Chapters, being gay is taboo even for super “open-minded people like the Dolmari”. Even though I am annoyed when developers feel like it’s open season on inserting hot-button issues into their products when it doesn’t feel at all relevant to the story, it wouldn't have been a big deal to me if it didn't feel so awkwardly placed. Like the two lesbians in Stark (I can't remember their names) felt totally natural and well-written, but Kian and Likho? Ragnar says he always intended for Kian to be gay, which I have a hard time believing, but maybe so. But Likho? He was once April Ryan's lover, and for him to suddenly be gay felt like a last-minute alteration so Ragnar could make a point, which ultimately felt like it cheapened the relationship he had with April. Not to mention the awkward placement of Kian’s reveal (was completely forced) and the repetition of this fact. For example: in the end of the game, when you are rowing across a lake to save the world, Crow asks you if you were ever lovey-dovey with April just so Kian can reinforce how gay he is. I almost threw my keyboard across the room. Instead of showing us what was happening with the rescue efforts of Benrime and the other captives or how the final assault was going (you never find out about that, by the way) or a last minute heartfelt chat, we need to talk about how gay Kian is ONE MORE TIME. Kian being gay is not what bothers me; the fact that it felt like Ragnar switched things around to make a point that didn’t need to be made in this story and then drill it into our heads in place of other much more important action is.
-Aside from burning April in the beginning, you don't see her again until the very end for five minutes where she basically says, "Yeah, duh, me dying was me being saved because, you know, it’s hard out here for a pimp." And then she leaves. I was soooo insulted at how cheap that felt.
-"Be careful, Dad. That's not Reza." Remember that line? Well it means nothing, nada, zip. You start the game off living with him, thinking, "Oh my gooooosh, how is this going to turn out?! >_< She's in a romantic relationship with a Wati Corp body clone spyyyyyy!" But no, turns out...he WAS Reza in sleeper agent format...and he was NEVER activated. They made his character disappear halfway through and never resurface until the epilogue with a bit of a confused headache.
-Zoe's character loses so much momentum by the end. Seriously, she "heroes it up" by being scientific.
-You never find out what happened to Benrime. She’s taken prisoner and that’s it. Someone says they are going to try to rescue her, but you never find out if they succeed.
-The Guardian. Apparently, whatever was happening between Stark and Arcadia didn’t affect the balance…ONLY IT WAS GOING TO MERGE THE WORLDS. But definitely not a balance problem. Nope. Not one bit.
-The death of the White of the Draic Kin. Just not very important other than a passing mention.
-Kian! He was so strong in Chapter 1, and that's where it ends. He goes from being a warrior and believer who was moved by the rebels and ultimately let down by the corrupt zealots he thought were allies...to being a super bitter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a beard. He was seriously really bland and "I'll do it...but only because I don't care about anything anymore!" until he suddenly starts caring about everyone because the plot demanded it.
-Kian's mother. Everything about her, her story, her place in the world and with the other characters (especially Crow) was awful, last minute, and poorly explained.
-Anna. Really, what was even the point of her? She shows up out of nowhere with zero context and barely appeared again until the very end where she made such small contributions that they could've easily been taken over by another character. She seemed to be there simply to reinforce that Kian is gay, so she was just a hair-clipping nightmare of a wasted character.
Saga. In general, I liked her character. If you took her out of this game and put her into anything else, I would've been like, "Awesome." But in Chapters, she is awful. I don't even care if she's supposed to be April reborn, as many people feel is hinted at. She only exists to resolve the plot because Ragnar couldn't do it any other way, apparently. There's really very little context for her character - you play her at various stages of her life and all you know is she's "special". She's special, all right. A special spoiled sassy teenager who shows up at the end knowing everything with undefined powers to resurrect Kian, open a portal between Stark and Arcadia so Zoe can "science the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this", and then be the answer to Lady Alvane because PROPHECY so Ragnar can stick it to everyone who spent a decade of their life believing April Ryan was Lady Alvane and theorizing where it was all headed.
Just like the Mass Effect series, TLJ and Dreamfall have been ruined for me. I can’t go back and play them again without knowing how the devs destroyed something so interesting and well-written into a steaming pile of garbage.

This review will contain some spoilers and is subjective.
First, the disclaimer: I let the world burn. In the beginning of the second book (out of five?), my brute was offered to be railroaded by the inexorable hand of  fate or he could choose free will. I chose, like Geddy Lee, and the game rolled me the ending credits. For my trouble, I got an achievement with a withered, creepy skull. So the story ends, and the world. The uninstall will soon liberate the bits from the Dreamfall squatters.
I liked
- Zoe was pretty as a button and Kian looks hot without a shirt
- Your choices have some effects on the story
- The game is available natively on Linux and worked ok
- There was a pessimistic, introverted robot side-character I could relate to
I didn't like
- The game patronizes; when there is a choice, the screen says, loud and clear, look here, this is a choice, careful now. Later, it rubs into your face what you chose, and that there will be consequences.
- The choice is yours, and as in school test, only one choice is sometimes right: the one that the teacher wants to hear, or else (see above).
- In matters regarding your personal preferences and tastes as a player, there is no choice. Zoe is an activist for the social democrats. So are you, as Zoe. And no, you are not allowed to choose to be an activist for the fascists or the anarchists instead. Zoe has a boyfriend, and so have you. Hope you like him. He works in the new media making the world a better place.
- As Zoe, you wake up from a coma and one of your first quests is to bring your boyfriend lunch to work. Not bringing it is not an option. Would Commander Shepard run meal errands for her boyfriend? Can't I play a feminist? Why is not the boyfriend bringing me the meal instead?
- The game has fake puzzles. You encounter what looks like a puzzle. There's a diagram, and there's parts. In any case, the thing just blows up. What you do with it doesn't matter. There was no puzzle. It was meant to explode. I googled just to be sure it was not just me.
- Children. Dreamfall Chapters really likes them. If I counted right, the intro has a few, then one childbirth, then you help a little girl that has nightmares. Sometime later -- before the world ends at the beginning of the book 2 -- you even get to toddle along as a toddler. Can you imagine how slow is that? The toddler makes toddler noises as it toddles. Happy immersion, hope you can relate to that!
- Unfortunately Zoe or Kian are not much faster walking than the toddler, and often some miraculous force prevents them from running (which is slow as well).
- Everybody has the *net and a heads-up display. But when you want to know where to go in the  pointless future city, you go ask a terminal for directions. Luckily there's many of them. I mean... What happened to openstreetmap and gps they had way back in 2017? On the similar vein, your friend gets into trouble. You are given two choices, either you can get into trouble as well, or you can stand aside to watch him get beaten. No, you cannot record it all on your smartphone and upload it live to Dreamscope or Solidaritube. Why not? You could already do that in 2017. The game seemingly has futuristic content, but it hasn't even grasped what people do with technology today. In the games' world where even the homeless have VR helmets and HUDs and wireless and who knows what, Zoe has a television at her place.
- Unmemorable graphics design. Things generally do not look like you'd want to stop and stare at it in awe. Its more generic fantasy/scifi trope. The architectures, the dreamscapes, the fantasy parts. Photoshopped, sterile, without real artistic vision. This could be a matter of taste, but compare to the beauty of Child of Light, the impressiveness of Metro, or the visual cleverness of the Arkham-brand Batman francise. You see no such originality in the first book of Dreamfall Chapters. And the characters are pretty, but look at Zoe. She is pretty. Pretty, perfect like a chocolate-eyed doll, straight from Blender. What future grizzliness the game attempts to convey vanishes under the overall photoshop candy varnish.
- Evil characters are cartoonish, big noses, bulky, ugly, buffoons. Good characters are smoking hot and perfectly shopped. I thought the game was against discrimination?
- You discover what can be interacted with by waddling close to everything, everything in turn... to discover most of it is meaningless, doors that do not let you enter, people that tell you some uninspired one line comment. Objections that you do not want to put your hand into the trashcan (in every adventure game you should).
The judgement
I could go on. Basically there appears to be very little game in the Dreamfall Chapters. With its far and few problems, solved by trial-and-error typically, it is not a good adventure game. With its nonrewarding, pointless movement from As to Bs, its not a satisfying game of exploration and discovery. Going the extra mile to some nook or cranny gives you... nothing. It is a role-playing game in the sense that you're forced to play certain roles and to do what the characters are intended to do and to think what they're intended to think.
With its endless cutscenes and dialogue, Dreamfall Chapters is finally best described as an interactive movie. If the offered content and political undercurrent floats your boat and you don't mind the missing 'game', that is nice. My boat caught a bit of fire along with the world.

This game has neither neat-looking graphics, a fun combat system, nor likeable/convincing characters.
So why am I giving this game a thumbs up?
It's highly motivating and even if the charakters are either uninteresting and/or annoying, I wanted to know how the story progresses.
Motivating because during the game you'll get PLENTY of experience points and there are many ways how to spend them. Even if the combat system is really awkward and wooden, I still wanted to continue, because I was rewarded for every single action. And the XP was motivating to the end.
About the story - don't worry, I won't spoil here - it had many "WTF"-moments at the beginning, where I thought that the characters made absolutely no sense at all. I was about to dump the game, but gave it one more shot and in the end everything will be explained. It's high-fantasy and sometimes very much over-the-top, but that's a characteristic of The Black Eye. And well, if the game is called "Demonicon", you kind of gotta expect that there are indeed tons of demons to fight against.
Another reason which made me keep playing was the atmosphere: it was dark and gritty, sometimes a bit insincere, but it managed to keep me hooked. If you played Drakensang, another The Black Eye - RPG, you will be surprised how dirty, cruel and hopeless the world seems in a sudden.
Beside this, you have many choices in the game and they do matter. Not gameplay-wise, but storywise and this is something I miss in many other games (Telltale Games, I'm looking at you!).
So all in all I can say, this game was good entertainment. Don't expect too much, though. I wouldn't reccomend spending more than 10€ for this game, but if it's on sale and you like a diverting, interesting RPG, go for it.

Demonicon is a 3rd person action RPG. You follow the story of a brother and sister, which takes place in the Dark Eye universe, who find out they have special gifts when their blood was mixed. You only play as the brother leveling up through action points and gift points you earn through battles. You can level up main stats like strength and vitality, skills like lockpicking, medicine, and speech or combat skills with the action points you earn. The gift points go towards your gift skills which are like magic powers.
Combat in the game is ok. You have one mainattack besides the combat and gift skills. When attacking you need to time the button pressing right to continue your combo attack. Enemies can become bothersome or annoying sometimes when you go to attack and they keep hitting you and stopping your action. Controls did feel a little sluggish and slow when attacking. You do have a dodge roll which helps a little but your character seems to move slower than everyone else.
Graphics look to be from something 10 years ago which isn't bad just not up to par with some games today. Plus it doesn't matter how a game looks if you enjoy it. Sounds were pretty generic and sometimes annoying. There are some parts in town when you are running around and NPC dialog got load and cluttered when it seemed like 10 people are trying to talk over one another.
Characters were pretty interesting and funny. You can choose different ways to go in the game and I chose mainly the good side of things. What was weird though was in some conversations it seemed like my character was rude and evil even though I would pick the better dialog route. The story overall wasn't bad and get me interested to see how it all panned out in the end. You could even do another playthrough to see where other actions would take you.
There were some issue with the game though. Framerate issues were a problem throughout the game. No matter where I put the settings I would drop as low as 15 frames sometimes which made for some rough video. I also would see pop in at times and screen tearing. I even had the game crash on me about 5 times when I was more than halfway though the game.
Despite these flaws the game was still fun and intriguing. I liked some of the characters and even had some laughs here and there. It also has replay value if you'd like to see where the different choices would take you. If you can get the game on sale than pick it up and enjoy your time.

All in all, if you see this on sale and you like linear action rpgs, give it a chance and grab it =)

This title is definitely worth the price.
Admitedly, I really didn't expect much from a $3 game. I completely misjudged Investigator and was pleasantly surprised with a solid story that had me playing from start to finish which is unusual for me and my short attention span. I have a lot of strong(and probably unpopular) opinions about the game.
Things I liked:
1. The story was interesting, although a little shallow. I got the jist of how the world became the way it was and who the pro/antagonists were, but I felt like there could have been more depth. This could have been easily accomplished with some notes placed here and there. Maybe a diary belonging to the bad guy?
2. Stamina! I almost never ran out of stamina and I was sprinting everywhere I could. I always hate when games give you too little juice so to speak so I was thrilled to be able to run everywhere since there isn't much danger in the game anyway(walking simulator).
3. Gnomes. They have a special place in my heart. That is all.
4. Achievements add another small dimention to the game and give people who like to explore a cookie for finding all the cool things or just playing the story.
5. Free DLC! This is a rare thing nowadays so I commend the Devs for adding more content at no additional cost to the customer. Thanks guys <3
That being said, I have a few nitpicks:
1. Head bobbing should always have a toggle in my opinion. Some of us get motion sick much easier than others. Although, it's not as bad in this game as it is in others, it only really becomes bothersome in small spaces.
2. The camera movement in cutscenes. I felt like I was transported back to the 90's when the Blair Witch was released and the camera was swinging everywhere. Again, not fun for people who easily get motion sick. I managed to soldier through but it was tough.
3. At one point you get a weapon and for some reason you can only walk at a snails pace with it. I don't understand this but it bugged me so on the list it goes. :P
4. It doesn't save my video settings! Luckily it isn't a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to put them back, but I wish it could save them somehow when I exit the game.

A fantastic game and a genre-defining one at that. Many would say it's a masterpiece.
First off, the best thing you can do for yourself is indeed to prepare to die, especially if you enjoy going in blank into the world and not do research online, but if you struggle too much, use the tools and tips you find online in order to not give up on this game. It will throw tests at you that you'll struggle with and the feeling you get from overcoming those struggles will re-define how you feel about games today.
Personally I'd recommend going for a more offensive fighting style using dodging, because the game starts out incentivizing you to hide behind a shield. While a shield can be a good option, you should be careful not to make the option of the shield limit your playstyle.
Personally I think there are issues with menus and optimalization, but there is a must-use mod for the game that sorts out a lot of those issues for optimalization, making the game playable despite a relatively poor port. Take a look at the community-page in order to find it and have fun.
Overall playing this game can lead you to a ton of enjoyable gametimes and actually feeling like you've achieved something, and if it does you'll have tons of new games to play like dark souls 2 & 3, Lords of the fallen, Bloodborne (PS4 exclusive) & Nioh.

Game Corp DX reminds me a lot of the indie hit Game Dev Tycoon, but with a different focus. Game Dev Tycoon's system is more complex, with a focus on making sure you match the right genre and platform and feel of the game, creating a sort of matrix of what works and what doesn't. Game Corp DX instead asks you to focus on worker management and ensure the right people for the job are working on the right teams.
The game feels a bit clunky in spots -- not being able to rotate items when building is a huge oversight. And there's not as much going on concurrently as there is in Game Dev Tycoon. This is still a solid way to spend a couple of hours. I blew through the campaign in about 2.5 hours, though I'd imagine it's possible to do it much quicker if you're not a perfectionist.
In short: definitely a fun game, but lacks complexity and is over too soon

I really wanted to love you, Corgi Warlock. I like goofy games with flash art that looks like it was drawn by someone who played a ton of games from The Behemoth. Even when a game lacks overall polish but has a lot of heart I’m often ready to defend its merits to anyone who wants to point out its shortcomings. Sadly I don’t think our romance was meant to be.
Corgi Warlock’s gameplay is a variation of the standard side-scrolling brawler, except unlike many of these games with horizontal and limited depth movement field, Corgi Warlock’s enemies all attack in a single-file line. Because of this, the player has only the option of jumping from the ground to have any variation in position. The game is designed to support play for up to four players, though this is local multiplayer only as of the time of this article’s publication.
The player will fight wave, after wave, after wave of identical mooks, and then possibly more waves of functionally identical but reskinned mooks after that. Once you have survived these waves you will fight a mini-boss, which is generally a larger mook with a health bar to tell you that you’ll have to hit them more than just once to get the job done. Don’t worry, most of the mini bosses stand stock-still and assault you with no more than three variations of their attack, in a cycle, forever. Should you survive the mini-bosses you’ll probably kill a flying enemy or two that have been tossed in for fun, and by fun I mean totally randomly for no discernible reason before running into an open doorway at the end of the level that automatically teleports you away once you’re over it, ending the level.
Each section of the game is broken into multiple sub-levels leading up to the final confrontation with the Level Boss. Between the sub-levels, the magical transport doors will take you to a town where the NPCs will shout dialog at you as you pass that doesn’t really affect the game at all. There is also a store, which is a fancy way of saying that text floats above orbs you can grab if you’ve murdered enough mooks to get gold, which you have, because otherwise you’d have died because you can’t avoid combat. Neat, right?
At the very end you’ll battle the Level Boss, which you can tell is happening because you’ll door-port into a room with a big sprite that attempts to murder you. Just a little though, all the bosses in Corgi Warlock are unable to move, and like the mini-bosses, limited to the same three-variation attack cycle. This makes defeating them more of an exercise in timing and pattern recognition than it is a challenge.
Overall, Corgi Warlock suffers from some serious limitations because of the way it was designed. According to the developer’s blog the game was created in Construct 2, which is a game creation engine that allows code-free game building. As with most ready-made engines, you have to work around the limits imposed by the simple options if you want any hope of having a game that isn’t brought down by them, and Corgi Warlock just isn’t up to the task.
For a game from a single person, and what seems to be a freshman effort, I think it could have been a lot worse, but I don’t think it was ready to be on Steam Greenlight. This feels like it would have fit right into the throngs of free flash games on sites like Newgrounds in the mid-2000s, where its lack of polish and variation would have been so much more forgivable.

I would strongly recommend the combat arena before starting a new game!
Fighting is hard to get your head round at first but the combat physics are uniquely superb. Fighting someone with a chair leg is very different from using a machete. Add to this the range of weapons both you and the opponents can use combined with where you fight them, a corridor, around a table and no two fights are ever the same.
A few people have been complaining about the permadeath but its worth noting that as you progress you get better Armour which means when you fight you don't loose any permanent health, just stamina which is regenerated after the fight, so essentially it does become easier than when you first wake up wearing rags and have no equipment.
There is health potions that do heal anyway but they are considering adding 'checkpoints' to the early content to save your progress. There is also a skill system on its way so you will be able to earn permanent skill points for starting builds on new characters.
It's worth noting that not all enemy's will attack on sight, which is handy if you want to hide out the way till they go past and have an explore about.

This review is basically for people scared of the difficulty...
My first few hours with Exanima were some of my most frustrating gaming experiences ever.
The camera all but got me killed, I tripped over on gusts of wind, enemies spilled my guts.
6 or 7 hours of practise later, it clicked.
The combat got less frustrating. My attacks landed more often, I dodged more. I was getting better. I went from struggling on the first two enemies in Novice Arena, to cleaning Novice Arena in minutes. My first time in Expert Arena, I got two enemies away from the end on my first try, and that's when I realised just how addicted I had become. From now on, there is no resting until I've beaten Expert Arena in my underpants.
There's nothing like the feeling of killing an enemy that has beaten you SO. MANY. TIMES. with a lucky backhand slash after dodging an overhead cut. It's the most lifelike, engaging, physical combat I've ever played in a game. It looks great, feels great, it's satisfying and difficult and rewards patience, practise, and learning. The story mode is pant-browningly creepy, as you're armed with sod all except your wits and however much practise you bothered to put into Arena, and left to explore and escape a classic dungeon that could've been taken straight from Ultima legend. Patience and methodical advancement are the ONLY way you'll survive. I haven't gotten past the first level yet!
Bottom line, don't be put off by the difficulty or controls;
you get used to them, and you'll be glad you did!
Edit: I just finished the Expert Arena as of the v6.0 update, 21hrs played.
A damn rewarding game!

This game requires a special mindset. It's not necessary a "hard" game but you need to use your brain to survive. Is it worth attacking the enemy who seems to be using a two handed sword and heavy armor when you yourself is wearing cloth or leather armor? Probably not. Is it worth fighting every enemy that you encounter throughout the dungeon? Probably not.
The game has a very advanced fighting system though and it might take a few hours (which are wisest spent i the Arena) to figure it out. I've gone from dreadfully bad to just pretty bad by dying and retrying. The sense of accomplishment is similar to that of the Souls games (or any hardcore game for that matter), though.
In my opinion this is well worth your money. If not for the enjoyment of the game, at least to open your eyes to the possibilities of what a completely physics driven game actually means. You might not like this game in particular but you will definately be curious to what the future has to offer in terms of gameplay.
And lastly: If you suck in the beginning, don't worry too much about it. Try to see what your caracter does when you swing "this" or "that" way. If you cannot get the hang of it watch some videos. I, myself, SUCKED COMPLETE BALLS and was dreading I was never gonna learn to maneuver. But I'm getting there. Slowly. So will you.

This is a game in the early stages of being completed.  At least, that's the way it seems.
So, the very, very short and vague instructions don't really tell you how to play the game.  I'm actually happy for games like that that let you figure it out for yourself.  But, not when key points of how to play the very limited range of the game aren't explained (like how to attack other people, for example).
The graphics are nicer than I expected
The sound is relatively inconspicuous but helps set the mood of being in a dungeon of sorts
The learning curve for playing the game is relatively high and may require some youtubing in order to figure out
As far as the gameplay... let's just say it's fairly punishing and takes some getting used to.
Combat is basically luck of the draw.  If you happen to get the last hit in, you win.  Otherwise it's like flailing at each other with wet noodles until you get the hang of it.  Then it's like flailing at each other with wet cardboard.
Don't forget to open your inventory when you pick something up to actually take it.
Don't forget that the combat interaction button IS NOT the combat button... that's the "turn toward cursor" button
The ability to learn how to dash can't be understated... because it's OP.  And, literally, is the only thing you need to learn how to do beyond opening doors and figuring out what to pick up.

I was born from the depths of the demon realm, fought monsters, demons, warriors and even my own kin to build my powers and seek the truth of my existence. Demonicon was an above average action RPG overall. At the current price of $20 it is not worth buying this game, but at $5 or less it might be worth it. The storyline is pretty straight forward and the choices you make, good or bad, mainly influence what hidden achievement you get and does not really affect the final ending other than some dialogue differences.
For achievement hunters this game will require multiple playthroughs as the hardest difficulty is unlocked after beating the game. The lack of a manual save might be a deterrant for some people, but the auto-save does appear after each fight ends, and there are some pre-set auto save points to get the other hidden achievements if you wanted to make another dialogue decisions, but it would be better just to start a new playthough on the hardest difficulty if you're aiming to be a completionist.
The leveling system is pretty straight forward and there is no real grind as monsters do not respawn in the areas you defeat them unless it's a new story progression. By endgame you will get most of the AP stat point skills to maximum, but the GP will be limited and at most you will max out two skills with GP.
Overall I give the game a 5.5/10 as the gameplay can be monotonous and the parry system is almost redundant by the end of the game and relies more on dodging. It's a decent linear RPG but going from point to point and backtracking is what made the game longer than it should be when doing side quests and main quests. Some of the puzzles do require you to memorize some obscure sentences that might not be obvious as well if you skip dialogues or lore.

Grow Up is a perfect example of how to make a sequel, you remove/ change what didn't work, you add new stuff, you make the game bigger and you make it a better experience all around.
So you are BUD, after the success that was the previous mission you have set off (presumably), back home but because MOM was busy playing Tic Tac Toe with you she hit a moon and MOM was blown apart into separate pieces, sprinkled all around the planet that the moon is orbiting, you must explore this planet to find MOM's pieces, fix her up on the moon and get back on track with your mission.
This time you have POD helping you out, POD is a flying drone essentially that allows you to access a birds eye view at any time by pressing TAB, from here she can point out crystals, teleporters, challenges, ship parts and abilities that you can utilise.
This time instead of a exploring a small island with a heck load of vertical, you get a whole planet with a heck load of vertical to explore, with unique biomes, which contain their exclusive plants, animals, challenges and mode.
This time you have 4 Star Plants to grow, growing them is not the main goal of the game but they also count for 100% completion, they can help you easily reach higher places and they have their own unique stems, foliage and designs from each other.
Around the world you can find these capsules which contain new abilities for BUD, some old, some new, BUD can then freely use these abilities to help in the exploration of the world.
These abilities consist of:
Floradex 3000: Back but with a twist, while also tracking what flora you have found in the world, you can generate a seed of any plant you find to plant anywhere you like, plant down a Champoline to make a springboard up a cliff, or make a bridge of Lily Pads to avoid deadly water.
Jetpack: Returning from the first game, it's a jetpack, I think you can figure this out.
Air Brake: The parachute flowers return but now it's a natural ability of BUD, once found you can press F any time in mid-air to slow your momentum and float down to safety
Ball Form: A whole new ability that allows BUD to curl up into a form resembling a ball, funny that, it can primarily be used to absorb fall damage and bounce back up to not die from high falls, you can also charge up a boost while in this mode and spin dash like your favourite neighbour hood speedman.
Glider: The Leaf is back from the first game but with a twist like the Air Break, once unlocked, by holding the Air Brake button (F default) you bring it out, it's unlimited and you can glide around like you'd expect, if you get enough crystals you can add rockets to it which are powered by you, so you can accelerate the the skies using it!
Crystal Detector: Returning from the first, allows you detect crystals within a radius, yep.
Crystals are also back from the first game but now there are 150 of them! Scattered throughout the world as you'd expect, getting past certain thresholds grant BUD more power over his abilities, such adding rockets to the glider, as more batteries to utilise the FloraDex, Jetpack, and Glider rockets, upgrading the Jetpack. Many things.
Challenges are a whole new thing added for this game, they consist of time trials in which you must use your abilities to climb, jump, plant and glide through all the waypoints, showing you new areas and even a couple of crystals along the way, encouraging exploration.
Completing the challenges grant new entirely new costumes (including the return of Ninja BUD from the first game) which grant whole new abilities and have their own unique visuals for each ability while in use, and all of them are helpful in their own way which I won't spoil.
I haven't experienced any bugs in the game (outside of a sound glitch at 250 consecutive minutes in game), but people have reported having technical issues for the game but I can't really comment on that.
Grow Up has done everything a sequel should do and it should be a insta-buy if you liked the first game at all. And for those who haven't played the first, Grow Up is the same price with more stuff and the kinks ironed out.

Shantae: Risky's Revenge - Director's Cut is a pretty average metroid-vania. Has all the backtracking you should expect, but often feel very artificial, the way you have to go much further left/right to keep things moving forward for very little reason.
The combat and the controls in general could be better, as I often missed attacks and platforms that seemed like a hit because of dodgy hitboxes... But other than that, it's okay.
The progression is rather bland, in comparison with many other Metroidvanias - the abilities you gain are transformations into animals with different abilities. These, however, don't serve much purpose aside from clearing "progress walls". Without X transformation, you can't get past this wall, but other than that, the game plays the same throughout... which defeats the purpose, to me. Take Guacamelee, for example: each ability gave you both platforming and combat possibilities you didn't have before, with challenges to match it. By that end, you had a pretty wide array of abilities and combos that you learned as you played. None of that here. The combat is simply about keeping your distance and spamming attack.
The exploration element is rather weak as well, only gaining "jam" that you can use to upgrade your magic abilities (which aren't very interesting either) or your attack speed.
The graphics are pretty nicely done, though, and the music as well, although it's not my favourite of Jake Kaufman's soundtracks.
There are also some sequence issues that can very easily throw you off, because characters are hinting at the next sequence, thinking you've completed an objective that you have not. This happened to me twice, which is not good at all. Especially since the game's map is rather awkward, and you have no ability whatsoever to mark places on the map.
To make matters worse, it deleted all of my progress. It may be because I changed the controls (although I changed them when I first started playing, and only now, after restarting the computer, as the progress been deleted)... which is another can of worms: the game has confirm on B and back on A, for some reason. And doesn't let you rebind the keys properly, requiring you to alter a hex file, etc. etc.
Yeah, not a very positive review, is it?
Despite all of the issues, the game is okay. I mean, if you're looking for a simple metroidvania, it will do the job. But aside from that, there really isn't anything special here. It seems like a game made for the sake of the classics rather than its own thing, but hey, it works.

Finished the game both on the DSi and on Steam. A beatifully polished example of what a retro platformer should be, though it's far better to play the initial game on the Gameoy Color in order to understand the plot fully.
First and foremost: when you start out, you'll find that your main method of attack is your hair whip. The hitbox is smooth and quick enough, but you're going to have to force yourself to get used to its awkward positioning. It's more comfortable hitting enemies on the far side of a cliff than directly next to them, and this is one of those types where you actually need to crouch to hit basic foes, so... be careful about that.
The game takes advantage of a 2.95-D sidescrolling map where you find arrowed platforms which send you to and fro layers of sidescrolling dimensions. This is a double-edged implementation for the game. For one, it's very nice to look at, and can help you see your exact location from the z-axis. On the other hand, it's a pain to navigate easily through the maps, let alone to actually FIND the arrowed platforms.
Menu navigation is also a bit hard to navigate. You have to kind of learn your way through it by accidentally chugging down potions you don't mean to, and I really wished the Map was more quickly accessed.
Throughout the game you learn new flirty dances and transformations of all kinds, which (as a platformer does) allows you access to many secrets. And this game loves secrets. It rewards you with a healthy amount of gems and health as a Zelda game would, and finishing dungeons leaves your pockets overflowing with them, which you can spend on useful but optional weapons.
There's not a single unlikeable character in this game, either, and I can nearly guarantee that for anybody! Even poor ol' Bolo is never forgettable, or the absolutely hilarious Rottytops, can sneak a grin or three up your face. WayForward tends to go for subtle though light-hearted sorts of humor, so definitely pick this game up if you're into that.
Though the dungeons are nice, creative and keep you busy, sometimes they get slightly frustrating. Despite they're seemingly innocent linearity, they can either get very confusing, or just straight painful to fight through. I never really enjoyed climbing the vertical wells with the small octopus running around, cause it requires slightly precise timing to hit.
The animations are insanely smooth, yet qucik enough to keep the pace up-beat. It does a very good job in making use of all the pixels it has for subtle shading and contrasting colors, to help make jazz easy on the eyes though bright and vivid.
Risky's Revenge is a game that takes your expectations of a classic platformer, and blows it out the window without even trying to make it into something it's not. Future games like it should look at it and see what it does right. Very polished!

This gameplay itself is extremely polished with a fun world and interesting mechanics and combat. However as a metroidvania game I feel the map system is woefully obsolete as it gives no real information regarding points of interest and your next quest location. You will get lost, and though the world is small enough to allow you to revisit everything and brute force your way to the next quest, it's not exactly fun to have to do so. The lack of direction there feels like a way to pad the game out and you'll see the same screens over and over again. Solid, but unmemorable, and I feel there are better alternatives in the genre. The world is charming though, and the core gameplay is fun, so I still would consider trying the newer, more polished sequels.
