is an independently developed first-person horror exploration game, in which you play as a man named Thomas, who once was a police detective. You roam from place to place, seeking shelter from the vicious weather.
That’s pretty much the gist of the story. After completing the game, I’m not quite sure what to make of it, as it’s more or less non-existent. 95% of the game is you by yourself, isolated from other people, until the last few levels, where you catch a glimpse of humanity, and proceed from there. All I know is there was some catastrophic weather event that basically eliminated the population, and put everyone else into a non-nuclear, non-zombie post-apocalyptic wasteland. I will admit, though, there is a nice twist at the end that I did not see coming.
For a game developed by one person, it looks astounding. Using CryEngine, the world is lush and heavily detailed, and draws you into the world, which is what a good horror property should. Curtains and such billow, lights flicker with eerie glows being cast, and everything just has such a high level of detail, that you’d probably think it was a team of many people.
Your character speaks Russian, and has English subtitles. Not being Russian, and not knowing anything about the language, I can’t say how good or bad the acting is, but I’m quite happy that the developer opted not to add English voiceovers; it makes the game feel more realistic. The rest of the sound, from the patter of what sound like footsteps, to harsh winds, to the crunch of the snow underfoot are all very well done. Between the amazing visuals and sound effects, if this game were available on the Vive or Rift, I would definitely play it again.
I don’t like to use the phrase myself, but
is definitely a walking simulator. The majority of your time will be spent walking (or running) from place to place and exploring. The game is very linear, and basically instructs you where to go by having your character look somewhere, or with some obvious lights. If you try to go where you shouldn’t, you’ll encounter invisible walls or locked doors, and if you find a door that you can actually open, then you know that’s the way to go. There are a couple of instances where you need to find an item or turn a valve to proceed, and one or two jump scares.
is rather short. I finished it in just over two hours, and that was exploring most nooks and crannies (remainder of my game time was letting the game run for cards). You can play the levels in any order, but there’s no reason to replay it once you’ve finished it.
Well worth it for such a low price,
will appeal to those who like slow-paced explorative games, and those with a hankering for anything horror. I know that, as a horror buff myself, we have to put up with tremendous amounts of garbage to find the good, and I’m happy to say that this one here does not belong in the trash pile.

I just got done playing Investigator and I was genuinely surprised at how well it was made. After purchasing this game from the steam summer sale I had very little to no expectations for it. If you're thinking about buyin the game I'd wait till it was on sale because it's so short and the replayability is close to none.
PROS:
+Ambience: Very few horror games that I've played have been able to evoke a feeling of anxiety and fear like this one had.
+Setting: The game altogether is beautiful, if playing horror games has taught me anything at all its that scares and foreboding music will do nothing if the setting isn't just right. Investigator achieves so much by letting the protagonist explore in multipe places including caves, buildings, tunnels, huts, the wilds, etc.
+Soundtrack: The music fit the story very well and I really enjoyed the few cutscenes where I got to just watch the player and listen to the music.
CONS:
-Short: The game took me only about 2 hours to finish and that was with me taking my time to explore and take screenshorts, etc. I realize there are more parts to come, but I felt it was lacking a little in length.
-Subtitles: The game is voiced in Russian so the developers kindly put subtitles over the voice acting, however the subtitles don't always make coherent sentences and don't make sense. It didn't detract too much from my experience, but still enough to be a hinderance.
-Slow: A few time throughout Investigator you're tasked with either solving a few puzzles or finding miscellanious objects. While this enabled me to explore a little more I found myself getting frustrated at having to do said puzzle/search and ended up rushing through a few parts in frustration.
All in all I'd give it a 7/10 and the ending has given me enough interest to want to keep looking into the game and play a future installment.

While I like that there are Half-Life mods still being developed and now released on Steam (for free I might add), I'm pretty sure the only reason this is even on Steam in the first place is Greenlight. Before is short: only 3 levels long and that's
the credits. It has its good points, but it is very extremely obviously an amateur product.
The plot is explained in the main menu background. It is a bit strange and laden with typos, but from what I can gather this is how Mr. Winning (presumably related to Charlie Sheen) 'acquired' the Xen crystal used in the last experiment Black Mesa would ever perform. I don't know why they'd tell him so much about it other than to inform him of how to get back to his dimension, and I think it's handled pretty damn quickly and unceremoniously, but I guess it's not an unworkable plot.
I found the atmosphere mostly great, with the rain and the storm and everything. More background information/flavor about the parallel universe Mr. Winning is in and what's happening on the ship (other than CONTAINMENT TEAM and ICKY MONSTERS) would have been great, but alas I didn't find much.
The music was also pretty good, the custom textures and scripted events weren't bad, and the new pistol is
- probably one of the best things about the mod.
Now, the bad news.
There are some obvious graphical glitches: bodies of Controllers that you kill in the first level float in the air, and hitting certain crates with the crowbar actually colors them white. I should also mention that every level (all three of them) needed to rebuild their node graphs when I first loaded them.
The game gives you a good number of weapons early on, but you don't exactly have a ton of ammo. I'd say it can't be helped considering how damn short this mod is.
Not to mention that some of the ways to advance in the first level could be made more obvious, including where the weapons are lying in front of you when you first start. The first level is good aside from that - it remined me of the ship level from Counter-Strike Condition Zero's Deleted Scenes - but the boss battle is just stupid and weird: the first time I tried it, the boss just traveled through the wall and eventually the level restarted. Turns out you just have to shoot it a lot while dodging enemy attacks.
After it died, the game ended and I got to see the 'Spacial Thanks' in the credits, which were otherwise nicely scripted.
I'd say give this a try if you
like Half-Life and don't mind playing a seriously weird level with a great custom pistol. Otherwise, there's not much to recommend about Before in comparison to the multitudes of other, superior HL mods. I really wish there was an option between 'yes' and 'no', because I'd use it here.
At least it's free.

One of the most rewarding, yet most complicated games I have ever played.
PROS:
-The game itself is very complex, yet not so much as to bar entry. It directly influences the reward from building right.
-The "Tiering" is very extensive. 7 factions, each with ship in 4 subtiers of quality. Add in that speciffic builds can directly couunter other builds that would otherwise be universally strong, and you end up having a reason to build a varied fleet.
-Due to both prior reasons, along with general immersion, gameplay time on this title is quite long.
-A unique take on sandbox building. Despite a surface level similarity to Empyrion: Galactic Survival, it is entirely a new spin on these types of building games, derived mostly from it's complexity. You can't just slap thrusters on a box and use it. You have to plan ahead, and quite often make last moment modifications. The first game I have seen to ACTUALLY offer building that rewarded smart thinking more than abusing exploits.
-The RTS feel is actually quite nice when you finally get some footing in your compaign.
CONS
-The interface is harder to learn than the game itself. After building a few successful models, even managing to 1v1 most of the godly enemy ships, I looked back and realized I had spent about half of my entire playtime learning to navigate the GUI. I feel that a more thorough tutorial is required on all the unlisted keybinds, menus and functions, and that this would remove a very large barrier to new player immersion.
SUMMARY:
-One of the best and most addicting games I have played in the past few years.
-Satisfying, complex, and yet STILL open to casual players who play only a little each day.
-The interface is extensively unintuituve, and thus I advise you to check YouTube or twitch for any tips on hidden screens you didn't know existed. The only significant suggestion I could give to add to the game's experience. I state this as a warning, not as a reason not to buy. It can be learned, but you will be far more pleased if you take the time to figure it out before trying to play as usual.
-It is very fun to spend hours in Designer because you got your butt kicked trying to design a new ship.. Then go back to campaign and just steamroll everything in sight. It makes you feel like you learned something and it shows in volumes how much it mattered.

What makes this game great is that it is different. It's rare nowadays to find a video game that can be described as innovative. I believe that Exanima, or Sui Generis as it will eventually become, is exactly that.
What makes this game different is that it uses a very unique combat system that's entirely physics-driven. For a powerful attack, it requires weight and momentum behind it, along with connecting the correct part of your weapon with the enemy. There is no such thing as button mashing in this game. Within minutes of trying the combat for the first time you will see why. Button mashing, or in this case, continuing to hold the left click, will result in a weak display of tapping the enemy with your weapon and finding yourself dead shortly afterward. Each attack requires you to turn and move your character to put your body weight into the swing, and be at the proper distance to connect with the enemy. Too close, and you'll hit them with the haft or bump into them awkwardly. Too far, and you'll swing wide due to the momentum and leave yourself open to attack. This is very much like real life. No person wielding a melee weapon will stand rigid and swing it with just their arms. Weight and force is placed behind a weapon swing through the hip and torso rotation, foot placement, and overall movement of the body (stepping forward along with a swing), all combined with the motion of the arms themselves.
Each battle ends up a frantic and tense endeavor, but also feels very real and organic. Battles move around as you dodge and maneuver, which in turn causes the scenery to come into play. Attack too close to a wall, and your attack will bounce off and be interrupted. Try to move around some debris on the floor, and you might trip and fall, leaving yourself open to a deadly overhead chop.
It took me about an hour to get used to the combat and start to be able to sense the flow of it, but once I have, I couldn't be more excited to get the full release of this game. Combined with the satisfying and unique combat, the entire game in the single player mode has a dark, bleak, and cruel feel to it. You explore what seems to be an abandoned prison filled with roaming undead, scavenging gear and discovering subtle lore while trying to escape. It
does
hold your hand in any way. I compare it to Dark Souls in this aspect.
In summary, this game requires actual skill to play, and is very unforgiving. These are both positive things. If you, like myself, are sick of how cliche, hollow, and unsatisfying modern day games have become, I have a feeling you will enjoy this. This is a game for people who want a legitimate challenge, who enjoy realism or physics-based gameplay, and who enjoy a dark/low-fantasy themed RPG setting.

I must say that this game is incredible.  It is difficult, but also very engaging.  The music, the lighting, the way the camera works, and especially the combat, keep your eyes peeled.  You are constantly trying to see or listen for your next potential opponet, because you know that if you engage them in the wrong area you are sure to lose.
I think my favorite aspect of this game is that each enemy presents a challenge.  Even a poorly equiped zombie with a crutch (yes a crutch) for a weapon can kick your a#@ if they take you by suprise.  Even after you have geared up, if you pick too many fights you put yourself at great risk.
This game take a while to figure out, but playing the arena is immensely helpful.  You will learn the basics of combat, and simply how to control your charecter, as it is quite unique.  Once you have figured out how to fight, the expert arena allows you to refine those skills and try out some of they higher end gear.  **Spoiler** the later enemies in the arena are full plate and ready to smash you in a few blows.
I actually managed to reach the end, but it took me about 20 runs.  I call them runs because the game functions essentially like a rouge-like.  If you die you're done.  You can quit/save at any time, but that save is scrubed when you start again and should you die you start back at square one.  Each playthrough is somewhat unique in the gear that you will find, but many useful items are consitently there.  Also, the layout of the map is the same, but there are many places to explore, and you are constantly faced with the decision to push deeper into the dark (where the best items are) or stick to the places that are well lit, and safer for combat.
All in all, I highly recommend this game, and I hope to see it prosper.  It is innovative, exciting, and frankly exactly what I have been wanting for a long time.
Thank you for making this game, and please continue to develop this gem.  I am anxiously awaiting more content.
Good luck to everyone who decided to try this game out, and if it feels akward at first, give it a few hours, and it will quickly become addictive.

This is going to be a bit of a two part review I'll start with the negatives and end up telling you "Why I actually recommend this game".
Anno 1602 was my first PC game ever, in christmas 1998 we received our first computer. A compaq pressario, and Anno 1602 came with it. This franchise remained close to my heart even though I only played 2070 and 2205.
Let's start right out of the bat with what's wrong about this game:
1) It uses uplay. Uplay has always been gimmicky, and a bad substitute for steam integration. Rewards are meaningless, separate friend list. -for me- the game worked on the -second- try. Though it worked without problem, The first time it failed to register the game. Ever since the game has worked flawlessly and there isn't one of those annoying uplay launcher that came with previous games, but as always, that's my experience and your milleage will vary. It's not the worst uplay integration I've seen and that's not saying much. I hope one day corporate will finally give up on uplay and trying to be steam. But until that day, it's there, its a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ drm.
2) No multiplayer. I don't have much to say about this as I maybe played anno in multiplayer twice.
3) Worlds aren't randomly generated, thus lack replayability. Now that's true but I'll go out and bat as to why this isn't a bad thing. For each biome (except dlc) you got 3 fixed maps. Now if you remember your anno, while maps were randomly generated, they were more or less always the same assortment. In anno 2070, there were big islands, small islands, starting islands had tea coffee and rice, your second island would have vegetable, etc. It was the same map every time, except the tile would be randomized. This time, each map are custom made, they are unique, and in my opinion, well crafted. I think you get more replayability by having an assortment of 3 custom map than just by having the same map regenerated. But that's just me
4) There's no free play, its all mission... Yeah I can't argue with you here, although the missions are more or less light and are simply what you would do anyway, and if you don't like the combat missions, you can skip them altogether and just wait it out.
5) combat is relegated as its own separate minigame. Yeah, its gimmicky, but it was ok fun for me. Not great, not bad, the combat in Anno has never been a strong suit of the franchise and the combat in 2070 felt painstaking to me. I'm not going to regret not having to fight during my regular base building game.
6) (not mentioned anywhere else) you play alone. You rarely ever interact with any other faction or player, its sad but its true, I miss raging at when the ai just take the one island I wanted.
7) Always online ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Here you're connected to a global market, I assume it's the game drm so to speak to force people to play online. But if Sim City back pedalled and removed it and allowed you to play offline, so can you.
Now that I'm done with that, here's why as a long time Anno fan I love this game:
1) They got rid of the area of control silliness. Now there's still some area of controls in this game. But now it make sense. On temperate island, why would you -ever- have problems building somewhere ? It doesn't make sense, and its not in this game. Here (sorry if it spoil the gameplay):
In the arctic biome, your factories generate heats and houses need heat in order to be habitable. Ok that make sense !
On the moon there are asteroid strikes and radiation therefor you need to be under a shield to protect your employee from radiation. That make sense !
On the temperate or tundra biome, you need to have... Haha I'm just kidding, you see it ? You can connect back to the wherehouse with it ? You can build it. Gone are the days you needed depots, markets and city centers.
2) I love the biomes, I love the restrictions they put in them, they felt much more varried than the "this island can grow wheat, this island can't, this island has gold, this one doesnt". The gameplay on each place is much more varried, much more fresh, instead of factions, you have biomes, what you had with eden and global trust, you now have 3 different gameplay style for each place. 3 different layouts style, 3 different tech tree. And you get to experience it all in one game.
Yeah my list of positive right now, is much shorter than my list of criticism. But it overshadow one part that can't really be conveyed by a review: I had a blast. I loved this game, much more than I did Anno 2070. I bought it at half price and already spent 14 hours inside it. That's like 2$ an hour, I got my money's worth and I'm still looking forward to play more of it. I'm sure I'll tire of it eventually, but it's not the case yet. Now if you excuse me, I got an hydrodam to rebuild and a space hotel to restore.
See ya!

How I got Anno 2205 to INSTALL & RUN/play:
1. Buy game on Steam.
2. Install uPlay if you don't have it.
3. CTRL+C your Anno 2205 Steam key from Steam.--You can find the key when you start the game and Steam tell's you that you may need the key. The game may not run or will crash or uPlay will state an error, but just go into the Steam SHIFT+TAB menu at that point and you may find the key--since this window always comes up until you tell Steam to not show it anymore.
4. Launch uPlay.
5. Select "Activate a Key" (Top Right--select the game controller icon with the + symbol).
6. CTRL+V your Anno 2205 Steam key.
7. Launch Anno 2205 from uPlay.
8. You can also Launch from Steam at this point.
9. Play Anno 2205!
10. I really like this Anno 2205 game, so should you!

This is not the worst Dark Eye game on the market. That distinction goes to a platformer whose name escapes me, and the less said about it the better.
But this is certainly the 2nd worst Dark Eye game out there. It's saving grace (if you're going to be generous) is that there is a modicum of Dark Eye plot content, some of which is quite interesting because it involves Borbarad and a geographical area of Aventuria that the other Dark Eye games (Realms of Arkania 1,2, and 3 and the remake of 1, Drakensang and Drakensang River of Time + Phileasson's Secret, Chains of Satinav and Memoria, and Blackguards 1 and 2) don't explore.
Without going into details, the other games take place in areas to the northwest, west, and southwest of Gareth, the capital of the Middenrealm. Demonicon takes place to the southeast of Gareth.
All of the other Dark Eye games (apart from the un-named sidescroller and the two adventure games use variations on the Dark Eye role-playing system. The two adventure games (Chains of Satinav and Memoria) don't use the RPG system because they're (surprise !) adventure games, but are brilliant and poignant additions to the Dark Eye tradition. The whole point of a Dark Eye RPG is that it is supposed to be an exercise in tactics and party management, elements which are conspicuously absent from Demonicon.
Demonicon does not use the Dark Eye roll playing system. It's a first person slasher that reminds me a bit of an Asian console game. I generally avoid this kind of game, but the only one that I ever really played (and almost liked) was Joan of Arc, and Demonicon seems to share a lot of game conventions with it. My approach to the combat has been to set it to easy and hold my nose and just do it, but I must admit I haven't been too successful in overcoming the gag reflex. I'll give it another try at some point out of academic curiosity, but this is most certainly a game that you only buy when it's been deeply discounted.
So I wouldn't go so far as to say it's crap, but it's not good and an unfortunate experiment to expand the genre made by people who probably didn't understand what the genre was about.
It's possible that someone might play Demonicon and enjoy it, especially if their idea of tactics was zipping around a battlefield clicking a lot. That doesn't appeal to me, and it's unlikely to appeal to anyone who is interested in the world of DSA and the Dark Eye.

I disagree with what a lot of people have said about this game not being worth full price. Maybe because it's a few years old now, but definitely not because of any flaws in the game.
I feel like the game developers definitely put the effort where it counts - i.e good gameplay, character progression and story. So who cares that the animations are a bit laughable and repetative? Who cares that it's linear? Linear doesn't have to be bad and you quickly forget about all that when you have so much fun in the combat and choosing your skills as this game offers.
I love how this game doesn't muck about like similar games in the genre. Things like stamina and inventory space are thrown out to make a more accessible and less time sink-filled game, thank you! This game tells you what you need to know and gives you fun tools to go about it. The skill system is excellent where they've really done a great job making every profession worth while (even a skill like Legend Lore!). There is just so much to put your points into but you will be getting points in a steady pace allowing you to always feel like you're progressing. And I have never had to make choices as difficult as they are in this game, where I truly feel like either is both good and bad and it comes down to your own personal morals. In the end you will still be thinking "what if I had done it differently?" opening up for a replay.
This game gives me the lovely "just a little bit more" feeling, and that's really all I require from a game.

Is "Shantae" the ultimate series of 2D action/platformer games? Maybe. Does it wipe away its competition in spectacular fashion? Well, it depends on the player's opinion (and, in my opinion, it certainly does so). Is Shantare: Risky's Revenge Director's one of the best games available for the PC? Definitely.
Risky Boots is on the loose again and it's up to you - playing as Shantae - to solve everything! Shantae, the title character, is a half-genie girl with magical powers and lots of purple hair, which is whipped back and forth while you get rid of monsters, enemies and other hazards in a variety of environments. The player meets other characters (which are charismatic in their own right) and gets to know more details of the plot by advancing through the different stages, collecting itens and learning different abilities until the final showdown. The graphics are gorgeous, with incredibly-detailed, colorful environments, superbly-animated sprites and great character design. Sound is also excellent; the soundtrack is catchy and blends well with each area, and the sound effects are also great.
But what stands out the most is the gameplay. The controls are superb, very intuitive, and the learning curve isn't steep at all. Once the player graps the basic concepts, Shantae: Risky's Revenge becomes a delightful experience. The characters learns how to morph into different animals in order to surpass certain obstacles and environmental hazards, and the player can also buy different magical itens and potions. There is no input lag whatsoever, and the game maintains a steady pace of 60 frames per second throughout the quest. The beautifully-designed levels may pose a serious challenge and will keep the player occupied for a while.
"Superb action in an outstanding package" certainly is a truthful statement, as Shantae Risky's Revenge offers just that (and much, much more)! It is a thrilling experience for a reasonable price, and you ought to pick it up whenever there is a special offer (like Steam's Summer Sale). It certainly is one of the best titles available on Steam. In fact, I could say it is one of the beat games I've ever played, if not the best. - 10/10

I find myself becoming a bigger and more vocal fan of this series; and as a result, falling more in love with WayForward's practices after finishing
a week or two ago. This game, as well as Pirate's Curse, harken back to a sense of SNES/GBA mainline platformer. And while mainline Nintendo games are known for having many titles under the umbrella, the two out of three
entries I've played have been really solid. I adored Pirate's Curse, and I'd be hard-pressed to say that game isn't near-perfect.
Risky's Revenge is fantastic and you should pick it up for whatever the devs are asking (I got my copy for a dollar out of the Humble Bundle which I think is criminal, but I don't normally negotiate price points to experiences). If you're the kind of person who draws comparisons between length and price, it might bother you to mention that I finished the game in under seven hours. Where the game itself is concerned, the level of polish and attention to detail in Pirate's Curse does exceed Risky's Revenge. And as a natural step in the evolution of the series, a lot of what makes Pirate's Curse great was present in Risky's Revenge.
While Pirate's Curse is overall a more beautiful and intuitive experience, I want to move away from that for the sake of the review. Maybe I’m just vexed that Wii U doesn’t support a reviewing function in the first place. Risky’s Revenge is short, but it works for what it is. Out of the four dungeons in the game, two are brief and formula-breaking, and this scratches and itch I didn’t realize I had. The design is intelligent and takes note of what makes 2D platforming so engaging in the first place. Nuances in the scenery will suggest walls you should press against in order to find secrets, encouraging a form of exploration which is so dear to me. Your hair is your greatest weapon, and the animal transformations are so satisfying.
But before I forget, I want to point out what I found unintuitive and pace-breaking about Risky’s Revenge. In Polyp Bay, near the end of the game, there is a gap between two piers which I could not possibly reach with the items and power-ups at my disposal. That was until I realized you can dash midair as an elephant so long as your character doesn’t drop even a pixel. And even then, I’m convinced what I accidentally managed to pull off once or twice after thirty minutes of fumbling around was a glitch. I couldn’t tell you how to get across that gap, and I don’t understand how that went under the radar during production.
Risky’s Revenge has some very cute, well-designed characters with expressive animations (both idle and not); the majority of whom I’m assuming came from the 2002 GBC title. The cute girl motif extends even to common enemies, much appreciated. Risky’s Revenge won’t be remembered for its story, so interactions are kept on the horizon at a healthy place. Character dialogue is light, but having to click through dialogue boxes containing two lines of large text could have been facilitated (this might be an issue with the port).
Sequin Land is varied, vibrant, and tropical; the pixel work really is stunning. Risky’s “Steam Powered Oceanic Tinker Tub” with its grand scale and fluid motions contribute to a few gorgeous boss fights in particular. Visuals alone hold your attention and continue to make the world worth exploring; items tucked away in Sequin Land are always beaming and rewarding to reach. You could take this game on visuals alone and it would still be a blast.
Overall impressions were great, and I’m convinced WayForward has it in the bag for Half-Genie Hero come September. If you’re playing with the Steam controller, save yourself the trouble and move with the control stick as directional pad minus radial overlap. I saw myself using the janky directional pad for what little crouch-walking I needed to do.

After years, this was the moment i was waiting for. 3 days ago, i revisited the 2nd game and finished it to refresh my memory. Now it's time to see if it was worth the wait. Here are the pros and cons of the game:
The soundtrack is brilliant, my favorite track was the
.
Great graphics. You'll revisit many places you "knew" and meet many characters you met in previous games. Dreamfall Chapters is full of nostalgia and references to the old games.
In this game, choices matter. Not all of them, but few matter a lot. The system is very similar to the ones in Telltale Games.
Atmosphere is great, i love the design. Especially
was such a great place to visit. I found myself just simply walking around, enjoying the view, taking screenshots and appreciating the art and little details.
I was really enjoying the cutscenes. Sometimes i wished this was an 3D animation movie instead of a game :) I enjoyed watching them.
Full of emotions. Slightly humorous and slightly (!) depressing...
There is an easily accessible "Goals" screen which shows your current goals. It was handy.
It automatically saves the game so you won't need to think about it.
Zoe's journal is more detailed, i suggest you to read it. But it gets cringy most of the time, you have been warned.
There are again, lots of conspiracy theories involved.
The last book of the story is enough reason to love this game!
Here is the biggest issue. In older games of the trilogy, the game always managed to hook me in. I was constantly facing with a new trouble, i was solving puzzles, fighting evils or solving mysteries all the time. The quests were always fun because it felt like all the quests i do were very important, interesting and directly related to the main plot. I always wanted to know what will happen next. BUT, Dreamfall Chapters felt so "slow paced" until the last book. In first chapters, you'll waste so much time with quests such as "Find this, find that, go there and do that" etc and i generally wasted so much time getting lost in the map, trying to find something etc. It wasnt fun. Sometimes i even wanted to just watch the cutscenes instead of playing the game. So, why i recommend this game? and for who i recommend for? I'll anwer these questions in the
part of my review.
There are performance issues. First of all optimization wasnt great, frame drops here and there (My specs: i7 5820k, 32gb ddr4 3000mhz, gtx 1060 oc, w10). Also i had various screen glitches few times, it is hard to tell but i got sudden visual glitches which looked like "white lines", i dont know, it was weird. Game also crashed and gave "Access Violation" error 1 time. And lastly, i had lots of weird and funny glitches in the cutscenes.
Most of the times i got voice overlaps. You inspect something while someone is talking? No luck, you can't stop your character's speech. So it becomes a mess.
I was expecting better facial expressions; sometimes it felt like characters couldnt express their emotions, their reactions felt dull.
There are few errors in subtitles.


You can't crouch in stealth missions, instead, you just "walk". It felt weird after playing Dreamfall. But this is an adventure game, not a stealth game etc. etc. i know..
I don't know why they tried so hard to emphasize sex in Zoe's journal.
There were some things which reminded me Beyond Good and Evil. Like the sound when you acquire new item, or the EYE soldiers or the.. "No"? Okay...
So should you play this game? The anwer is "Depends.". Depends on if you have played the previous games and liked them. I honestly think that if you havent played the previous games, you will have less fun, you'll understand less about the plot, you wont get the references, you won't feel the nostalgia and so on... For those who played the previous games and really want to know what happened to the characters, definately worth it. BUT if you think this game will answer all of your questions, you are wrong. The are huge twists and complex situations. There are some questions left unanswered. The last book is the defination of MINDF*CK, so much is going on in the last chapters, which was the thing saved the game and made me love it. It even felt like they left all the great things to the last chapters, the fast-paced progress was awesome! After i finish the game, i found myself searching forums, reddit and the wiki for answers. You'll get confused as HELL, but that was the fun after all... Is this game has sequel potential? Yes. Will it happen? Probably no... Was it worth it? For me, The Longest Journey Saga WAS and IS the best of all time...

TLDR: The is my favorite story-driven, decision making game by far. It's easy to connect with the characters and become attatched. Choices feel like they have actual consquences and there are so many different ways you can end the game. IF YOU HAVE NOT PLAYED THE PREVIOUS GAMES, MAKE SURE YOU KNOW THE LORE. PLAY THE GAMES, WATCH WALKTHROUGHS, READ ON EVENTS BEFORE THIS GAME. It will help a lot, I would of been lost if I didn't.
This game is probably the best story-driven game I've played in a very long time, and I am honestly so happy I ended up purchasing this. I, unfortunately, have not played the previous two games but I did watch full play throughs of the events as well as reading up on the lore prior to this game. I now wish I had played the previous two prior to playing this, and I only didn't because I wasn't sure if I wanted to spend money on two games not knowing what to expect.
After finding all the knowledge I needed to play the game, I dived right in and the story, to me, was very compelling and the universe in place is so fantastical. I was initially drawn in by the screen caps in on this page because it seemed to have this whimsical world and it did, it was a universe that was right up my ally. I'm a sucker for eutopias that are the exact opposite.
I found myself quickly engrossed in the story, the characters, what motivates them and the choices I was able to pick. I am a huge fan of the way the cause/effect system works in this game because it isn't just: Choice A = Choice A ending, Choice B = Choice B ending.  While the end results could always be the same, I love that each decision can effect something in the future, and it does. Most other games I've played will say things like "They will remember that," but they never do, it holds no real consequence. You can pick various different choices and they will  have an effect even to the end of the game.
The animation is clunky, I will admit that, and I am usually someone who prefers to be immersed and a person doing a smooth 180 degree turn to turn around is very unimmersive. Despite this, I was so immersed because of how great the voice acting is, the characters feel real and you get their emoitions instead of terrible voice acting. I am someone who doesn't cry when someone dies in movies or games ever, and this game is probably the first in my life to ever make my cry at a character death. Even though the scene of it might not be smooth and realistic looking, it was the voice acting, the script, the character that moved me.
The game lasts far more than other story-based decision games that I've played, this took me 20 hours to complete, while the others would be 4 hours or so. I was extremely happy with the play time and how the game kept me motivated and interested in playing.
I can't find an honest complaint while playing the game, I am in love with the series and I'll just keep my fingers crossed for more!

The developers cared more about stuffing the game with leftist propaganda, than making it an enjoyable gaming experience or telling a good story.
- The baffling design choice of making the player walk so much through a city before reaching a location, where the story progresses is supposed to happen might be relevant in an open-world RPG/sandbox game, and here it just wastes your time.
- The devs decided that dull puzzles are supposed to make you enjoy the game more. However, I didn't feel proud of myself figuring out, that I should "pick up that thingy and using it on that thingy", I felt like I'd rather be playing a TellTale game instead and play a proper puzzle game when I'll want to solve puzzles and not be bored to death while at it.
- The characters just stand there blankly staring forward during dialogues, even when voice overs are dramatic and believable, their poker-face and default idle pose just kills it. Character animations are only done in segments, when the scene wouldn't make sense at all otherwise.
- The game looks slightly better than its decade-old prequel, yet the performance is quite poor.
- The story is stuffed with heavily biased toward left political statements, while hardly gave me a reason to care about things that are going on, may the people who wrote it be haunted by Pepe.
Avoid this game if you value your time and money, go play something made by Telltale, Microids or Harvester Games, you'll have a good time, better time for certain anyway. This mind-numbing abomination should've never been made.

What is this game? It's the ultimate naval ship building game that just so happens to have excellent aircraft and ground vehicle construction as well.
Everything is considered with this game, drag, buoyancy, center of gravity, everything comes together to either make or break your designs. And that can be a serious problem for people who don't have the mindset for this type of game. And I'm not talking stupid people I mean the kind of people who could probably be engineers if they wanted to should play this game.
Everything is complex, and not in the stupid way. Every part has a role, every component has a job and it's up to you to use them to produce truly devastating weapons to crush your enemies. Do you want to make a 10 barreled 500mm cannon? Go for it, have fun finding a ship that'll use it but you can do it! Want to recreate the USS Missouri or the German Bismarck? You can do it. Want to recreate the Space Battleship Yamato? You can do it. Complete with giant laser cannon and all.
This game also has a really robust and active steam workshop community which is a huge plus in my book.
The UI needs work though. If you do buy this game, please please please don't write it off because of the UI. Because once you learn the quirks it's not bad to work with.
So do I recommend it? Absolutely.

username: Team Fortress Two is a bad game
text:
Want to build a giant starship that drops nukes? You can do that. Want to build a underwater base? You can do that too. Want to build a block of wood with a huge cannon with balloons on it that defies all logic and engineering? Go ahead. Want to build a rainbow that does nothing? It's all there.
I have played this game so much ever since i found it. Seriously, just look at my hours played! Everything about this game is so well thought out.
Gameplay 10/10
I don't know what to ever compare this to, becuase it's so unique. It's got traces of Robocraft, a chunk of Scrap Mechanic, a tiny bit of RTS gameplay, and can somewhat bear the title of "What No Man's Sky SHOULD have been". It's fun to build crazy vehicles, then adapt and expand them based on how they work, and just keep on repeating that until you made a campaign-winning flagship. It's fun to watch enemy fleets explode under the rain of shells, bullets, and missiles.
It's fun to jump out of planes, land on enemy ships, and destroy them from the inside out. It's all fun, and it never gets old.
Story 8/10
It's expected for games like this to have some kind of plot or motive. But this game goes beyond that. It somehow manages to cram enough story to make a movie off of. You can see patterns and traditions work into the designs of each faction, the DWG making steampunk sailing ships, the OW making giant galleons, the WF outfitting their ships with brutal and intimidating spikes, saws, and blades of every kind, the SS have battleships and cast-iron planes(How do those hunks of metal even fly?), the TG building swarms of little drones, the LH with futuristic high-speed crusiers and planes, the GT and their oversized space dreadnaughts, and the SD with sci-fi spaceships and planes.
Soundtrack 6/10
The soundtrack isn't a highlight, but it certainly isn't a downfall either. The songs are fitting, but somewhat lacking at the same time. There are only about 5 or 6 songs, and they all have the same feel to them. Strings and Calm Before The Storm do a good job of being a good fit for the menu and RTS screen, as does Clouds somehow manages to fit all 3 kinds of combat.
Boy, does Clouds get annoying over time though.
Community support/moddability 9/10
You can never go wrong with Steam Workshop support, especially with a creativity-inducing(Is that even a word?) game like this. I personally suck at making vehicles, so it's much more fun(for me) to download stuff from the workshop and vicariously win campaigns. The community is quick to respond to help requests and is made of mostly nice people, and dev updates are somewhat frequent, acting much in the ways that MC's updates work.
Learning curve 8/10
This is one of my favorite parts of this game. This game is a mountain, try to charge up it all and it's way too steep. Intead, you discover and experiment with the game, piece by piece. Each part you spend about a week on, then as you get bored you realize there's a whole new layer to explore. Here's what i could pick apart as the order i went in: Basic building=>Engines=>Basic Boat Construction=>Basic Missiles=>Basic CRAM Cannons=>Advanced Boat Construction=>Basic Planes=>Lasers=>Spaceships=>Advanced Missiles=>Advanced Planes=>Advanced CRAM Cannons=>APS System=>Story Mission development=>Campaign development=>Mod development=>Planet development
Graphics 6/10
Okay, this aint your HD ultra-smooth graphics simulator game, but it's not low-quality trash at all. This game wasn't made to be pretty, you won't be looking at those sunsets, you'll be looking at the ball of fire that was a enemy boat a few seconds ago. It's not good or bad, but it doesn't really matter. What's more important is how it affects what's next.
Performance 7/10
Okay, so let me talk a bit about my PC. I'm not a total geek, so i don't know everthing about it, but let me tell you this: All my games run at a averge of 20 fps. I have never gotten 50 fps of anything, and i consider 10 to 5 as lag. And if this game runs at about 15 for me on high graphics settings, i think it'll run at 60 or 70 for you.
Bugs, glitches, ect 8/10
This part "bugs" me a lot. (I'm so sorry) No, really it does. The physics are realistic enough, and things don't flip out on a regualr basis, but one thing gets me. Typos. In the game's writing there are little bits here and there that drive me nuts. Foramtting being inputted incorrectly on the tutorial. Misspelled words. Calling two seperate pages "Page 5" on the update notes. It gets to me.
I have seen many games like this, but none of them can ever have the depth of From The Depths(I'm sorry, again) I love this game to
death, and has given me (At the time of writing this) 1,288 hours of fun, and i look forward to what it will become in the future.
That being said... I don't like the most recent updates. The new material system i find just... lacking. For those who are unaware, in the past there have been 5 resources. Natural(Basic cheap wood, rock, ect) Metal(Iron plating, refined steel, ect) Oil(Used in fuel and electronics) Scrap(Gears, machinerey, electronics, ect) and Crystal.(Rare crystal, used as large currency and in advanced electronics) Each had specific containers and each block had unique resource value to it. (Wood needed just N, Alloy needed M and S, Lasers needed M, S, O, and C, ect) Now there's only one resource, Material. I found the game much more complex and fun with lots of resources, and i think they could be added in the style of Localized/Centralized resource, as a way to get extra EXP. The other thing i don't like is the radar update. While it makes it realistic, me and a lot of other people struggled to adapt to the new requirement on our old ships and planes.
In conclusion, if you're looking for a quick bit of fun you can play every now and then, FTD may not be the game for you. If you're looking for a game you can play for a long time and not get bored of, and are a fan of either RTSs or FPSs, From The Depths is a great game! It's worth the 20 bucks, but if you don't get to play it often, you may want to wait for a sale. After all, you should only pay into a game how much you want to get out of it, right? So get out there, nuke some boats, and have a good time!

Corgi Warlock is a simple 2D side-scrolling action game that puts you in the paws of Maia, a Corgi that belongs to the one-man development team. This is clearly a labor of love and one that succeeds on many levels, but is a little shallow and repetitive. The game only lasts for a few hours, and that is long enough to keep you entertained while not overstaying it’s welcome.
The setup is simple, you are Maia, a Corgi dog, who also happens to be a warlock. You need to use magical powers that you pick up along your journey to defeat the evil that has invaded the land. The story is extremely basic and is all conveyed through text blocks. It’s really just a way to move the action forward and never feels forced upon you in anyway.
The story telling is very simple, but never gets in the way.
The gameplay is also very simple, you move forward through largely linear levels blasting every enemy in your path. You start out with a basic fireball spell, but pick up all sorts of new spells along the way. My favorite spell was a laser beam that is both powerful and capable of hitting multiple enemies… It also sounded really cool. You also get access to a basic shield spell and multiple healing spells throughout the game.
One major issue I had with the game is the lack of enemy variety. While new enemies are introduced at a steady rate, the variety in their attacks and how they moved is very limited. In my opinion, too many enemies are damage sponges that require you to attack, run, attack, run, and attack until they die. This gets tedious very quickly. That’s not to say the game isn’t challenging, because it is. Some of the boss battles are very tough and mix things up, but unfortunately all the stuff in between gets very repetitive.
The game offers four player local co-op where the other players take control of either a pug dog, a pig, or a fish. I was unable to try out the co-op mode for myself, so I am not sure if the difficulty scales based on the number of players or if stays the same. I can see how it would be fun to get some family members or friends together to blast through this game. It has a similar look and feel to Castle Crashers, which is another great co-op experience.
The game looks great!
This game’s art style really shines for me. The game looks deliberately hand-draw, with thick lines like a cartoon. The characters and enemies all look unique with some fantastic facial expressions. It also runs smooth for the most part. I will say that the background seems to move and animate more smoothly than Maia, so sometimes when jumping or moving forward it can feel like the game is stuttering. The developer has been good about releasing updates since launch, so maybe this will be addressed in a patch. Chances are you won’t notice it, but I felt like I had to mention it. Other than that everything looks and plays very well.
I do want to mention the music and specifically the main theme. It reminded be a lot of the Minecraft theme music and that is a good thing. It is appropriately whimsical and relaxing; very enjoyable.
If you don’t expect the world from Corgi Warlock you won’t be disappointed. The game is a fun romp that lasts just as long as it needs to and seems like it would be a blast to play co-op. While there are a few issues with enemy design and repetition, it is hard to complain too much at this price point.
Corgi Warlock is currently 50% off on Steam right now for the remainder of the Steam Winter Sale. I’d recommend you grab it now if you’re interested.

This game is epic. I played a game year ago similar to this and this one comes out on top easy while keeping all the same elements. Right now there are two game mods, both are amazing.
First off you have the adventure "Story" mode. In this mode you spawn with nothing but the clothes on your back. You see a torch and grab it since it's really your only light source and possibly the only things you got to smack something with. With that you head off in a physics based adventure. My first task was trying to open up the door without knocking myself down when I smacked my face with it. In good time I managed to get the door open and head down a hallway. I saw a lot of these hallways and got lost everytime I've been in them. I could only remember the first two doors, the rest became a jumbled mess. I eventually came face to face with my first opponent. I grab my torch and start smacking the zombie looking thing. Within seconds I'm on the floor beeling. This repeats about nine or so times. I do eventually kill him and get his axe he was wileding. I find a chest in the room which I find randomizes each time I kill that guard. Sometimes I found leggings, other I found metal staves and daggers. It was a nice touch that adds to the dynamic of gameplay.
In the end of all this I could never make it past three enemies. Not at once, alone. The A.I. in this game is tough, and they will whoops your♥♥♥♥♥many a time. I have a good understanding of the combat from the ingame help, which I recommend reading the settings menu for combat help. With that I could hold my own, but all it took was the drunk looking oponent to trip and throw his blade in my face by accident. It really comes down to timing. You can end some fights in one hit, while others last minutes. I had one fight go for nearly ten minutes once, constant blocking and evasive manuevers on both parties proved to be a difficult fight. I did kill the guy, but it shows true skill because the guy was using a stick.. I died moemnts later when I opened a door and three came rushing at me.
The Arena is the other game mode the game comes with. In this mode you basically get to do 1v1 fights with increasing difficult. It starts you off fighting a guy with a club, then we go to a two handed axe, it then moves up to a two handed bo staff wielding guy, from there a maul and shield. They also start getting more geared up by getting better weapons, spawning with armor, etc. The awesome thing about this is that you can pick up all the loot off of the enemy and use it. So if you run against a guy with a sword and board and want some defense, you just swap out your gear at the end of the turn. You can't buy armor or anything like that so you need to kill to earn it by taking it off of their body.
Honestly this game is awesome. Anyone who like to dungeon crawl, get scares, feel hopeless, die endlessly, and mess around with phusics, this is the game.

The dynamic physics based fighting system in this game is really fantastic and something you've probably not experienced before in this genre, but it works wonders and I wish more games could implement something similar.  It is difficult to get used to the unique controls in this game because it is such a different concept compared to how these kinds of games usually approach the controls, but even though it is difficult it is entertaining the entire time you are getting familiar with it.  The character dynamics make each fight different, and there are occasionally hilarious and brutal moments that occur as a result of the physics. Exanima is a fresh approach to the genre. The game tries to introduce real physics based melee combat and it succeeds in a high degree. Every little detail counts, the weight of your armor, the weight of your weapon will have a huge impact on the way your character moves and fights. Going around smashing your keys will get you nowhere. To survive in Exanima you must proceed carefully, think your next move and try to plan ahead.
The world in which Exanima takes place is the second best thing about the game. You find yourself locked inside a dark dungeon, with absolutely no idea of what is going on or why you are there. It is up to you to push forward and start collecting clues and items that will help you understand the story of this place and in the end survive and escape the dungeon. Every little room, every corridor in Exanima is fully interactive and you have to search under every crate or in every shell in order to find useful information and objects. The dungeon is dark and creepy but the game does not have any horror elements, providing jumpscares is not what Exanima is trying to achieve.
Obviously, going around searching for clues, is not as easy as it sounds. There are others locked in this dungeon as well. Most of them will ignore you, but there are some that will try to stop and kill you. This is where you have to use your sword, your axe or whatever else you have found already and using as your weapon. But combat is not the only way to move forward. Exanima allows you to outsmart your enemies or even outrun them and avoid conflict if that is what you desire.
Exanima offers a unique experience not only with the main game, where you try to find the exit of a dark dungeon but also with the arena mode. In arena you will have the opportunity to test different weapons and fight against opponents that use various other weapons and a plethora of tactics to take you down. In there you will have the possibility to test your skills and become better. Something that will help you in the main game a lot.
Exanima is the prelude to Sui Generis, an open world RPG, and it gives us a first look at the dark and unforgiving world of this upcoming game. At the moment, the main game does not have a lot of content to offer but the amazing combat system, the fully interactive environments and the general dark atmosphere make Exanima a must buy for fans of the genre and everyone that is looking for a great challenge.

Edit: Commenters have told me the price of the game has been halved. Because I wrote the review when the game was fresh in my mind (it isn't anymore), and the issues I had with the game still exist, I'll leave the written review unchanged so people can see my complaints. However, from what I remember of the game, $20 is a much fairer price for what you're getting. So, I think I can now recommend it.
I want to clarify first off that this is not a bad game. I'm not recommending it not because it's a bad game, but merely because it offers nothing over other games in the genre. It is, in almost all respects, perfectly average and mediocre. Were it priced a little more reasonably I might recommend the game in spite of its shortcomings, but $40 for something that I would only describe as "painfully average" is a bit too much.
One thing I think is worth praising is the story. Apparently this is based on a German tabletop series akin to DnD. I know nothing about it, but the game does seem to have a great deal of backstory and lore that is only barely touched upon within the actual game, and that does breathe a little life into the story. Not everything is explained within the context of the story (you'll probably spend half of the game wondering just what in the hell a Borbaradian actually IS), but the game does provide a fairly robust codex that describes things not expounded on in dialogue. And the story itself is fairly interesting. Many of the characters were also enjoyable. I especially liked Feodor, Argus, and Solus; it is a shame that the last two are only available in the last area of the game.
That is, however, where my praise basically has to end. You're given several choices during the story, but it doesn't really seem like that has any impact on how the story plays out, at least not to an appreciable degree. Most of the choices are binary, and the only difference is whether you're a♥♥♥♥♥♥about what you're doing or whether you're not a♥♥♥♥♥♥ "Banish him" or "execute him" result in the exact same ending plotwise; the character is gone and has no impact for the rest of the game. That's basically what every choice boils down to. Which of these characters do you accept as your father? Doesn't matter; either one has absolutely nothing to do after the choice. The worst of anything is the ending; I had hoped for a little more variation, but it's just another generic, binary ending. To be fair, this is not a problem specifically with Demonicon; many RPGs suffer from a similar problem.
Combat is monotonous and dull, made at times even painful because of a lack of lock-on. I can't count the number of times I cast an ice spell and Cairon threw it in a direction I wasn't aiming at towards an enemy I didn't care about. He does it with melee attacks too, which is especially egregious. If you're not going to have the character attack in the directions I'm inputting, at least give me a lock-on so that he doesn't roll across half the screen to hit an enemy I have no reason to go after. There are several points in the game where you'll face summoners constantly bringing in new enemies and all you want is to kill them but Cairon keeps going off trying to hit some damned small fry who's just going to be replaced even if it dies. And that's awful.
At least, however, that adds some element of difficulty. I played through on Normal and the game is just pathetically easy. I apparently got an achievement for not using any potions throughout the entire game; I wasn't even TRYING to get this achievement, there's literally just no need for the things, at least on Normal. Doubtless the game is harder in one of the other difficulty modes, but it should bear mentioning, shouldn't it, that throughout the entire game I didn't need even a SINGLE healing potion? Perhaps allowing Cairon to heal by attacking was a bit too much. As long as your combat multiplier is high enough (hit enemies without them hitting you, basically), every attack heals Cairon for a fairly substantial amount of health. Since almost every enemy in the game has hitstun from being hit, and Cairon can roll indefinitely and is invulnerable during these rolls, it's child's play to rack up a large combat multiplier and just heal, heal, heal.
The camera, for the most part, is fine, but there are a few sections where it gets in the way. There was one section in a building in Kreutzer Alley where the camera was so bad I literally could not see what I was doing and nowhere I could move to fixed it. I simply had to mash the attack button until combat ended and then I was able to move to an area where the camera was not so screwed up. I have a feeling this was due to the relatively low ceiling in the building, and this WAS the only place in the game where the camera screwed up to such a degree. As I said, for the MOST part, the camera is entirely serviceable, but when it screws up it's very noticeable.
I honestly can't remember any of the music except for the battle music. That means it didn't stick out, which means it was neither offensively bad nor enjoyable. I actually did like the combat music at the start, but since combat takes so long and there's so much of it I tired of it a few hours in. The sound direction is also fine, although there were a few cutscenes in the game where the sound cut out entirely. It did fix itself once the scene switched, however.
I would have liked some greater ability to customize Cairon's equipment. Early on you have a fair number of choices and you can mix and match them, but later on all you seem to get is equipment sets which cannot be broken up; you either have to wear the entire set or none of it. It's a little disappointing.  There are only two weapon types, bladed and blunt (axes are, for some reason, considered blunt weapons, which is as mystifying here was it was in Oblivion). There are also throwing weapons, but I hardly used those as there was little point using them over your ranged ice spell. There are some interesting weapon and armor designs. You can use weapon/armor enhancements to beef up your equipment, but so far as I can tell there's no way to remove them.
I do have a bit of a problem with how often you're sent running back and forth and how often environments are reused. About a quarter of the way through the game you're given access to the Market and Kreutzer Alley; learn to love them because you'll be running back and forth between them for the next few hours. You start the game in Moloch Mountain, about halfway through the game you're sent there again (and you have to open all of the gates again; who closed them?), and then at the end of the game you're sent there AGAIN. And you have to open the gates AGAIN (although there is a reason for the gates being closed this time). The monastery, the last original area in the game, has two main sections and a courtyard between them; you're sent running back and forth collecting gems and I began to truly despise that courtyard because of how often I had to run between sections. That entire area felt rushed, actually.
The last thing I want to mention are the bosses. They're major letdowns. Only one boss in the entire game killed me, and that's merely because he heals himself four times throughout the fight. This is largely a symptom of the general easiness in combat I mentioned earlier; you see the boss's attacks (of which they generally only have three or four, all heavily telegraphed), dodge them, and rack up your combo multiplier allowing you to heal directly as you deal damage. If you use Demonic Aura, increasing your attack and movement speed, it becomes even easier.
At $40, I  just can't recommend the game. I bought it for a heavy discount during the summer sale, and I wasn't ENTIRELY dissatisfied with my purchase, but if I had spent $40 I surely would have been. If you're hard up for an action RPG, this isn't the worst choice...but it's definitely not the best, either.

I bought this game on Summer Sale because I was concerned with the Mixed reviews it had received from launch and I didn't want to pay full price for it on the chance it was bad.  The only other Anno game I own is Anno 2070, which I enjoyed.  I also enjoy this game.  I feel too many reviewers are unfairly judging this game based on what they liked about Anno 2070 without understanding that not every game is going to be a copy of its predecessor with better graphics.  Here is an indepth analysis of why I like the game and why I recommend people try it.
In my opinion, Anno 2205 is a shift towards a simpler and more casual gamer, which admittedly is a saavy business move as casual gamers are a much larger demographic.  The things some people have been saying are negatives I actually find to be positives.  The simplified supply chains for example.  This game moves from micro level resource management to macro level resource management.  The amount of micromanaging required in setting up trade/supply routes in Anno 2070 meant I was spending more time managing those than I was actually enjoying the game.  Now the game takes care of that for me.  I set up a trade/supply route and/or start up a new settlement and instantly I see the recognizable trade ships from 2070 begin to head to and from my various warehouses automatically.  It's all aesthetic sure but before you'd actually have to have set all those routes up yourself.  Personally I find the automation a welcome adjustment.
The removal of combat from the standard gameplay has the same tone.  Nothing annoyed me more in Anno 2070 than when a pirate fleet would arrive and mess up a trade route before my fleet could intercept them, forcing me to then have to rebuild lost ships in order to resume my previous trade route(s).  I'll agree that now there doesn't seem to be any penalty in not dealing with hostile forces; I was expecting there might be some timers on combat missions or you'd suffer some penalty.  I'm glad there isn't because that would also have been annoying but still, the lack of any necessity to deal with combat missions other than to collect Iridium (which seems to be the super resource I tend to run out of the quickest) and Achievements does seem a touch hollow, but I'm generally okay with that.
As for replayability.  There is a valid point there.  Generally City Builders are best when they have replayability.  Anno 2070 was ok with this.  I played that game four times; once as Eden/GT, once as GT/Eden, once as Eden only, and once as GT only (I called that one Hard Mode).  Thing is outside that there wasn't much for me that made replayability interesting.  I'm fine with the story mode.  Besides, obviously with there already being two DLC's they intend on expanding playability through expansions, which is in line with the way games are going these days.
Another thing I saw in a lot of negative reviews is that service buildings no longer have areas of effect and rather offer a flat service value (I think maybe with some penalties for being close to each other and/or distance away from population?  Haven't actually paid that much attention to the nuance of it).  I for one think the way it works now is overall better.  Sure, it reduces some of the micromanaging aspects of city designing, but this new way is the way City Builders are going these days.  I've seen this change in Sim City games, Tropico, Caesar, now Anno, generally speaking game designers are moving away from unnecessarily complex mechanics in favor of more accessible entertainment.  Again I feel the shift is towards accessing more of the casual gaming market, of which I am a member, so I'm okay with that.  If you want harder then artificially make the game harder.  Say to yourself "I won't build a Community Center building unless it is within a certain range of population structures and a certain distance from any other Community Centers".  There, you've increased your own difficulty while not impacting those who prefer to have fun rather than be restricted in their expansion options.  Or, presuming the games permits it, make a mod that does that.  I'm a big fan of making games as accessible as possible in their base mode then allowing more hardcore gamers the ability to make it more difficult on their own terms.
So that's my review.  All told the game is beautiful, I enjoyed the story aspects, I found it accessible yet still challenging at times, and I'd definitely say it was worth the price I paid.  I hope others will give it a try and discover the same.

Only us honest-to-God, hardcore horror gamers truly appreciate that most great horror games depend heavily upon the SCENERY, and the player's compulsion to explore said scenery. There's a few exceptions, of course: Five Nights at Freddy's, for example, essentially takes place within the confines of a single, tiny office (though with the aid of cameras, one can take a peek at a number of other locations besides). But in 98% of occasions, horror games arguably live or die by the "spookiness" of their environments, and Investigator certainly gets off to an amazing start in this department.

The very first thing you'll notice about this game is, in fact, the visuals. An instant "whoa" from my mouth, I gotta say, and I wasn't even playing at top graphics (I tend to hold off and find out how laggy a game is gonna be 'til I commit to such heights). The sound is quite gob-smacking also, as I found when I wandered under the plastic roof of a greenhouse in an abandoned farmyard, and admired the vividly-realised raindrops pitter-pattering overhead. All around, an instantly immersive experience, which could perhaps be improved only by the presence of a VR headset.

But what about the STORY, I hear you ask? And the GAMEPLAY, for ♥♥♥♥'s sake? Okay, okay, I was getting to that. Um...okay...honest truth? They're both pretty close to non-existent.
When all is said and done, this is essentially a "walking simulator" in which you can't really die - well, okay, there was one fatal jump I failed to make, but this only set me back a couple of metres of gameplay - and none of the danger you appear to be in (crazy masked dudes with guns, giant spiders, various weather-based forces of nature) is particularly time or skill-dependent, as the game simply shifts to a cut-scene whenever your character needs to be nimble enough to make a desperate getaway.
All of this might be perfectly acceptable, if only the story was involving enough to feel like a bona fide "experience". As it is, there's almost bugger-all suspense once you realise you're basically strapped safely into a very linear rollercoaster ride with virtually no chance of derailing; and on the whole, there doesn't seem to be a great deal of reason why this is a video game as opposed to, say, a movie, as the interactivity is ultimately borderline inconsequential.
Now, I recently gave a very praising review to a game called Layers of Fear, at which much the same criticisms could perhaps be leveled. But that game not only threw the odd semi-challenging puzzle at the player, but also somehow managed to make you feel like you were on a very personal and delirious "journey", whereas Investigator never seems to overcome an undeniable sense of detachment from events. Perhaps this isn't helped by the fact that we frequently get to SEE our protagonist, the back of whose head we zoom in and out when it's time to have a cut-scene portrayed in third-person. At least this little technique, along with the aforementioned graphics and sound, assures us that we're not just looking at some typical, lazy knock-off job by some European hack who got their hands on a copy of the Unreal engine roughly this time last week.
Regrettably, though, the STORY could easily have been penned by any one of those bored bedroom warriors. Try this spoiler on for size:
Look, I'm guessing you know by now whether you'd consider this a game worth buying or not, and for what price (I certainly wouldn't recommend full). It's a bit of silly and atmospheric fun, and certainly rather impressive on the technical front (especially for an "indie" game). I'm sincerely hoping, however, that these devs are looking to use this game to advertise their skills as audio-visual artists, as opposed to competent storytellers. There's also some irritations to be endured in regard to settings, etc. - i.e. you have to reset them every single time you play - and there's some minor lag and "getting stuck on the scenery" problems as well. But on the whole, it's a long, long way from the most insulting thing Steam has thrown at us die-hard horror fans in recent years.
I wish the devs the best of luck, and hope that they use this game as the "learning experience" which I'm sure they'll be sensible enough to see it as. Not a bad effort at all, just not a particularly extraordinary one, and definitely not recommended to anyone who hasn't already enjoyed the far superior likes of Outlast, Amnesia, Alien: Isolation, Among the Sleep, etc etc, ad nauseum.
Verdict: 7.5/10.
(Oh, and PS: I probably failed to mention some of the most ludicrous "jumping" bits you're sure to experience this side of Cry of Fear; but these are fortunately few and far between.)

There's a very common saying, "You get what you pay for".  I got this game for $4 and it felt like a played a $4 game.  I would NOT, however, suggest to anyone paying for this game full price.
So the game itself... It wasn't terrible... but it was far from great.. actually it's not great at all.  Boring really.  I'm giving it a thumbs down because I personally feel it could have been better.
Let's talk about what the game did RIGHT.
Pros:
+ Graphics are pretty darn good.  For an indie title like this I was quite surprised.  Some areas in the game were lackluster, but for the most part, graphics were solid and lighting was great.
+ A couple decent jump cares that got me pretty good.
+ Smooth. No tearing or anything.
... That's about all the pros I could really think of.
Cons:
- Here's my biggest con and I'm really curious to see if I was the only person who had this problem.  The game consumed 99% of my GPU the WHOLE time!  This was insane! I have an I7, 32GBs of RAM, GTX 970, and great cooling, but this game was making my GPU run at 60c-69c (140f-154f) non stop.  I've ran extremely GPU and CPU demanding games and have always had temperatures ranging from 110f to 125f under more intense loads than this game.
- Another con was the enemies... There were only two: a dude with a mask and a S**T ton of spiders, and not even good spiders to be honest, these were some crap spiders, didn't even have eyes and moved like stiff cardboard.  At the the beginning of the game, it felt like this could be real promising, but once you come to the conclusion that "this is it? this is the only thing I'm going to encounter" the game quickly loses it's charm it had in the beginning.  It gets even more ridiculous when you come across this GIANT spider that roars like a dinosaur... I literally shook my head and thought wtf...
- At the times the game did this forced camera perspective to force you to look at something the game thought was "important".
Example: *Pool of blood on ground*
Camera: "WOAH LOOK AT DIS POUL OF BLOOOD ON THE GROUND, SUUPR SCARI RIGHT?!"
ME: "F**ks sake that's annoying, get off me camera, let me discover it on my own, please."
Camera: "I CANT RISK U MISSIN THISS!!"
(You get the idea).
- Game does have it's occasional bugs.  My favorite one is if you jump on a surface of the game you're not suppose to jump on a square with the words "No surface type - assign something to this" appears where you're jumping and it's a good reminder that this game is clearly not finished.
- Lastly, this is a walking simulator straight up.  You cannot die.  Running is the equivalent of an elderly person doing cardio.  The GOOD scares are few and far between making each moment until then a total drag.
Conculsion:  If you want a well polished, FUN, apocolypse style, Russian, etc. type of game, just play Metro or STALKER.  This game just doesn't do it.  It quite possibly could have done well as a paranormal horror game, due to it's lighting and enviroments, but it's not, and I'm out $4 and 2 hours of my life.

Investigator is the second game from Russia that I’ve experienced this week with fantastic atmosphere, and I find myself wanting someone to curate a list of the best that Steam has to offer. Although a walking simulator, it fits more into the horror genre with a bevy of ‘holy ****’ moments during your playthrough.
The graphics are impressive, doubly so coming from a small indie team. Each new level of the game is varied and detailed, and asset reuse is at a bare minimum. A lot of love and attention went into their design, and the game benefits greatly for it. Playing over top of these expeditions is the beautifully haunting soundtrack by Nikolay Semenov, which is included for free. These pieces really help to sell the feeling of what is happening on-screen, and their melancholy notes have secured a place in my personal playlist.
As a walking simulator, you can expect very little puzzle-solving, and I for one was fine with that. I place these type of games into a ‘slightly-interactive movie’ experience, and filling my time with logic-defying walls of convolution only serves to break immersion. If time-versus-money is an issue for you then I suggest you simply explore, it’s really the whole point of this type of game.
There are a few things that mar an otherwise fantastic experience. First, the sparse dialog within the game is voiced completely in Russian with English subtitles. I have no problem with that, but your mileage may vary. There are also a few disjointed moments during the game where you are thrust from one point of view to another without any explanation. While many will just roll with the punches, it just breaks the story telling for me. Another wrinkle is that the various antagonists of the game show up for scripted events or jump scares, they are never really in a position to hurt you. This relegates the tension to a movie watching experience, and something you may not like if you’re a hardcore Outlast player.
Investigator is a solid title, and it’s category should be enough to tell you what to expect. I would have liked to see background or side story points thrown in for those intrepid wanderers who scour the maps, but the imagery maintained enough beauty to remain rewarding. Overall, I found the experience to be far and above many other titles that profess to be ‘real games’, and look forward to what AdroVGames have in store for their next title.
