NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Investigator is a first-person horror adventure game set on a post-apocalyptic Earth in 2050, where Mother Nature was the bringer of the apocalypse, with the Earth's climate now fierce and inhospitable.
You play Tom, a Russian ex-private-investigator, who's been surviving on his own and searching for other people. Seeing signs of habitation while exploring the flooded area in which you find yourself, you tie up your skiff nearby and go in search of the people who must be nearby. Unfortunately what you find isn't quite as friendly as you'd hoped.
Graphics - At first glance, the graphics are astoundingly good for a small-team indie game. At second glance, in the starting outside area, the graphics are even better! Trees and plants look fantastic and give a great impression of an overgrown world. Water and rain look terrific, as do reflections, fire, shadows, and the fantastic dynamic lighting.
A significant portion of my praise for the beauty of the graphics has to go towards the CryEngine, of course, which has a tendency to make beautiful looking games. But the tree and character models are excellent and the level design, particularly in that first area, is spot on. Unfortunately there is a bit of inconsistency in the quality while you play and the spiders in particular look very angular and not very detailed, which is a shame. The indoor environments in general are far less impressive than that first outdoor area, but overall the game still looks very good.
The game features only limited graphics options: resolution, full screen / windowed, and vsync. The included 'Detail Settings' seems to do nothing, at least on my system. In fact, the whole menu system looks like the default CryEngine menu, complete with "CRYENGINE" text at the top of the main menu. It's a bit unprofessional and, together with the very plain and jarringly amateur loading screen, detracts from the overall presentation of the game.
But that first level, with the great variety of vegetation, birds, rain, puddles ... it looks so good!
Sound - Sound, too, is pretty top notch: snow crunching, rain, storm sounds, and the other sounds used throughout the game are all perfectly sampled and normalised, and sound great. I can't think of a single one that annoyed me or seemed out of place.
There's also full voice in the game, in Russian. It sounds great, though since I don't speak Russian I'm not sure if it matches the subtitles displayed whenever Tom or the other characters you encounter speaks
Finally, Investigator includes some hauntingly beautiful original music that suits the atmosphere very well. It's used only sparsely, but that makes it all the more appreciated.
Gameplay - You control Tom like a character in any FPS, using WASD to move him around, C to crouch, Space to jump, Shift to run, and mouse to look around. Since it's more an adventure horror game than a shooter, though, you don't use the mouse buttons to attack. Instead, the left mouse button interacts with objects in the game world, which always display a large "LBMouse" prompt when nearby to show they are interactive. These interactions usually consist of a small, uninterruptible scripted camera movement to examine the object, and Tom's comments about what you see.
The game is largely about exploration and discovery in the rather foreboding world. The outside levels do a great job of making the world appear large and open, even though Tom is fairly restricted to only travelling on set paths and to certain areas. The inability to walk off most ledges and walkways breaks the suspension of disbelief a little, but makes the game less frustrating and more fun to play than if the areas were all been truly open, especially since controlling Tom is a bit clunky. He also walks very slowly and jumps somewhat erratically, making the (thankfully brief) platformer-like sections much harder than they should be.
Like most horror games, Investigator includes a healthy serving of jumpscares, but I'm proud to say I didn't even flinch until one got me on Level 4 when I really wasn't expecting it. It's a bit of a cheap trick, but is pretty standard in this sort of game.
The plot is revealed through a relatively small amount of dialogue and the subtitle translations are a bit rough, with some badly worded sentences and poor grammar in a few places. It's mostly not hard to understand the writing, although there were a few bits of the (short) plot that didn't make a whole lot of sense to me.
Pros:
+ Mostly fantastic graphics, particularly outside
+ Interesting and atmospheric (hah!) weather-based post-apocalyptic setting
+ Haunting music and great Russian voiceover
+ Most convincing overgrown vegetation areas that I've seen in any game
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- Relatively short story that didn't make a whole lot of sense in some places, and didn't take full advantage of the great setting
- Some menu weirdness ("CRYENGINE" is the menu title, 2x 'invert' settings, 'detail settings' doesn't do anything)
- Loading screen looks pretty bad, especially when compared with everything else
- Game doesn't remember video settings between restarts, reverting to windowed mode each time
- No way to save, just start on different 'levels'
- Scripted camera movements tend to wobble a lot, presumably simulating head bob, but it's a bit too much sometimes
- Some poorly worded subtitles
Investigator is a mixed bag. It has some amazingly good graphics, particularly in the outdoor environments, and it has a really interesting setting with a lot of potential. But the graphics are let down a bit by some of the indoor models and the spiders, and the setting just isn't realised effectively in the short story that Investigator tells.
That said, I enjoyed playing Investigator, even if it felt like I wasn't doing very much while I did so. I look forward to seeing what the developers make next, especially if it's set in this great world they've created.

Game Corp DX is an exceptionally cheap, highly addictive strategy game that casts you as head of a new software company. If you enjoy strategy games, you can't go wrong for the price.

Do you like Corgis? Do you like warlocks? Have you ever thought about combining them!?!? Well neither  had anyone else. Until now! Corgi Warlock follows the 'epic' quest of Maia the Corgi who is attempting to free the world of the evil forced of the undead rabbit king. Along the road, in this throw away story, Maia and up to three other friends (through local only co-op) must fight through waves and waves of enemies and bosses.
Corgi warlock is a side scrolling... game. It's one that doesn't really fit into any of the current categories. It's most like comparison comes from the old 'Armour Games' that you would play through whatever site your school hadn't managed to block. Things like 'Black Knight' and such where your main aim is just to move to the end of the level in a beat 'em up style but without any of the combat complexity. You start with just a simple fireball and throughout the game unlock more powerful spells. However these spells are really just larger beams that do more damage with a longer cool down and that's about it. There's not much complexity to the combat even with the added special 'Corgi Power' and shields. It's really quite simple.
Any complexity then comes from the sheer variety of monsters in the game. There's a huge number and many of them act very differently. Ultimately the combat comes down to avoiding any projectiles and ensuring that most things are dead before they can reach you. This mostly requires learning monster attack patterns and being able to act accordingly. Most likely as a direct result as this the game is not very hard at all. I died a handful of times at the most and the majority were from missing a platform and falling into the water/lava.
For a game made by a former animator for Pixar, Sony and Dreamworks that animation is nothing to write home about. Much of it feels quite slow and without much of a flow. What the animations do have however (and the rest of the game for that matter) is character. This game oozes character. From the stylistic choices of the characters and backgrounds, to the dialogue and animation. Every single bit of this game feels somewhere between a Saturday morning cartoon and the old flash games we loved growing up.
All in all Corgi Warlock isn't great. It's repetitive combat gets boring quickly and it's lack of depth means that whilst it only takes 2-3 hours it starts to outstay its welcome. The Co-op battle arena is fun for a few rounds but again quickly loses its appeal. But if you're looking for a fun little experience you could do far worse than this.

This is a game where every time you encounter an enemy, you step aside and let him pass; hoping upon hope that he does not take notice of you and just continues his or her eternal routine of endlessly roaming around a sinister dungeon. If you antagonize them for whatever reason, however, then they will descend upon you with the wild swinging of an undead barbarian backed with the power of this game's fantastic, all-encompassing physics engine.
Every single fight in this game could be your last. Against every enemy. This is a game where you are constantly on edge, never able to relax and torn between searching every single room in hope of finding a better piece of gear to protect yourself or avoiding them out of fear of a wild prisoner slamming a lumber axe into your face.
Throughout the environment there are signs of a story. A note here, or a room where a man has attempted to barricade himself in before eventually falling to a horrific onslaught. In another, a man is slumped against a desk, presumably murdered by inmates or servants. The graphics are gloomy and the sound design sinister; it's a dungeon crawler that has  the potential to scare you witless.
As mentioned before, physics are a huge part of the game. It boasts that it simulates everything and I would be inclined to agree that they're not too wrong. The player is able to drag objects around the world to create obstacles or block doors, even throw wooden planks and crates at enemies to hinder their progress. Combat consists of force, momentum and locational damage. Swing a hammer hard enough and at the correct distance and you can bash your enemy to the ground; but misjudge the distance and your forearm or weapon handle will bounce harmlessly off them. Weapons swung at the same time into each other will collide and blocking is done automatically depending on the availability of your character to adequately protect himself and where you choose to face. You can even swing your character around while holding the attack button to perform larger, more powerful attacks with momentum and force behind them - but the enemy can see these coming and either avoid the attack completely or attack you while you're open.
Enemy AI is fantastic. At first, you may find yourself at every disadvantage. You might find the controls awkward and unfriendly and your character slow or clumsy. But then you realize that your enemy has all those disadvantages too; bound also by the power of the game's physics engine and subject to all the same laws as you. To compensate, each enemy plays almost like you would expect a player too; right down to simulating reaction times and attempting to read your movement to best figure out how to defeat you. It has, by far, the most realistic and engaging melee combat I have ever seen in a video game.
You need to re-learn how to fight if you plan to play this game - and you should. You need to treat it as though it's as real as any fight you've been in personally. This is not just a game where you have to learn the controls, but a game where you have to truly master your chosen weapon and stay one step ahead of your opponent at all times, because once you die? That's it. You have to start all over again.
If real men play Dark Souls, then only the baddest of the badasses play Exanima.

As a huge supporter and believer in indie titles and developers as the saving grace of the gaming industry as we know it, do not read the following statement thinking I am a hater, or that I didn't "get" what the devs were trying to achieve here.  That being said, read away.  I say the following with love and guidance, not ignorance and hatred.
I'm reading a lot of reviews about just how ground breaking and earth shatteringly, awe inspiringly glorious the ohysics based combat system is.  The truth is that bestowing such praise to a combat system that BARELY functions in the state that it's in currently is actually damaging towards the progression of this system.
There is SO much potential here for this game to blossom into somthing so much more than what we are used to, that challenges us and changes our perception of what it is to interact with a video game and I am extremely excited to see the devs achieve this and I wish them all the luck and best wishes someone can wish upon them.
BUT the combat and animation system in it's currant state is borderline unplayable, I love the IDEA, I love the TECHNOLOGY behind it, but the actuall gameplay just stinks, the devs are falling into the exact same pitfalls that other devs games have fallen into that have tried to use a revolutionary physics and animation system for their game.
I feel like we need to be critical and concise about our feedback to help the devs really refine and galvanise this system.
But I'm at a loss?.... I just play games... I can only tell you how your game FEELS when I play it, I can't tell the devs how to actually improve their system, and I want it to be great, I want it to kick♥♥♥♥♥♥but I feel like the most we could give the devs as meaningful feeback is just that it's infuriatingly difficult during combat, I HATE the control scheme.
The way when youre locked on in combat mode that the cameras angle doesnt dictate what directions the WASD keys move you in make it frustrating as hell and the animations need to be more fluid and less sluggish.
People need to be able to pick this up and at least have the control scheme actually click in their brain, the way the controls are now, it's complicated and confusing, combine that with the fact that you need precise angles, distances and timing to actually win in combat and you have an infuriating combat system.  I fail to see how a game so full of promise and a team of devs so pationate and driven havn't clocked onto this and actually done somthing about this before opening their game up and making it playable??!!  Most of this games demographic will buy this in its early access stage and now say bad things about it to their video game playing friends because the controls are awfull.  Word of mouth is what makes games like this successful!  You've just damaged your buisness model!!!
The devs need to very quickly get some taleneted, experienced, pationate animators and gameplay designers on board, use the money they've gained from the sales of the early access and get the combat and controls working ASAP.
These devs are coders, not designers and it shows, no offence, you need to get the right people for the right job on this.
I'm going to recommend the game because the more money the devs get then the better it will be (hopefully) but as it stands right now, theres a LOT of work that needs doing, forget "fleshing out" the game world, nail the combat and controls and animations first.

A prelude to Sui Generis, an open world RPG, Exanima is a dungeon crawler that uses a completely unique physics-based combat system to test out everything before Sui Generis' release. Should you wait until Sui Generis? Absolutely not. Exanima, unlike most Early Access games, feels complete, polished and worthwhile. Here's why:
Exanima is genuinely one of my favourite games, which seems like a good start to a review. It's incredibly atmospheric, nail-bitingly tense and, above all else, completely satisfying. Starting off in a dungeon with nothing but some flimsy clothes, you have to scavenge and gather increasingly powerful gear, fighting your way through until you, hopefully, find an exit. I assume there's an exit, anyway, despite the 2 weeks I spent playing the game, I still didn't complete it.
All of this is done through entirely physics-based animation. The walking/running and the combat is all managed by physics, meaning you can stumble over clutter around the room which leads to either hilarious results, or your death in combat. The combat itself, however, is the most unique I've seen in any game. As you swing your weapon you have to manually twist your body to generate more force behind the swing, dealing more damage. When the enemy attacks you will have to manually position your body to either dodge or block the attack. And the enemies act exactly the same, meaning you will have to time your attacks to get in between the enemies defence and deal damaging blows. Each battle is totally unique from the last, as enemies move differently, attack in different patterns and react to the world around them. As a result, each battle feels personal and unbelievably tense. Even low level enemies right at the start of the game can beat you to death if you don't pay attention.
The game has a tough learning curve. Upon launching the game you get a warning "This game is unlike others, throw away all expectations." It's not lying, and when I first played it, I ignored it. As I stumbled through doors and drunkenly fell over rubble in Goat Simulator levels of hilarity, I could have put this game down and said "Wellp, dumbest game I've ever played." Stick with it. Seriously. Once you get to grips with it you will be able to perform some fantastic moves and defeat enemies quicker and quicker. And it will all be because of your skill, not because you pressed X at the right time like most other games.
And then there's the arena, a battleground to test out your combat against a series of enemies with increasing levels of gear and skills. I spent far too long fighting and dying and fighting and dying until I reached the final "boss". It was a heart pounding battle rivalled only by Ornstein and Smough in Dark Souls, and the satisfaction of defeating him was just the same.
Also, if things get too tough, you can put a bucket on your own head, or drop a chair on an enemy to throw him off balance. Seriously.
Exanima is incredibly unique with a very bright future, and I can't wait to see how it progresses.

For a combat system that is built around precision, forethought, and split-second timing...there's still an awful lot of dice-rolling here. The core design of the game truly promises to be something new and completely unique. And, it does deliver on that. The problem is that the core mechanics are still in competition with themselves. One part of the game wants to be a precision-based brawler on par with Dark Souls. The other part of the game wants to be a roguelike that's willing to kill you without warning if you so much as open a door.
The final outcome is an overall frustrating experience that will leave the vast majority of players sneering and uninstalling. But I can easily see a fair few of those players re-installing later...just to make sure they don't like it.
As I have already posted ad nauseam, I wish the developers would simply adhere to a skill-based system.  There are presently critical flaws:
+ Timing and precision mouse-movement are critical --- but attack placement is almost completely randomized.
+ Your character is given no viable ability to realiably recover from wounds --- but all defense is ultimately based on chance.
+ You are given but one life (with a limited number of reloads) --- but the game is perfectly willing to drop you into impossible situations.
So the experience is not a carefully calculated adventure that rewards intelligent play and mastery of its systems; the experience is a carnival game that asks you to throw darts blindfolded without ever seeing the target. The game does not rely on player input; it relies on sheer, dumb luck. There will be some who persist (like me!), but most people will throw a few darts, roll their eyes, and walk away.
However...if you have the money to burn...it's worth a shot! It is pretty cool, even if just as a novel distraction.

Where do I start...? I followed this game via Kickstarter a couple of years ago now. And whilst the team are behind schedule in terms of development, they are way ahead of the industry in terms of intuivity, innovation and most importantly listening to the customers/backers/followers/fanatics...
The first thing to happen when you play this game, you will die, and at times you will feel you have done enough to vanquish your opponent, let me tell you the game doen't lie!
Armored opponents will take stamina damage... Unless you hit them in the cracks of their armor and you will see a spray of blood, this is more satisfying than I am describing. If you bring a heavy weapon down on their helmet, their legs will buckle and I can't remember if I read this on the forums or not, but will make them very aggressive and clumsy for a few seconds (concussion).
Attacks feel random, but they are not, its your movement, cursor position and mouse clicks that are at fault. Side step an attack, perform a counter on a off balance enemy and you will send him hurtling across the room buying yourself some valuable space. You will soon learn how to feint and riposte in this strikingly accurate portrayal of medieval/fantasy combat.
Don't get me wrong, there are weird little bugs sometimes (very rare) and some things do need balancing. But the combat draws away from the main idea behind this game, they hope to acheive an RPG never seen before in terms of freedom. And if you are really serious about purchasing this game, I advise you to check out the videos on the official website, they will give you an idea of the mechanics and how interesting this game can truly be.
When I backed this I spent £60 because I believed in it so much, for £9.99 it's a steal...

Sacred was the first game to introduce me to the Hack n Slash genre. That's right, I never played Diablo at the time even though I'm old enough to should have been doing that back then. But somehow I skipped it and it was this game that taught me what I was missing out on, and then some. Highly addictive gameplay, appealing graphics (there is something about the grittiness of Sacred 1 that I really prefer to its smoothed out successor), badly voiced but fun characters. It's a game that doesn't take itself too seriously but at the same time may provide some challenge, especially early on if you want to advance too far too soon.
The skill progression is simple yet diverse. The difference in skills and weapon use are well implemented; each character does feel unique. After finishing the main Ancaria campaign (which took ages since I felt I had to explore every inch of the map)  I must admit I didn't have much interest left to complete the Underworld campaign. To me it didn't feel as a real part of the game, both storywise and mapwise. But I do love the two extra characters, they are both my favorites to use. The demon's spells are interesting to play around with (more then just your common fire ball, you'll need the battle mage for that kind of work) and the dwarfs cannon gun and use of mines is quite satisfying.
I like both Sacred and Sacred 2, but this is the game that will remain somewhat special to me. Even though by now I do understand what Diablo (1 & 2) is all about. So yes, of course I would recommend this game, play it!

The Good:
-Graphics. While the game isn't the next Crysis it looks quite nice. Most of the game takes in places with limited lightning. This allows for two things. First it allows to somewhat enrich the graphics with nice use of lightning and shadows. Second, as I said this ain't Crysis, so this allows to mask many graphics deficiencies.
-Sound, nothing great but it definitely fits the game atmosphere.
-Solid voice acting.
-Interesting, funny main characters and few minor characters (Kian, Zoe, Crow, Enu, Mira, Bip).
The Bad:
-Absurd system requirements. You think that your high-end desktop will run 1080p+maxed everything without any sweat because this is a adventure game? Think again!
-Numerous awkward animations.
-Issues with plot. Let's be cryptic! Because.
-Outside of cutscenes the player characters will say numerous things but his/her lips won't move a muscle during that time.
-This game features the worst ending I've ever witnessed in a story heavy game.
-Bad "puzzles", some are simply "try everything, because" and some "navigate the whole map, because".
-Your characters move slow. They can't run, they only jog. You waste large amount of time because of this.
-In many games the creators advertise how the choices in the game matter sooo much. It is similar in this game, no It's even worse, you're reminded after each episode about you're decisions, during gameplay it's similar, big text with big words, I would say it's even insulting to the player, especially considering the fact that your choices don't matter that much.
-Some talk you can skip, some you can't. Because.
-The game is now finished but you have to remember this was and episodic game. The episodes unfortunately weren't the same length. So this has lead to a situation where you got a fairly long episode, expected that another will be the same length but in the end another episode was shorter.
-The political message. LGBT, left vs right, misogyny, racism. Lets face this, this will always be a touchy subject, but it can be done in a convincing way. In this game it's done in ham-fisted way. Protip: If you can't do it right don't do it at all.
In the end, despite it's flaws the journey was interesting and worth playing. It's sad that the same can't be said about the ending.
Zoe's butt wins everything.

We thought it couldn't get any worse than the second game. We were wrong.
While the clumsy action combat is gone, in it's place is terrible writing, butchered/boring characters, and bugs to hell and back. Nearly all of the most interesting lore from TLJ is gone, and the new stuff is either dull or poorly concieved. All of the characters have the worst facial animation possible, with their lips barely moving in time with the syllables and their expressions NEVER change; they just keep staring dead-eyed straight in front of them.
Unlike TLJ, which gave pretty much everything at least some explanation or snarky note from April, neither Stark nor Arcadia get the attention they deserve outside of the immediate plot. What little IS there is usually tied in to the game's ham-fisted political commentary (of course aimed at America, despite the game being developed in Poland and the half that isn't in Arcadia is in EUROPE).
Almost none of the questions raised in TLJ and Dreamfall are answered, and those that are answered are done so in the laziest way possible in the last episode, as if the writers were getting ready to submit their final draft and went, "Oh yeah, we were supposed to do that, weren't we?" and shoved it all in in the last second. Characters' motivations and even personalities completely change between Dreamfall and this game, with absolutely no reason given.
Oh yeah, it also falls for the ever lovely "choice" illusion so many games are doing now, and it's especially obvious that your choices don't actually mean that much. I can think of one or two that have signifigance, and even then it only applies for a few scenes and then goes away.
And to cap it all off,
tl;dr - this game sucks, just play the first one and pretend the other two don't exist.

I was very disappointed by Dreamfall Chapters, and I cannot recommend this game to anyone. Moreover, after playing Dreamfall Chapters I think it would be wise to have a healthy skepticism towards any future game by Red Thread Games.

- The game ignores big parts of the story from the previous games - there are for instance almost no references anymore to the Draic and many questions from the previous games are left unanswered.
- Most of the characters lack any dept or charm. Their personality have often changed drastically from the previous games, and not in a good or even logical way.
- The game is trying really hard to be political and make references to contemporary events. However, it does so in a almost childlike manner, it comes off as very crude and simple.
- There are a lot of bugs in the game.
- Your characters move so freaking slow - and I am sure this was done on purpose. You probably spend 40 min extra on the game due to how slow your characters move.
- The game offers a very unsatisfying ending to the entire franchise.
An amazing end in my favourite adventure game series :)

The third and [so far] final in The Longest Journey series, this game was absolutely phenomenal!
First of all, I HIGHLY SUGGEST that potential players first play The Longest Journey, then Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, before playing this game to achieve a full understanding and appreciation for a lot of the lore and backlore that sits heavily upon this game in particular, being a story-driven, choices matter game.
Personally, I have never been interested in wanting to try a choices matter game, being an old school gamer of point-and-clicks and like in classic Tomb Raider just shoot shoot to kill, but I am so happy that my first experience with one was Dreamfall Chapters! Maybe it had to do with my personal bias for the story itself, but the thing is that this game brought to life such a magical, futuristic, truly out of this world experience just like its predecessors, leaving nothing behind as many sequels do in entertainment. You can just feel yourself immersed in the surroundings, in the story, and even smaller characters you will find yourself caring for very much (Bip!!), and not many games these days can do that.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys beautiful, imaginative storylines of fantasy and sci-fi, though like I stated above, I would try to play the other games first to fully enjoy this game for what it is, though I'm sure you could enjoy it just the same if needed.
*The only thing I need to say is there IS a technical issue/bug you MAY experience in which halfway through the game there is a bug in which the game freezes and will not continue, but there ARE fixes on it, for instance I just re-installed the game once and your game saves won't be harmed as this is a steam-cloud game.
OVERALL I give Dreamfall Chapters 10/10.
And the whole series? 200/10 for giving the little fantasy/sci-fi geeky girl in me wonderful places to escape to, and in which I have wonderful memories playing in! (The series overall spanned around 2 years of my life including during the birth of my daughter! hehe). So much love to this series <3
